passages.t: Explains what supply and demand is, where the zone-trading method comes from, and how banks leave footprints as a pause in the market followed by a big, fast move away. The strategy in a nutshell: find the large move away, go to its origin (the basing), draw the zone, and buy/sell the pullback, using the two zone families (reversal and continuation).

Only mark zones with a large/fast move away; small drifting moves are not tradeable demand/supply. Always wait for the pullback to the zone - never chase the move away. Sideways price = balance = no zone; we only trade imbalances.

Nobody created supply and demand; every market (clothes, food, stocks, currencies, commodities) moves as a function of it. More demand -> price goes up. More supply -> price goes down. It is a natural law.

What does have a founder is the method of identifying it on a price chart: he credits the trader the captions call 'Sam Sein' (likely Sam Seiden), who worked on a trading floor facilitating orders and learned to spot on the chart where big order stacks sat.
He recommends watching that founder's videos as starter material; this course goes into much more depth.

passages.h: How a demand zone forms (the trading-floor logic)
passages.t: Example: a big stack of buy orders sits at, say, $62. Price pushes down into it and shoots up because of all those orders.

passages.h: How a demand zone forms (the trading-floor logic)
passages.t: On the chart this shows as price pushing down, then 'boom' a push up: price could not stay at that level long before shooting out.

passages.h: How a demand zone forms (the trading-floor logic)
passages.t: Idea: there are leftover buy orders from large banks/institutions at that level, or, having bought there once, they may want to buy there again. That is the reason to trade the return.

passages.h: How a demand zone forms (the trading-floor logic)
passages.t: Only banks or large institutions can move a market up or down like that, so the big move is their footprint, and we want to trade with them.

passages.h: What to look for on the chart
passages.t: For demand: a pause in the market (basing) followed by a strong, fast move out, e.g. a large green candle.

passages.h: What to look for on the chart
passages.t: Small moves away (little candles drifting off) contain no demand you would trade. Technically S&D is everywhere, but we only mark the big moves away.

passages.h: What to look for on the chart
passages.t: Process: identify the large move away -> go to the origin of the move (the basing) -> draw the zone capturing the basing candles -> wait for and take the pullback.

passages.h: What to look for on the chart
passages.t: Example shown: a large red candle, basing, then a large green candle -> draw the demand around the basing. Supply is the exact opposite: basing then a strong move down.
Sideways price action = a balance of buyers and sellers. That is NOT what we want. We want an imbalance: price pushed into a level, could not stay there, and shot out.
A small push up out of a sideways range is at best 'borderline' demand; he treats the range as balance, no demand.
S&D is an imbalance - way too much demand and lack of supply (demand zone) or way too much supply and lack of demand (supply zone).
Demand: Drop-Base-Rally (DBR) and Rally-Base-Rally (RBR). Supply is opposite: Rally-Base-Drop (RBD) and Drop-Base-Drop (DBD). DBR/RBD = reversal type; RBR/DBD = continuation pattern.

His opinion: continuation zones (RBR/DBD) are better in trending markets - that is how you trade with the trend. Any DBR demand is pretty much going to be counter-trend. There are a few more zone types that he will cover later in the course.
He deliberately showed a failed supply zone (basing of two red candles + big move away) and zones that never filled. Not every trade works; we are stacking the odds by trading with the large players.
The strategy is not just 'spot demand, buy the pullback' - you also need the trend, the structure of the zone and more (later lessons: multiple timeframe analysis etc.).
Goal of the course: combine everything (incl. multiple timeframe analysis) to build your own strategy. Ask him questions anytime if something is unclear.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Why a chart method was needed

How he draws zones: a filled rectangle (green demand, red supply) wrapped around the basing candles, extended right until price returns. Some zones carry exact proximal/distal price tags (for example 81.235 / 83.183).

The "large red candle, basing, then a large green candle" example is the August 2021 WTI base. The failed supply he shows is the November 2021 WTI supply (about 78–80), which the January 2022 rally broke.

passages.t: An old zone retested many months later. The zone is a level to trade the return to, not a guarantee.

Drop-Base-Rally as he shows it on WTI: drop, a short pause (basing), one large green candle away, and a box wrapped around the basing (proximal on top, distal at the lowest wick). It extends right until price pulls back into it.
Balance vs imbalance: sideways candles mean buyers and sellers are balanced, so no zone. A pause followed by an explosive move out is an imbalance, so a zone.
The two zone families. Demand is DBR (reversal) or RBR (continuation). Supply is the exact opposite: RBD (reversal) or DBD (continuation). The shaded base is where the zone is drawn.
Marking every little move as demand/supply because 'S&D is everywhere'. Treating a sideways range with a small push out as a demand zone.
Thinking the strategy is only 'find a zone and buy the pullback' without trend, structure and timeframe context. Expecting every zone to work or to fill.

Is there a clear pause (basing) followed by a large, fast move away? Is this an imbalance rather than sideways balance? Am I waiting for the pullback instead of chasing? Do I know whether this is a DBR/RBD (likely counter-trend) or RBR/DBD (with-trend) zone? Have I checked trend and higher-timeframe context, not just the zone?

“We are looking for a pause in the market and a strong fast move out.” “Sideways price action basically means that there's a balance of buyers and sellers - that's not what we are looking for.” “That's how they leave their footprints on a price chart.” “We always wait for the pullback.” “There was so much demand here and such a lack of supply that price pushed out.”
“Price could not stay at this level long enough and we just shot up out of that area.” “We are stacking the odds in our favor by trading with these large players.”
Credits the founder of the chart method (captions: 'Sam Sein', likely Sam Seiden) and his trading-floor order-stack origin story.
Explicitly frames sideways action as 'balance' vs zones as 'imbalance' with the borderline-demand example.
His opinion that continuation zones (RBR/DBD) suit trending markets and that DBR demand is pretty much always counter-trend.
Second reason for the return: banks that bought there once may want to buy there again (PDFs only mention leftover unfilled orders).

Big players leave footprints: a pause, then a jump. Wait for the return. Imagine a toy shop. One morning a giant truck of kids arrives and buys every toy at $5, so the price shoots up. Some kids did not get a toy, and they are still waiting at $5. Later, when the price drifts back down to $5, those kids buy again and the price jumps once more. On a chart, the waiting spot is the little pause just before the big jump.
A zone is like the spot where the ice-cream truck stopped and a crowd rushed in. When the truck comes back to that same corner, the crowd is still there waiting.

Only a big, fast move away shows a bank was there. Small drifting moves do not count. Go to where the move started (the pause, called the basing), box it, and wait for the pullback. Sideways price is balance. We only trade imbalance.

passages.h: Step: Spot the big, fast move
passages.t: First look for a candle (or two) that is much bigger than the ones around it, moving fast in one direction. Only banks and big institutions can push price like this. That is their footprint.

passages.h: Step: Walk back to the pause
passages.t: Now look at where that move came from. Just before it, price paused with small candles. That pause is the basing. It is where the big buy orders were sitting.
Draw a box around the basing candles. Price came down (drop), paused (base) and shot up (rally), so this is a Drop-Base-Rally demand zone.
We never chase the big move. We wait. When price comes back into the box, some of those big buy orders may still be there, so price can push up again.
Supply is the exact opposite: price rallies, pauses, then drops hard. The box goes around that pause, and we look to sell when price comes back up into it.

passages.h: Step: Sideways is not a zone
passages.t: When price just goes side to side, buyers and sellers are in balance. A small push out of the range is not a strong move away. No zone here.

What does a bank footprint look like? - A pause (basing) followed by a big, fast move away. Where do you draw a zone? - Around the basing candles at the origin of the big move. Do you chase the move away? - No. Always wait for the pullback into the zone. Sideways price means...? - Balance of buyers and sellers. No zone. Two demand zone types? - Drop-Base-Rally (reversal) and Rally-Base-Rally (continuation).

Two supply zone types? - Rally-Base-Drop (reversal) and Drop-Base-Drop (continuation). Which zone type fits a trending market best? - Continuation zones: RBR and DBD. Does every zone work? - No. We stack the odds by trading with the big players.

Covers how to qualify a zone: the highest-quality zones remove an opposing zone or a trendline, but because his edge comes from multiple timeframe and multiple sequence analysis, a clean base with a decent move away inside a higher-timeframe zone is acceptable even if it removed nothing.
Also separates drawable-but-not-tradable zones from tradable ones and shows what is NOT supply and demand (support/resistance boxes).

Highest-quality zones remove an opposing zone or a trendline. A tradable zone needs clean basing and a strong move away. Wrap the zone tightly around the basing candles; no randomly started S/R boxes. A broken zone is violated and no longer valid. Pure price action - no indicators.
There is supply and demand everywhere on a chart, so finding one does not mean it qualifies. No zone on the daily at a spot does not mean there is none on the 1m or 5m chart there.

passages.h: Highest-quality qualification: remove an opposing zone or trendline
passages.t: For the highest-quality zone, it must remove another (opposing) zone or a trendline. Example: price pushes up into a supply zone (may react a bit, doesn't matter), then breaks it - supply is now removed. Something must have removed it: the demand zone at the origin of that move. That demand qualifies and is the potential trade.

passages.h: Highest-quality qualification: remove an opposing zone or trendline
passages.t: On his chart link you see this: a supply zone that removed several little mini demand zones, and a demand that took out a supply. Removed zones are shown in tan on his chart link.

passages.h: Where the real edge comes from
passages.t: His personal edge comes from multiple timeframe analysis and multiple sequence analysis (top-down), covered later - don't skip ahead.

passages.h: Where the real edge comes from
passages.t: So as long as the zone looks good (clean basing, decent move away), it can be traded even if it removed nothing - provided the higher timeframes make sense.

passages.h: Where the real edge comes from
passages.t: Example: a 1-hour demand zone that did not remove the supply above it is still a candidate if it sits inside a daily demand zone.

passages.h: Where the real edge comes from
passages.t: Summary: highest quality = removes opposing zones; but if trading with MTF + MSA, what the zone removed 'doesn't matter quite as much' as long as it looks good.

Decent zones: decent basing + large move away. Mediocre/lower quality: only about one candle staying away and a move away that isn't large - the trade may still work, but it's mediocre. The bigger and cleaner the move away the better.
Time away matters: a zone price stayed away from for a long time before rallying back is better than one price couldn't stay away from.
Drawable zone: he draws it to track the chart (what removed what) so he can find the highest-quality zones when the time comes - not to trade.
Not tradable examples: a very large zone with a very large wick that only removed things later; a supply zone that did remove demand but whose move away was a ~50% candle (weak move away).
Tradable zone: very clean basing + very nice, strong move away (shown on both supply and demand, incl. a daily demand that still failed - that's okay).
Low-quality, drawable-only signs: very poor move away, not much time spent away from the zone. Using MTF/MSA makes the drawable-vs-tradable distinction 'a little less important'.

passages.h: What is NOT supply and demand
passages.t: Example: a DailyFX article ('whoever wrote this should be fired') with boxes started randomly far back and drawn straight across - that is support/resistance, not S&D.

passages.h: What is NOT supply and demand
passages.t: Those boxes 'work' as S/R (break, retest, support turns resistance), and that's fine, but there is no structure.

passages.h: What is NOT supply and demand
passages.t: Real zones are tightly based: lines wrapped around the basing candles, zones roughly the same size, drawn consistently - because that is how you shape the trade (entry/stop).

passages.h: What is NOT supply and demand
passages.t: Once a zone is broken it is violated/removed; you don't start a box from some random earlier price.

passages.h: What is NOT supply and demand
passages.t: He redraws the article's chart: the actual demand is where price rallied, based, then shot up - wrap lines around that base (he admits it isn't the best demand). No indicators - S&D is traded on pure price action. Lots of 'junk' on social media/Google isn't the original methodology he follows.
Open a chart and use the arrow tool to POINT to where you think demand and supply are (point at the basing) - don't draw zones yet. Post a screenshot in the Discord homework tab; he will check it.

The article is DailyFX "Supply and Demand Trading: A Forex Trader's Guide" (its byline, Richard Snow, is visible in lesson 1 at 02:18). Its charts are USD/JPY weekly, GBP/USD ("Sharp moves off supply and demand zones") and USD/SGD (stop placement), and he criticises all three.

The "second article chart, a zone price had already broken through" is the GBP/USD "sharp moves" chart, where price closes below the blue demand box on the right. The "boxes started randomly far back" point is made on the USD/SGD chart, where he arrows the boxes' left ends.
The article's tip 3 literally says "Use indicators for confirmation of support and demand zones" (pivot points). A stochastic example follows. This is exactly what his "no indicators" rule rejects.

His chart link is WTICOUSD in four panes (1W/4h/1D/1h), not a single chart. Removed zones are tan, live zones carry proximal/distal price tags, and a three-month zone is projected onto the weekly as "3m Proximal" and "3m Distal" lines.
Trendlines are drawn on all four panes of his layout, which fits removing a trendline as the other way a zone qualifies.

passages.t: Starting point for "what removed what": the 91.5–94.5 demand was later broken by the drop out of the 103–106 supply. Every zone is a tight box around a basing, never a broad band.

Dashed "3m Proximal" and "3m Distal" lines sit on the weekly. Trendlines are drawn on the weekly, daily, 4h and 1h.

passages.t: This is the article he criticises: the boxes are support and resistance, started at a random price and drawn straight across.

passages.h: Chart: [10:30] The same USD/JPY chart zoomed in, with his black pen trace showing price chopping in and out of the "supply zone" and then falling into the "demand zone".
passages.t: Price trades back and forth through the box, so nothing is being removed and there is no basing + move-away structure. His point: these zones "work" as S/R (break, retest), but there is no structure to them.

passages.h: Chart: [12:11] The article's tip 3 on screen: "Use indicators for confirmation of support and demand zones" (daily or weekly pivot points).
passages.t: He rejects this. Supply and demand is traded on pure price action, with no indicators.

passages.h: Chart: [12:37] DailyFX "Sharp moves off supply and demand zones" (GBP/USD): a long red supply box and a blue demand box spanning the whole chart. On the right price has already pushed below the demand box.
passages.t: This is the second "not S&D" example: a broad, randomly placed box that price has already broken through. A broken zone is violated. A real S&D trader would not keep drawing it.

passages.h: Chart: [13:07] DailyFX USD/SGD "stops for short/long positions" chart. His arrows point at the left ends where the supply and demand boxes start.
passages.t: The boxes begin at arbitrary earlier prices rather than at a basing that caused a move away. He calls this out explicitly.

passages.h: Chart: [13:07] DailyFX USD/SGD "stops for short/long positions" chart. His arrows point at the left ends where the supply and demand boxes start.
passages.t: Real zones start at the basing candles and are drawn tight around them, so they can shape the entry and stop.

passages.h: Chart: [14:47] The article's USD/JPY example again, now with a stochastic oscillator underneath (circled overbought/oversold points).
passages.t: The indicator-confirmation idea he dismisses. None of this is part of his method.

passages.h: Chart: [14:54] Google Images for "supply and demand trading zones": a grid of generic examples, with one opened ("SUPPLY ZONE" from Colibri Trader).
passages.t: His warning: most of what Google and social media call supply and demand is not the original methodology he follows.

passages.h: Chart: [14:59] Back on his four-pane WTICOUSD layout (1W, 4h, 1D, 1h) with tan removed zones, live green/red zones and trendlines.
passages.t: His contrast: tight, consistently sized zones, each one wrapped around a basing.
Highest-quality qualification: a supply zone is broken by a rally and turns tan (removed). The demand at the origin of that rally is what removed it, so it qualifies.
The DailyFX-style boxes he criticises (wide, started at a random price, drawn across many touches) next to a real zone wrapped tightly around the basing that caused the move.
His worked hypothetical: a 1H demand that did not remove the supply above it. With a clean base and a decent move away inside a daily demand zone, it is still a candidate.

Assuming any S&D you can find qualifies as a tradable zone. Assuming no zone on the daily means no zone on lower timeframes. Trading drawable-only zones (huge wick, ~50% candle move away, little time away). Drawing support/resistance boxes from random prices and calling them supply and demand. Using indicators on S&D charts. Getting too hung up on what the zone removed when the higher-timeframe context is right.
Starting a zone from a random earlier price instead of at the basing that caused the move away.

Did this zone remove an opposing zone or a trendline (highest quality)? If not, is it inside a matching higher-timeframe zone? Is the basing clean? Is the move away strong (not a ~50% candle) and did price stay away for a while? Is the zone drawn tightly around the basing, not as a broad S/R box? Is the zone still unbroken (not violated)?

“Just because you can find it, it doesn't mean that it's qualified as supply or demand.” “Our edge comes from that top-down analysis.” “Clean basing, good move away - that's a drawable and tradable zone.” “This is not supply and demand, this is basically a support and resistance zone.” “Supply and demand is very tightly based.” “There's just no structure to anything they're doing here.”
Concept of 'drawable vs tradable' zones and drawing zones just to track what removed what.

His view that with MTF/MSA, a zone need not remove anything as long as it looks good and sits in a HTF zone (PDF slide says neither removal = NO TRADE). Time spent away from the zone as a quality sign. A ~50% candle move away cited as not tradable; very large wick zones as not tradable. No zone on the daily doesn't mean none on the 1m/5m. Mentions 'multiple sequence analysis' as part of his edge (a later lesson).
No indicators - pure price action; a DailyFX-style S/R box example of what is not S&D. Homework: point to demand/supply with the arrow tool and post in Discord.

Not every zone you find is good enough to trade. Qualify it first. Two kids arm-wrestle. The winner is the strong one, so you would bet on him next time. On a chart, when buyers smash through a sellers zone, the buyers zone below proved it is the strong one. A clean pause and a big, proud move away make a zone worth trading. A wobbly pause with a weak move is just a note in your notebook.
Finding a zone is like finding a fruit. You can find fruit everywhere, but you only eat the ripe one. Ripe = clean basing, strong move away, and price stayed away a long time.
Highest quality: the zone removed an opposing zone or a trend line. Tradable = clean basing + strong move away. Weak ones are drawable only (to track the chart).
Real zones wrap tightly around the basing. Random wide boxes are support/resistance, not supply and demand.

passages.h: Step: A supply zone sits above
passages.t: Price rallied, paused, then dropped hard. That pause is a supply zone. Sellers were strong there.
Later, price pushes up into the supply and breaks right through it. A broken zone is violated: it is removed. Something strong must have done that.

passages.h: Step: The winner: demand at the origin
passages.t: The strong move started from this basing. This demand zone removed the supply, so it is the highest quality kind of zone. That is our potential trade.
When price pulls back into the qualified demand, that is the trade. Clean basing, strong move away, and price stayed away for a while: all good signs.
Here the basing is only one candle and the move away is weak: a half-size candle with a big wick, and price came straight back. You can draw it to track the chart, but it is not a zone to trade.

A zone that removed nothing can still be traded if it looks good AND it sits inside a higher-timeframe zone (for example a 1-hour demand inside a daily demand). That top-down view is where his edge comes from.

Highest-quality zone? - One that removed an opposing zone or a trend line. Tradable zone needs...? - Clean basing + strong move away. Drawable-only signs? - Poor move away (~50% candle), huge wick, little time away. What happens to a broken zone? - It is violated and removed. It is no longer valid. Does time away matter? - Yes. The longer price stayed away before returning, the better.
Indicators in S&D? - None. Pure price action. Zone removed nothing - can I trade it? - Yes, if it looks good and sits inside a higher-timeframe zone.

Shows how to draw PV (drop-base-rally / rally-base-drop) and CP (rally-base-rally / drop-base-drop) zones: the distal line is objective and always includes the wick, while the proximal line is partly subjective and trades fill rate against R:R. Zones should look visually similar in size on a timeframe, and an overly large zone can be cut in half.

The distal line goes at the extreme wick of the basing - always include the wick (exceptions are a separate lesson). Use the basing candles to place both lines. Keep zones visually similar in size on the same timeframe. Use the magnet tool to hit the exact high/low.
Drawing has some subjectivity; some parts are completely objective. Aim for zones that look visually similar in size - not measured to an exact pip count (e.g. not forcing 68 or 78 pips).

passages.h: Two zone types: PV and CP
passages.t: Demand: drop-base-rally and rally-base-rally. Supply is the complete opposite: rally-base-drop and drop-base-drop. He calls DBR/RBD 'PV' zones (peaks and valleys). He calls RBR/DBD 'CP' zones (continuation pattern - a continuation move).

passages.h: Two zone types: PV and CP
passages.t: Each zone = basing candles + the move away; the move away is how we identify that there is demand; then wrap the lines around the basing candles. Other zone situations exist; odd ones get broken down in the Sunday meetings.

Distal = the line furthest away. Demand: distal at the bottom; supply: distal at the top. Proximal = the near line. Demand: proximal on top; supply: proximal at the bottom. Knowing the names isn't super important, it's part of the theory.
The distal line is usually always completely objective: at the extreme wick of the basing (lowest low for demand, highest high for supply).
Always include the wick - leaving the wick outside the zone is incorrect (a common mistake he sees).
Exceptions where wicks are excluded exist, but they're for another lesson; in general always include the wick.
Use the TradingView magnet tool (hold Ctrl) to snap exactly to the candle high/low instead of eyeballing it - manual placement misses the exact pip.

passages.h: Drawing the proximal line (subjective) and the R:R trade-off
passages.t: Usually put the proximal on the top of the body of a basing candle (demand); or use the wick if the body version makes the zone tiny. Use parts of the basing candles to pick where the lines go.

passages.h: Drawing the proximal line (subjective) and the R:R trade-off
passages.t: Example with a 3:1 trader: the smaller the zone, the less price has to travel to hit 3:1; a bigger zone needs a bigger move. A very tiny zone turned the same move into 13:1.

passages.h: Drawing the proximal line (subjective) and the R:R trade-off
passages.t: Small zone: better R:R but you'll take a decent amount of losses, get filled less and miss more trades. Large zone: more trades and more fills, but smaller R:R.

passages.h: Drawing the proximal line (subjective) and the R:R trade-off
passages.t: As long as the distal is right (the most important thing), experiment with the proximal and build your own strategy. He prefers a middle, decent-size zone - not too small, not too big.
Try to copy the size of a properly drawn zone onto others on the same timeframe so zones are the same size.
Example measurements: 33 pips and 43 pips are fine/similar; a 79-pip zone is much larger - 'you don't really want that'.

To match size on a CP zone he ignores a wick at the top (proximal side), giving ~31-39 pips - 'somewhat similar' is fine; a slightly bigger zone 'who cares'. If a zone is a little too big, tighten it up a bit.
Real trade example: a DBR with a very large range (red basing candle + several green). Don't ignore the large candles - distal at the far low, proximal at top of the basing body.

If the zone is too large, you can simply cut it in half. 'I know this looks weird' but he has done it a long time and it works for him. Optional. Effect: the same move goes from roughly 3:1 to roughly 4:1-5:1.
Supply examples: proximal on the green basing candle; distal at the objective high; choose the version that keeps size similar.
Draw 2 supply zones (one RBD, one DBD) and 2 demand zones (one continuation/RBR, one DBR), all drawn similar in size.
Post in the homework chat labelled lesson 3 homework. Getting it wrong is fine - that's the point.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Worked 3:1 example (proximal choice)
passages.t: With the proximal drawn low (small zone), a 3:1 trader only needed price to reach 2.205. Drawing the proximal higher made price travel further for 3:1; drawing it even bigger, price only just hit 3:1. Whether you hit it depends on how far your stop is.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Other notes
passages.t: His example chart had three demand zones: two CP (rally-base-rally) and one PV (drop-base-rally).

passages.h: More from the lesson: Other notes
passages.t: He says there are really only two types of zones; there are 'different situations', but he doesn't want to confuse anyone. He won't repeat everything for supply because it is the complete opposite.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Other notes
passages.t: The rules to apply: zones similar in size, distal line at the extreme of the basing candles. Beyond that the proximal is up to you.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Other notes
passages.t: Example identification: 'two basing candles' and the green candle is the large move away; then wrap the lines around the basing.

passages.t: The two zone types for each side. Demand is on the left (DBR, RBR) and supply is the exact opposite on the right (RBD, DBD). Each shape is a move in, a flat base, and a move away.

passages.t: The example chart from the notes: two CP zones and one PV zone. The magenta trace shows the "rally, base, rally" step the CP zone is drawn around.

passages.t: For demand, the proximal is the top line (near price) and the distal is the bottom line (further away). Supply is the mirror image: distal on top, proximal at the bottom.

passages.h: Chart: [05:58] Zoomed right in on the basing candles: he drags the zone's corner handle until it snaps onto the candle body/wick.

passages.t: The zone defines the trade. Entry is at the proximal and the stop goes beyond the distal, so the zone size sets the risk.

passages.h: Chart: [09:17] The upper CP demand redrawn as a very thin box (proximal pulled right down to the distal).

passages.t: His real-trade example of a large DBR. He does not ignore the large candles: distal at the far low, proximal at the top of the basing body.

passages.t: Distal at the objective high and proximal chosen to keep the two supplies a similar size.

passages.t: The homework target: zones of similar size, each wrapped around its basing, with the distal on the extreme wick.

Where the lines go. Demand: distal at the lowest wick of the basing (objective, wick included) and proximal at the top of a basing body, or at the wick if that makes the zone too small. Supply: the mirror image.
His whiteboard, labelled the way he labels zones on his chart: Drop-Base-Rally = PV demand, Rally-Base-Rally = CP demand, Rally-Base-Drop = PV supply, Drop-Base-Drop = CP supply.

The same distal and the same high, but three proximals. A tiny zone shows about 13:1 but rarely fills, a medium zone about 3:1, and a large zone about 1.3:1 that fills often. If a zone is too large he cuts it in half.

Leaving the wick outside the zone when placing the distal line. Eyeballing the line and missing the exact pip. Drawing a tiny zone just to show a huge R:R (e.g. 13:1) - fewer fills and more losses. Drawing very oversized zones (e.g. 79 pips next to 33-43 pip zones). Ignoring the big candles of a large basing when drawing the zone.

Is the distal line on the extreme wick of the basing (wick included)? Is the proximal on a basing candle body or wick? Is the zone similar in size to my other zones on this timeframe? If the zone is oversized, have I considered cutting it in half? Is my zone size giving a deliberate fill vs R:R trade-off, not a fantasy R:R?

“Distal is always going to be the one that's further away.” “You need to include this wick.” “As long as you have the distal line, that's the most important thing.” “You simply just cut that in half.” “There is some subjectivity here. It's not all completely objective.”
“If you send me homework and it's incorrect or it's not good, that's great. That's the point of it.”

He calls DBR/RBD 'PV' (peaks and valleys) - the PDF calls them VP. Visual size consistency across zones on a timeframe, with pip examples (33/43 ok, 79 too big; ~31-39 similar). Cutting an oversized zone in half (3:1 becomes ~4-5:1). Magnet tool (hold Ctrl) to snap lines exactly. Distal is objective, proximal is subjective; tiny-zone 13:1 example.
Exceptions where wicks are excluded are mentioned but deferred to another lesson. Homework: draw RBD, DBD, RBR and DBR zones of similar size.

The far line goes on the wick tip. The near line is your choice. Think of drawing a fence around a sleeping puppy. The back of the fence must go behind its tail, even the very tip, or the puppy is not fully inside. That is the distal line: it always includes the wick. The front gate (the proximal line) you can place a little closer or further. A close gate means a small, tight pen. A far gate means a bigger pen that is easier to walk into.
Distal is the wall behind you, proximal is the door in front. The wall is fixed. The door you can move.

Distal line (furthest away) = extreme wick of the basing. Always include the wick. Proximal line (near side) is subjective: smaller zone = better R:R but fewer fills; bigger zone = more fills, smaller R:R. Keep zones on one timeframe similar in size. An oversized zone can be cut in half.

passages.h: Step: Find the basing and the move away
passages.t: Drop, then two or three small basing candles, then the big green move away. The move away tells us there is demand. Now we wrap lines around the basing.

passages.h: Step: Distal line: the lowest wick
passages.t: For demand, the distal line is at the bottom: the lowest low of the basing, wick included. See that long wick? It must be inside the zone. Leaving it out is a common mistake. Use the magnet tool to snap to it exactly.

passages.h: Step: Proximal line: top of the basing body
passages.t: For demand, the proximal line is the top. Usually he puts it on the top of a basing candle body. That part is your choice.
Now fill in between the two lines. That is the demand zone. If the body version is tiny, you can use the wick top for the proximal instead.
For supply the distal is on top (highest wick of the basing) and the proximal is at the bottom (a basing body). Same rules, flipped.

passages.h: Step: Too big? Cut it in half
passages.t: A wide basing makes a big zone. Do not ignore the big candles: distal stays at the far low. If the zone is much larger than your others, you can cut it in half. It looks weird, but it turns about 3:1 into about 4:1 or 5:1.

Distal line? - The line furthest away: bottom for demand, top for supply. Where does the distal line go? - On the extreme wick of the basing. Always include the wick. Proximal line? - The near line, usually a basing body top (demand). It is subjective. Small zone trade-off? - Better R:R, but fewer fills and more losses. Big zone trade-off? - More fills, but smaller R:R. PV zones? - Peaks and valleys: DBR and RBD.
CP zones? - Continuation patterns: RBR and DBD. Oversized zone? - Tighten it, or cut it in half (optional). Tool to hit the exact high/low? - The magnet tool (hold Ctrl in TradingView).

Multiple timeframe analysis (MTA) means only taking entry-timeframe zones that sit inside a higher-timeframe zone of the same direction, so the odds and the R:R are on your side. His edge: find the HTF zone, refine the entry on a lower timeframe, then hold as long as possible.

Pick one entry timeframe (if you are new) and stick to it. Use the correct HTF for your ETF (1m→15m, 5m→H1, 15m→H4, H1→D, H4→W). Inside a HTF demand zone, only look for buys. Inside HTF supply, only look for sells. Hold as long as possible when the entry is inside a HTF zone.
He calls it arguably one of the most important parts of the whole strategy, and says it helps whatever you trade (S/R, bull flags, etc.).
MTA = knowing that entry-timeframe zones have higher odds when they sit inside a higher-timeframe zone of the same type.
Natural gas example: three or four H4 demand zones, all inside a weekly demand zone. A couple of them failed, but one worked big. 'That's okay because eventually the one did.'
Buying higher up the chart, inside HTF supply, gave only small R:R even on the trades that worked. 'You do not wanna be buying in a supply zone.'
ETF = entry timeframe (the one you enter on). ITF = intermediate timeframe. HTF = higher timeframe.
For now, almost ignore the ITF. Focus on the ETF and the HTF. He says the ITF is there for a reason that comes up later.
1m entry → 15m HTF · 5m entry → H1 HTF · 15m entry → H4 HTF · H1 entry → Daily HTF · H4 entry → Weekly HTF.
The daily-entry row in the captions is unclear ('daily three month'). In the MSA lesson he says the HTF for daily is the monthly.
The combinations are also on the 'High Probability Trading Solver' spreadsheet that members get.
The same process works on any combination (5m with H1, 1m with 15m, 15m with H4, and so on).

First step in building a trading plan: decide which timeframe you will enter on. He enters on H1 and H4, and occasionally on a daily zone. He can do three because he understands MTA and MSA well enough not to get confused. If you are new: pick ONE entry timeframe, not three, and stick to it. If you cannot day trade: enter on H1 or H4. If you day trade: enter on 1m, 5m or 15m.
He suggests a four-chart layout as probably the best option.
1) Decide your ETF (example: 5m). 2) Go to its HTF (H1) and mark the demand and supply zones. A tested zone can still be marked.
3) Wait for price to reach those HTF zones. 4) Drop to the ETF and trade the ETF zones that form inside or off the HTF zone.
EURUSD 5m example: a 5m demand zone removed a 5m supply zone (large move away, basing candle, stay-away candle), and price pulled back into it. That was the trade, coming off the H1 zone.
In that example a wick may have stopped the trade out. 'That's why it's nice to have your stop a little bit lower, but that can happen.'

In the same example the overall trend was down, so he thought shorts were higher odds. Trend is covered in another lesson. He says there are times you will adjust the timeframe pairing, to be covered later.
Find the HTF zone, refine the entry on the lower timeframe, then hold as long as possible.
He is 'taking this weekly zone and making it smaller on an H4 chart'. He tries to trade the whole weekly move while entering only at lower-timeframe zones (he calls this confirming the entry).
Inside HTF demand you only BUY. You ignore the supply-zone trades. 'We buy at demand. We do not sell at demand.'
Supply trades inside HTF demand can work, but usually only briefly (about 1:1, maybe 2:1). The long inside weekly demand reached 12:1.
MSA (next lesson) is 'basically this times two'. It is how he gets '50 to one' trades, but you cannot understand it until you master MTA.
Post two screenshots of one setup (a win or a loss is fine): 1) your HTF zone, 2) the ETF setup inside it ('a zone within a zone'). Post it in the Discord homework chat and label what it is.

passages.t: This is the "hold as long as possible" part of his edge: enter low on the lower timeframe and aim for the full higher-timeframe move.

Zone within a zone, as on his NATGAS chart: three H4 demands (two CP, one PV) inside a weekly demand band. The CP zones gave way, the PV demand held, and the long from it ran beyond the 2.81 R:R first shown.
His timeframe-combinations table as it appears on screen. Read by column: ETF, then ITF, then HTF. Daily entries use 1M and 3M.
The process on his EURUSD replay: mark the H1 zone, wait, drop to 5m. A 5m demand that removed a 5m supply, inside the H1 demand, gives the pullback entry.

Buying while price is inside a higher-timeframe supply zone, or selling inside HTF demand. New traders entering on several timeframes at once. Trading entry-timeframe zones without checking where price is on the HTF. Taking quick counter-HTF trades. They only give about 1:1 to 2:1.

Have I chosen ONE entry timeframe? Am I using the correct HTF for that ETF? Is my ETF zone inside a HTF zone of the same direction? Am I avoiding longs inside HTF supply and shorts inside HTF demand? Is my plan to hold toward the opposing HTF zone, not take a quick 1:1?

“Our edge comes from identifying these higher timeframe zones, refining our entry lower, and then holding as long as possible.” “We buy at demand. We do not sell at demand.” “Pick one timeframe guys and stick to that timeframe.” “A couple trades did not work, but that's okay because eventually the one did.” “I would screenshot this, I would learn this.”
“This is golden information here. This is how we get those 50 to one trades.”
The ITF (intermediate timeframe) row exists, but he says to mostly ignore it for now. He enters on H1, H4 and sometimes daily, and tells beginners to pick only one. Four-chart layout recommendation.

Quick trades against the HTF zone usually give only 1:1 to 2:1, against 12:1 for the long inside weekly demand (natural gas example). His edge is stated as: HTF zone, refine the entry lower, then hold as long as possible. Members get a 'High Probability Trading Solver' spreadsheet that lists the combinations.

Small zone inside a big zone of the same kind = better odds. A small fish swims inside a big school of fish going the same way. It is much safer than a small fish swimming alone toward a shark. On charts, a small entry zone inside a big higher-timeframe zone of the same type has the big crowd behind it. We buy small demand inside big demand. We do not buy inside big supply.
Russian nesting dolls: the small doll (your entry zone) sits inside the big doll (the higher-timeframe zone). Same shape, same direction.
Only take entry-timeframe zones that sit inside a higher-timeframe zone of the same direction.
Pairs: 1m to 15m, 5m to H1, 15m to H4, H1 to Daily, H4 to Weekly. New traders pick ONE entry timeframe. Edge: find the HTF zone, refine the entry lower, then hold as long as possible.
Step one of a plan: choose ONE entry timeframe (ETF). Say 5 minutes. Its higher timeframe (HTF) is the 1-hour. This chart is the 5m.
On the 1-hour, mark the demand and supply zones. Here we copy them onto the 5m chart as big shaded boxes: H1 demand below, H1 supply above.

passages.h: Step: Wait for price to reach the HTF zone
passages.t: Now we wait. Price drops into the big H1 demand. Inside HTF demand we only look to BUY.

passages.h: Step: A small zone inside the big zone
passages.t: A 5m demand forms inside the H1 demand: a zone within a zone. That is the trade. We buy the pullback into the 5m zone.

passages.h: Step: Hold toward the opposing HTF zone
passages.t: We hold as long as possible: all the way to the H1 supply. A small entry with a far target is how the big R:R happens.

passages.h: Step: Do not buy inside HTF supply
passages.t: Here a 5m demand formed INSIDE H1 supply. Buying it gave a tiny bounce at best, then price fell. We buy at demand. We do not buy at supply.

What is MTA? - Taking entry-timeframe zones only inside a higher-timeframe zone of the same direction. HTF for a 5m entry? - 1 hour. HTF for an H1 entry? - Daily. HTF for an H4 entry? - Weekly. HTF for a 1m entry? - 15 minutes. Inside HTF demand you...? - Only buy. We do not sell at demand.
Where does the edge come from? - Find the HTF zone, refine the entry lower, hold as long as possible. How many entry timeframes for a new trader? - One. Stick to it.

A trend has clear, obvious peaks and valleys and is sustainable. Momentum is a steep, near-straight move with tiny pullbacks and is not sustainable. He trades only with trends and trend lines, and covers momentum lines only to show what not to use.

Trade with trends and trend lines, never momentum lines. Draw a trend line only after the prior swing low (downtrend) or high (uptrend) is broken. A trend line must be angled, not near-flat. For confirmation, use a break of a proper trend line, not a momentum line. Do not draw momentum lines on your chart.
He does not trade momentum or momentum lines. He only pays attention to trends and trend lines.
Trend: very clear peaks and valleys that anyone can see. 'Show your mom', or any beginner, and they could tell you the trend.

Momentum: a steep, almost straight-line move with only small pullbacks and no clear peaks or valleys. In his opinion it is not sustainable. When he says 'trade with the trend', he means a proper, sustainable trend, NOT momentum. A trend, even a weak one, is always better than momentum.
Downtrend line: you need peak → valley → lower peak, then price must BREAK BELOW the valley low. Only then do you connect the peaks and extend the line.
Uptrend: the mirror image. Price must break above the prior high before you draw the line.
You cannot draw a trend line if the swing point was not broken. 'This doesn't make any sense.'
After a new lower low, re-anchor the line to the newer high to clean it up (his example: price wicked above the old line, then made a new low). The line must slope. A near-flat line is not a trend.
Arrows on his main chart link show the trend. Study his charts to learn what he counts as a trend line.

A real trend line can still be low quality. If the peak-valley-peak-valley structure is small, or formed over a short time, the trend probably won't last. A larger trend, with big swings over a long time, is much better to trade with.
You can have a trend (for example a lower low) without a valid trend line. Then he marks the trend arrow but draws no line.
AUDUSD example: the H1 was only momentum (no trend line), but the H4 had a clear trend line. The H1 arrow still said downtrend.
Repeated momentum with many small peaks and valleys, falling again and again, can eventually be called a trend.
No set number exists, and no pip distance (such as '600 pips') turns momentum into a trend. Use judgement. Borderline cases exist where he could argue either way, so he leaves the line off.
Example: HTF supply, H4 context, 15m entry. Breaking a small momentum line can be a false breakout, and price can continue higher.
The real signal is the break of the proper trend line from further back, so use trend lines, not momentum lines, for confirmation.
Draw one momentum line and one proper trend line (clear higher highs/higher lows, peaks and valleys) and post both.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Momentum with no trend: how a trend would have formed
passages.t: Example: momentum currently up, but no clear peak or valley. It is hard to call it a downtrend, sideways, or anything else; there is no trend, only momentum.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Momentum with no trend: how a trend would have formed
passages.t: How it would have become an uptrend: push up, push down lower, push back up and break the high. Then you have a clear valley and a clear peak, and you draw the trend line. That did not happen.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Downtrend without a trend line (sketch)
passages.t: Sketch: valley, peak, then price broke the low but never broke the prior high in the right way. There is a lower low, so it is pretty much a downtrend, but you cannot draw a trend line there. He says this does not happen too often, so examples are hard to find.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Judging when momentum becomes a trend
passages.t: Example: price came down to the trend line and kept rallying. At some point further up he would say the trend is up, but at the time there was not enough price action.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Judging when momentum becomes a trend
passages.t: Zoomed in on a slice, price can look sideways; zoomed out, it keeps breaking down and the trend is down. He calls this 'reality-based thinking': if price keeps going for long enough, that is the trend. He uses subjectivity and best judgement here, not a measurement.

Colour code on his real charts: red lines are momentum lines and black lines are trend lines. The whiteboard uses purple for both, and he puts an X over the momentum example.

The re-anchor example is EURUSD 4h, Feb 2023, not an abstract case. Both lines start at the Feb 2 top (about 1.103). The steep red momentum line through the Feb 9 high was broken by the Feb 13–14 rally. The black trend line through the Feb 14 lower high held, including a Feb 21–22 retest, until the late-Feb low (about 1.053). The line that "price wicked above" was the momentum line, not the trend line.

Re-anchoring also happens in uptrends: Mar 15 low → Apr 3 valley, then a new, flatter line Apr 3 → Apr 10 valley. The Apr 10 dip poked slightly under the first line but held as a higher low, so he redrew the line from the newer valley instead of calling the trend over. Each re-anchor is shallower.

Trend without a trend line is shown twice, not once. AUDUSD has a red arrow on the 1h with no line (the 4h and 1D have lines). EURUSD in May 2023 has red arrows on the 4h and 1h and no line, while the 1D still shows a rising trend line.
The "momentum becoming a trend" example is the EURUSD 4h fall from the May 4, 2023 high (about 1.109) to about 1.071, circled in red. It came right after the Apr 3 → Apr 10 uptrend line broke.
The "small, short trend" example is the late Dec 2022 – early Jan 2023 EURUSD 4h down line: one peak and one valley over a few days. Price then rallied sharply.

passages.t: The extended trend line keeps working as a ceiling, which a momentum line would not have shown.

passages.h: Chart: [05:58] EURUSD 4h, late Dec 2022 – Jan 2023: a short black down line from the Dec 30 top, with the top and the Jan 3 valley circled. A steep red momentum line runs up from the Jan 6 low.
passages.t: A real but small trend line: one peak, one valley and a lower low, all within a few days.

passages.h: Chart: [07:00] Same area, the whole small down-structure (late Dec – Jan 6) circled.
passages.t: Trend quality: this structure is small and formed over a short time, so the trend probably will not last. It did not: price rallied hard right after.

passages.h: Chart: [06:35] EURUSD 4h, Mar–Apr 2023 uptrend: black lines from the Mar 15 low (about 1.052) through the Apr 3 valley, then a second line from Apr 3 through the Apr 10 valley. He circles the peaks and the Apr 3 valley and sketches how the trend formed.
passages.t: His sketch: push up, pull back to a valley, push up and break the high. Only then draw the line along the valleys.

passages.h: Chart: [07:12] The same uptrend, clean: a steep red momentum line from the Mar 15 low, a black line Mar 15 → Apr 3 valley, and a flatter black line Apr 3 → Apr 10 valley that runs to early May.
passages.t: Re-anchoring in an uptrend: after a new higher low, the line is redrawn from the newer valley. Each redraw is flatter.

passages.h: Chart: [07:49] Sketch: a box labelled "H4" (orange = supply) with a "15" (15m) price path rising into it as momentum, with small steps.
passages.t: His confirmation example: on the 15m, breaking the small momentum line under that climb can be a false breakout. Wait for a proper trend line to break.

passages.h: Chart: [08:14] EURUSD 4h, May 2023: after the Apr 3 → Apr 10 line breaks, the fall from the May 4 high (about 1.109) to about 1.071 is circled in red. No trend line is drawn on it.
passages.t: Steady, repeated lower pushes with small pullbacks. At some point this momentum becomes a downtrend, but he still draws no line.

passages.h: Chart: [08:38] His DXY layout: 1W, 4h, 1D and 1h panes with zones. Green up arrows on the 4h and 1h; the 1h also has a rising trend line.
passages.t: This is the "main chart link" he refers to. Each pane gets a trend arrow; a trend line is added only where one is valid.

passages.h: Chart: [10:17] AUDUSD layout (1W/4h/1D/1h): the 1D and 4h each have a falling trend line and a red down arrow. The 1h has only a red down arrow, no line.
passages.t: His AUDUSD example: the 1h fall is momentum with no valid trend line, but the arrow still says downtrend because the 4h has a proper line.

passages.h: Chart: [11:07] EURUSD layout: red down arrows on the 4h and 1h with no trend lines, while the 1D still shows a rising trend line that price is dropping through. The weekly is marked "3m Proximal" and "TARGET".
passages.t: A second "trend without a trend line" case: the arrows carry the trend call when no line can be drawn.

passages.h: Chart: [10:54] EURUSD 4h May decline with the swings marked: the top circled, a "1" valley, a "2" bounce, and the latest low circled.
passages.t: He counts the swings to show there is no clean peak–valley–lower-peak sequence to anchor a line, even though price keeps making lower lows.

passages.h: Chart: [11:44] Sketch over the May decline: what would have made a valid downtrend line. Drop, valley, rally to a lower peak, then a fall through the valley low.
passages.t: Only after the valley breaks can you connect the top and the lower peak. This did not happen in May, so there is no line.

passages.h: Chart: [13:47] Back on the Mar–Apr uptrend: he circles the steep momentum leg off the Mar 15 low and, separately, the Apr 3 valley where the proper trend line is anchored.
passages.t: Same move, two lines. The momentum line (red) hugs the first leg; the trend line (black) needs a valley and is the one he uses.
His opening whiteboard: the trend has clear, circled peaks and valleys with the line along the valleys. The momentum leg has only tiny pauses, and he crosses it out.

His EURUSD 4h February example: the steep red momentum line was broken by the Feb 14 rally without ending the fall, while the black trend line (Feb 2 top through the Feb 14 lower high) held, including the Feb 21 retest.

The uptrend he walks through: a steep red momentum line and two black trend lines (Mar 15 low → Apr 3 valley, then re-anchored Apr 3 → Apr 10). After line 2 broke in May, the steady fall was circled as momentum that becomes a downtrend, with no line drawn.

Drawing momentum lines and treating them as trend lines (he sees this a lot in the community). Drawing a trend line before the swing point is broken. Treating a tiny, short-lived trend as equal to a large, established one. Taking the break of a small momentum line as confirmation, which can be a false breakout. Looking for an exact pip or candle count to call a trend.

Does the trend have clear, obvious peaks and valleys? Was the prior swing low/high broken before I drew the line? Is the line angled, not flat? Is this a sizeable, established trend rather than a short one? Is my confirmation a break of a trend line (not a momentum line)?

“Momentum lines are steep and aggressive and trend lines are very, very obvious.” “You could probably show your mom who has no idea what trading is, and she'd be able to tell you.” “Not everything is black and white.” “The reason I'm showing you momentum lines is to show you what not to do.” “This is always gonna be better than that momentum.”
“Not every trend line's gonna be the exact same. Not every momentum line's gonna be the exact same.” “Study my charts, look at my trend lines, get used to it.”
The PDFs only define a trend by HH/LL plus a blatant trendline. They do not cover the separate concept of momentum vs trend.
Trend line is valid only after the prior swing point breaks, then re-anchored after each new low or high. Trend quality depends on the size and duration of the swings.
A trend can exist without a trend line, and repeated momentum can become a trend. No fixed measure. Breaking a momentum line can be a false breakout for confirmation.

A trend is stairs anyone can see. Momentum is a slide that does not last. Walking down a staircase, you step down, rest on a landing, then step down again. You can see each step and each landing. That is a trend: clear peaks and valleys. Now picture a slippery slide: whoosh, straight down, no landings. Fun, but it ends fast. That is momentum. We follow staircases, not slides.
Trend = stairs with landings (peaks and valleys). Momentum = a slide (steep, no landings). Even your mom could point at the stairs.
Trade with trends and trend lines. Never use momentum lines. Draw a downtrend line only after peak, valley, lower peak AND a break below the valley. Mirror for uptrends.
Bigger, longer trends are better. Confirmation = a break of a proper trend line, not a momentum line.
Price climbs and turns down. The top is a peak. One peak alone tells us nothing yet.

passages.h: Step: A valley, then a lower peak
passages.t: Price falls to a valley, bounces, but turns down BELOW the first peak. That is a lower peak. Still no trend line yet!
Now price breaks below the valley low. The swing point is broken. Only now does a downtrend exist and only now can we draw the line.
Connect the peaks and extend the line. It slopes clearly: a flat line is not a trend. Price respects it as the staircase keeps going down.
This is momentum: steep and almost straight, with tiny pullbacks and no clear peaks or valleys. He shows momentum lines only to show you what NOT to do.
Breaking a small momentum line can be a false breakout. The real signal is a break of the proper trend line from further back.
Trend? - Clear, obvious peaks and valleys. Sustainable. Momentum? - Steep, near-straight move with tiny pullbacks. Not sustainable.

When can you draw a downtrend line? - After peak, valley, lower peak, and a break below the valley. Uptrend line rule? - Mirror: price must break above the prior high first. Flat line? - Not a trend. The line must slope. Which trend is better? - A larger one, with big swings over a long time. Confirmation uses...? - A break of a proper trend line, never a momentum line.
Fixed number to call a trend? - None. Use judgement.

Basic method: enter a little before the proximal line, stop a little beyond the distal line, with the spread as buffer. Take-profit methods vary and should be tested. He takes 25% off at 3:1 and holds 75% toward the next HTF opposing zone.
Stop goes just beyond the distal line (spread/few pips). If the zone breaks, the trade is void. Enter just before the proximal line. Base your entry and take-profit choices on your own testing.
As with drawing zones, entries and take profits are subjective. There is no right or wrong. Test what works for you, and you may find an entry he has not tested.
Once the zone is broken the whole trade is void, which is why the stop goes just beyond it.
Size the long/short position tool to the zone, then add the spread on both sides. With a 1-pip EURUSD spread, entry about 1 pip before the proximal line and stop about 1 pip beyond the distal line.
Entering just around the proximal line is usually fine. You don't need a wide buffer or an entry far ahead of the zone.

Give the stop a little more room, judged visually, because price sometimes peeks just through a zone and then goes. The stop is 'usually always' a few pips/spread beyond the zone. Nothing else to it. Supply is the exact opposite: short just below the proximal line, stop above the zone.
Split entry: 50% at the proximal line and 50% halfway through the zone. This tightens the entry and raises R:R, but has cons ('no free lunch'). The split entry may suit a bigger zone.
Zone within the zone: drop to a lower timeframe (for example 15m inside an H4 zone) and use a lower-timeframe zone to refine the entry.
There are hundreds of entry types. More may be covered in the Sunday sessions or a later video.
Two orders: 25% of the position with TP at 3:1 (set on the R:R tool → create limit order).

The other 75% targets higher-timeframe supply/demand, for example holding H4 longs inside weekly demand up to the next weekly supply. On the runner he bumps the stop under new zones to lock in profit.
Target the most recent high or pivot. Fixed R:R such as 2:1 or 3:1, ignoring structure. Example: maybe your tests show 30% wins and a lot of trades reach 3:1, so a fixed 3:1 rule fits you.
Target the next opposing HTF zone. With MTA, an H4 entry can target weekly supply, which raises overall R:R.
Context decides: in weekly demand with room above, hold to weekly supply. If it is a riskier trade with a supply zone close above, take profits quicker.
As price moves in your favour and fresh demand forms below, you can bump the stop under it to lock in profit.

With a deeper entry inside the zone (about 1.939, 38-tick stop) it closed at R:R 3.76. This puts numbers on "a deeper or split entry raises R:R".

passages.h: Chart: [01:34] Long Position tool on the PV demand: entry at the top (proximal) of the zone, stop just under the bottom (distal, red tag 1.899), profit box up to about 2.205.

passages.h: Chart: [01:43] He marks the entry line on the proximal edge and the stop line under the distal edge (also the bottom of the weekly band), then draws a big X below the zone.
passages.t: The X is the "trade is void" area: once price closes through the zone, the zone is broken and the setup is gone. So the stop sits just past it.

passages.h: Chart: [02:11] Sketch on a hypothetical green demand: price chops inside the zone several times, one final dip pokes just below the bottom edge, then price shoots straight up.

passages.h: Chart: [03:17] EURUSD 4h, test demand (about 1.0580–1.0622): the tool reads "Stop: 0.00402 (0.38%) 40.2" pips with entry on the proximal and stop on the distal line.

passages.h: Chart: [04:13] After adding the spread: "Stop: 0.00416 … 41.6" pips, Risk/Reward Ratio 3, "Target: 0.01247 … 124.7" pips.
passages.t: Entry about one pip above the proximal line, stop about one pip below the distal line. With a 3:1 target the TP is 124.7 pips away. This is his 25% portion: a fixed 3:1 order.

passages.h: Chart: [04:32] Same 41.6-pip stop with the target dragged much higher: Risk/Reward Ratio 6.71, target 279.1 pips.
passages.t: The runner idea: the other 75% is held toward a higher-timeframe opposing zone, which can be many R away.

passages.h: Chart: [05:47] NATGASUSD 4h, March 2023: "Rally Base Drop Supply (PV SUPPLY)" at about 2.945–3.010 at the spike top, and a second supply at about 2.68–2.72 under it.

passages.h: Chart: [06:25] Dropped to the 15m inside that H4 PV supply: a thin 15m zone at about 2.993–3.004 sits at the very top (distal side) of the H4 zone.

passages.h: Chart: [06:53] NATGAS 4h long from the PV demand with a deeper entry (about 1.939): stop 0.038 (38 ticks) at 1.901, target 2.082, "Closed P&L 0.143", Risk/Reward Ratio 3.76.
passages.t: Entering inside the zone instead of at the proximal line shrinks the stop and raises the R:R toward the same target.

passages.h: Chart: [07:40] He draws a double arrow over the whole height of the yellow weekly band and sketches choppy price beside it.
passages.t: Context for take profit: inside the weekly demand price can chop, and the bigger move is the run out of the band.

passages.h: Chart: [08:09] Zoomed out NATGAS 4h: the weekly demand band at the bottom (April–May demands) and the March supplies at about 2.70 and 3.00 above. Price has already rallied to about 2.60.

passages.h: Chart: [08:56] Same PV demand, entry at the proximal line (about 1.962): stop 0.060 (60 ticks) at about 1.902, target about 2.103, Closed P&L 0.143, Risk/Reward Ratio 2.38.
passages.t: Compare with 06:53: about the same target, but the proximal entry has a larger stop, so the R:R is 2.38 instead of 3.76.

passages.h: Chart: [10:20] Final recap on the PV demand: a short black line just above the proximal edge (entry) and one just below the distal edge (stop).
passages.t: The basic method in one picture: enter a hair before the zone, stop a hair beyond it.

The basic method as he sets it on the TradingView tool: entry about one pip above the proximal line, stop about one pip below the distal line (40.2 → 41.6 pips on his EURUSD example), 25% closed at 3:1 (124.7 pips) and 75% held toward the next HTF supply.

The two natural gas trades he shows on the same PV demand: the proximal entry (A, R:R 2.38) and a deeper entry inside the zone (B, R:R 3.76). Both closed at about the same 2.08–2.10 target. A deeper entry gives a smaller stop and a better R:R, but price may not fill it.

Two entry refinements he shows. Left: his "50%" split, with half at the proximal line and half halfway in. Right: zone within the zone on the NATGAS H4 PV supply, where a thin 15m zone at the top of the H4 zone allows a much tighter short.

Stop exactly on the zone edge with no room (zones can peek through). Holding for a big target when an opposing zone sits close above. Take profit quicker then. Copying someone else's entry or TP style without testing it.

Is the entry just before the proximal line (spread added)? Is the stop just beyond the distal line with a little room? Did I choose a TP method I have tested? Is there an opposing zone close to my target? If so, did I plan to take profit sooner? Do I have a plan for bumping the stop under new zones?
“Once the zone is broken, the whole trade gets voided.” “There's no free lunch. There's pros and cons to everything.” “It's all about testing.”
“The stop loss is usually always the same, but as far as entries go and take profits, it's definitely subjective.” “It's all based on different market conditions.”

Spread-based buffer: about 1 pip before the proximal line and about 1 pip beyond the distal line, with the stop given a bit more visual room. His split: 25% at 3:1, 75% held to the next HTF opposing zone. Split entry: 50% at the proximal line, 50% at mid-zone. Refining the entry with a lower-timeframe zone inside the zone (15m inside H4).

Enter at the front door, put the stop just behind the back wall. You wait for a friend at the front door of a house. You step in the moment they arrive: that is your entry, just at the near line of the zone. If a burglar breaks through the back wall, the house is not safe any more and you leave: that is your stop, just past the far line. When you win, you put a quarter of your toys in the bank early, and let the rest ride to the next big town.
The zone is a house. Entry = front door (proximal). Stop = a step past the back wall (distal). Once the wall breaks, the trade is void.
Entry just before the proximal line; stop a little beyond the distal line, with the spread as buffer. Once the zone breaks the trade is void, so the stop sits just past it with a little room.
His method: 25% off at 3:1, 75% held toward the next HTF opposing zone. Test your own TP style.
Here is a clean demand zone. Size the long-position tool to it.

passages.h: Step: Entry: just above the proximal
passages.t: Place the buy order about one spread before the proximal line (for example 1 pip on EURUSD). Entering around the proximal is usually fine; no need to go far ahead.

passages.h: Step: Stop: just past the distal
passages.t: Put the stop a little below the distal line, adding the spread and a bit of visual room, because price sometimes peeks just through a zone and then goes. If the zone breaks, the trade is void.
His personal method uses two orders. The first is 25% of the position with take profit at 3 times the risk.

passages.h: Step: Runner: 75% to the HTF supply
passages.t: The other 75% is held toward the next higher-timeframe supply. If a supply zone is close above, take profit quicker instead.
As price moves your way and fresh demand forms below, move the runner stop under it to lock in profit.

Entry on a demand zone? - Just above the proximal line (about one spread). Stop on a demand zone? - A little below the distal line, spread + small room. Why stop just past the zone? - Once the zone breaks, the trade is void. His exit split? - 25% at 3:1, 75% to the next HTF opposing zone. Split entry? - 50% at proximal, 50% halfway into the zone.

Zone within the zone? - Refine the entry with a lower-timeframe zone inside your zone. Opposing zone close above? - Take profit quicker. Managing the runner? - Bump the stop under new demand as it forms.

Multiple sequence analysis (MSA) adds a third timeframe: the HTF of your HTF. It asks why the higher-timeframe zone should hold, and three-timeframe confluence is when he risks the most. Without that third-timeframe zone he still may trade, but at 0.25–0.5% instead of 1%.
Master MTA before trying MSA. For every HTF zone, ask why it should hold: check the next timeframe up.
Risk the most only with three-timeframe confluence. Without a HTF or MSA zone, risk 0.25–0.5% instead of 1%. Use the correct sequence for your entry timeframe.
MTA = multiple timeframe analysis. MSA = multiple sequence analysis. He writes them as 'MTA' and 'MSA'.

You must master MTA first. 'If you do not understand multiple timeframe analysis, you will not understand multiple sequence analysis.' MTA: look for ETF trades inside HTF zones (example: H4 longs inside weekly demand).
MSA asks: why should that weekly demand zone hold? Treat the HTF as if it were your entry timeframe, then look at ITS HTF.
1m ETF → 15m HTF → H4 MSA. 5m ETF → H1 HTF → Daily MSA. 15m ETF → H4 HTF → Weekly MSA. H1 ETF → Daily HTF → Monthly MSA.
H4 ETF → Weekly HTF → in the natural gas example he used a 6-month 'macro' zone. The captions do not state a fixed MSA timeframe for the weekly.
Any timeframe works if you use the appropriate sequence (see the High Probability Trading Solver spreadsheet). You can message him to check yours.

Weekly demand was a drop-base-rally with two basing candles and a clean move up. On the 6-month chart there was demand (basing candle plus large stay-away candles), and the weekly demand sat inside it. H4 demand inside weekly demand inside 6-month demand gives three-timeframe confluence.
This is why he felt comfortable taking loss after loss in the H4 zones and holding for one large win. These are the trades where he applies the most risk/capital.
Without a HTF zone and an MSA zone in play he would risk about 0.25% or 0.5%, not 1%. With MSA confluence and price moving because the higher timeframes are in play, he applies more capital.
Low-quality example: EURUSD, find a weekly zone and an H4 zone in it, with no reason for the weekly to hold. He says this is fine, and better than S/R, but low quality: 0.25–0.5% risk.

5m day-trade example: H1 demand, but on the daily there is no demand where price is (only a low-quality one elsewhere). No MSA confluence, so very low risk on 5m confirmation. If the area were daily demand too, it becomes higher odds. You can still take H1 trades in daily zones with no monthly zone. Just risk less.

The edge: identify the top-level zone (for example daily), enter on the 5m, and try to hold the whole daily move by repeatedly finding 5m entries. Expect a very large R:R but a not-amazing win rate. 'That's just my strategy.'
Once he started applying MSA his trading 'took a turn for the best'. Without it 'you're gonna have a hard time trading'.
Three screenshots: 1) entry-timeframe zone/entry, 2) higher-timeframe zone, 3) MSA-timeframe zone. Label each timeframe (arrows help). Any valid sequence is fine.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Where MSA came from
passages.t: He says he asked himself one day, while only trading HTF zones, 'why should this weekly demand zone hold?', and then went to the timeframe above the weekly. The weekly zone in the natural gas example had 'beautiful reactions' off it.

passages.h: More from the lesson: The question above the weekly
passages.t: In the EURUSD low-quality example he says that to justify the weekly demand you would have to ask whether there is a three-month demand there 'or whatever'.

passages.h: More from the lesson: The question above the weekly
passages.t: In the natural gas example he used the 6-month ('macro') chart. He adds that MSA can also be applied to the lower timeframes.

passages.h: More from the lesson: EURUSD daily-to-5m hold idea
passages.t: Example: a daily supply zone was on his chart at the time. Plan: get long at daily demand, find a 1H demand inside it, enter on 5m, and try to hold from the daily demand toward the daily supply by repeatedly finding 5m entries. He calls the 5m 'a pretty popular entry type'.

passages.h: More from the lesson: How to build your own sequence
passages.t: Take the HTF of your entry timeframe, act as if that HTF is now your entry timeframe, and apply its HTF. That third timeframe is your MSA timeframe.

The EURUSD daily hold idea uses a daily demand at about 1.055–1.062 and a daily supply at about 1.095–1.101.
The EURUSD weekly zone for the low-quality example is about 1.022–1.038 (drawn as two nested boxes, inner 1.029–1.034), formed in Nov 2022.

passages.t: Opening setup: H4 zones drawn inside a higher-timeframe (weekly) demand. He labels every zone by its formation and its role: "CP" (continuation pattern) or "PV" demand. The lowest H4 DBR zone was hit again in early May and price rallied from it.

passages.h: Chart: [02:56] NATGASUSD weekly: after the 2022 collapse from about 10, a yellow weekly demand at about 1.9–2.2. A Rally Base Drop supply (PV supply) is labelled just above it.
passages.t: This is the HTF zone in the MTA step. Next he asks why it should hold. Labels on the weekly: Rally Base Drop Supply (PV SUPPLY), Rally Base Rally Demand (CP demand), Drop Base Rally Demand (PV demand).

passages.h: Chart: [03:27] NATGASUSD 6-month chart, zoomed out: the 2005–2008 spikes up to about 15, and current price back near the lows around 2.
passages.t: He goes ABOVE the weekly to the 6M ("macro") chart: this is the MSA step.

passages.h: Chart: [03:35] NATGASUSD 6M, zoomed in: the yellow 6M demand at about 1.9–2.2 sits under the last big red 6M candle. The labels mirror the weekly ones (RBR CP demand, DBR PV demand, RBD PV supply).
passages.t: Basing candle plus big stay-away candles on the 6M give the macro demand. The weekly demand sits inside this 6M demand, so the weekly zone has a reason to hold.

passages.h: Chart: [04:20] NATGASUSD H4 with all three timeframes overlaid: a peach 6M zone (widest, about 1.9–2.25), the weekly zone inside it, and the green H4 demands inside both.
passages.t: This is what three-timeframe confluence looks like on the entry chart. H4 demand inside weekly demand inside 6M demand. This is where he applies the most risk and holds through repeated H4 losses for one large win.

passages.t: The low-quality example: an H4 zone inside this weekly demand is fine but low quality. There is no reason shown for the weekly demand to hold (no 3-month zone checked), so the risk is 0.25–0.5%.

passages.h: Chart: [06:39] EURUSD weekly 2017–2023: the weekly demand (about 1.022–1.038) formed in Nov 2022 after the rally off the 0.95 low.

passages.t: No daily (MSA) demand where price is means no MSA confluence for a 5m long. If he took it, the risk would be very low.

passages.t: The "hold" idea: get long at the daily demand, find an H1 demand inside it, enter on the 5m.

passages.t: Keep finding 5m entries to hold the whole move toward the daily supply. Big R:R, modest win rate.

passages.t: Screenshot 3 of the homework: the MSA-timeframe zone, labelled. The 6M box is drawn much wider than the weekly box, and the weekly sits in its upper part.
