passages.t: Homework screenshots 1 and 2: the entry-timeframe zone and the HTF zone, each labelled with its timeframe.
How he shows MSA on the entry chart: the 6M zone (dashed, widest) contains the weekly zone, which contains the H4 RBR (CP) and DBR (PV) demands. Price returned to the H4 PV demand and rallied.
The sequences he lists. Each HTF is treated as an entry timeframe, and its own HTF becomes the MSA timeframe. For the H4/weekly natural gas trade he used the 6M chart.
EURUSD daily: the H1 demand at 1.0702–1.0714 has no daily demand under it, so it is low risk only. His preferred plan is to buy at the daily demand and re-enter on the 5m toward the daily supply.

Taking an ETF zone inside a HTF zone without asking why the HTF zone should hold. Using full risk on low-quality, single-timeframe or two-timeframe setups. Expecting a high win rate from a big-R:R hold strategy.

Is my ETF zone inside a HTF zone? Is that HTF zone inside a zone on the MSA timeframe? If there is no MSA zone, did I cut risk to 0.25–0.5%? Am I using the correct ETF/HTF/MSA sequence? Do I accept a lower win rate for a larger R:R?

“Why should this weekly demand zone hold?” “If you're not using multiple sequence analysis, you're gonna have a hard time trading.” “Our risk reward is gonna be very large, but our win rate is not gonna be amazing.”

“If you do not understand multiple timeframe analysis, you will not understand multiple sequence analysis. I can guarantee you that.” “When I started to apply this, my trading took a turn for the best.”
MSA (a third timeframe above the HTF) does not appear in course.ts. Sequence list: 1m-15m-H4, 5m-H1-D, 15m-H4-W, H1-D-M, plus a 6-month macro for the H4/W example.
Risk tiers: about 0.25–0.5% without HTF/MSA confluence, more (up to 1%) with three-timeframe confluence. He says his strategy has a big R:R and a modest win rate.

Ask why the big zone should hold: check one more timeframe up. You want to stand on a box. Is the box strong? Look under it: it is on a table. Is the table strong? Look under it: it is on the floor. Box on table on floor: safe! That is three timeframes agreeing. When all three line up, he risks the most. When the table is missing, he still might stand there, but more carefully.
Three nesting dolls: entry zone inside a higher zone inside an even higher zone. Three dolls = confidence.

MSA = MTA times two: entry timeframe, its HTF, and the HTF of that HTF. Three-timeframe confluence is where he risks the most. Without the MSA zone: 0.25 to 0.5% instead of 1%. Expect a big R:R and a not-amazing win rate. Hold the big move with repeated entries.
You must master MTA first. Here an H1 demand (entry) sits inside a daily demand (HTF). That is a zone within a zone.

passages.h: Step: Ask: why should the daily hold?
passages.t: MSA asks one more question. Treat the daily as if it were your entry timeframe. What is ITS higher timeframe? For daily, it is the monthly.
The daily demand sits inside a monthly demand. H1 inside daily inside monthly: three-timeframe confluence.
These are the trades where he applies the most risk, around 1%. Confluence is why he can accept loss after loss in the small zones and hold for one big win.
The goal: hold the whole higher-timeframe move by finding new entry zones again and again as price climbs.

passages.h: Step: No MSA zone? Smaller risk
passages.t: If there is a daily zone but nothing on the monthly, you can still trade it, but risk only 0.25 to 0.5%. It is fine, just lower quality.

MSA? - Multiple sequence analysis: entry, its HTF, and the HTF of that HTF. Question MSA asks? - Why should this higher-timeframe zone hold? Sequence for 1m? - 1m, 15m, H4. Sequence for 5m? - 5m, H1, Daily. Sequence for 15m? - 15m, H4, Weekly. Sequence for H1? - H1, Daily, Monthly. Risk without an MSA zone? - 0.25 to 0.5% instead of 1%. Expect what win rate? - Not amazing, but a very large R:R.

Trend trading means the higher timeframe AND the entry timeframe are both trending, and you buy or sell the nearest entry-timeframe zone until it is removed. After three continuation patterns in a row, price is overextended: stop or cut risk, and do not chase.
The HTF trend and the ETF trend must both point the same way. Trade only the NEAREST ETF zone until it is removed.

After the nearest zone is removed, the next zone is only valid if it sits inside an ITF zone. Otherwise wait for the HTF zone. After three CPs in a row, stop, or use reduced risk and aggressive management. The zone must still be high quality.
Some call it momentum trading. The idea is trading with the trend. Just buying the nearest H1 demand because the H1 is up is 'right to an extent', but it ignores the higher-timeframe trend.
His trend trading: the HTF of your ETF must be trending, AND the ETF must be trending (trend line respected). Then buy or sell the NEAREST ETF zone.
Example: H1 ETF, daily HTF in an objective uptrend, H1 uptrend line respected. The nearest H1 demand is valid. Once the H1 demand was removed, his chart showed the H1 trend as sideways.

passages.h: When the nearest zone is removed
passages.t: Trade the nearest zones in play until that zone is removed. After the nearest zone breaks you lose the ETF uptrend. You cannot buy the next zone down UNLESS it sits inside an ITF zone (H4 for an H1 entry).

passages.h: When the nearest zone is removed
passages.t: Otherwise wait for HTF (daily) demand to be hit. In the example the nearest H4 zone was far lower, so buying the next H1 zone was risky.
In his experience, after three continuation patterns (CPs) in a row you should stop trading in that direction. Price is overextended and you are waiting for a pullback.

You CAN still take it, but with less risk and more aggressive management. His example: move the stop to break even by about 1:1 (or take profit), half-risk then into profit. At only the second CP he might risk the full 1% and look for 5:1.
Not always exact: one run went CP 1-2-3-4-5 and still worked as a trend trade. He skipped the later one because of the three-CP overextension.
Price will sometimes go straight up and you will miss trades. Do not chase price ('I cannot stress that enough').

A trending HTF does not mean buy every nearest zone. The zone must still be high quality. Example: H4 entry with the weekly trending up. The nearest H4 demand was not great, so not automatically a buy.
Two labelled screenshots: the HTF trend (any sequence), and the nearest-zone setup on the ETF.

'Momentum trading' from him can also mean a different method that he does not cover here.

passages.h: Chart: [02:44] GBPJPY 1h with his drawing: an X through the nearest zone (180.89–181.30), a scribbled path down through 180.10–180.48, and a horizontal line at about 179.20 on the 179.20–179.72 zone.

passages.h: Chart: [02:44] GBPJPY 1h with his drawing: an X through the nearest zone (180.89–181.30), a scribbled path down through 180.10–180.48, and a horizontal line at about 179.20 on the 179.20–179.72 zone.

passages.t: Homework template: one screenshot for the HTF trend and one for the nearest-zone setup on the entry TF.
GBPJPY H1: buy only the nearest demand (180.89–181.30). If it breaks, skip 180.10–180.48 (no H4 zone under it) and look for the H1 zone that overlaps the H4 demand at 178.13–179.40.
The three-CP rule: full risk on early continuation patterns, reduced risk and break-even by 1:1 on the third, and stand aside after that.
His four-pane layout for GBPJPY: weekly, 4h, daily and 1h all trending up (green arrows), with the nearest 1h demand as the entry.

Calling it a trend trade off one timeframe only. Chasing price after an extended run. Buying deeper ETF zones after the nearest one breaks, when they are not inside an ITF zone. Buying every nearest zone regardless of quality.

Is the HTF trending in my direction? Is the ETF trending (trend line holding)? Is this the NEAREST ETF zone? If the nearest zone broke, is this zone inside an ITF zone? Is this the 3rd+ CP in a row? If so, did I cut risk or skip? Is the zone itself high quality?

“Do not chase price. I cannot stress that enough.” “After three CPs, continuation patterns, we should stop trading to the upside.” “We simply buy or sell the nearest zone.” “We don't just want to just be buying every zone with the trend.” “We still need to make sure that the zone is high quality.”
Rule: buy or sell only the NEAREST ETF zone; the next zone is valid only if inside an ITF zone.

Three continuation patterns in a row means overextended: stop, or reduce risk and manage aggressively. Full 1% and a 5:1 target at an early (2nd) CP. His meaning of 'momentum trading' may differ in other contexts.

When both big and small charts go up, buy the closest step. Climbing a ladder, you step on the rung right below your foot, not one far down. When the big picture and the small picture both go up, we buy the nearest zone. But after climbing three rungs in a row really fast, you are out of breath and should rest. And if the rung under your foot snaps, you do not jump to a lower rung unless it has extra support.
A ladder: step on the nearest rung; after three quick rungs, rest; a broken rung means the climb pauses.
Trend trading = HTF trending AND entry timeframe trending. Then trade the NEAREST entry zone.
Trade the nearest zone until it is removed. The next zone down counts only if it sits inside an ITF zone; otherwise wait for HTF demand.
After three continuation patterns in a row, price is overextended: stop, or cut risk and manage aggressively. Never chase.
The daily (HTF) is in an objective uptrend, and the H1 (entry) trend line is respected. Only now is it a trend trade.
Each new rally-base-rally is a continuation pattern (CP). We buy the nearest H1 demand: the newest one closest to price.
At the second CP he might still risk the full 1% and look for 5:1. Keep counting.
After three CPs in a row, price is overextended. Stop trading that direction, or take it with less risk and move the stop to break even by about 1:1. Price may run without you. Do not chase.
Price breaks the nearest zone (CP3). The H1 uptrend is lost and now looks sideways. CP2 below is only valid if it sits inside an H4 (ITF) zone. Here it does not, so we wait for the daily demand.
Trend trading needs...? - HTF trending AND entry timeframe trending, same direction. Which zone do you trade? - The NEAREST entry-timeframe zone, until it is removed.

Nearest zone broke. Next zone down? - Only if inside an ITF zone. Otherwise wait for HTF demand. Three-CP rule? - After 3 CPs in a row, stop or cut risk: price is overextended. Third CP management? - Less risk, break even by about 1:1. Second CP? - Full 1% risk possible, look for 5:1. Price runs without you? - Let it go. Never chase.

For long-term dividend stocks he buys supply-and-demand zones on the 12M, 6M, 3M and 1M charts with no stop loss (about 99% of the time). He sizes up on higher-timeframe zones and buys pullbacks instead of chasing.
No-stop zone buying is for dividend investing only. Buy only at zones on the 1M/3M/6M/12M charts; bigger timeframe zone means bigger buy. In uptrends, buy pullbacks to new demand; never chase.
Only keep buying a falling stock if you believe in the company, it still pays a dividend, and your capital is consistent.
This is ONLY for dividend investing, because there is no stop loss about 99% of the time. Otherwise it is the same supply-and-demand method.
Charts: 12-month, 6-month, 3-month and 1-month (his macro charts). He maps zones on each and buys them.

Illustration only ('keep it simple'): $100 at a 1M zone, $200 at 3M, $300 at 6M, $500 at 12M. The larger the timeframe, the bigger the pullback, so the bigger the buy. Buy according to your risk parameters, your capital and how consistent your income is.

Coca-Cola: no fresh zones on the 12M. A 1M zone buy at 56.65, no stop. 3M (MMM): buying 1M zones all the way down while it trended down, collecting dividends. Now at a 12-month demand zone, about 62% down from the highs. He plans heavy capital while it stays in that 12M demand.
If it goes sideways for five years he doesn't mind; he keeps collecting the dividend and buying while it is paid.

Don't chase after a big run (S&P monthly example). Wait for price to base, create demand, then break the prior high. The new demand zone below becomes a discount buy on the pullback. For more active investing you can buy small pullbacks on a daily/lower timeframe.
Buy demand zones on the way down, as long as you have consistent capital, believe in the company long term, and it pays a dividend.
Buying at the highs still collects dividends but can leave you down 50%. Buying low adds capital gains on top of dividends.

passages.t: S&P 500 monthly: trending up and coming off a pullback. Buying the dips on the way down is 'not mentally easy', but it is easy to justify because you are buying after -20%, not after +20%.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details from the examples
passages.t: S&P scenario: right now, up at the highs, is not a great time to buy. If price breaks the prior high and leaves demand below, that demand becomes a great buy 'because we prove that price can push all the way up to here'.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details from the examples
passages.t: Buying at the highs and riding a 50% drop is 'still all right if you don't plan on selling', because you still collect the quarterly dividends. Buying low is much better because you get capital gains as well.

His macro method: zones on the 1M/3M/6M/12M with a dotted BUY at each proximal and no stop. The size scales with the timeframe (his illustration: $100 / $200 / $300 / $500).
The S&P drawing at 03:37: do not buy at the highs. Wait for price to break the monthly supply and leave new demand, then buy the pullback into it.
MMM: buying 1M zones on the way down under the 3M/1M downtrend lines, then heavy buying in the 12M demand (proximal about 98; 3M/6M BUY 95.46).
Using the no-stop approach for trading. Chasing a stock after a big run instead of waiting for a pullback to demand. Buying at the highs.

Is this a dividend stock I want to hold long term? Is price in a 1M/3M/6M/12M demand zone? Is my buy size scaled to the zone's timeframe? Am I buying a pullback rather than chasing a run? Is my capital consistent enough to keep buying lower?
Has price proven it can push up (broken the prior high) before I buy the new demand on the pullback?

“It's basically the same strategy as supply and demand, but it's just with no stop loss.” “The larger timeframe we go, the bigger the pullback.” “Wait for price to go up and then buy pullbacks.” “We prove that price can push all the way up to here.” “It's a great source of income to put your cash at work.”
The whole dividend-investing approach: 1M/3M/6M/12M zones, no stop, size scaled by timeframe. Coca-Cola 56.65 1M zone and 3M (MMM) 12M demand examples.

For dividend stocks, buy zones on giant charts, and buy more the bigger the zone. Think of a fruit tree that gives you apples every few months. You want to own more of that tree. You buy a little when the price dips a bit, and a lot when the price dips a lot. You do not sell when it gets cheaper, because the tree still gives apples. But you never rush to buy right after the price shot up.
A sale at your favourite shop: small sale = small basket, huge sale = big basket. And you do not pay full price right after a price jump.
Dividend investing only: buy zones on 12M, 6M, 3M and 1M charts, with no stop loss about 99% of the time.
Bigger timeframe zone = bigger pullback = bigger buy (for example $100 at 1M up to $500 at 12M).
Rising market: do not chase. Wait for a base, new demand, a break of the prior high, then buy the pullback.
On the 1M, 3M, 6M and 12M charts, mark the demand zones. These huge zones are where he buys.

passages.h: Step: Buy the zones on the way down
passages.t: While the stock trends down, he keeps buying 1M demand zones and collecting the dividend. No stop: this is investing, not trading.
Now price reaches a 12-month demand zone, about 14% down from the highs. The highest-timeframe zone gets the biggest buy.
Keep buying lower only if you believe in the company long term, it still pays a dividend, and your capital is consistent. If it goes sideways for years, you still collect the dividend.

passages.h: Step: Rising market: do not chase
passages.t: After a big run up, buying at the highs is not a great idea. Wait.

passages.h: Step: Base, break the high, buy the pullback
passages.t: Price pulls back, bases, and rallies through the prior high. That proves price can push up. The new demand below becomes a discount buy on the pullback.

Charts for dividend investing? - 12M, 6M, 3M and 1M. Stop loss for dividend investing? - None, about 99% of the time. Dividend investing ONLY. Sizing rule? - Bigger timeframe zone = bigger buy (e.g. $100 at 1M to $500 at 12M).
Rising market buy? - Wait for a base, new demand, a break of the prior high, then buy the pullback.
Keep buying a falling stock only if...? - You believe in it, it pays a dividend, and your capital is consistent. Why buy low, not high? - You get dividends plus capital gains.

No time or candle-count rule. Remove or move a limit order when the context changes: the HTF zone becomes tested or loses control, a newer nearer zone forms (set & forget), or the trend line or ITF support is lost. Everything is subject to your own testing.
A zone is tested once a candle closes fully outside it (no wick or body touching). Confirmation: remove the order if price hits the opposing HTF zone before pulling back to your entry zone.
Set & forget: keep only the order at the nearest zone. Move it when a newer nearer qualified zone forms.
After the nearest ETF zone fails, lower ETF orders stay only if inside an ITF zone with the ITF trend line holding. No time-based or candle-count removal.
Counter-trend trades are lower odds anyway, so they need to be the highest-odds version of the setup.
Question: how long should limit orders sit, and do you remove them on a condition or after a time?

Everything here is 'subject to testing'. He is explaining what he was taught and his own experience. There is more room to leave orders in longer with set & forget than with confirmation. No time limit and no candle count apply.

passages.h: When a zone counts as tested
passages.t: Price pushes into the HTF zone and reacts. The zone is officially TESTED once a candle CLOSES fully outside it, with no body or wick touching. Until then it is 'being tested'. Pulling back into a tested HTF zone to a lower-timeframe zone is lower odds.

passages.h: When a zone counts as tested
passages.t: A quick return right after it was tested is different from returning much later after a long move ('even more tested').

passages.h: Confirmation: what can offset a tested zone
passages.t: A trend can negate it: H4 downtrend pulling into H4 supply plus a daily downtrend makes 'tested' less important.

passages.h: Confirmation: what can offset a tested zone
passages.t: Counter-trend (for example H4 down, daily up) at a tested zone: he would not feel comfortable. 'With the trend always increases your odds.'

passages.h: Confirmation: what can offset a tested zone
passages.t: If you are not with the trend, prefer the confirmation to happen while the zone is still being tested, not after.

passages.h: Confirmation: what can offset a tested zone
passages.t: Embedded zones: two 15m supply zones in a tested H4 supply both worked over 3:1. The one inside an H1 supply was higher odds. He would have pulled the order on the one that wasn't embedded.

passages.h: Confirmation: the zone you trade must stay in control
passages.t: Example: a daily demand becomes in control, and an H1 demand forms from confirmation. Leave the order as long as price pulls back BEFORE hitting the opposing daily supply.

passages.h: Confirmation: the zone you trade must stay in control
passages.t: If price hits the opposing daily supply first and pushes down, daily supply is now in control. He removes the entry for sure.

passages.h: Confirmation: the zone you trade must stay in control
passages.t: Exaggerated case: an H4 confirmation that only pulls back after price has reached weekly supply is not a confirmation trade anymore. The move already happened.
Rule of thumb: the confirmation should form within about the size of the HTF zone away from it. Further away, other things come into control.
Best case is an immediate pullback after the confirmation. If not, make sure the ETF zone is inside a HTF zone.

After sharp moves off a zone that becomes in control, trades outside the HTF zone can still work. Inside is better. Once price leaves and breaks the low, it is 'more of a momentum' trade than confirmation.

passages.h: Set & forget: move the order to the nearest zone
passages.t: Set & forget requires price to be trending. Keep the order at the nearest ETF zone as long as the trend line holds.

passages.h: Set & forget: move the order to the nearest zone
passages.t: When a NEW nearer zone forms, remove the old order and move it to the new nearest zone, if it is a qualified, decent-looking zone and there is room to the trend line. The trigger is a newer nearer zone, not time or candles.

passages.h: Set & forget: after a loss or trend-line break
passages.t: Example sequence: H1 (HTF), 15m (ITF), 5m (ETF). If the nearest 5m zone fails, pull any lower 5m orders UNLESS that 5m zone is inside a 15m zone (H1 even better) AND the 15m trend line is still holding.

passages.h: Set & forget: after a loss or trend-line break
passages.t: If the ETF zone is below the ETF trend line it is lower odds. He takes it only if it is inside an ITF zone with the ITF trend line holding.

passages.h: Set & forget: after a loss or trend-line break
passages.t: AUDUSD example: a 5m zone just under the 5m trend line was inside a 15m rally-base-rally, with no real 15m trend line (only momentum). He would leave it. When price is trending, the criteria can be looser; trend raises odds.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details from the examples
passages.t: Tested example (US dollar H4 supply): a red candle that closed outside the zone did not count as tested, because part of that candle was still touching or inside the zone. Only the green candle with no wick or body touching made it tested.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details from the examples
passages.t: He says he no longer trades confirmation much. When he did trade it heavily, he never felt comfortable shorting a supply zone after it had become tested.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details from the examples
passages.t: Hypothetical demand ('two bases and a nice rally stay-away candle'): while no demand zone is in control, the daily supply is still in control, which is better for shorts. Once a daily demand forms below and takes control, shorts become lower odds.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details from the examples
passages.t: Embedded example: he would have drawn the H1 supply around the 15m zone a bit bigger than shown. He called the lower, non-embedded 15m zone 'definitely a risky setup'.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details from the examples
passages.t: Your own testing may disagree with him. For example, you might find over 100 tested trades that taking both zones and aiming for 3:1 works even at a tested zone.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details from the examples
passages.t: AUD (Aussie) example: on a 1H uptrend he looks for 5m longs. The only 15m line there was an aggressive momentum line, not a trend line; the real 15m trend line was further back, so the 5m zone was fine.

passages.t: A red candle closed below the zone, but part of it still touched the zone, so it is NOT tested yet. Only a candle with no wick or body touching makes the zone officially tested.

passages.h: Chart: [05:26] DXY 4h: price came back into the 102.430–102.803 supply, chopped inside it, dropped, and retested the 102.430 proximal before falling again.
passages.t: Shorting back into a tested zone is lower odds, unless the H4 and daily downtrends are with you.

passages.t: The daily demand is where a confirmation long would come from. The 4h and 1h supplies above are the opposing zones that must not be hit first.

passages.h: Chart: [13:31] EURUSD 1m sketch: he draws price stair-stepping up from below, dipping into the drawn box, then rallying straight through it.
passages.t: This illustrates the confirmation timing and distance discussion: what happens to an order when price moves sharply away from, or through, the drawn zone.

passages.h: Chart: [13:31] EURUSD 1m sketch: he draws price stair-stepping up from below, dipping into the drawn box, then rallying straight through it.
passages.t: An immediate pullback after confirmation is best. The further price runs before pulling back, the less it is a confirmation trade.

passages.t: Several opposing zones are close to each other here, and each one decides whether an order stays.
His "tested" definition on the DXY 4h supply (102.430–102.803): a close below with a wick still in the zone is "being tested". A candle with nothing touching the zone makes it officially tested.
Confirmation order: keep the H1 confirmation order while price pulls back before reaching the opposing daily supply (A). If the supply is hit first, it is in control and the order is removed (B).
Set & forget: move the order to each newer, nearer qualified zone while the trend line holds. After a loss, keep lower 5m orders only inside a 15m zone with the 15m trend line intact.

Leaving an order after the opposing HTF zone was hit, when your zone is no longer in control. Counter-trend trades at a tested zone. Keeping an old set & forget order below a newer nearer zone. Taking ETF zones below a broken trend line with no ITF zone support. Treating confirmations far from the HTF zone as confirmation trades.
Expecting exact, to-the-letter rules for when to pull an order. He says there aren't any; it evolves with your own testing.

Is the HTF zone tested (candle closed fully outside)? If tested, am I with the trend on the ETF and HTF? Has price hit the opposing HTF zone before my entry? If so, remove. Is my order at the NEAREST zone (set & forget)?
Is the trend line still holding? If not, is my zone inside an ITF zone with the ITF trend line intact? Did the confirmation form within about one zone-height of the HTF zone?
Is the zone I'm keeping an order on embedded inside a higher-timeframe zone (H1 for a 15m zone)?

“It has nothing to do with time or anything or the amount of candles.” “When a zone is tested, it becomes lower odds.” “With the trend, it always increases your odds.” “It's all going to be subject to testing.” “There are rules that I would break if price is trending.” “When price is trending, it just makes the criteria have to be less.”
Definition of a 'tested' zone (a candle closes fully outside it). Order-removal triggers: opposing zone hit first, newer nearer zone, trend-line loss without ITF support.
Rule of thumb: confirmation within about one zone-height of the HTF zone; an immediate pullback is best. Trend can offset a tested zone; an embedded lower-timeframe zone raises odds.

Pull your order when the story changes, not when the clock ticks. You save a seat for a friend at the cinema. You do not leave after ten minutes just because time passed. You leave if the friend says they went to a different cinema, or if a closer seat opens up for them. Limit orders are the same: remove or move them when the chart story changes.
A saved seat: move it when a better seat opens (nearer zone), give it up when the plan changes (opposing zone took control).

No time or candle-count rule. Remove or move an order when the context changes. A zone is officially TESTED once a candle closes fully outside it with no body or wick touching. Tested zones are lower odds.
Confirmation: remove the order if price hits the opposing HTF zone first. Set & forget: move the order to a newer, nearer qualified zone.

passages.h: Step: Price reacts from the zone
passages.t: Price pushes into the H4 demand and reacts. Right now the zone is "being tested".
This candle closed above the zone, but its wick still touches it. That does NOT count as tested.
This candle closes fully outside, no body or wick touching. Now the zone is officially tested. Coming back into a tested zone is lower odds, unless the trend is with you.

passages.h: Step: Confirmation: who is in control?
passages.t: Daily demand took control and an H1 demand formed from confirmation. Leave the order only if price pulls back BEFORE it hits the opposing daily supply.

passages.h: Step: Opposing zone hit first: remove
passages.t: Here price hit the daily supply first and pushed down. Daily supply is now in control. He removes the entry for sure.

passages.h: Step: Set & forget: move to the nearer zone
passages.t: In a trend, keep the order at the NEAREST zone while the trend line holds. When a newer, nearer qualified zone forms, move the order up to it.

Time limit on limit orders? - None. No candle count either. Context decides. When is a zone officially tested? - When a candle closes fully outside it, no wick or body touching. Tested zone odds? - Lower, unless the trend is with you.
Confirmation: opposing HTF zone hit first? - Remove the order. The other zone is in control.

Set & forget: new nearer zone forms? - Move the order to it (if qualified and room to the trend line). Set & forget needs...? - Price to be trending. Confirmation distance rule of thumb? - Within about one HTF-zone height of the HTF zone.

A no-chart psychology bonus video, a solo recording rather than a live webinar. Main points: focus on the process, not the money; being flat is a position; predict but don't trade predictions; stick to one side; judge a strategy over months, not three losses.

Stick to one side of the market (long, short or flat) and change only when the zones or trend change. Don't trade predictions that go against the trends in play. Don't change a strategy after a short losing streak. Evaluate over about two quarters. Protect capital; being flat is a valid position.
Stop asking others 'where is it going?' or 'should I buy here?'. Even if you make $5,000 off a tip, it doesn't make you consistent.
He wanted consistency and to learn to do it himself. Once you understand MSA you'll have your own view of where price is headed.
Focus on the strategy and the process, not the money. If you don't enjoy charting and tracking zones, trading may not be right for you.
Sharing profits in Discord is irrelevant to him. Get consistent first and the money follows.

Having no trades open is a position. It means you see no good quality setups. EURUSD example: daily supply in control, H1 demand in play. He missed his entry, pulled the order, and is waiting for the zone to be removed so he can look for H1 confirmation.
Not losing money is part of the process. Preserving capital matters more. Breaking even over three years beats losing thousands or blowing accounts. Patience comes only with experience.
He predicted pullbacks on overextended GBPJPY/AUDJPY from history and experience, but would never trade that.

Reason: weekly momentum, daily, H4 and H1 trends were all up. Price could easily shoot back up, unless some HTF supply was in control. 'I will predict these things based on history, but I will not trade them.'

passages.h: Stick to one side: long, short or flat
passages.t: Traders try to catch every move: they trade the daily uptrend and also try to short the lower-timeframe pullback.

passages.h: Stick to one side: long, short or flat
passages.t: Pick one bias from the trends in play. Example: daily uptrend pulling into daily demand, so only longs.

passages.h: Stick to one side: long, short or flat
passages.t: Change accordingly: if those longs lose and price breaks below daily demand, you lose the uptrend (now sideways), and shorts become viable. Counter-trend is possible, but your MSA must show higher-timeframe zones in control.

passages.h: Stick to one side: long, short or flat
passages.t: You will take fewer trades. It feels hard at first, and like working out, it becomes natural with repetition.

passages.h: Each setup is one of thousands
passages.t: Each setup must match your exact criteria, but it is one of thousands over your career. Stick to the plan and R:R. His average R:R is about 5:1. Three losses in a row still hurts.

passages.h: Each setup is one of thousands
passages.t: Run a simulation on a calculator or notepad. For example: lose 6, win 1, lose 3, win 1; or 5 losses then 2 wins. See that it is still profitable.

passages.h: Each setup is one of thousands
passages.t: Don't change strategy after three losses, especially a high-R:R one. Give it a few months. If it still isn't working after about two quarters, then change something.

passages.h: Each setup is one of thousands
passages.t: Holding to the final TP takes experience. Example: up $1,500 with a $2,000 target, a new trader closes early and loses out on $500.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details and his own experience
passages.t: When he was learning, he watched a few people but never asked them where price was going. He was more interested in the process and in being able to do it on his own.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details and his own experience
passages.t: He wanted something where he could make a profit consistently every month or every year, 'not just make some money'.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details and his own experience
passages.t: You have to enjoy what you do; if you don't, 'there's almost no reason to be doing it'. He would not track zones all day for members if he hated it, because it doesn't pay him enough for that.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details and his own experience
passages.t: Before his current strategy he took 2.5:1, 2:1 and sometimes 3:1 trades, and after three losses in a row he would want to change his strategy. He says he has been guilty of this and it is not a good thing to do.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details and his own experience
passages.t: Even when he gives a new trader an exact entry, stop and TP, the new trader may not be able to hold. In the $1,500 / $2,000 example, he himself would move the stop to breakeven and let it play out to the final TP.

EURUSD 1h (05:07): he missed the entry under the daily supply and pulled the order. The 1h demand and trendline must be removed, and price must pull back for 1h confirmation, before he shorts. Until then he is flat.
AUDJPY (06:36–08:57): he draws the pullback he expects into the 4h demand (or the daily zone), but weekly, daily, 4h and 1h are all trending up, so he will not short on that prediction.
One side at a time. Longs while the daily uptrend pulls into daily demand. Shorts only once that demand breaks and the trend is lost. Flat whenever nothing qualifies.

Asking others where price is going. Focusing on money instead of process. Trying to catch every move (trading both directions). Trading a prediction against the trend. Abandoning the strategy after three losses. Closing early before the final TP out of fear. Switching to a new strategy after three losses, as he did when he traded 2:1-3:1.

Is this trade on my one chosen side (long/short/flat)? Is it a prediction against the trends, or a planned setup? Does it exactly match my setup criteria? Have I simulated a losing streak at my R:R so I can sit through it? Am I staying flat when nothing qualifies?
“Being flat, being in no position is actually a position.” “I will predict these things based on history, but I will not trade them.” “Stick to one side of the market: long, short or flat.”

“It should be about the process and learning how to trade; the money will just flow in naturally.” “Not losing money is actually part of the process.” “Psychology only comes with experience and time.” “You have to enjoy the process.”

'Flat is a position' and 'predict but don't trade it'. 'Stick to one side: long, short or flat', switching only when the trend is lost. Evaluate a strategy over about two quarters, not after three losses. Simulating a loss sequence at your R:R (his average is about 5:1).

Care about doing it right, not about money. Doing nothing is allowed. Learning to ride a bike, you fall a few times before it clicks. If you quit after three falls, you never learn. Trading is the same: a few losses in a row are normal. Sometimes the best move is to wait on the bench until a good path appears. And pick one direction to ride, instead of zig-zagging everywhere.
A fisherman: he does not throw the net at every ripple, he waits for the fish. Some days he catches nothing, and that is fine.
Focus on the process, not the money. Being flat (no trades) is a position. Predict if you like, but do not trade predictions that go against the trends. Stick to one side: long, short or flat.
Each setup is one of thousands. Judge a strategy over about two quarters, not three losses.
No clean zones, no trend: no setups. Having no trades open means you see no good quality setups. Preserving capital is part of the process.
Daily uptrend pulling into daily demand means only longs. A little H1 supply on the way down tempts a short. Do not try to catch every move.

passages.h: Step: Predict, but do not trade it
passages.t: Price looks overextended and you may predict a pullback. But every trend is up. He would predict it, but never trade it.
Each candle here is one trade at about 5:1. Six losses in a row feel terrible.
One 5:1 win almost erases six losses. Keep going: lose 3, win 1, lose 5, win 2.
With more losses than wins, the account still ended higher. Run this simulation yourself. Do not change strategy after three losses; give it about two quarters.
Being flat? - A position: you see no good quality setups. Focus on...? - The process, not the money. Predictions? - Predict if you like, but do not trade them against the trends.
One side? - Long, short or flat, from the trends in play. Change when zones or trend change.
Three losses in a row? - Normal. Do not change strategy; evaluate over about two quarters. His average R:R? - About 5:1. Asking others where price goes? - A mistake. Learn to do it yourself.

Kevin walks through the pros and cons of day trading, the three day-trading timeframe sequences, and a full top-down day-trading plan on EUR/USD using entry, higher and curve timeframes. He finishes with session times (Eastern) and how to handle news: be aware of it, never predict it, and never trade into it.

Do a top-down analysis: assess the HTF trend first, then draw zones, then check one timeframe higher (multiple sequence analysis) before looking at the entry timeframe. Do not day trade the news; wait for the release and for spreads to settle. Never let news or your opinion of it change a valid technical setup. Day trading as a beginner only with money you can afford to lose - not 1-2% per trade.
You do not need to take a trade every day. Don't just find HTF zones and look for trades inside them: assess the trend first.

passages.h: Pros and cons of day trading
passages.t: Pro: far more setups, so you get involved in many trades and build emotional experience fast.

passages.h: Pros and cons of day trading
passages.t: He thinks day trading is a great way to START learning, but only if you risk tiny amounts you can afford to lose (he started risking about $5 a trade). Risking 1-2% of the account per trade as a beginner day trader is 'not a great idea'.

passages.h: Pros and cons of day trading
passages.t: Con: decisions have to be made quickly, so mistakes are easier (e.g. chasing a 1m/5m zone you 'missed' because the candle is about to close - he never recommends that).

passages.h: Pros and cons of day trading
passages.t: Con: much more stress; you have to be at the screen at exact times. On H1/H4 he has all day to decide and only rarely has to act live (his big gold trade: H1 zone inside H4 zone, price already inside both).

passages.h: Pros and cons of day trading
passages.t: Con: you start to believe you must take a trade every day. That is not true and it messes with your emotions.

passages.h: Pros and cons of day trading
passages.t: Price is fractal: a zone that works on H4 works on 1m, daily, monthly. The only differences between timeframes are how many trades you get and how fast you must react.

passages.h: Pros and cons of day trading
passages.t: His suggested learning path: start day trading (small risk) -> move to swing trading (where you really start to master it) -> optionally go back to day trading, which then feels much easier.

passages.h: Pros and cons of day trading
passages.t: To make more money he prefers risking more per zone (e.g. 2% instead of 1%, if the strategy's drawdown allows) rather than taking more trades on lower timeframes.
His own layout: four charts - weekly, daily, H4, H1 - plus a separate macro chart for the overall curve. He enters on H4 and H1 (mostly H1 lately).

Day-trader members: keep his chart link open to see his HTF zones (e.g. if price is inside his daily supply, lay off day-trading longs). On your own two-chart layout: one side = higher timeframe, other side = entry timeframe.

H4 -> 15m entry (captions say '50 minute'; context and the H4 HTF show it is the 15-minute). For people who can only check the chart every 15-20 minutes. 15m is the highest day-trading entry; trades can last longer than expected, so expect to hold overnight - it is 'day trading / intraday swing'.
H1 -> 5m entry. For checking every 5-10 minutes. His pick if he started day trading tomorrow - a good middle ground (e.g. 30 minutes away = 6 candles on 5m vs 30 on 1m).

15m -> 1m entry. Most trades, but you must be on the charts constantly; a 1m zone can form, pull back and hit TP in minutes while you answer the door. Fine only if you accept missing trades. Expect to be out of a 1m trade within roughly 10-15 minutes depending on conditions.
Anything higher than a 15m entry is intraday swing. Seconds charts (1s, 5s, 10s, 30s...) are extreme scalping - stay away. Even 1m is borderline scalping.

passages.h: Top-down plan example (15m HTF, 1m entry, EUR/USD)
passages.t: Step 1 - assess the trend on the 15m. A member called it sideways because no clean trendline could be drawn; Kevin called it a downtrend: high, low, higher high, then the low broke (clear valley + clear peak, then a lower low). He admits it is 'not the best trend' and a 'weird looking trend' - he would prefer a cleaner one.

passages.h: Top-down plan example (15m HTF, 1m entry, EUR/USD)
passages.t: Step 2 - draw significant 15m supply and demand zones (two 15m supply zones above, demand below; ignore areas with basing but nothing worth drawing).

passages.h: Top-down plan example (15m HTF, 1m entry, EUR/USD)
passages.t: Step 3 - multiple sequence analysis: go one timeframe higher than the 15m, i.e. the H4 (the 15m's higher timeframe). H4 supply was in control, so the 15m supply zones become higher odds and the 15m demand (counter-trend) lower odds.

passages.h: Top-down plan example (15m HTF, 1m entry, EUR/USD)
passages.t: You can still trade any of the zones, but size them by the analysis: e.g. 1% on the with-HTF shorts, 0.25-0.75% on the longs that have no real reason to hold.

passages.h: Top-down plan example (15m HTF, 1m entry, EUR/USD)
passages.t: Step 4 - drop to the 1m inside the 15m supply: either a set & forget order at a 1m supply zone embedded in the 15m supply, OR wait for the 15m zone to be contacted and look for confirmation (removing 1m demand and trendlines) then short.

passages.h: Top-down plan example (15m HTF, 1m entry, EUR/USD)
passages.t: Same process on any sequence: for a 5m entry the zone is an H1 zone and you check the daily (the H1's higher timeframe). Three timeframes in total: entry, higher, and curve/bigger-picture.

passages.h: Top-down plan example (15m HTF, 1m entry, EUR/USD)
passages.t: Recap he gives: 15m downtrend -> shorts higher odds; 15m demand is counter-trend; H4 supply on top -> the 15m supply is '15m confirmation coming off H4 supply'.
All times he gives are Eastern; convert to your own. New York session: wake around 8:00 AM, plan and look for trades. London session: around 1:00-2:00 AM Eastern.
Pick one session and stick to it, based on where you live (he can only day trade the New York hours).
Always check economic data and big speakers (the president, Fed chair Jerome Powell) - for day traders this is 'an absolute must'.

Example: price about to hit 15m supply at 8:59 AM with unemployment data at 9:00 AM -> wait. Even if price goes straight to TP, staying out was the better decision. Spreads widen around news and can stop you out even though price never reached your stop.

Do not day trade the news. Two options: (a) place the order early, betting on a spike into the zone then a drop - 'definitely risky'; or (b) wait for the release and the spike, let spreads calm down, then place the order.

Never predict the news or form your own opinion of it and trade that - many releases are subjective. Even objectively positive news should not sway a valid technical setup: 'If you have your setup in play, take it.'
Trade the charts because zones are objective: a base followed by a sharp drop is objectively supply; a huge push up is not.
Q: What is the higher timeframe for the 15m chart? A: The H4 (not the H1). Q (trend read): sideways? A: Downtrend - valley, peak, then lower low - though not a clean one.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details
passages.t: Why he personally avoids day trading: the stress is much higher and he calls himself an uptight person who gets overwhelmed easily, so it does not suit his personality.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details
passages.t: Signal and course sellers who call themselves full-time traders are, in his view, not really day trading full time.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details
passages.t: Swing trading gives you freedom: you don't always have to be looking at the chart. He spends only as much time as he needs to update zones for members.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details
passages.t: Objective vs subjective news: a war with Russia or high unemployment is objectively negative. Something like the US debt-ceiling decision is subjective; he thinks it is very negative for the dollar while others think it is positive. That is why he trades the charts.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details
passages.t: Pre-news scenario: if price is BELOW your zone at 8:59 with data at 9:00, you could leave the order in expecting a spike up and then a drop (risky), or wait for the spike candle, let spreads calm down, and then place the order.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details
passages.t: Practical setup: keep his chart link open in one browser tab and your own two-chart layout in another, so you can check whether price is inside one of his HTF zones (e.g. 'price is right at my four-hour supply, maybe not the best time to go long').

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details
passages.t: Day trading can be very rewarding if you have a very good understanding of multiple sequence analysis.

passages.t: This shows how small and fast 1m zones are. The whole zone is about half a pip. If you miss a 1m zone, never chase it because the candle is about to close.

passages.h: Chart: [19:32] EURUSD 15m top-down example: two 15m supplies at 1.07692–1.07738 and 1.07567–1.07604, and a 15m demand at 1.07334–1.07385. Price is chopping near 1.0749 after the drop.
passages.t: Step 1, trend: high, low, higher high, then the low broke. He calls it a downtrend, though not a clean one. Step 2: draw the significant 15m zones, two supplies above and one demand below.

passages.h: Chart: [19:32] EURUSD 15m top-down example: two 15m supplies at 1.07692–1.07738 and 1.07567–1.07604, and a 15m demand at 1.07334–1.07385. Price is chopping near 1.0749 after the drop.
passages.t: With the downtrend, the supplies are the higher-odds side and the demand is counter-trend.

passages.h: Chart: [19:51] EURUSD 1m inside the 15m supply (peach, 1.07567–1.07604). A purple 1m supply at 1.07574–1.07586 sits inside it.
passages.t: Step 4: drop to the entry timeframe inside the HTF zone. Option A: set & forget a sell at the 1m supply embedded in the 15m supply. He draws the embedded lower-timeframe zone in purple inside the peach HTF zone.

passages.h: Chart: [21:02] Side by side: the 15m with both supplies and the demand on the left, and the 1m zoomed in on the 15m supply and its purple 1m zone on the right.
passages.t: Option B: wait for price to contact the 15m supply, then look for 1m confirmation (1m demand and trendlines removed) before shorting. He calls it "15m confirmation coming off H4 supply".

passages.h: Chart: [21:03] Same layout with the 1m zoomed out. Price is still below both 15m supplies, and the 1m is making higher lows into them.
passages.t: The 1m rally runs straight into the 15m supply: the exact spot where you either have a set & forget order or start watching for confirmation.

Weekly: "<50% Body Candle" label, dotted "3m Proximal" at 1.10657, weekly demand 1.04833–1.07023. 4h: supply 1.07774–1.08014, green up-arrow and rising trendline. passages.t: This is the chart link members keep open to avoid day trading against his HTF zones. The 15m supplies in the day-trading example sit just under this 4h supply (1.07774–1.08014): the HTF zone in control for the short idea.

Weekly: "<50% Body Candle" label, dotted "3m Proximal" at 1.10657, weekly demand 1.04833–1.07023. 4h: supply 1.07774–1.08014, green up-arrow and rising trendline. Daily: purple supply 1.09416–1.10070, demand 1.04833–1.06044. 1h: up-arrow, demands 1.06901–1.06978, 1.06618–1.06684, 1.06352–1.06528.
passages.t: Price is also inside the weekly demand, which is why he sizes the trade by multiple sequence analysis rather than going all in.
The three day-trading sequences with the third, "curve" timeframe above each: H4 → 15m, H1 → 5m (his pick) and 15m → 1m. Each is shown on screen as a two-chart layout, HTF left and entry right.

The EURUSD 15m plan as drawn: a downtrend (high, low, higher high, low broken), two 15m supplies and one 15m demand, all under the H4 supply 1.07774–1.08014. Shorts get normal risk; counter-trend longs get 0.25–0.75%.

Two ways into the 15m supply on the 1m: A, a set & forget sell at the purple 1m supply (1.07574–1.07586) embedded in it; B, wait for contact, let the 1m demand and up-trendline break, then sell the pullback to the new 1m supply.
Jumping into a 1m/5m zone you missed because the candle is about to close. Believing a 'day trader' must trade every day.

Entering just before a scheduled release - spread spikes can stop you out without price touching the stop. Predicting news or trading your opinion of it. Going long on lower timeframes while price is inside a higher-timeframe supply zone. Using seconds charts (extreme scalping). Pricing your own opinion of a subjective news event into a trade.

Have I checked the trend on my higher timeframe (15m / H1 / H4)? Have I checked one timeframe higher (H4 for a 15m, daily for an H1) for a zone in control? Is my trade with the higher-timeframe zone in control? If not, have I cut my risk? Is price inside a Kevin HTF zone that opposes my direction? Is there economic data or a major speaker in the next few minutes? Have spreads normalised after any release?
Is this my chosen session? Can I actually watch this timeframe (1m needs constant screen time)?

“Price is fractal - everything works on every timeframe.” “Do not day trade the news.” “It's not about predicting the news.” “If you have your setup in play, take it.” “It's not about predicting what they're gonna say.” “This huge move up is not objectively supply.”

Day-trading sequences H4->15m and H1->5m (PDF lists 1m=15m, 5m=H1, 15m=H4 but not his reasoning on screen-time per sequence). Seconds charts = extreme scalping; 1m is borderline scalping. Session times in Eastern: NY wake ~8:00 AM, London ~1-2 AM; pick one session.

Spread widening around news can stop you out; two ways to handle a release (pre-placed order = risky, or wait for spike then place). Do not form opinions on news or let it sway a setup. Size risk by multiple sequence analysis (e.g. 1% with-HTF, 0.25-0.75% counter). Learning path day -> swing -> day; risk tiny amounts while learning day trading. Prefers raising risk per trade (within drawdown) over taking more trades.
Using his shared chart link to avoid day-trading against his HTF zones.

Day trading = same zones, faster clock. Check the big picture and the news first. A zone works the same on a tiny chart or a giant chart, like a cookie cutter that is the same shape in any size of dough. The only differences are how many cookies you get and how fast you must move. Before you play outside, you check the weather: big news is a storm. You stay inside until it passes, even if you miss a little sunshine.
News is a thunderstorm: do not walk into it. Wait for it to pass, let the puddles (wide spreads) dry, then go out.
Three sequences: H4 to 15m, H1 to 5m (his pick), 15m to 1m. Entry, higher, and bigger-picture timeframe.
Top-down: trend on the HTF, draw zones, check one timeframe higher for the zone in control, then drop to the entry. Never predict or trade the news. Wait for the release and for spreads to calm down.
A high, a low, a higher high, then the low breaks. He calls this a downtrend, though not a clean one. Shorts become higher odds.
Mark the significant 15m supply zones above. Ignore areas with basing but nothing worth drawing.
Multiple sequence analysis: for a 15m chart, go to the H4. H4 supply is in control, so the 15m supply zones are higher odds and 15m demand (counter-trend) is lower odds.
You can still trade any zone, but size it: about 1% on shorts with the HTF, 0.25 to 0.75% on longs with no real reason to hold.
Inside the 15m supply, either set a 1m supply order embedded in it, or wait for the 15m zone to be hit and look for 1m confirmation, then short.
Price is about to hit supply at 8:59 with data at 9:00? Wait. Spreads widen around news and can stop you out even if price never reached your stop.

HTF for the 15m? - The H4. Three day-trading sequences? - H4-15m, H1-5m, 15m-1m. His pick to start day trading? - H1 HTF with a 5m entry. Seconds charts? - Extreme scalping. Stay away. Trade the news? - No. Wait for the release and for spreads to calm down. Beginner day-trader risk? - Tiny amounts you can afford to lose (he started at about $5).
Sessions (Eastern)? - New York: wake around 8:00 AM. London: around 1-2 AM. Pick one. Must you trade every day? - No.

Kevin argues that zone quality is decided mainly by the higher timeframes, trend and testing history, not by how pretty the zone looks or a score out of 10. He grades the look of a zone simply as good or bad, then lets HTF zones, trend, tests and depth of tests decide whether it is high or low quality, followed by live market Q&A on overextended trends, embedded zones and macro confirmation.

Higher timeframes in play decide quality more than the look of the zone. Always want a large move away; tight basing is a plus. Do not take a very low quality (wicky, barely-a-zone) zone no matter what the HTF says. A zone tested over 75% of the way is out. His non-negotiable: daily uptrend + H1 uptrend before buying pullbacks to demand. Do top-down analysis first; do not start on the entry timeframe as a new trader.
Every trade needs logic you can explain. Starting from the entry timeframe is something only experienced traders can get away with; new traders must go top-down.
With high R:R you can take several valid zones in a row: -1, -1, +5 still nets +3%. Even four losses and a fifth winner is about breakeven or +1%.

passages.h: Look of the zone: good or bad, not a score
passages.t: Classic teaching: tight basing + large move away = high quality. He agrees only to an extent - you always want a large move away (the bigger the better) and tight basing is good.

passages.h: Look of the zone: good or bad, not a score
passages.t: Problem: some groups score zones out of 10 (candle count in the base, 3:1 or 4:1 move away) and only trade 8-10/10 zones. That misses the HTF, the intermediate timeframe and the trend.

passages.h: Look of the zone: good or bad, not a score
passages.t: He ranks the look of a zone as just good or bad. The range inside 'good' is wide on purpose because the higher timeframes matter more.

passages.h: Look of the zone: good or bad, not a score
passages.t: Good example: 1-2 candle basing + large move away. A small wick does not matter ('whoopty do').

passages.h: Look of the zone: good or bad, not a score
passages.t: Bad example: fine basing and initial move away, but a 50% indecision candle in the move away -> bad.

passages.h: Look of the zone: good or bad, not a score
passages.t: Never-take example: lots of candles and wicks, a candle wicking right back into the zone - 'barely even a zone'. He would not take it even if every HTF zone was in control (even though price reacted off it).

passages.h: Look of the zone: good or bad, not a score
passages.t: Stair-step basing / big wick = lower quality no matter how many HTF zones stack up (weekly in monthly in six-month). It could still work, but lower odds.

passages.h: Look of the zone: good or bad, not a score
passages.t: You want clean basing and a clean move away (shape for a CP; similar for a peak & valley zone). Extra messy price action inside the base is not ideal, but you cannot always get perfect zones - trade with the higher timeframes.

passages.h: HTF context changes quality without the look changing
passages.t: A 'bad' H4 demand can become a decent, tradable zone if it sits at weekly demand and removed supply.

passages.h: HTF context changes quality without the look changing
passages.t: Trend: an H4 supply in an H4 downtrend is higher odds; an H4 demand in that downtrend is counter-trend and lower odds even if it is the best-looking demand ever.

passages.h: HTF context changes quality without the look changing
passages.t: That counter-trend H4 demand turns from low quality to high quality if it sits inside a weekly demand zone (captions say 'weekly supply in control' at one point - he clearly means the weekly demand he just drew). Without the weekly zone, a random counter-trend H4 demand is low quality.

passages.h: HTF context changes quality without the look changing
passages.t: Conversely, a picture-perfect zone (clean move up, tight base, clean move away) becomes much lower odds if higher-timeframe supply sits above it.

passages.h: HTF context changes quality without the look changing
passages.t: Bottom line: what makes a zone high or low quality is basically the higher timeframes in play - you are stacking the odds.

passages.h: Tests: how many, and how deep
passages.t: A weekly DXY demand: nice rally-base-rally, strong move away, good zone on its first test.

passages.h: Tests: how many, and how deep
passages.t: After price reacted off it once, twice, three times (almost four), the look has not changed but it is now low quality.

passages.h: Tests: how many, and how deep
passages.t: Depth matters: split the zone into 0 / 25 / 50 / 75 / 100% lines. Tests that only went ~25% in make it a 'mid' zone - a deeper pull into it with a decent LTF zone could still be a setup. If a wick tested it over 75% of the way, 'everything I just said goes out the window'.

passages.h: Tests: how many, and how deep
passages.t: Count matters too: 25% deep but tested 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 times is not the same as tested once.

passages.h: Tests: how many, and how deep
passages.t: Factors to weigh: how many times tested, how deep, is it fresh, is it just a reaction off a previous zone. He admits much of this is experience rather than a written rule.

passages.h: Trading a good zone against a HTF zone
passages.t: If a great-looking H4 demand sits right under weekly supply: ignore the zone, OR wait for it to be hit and look for extra confirmation. Price often does give an initial reaction off a LTF zone just before a HTF opposing zone.

passages.h: Trading a good zone against a HTF zone
passages.t: If you trade it anyway: day-trading confirmation, take profit at 2:1 instead of 5:1, and half risk - a quick low-risk scalp. He calls that a great plan.

passages.h: Trading a good zone against a HTF zone
passages.t: A winning trade with no logic behind it is luck - he would not give it a thumbs up. The logic has to make sense.

passages.h: Rules vs subjectivity, and his views
passages.t: You need a set of rules. His non-negotiables: a daily uptrend AND an H1 uptrend, then he buys pullbacks to demand (mirror for shorts).

passages.h: Rules vs subjectivity, and his views
passages.t: The look of zones is where it gets subjective, and some rules cannot be super strict because the market is never exactly the same. Stick with one teacher (it does not have to be him).

passages.h: Rules vs subjectivity, and his views
passages.t: Even retail tools (RSI, support/resistance) would probably work if used only at higher-timeframe zones on the right side; RSI on its own is lagging junk. Order blocks are just supply and demand renamed; markets move only on supply and demand.

passages.h: Rules vs subjectivity, and his views
passages.t: Never start analysis on the entry timeframe if you are new - do top-down first, or a pretty H1 zone will tempt you into ignoring the daily.

passages.h: Overextended trends and embedded zones (GBP/JPY, USD/JPY Q&A)
passages.t: GBP/JPY: weekly, daily, H4 and H1 uptrends - look for longs - but 5 continuation-pattern (rally-base-rally) zones in a row.

passages.h: Overextended trends and embedded zones (GBP/JPY, USD/JPY Q&A)
passages.t: Usually after 2-3 CPs you get one final move and then price rolls over back to a deeper zone (not 100% of the time - it could keep going).

passages.h: Overextended trends and embedded zones (GBP/JPY, USD/JPY Q&A)
passages.t: When overextended, prefer H1 zones embedded inside an H4 demand. If the H4 demand is just a reaction off another demand, it is lower quality but still an area to look for buys.

passages.h: Overextended trends and embedded zones (GBP/JPY, USD/JPY Q&A)
passages.t: Overextended H1 demand: tradable but risk a bit less. Apply full 1-2% only when price pulls back into the daily/deeper demand - the bigger pullback with the trend.

passages.h: Overextended trends and embedded zones (GBP/JPY, USD/JPY Q&A)
passages.t: His biggest trades that month were H1 zones embedded inside H4 demand (USD/JPY: fresh H4 demand after an overextended run, H1 zone inside it, 5:1 with no drawdown).

passages.h: Overextended trends and embedded zones (GBP/JPY, USD/JPY Q&A)
passages.t: With 5:1 R:R you break even winning roughly 17-18% of the time, so you can take the nearer zone and still wait for the deeper one if it fails. Rather wait for a deeper zone than chase price and lose.

passages.h: Macro confirmation (EUR/USD Q&A) and other markets
passages.t: EUR/USD: three-month supply in control and a three-month downtrend; one-month supply too, six-month demand also somewhat in control - 'tricky', but shorts only.

passages.h: Macro confirmation (EUR/USD Q&A) and other markets
passages.t: A daily supply under the three-month supply is itself a confirmation zone - a daily chart can be a confirmation trade - so keep looking for shorts on lower timeframes.

passages.h: Macro confirmation (EUR/USD Q&A) and other markets
passages.t: If that daily zone breaks, that is fine - then look for longs, even with three-month supply in control.

passages.h: Macro confirmation (EUR/USD Q&A) and other markets
passages.t: Ways in: set & forget at the H1 supply above ('very risky'), or confirmation: H1 demand removed, leaving H1 supply. Longs off the H4 demand would be low odds against three-month and daily supply.

passages.h: Macro confirmation (EUR/USD Q&A) and other markets
passages.t: Natural gas: wait for daily supply to be removed, then look for H1 confirmation inside the daily demand.

passages.h: Macro confirmation (EUR/USD Q&A) and other markets
passages.t: USD/CHF: no weekly or daily zone in control -> not trading it. Oil: sideways -> not interested.
Trading is about 50% strategy and 50% applying it time and time again without changing it - not '90% emotions'.
You must be able to take zone 1 (loss), zone 2 (loss), zone 3 (win). At 5:1: -1%, -1%, +5% = +3%. Do not cherry-pick between equally valid zones out of fear of missing out.
He wants to move stops to breakeven quicker - e.g. a trade that went almost 3:1 before stopping him out should have been at BE.

Build your own strategy from his: you might use his H4 zones with a different HTF or only 1:1 targets - but 1:1 needs very high accuracy; it all depends on your testing. Backtest with the replay tool and his tracked zones; tracking zones = tracking the story.

Build a relationship with a few markets; day traders should stick to a couple of pairs (e.g. two pairs plus oil). Swing traders can follow more because stories are easier to remember. Swing trading on the H1 is 'the perfect mix' - decent setups without the stress.
Patience: his results improved drastically when he stopped thinking he must trade every day.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Why he rejects score-based rule books
passages.t: Rule-book example he was taught: count the basing candles (e.g. six; 'six to seven candles is max'), measure the move away (over 4:1), call it 10/10. He says it makes trading too simple; anybody can learn to count candles and measure with the R:R tool.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Why he rejects score-based rule books
passages.t: He compares it to 'wait for the EMA cross and you're short', or '9/10 buy, below 8 buy with less risk, below 7 don't trade'. It is better than random buying and selling, but not enough to be successful.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Why he rejects score-based rule books
passages.t: He would not even call a zone 10/10, because that implies many factors; it is just 'good' (or 'three out of three'). There are basically tradable zones and non-tradable zones.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Why he rejects score-based rule books
passages.t: EUR/USD chart: good, good, good, good, good, bad. The purple zone gets higher odds from the daily supply above (for shorts) than a long against that daily supply.

passages.h: More from the lesson: His own trading notes from the session
passages.t: In June he started adding more H1 entries and got a lot of trades. Win rate 'isn't great', but he stayed profitable by managing stops aggressively and risking less.

passages.h: More from the lesson: His own trading notes from the session
passages.t: Mistake he admits: on EUR/GBP he took a trade at what he calls a dead demand zone. 'It's actually not a trade I would take.'

passages.h: More from the lesson: His own trading notes from the session
passages.t: GBP/JPY: he skipped an H1 zone at about 4 CPs because price was overextended, and regrets it. The embedded H1 zone at 179.719 was large with wicks he didn't love; he was waiting for the deeper zone around 175.545.

passages.h: More from the lesson: His own trading notes from the session
passages.t: EUR/USD: the three-month chart itself looked bullish (green candle, two 50% basing candles), so he admits he could be wrong. He is just reading 'the story': higher-timeframe supply in control means shorting, if anything.

passages.h: More from the lesson: His own trading notes from the session
passages.t: A daily supply could in theory be traded on its own (stop above, TP below), but on a daily you would rather get a lower-timeframe entry.

passages.h: More from the lesson: His own trading notes from the session
passages.t: Many traders never go above the daily, weekly or monthly chart. Looking at macro charts shows how much higher quality a daily zone really is.

passages.h: More from the lesson: His own trading notes from the session
passages.t: Silver: an H4 demand below that price didn't quite reach; he called a nearby zone one he 'would never have taken, very poor quality'. Zones in red on his watchlist mean he is looking for momentum trades.

passages.h: More from the lesson: His own trading notes from the session
passages.t: Week plan by relationship with markets: EUR/USD shorts, silver longs off daily demand, natural gas waiting for daily supply removal, oil sideways (skip), USD/CHF no weekly or daily zone in control (skip).

passages.h: More from the lesson: Retail strategies vs S&D (member Q&A)
passages.t: A member who traded S/R for three years kept getting stopped out. Kevin's explanation: price breaks the S/R level into the real supply or demand and then moves back the other way.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Retail strategies vs S&D (member Q&A)
passages.t: AUD example: a purple daily demand zone that S/R traders saw as support held with barely any drawdown. S/R sellers were stopped out, and their sells were probably the banks' buys.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Retail strategies vs S&D (member Q&A)
passages.t: USD/CAD weekly: an obvious support level with fresh demand below. He expected at least 1.33 and said 'let's say I'm completely wrong, who cares' because of his 5:1 or 3:1 R:R. Emotional experience comes into play only after you have your strategy in place.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Retail strategies vs S&D (member Q&A)
passages.t: Everybody should start with supply and demand. You can add S/R or other tools, but only while trading with the higher timeframes.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Memory, testing and timeframe
passages.t: He can tell you the weekly and daily picture of the major pairs, major indexes, oil, natural gas and gold from memory, because he has built a relationship with those markets. Cross pairs he tends to forget.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Memory, testing and timeframe
passages.t: He finds TradingView's backtesting software poor. He tests by going back over the zones he has tracked. On the H1 he can skip the charts for a couple of hours and not miss a trade.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Memory, testing and timeframe
passages.t: If you are day trading and it's working, stick with it; you can move to swing trading as you get more experienced. It's all fractal; the differences are time and emotional involvement.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Memory, testing and timeframe
passages.t: Copying someone exactly only makes sense for personal friends. Members should take what he does, tweak one thing (e.g. 9 of his 10 rules) and test it.
