How he grades the look of a zone: good (1–2 candle base plus a large move away, as in his 00:43 sketch), bad (an indecision candle in the move away), never (stair-step, wicky basing like the circled AUDJPY base). Quality then comes from the higher timeframes.
The DXY weekly demand 99.571–101.118 split into 0/25/50/75/100% lines. Three to four shallow (~25%) tests leave the look unchanged but turn the zone low quality. A wick past 75% puts it out.

GBPJPY 1h: five continuation demands stacked on an overextended run. Take 1h zones embedded in the 4h demand (178.133–179.404) at reduced risk, and keep full risk for the deeper 4h/daily pullback (about 175.1–175.5).

EURUSD macro confirmation: the daily supply 1.09416–1.10070 sits inside the 3M supply 1.09353–1.14950. Short the 1h supply after the 1h demand 1.08991–1.09151 is removed. If the daily supply breaks, switch to longs.

Trading a zone because it looks like a 10/10 while ignoring HTF, trend and intermediate timeframe. Counting basing candles from a rule book as the whole system. Buying a beautiful demand zone right under weekly supply with full risk and full target. Treating a zone tested many times (or deeply) as fresh. Taking a zone with a 50% indecision candle in the move away.

Buying overextended trends after 4-5 CPs with full risk. Chasing price instead of waiting for the deeper zone. Claiming a lucky win as a good trade without logic. Changing the strategy after two losses / cherry-picking zones. Taking a trade on a dead (already-spent) demand zone.

Believing trading is '90% emotions and 10% skill'. A perfectly emotionally stable trader still fails trading bad patterns. Following signal or podcast-clip 'full-time traders' instead of being patient.

Is the look of the zone at least 'good' (clean base, large move away, no indecision candle in the move away)? Is the zone free of messy stair-step basing and wicks back into the zone? Is there a higher-timeframe zone supporting my direction?

Is there a higher-timeframe opposing zone right above/below? If so, am I using half risk, ~2:1 TP and confirmation - or skipping it? Is the zone with the trend? How many times has the zone been tested, and how deep (under 25%? over 75%)? Is the zone fresh, or just a reaction off a previous zone?

Is the market overextended (several CPs in a row)? If so, am I reducing risk or waiting for an embedded zone in a deeper HTF zone? Can I explain the logic of this trade? Have I checked the macro charts (monthly/3M/6M) above my daily zone? Is this zone actually spent (a dead zone), even if it still looks fine?

“The quality of the zone changed without the look of the zone changing.” “It's all about the higher timeframes.” “You got lucky in my opinion.” “I would rather wait for that than chase price and lose.” “There's basically tradable zones and non-tradable zones.”

“It's 50% strategy and 50% of just applying that strategy time and time again and not changing it.” “The markets function based on supply and demand, nothing else.” “All this price action is a story.”
Rejects scoring zones out of 10; grades the look as only good or bad. A 50% indecision candle in the move away makes a zone bad. Stair-step basing = lower quality regardless of HTF stacking.
Test-depth grid 0/25/50/75/100%: ~25% tested = mid quality, over 75% = out; number of tests also counts.
Good zone under opposing HTF zone: half risk, TP 2:1 instead of 5:1, day-trading confirmation.

After 2-3 continuation patterns, expect one final move then a roll-over; reduce risk when overextended, full risk at the deeper daily zone. Embedded H1 zones inside H4 demand as his best trades. A daily zone under a three-month zone counts as a confirmation zone. His non-negotiable: daily uptrend + H1 uptrend before buying pullbacks. Trading is ~50% strategy / 50% consistent execution; -1, -1, +5 = +3% example.
Wants to move to breakeven sooner (e.g. near 3:1). Order blocks = S&D renamed; indicators only work at HTF zones.

A zone is strong because of the big picture around it, not its looks. Two lemonade stands look exactly the same. One sits next to a busy park on a hot day. The other sits on an empty road. Same stand, but only one will sell lots of lemonade. A zone is the same: where it sits on the bigger charts decides how good it is. And if thirsty kids already bought most of the lemonade, there is not much left for the next visit.
A house: the neighborhood (higher timeframes, trend) matters more than the paint (how pretty the zone looks).

Grade the look of a zone simply: good or bad. No score out of 10. Higher timeframes, trend and test history decide if a zone is high or low quality. Every test uses up the zone. A test deeper than 75% means the zone is out.

passages.h: Step: Look first: good or bad?
passages.t: Here is a drop, two small basing candles, then one big fast candle up. Tight basing plus a large move away is a good-looking zone. Kevin does not score it 8 or 10 out of 10. It is just "good".
Wrap the basing candles. The distal line goes on the lowest wick. The proximal line sits on top of the basing bodies.

passages.h: Step: The big picture changes quality
passages.t: Now we zoom out. This zone sits inside a weekly demand and the trend is up. The zone did not change its look, but its quality went up. If weekly supply sat right above it instead, the same pretty zone would be low odds.

passages.h: Step: Split the zone into depth lines
passages.t: Cut the zone into 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100% lines. The first pullback only dipped in a little. A shallow test leaves the zone in decent shape.

passages.h: Step: Count the tests, check the depth
passages.t: Price came back a second time, then a third time. The third wick went past the 75% line. Kevin says once a test goes over 75% of the way in, the zone is out. The look never changed, but now it is low quality.
The tired zone broke. That is why many tests and deep tests matter. Each visit uses up the orders sitting there.

How does Kevin grade the LOOK of a zone? - Only good or bad. No score out of 10. What mostly decides zone quality? - The higher timeframes in play, the trend, and the test history. What does a 50% indecision candle in the move away do? - It makes the zone bad. A test went past 75% of the zone. Status? - The zone is out.

Good zone right under HTF supply: how to trade it? - Skip it, or confirmation + half risk + about 2:1 target. Kevin's non-negotiable before buying pullbacks? - A daily uptrend AND an H1 uptrend. Breakeven win rate at 5:1? - About 17-18%.
Overextended after many CPs: how to risk? - Risk less on near zones; full risk at the deeper daily demand.

A short chart walkthrough of how Kevin draws a trendline: it needs a higher high (or lower low) and an obvious peak and valley, and it must be adjusted when it cuts through candles after a new high. He also separates trendlines from momentum lines and explains when a wick is not enough to count as a new valley.

No higher high (or lower low) = no trendline. Anchor only to an obvious peak and an obvious valley. A trendline must not cut through candles once a new high is made - adjust it. A lone wick is not a new valley; adjust the line rather than draw a new one.
A higher high is required (lower low for a downtrend). The high must be broken after the peak.

If price rallies from the valley and just barely misses the previous high, then drops, you cannot draw a trendline - no higher high. The higher high is only one requirement - 'there's many other things'.
The trendline anchors to an obvious peak and an obvious valley, with a clear distance between them. A shallow dip that is 'not really that obvious' is not a valley.
Price stepping up with small shallow pullbacks is a momentum line, not a trendline - technically price went up and down, but it is not deep enough.
A first trendline can be drawn from the valley once the high is broken. If the line cuts through candles, that is fine at first - until price makes another new high.

Once a new high is made and the line cuts through candles, re-anchor it so it no longer cuts through candles. The two touch points on his chart are then the adjusted ones, not the original ones - this is why members get confused by his lines. If price cuts through candles again, the trendline is removed and must be updated.

He does not like calling a single wick a new low / peak-and-valley. If there were real price action down there (several candles forming a clear new valley and new peak), draw the new trendline from the most recent valley.
If it is just a 'weird wick' without real price action, simply adjust the existing line instead of starting a new one.
Trendlines are 'not the easiest thing ever' - there are rules and nuance; the Sunday meetings cover them in more depth.

00:00 SPX500USD 1h (OANDA, 28 Aug 2025): 1h demand 6383.4–6399.2 under a vertical 22 Aug rally; the supply at ≈6475–6482 is marked removed (green up-arrow). 00:30 Horizontal line at the previous high (≈6480) to show the higher-high requirement.
00:36–00:42 He draws a V from the peak to the 26 Aug valley and back, then the case where price misses the high and drops straight into the 1h demand: no trendline.
00:54 The 22 Aug valley (≈6349–6355) to ≈6480 impulse: the first anchor is the valley that started the move.

01:00–01:30 He scrolls back to 7–20 Aug: rising trendline from the 7 Aug valley through the 12 Aug valley after the ≈6410 peak broke, later broken to the downside; a falling trendline from the 15 Aug peak. 01:42 First 22–28 Aug trendline: 22 Aug low → 26 Aug valley. 02:06–02:30 Arrows show the 27 Aug candles cutting through that line after the new high.

03:12 He highlights the 27 Aug lower wick (≈6452): a lone wick, not a new valley. 03:30–03:48 He re-anchors the line from the 22 Aug low to the tip of that wick and extends it. The 26 Aug valley is no longer a touch point.
The chart is SPX500USD (S&P 500 CFD) 1h on OANDA, 28 Aug 2025, built around a 1h demand 6383.4–6399.2. The notes give no instrument or levels.

The adjusted trendline is anchored at the 22 Aug valley (≈6349) and the tip of the 27 Aug wick (≈6452). The original second touch, the 26 Aug valley (≈6420), is no longer on the line. This is the concrete case behind "the two touch points are the adjusted ones".
In this case, "adjust instead of drawing a new line from the wick" means pivoting the existing line down to the wick tip from the same first valley. The first anchor does not change.

The "missed the high" example is drawn as price rallying back from the 26 Aug valley to just below the ≈6480 high, then dropping straight into the 1h demand. A horizontal line at the previous high is his reference for the higher-high test.

passages.h: Chart: [00:00] SPX500USD 1h (OANDA, 28 Aug 2025). 1h demand 6383.4–6399.2 at the base of a vertical 22 Aug rally. Supply ≈6475–6482 at the top with a green up-arrow (removed). An old falling trendline on the left.
passages.t: The whole lesson is on this one S&P 500 1h chart, with an earlier stretch of the same chart.

passages.h: Chart: [00:30] Same chart: he draws a horizontal line at the previous high (≈6480, top of the 22–23 Aug impulse) and an arrow to where price later broke above it.
passages.t: First requirement: a higher high. The peak has to be broken after the valley.

passages.h: Chart: [00:36] A V drawn from the ≈6480 peak down to the 26 Aug valley (≈6418) and back up to the high.
passages.t: Obvious peak, obvious valley, clear distance between them.

passages.h: Chart: [00:42] He extends the V: price rallies back to just under the high and then an arrow runs straight down into the 1h demand 6383.4–6399.2.
passages.t: If price misses the previous high and drops, there is no higher high, so no trendline can be drawn.

passages.h: Chart: [00:54] Line from the 22 Aug low (≈6355) straight up to the ≈6480 peak: the impulse that created the demand.
passages.t: The valley at the start of the impulse is the first anchor.

passages.h: Chart: [01:00] Earlier on the same chart (7–20 Aug): a long rising trendline from the 7 Aug low, a falling trendline from the 15 Aug peak (≈6485), and price later breaking below the rising line.
passages.t: A second example of a clean uptrend line with obvious valleys.

passages.h: Chart: [01:18] Zoomed: a leg drawn from the 7 Aug valley (≈6315) to the 11 Aug peak (≈6410).
passages.t: Obvious valley → obvious peak.

passages.h: Chart: [01:24] Arrow up to the 12 Aug valley (≈6372) sitting on the rising trendline. The next rally takes out the ≈6410 peak.
passages.t: The second anchor is the next obvious valley, and it only counts once the peak is broken (higher high).

passages.h: Chart: [01:42] Back on 22–28 Aug: first trendline from the 22 Aug low (≈6349) through the 26 Aug valley (≈6420), extended up to 27 Aug.
passages.t: First line: valley-to-valley once the ≈6480 high broke.

passages.h: Chart: [02:12] Arrows: one points to where the 27 Aug candles cut through the first line, one back to the 26 Aug valley touch.
passages.t: After a new high, a line that cuts through candles is no longer valid as drawn.

passages.h: Chart: [02:30] A second line projected from below to the 27 Aug dip (≈6455) shows where the drop pierced the first trendline.
passages.t: The 27 Aug sell-off goes through the line, so the line has to change.

passages.h: Chart: [03:12] He highlights the long lower wick on 27 Aug (to ≈6452). It is a single wick, with no cluster of candles forming a new valley.
passages.t: A "weird wick" like this is not a new valley.

passages.h: Chart: [03:30] Adjusted trendline: still anchored at the 22 Aug low (≈6349), now re-anchored to the tip of the 27 Aug wick and extended into September.
passages.t: He adjusts the existing line to the wick rather than starting a new trendline from it. The 26 Aug valley no longer touches the line, which is why his lines can look "wrong" to members.

passages.h: Chart: [03:48] Final view: the adjusted line runs under every candle from 22 Aug to now (≈6487), clear of the 26 Aug valley and touching only the 27 Aug wick.
passages.t: If price cuts through this line again, the trendline is removed and has to be redrawn.
Higher-high requirement (00:30–00:42). The line from the valley is valid only once price breaks the previous high. A rally that just misses it and drops to demand gives no trendline.
SPX500USD 1h, 22–28 Aug 2025. First line: 22 Aug low → 26 Aug valley. The 27 Aug wick cuts through it after the new high, so he re-anchors to the wick tip. The 26 Aug valley is now off the line.
A trendline needs an obvious peak and an obvious valley with real depth. Shallow step-ups make a momentum line, not a trendline.

Drawing a trendline when price narrowly missed the previous high. Treating a momentum line (shallow step-ups) as a trendline. Anchoring to an unobvious dip. Leaving a trendline that cuts through candles after a new high. Treating a single wick as a new valley.

Did price make a higher high (or lower low) past the peak? Are both the peak and the valley obvious? Is this a real trendline, not a momentum line? Does my line cut through any candles after the latest new high? Is my latest 'valley' real price action, or just a wick?

“This is a momentum line.” “It's not the easiest thing ever. There are some rules to it and there is some nuance to it as well.” “The higher high is one thing that we need as far as how to draw a trend line.”
Trendline needs an obvious peak and obvious valley with real depth; the PDFs only say 'blatantly obvious trendline'. Momentum line vs trendline distinction.
Re-anchor the line once it cuts through candles after a new high; cutting through again removes it. A lone wick is not a new valley - adjust instead of redrawing from it.

A real trendline needs a clear hill, a clear dip, then a new higher hill. Imagine climbing stairs on a big hill. You go up to a bump, walk down into a deep dip, then climb past the first bump. Now you can lay a stick along the bottoms of your path. Tiny wobbles on flat steps do not count. And if your stick pokes through the ground, you move it so it rests on top.
A handrail on a staircase: it rests on the lowest points and never goes through a step.
Uptrend line = obvious peak, obvious valley, then a higher high (mirror for downtrends). Shallow little step-ups make a momentum line, not a trendline.
After a new high, the line must not cut through candles: re-anchor it. A lone wick is not a new valley.
Price climbs and makes a clear top. This is the peak. It must be easy to see, not a tiny bump.
Then price falls into a clear, deep dip. Everyone can see it. That is the valley. A shallow dip would not count.

passages.h: Step: Wait for the higher high, then draw
passages.t: Price breaks above the peak. That is the higher high we need. Now draw the line from the low through the valley. It rests under the candles and cuts none of them.

passages.h: Step: The line cuts a candle
passages.t: Price dips and pokes through the line. That is okay for now, because no new high has formed yet. The candle still touches the line, so it is not a removal.
Price makes a new high. Now the line must not cut candles anymore, so we move it to the new low point. This is why Kevin's touch points can look different from the first ones.
Here price steps up with tiny, shallow pullbacks. Technically it went up and down, but the dips are not deep enough. Kevin calls this a momentum line, not a trendline.

Three things an uptrend line needs? - Obvious peak, obvious valley, then a higher high. Price just misses the old high and drops. Trendline? - No. No higher high = no trendline. Shallow step-ups with tiny dips are called? - A momentum line, not a trendline. Line cuts candles after a NEW high. What now? - Re-anchor it so it cuts no candles. Is a lone wick a new valley? - No. Adjust the existing line instead.
Line cuts candles again after adjusting? - It is removed and must be updated.

Confirmation trading means waiting for price to contact a higher-timeframe zone, then dropping to the entry timeframe and waiting for opposing zones and/or a trendline to be removed before entering on a pullback (or a breakout).

He covers the two entry methods, which timeframe pairs to use, when confirmation is worth it (counter-trend, around trendlines, large or doubtful zones, overextended price), plus Q&A on wick removal, stacked zones, targets, adding to winners and homework reviews.

Price must contact the HTF zone before you look for confirmation on the entry timeframe. Confirmation = an opposing zone and/or opposing trendline removed on the entry timeframe. Breakout method only with a proper basing structure to put the stop under.
The deeper you refine below the zone timeframe, the bigger the R:R target must be (hold toward the opposing HTF zone).

Use confirmation for counter-trend trades, zones around trendlines, oversized zones and zones you don't trust. Only add to a trade on a clean new zone that meets your criteria. Test everything before trusting your R:R.
If you don't trust a zone or think it is questionable, always use confirmation, then track the data with screenshots to decide later whether to ignore such zones or just trust the R:R.
Mark the HTF zone first (his example: H1 demand). Then go to the entry timeframe (example: 5m) and wait. Step 1: price must come down and contact the HTF zone.

Step 2: on the entry timeframe, look for opposing zones to be removed - e.g. a new demand zone that removes the opposing supply zones above it. That removal is the confirmation. Removing a downward trendline also counts as confirmation (see trendline section). He uses 'HTF' as shorthand for higher timeframe on his charts.
Pullback method (his personal choice): after the zone(s)/trendline are removed, wait for price to pull back to the new entry-timeframe demand and buy there with a limit order.

Breakout method: if there is a clear basing structure that looks like demand on the way up, place a buy order above the supply zone (trade the breakout), stop below that basing structure. Needs a proper zone/structure to put the stop under.
Why breakout exists: sometimes price pushes up, confirms, only makes a minor pullback and runs to TP without filling the pullback order.
No free lunch: in his example to the same target (1.206) the breakout gave roughly 1.5R while the pullback gave roughly 10R.
Trade-off in his opinion: pullback = bigger R:R, tighter stop, stopped out more, lower win rate; breakout = higher win rate, smaller R:R. Test which fits your personality.
He is fine losing more trades than he wins and still being profitable - that is why he uses the pullback method.
These are the only two confirmation methods he knows. He does not use candlestick patterns (hammers etc.) and will not teach what he does not know.
First decide the timeframe you want to trade and the one you enter on - it must fit your personality AND your schedule.
1m entries = checking charts constantly, high stress. 1H entries = less stress, fewer trades. 4H/daily = a lot of patience.
His own plan: enters on the 1H inside daily zones. When he does enter on a 4H he refines into a 1H.
Example pairing: 5m entry with 1H as the HTF. The chart is a guide, not 'the Bible' - you can switch it up (e.g. 5m confirmation in a 4H zone), but expect more losses.

Extreme example: 1m confirmation in a daily zone = a ton of losses, but huge R:R. If you refine that far you must hold as long as possible, ideally to the next opposing daily zone (20:1-type trades are possible).
Rule of thumb from him: the lower your refinement vs the zone timeframe, the higher your R:R needs to be.
He would not go 1m all the way to daily (too risky). 1m to 1H is fine; 1m to 4H is more risky but doable.
'Lower timeframe' is relative: the entry timeframe can be a daily or 4H chart. A daily zone inside a 6-month/weekly demand is itself daily confirmation.
He offered to help members pick timeframes by private message; a trading-plan-by-schedule Zoom session exists that he plans to repost.
You can always use confirmation, never use it, or use it sometimes - no right or wrong; it depends on your testing. He trades both S&F and confirmation.
First question before a 1H trade: what is the HTF of the 1H? The daily. Check the daily trend.
HTF trend up (clear highs, obvious trendline) = longs are the highest-odds thing; a 1H demand pullback there is a valid set & forget.
Overextended price: does not mean it will drop, but if you hesitate you can wait for confirmation instead of S&F.
Counter-trend (relative to your HTF) = confirmation is best used / recommended. Example: weekly supply against a strong daily uptrend on GBP - look for extra confirmation on the 4H.
With the HTF trend: confirmation is not needed as much; a 1H demand inside daily demand in a daily uptrend can be a S&F.
Zone sitting around a trendline: confirmation is always best because of stop hunts that happen around trendlines.
Zone too large (e.g. natural gas daily zone inside macro demand): refine the entry with confirmation instead of taking the whole zone.

If you do not trust the zone, it looks questionable, or the ITF trend is down but multiple sequence analysis says that downtrend may be ending (e.g. 4H supply under 6-month demand in control) - only take a confirmation trade off it.
He was taught that counter-trend trades need confirmation on the intermediate timeframe (e.g. 4H). His view now: with a proper, tested R:R you don't really need that.
The ultimate confirmation: a supply zone AND a downward trendline both removed. Even better if there is another supply zone also removed.

If price breaks the downward trendline but respects (does not remove) the supply zone, a quality demand zone that meets your criteria is still a trade in his opinion - but it is a WEAKER confirmation (trend went from down to sideways).
He has no math on that case. Ideas to test: risk less (half or a quarter of a percent) or keep 1% but take profit earlier.
No two profitable S&D traders trade exactly the same - test your own strategy and management.

passages.h: Q&A: is a zone removed by a wick?
passages.t: A small body with a huge wick through the zone = he does NOT call it removed; it looks like an emotional wick. A big body with a proportionately large wick = he would probably call it removed.

passages.h: Q&A: is a zone removed by a wick?
passages.t: Best case: a normal-looking candle with a normal wick closing through - that is clearly removed.

passages.h: Q&A: is a zone removed by a wick?
passages.t: The wick should be proportionate to the body. He admits this is pattern recognition, hard to explain exactly.

passages.h: Q&A: stacked zones (level on top of level)
passages.t: After a removal you may get two or three demand zones stacked (e.g. basing before the big move AND the origin of the whole move lower down). He has no data on which works more often; from experience it feels close to 50/50.

passages.h: Q&A: stacked zones (level on top of level)
passages.t: Options: test which one to take; take the extreme one only and accept missing fills; or take all of them and trust the R:R.

passages.h: Q&A: stacked zones (level on top of level)
passages.t: Natural gas reel example: he took all three zones, only the bottom one worked, and he still made a lot because of R:R.

passages.h: Q&A: stacked zones (level on top of level)
passages.t: With three zones he would probably take all three, or the top or bottom one, and ignore the middle one.

passages.h: Q&A: stacked zones (level on top of level)
passages.t: He prefers to take all and leave the emotional decision out, as long as the R:R makes sense. If the far TP is only justified from the extreme zone, take only the extreme one and accept missed trades.
Targets: opposing zones; also notice selling areas (bearish candles/basing that are not supply) for a first TP, then the high.
After a sharp move it is hard to place a target based on a zone - you can bump the stop instead.

What he does now: set a 5:1 TP, then adapt per trade. If stop is at breakeven, price breaks supply and a new demand forms before 5:1, he may remove the TP (set it far away) and trail the stop below each new zone.
If price runs in one big candle with nothing to put a stop under, he just lets the 5:1 TP get hit.
Trading rules matter, but not every trade goes exactly to plan - each situation is a bit different.

His plan: S&F trades and confirmation trades, generally inside daily zones. Example: take a 1H S&F in a daily demand; price breaks supply and forms new demand. He moves the S&F stop to below the new demand and takes a confirmation trade there with its stop in the same place. Result: likely around breakeven, or two big winners targeting the opposing daily supply.
He only adds if there is a clean new zone that meets his criteria. Sometimes he will not add if he does not think price is going all the way (does not want two positions).
Journal: he logs these as TWO separate trades. A split-risk trade across two pairs (e.g. EURJPY and ZARJPY shorts) is logged as ONE trade.
Test everything: backtest, paper trade, or live trade risking a super small amount. Without testing you won't trust your R:R.

He is collecting data to see which setup is more profitable; e.g. if S&F made 6% and confirmation 2% in a year, he might risk 2% on S&F and keep confirmation risk the same. Increase risk on the more profitable strategy. Nobody has it all figured out; keep improving.

Multiple sequence analysis finds the best HTF zones for confirmation: e.g. 6-month demand -> daily confirmation -> 1H confirmation inside the daily. Stacking this way raises odds AND confidence (fixes hesitation to pull the trigger).
When he only used 15m inside 4H zones he was around breakeven; opening up to higher timeframes changed that.
Homework (MSA): daily supply -> 1H supply -> 5m supply at the extreme gave ~10:1+; refining that deep requires a bigger target (opposing zone) or moving stops.
Homework (zone drawing): he would draw the supply using the wick to leave a little space; supply's move away should be fast candles. 50% candle indicators make basing more obvious.
Homework (trend trading): weekly demand with 4H confirmation in a weekly uptrend = tradable, with the trend.

Homework (GBPUSD daily/1H): valid with the trend only if the pullback comes before price reaches/breaks the trendline; if it takes a long time and breaks the trendline it is no longer a trend trade and he would ignore the zone.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Q&A: EUR/USD daily supply short (targets)
passages.t: A member asked about shorting EUR/USD off daily supply once the H1 demand breaks. Kevin is personally not interested: weekly momentum is up and the daily trend is up, so a 1H supply short is against both. Confirmation is needed and he wouldn't short until he gets it.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Q&A: EUR/USD daily supply short (targets)
passages.t: Targets for that short: the nearby area, or something like 1.11 for a big move. Your target could also be a fixed 2:1 or 3:1 based on what your journal and testing show.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Q&A: EUR/USD daily supply short (targets)
passages.t: If there were an opposing zone close by, you could see your target clearly. After a sharp move it is hard to set one, so you can bump your stop instead. 'There's not one right way.'

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details
passages.t: In the H1/5m teaching example, he says you wouldn't actually take 1H confirmation there, because no daily zone was in control. He teaches it anyway because 'chart work is chart work': it works on any timeframe.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details
passages.t: Stacked zones: a member said price often breaks the top zone and comes back to the deeper one. Kevin has seen all three work, and he used to like the ones at the trendline.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details
passages.t: With confirmation you will miss some trades and have to be okay with that. That is why he uses both S&F and confirmation.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details
passages.t: His results are slightly better with set & forget, which you want to trade with the trend because it is the highest-odds thing to do.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details
passages.t: He finds TradingView's backtesting tool glitchy and laggy, and hard to use without his four-chart layout.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details
passages.t: Natural gas: six-month demand in control (weekly too), so the daily zone is daily confirmation and 'very likely to work'.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details
passages.t: When he only traded 15m inside 4H supply zones he was breakeven, 'winning small'. Opening up to the higher timeframes changed that.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details
passages.t: Hesitation to pull the trigger is really not trusting your process, plan or R:R. Using multiple sequence analysis builds that trust.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details
passages.t: Gold homework (daily -> 1H -> 5m): the 1H supply's move away wasn't great. The basing was identified well; he would draw it to the wick to leave a little space.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details
passages.t: GBP/USD homework: a slow pullback that reaches the trendline is 'very low odds' to even take place.

This is for an H4 demand bought against a daily and weekly downtrend, where he says day-trading confirmation is the best option.

US30 homework (HTF 4H, ETF 15m): Kevin answered "yes, as a set and forget". An H4 uptrend is the best and least risky case. If the H4 is downtrending, it is still tradable but riskier, with aggressive management.

passages.h: Chart: [00:33] EURUSD 1h (OANDA): he draws a green higher-timeframe demand box under the rally and opens the text tool to label it.
passages.t: Step one of confirmation: mark the HTF zone first. In his example it is a 1H demand. He labels zones as "HTF" for higher timeframe on his charts.

passages.h: Chart: [10:44] His hand-drawn 5m sketch on EURUSD: price falls from a peak into the green HTF demand at the bottom, turns up in a V, forms a small green 5m demand, and an arrow points up through two salmon 5m supply zones.
passages.t: Step 1: price must contact the HTF zone. Step 2: the new 5m demand removes the opposing 5m supplies above it. That removal is the confirmation.

passages.h: Chart: [10:44] His hand-drawn 5m sketch on EURUSD: price falls from a peak into the green HTF demand at the bottom, turns up in a V, forms a small green 5m demand, and an arrow points up through two salmon 5m supply zones.
passages.t: Pullback method: buy the new 5m demand with a limit. Breakout method: buy above the supply with the stop under the basing.

passages.h: Chart: [06:36] "Timeframes To Trade - Use these timeframe combinations". Entry / Higher / Higher +1: 1m/15m/4H, 5m/1H/1D, 15m/4H/1W, 1H/1D/1M, 4H/1W/3M, 1D/1M/6M.
passages.t: Pick the entry timeframe that fits your personality and schedule, then read the higher and curve timeframes across the row. His own row is 1H entries inside daily zones. He calls the chart a guide, not "the Bible".

passages.t: He uses this 1h demand as the live version of the sketch: a 1H zone with a lower timeframe for confirmation.

passages.h: Chart: [13:29] GBPUSD weekly: price is pushing into the weekly supply (1.29736), above weekly demands 1.23081–1.25087 and 1.11468–1.16084, after breaking a falling trendline.
passages.t: Counter-trend case: a weekly supply against a strong daily uptrend. Look for extra confirmation on the 4H rather than a set & forget.

passages.t: The member's question was about shorting this daily supply. The weekly momentum and daily trend are both up, so he is not interested without confirmation.

passages.t: Targets: the nearby area, about 1.11 for a big move, or a fixed 2:1–3:1 from your own testing.

Daily: supplies 1.11926–1.12744 and 1.13055–1.13909, demand 1.08336–1.08792. 1h: supply 1.12770–1.12940, demand 1.11807–1.11962, rising trendline.
passages.t: Price is inside the daily supply while every trend arrow points up. That is why a 1H short here would be against both the weekly momentum and the daily trend.

passages.h: Chart: [39:08] EURUSD 1h close-up: demand 1.11803–1.11962 at the base of the last leg up. Price is chopping above it near 1.122.
passages.t: The 1H demand has to break before any short idea off the daily supply even starts.

passages.t: For supply, the distal is the top of the highest wick, snapped with TradingView's magnet. The same channel shows members labelling their charts MTA / HTF / ETF.

passages.h: Chart: [49:04] #homework: "US30, HTF is 4H, ETF 15 min, is it valid to enter buy trade here?" Kevin: "It would be yes, as a set and forget. The H4 trending up would be the best scenario and less riskier." Then: "If the H4 is downtrending? You could still take the trade, it's just more risky at that point. And you should be aggressive with your trade management."
passages.t: A with-trend HTF makes a set & forget fine. Against the HTF trend you can still trade it, but manage it aggressively.

passages.h: Chart: [49:07] #homework: "If H4 is having uptrend but Daily and weekly are having downtrend, can we enter buy from H4 demand level?" Kevin: "I would only really say using day trading confirmation is the best thing to in that situation… extra confirmation is needed." "Aggressive" means "move your stops to breakeven soonest. And have a TP that isn't asking too much based on the overall downtrend."
passages.t: Counter-trend relative to the bigger picture means use confirmation, not set & forget. Aggressive management is defined on screen: breakeven sooner and a modest TP.

passages.t: Daily supply, then a 1H supply, then a 5m supply at the extreme. Refined this far, it gives about 10:1 or more. A refine that deep needs a bigger target (the opposing zone) or moved stops.

passages.h: Chart: [51:42] The same homework's "MTA- D1" chart: XAUUSD daily supplies 1950.420–1967.920 (price inside), 1970.348–1985.390 and 2035.230–2075.282.
passages.t: The daily supply is the macro zone in control for the gold short idea.

passages.t: He says the 1H zone's move away wasn't great, but the basing was identified well. He would draw it to the wick to leave a little space.

passages.t: Weekly demand in a weekly uptrend: a 4H confirmation off it is tradable and with the trend.

passages.h: Chart: [52:38] The same homework on USDCAD 4h: supplies 1.33651–1.33870 and 1.32843–1.32997, a red down-arrow, a broken rising trendline, and a 4h demand around 1.3159–1.3174. Kevin draws a blue "V": dip into the demand, then rally.
passages.t: The member asked whether the zone is tradable when the 4h (the entry timeframe) is not in an uptrend. Kevin's blue path shows the pullback into the 4h demand he expects to work, because the weekly trend is up.

passages.h: Chart: [53:24] Homework Lesson 8, GBPUSD 1h (HTF D1, ETF H1, both in uptrend): a large demand 1.27504–1.28684 with a yellow entry zone in its lower part, a deeper demand from 1.25858 on a rising trendline, and a black box around the latest high.
passages.t: Valid with the trend only if the pullback comes before price reaches or breaks the trendline. A slow pullback that reaches the trendline is "very low odds" to even take place.

His 5m confirmation sketch: (1) price contacts the 1H demand; (2) a new 5m demand removes the opposing 5m supplies and the downtrend line. Pullback entry at the new demand (his choice, about 10R) or breakout entry above the supply with the stop under the basing (about 1.5R).
The "Timeframes To Trade" slide he shows twice: entry, higher and higher+1 timeframe for each style. His own plan is the 1H → 1D → 1M row.

The gold homework stack: a 5m supply inside a 1H supply inside the daily supply 1950.420–1967.920, plus his drawing rule from #homework: attach the supply distal to the top of the wick with the magnet tool.

Calling a zone removed by a huge emotional wick with a small body. Refining to a very low timeframe and then taking a small target. Going from 1m straight to daily zones (too far). Picking timeframes that don't fit your schedule (1m entries without screen time).

Not accepting missed trades when waiting for confirmation or taking only the extreme zone. Trading counter-trend zones without confirmation. Not testing - then not trusting your R:R and hesitating to pull the trigger. Taking 1H confirmation when no daily zone is in control. Asking which timeframe a setup was on. Price action is price action on every timeframe.

Has price actually contacted the HTF zone? Has an opposing zone and/or trendline been removed on the entry timeframe? Was the removal a real candle (not just an emotional wick)? Is this trade counter to the HTF trend? If yes, am I waiting for confirmation? Is the zone near a trendline, oversized or doubtful? If yes, am I using confirmation?

Does my timeframe pair fit my schedule, and is it not too far apart (e.g. not 1m into daily)? If refining very deep, is my target toward the opposing HTF zone? Pullback or breakout - is there a basing structure for the breakout stop? If adding on, is the new zone clean and does it meet my criteria? Is there a daily zone in control before I look for 1H confirmation?
Am I shorting against a weekly momentum and daily uptrend? If so, has confirmation actually happened?
“Remember, there's no free lunch.” “Confirmation is best used when trading counter trend.” “Price action is price action.”

“If you ever meet a trader that says I've got it all figured out, they're probably full of it.” “Chart work is chart work.” “You will miss some trades on confirmation. You have to be okay with that.” “With my strategy, I'm gonna lose more than I win and it's gonna work out.”
Pullback vs breakout trade-off with numbers (~1.5R vs ~10R to the same target) and his view on win rate.
Lower refinement = higher R:R needed; 1m-to-daily too far, 1m-to-1H fine, 1m-to-4H risky but doable.
When to use confirmation: counter-trend, around trendlines (stop hunts), oversized zones, overextended price, zones you don't trust.
Taught to confirm counter-trend on the intermediate timeframe - he says with tested R:R it is not needed. Wick-vs-body rule for deciding whether a zone is removed.

Trendline broken but supply respected = weaker confirmation; consider smaller risk or earlier TP. Stacked zones: no data, ~50/50, take all / extreme only / skip the middle one. His 5:1 default TP, then removing TP and trailing below new zones. Adding to a S&F with a confirmation trade; journaling as two trades vs split-risk as one. Increase risk on whichever setup your data shows is more profitable.
'Lower timeframe' is relative - a daily zone can itself be confirmation off a 6-month zone.

Wait at the big zone until the small chart proves buyers took over. You want to cross the road at the crossing. Reaching the crossing is not enough. You wait until the cars stop and the light turns green. On a chart, the crossing is the big zone. The green light is when buyers break the sellers' wall and the down line. Then you cross, calmly, on the small pullback.
A crossing (higher-timeframe zone) plus a green light (opposing zone or trendline removed on the entry timeframe).
Step 1: price contacts the higher-timeframe zone. Step 2: on the entry timeframe, an opposing zone and/or trendline gets removed.
Enter by pullback (bigger R:R, lower win rate) or breakout (higher win rate, smaller R:R).
Use confirmation for counter-trend trades, zones near trendlines, oversized zones and zones you do not trust.
First mark the HTF zone. Here it is an H1 demand: basing, then a big move away.
Price falls back and touches the H1 demand. Contact is step 1. We still do not buy. Now we drop to the entry timeframe and wait.
On the way down, sellers left a small supply zone and a downtrend line. These are the walls that must break for a long.

A big candle closes above the supply and through the downtrend line. Both are removed. Kevin calls supply plus trendline removed the ultimate confirmation. The basing before that candle is our new demand.
Place a buy limit at the new demand's proximal line. Stop below its distal. Target 5:1 or the next opposing zone. Price pulls back, fills, and runs.

Breakout method: a buy stop just above the supply, stop below the basing. It fills more often, but to the same target the R:R is much smaller. Kevin's example: about 1.5R breakout versus about 10R pullback. No free lunch.

Confirmation trading: step 1? - Price must contact the higher-timeframe zone. Confirmation trading: step 2? - On the entry timeframe, an opposing zone and/or trendline is removed. Kevin's ultimate confirmation? - A supply zone AND a downward trendline both removed.
Pullback vs breakout? - Pullback: bigger R:R, lower win rate. Breakout: higher win rate, smaller R:R.
When is confirmation best used? - Counter-trend, near trendlines, oversized zones, zones you do not trust.
Deeper refinement means what for the target? - A bigger R:R target (hold toward the opposing HTF zone). Huge wick, small body through a zone: removed? - No. That is an emotional wick.
Trendline broken but supply respected? - Weaker confirmation: test smaller risk or earlier TP.

A Sunday session on what is and is NOT a supply and demand zone: everything on a chart is supply and demand, but zone trading needs structure - basing, a strong move away, and proximal/distal lines drawn from the wicks, marked before the fact.
He also explains why he avoids zones that sit on trendlines or old support/resistance (trading against retail, explained with poker), and rants on testing, journaling, drawdowns and fake gurus.

A zone needs basing plus a strong move away; no structure = no zone. Draw from the wicks (distal at the extreme wick of the basing); never cut through candles. Draw zones before the fact - not because price reacted there. If a zone is clearly broken, take the loss and move on; don't keep trading it.
Be cautious of zones sitting on trendlines or obvious old S/R; prefer the zone below/beyond where retail stops sit. Once you have a working system, stick with it for at least six months.
Be aware of obvious retail levels (S/R and trendlines) and adjust. These are the only two times he looks for 'retail things'.

passages.h: Supply and demand vs supply and demand ZONE trading
passages.t: Essentially everything is supply and demand (a green candle is demand, a red one supply) - but that is not a zone.

passages.h: Supply and demand vs supply and demand ZONE trading
passages.t: He trades supply and demand ZONES; pointing at 'supply up here, demand down here' is not the methodology.

passages.h: Supply and demand vs supply and demand ZONE trading
passages.t: A real zone has structure: rally-base-drop (supply) or drop-base-rally (demand), a large quick move away, and a specific start point.

passages.h: Supply and demand vs supply and demand ZONE trading
passages.t: Every zone is basing plus a move up (demand) or move down (supply); wrap the lines around the basing, extend them, and wait for the pullback to go long/short.

passages.h: Supply and demand vs supply and demand ZONE trading
passages.t: Every zone pretty much needs a strong move away. Zones with a weak move away exist (e.g. one that removed a downtrend line) but he would not feel comfortable trading them.

passages.h: Supply and demand vs supply and demand ZONE trading
passages.t: He credits the methodology to Sam Seiden; his entry/strategy is his own. ICT/SMC/order blocks/FVGs are rehashed supply and demand in his view.
Demand: distal line at the lowest wick of the basing (the low of price) - not a random wick. Proximal at the top of the basing.
Exception: if the low wick is huge/emotional you can ignore it and use the body low instead. Never cut through candles; use the wicks/price to draw.
Some subjectivity is fine: tighter zone = better R:R but you may not get filled; wider = filled more but less R:R.

Use TradingView's magnet tool by holding Ctrl (instead of leaving it always on, which snaps to everything) so lines grab the exact wick. Price often holds a zone to the pip. When he marks a zone as removed he doesn't bother drawing it precisely.

passages.h: What is NOT a zone (red flags)
passages.t: Zones that start at a random place with no basing or move away - test: black out price to the right of where the zone starts; if there's no reason for it, it was drawn after the fact.

passages.h: What is NOT a zone (red flags)
passages.t: Zones drawn because price reacted several times at an area = support/resistance, not supply and demand.

passages.h: What is NOT a zone (red flags)
passages.t: A big general area with no obvious tight zone is basically just a zone on a higher timeframe.

passages.h: What is NOT a zone (red flags)
passages.t: If price clearly breaks a zone, it's gone - don't keep trading it as 'supply'. With a real zone your order, stop and TP were already in place; if broken you take the loss and move on. Support/resistance is a retail strategy, and most retail traders are not winning traders.

passages.h: Analysis must be done before the fact
passages.t: Your zone should already be on the chart before price reacts; that is how you get an entry, stop and TP.

passages.h: Analysis must be done before the fact
passages.t: He sometimes draws a zone after the fact (missed it), but it would have been objectively the same zone.

passages.h: Analysis must be done before the fact
passages.t: Be cautious of people who point out zones after the fact - it looks great but they couldn't have called it beforehand.

passages.h: Avoid zones on trendlines and old S/R (trade against retail)
passages.t: Q: why not take a zone that sits right at a trendline? Trendline trading is a very popular retail strategy; around trendlines he sees whippy price action and stop runs ('liquidity search').

passages.h: Avoid zones on trendlines and old S/R (trade against retail)
passages.t: It's okay if trading with the trend and the R:R is good - he would take it if decent - but it's something he watches for.

passages.h: Avoid zones on trendlines and old S/R (trade against retail)
passages.t: Once price breaks a trendline, zones become lower odds because the trend has officially changed.

passages.h: Avoid zones on trendlines and old S/R (trade against retail)
passages.t: A demand zone right at an obvious old high ('old resistance becomes new support') is also a S/R trade. Retail stops sit just below that level, so he'd rather take the zone below it.

passages.h: Avoid zones on trendlines and old S/R (trade against retail)
passages.t: Obvious repeatedly-tested areas just before supply are like a trap setup: stops sit there and fuel the real zone. Only two times he looks for 'retail things': around S/R areas and around trendlines.

passages.h: Avoid zones on trendlines and old S/R (trade against retail)
passages.t: He noticed the trendline issue himself after being stopped out several times - nobody taught him. Goal: trade with the banks and against retail; retail traders are who pay us.

GTO poker = fixed system; exploitative poker = read the opponent and adjust. He plays exploitatively: tight player re-raises -> respect it; loose aggressive player -> slow down and let him hang himself.
In trading, the opponent is retail. Adjust your normal setup when it sits where retail trades (trendlines, S/R).
Learn what he knows, then build your own system with your own R:R, risk tolerance and win rate through testing.
Once you have a system that works, stick to it for at least six months, even through a drawdown.
His Excel journal: his five setups with wins, losses, breakevens, half wins and half losses per setup, max drawdown and max winning streak (tracked back to January). No screenshots yet.
Knowing max drawdown means three losses in a row is nothing - he can check the journal and see it's normal.
With 3:1, breakeven win rate is 25%; that can mean six losers in a row - anything is possible (like 20 heads in a row).
Play out a month on a calculator (e.g. five losses then two winners) so you understand what your system can look like.
A system with 10R+ will hit those trades every now and then - that's probability, not gambling.
He backtested a 1:1 system on 1m EURUSD for a week (+2%), but low R:R strategies bother him.
If your setup says take the trade, take it even if price looks overextended - price has looked overextended many times before.
One weekend of testing, focused on trend and old S/R, changed his trading forever. Test on weekends.
Anyone is a genius in a bull market; there are always trades in any trend if you know what to look for.

P&L screenshots and withdrawals can be faked; judge mentors by their timestamped forecasts (e.g. YouTube) compared to the charts. The membership doesn't hand out exact entries/stops/TPs - it's for learning. Post your trades in the trade review channel. Stacking odds: trade with the trend and inside higher-timeframe zones.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details on zones
passages.t: Demand is identified by the move away; then you draw the structure. Everyone drawing the same demand zone should end up with the same distal line, on the very bottom wick of the basing.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details on zones
passages.t: Black-out test, repeated: when an 'area' zone has no structure where it starts, 'it is always a zone that is drawn after the fact'.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details on zones
passages.t: Example of someone doing it right: identified the move down and the basing, then drew the distal and proximal lines using the wick. 'This guy clearly knows what he is doing.'

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details on zones
passages.t: Pound example: he ignored a huge emotional wick and drew the zone to the body because 'it makes logical sense'. With tight basing, though, include the wick.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details on zones

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details on zones

passages.t: USD/JPY: his buy sat below an 'old resistance becomes new support' level where S/R buyers' stops were, so 'I bought all their sell orders'. He says it wasn't his plan, but it makes sense in hindsight.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details on trendlines and retail traps
passages.t: If you traded old-resistance-becomes-new-support levels there, you would have been stopped out a lot. The real demand was below and that one worked.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details on trendlines and retail traps
passages.t: Banks move price, but they need to make money too: 'we're all trying to make money from retail traders'.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details on trendlines and retail traps
passages.t: Poker detail: if a super-tight player re-raises your aces, he probably has kings, ace-king or queens, so get the money in now. Against a loose aggressive player, call rather than raise and let him put the money in.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details on testing and systems
passages.t: Example tweaks to test: maybe you only take zones at the extreme and not both zones. He could tell members his strategy to a T and they might still not be able to execute it, because it needs a lot of patience.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details on testing and systems
passages.t: From his journal: after three losses in a row he can see he could lose two or three more and still be back to breakeven or up with one winner.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details on testing and systems
passages.t: GBP/JPY setup at the time: price looked very overextended, with a possible deep pullback to the 177 area. It had looked overextended many times before in the same run.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details on testing and systems
passages.t: There is probably a chart-pattern, S/R or trendline system with a win rate under 50% that is profitable. Some people need to win more than they lose and cannot trade such systems.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details on testing and systems
passages.t: Instagram example: a trader who struggled with losing didn't know his win rate or R:R, only that he 'usually goes for 3:1'.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details on testing and systems
passages.t: Until you test your own system, you probably won't be profitable. You never truly 'figure it out', but you can figure out a system that works for you.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details on testing and systems
passages.t: He had a few mentors. Before joining, he spent hours comparing their timestamped YouTube forecasts with the charts.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra details on testing and systems
passages.t: Faking is easy: someone could run two accounts, short one and long the other, and show the winner. That is why he points to timestamped forecasts instead of P&L.
