Black-out test: hide everything after the zone's origin. A real zone already shows basing and a large quick move away. An area box that starts at a random candle has no reason there; it was drawn after the fact.
EURUSD daily: the 1.48629–1.49801 supply formed in September 2008 and was hit again in November–December 2009, followed by the fall to about 1.19. That is analysis before the fact.
Trading against retail: a demand on a trendline or an old high (A) has retail stops just below it. He prefers the zone below those stops (B), where the stop run tends to end.

Drawing zones from areas price reacted to several times (that's S/R). Starting a zone at a random point with no basing. Ignoring a normal-size wick when setting the distal line. Trading a zone that has been clearly broken. Analysing after the fact. Buying a demand zone right on a trendline or on 'old resistance becomes new support'. Not knowing your win rate, R:R and max drawdown, so losing streaks shake you.

Skipping a valid setup because price 'looks overextended'. Not knowing your win rate and R:R, so normal losing streaks feel like the system is broken. Treating a big-R:R system as gambling or 'trying to hit a home run'. It is probability.

Does the zone have clear basing and a strong move away? Is the distal line on the extreme wick (no cut-through candles)? Was the zone identifiable before price reacted to it? Is this zone just an area of repeated reactions (S/R)? Has the zone already been clearly broken? Does the zone sit on a trendline or an obvious old high/low? If on a trendline, am I trading with the trend and is R:R good?

Do I know my win rate, R:R and max drawdown for this setup? Are retail traders' stops likely sitting just beyond my zone (old S/R, trendline)? Is there a better zone below/above them? Is my distal line exactly on the wick (magnet tool)?

“There's supply and demand, and then there's supply and demand zone trading.” “We don't cut through a candle.” “We want to trade with the banks and against retail.” “Anybody is a genius in a bull market.” “There's always trades to be taken. You just need to know what to look for.” “The discord can only be as active as you make it.” “If your setup says you take this trade, you take that trade.”
“I am a trader. I am not an influencer.”

Black-out test: hide price to the right of a zone's start - if no reason for it, it was drawn after the fact. A large vague area = basically a higher-timeframe zone. TradingView magnet tool via Ctrl for exact wick placement.
Avoid demand right at a trendline (retail stop hunts) - he found this himself after repeated stop-outs.

Avoid demand right at an obvious old high (old resistance = new support); take the zone below where retail stops are. Zones become lower odds after price breaks the trendline (trend changed). Poker GTO vs exploitative analogy for trading against retail.
Stick with a working system for at least six months; his journal fields (5 setups, half wins/losses, max drawdown, max win streak). Judge mentors by timestamped forecasts, not P&L screenshots.

Everything is supply and demand, but a ZONE needs a base and a big escape. Every time someone buys or sells, that is supply and demand, like every step you take is walking. But a race has a start line. A zone is a start line: price rests for a moment (the base), then sprints away. We draw the start line before the race, not after. And we avoid the spot where everyone else stands, because that is where traps are set.
A sprinter's starting blocks: a short rest, then a burst. You mark the blocks, not the whole track.
A zone needs structure: basing plus a strong move away. A place price bounced several times is support/resistance, not a zone.
Distal on the extreme wick of the basing, proximal at the top of the basing. Never cut through candles. Draw it before the fact.
Be careful with zones on trendlines or old highs/lows: retail stops sit there. Trade with the banks, against retail.

passages.h: Step: Find the base and the big move
passages.t: Every candle is supply and demand, but that is not a zone. A zone has a base (here 3 small candles) and then a large, quick move away.

passages.h: Step: Distal line on the lowest wick
passages.t: For demand, the distal line goes on the lowest wick of the basing. Not a random wick. If the wick is normal-sized, include it.

passages.h: Step: Proximal line on top of the basing
passages.t: The proximal line sits at the top of the basing. Wrap the base, never cut through a candle, then extend the lines to the right.

The zone was on the chart before price came back. That is how you have an entry, stop and target ready. Black-out test: hide everything right of the zone's start. If there is no reason for the zone there, it was drawn after the fact.

Price bounced off 150 again and again: that is support/resistance, not a zone. Retail traders buy "old resistance becomes new support" and put stops just below. Kevin prefers the real demand lower down, where those stops fuel the move.
Supply and demand vs zone trading? - Every candle is S&D; a ZONE needs basing + a strong move away. Demand distal line goes where? - On the lowest wick of the basing.
When may you ignore the low wick? - Only if it is huge and emotional; then use the body low.
What is the black-out test? - Hide price right of the zone start. No reason there = drawn after the fact.
A level price bounced off many times is? - Support/resistance, not a supply and demand zone.

Why avoid demand on an old high or trendline? - Retail stops sit there; price often runs them first. Breakeven win rate at 3:1? - 25%. How long to stick with a working system? - At least six months, even through a drawdown.

An informal garage podcast recorded on 12 July, after a breakeven trade and two losses in a row just after he raised his risk. He uses his own stats and his new gym habit to argue that trading is mostly discipline: stick to the plan, keep losses short-lived emotionally, and trust R:R over win rate.
Stick to your trading plan even when emotion says otherwise (e.g. move the stop to BE when your plan says so).
His own plan rule: in that specific setup type, move the stop to breakeven after about a 2:1 move (based on his own trade observations). Riskier setups get half risk; standard setups get full risk.
Decide risk changes in advance and in writing (e.g. 'if June is profitable, increase to full risk'). After a loss, feel it briefly, then get straight back to looking for the next setup.
Once a system is proven, trust the R:R and the probabilities. Do not rewrite it after a losing streak.
When a losing streak hits, re-read the notes you wrote in advance (e.g. 'expect big drawdown, do not get discouraged') before reacting.
Get used to losing: the system's few winners pay for the many losers, so keep taking the next trade.
USDJPY: H1 set & forget trade inside a daily demand zone (one of his typical setups). It went his way almost immediately with basically no drawdown.

It reached a little over 2:1. His targets are much larger than that, so he moved the stop to breakeven. Price pulled back and stopped him at BE (a tiny profit from overnight swap, so call it breakeven).

USDCAD: set & forget on a daily confirmation. It is on the riskier side of his plan, so it was a half-risk setup. It lost, so he lost half a unit. EURGBP: a standard setup for him, so full risk. It was also stopped out.
Result: BE, then two losses in a row, right after he increased his risk. He says it felt like being punched in the face and then stabbed.

passages.h: Why the BE trade was a win for his process
passages.t: A month or so earlier he would not have moved to BE on that trade. It would probably have been a half or a full loss.

passages.h: Why the BE trade was a win for his process
passages.t: By observing his own trades and thinking critically, he concluded that in that specific situation it is best to move the stop to BE after about a 2:1 move, because when price pulls back from there it very rarely goes his way.

passages.h: Why the BE trade was a win for his process
passages.t: The positive takeaway is that he stuck to the plan. If emotion had made him think 'it will react a second time' and leave the stop where it was, that would have been breaking his plan. Even with no money made, sticking to the plan is the important thing.
Over the last month he tweaked his strategy to take only H1 zones. If he wants a H4 zone, he refines it to an H1 zone. He added more trending trades. This worked well for him in June.
His plan has two risk tiers: full-risk setups (standard) and half-risk setups (riskier, e.g. the USDCAD daily confirmation set & forget).
Swap fees can eat a lot of profit when you hold for a long time. That is part of why he now enters on H1. He has also been experimenting with his take profit, so his June winners were not 10:1.

Before 1 June he wrote in his P&L spreadsheet/journal: if June is profitable, he will increase his risk to full risk. June was profitable, so he increased risk in July. His notes say 'Risk increase'. He still risks only half on the one riskier setup.
He also wrote 'Expect big drawdown, do not get discouraged', because he knew losers would hit bigger after the increase.
His P&L journal is broken down by month, by quarter and by half-year. He was half expecting the next quarter to be a losing quarter after the risk increase, unless a couple of winners came early.

passages.h: His stats: losing more than winning and still profitable
passages.t: June: +0.89% (almost 1%) while not even risking 1% per trade. He says you could roughly double it to get a 'true' return, then says 1.6% to 1.9% at 1% risk (an off-the-cuff estimate).

passages.h: His stats: losing more than winning and still profitable
passages.t: June record: 4 wins, 11 losses, 1 breakeven. He corrects it to probably 4 wins, 10 losses, 1 BE, because two trades where he split the risk (on AUDJPY and a EURJPY trade, both yen) were logged separately. He is unsure of the details. July so far: 3 losses and 1 BE (4 trades counting the split-risk pair).

passages.h: His stats: losing more than winning and still profitable
passages.t: He tracks max drawdown as losing trades in a row. His current max is 6 in a row, and June had 4 losses in a row. He still had a profitable year so far.

passages.h: His stats: losing more than winning and still profitable
passages.t: He loses more than he wins and is still profitable. Average people think that is delusional, but it works if you have the discipline. Not every strategy has more losers than winners. This is just his system.
It is basically impossible to feel nothing. Winning brings joy, and losing brings anger, sadness or defeat. That is normal and human.
The key factor is how long you feel it. A few minutes is fine. Then get straight back to your discipline and look for the next setup.

His scale: after one loss you should feel basically nothing. After two in a row: 'damn'. After three: 'does this even work?'. Then remind yourself that you know your system and your R:R, and it will be fine long term.
Take your losses like an adult. Understand the maths and the probabilities, and keep taking the next trade. It gets easier every month.

passages.h: The old mistake: tweaking after every losing streak
passages.t: He used to lose two or three in a row and immediately decide the system did not work ('trading is a scam'), then tweak something.

passages.h: The old mistake: tweaking after every losing streak
passages.t: He would blame things like a bad approach to the zone and go hunting for a pattern behind every loss. Back then he was around breakeven, losing small or winning a little. Identifying patterns IS necessary. That is how he found the move-to-BE-after-2:1 rule.

passages.h: The old mistake: tweaking after every losing streak
passages.t: But once you have seen the strategy work and know the system works, you must trust the overall R:R and the probabilities and take the next trade.

He started weight training on 13 June (one month before recording). The goal is not to be a frail old man and to keep a sharp mind. In the past he always quit working out after a week or two. This time he has stuck to it.
Seeing results from trading discipline helped him stick to the gym, and the gym discipline now helps his trading. He feels more clear-minded.
His suggestion: changing something in your actual life to build discipline can help your trading.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Context and extra details from the week
passages.t: Start of a new month: he took no trades at first, then several setups showed up at once. The USDJPY trade was posted in the Discord group.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Context and extra details from the week
passages.t: On USDJPY his stop went to breakeven almost immediately because the trade had basically no drawdown. He says a no-drawdown trade feels like hype, and it is a bummer to watch that return pull back, but 'not that big of a deal... onto the next one'.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Context and extra details from the week
passages.t: Why he wanted the first trade after the risk increase to win: a winner first would mean any following losses are only a drawdown from profit, not a true drawdown.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Context and extra details from the week
passages.t: After the two losses he went back to his journal notes and re-read his own 'do not get discouraged' note. He says reading it is what you have to do in that moment.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Context and extra details from the week
passages.t: The analogy in full: running down the street for a free ice-cream truck (the USDJPY trade going great), getting punched in the face (stopped at BE), getting up and walking away, then getting stabbed (two losses in a row after raising risk). He says it no longer really feels like that, because of his discipline.

passages.h: More from the lesson: R:R mindset he spells out
passages.t: The losses will hurt, but one or two winners will make up for them. You will lose more than you win and still be profitable over the long run.

passages.h: More from the lesson: R:R mindset he spells out
passages.t: If 1:1 or 2:1 does not fit you (he does not like it either, he finds it difficult), master the discipline to keep taking the next trade with a lower-win-rate, bigger-R:R system.

passages.h: More from the lesson: R:R mindset he spells out
passages.t: With 1% risk on every June trade, he estimates the return would have been about 1.6% to 1.9% instead of 0.89%.

passages.h: More from the lesson: R:R mindset he spells out
passages.t: June also contained four losing trades in a row. He reminds himself that this 'is what it is' and moves on.

passages.h: More from the lesson: R:R mindset he spells out
passages.t: He expects a temporary drawdown while the bigger risk is in place, and says you just have to understand that it will happen.

passages.h: More from the lesson: R:R mindset he spells out
passages.t: Trading 'a lot of it is just that discipline'. You do not have to win a lot if you get used to losing.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Why he shared this
passages.t: He recorded it right after the losses so that anyone with the same thoughts or feelings knows other traders feel this too. It is completely normal, and it does not mean you won't be successful.
Not moving the stop to BE when your plan says to, because you think price will react a second time. Declaring the system broken or a scam after two or three losses in a row.

Constantly tweaking the strategy after each loss (e.g. blaming the approach to the zone) instead of trusting the probabilities. Staying upset for too long after a loss. Holding trades very long without accounting for swap fees eating profit. Being shocked by a drawdown after raising risk instead of expecting it. Letting a no-drawdown 'hype' trade that comes back to BE throw you off the next setup.
Choosing a 1:1 or 2:1 style only because a low win rate feels uncomfortable, when the real fix is the discipline to keep taking trades.

Is this a full-risk (standard) or half-risk (riskier) setup in my plan? Is my risk size the one I decided in writing in advance? Do I know the point (e.g. ~2:1) where my plan moves the stop to BE? Have I accounted for swap fees if I plan to hold for a long time? Am I calm, with no lingering frustration from the last loss? Am I taking this trade because it fits the plan, not to 'fix' a losing streak?
Have I re-read my pre-written journal notes for this month (risk plan, expected drawdown)?
Do I know my current losing streak compared with my recorded max drawdown (his is 6 in a row)?
“Expect big drawdown, do not get discouraged.” “I lose more than I win and I'm still a profitable trader.”
“It's okay to feel that way for a few minutes, then you have to immediately get right back into it.” “Take your loss like an adult and understand the math and the probabilities.”
“Obviously supply and demand works. Obviously the system I have works, I just need to move on to the next trade.”

“These losses are gonna hurt, but you're gonna have that one winner... those two winners that are gonna make up for your losses.” “It's completely normal and it doesn't mean that you aren't gonna be successful.” “You don't have to win a lot if you get used to losing.”
His personal rule: move the stop to BE after about 2:1 in that setup type, derived from his own trade observations (the PDFs mention BE after a set R:R only generically).
Two-tier risk in his plan: full risk for standard setups and half risk for riskier ones (e.g. daily confirmation set & forget).

Pre-committing a risk increase in writing, conditional on a profitable month, with a note to expect a bigger drawdown. Taking only H1 zones and refining H4 zones to H1, plus adding more trending trades. Swap fees eating profit on long holds as a reason for shorter-timeframe entries.
Real stats: June 4W/10-11L/1BE = +0.89% at under 1% risk; max losing streak of 6; losing more than winning while profitable.

Emotional time-limit idea (feel it for minutes, then move on) and the 1/2/3-loss reaction scale. Splitting risk across two correlated yen trades (mentioned in passing; details unclear). Building discipline outside trading (weight training) to support trading discipline.

Follow your plan every time, even when a loss stings. You are learning to ride a bike. You fall twice and your knee hurts. It is okay to feel sad for a few minutes. Then you get back on, because you know riding works. If you change the bike after every fall, you never learn. Trading is the same: a few wins pay for many small falls.
A gym routine: one bad day does not mean the routine is broken. Showing up again is the skill.

Discipline means doing what your plan says, even a breakeven move, even after losses. Feel a loss for a few minutes, then go straight back to the next setup. Trust R:R over win rate: Kevin loses more than he wins and is still profitable.
Kevin buys at demand: entry at the proximal, stop under the distal. Price fills.
Price moves a little over 2:1. His targets are bigger. But his own data showed: in this setup, when price pulls back from about 2:1 it rarely goes his way.

passages.h: Step: The plan says: stop to breakeven
passages.t: So he moves the stop to breakeven (the entry price). Emotion whispers "it will react again, leave it". The plan wins.
Price pulls back and takes him out at breakeven. No money made, but the plan was followed. That is a win for the process.

Look: price kept falling to the old stop. Without the breakeven rule this would have been a full loss. Then came two losses in a row. He felt it, re-read his note "Expect big drawdown, do not get discouraged", and moved on.

What counts as a "win" for the process? - Following the plan, even if the result is breakeven. Kevin's own BE rule in that setup? - Move the stop to breakeven after about 2:1. How long to feel a loss? - A few minutes. Then back to the next setup. Note he wrote before raising risk? - "Expect big drawdown, do not get discouraged." Risk tiers in his plan? - Full risk for standard setups, half risk for riskier ones.

His June record? - 4 wins, 10-11 losses, 1 BE: still profitable (+0.89%). Old mistake after 2-3 losses? - Declaring the system broken and tweaking it. Why can you lose more than you win? - Big R:R: one or two winners make up for the losses.

Sunday Zoom session (2 Feb 2025) that resets the basics for new members: the four parts every zone must have, drawable vs tradable zones, sizing zones consistently, and the exact rules for drawing and removing trendlines. It closes with homework reviews and a short psychology talk on not forcing trades, 1% risk and hard stops.

A zone needs all four parts: basing, move away, stay away, and space between the stay-away candle and the proximal line. Risk 1% per trade, always, whatever the account size. Always use a hard stop loss. Keep zones a similar size; never shrink a zone to make space. Never let wicks cut through the distal line, and never draw trendlines through candles.
A trendline is removed only when a candle closes fully (body and wick) beyond it. Ignore emotional wicks when judging zone removal. Don't force trades or zones — no opportunity is a valid decision.
The trendline is removed by the FIRST candle that closes fully (body and wick) beyond it. Later full closes are irrelevant.
If you are unsure whether a zone exists, draw it at the similar size first and only then judge the space.
Attach the distal line to the true lowest point of the base, even if that is another candle's body rather than a wick.
Every daily candle is supply and demand on a lower timeframe. Only the specific formation (basing, move away, stay away, space) is a zone.

passages.h: Psychology: the best trade is often the one not taken
passages.t: Seeing no opportunity and moving on is a decision — a position of patience and strength. Don't force trades.

passages.h: Psychology: the best trade is often the one not taken
passages.t: Beginners can press buy and win by luck; forcing your will on the market can work short-term, but trading is a long-term game.

passages.h: Psychology: the best trade is often the one not taken
passages.t: Sometimes there are tons of setups, sometimes none. When every pair on the watchlist has a zone it can get overwhelming — pick the best one (e.g. a 4H demand on EURUSD vs EURJPY: he would pick EURUSD).

passages.h: Psychology: the best trade is often the one not taken
passages.t: Hitting a trade that runs from a planned 5:1 to 10:1 feels better than skipping, but skipping bad charts is still a result.

He uses a four-chart layout to judge a symbol in seconds: e.g. EURUSD weekly floating in the middle with profit margin down to weekly demand, daily supply in control, a 4H confirmation trade setting up, 1H downtrend → could day-trade short on 5m. S&P 500: weekly and daily trends are fine but nothing on 4H/1H → move on.
USDCHF: 4H supply above — wait for it to be hit for shorts, or removed for longs (daily trend is up).
Doing this quickly across the watchlist and skipping what isn't there leads to better results.

passages.h: Risk: always 1% and a hard stop
passages.t: Never risk more than 1% of the account per trade — whether the account is $50 or $50,000. Don't drip-feed $500 deposits and blow them; if you are not comfortable funding more, put in the smaller amount, risk 1% on every trade and learn.

passages.h: Risk: always 1% and a hard stop
passages.t: If you can't make 10–30% a year on a $50 or $500 account, you can't do it on a $100,000 account.

passages.h: Risk: always 1% and a hard stop
passages.t: Always use a hard stop loss. Remove it and the 1% loss becomes 2%, 3%… 10% of the account. Losing positions also tie up capital and leverage.

passages.h: The four parts of a zone (all four required)
passages.t: 1. Basing candles. 2. Move-away candle(s). 3. Stay-away candle. 4. Space between the stay-away candle and the proximal line.

passages.h: The four parts of a zone (all four required)
passages.t: Missing any part = no zone. There is always basing, so the real tests are the move away, the stay away and the space.

passages.h: The four parts of a zone (all four required)
passages.t: Example: if the stay-away candle's wick comes down and touches the proximal line, there is no space → no zone.

passages.h: The four parts of a zone (all four required)
passages.t: He tells members to make the four-part diagram their phone/desktop wallpaper — it stops you drawing the wrong areas.

passages.h: The four parts of a zone (all four required)
passages.t: Not support/resistance: YouTube 'supply and demand' that just marks repeated highs as supply and lows as demand is technically buying/selling, but every candle is supply and demand. A zone needs the specific formation (methodology originally from Sam Seiden; his is slightly tweaked).

passages.h: Basing candles and the 50% candle indicator
passages.t: Basing candles do not have to be '50% candles' — a single small candle with barely any wick can be the base, as long as it is smaller than the move-away candle.

passages.h: Basing candles and the 50% candle indicator
passages.t: Bases come in endless shapes, which is why the homework and chart work matter more than any single example.

passages.h: Basing candles and the 50% candle indicator
passages.t: The 50% candle indicator just helps spot basing quickly ('like cruise control'); he can turn it off and still trade profitably.

passages.h: Basing candles and the 50% candle indicator
passages.t: The candle right after the proximal line must be a move-away candle. If it looks like another basing candle, it isn't a move away and there is no zone there.

Every tradable zone is drawable, but not every drawable zone is tradable. A wick that comes down to barely leave space still qualifies the zone — he draws it to see what removes it, but wouldn't trade it because the move away isn't great.
The faster the initial move away and the more price stays away from the zone, the better the zone. 'I cannot stress that enough.'
All zones on a chart should be a similar size; judge a new zone's size from the previous correct zones.
If you can't tell whether there is space between the stay-away candle and the proximal line, draw the zone at the similar size first — then check. Never shrink a zone just to create space.

There's no fixed wick-to-body or wick-to-wick rule. He prefers wick-to-body for a tight zone but makes it bigger when needed. Use the surrounding wicks/bodies of the base as anchors; if nothing fits, extend it to a similar size.
The proximal line sits right before the sharp move away — keep it tight against that move, not floating higher.
Distal line attaches to the lowest point of the base (for demand). Never let wicks cut through the distal line. Don't extend zones far back to the left; keep the chart clean.
It doesn't have to be picture perfect ('doesn't have to be a grand piano') — similar enough is fine.

passages.h: What qualifies a zone in chain analysis
passages.t: A zone qualifies when it removes an opposing zone, removes a trendline, or makes an all-time high/low (not just any high or low).

passages.h: What qualifies a zone in chain analysis
passages.t: Draw the zone whose basing happened before the opposing zone was removed, with the move away after it.

passages.h: What qualifies a zone in chain analysis
passages.t: New rule for members: when a trendline is removed, draw every zone that removed the trendline.

passages.h: What qualifies a zone in chain analysis
passages.t: Sometimes a zone or trendline is removed by nothing — no zone forms. That's fine; don't force a zone and the analysis just ends there.
Needs a clear peak, a clear valley and then a higher high (uptrend) / lower low (downtrend). Sideways basing at the top is not a clear peak — no trendline.
Attach to the lowest point (uptrend) / highest point (downtrend). If that line cuts through any candle or wick, move to the next point that doesn't cut through candles.

Never cut through candles: 'if it cuts through this much, why not that much?' — a rule-based system needs exact attachment. Trendline (clear peak/valley) is different from momentum (no clear peaks/valleys).

passages.h: When a trendline or zone is removed
passages.t: A trendline is removed by the first candle that closes fully — body AND wick — beyond it (below an uptrend line). A candle still touching the line does not remove it, even if it closed beyond.

passages.h: When a trendline or zone is removed
passages.t: It has nothing to do with the first or second candle or any count — it can be the 15th candle.

passages.h: When a trendline or zone is removed
passages.t: A zone is removed when price closes/pushes beyond its distal line. Price can float inside a zone forever without removing it.

passages.h: When a trendline or zone is removed
passages.t: Emotional wicks: a huge candle with a huge wick through the zone (looks like news/manipulation) is ignored — treat it as if it isn't there. It's about the size of the whole candle and wick, not the wick alone. Rare.
Submit screenshots, not unusable links. For multiple timeframe / sequence work, send every timeframe — a 4H zone can't be judged on a 15-minute chart.
Common misses: obvious zones after a trendline removal; trendlines drawn poking through candles; 'zones' whose next candle is basing, not a move away.

Indicators that flag strong moves can be fine to experiment with, but they don't follow the chain analysis (they flag moves that aren't zones). Next homework: January 2012 to January 2013 on the same chart.

passages.h: More from the lesson: More psychology details
passages.t: Someone who has never heard of trading can press buy and win. 'You can make a million dollars at the click of a button, but you could also lose it slowly over time.'

passages.h: More from the lesson: More psychology details
passages.t: He says the quote exaggerates a little: a trade you planned for 5:1 that runs to 10:1 probably feels better than skipping. The point is still not to force trades.

passages.h: More from the lesson: More psychology details
passages.t: Some very obvious-looking charts will still lose when you take them. That is all part of it.

passages.h: More from the lesson: More psychology details
passages.t: There is a balance between short-term and long-term thinking, but trading is about staying in the game long-term.

passages.h: More from the lesson: More psychology details
passages.t: Hard stop, as a YouTuber put it: it makes you accept you are wrong. Without it, 1% becomes the next stop at 2%, then 3%, 4%, up to 10% of the whole account. A losing position you keep also ties up capital, leaving you less leverage.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Why highs and lows are not zones
passages.t: Example: a sideways daily chart with repeated selling at the top and buying at the bottom. That is technically supply and demand, but every candle is supply and demand.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Why highs and lows are not zones
passages.t: Each daily candle seen on a lower timeframe (e.g. 1H) is its own run of buying and selling. That is supply and demand, but it is not a supply and demand zone under the original methodology.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Why highs and lows are not zones
passages.t: He learned from Sam Seiden's free YouTube videos (never his course). His strategy is tweaked from that, but much closer to it than to YouTube's highs/lows versions, which he says were changed to sell courses.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Zone sizing by measuring (clone method)
passages.t: Worked example: wick-to-body was far too small (a correct earlier zone fitted about 2.5 times inside it). Wick-to-wick was still too small (about 1.5 times). So he moved the proximal line up to wherever the zone matched the earlier correct zone's size. 'There's no reason that this is here other than I'm making it similar size to that one.'

passages.h: More from the lesson: Zone sizing by measuring (clone method)
passages.t: When first learning, clone a correct zone and measure the new one against it. With experience you won't need to. He clones only to demonstrate.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Zone sizing by measuring (clone method)
passages.t: Use the surroundings: try attaching the proximal line to different wicks and bodies within the basing and pick what gives a similar size. A zone a little smaller or a little bigger is 'similar enough'.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Zone sizing by measuring (clone method)
passages.t: Example: a too-small zone that you could fit almost two of the correct zone into shows the size is wrong. That would make a 'no space' zone look valid when it isn't.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Homework walkthrough details (Jan 2011 to Jan 2012)
passages.t: First zone qualified because it removed a trendline. When a supply was removed, he saw the move away and the zone immediately ('picture perfect obvious to me' after years of practice).

passages.h: More from the lesson: Homework walkthrough details (Jan 2011 to Jan 2012)
passages.t: Distal line example: a green candle's low sat below a red wick, so the distal line attached to that green candle's low (the true lowest point of the base).

passages.h: More from the lesson: Homework walkthrough details (Jan 2011 to Jan 2012)
passages.t: Trendline exercise: several candles technically closed below the line. The removal candle is the FIRST one whose body and wick both closed below. Members circled the wrong candle (one still touching the line). The later full closes don't matter.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Homework walkthrough details (Jan 2011 to Jan 2012)
passages.t: A trendline removed by no zone: everything after it was basing with no move away and no stay away, so the chain stopped there.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Homework walkthrough details (Jan 2011 to Jan 2012)
passages.t: A hidden zone he had to draw to see: basing, a move-away candle, then the stay-away candle and the space. His worry was whether the move-away candle was big enough. He judged it was, and it was 'a beautiful setup'.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Homework walkthrough details (Jan 2011 to Jan 2012)
passages.t: A supply zone: an extra red basing candle at the top could be included or left out. Including it made sense given the zone size he was aiming for.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Homework walkthrough details (Jan 2011 to Jan 2012)
passages.t: Trendlines placed very close to each other are hard to spot. Even he almost missed one, and he admitted missing another while marking homework.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Homework walkthrough details (Jan 2011 to Jan 2012)
passages.t: Emotional wick example (USDCAD): a huge candle wicked through a demand like a news event. He treated the wick as if it wasn't there and kept extending the zone. If the body had closed beyond it, the zone would have been removed.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Homework walkthrough details (Jan 2011 to Jan 2012)
passages.t: For next week: if you don't have this zone on your chart, draw it so you can see what removes it.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Move-away judgement in homework
passages.t: Technically every candle is a move away. The move away he wants is a nice, sharp move, not a run of wicks and basing candles.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Move-away judgement in homework
passages.t: Placing the proximal line says the next candle is a move-away candle. If that candle is clearly basing, there is no zone there.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Move-away judgement in homework
passages.t: 50% candle indicator use case: a candle you might think is a move away gets flagged as a basing candle, which helps beginners tell basing from move away. He says it is just a tool and that his work without it is 'spot on'. Your eyes should go straight to the sharp moves away on any chart.

His zones.JPG redrawn: basing candles, move-away candle, stay-away candle, and the space between the stay-away candle and the proximal line. If the stay-away wick touches the proximal line, there is no space and no zone.
Trendline removal: candles whose wick or body still touch the line do not remove it. The first candle that is fully beyond the line (body and wick) removes it, and later closes are irrelevant.

GBPUSD daily homework chain: (1) the January 2011 demand 1.54749–1.56394 removed the downtrend line, (2) the September 2011 supply 1.61167–1.62601 removed the uptrend line, (3) the next downtrend line was removed in mid-January 2012.
From the EURJPY 15m homework: the proximal line goes on the last basing, right before the sharp move. A box whose next candle is still basing is not a zone.

Calling repeated highs/lows supply and demand (support/resistance thinking). Treating a basing candle as the move away. Shrinking a zone just to create space for the stay-away candle. Proximal line floating above the sharp move instead of right before it. Cutting through wicks with the distal line or trendline. Calling a trendline removed while the candle still touches it.
Calling a zone removed by an emotional news wick. Judging a higher-timeframe zone on a lower-timeframe chart. Drip-feeding small deposits and blowing them instead of risking 1%.
Circling a candle that still touches the trendline, or a later candle, as the removal candle.
Measuring zones wick-to-body or wick-to-wick by habit instead of matching the size of the previous correct zones. Missing a second trendline that sits very close to an obvious one.
Removing the hard stop and letting a 1% loss grow to 10% of the account, and tying up capital. Not asking questions in sessions (he says people who never ask learn nothing).

Does the zone have all four parts (basing, move away, stay away, space)? Is the candle right after the proximal line a real move-away candle? Is the zone a similar size to my other zones on this chart? Is it tradable, not just drawable (fast move away, price stayed away)? Am I risking 1% with a hard stop? Is this the best setup on my watchlist, or am I forcing it?

Have I identified the FIRST candle that closed fully (body and wick) beyond the trendline? If I cloned a previous correct zone onto this one, would it be a similar size? If a wick broke the zone, was it a huge emotional (news) candle that I should ignore? Am I sending screenshots of every timeframe for MTA homework?

“The greatest trade is often the one not taken.” “You absolutely need all four of them.” “Every tradable zone is a drawable zone, but not every drawable zone is a tradable zone.” “It doesn't have to be a grand piano.” “The market rewards those who wait, not those who force their will upon it.” “To see no opportunity and move on is a decision, a position of patience and strength.” “Every candle is supply and demand.”
“How is that a rule-based system if you're cutting through candles?” “It's nothing to do with the first candle or the second or some arbitrary number.”

The explicit four-part zone checklist including the stay-away candle and the space to the proximal line. Drawable vs tradable zones. Zone sizing by similarity to previous zones instead of a fixed wick/body rule.

Exact trendline attachment and removal rules (full body and wick close; touching candles don't count). Emotional-wick exception for zone removal. 1% risk regardless of account size and the 10–30%/year small-account test. Four-chart watchlist scan routine.

A zone needs four parts: base, move away, stay away, and space. Think of a rocket. It sits on the launch pad (base). It blasts off (move away). It keeps flying and does not fall back (stay away). And you can see clear sky between the rocket and the pad (space). If the rocket drops back onto the pad, it was not a real launch. Miss one part and there is no zone.
A rocket launch: pad, blast-off, keeps flying, clear sky under it.
All four parts are required: basing, move-away candle, stay-away candle, space to the proximal line.
Every tradable zone is drawable, but not every drawable zone is tradable. Faster move away + price staying away = better zone.
Trendline removed only by the FIRST candle closing fully (body and wick) beyond it. Risk 1% with a hard stop.
Small candles where price pauses. They only need to be smaller than the move away.
Right after the proximal line comes a sharp candle. If the next candle looks like more basing, it is not a move away and there is no zone.
The next candle stays up there. It does not fall back toward the zone.
There must be space between the stay-away candle and the proximal line. Draw the zone at the usual size first, then check the space. Never shrink a zone to create space.

passages.h: Step: All four: a real zone
passages.t: All four parts are there, so it is a zone. Price came back later and it held.

passages.h: Step: Missing a part: no zone
passages.t: Here the next candle's wick fell right back to the proximal line. No space, so no zone. Kevin might draw it to see what removes it, but he would not trade it.
The four parts of a zone? - Basing, move away, stay away, space to the proximal line. Stay-away wick touches the proximal line? - No space = no zone.

Drawable vs tradable? - Every tradable zone is drawable; not every drawable zone is tradable. What makes a zone better? - A faster move away and price staying away longer. How should zone sizes compare? - Similar size to the previous correct zones on the chart. When is a trendline removed? - First candle that closes fully (body and wick) beyond it.

When is a zone removed? - Price closes beyond the distal (ignore rare emotional wicks). Risk per trade? - 1%, always with a hard stop. Best trade is often...? - The one not taken. Do not force trades.

Using EUR/JPY, Kevin shows that a trendline stops mattering when price runs so far away, for so long, that there is no price action around the line. He also repeats the difference between a trendline and a momentum line.
A trendline needs price action around it to stay valid; if price leaves for a long time and goes far away, remove it. A trendline that keeps getting tested stays valid until it is broken.
Only a clear peak and valley with a higher high (lower low) makes a trendline; otherwise it is momentum.
Review trendlines when you update charts. Remove any line that price has left far behind for a long time, even if it was never broken.
EUR/JPY example: the trendline made sense while price was close to it. Had price come back for another test with price action near the line, he might have kept it.

Instead price pushed up so far, and took so long to come back, that the line 'doesn't really matter anymore' - he removed it. Price action must be seen around the trendline for it to be considered valid.
Valid example: downward trendline with obvious valley, obvious peak, lower low, and price came back in for another test - it stayed valid until it was actually removed (broken).

Hypothetical: if price had dropped away, not come back for a second test, spent a long time far away and only returned much later, he 'would maybe' delete it. There is no exact time/distance threshold given.
A trendline needs a high, a clear pullback forming an obvious low (valley), then the higher high.
Steady movement without that clear peak and valley is just momentum - a momentum line, not a trendline.

passages.h: More from the lesson: How he spotted it
passages.t: He found this EUR/JPY trendline while updating the members' charts. It 'was looking good at first', then price pushed up so far that the line was no longer relevant 'at the time of recording'.

passages.h: More from the lesson: How he spotted it
passages.t: The reason to remove it was time: 'it took so long for price to come back to it' that it is basically irrelevant.

EUR/JPY 1h, Feb 2025: the uptrend line from the 155.51–156.10 demand had one valley test, then a steady run to ~161 and four days away. He deleted it even though price was drifting back toward it.
His 00:30–00:36 sketch: what would have kept the line valid, with price repeatedly returning to the line between higher highs.
The valid downtrend line (valley, peak, lower low, then retests before it broke) and his hypothetical drop to the 152.80–153.23 demand with no retest, which is when he "would maybe" delete it.
Momentum line vs trendline: a steady leg gives only a momentum line. A trendline needs a high, an obvious valley and then a higher high.
Keeping an old trendline that price left long ago and far behind. Calling a momentum line a trendline.

Has price shown recent price action around this trendline? Has price been far away from it for a long time? (If so, remove it.) Is it a real trendline (clear peak and valley) and not a momentum line? When updating my charts, is each trendline still relevant to where price is now?

“This is a momentum line, not a trendline.” “We basically have to see price action around the trend line for it to be considered valid.” “It took so long for price to come back to it, it is basically irrelevant.”
Trendlines become irrelevant when price leaves them far behind for a long time without price action around them (not in the PDFs). Momentum line vs trendline distinction.

A trendline only matters while price stays near it. A fence in your garden matters when the dog plays near it. If the dog runs off to a far field and stays there all summer, the fence is not doing anything. You stop thinking about it. A trendline is the same: when price runs far away and stays away a long time, the line stops mattering. So you end it. A fence only matters while the dog plays next to it.
A trendline needs price action around it to stay valid. If price leaves it far behind for a long time, end (remove) the line, even if it never broke.
A line that keeps getting tested stays valid until it is broken. Momentum is not a trendline.
Obvious peak, obvious valley, higher high. Then price comes back and tests the line. Price action around the line keeps it valid.
Now price pushes up hard. Every candle gets further from the line.

passages.h: Step: Far away, for a long time
passages.t: Price stays far away for a long time, with no price action around the line. Kevin says it "doesn't really matter anymore". There is no exact time or distance number; it is a judgement.
So we end the line on the chart. Leaving it extended would say it is still valid, which it is not. Check this every time you update your charts.

What keeps a trendline valid? - Price action around it (tests). Price left the line far behind for a long time? - End/remove the line: it is irrelevant. Is there an exact time limit? - No. It is a judgement of distance and time. A tested trendline stays valid until? - It is actually broken. Steady climb with no clear peak/valley? - A momentum line, not a trendline.
When to review trendlines? - Every time you update your charts.

On USD/JPY with every timeframe ranging, Kevin explains that trading is lower odds when the timeframe above your entry timeframe is going sideways. It is higher odds when that higher timeframe is trending (either direction) or price is at a higher-timeframe zone.
Lower odds when the higher timeframe of your entry timeframe is sideways. Higher odds when the higher timeframe is trending (either direction) or price is at a higher-timeframe zone.
Zones inside a big messy range are not setups for him - wait for price to leave the range.
It's always higher odds to trade with a trend on your higher timeframe. A sideways market is very, very difficult to trade.
Lower odds when the higher timeframe of your entry timeframe is sideways. H1 entry with a sideways daily = lower odds. H4 entry with a sideways weekly = lower odds.
Higher odds when your higher timeframe is trending (up or down - we are not biased) OR price is at a higher-timeframe supply/demand zone.
You do not need a trend if price is at a HTF zone: e.g. pulling back into daily demand that is not in a downtrend is still a long candidate.
Four-chart layout: every timeframe sideways - a 'picture perfect' example; real cases are often less obvious. Weekly sideways since August 2024 (over a year), so H4 zones are lower odds.
A weekly trend can take about a year to form; the higher the timeframe, the more you can ignore this rule and just trade with more caution.

5m entry: H1 sideways between two marked lines. Wait for a break: break the high -> peak, valley, higher high and a trendline that guides when to stop looking for longs; break the low -> mirror for shorts.
If H1 downtrend forms -> day-trading shorts are good. If daily downtrend or price at daily demand -> longs are good.
If he were doing a market breakdown right now: no trading options until a high or low breaks on the H1.
You can still trade inside a sideways market (e.g. a range on 5m) - it is just lower odds in his opinion.

H4 example: a supply and a demand inside a big messy range both got blasted through. He did not count them as setups - 'absolutely hate it'. Wait for price to leave the range into higher-quality zones above or below.
A pullback into the daily demand here would not form a downtrend (the peak and valley are not good enough for a trendline), but you can still go long because it is at a demand zone.

passages.t: Lower odds does not mean he stops trading the pair: 'it's not like we're not gonna take trades... we understand that it's just gonna be lower odds' for all the H4 zones.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra points from the USD/JPY example
passages.t: On H4 there were high-quality zones above the range but not really any below it. Wait for price to pull out of the range into those zones.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra points from the USD/JPY example
passages.t: Day-trading longs or shorts become good depending on which side of the H1 range price breaks out of.

passages.t: A pullback into the 144.18–145.24 daily demand would not make a downtrend (peak and valley not good enough), but it is still a long because it is at a daily zone.
The rule as he applies it to USD/JPY: 5m→H1, H1→Daily, H4→Weekly. Every higher timeframe is sideways, so everything is lower odds until a trend forms or price reaches a HTF zone.

His 03:12 sketch on the 1h: no trades between ~147.0 and ~148.15. A break of the high (peak, valley, higher high and trendline) toward 1h supply 148.585 means longs, and a break of the low is the mirror for shorts.

The 4h messy range (~146.2–149.1): zones inside it got blasted through. The quality zones are outside it: 4h/daily supply 150.38–150.92 above, daily demand 144.18–145.24 below (a long even without a downtrend), and the next 4h demand far down at 141.49–142.09.
Trading zones inside a messy range on the higher timeframe. Treating sideways as tradeable at full confidence. Waiting for a trend at a HTF zone when the zone itself is the reason to trade.

Is the higher timeframe of my entry timeframe trending? If not, is price at a higher-timeframe supply/demand zone? Is this zone sitting inside a big messy range? Am I waiting for a break of the range high/low before trading? If I trade sideways conditions anyway, am I trading with extra caution? Has the H1 broken its range high or low yet (if not, no day-trading options for him)?

“It's lower odds to be trading when your higher timeframe to your entry timeframe is going sideways.” “We're not biased long or short.” “That was just trading in a big messy range. Absolutely hate it.”
“It's always going to be higher odds when we are trading with a trend on our higher timeframe.”
“I don't see any trading options until we can break a low or break a high on the one hour chart.”

Weekly trends can take ~a year to form; the higher the timeframe, the more you can relax the sideways rule and just trade with caution. Zones inside a big messy range are not setups - wait for price to leave the range. A HTF zone alone (without a trend) is enough to make a trade higher odds.
Range breakout creates the trend and trendline that guides when to stop looking for longs/shorts.

When the bigger chart just goes sideways, trading is harder. Wait. Picture a ball in a hallway, bouncing between two walls. It goes left, right, left, right, and nobody knows which way it goes next. That is a sideways market. When a door opens and the ball rolls out one side, now it has a direction. Kevin waits for the ball to roll out, or for it to reach a big strong wall (a higher-timeframe zone).
A ping-pong ball between two walls: no direction until it escapes.
Lower odds when the higher timeframe of your entry timeframe is sideways (H1 entry -> daily; H4 entry -> weekly).
Higher odds when that higher timeframe is trending (up or down) OR price is at a higher-timeframe zone. Zones inside a big messy range are not setups. Wait for a break of the range high or low.

passages.h: Step: The higher timeframe is sideways
passages.t: Price bounces between a range high and a range low. If this is the chart above your entry timeframe, your trades are lower odds.
A demand and a supply form inside the range. They look like zones...
...but price blasts straight through both. Kevin did not count these as setups: "Absolutely hate it." Messy ranges eat zones.
The answer is patience. No trading options until price breaks the range high or low.
After the break: a peak, a valley, then a higher high. Now there is an uptrend and a trendline to guide when to stop looking for longs. Higher odds again.

When are trades lower odds? - When the HTF of your entry timeframe is sideways. HTF of an H1 entry? Of an H4 entry? - Daily. Weekly. Two things that make odds higher? - HTF trending (either way) OR price at a HTF zone. Zones inside a big messy range? - Not setups. Wait for price to leave the range. H1 range and you day trade on 5m? - No options until the H1 breaks its high or low.
Is Kevin biased long or short? - No. Trend up or down both work.

A short live Q&A clip on whether a wick through a zone removes it. A candle body closing through removes the zone; wicks generally do not, but he judges by the size of the wick relative to the candle body.
A body through the zone removes it. A big emotional wick through the zone does not remove it. Judge by the wick size compared with the body.
A candle body closing through the zone = removed. Obvious. Huge wicks through the zone = not removed.
It is about the size of the wick relative to the body: a big 'emotional' wick with a small body is not a removal.

His second comparison is ambiguous in the captions: two candles with similar emotional wicks - one with a body about as big as the wick, one with a much bigger body. He calls the one with the bigger body 'not removed', and says that when the body is that big the wick is not really big compared to the body, 'and we're not gonna call that removed'. The drawing is needed to be sure which case he means.

Clip from a live session: a member who joined late asked about a zone being violated by a wick. He says he had covered it in detail earlier and drew a 'removed' side and a 'not removed' side to compare examples.
00:00–00:06 EURUSD 1W/4h/1D/1h layout from the live session: each pane has a demand zone plus an uptrend line and a long bias.
00:12 He switches to a blank GBPUSD daily as a whiteboard. Pinned note: what qualifies as a zone = removes an opposing zone, removes a trendline, or makes an all-time high/low.
00:30 He draws one zone, splits the board, and marks ✓ (removed) on the left and ✗ (not removed) on the right.
01:24 Removed side: a candle body closes below the zone's distal line. Not-removed side: small bodies in the zone with very long lower wicks.
02:12 He adds more wick examples on the ✗ side, ending with two candles that share the same emotional wick: one with a small body, one with a huge body. Both stay on the not-removed side.

The drawing settles the ambiguous comparison in the notes. Both "emotional wick" candles (small body and huge body) are drawn on the ✗ "not removed" side. The big-body one is not a removal because its wick is small compared with its body.

Sharper rule from the board: a zone is removed when a candle BODY closes beyond its distal line. A body sitting inside the zone, or a wick of any length through it, does not remove it. The notes only say "a body closing through the zone".
The board example is a demand zone with price coming down into it: the wicks pierce downward and the removal is a body below the bottom line. Mirror it for supply.
The clip opens on a pinned note the notes do not mention: "What qualifies as a Zone? 1. Removes opposing zone 2. Removes a trendline 3. Makes all time high/low".

passages.t: His three conditions for a zone are pinned on the chart. Removal is the reason a zone exists, so knowing when a zone is removed matters.

passages.h: Chart: [00:30] He draws one zone (a rectangle), splits the board with a vertical line, and puts a tick (✓) above the left half and an X (✗) above the right half.
passages.t: Left (✓) = removed. Right (✗) = not removed. The same zone is used for both so only the candles differ.

passages.h: Chart: [01:24] Removed side: four candles in the zone. One BODY extends below the bottom (distal) line of the zone. Not-removed side: two candles with small bodies inside the zone and very long lower wicks reaching far below it.
passages.t: He draws a demand zone that price comes down into. Removal is a body closing beyond the distal (bottom) line.

passages.h: Chart: [01:24] Removed side: four candles in the zone. One BODY extends below the bottom (distal) line of the zone. Not-removed side: two candles with small bodies inside the zone and very long lower wicks reaching far below it.
passages.t: On the not-removed side the wicks are much longer than on the removed side. Wick length alone never removes the zone.

passages.h: Chart: [02:12] The finished board. The ✗ side now holds six candles: bodies inside or above the zone with long lower wicks, then the final pair. One has a small body above the zone and an emotional wick. The other has a huge body running from the zone up into the 1.52 supply band, with the same wick below.
passages.t: The final pair is the "two pretty emotional wicks" comparison. BOTH are drawn on the not-removed side.

passages.h: Chart: [02:12] The finished board. The ✗ side now holds six candles: bodies inside or above the zone with long lower wicks, then the final pair. One has a small body above the zone and an emotional wick. The other has a huge body running from the zone up into the 1.52 supply band, with the same wick below.
passages.t: The big-body candle's wick is small compared with its body, so "we're not gonna call that removed". Not one candle on the ✗ side has a body that closes below the distal line.
His board redrawn: the ✓ (removed) side has a candle body closing through the distal line. The ✗ (not removed) side has long wicks only, with every body inside or above the zone.
The final comparison: an emotional wick on a small body and the same wick on a huge body are both "not removed". A body closing through the distal is what removes the zone.
The note pinned on his whiteboard chart: a zone qualifies if its move removes an opposing zone, removes a trendline, or makes an all-time high/low.
Deleting a zone because a wick poked through it.
Did a candle body close through the zone? Or was it only a wick - and how big is the wick compared to its body?
“It's all about the size of the wick.” “They're two pretty emotional wicks.”
Wick vs body rule for zone removal - the PDFs do not define when a zone is removed by a wick.

A body closing through breaks a zone; a quick wick poke usually does not. Imagine a fence. A kid reaches an arm through the gap and pulls it back. The fence is still standing. But if the whole kid walks through and stays on the other side, the fence is broken. A candle body is the kid's whole body. A wick is just an arm reaching through. An arm through the fence (wick) vs walking through it (body close).
A candle body closing through the zone removes it. A big emotional wick through the zone does not remove it. Judge by the wick size compared with the body.
Base, big move away. We draw the demand: distal on the lowest wick, proximal on the top of the base.

passages.h: Step: A huge wick stabs through
passages.t: A candle shoots a long wick way below the zone, but its small body closes back up. The wick is huge compared to the body: an emotional wick.
Kevin does not call that removed. Treat the zone as still alive. Price rallied away again.
Later a normal candle closes its body below the distal line. That is obvious: the zone is removed. Mark it and stop extending it.

Body closes through the zone? - Removed. Huge wick, small body through the zone? - Not removed (emotional wick). How to judge a wick? - Size of the wick compared with the body. Common mistake? - Deleting a zone because a wick poked through.

A live Sunday session: a quick recap of what a zone and a trendline are, then a full 'chain analysis' homework walkthrough on the daily chart (Jan 1990 to Jan 1991). He covers when to draw a zone, how to draw, adjust, end and remove trendlines, borderline zones, all-time highs, and common homework mistakes.
A zone needs basing, an explosive move away AND a stay-away candle. No stay-away candle = no zone yet.
Only draw a zone if it removes an opposing zone, removes a trendline, or makes an all-time high.
Upward trendline = peak + blatant valley + a higher high above the peak. Downward = peak + valley + a lower low.
A trendline must not cut through any candles. Attach from the lowest point, adjusting to the next lowest if needed.
Upward trendline is removed only by a full candle close (body and wick) below it. Downward only by a full candle close above it.

A demand's basing must be below the supply it removed (supply's basing above the demand it removed). A wick poking past it disqualifies it. When a zone is removed, end it and mark it removed. Keep charts clean. Don't force zones. If nothing removed it, the chain ends. End an overextended trendline. Don't extend it. Use the magnet tool (or hold Ctrl) so trendlines and zone lines snap exactly to wicks.
Copy every one of his zones every week. At minimum, carry over the zones he lists, so the chain continues correctly.

passages.h: Recap: what a zone is (3 parts)
passages.t: A zone needs: (1) basing candle or candles, (2) an explosive move away, (3) a stay-away candle. The move away must be an explosive candle, clearly bigger than the basing.

passages.h: Recap: what a zone is (3 parts)
passages.t: Without a stay-away candle there is NO zone yet, even when the move-away candle is explosive. Price could open the next candle and pull straight back.

passages.h: Recap: what a zone is (3 parts)
passages.t: What you want is space between the explosive candle and the proximal line. The bigger the space, the better the zone.

passages.h: Recap: what a zone is (3 parts)
passages.t: Telltale sign of a basing candle: big wicks. A candle with big wicks is basing, not the move away.

passages.h: Recap: what a zone is (3 parts)
passages.t: Rally-base-rally example: 'barely a zone'. Look at the space and the stay-away candle before calling it.
Upward trendline: there is always a peak, then a BLATANT valley (a deep one everybody can see). Small dips don't count.
That isn't enough on its own: after the peak forms, price must make a higher high above that peak.
Downward trendline: a peak and a valley, then price must break to a lower low. Peak with no lower low = no trendline.
Momentum line vs trendline: a line across shallow pullbacks is a momentum line, not a trendline (watch the trendline vs momentum lessons).
Sideways price action, or a line that is 'too horizontal', is not a trendline even if there is a peak and a valley.
Borderline case: almost too much sideways action, but 'one last candle peak' made it a real peak for him. Quick peak-and-valley moves still count but are easy to miss.

Attach the second touch point to the valley, starting from the lowest point. The trendline must not cut through any candles (bodies or wicks). If it does, move it to the next lowest point that cuts nothing. With practice you place it right away. Use the magnet tool, or hold Ctrl while dragging, to snap the line to the exact wick.
Adjusting: if price reacts off the trendline and then makes a new high, redraw the trendline to the new swing.
Overextended trendline: put the channel tool on it (a normal trendline plus a parallel line attached to the first peak). If price trades above the channel, the trendline is irrelevant.
When a trendline becomes irrelevant, END it on your chart. It doesn't have to stop at an exact spot. Extending it says it is still valid, which it isn't.

Upward trendline: removed only by a FULL candle close below it, body and wick both below. A candle whose body or wick still touches the line has not removed it. Downward trendline: removed only by a full candle close above it.
Example: many would say the line broke on an earlier candle, but the wick still touched it. It was removed on the later candle that closed fully below.
He says these are his own rules to stay rule-based: 'I'm not saying this is the only way to do it.'

Map out every zone that removes an opposing zone and every zone that removes a trendline. Only draw a zone when it (a) removes an opposing zone, (b) removes a trendline, or (c) makes an all-time high. If you draw a zone, it had better have done one of these.
When a zone is removed, mark it with the remove tool (rectangle in a different colour) and stop extending it. Keep charts very clean. Extended zones are his 'biggest pet peeve'.
To find the zone that did the removing, take the zone NEAREST to the removed opposing zone. If that isn't valid, go further down (or up) to the next one.
Don't force zones. Don't draw a tiny zone to call it a gap zone. If no supply removed a trendline, the chain simply ends there. That is why his charts are sometimes empty.
One zone can remove several things at once (e.g. one demand removed 2 supply areas, or a supply plus an all-time high).
Put the rules on your chart (like Jeff did) and check each zone against them. If it didn't remove anything, you can't have it.
For a demand to count as the one that removed a supply, its basing must be below that supply, before the supply was removed. For supply it is reversed: the basing must be above the opposing demand.

Example: a group of 3 basing candles was respected by the supply, but one candle's wick peaked just above it. So that demand is NOT the one that removed the supply, even though it looks like a demand zone.
A wick barely above the supply counts the same as basing far above it. You only see this when you zoom in.
All-time high: zones also form when price makes an all-time high, using the same basing rule.
An all-time high doesn't have to be a blatant peak. Every high that price breaks past is an all-time high.
Example: he compared candle bodies as a quick visual check, 2.06 vs 1.96. It was very close to not being a demand zone. When unsure whether a zone is a zone, draw it and see how it looks.
He normally draws only ONE zone. Two are acceptable only when the case is 'very, very close'. Here he'd probably keep the more obvious lower one, but he wouldn't call either choice wrong.
'You're gonna have rules, but... it's gonna be very borderline' sometimes. Trading is never super easy.
In homework, drawing two zones for the same removal (when it isn't borderline) is wrong. Only one zone removed it.

passages.h: Q&A: proven zones, old zones, HTF control
passages.t: Q: If a zone is respected or tested and then removed, is the zone that removed it more valid? A: Yes. Several reactions off a supply prove it was real supply, so the demand that breaks it is more powerful.

passages.h: Q&A: proven zones, old zones, HTF control
passages.t: If price just blasts through a zone with no reaction, the zone that removed it is still valid and he'll still trade it, but it gives him less confidence.

passages.h: Q&A: proven zones, old zones, HTF control
passages.t: Old zones: a daily zone from 1990 got its first pullback in 1991. Good zone, but he would not take it. He wants a pullback in a reasonable time, not a year or more later.

passages.h: Q&A: proven zones, old zones, HTF control
passages.t: Very old zones have little liquidity and no support or resistance built up, which is why you see old zones break.

passages.h: Q&A: proven zones, old zones, HTF control
passages.t: When price hesitates for a long time, open a higher timeframe (weekly, monthly, 3-month). Often a macro HTF zone is in control. Not in this example, but many times it is.

passages.h: Zone drawing corrections from homework review
passages.t: Include all the basing candles and their wicks when they are close. Including them doesn't make the zone massive. Leave a wick out only if it is far away. Wrap the proximal line tight against the basing, right before the explosive move. Draw the lines around the basing candle(s), not around the explosive candle.

passages.h: Zone drawing corrections from homework review
passages.t: Tighten zones: there is no need to go wick to wick, but getting the right area matters most. Don't put a distal line randomly in the middle of a candle. Attach it to the wick.

passages.h: Zone drawing corrections from homework review
passages.t: Supply/demand is NOT 'old resistance becomes new support'. The S&D way: supply removed by demand, then buy the pullback to that demand.

passages.h: Zone drawing corrections from homework review
passages.t: 'Not a good enough move away' = not a zone. A drop-base-rally or rally-base-drop label alone isn't enough.
Use the daily chart. Homework not on the daily (e.g. 4h) can't be marked. Submit a chart LINK with sharing on, not a screenshot. Submit once only; duplicates confuse marking.

Copy his zones and trendlines exactly, to the pip, on the FXCM broker feed. Delete every zone he didn't draw before next week. He uses TradingView. Next homework: January 1991 to January 1992. Also map out the all-time high. Keep sessions to homework. Confused? Watch the welcome video.
Homework is optional, but practice takes you from confused, to about 90% right but slow, to mapping fast after 1-3 months. Chain analysis isn't the holy grail. Its value is keeping you rule-based.
Rules help psychology. A great move from a zone with no trendline or opposing zone removed is 'not a trade'. Missing it shouldn't bother you, and rules stop you forcing trades or changing your rules.

passages.h: More from the lesson: More walkthrough details (Jan 1990 to Jan 1991)
passages.t: First demand that removed a supply: three basing candles before 'not the best explosive move away'. He included all three in the basing.

passages.h: More from the lesson: More walkthrough details (Jan 1990 to Jan 1991)
passages.t: Respected supply example: price reacted off a supply many times ('clearly there is supply here, but it just couldn't hold'). Buyers took over and pushed price up, so the demand that removed it is a strong one.

passages.h: More from the lesson: More walkthrough details (Jan 1990 to Jan 1991)
passages.t: Not a downward trendline: there was a peak but no lower low. Another case was sideways price action: 'if we just had one more little spike down' there would have been a good enough valley.

passages.h: More from the lesson: More walkthrough details (Jan 1990 to Jan 1991)
passages.t: All the zones look a little different but very similar: basing, then explosive move away, every time.

passages.h: More from the lesson: More walkthrough details (Jan 1990 to Jan 1991)
passages.t: After a trendline removal, a demand gave 'a beautiful setup there to target the all-time highs'. A single-candle-basing demand that removed a supply plus an all-time high gave 'a nice little 1:1'. The zone didn't work that great.

passages.h: More from the lesson: More walkthrough details (Jan 1990 to Jan 1991)
passages.t: Final example: a supply and a trendline both removed by one demand with single-candle basing and an explosive move away, 'picture perfect'.

passages.h: More from the lesson: More walkthrough details (Jan 1990 to Jan 1991)
passages.t: When he can already see a zone was removed, he uses the remove tool directly rather than checking it with another tool (he mentions not needing his Fibonacci tool).

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra homework-review corrections
passages.t: Draw trendlines from the lowest touch point available. A line not attached to a valley 'from down there' makes no sense.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra homework-review corrections
passages.t: A line 'too horizontal' is not a trendline, and drawing it can make you ignore the real trendline nearby.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra homework-review corrections
passages.t: Don't call a candle the explosive move when it is really the basing candle. Moving the proximal line shows the real zone, and you then see the trade off it.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra homework-review corrections
passages.t: If two basing candles are close together, include both. Including them doesn't make the zone massive.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra homework-review corrections
passages.t: Use the magnet tool: either turn it on, or hold Ctrl while dragging a trendline or zone edge so it snaps to the nearest wick. Use different colours. Yellow zones are very hard to see.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra homework-review corrections
passages.t: Overcorrecting: a member who drew too many zones started drawing too few. The goal is to fine-tune what should be drawn.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra homework-review corrections
passages.t: Members' DBR/RBD/RBR labels were often technically correct even when the move away was 'barely good enough' to be a zone. Don't tag him in homework. He only looks at it on Sunday.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra homework-review corrections
passages.t: Screenshots are only for video-lesson homework. Sunday chain-analysis homework is a shared chart link.

passages.h: More from the lesson: Extra homework-review corrections
passages.t: If you're new and confused, rewatch old Sunday sessions (he keeps them up until his Zoom storage runs out) and the welcome video. Mute your mic during sessions. Homework at about 98% is very rare. A couple of members reached it in this session.
