Trendline.JPG redrawn: a peak, a blatant valley, then a higher high. The line starts at the lowest point and cuts no candles. Right: once price trades above the channel (a parallel line on the first peak), end the trendline.

From his GBPUSD 1990 example: the basing candles inside the 1.71486–1.74700 supply have wicks reaching its distal, so that demand did not remove the supply. A demand that removes a supply must base fully below it.
The member's AUDNZD idea ("4hr supply zone act as Demand zone now") is an S/R flip. The S&D way: the supply is removed by a demand that based below it, and you buy the pullback to that demand.

Homework corrections: wrap the lines around the basing, include close basing candles and their wicks, keep the proximal tight before the explosive candle, and put the distal on a wick, not mid-candle.

Calling a zone off an explosive candle before a stay-away candle forms. Drawing momentum lines, or sideways/too-horizontal lines, as trendlines. Trendlines that cut through candles or aren't attached to the low or wick. Treating a wick touch, or a candle still touching the line, as a trendline break. Extending removed zones or irrelevant trendlines. Messy charts. Drawing two zones for one removal.

Leaving out nearby basing candles or wicks, or wrapping lines around the explosive candle instead of the basing. Missing trendlines that need adjusting after a new high. Using the demand whose basing wick peaked above the supply as the one that 'removed' it.
Thinking of S/R ('old resistance becomes new support') instead of supply removed by demand. Taking a very old zone whose first pullback comes a year or more later.

Homework errors: wrong timeframe, screenshots instead of links, not copying his zones, submitting twice. Overcorrecting from drawing too many zones to drawing too few. Drawing zones in hard-to-see colours (e.g. yellow). Tagging him on homework or submitting screenshots for Sunday homework. Calling the basing candle the explosive move by misplacing the proximal line.
Is there a stay-away candle, with clear space between the explosive candle and the proximal line? Did this zone remove an opposing zone, remove a trendline, or make an all-time high?

Is the basing fully below the supply it removed (or above the demand), with no wick poking past? Is this the zone nearest to the removed opposing zone? For a trendline break: did a full candle (body and wick) close beyond the line? Is the trendline still relevant (not overextended beyond the channel)?

Is the trendline built on a blatant peak and valley plus a higher high or lower low, without cutting candles? Was the removed opposing zone respected or tested before it broke (more confidence)? Is the zone recent enough? No year-later first pullback on an old zone?
Are all nearby basing candles and wicks included, with the proximal line tight to the basing?
Is the trendline attached to the lowest available valley point (snapped with magnet/Ctrl)? Have I carried over all of his zones and trendlines from last week before starting?

“The bigger the space, the better the zone.” “We're not gonna force zones... the analysis just ends.” “Every single high we break is an all-time high.” “It just didn't follow my rules. There's nothing I can do about it.” “Clearly there is supply here, but it just couldn't hold.” “This isn't the holy grail, this is just the chain analysis... it keeps us rule-based.”
Stay-away candle as a required third part of a zone, and 'space between the explosive candle and proximal line' as a quality measure.

Chain analysis rule: only draw zones that remove an opposing zone, remove a trendline or make an all-time high. All-time high is a new qualifier not in the PDFs. 'Every high broken is an all-time high', with no blatant peak needed.
Exact trendline definition: blatant valley plus a higher high. Draw from the lowest point without cutting candles; magnet tool / Ctrl to snap to wicks.
Trendline removal requires a full candle close (body and wick) beyond the line. A wick touch doesn't count.
Adjusting a trendline after a new high. Ending overextended trendlines using the channel tool.
Basing must be below the supply it removed (above the demand for supply). A wick barely past disqualifies it.
Take the removing zone nearest to the removed opposing zone. Two zones only in very borderline cases.

A zone that removes a proven (respected/tested) zone is stronger than one that removes a zone price blasted through. Very old zones (first pullback a year or more later) aren't traded: little liquidity.
Long hesitation often means a HTF macro zone is in control. Check weekly, monthly, 3-month.
Include nearby basing wicks. Never put a distal line mid-candle. Big wicks mark a basing candle.
Rule-based system framed as a psychology tool: no regret over missed trades that broke the rules.

Only draw zones that beat something: a zone, a trendline, or an all-time high. Think of a tug-of-war. Sellers held the rope at the top twice. Then buyers pulled so hard they won and dragged the rope far away. The spot where buyers gathered before that big pull is our demand. We only draw zones like that, ones that beat something. If nobody beat anyone, there is nothing to draw, and that is fine.
A tug-of-war: draw where the winning team stood before the big pull.
A zone needs basing, an explosive move away AND a stay-away candle. Bigger space = better zone.
Only draw a zone if it removed an opposing zone, removed a trendline, or made an all-time high. Its basing must sit below the supply it removed (above the demand for supply).
Trendlines are removed only by a full candle close beyond them. End removed zones and irrelevant lines; keep charts clean.

passages.h: Step: A supply that is respected
passages.t: Sellers made a supply zone. Price came back twice and got pushed down both times. Clearly there is supply here.
Price pauses below the supply. The whole base, wicks too, is below the supply's proximal line. That position matters.

passages.h: Step: Explosive move removes the supply
passages.t: An explosive candle closes above the supply: removed. A stay-away candle follows. Mark the supply as removed and stop extending it.

passages.h: Step: Draw the demand that did it
passages.t: Now we draw the demand nearest to the removed supply. It removed a proven supply, so Kevin trusts it more.
Wait for the pullback to the demand: entry at the proximal, stop under the distal. The S&D way is "supply removed by demand, buy the pullback", not "old resistance becomes support".

Three parts of a zone (Sunday recap)? - Basing, explosive move away, stay-away candle. Three reasons to draw a zone? - It removed an opposing zone, removed a trendline, or made an all-time high. Where must a demand's basing be? - Fully below the supply it removed (wicks too). How is an uptrend line removed? - Full candle close below it: body and wick.

Which zone removed the supply? - The one nearest to the removed supply (if valid). Nothing removed the trendline? - Do not force a zone. The chain ends. Very old zone, first pullback a year later? - He would not take it: little liquidity. Overextended trendline? - Use the channel tool; if price trades above it, end the line.

On EUR/GBP H1 with a daily HTF, Kevin shows that the difference is when the entry zone formed: an H1 zone embedded inside the daily zone (formed with it) is set & forget, while an H1 zone formed after the daily zone was contacted is a confirmation zone. Both are still traded with an order you set and manage.
An H1 zone formed as part of the daily zone's move is embedded = set & forget, not confirmation.
A confirmation zone forms after the HTF zone is contacted and removes something (e.g. a trendline).
Technically any zone is a set & forget - you set the order and kind of forget it (still managing it). So the difference is not how you place the order but how the zone was formed.

Daily demand formed by removing a trendline; price pulled back to it and rallied out. Zone 1: an H1 demand inside the daily demand that was formed WHEN the daily zone formed - part of the daily move. That is an embedded H1 zone = set & forget.
Zone 2: price came back to the daily demand, contacted it, pushed out and removed a trendline, forming an H1 demand outside the daily zone = confirmation zone.
Common mistake: calling the embedded zone a confirmation trade just because it is inside the daily zone.

Formed while the HTF zone was forming -> set & forget (embedded). Formed after the HTF zone was contacted (with a removal, e.g. a trendline) -> confirmation. Both can look like set & forget trades in practice.

His position tool on Zone 2: entry 0.87340, stop 8.7 pips below the distal, target about 0.8750 under the prior H1 highs, R:R 1.89.

Calling an embedded LTF zone inside the HTF zone a confirmation trade.
Was my entry zone formed while the HTF zone was forming (set & forget)? Or after the HTF zone was contacted (confirmation)?
If I call it confirmation, did the move remove a trendline or opposing zone after contact?
“Technically any zone is a set and forget.” “This zone was formed when the daily zone was forming. This zone was formed after the daily zone was contacted.”
“So they may both look like set and forget trades... but just remember this is a confirmation zone.”

The timing test: embedded zone formed with the HTF zone = set & forget; zone formed after HTF contact = confirmation. The PDFs say confirmation trades zones formed after contact and S&F trades zones formed outside HTF zones; he adds that an embedded zone inside the HTF zone is also set & forget.

Same order type, different birthday: when the small zone was born decides its name. Two puppies live in the same house. One was born in the house when the family moved in. The other came later, after the family met it at the park and it proved it was friendly. Both are now house puppies, but they arrived differently. A small zone born together with the big zone is set & forget. A small zone born later, after price touched the big zone and broke something, is confirmation.
Born with the house (embedded = set & forget) vs adopted later after a test (confirmation).
The difference is not how you place the order. Any zone is "set" and managed. An H1 zone formed WHILE the daily zone formed (embedded) = set & forget.
An H1 zone formed AFTER price contacted the daily zone and removed something (e.g. a trendline) = confirmation.
Price falls, bases, then explodes up and removes a downtrend line. That base is the daily demand.

passages.h: Step: Zone 1: born with the daily zone
passages.t: Inside that daily base sits an H1 demand. It formed at the same time, as part of the daily move. That is an embedded zone: set & forget.

passages.h: Step: Price comes back and contacts
passages.t: Later price drops back with a new downtrend line and touches the daily demand. Contact.
Price pushes out, bases just above the daily zone, then an explosive candle removes the trendline. The new H1 demand formed AFTER contact and after a removal: a confirmation zone.

passages.h: Step: Both look like set & forget
passages.t: Both get a limit order you set and manage, so both can look like set & forget. Just remember which one is which: the timing of its birth decides.

Is the S&F vs confirmation difference in the order type? - No. It is how and when the zone formed. H1 zone formed with the daily zone? - Embedded = set & forget. H1 zone formed after daily contact + removal? - Confirmation zone.
Common mistake? - Calling an embedded zone a confirmation trade just because it is inside the daily zone.
What usually gets removed for confirmation? - A trendline or an opposing zone, after contact.

Kevin continues last week's chain-analysis homework, drawing only zones that remove an opposing zone, remove a trendline or make an all-time high/low, and walks through each new zone and trendline in order.

The big theme is trendlines: attach each new one to the most recent peak (or valley), move it only when it would cut through candles, fall back to the original starting point when it is too horizontal, and know that one missed trendline can cost several zones further down the chain.

He says he prefers a zone whose first explosive candle is followed by a second explosive move over one that bases again before moving, and he explains why some zones that won still were not trades he would take (already tested before they qualified, or a weak move away).

In Q&A he covers realistic stop placement (visual rather than measured, wider on gold/oil and in volatile conditions, and wider again when the zone sits at the proximal line of a higher-timeframe zone), keeping zones a similar size, and zones price comes back to straight away. The new homework is January 1992 to January 1993, with the all-time high mapped first.

Only draw zones that remove an opposing zone, remove a trendline, or make an all-time high/low. One of the three is enough. If nothing qualifies, draw nothing. The first candle after the basing must be an explosive move, every time. Do not stretch a zone wick to wick if that makes it too big. Use the core basing candles.
Attach a new trendline to the most recent peak (downtrend) or valley (uptrend), never to a random point.
If the trendline cuts through candles, move it to the next highest (or lowest) point that does not cut any.
If a new trendline from the recent peak is too horizontal, go back to the original starting point and draw from there.
A trendline is removed only when a candle closes beyond it with its full body and wick. A wick touch does not remove it.
If there is a trend but the trendline would be nearly flat, mark the trend with an arrow and draw no line.

If a new trendline is as good as the old one, usually remove the old one. Keep both when one is the overall line and the other is a temporary, aggressive line. Do not draw two trendlines from the same anchor point. There is only one. Keep removed or untradeable zones on the chart so you can see what removes them. Extend zones and trendlines until the point where they are actually removed.

A zone tested before it qualified (before it removed anything) is still the zone, but it is not a trading setup. A wick on the move-away candle is fine if the body is big enough. Put the proximal line where it belongs, even if the zone gets a little larger.
If you include a group of candles in a zone, include all their wicks. Do not ignore one wick. Keep zones a similar size and avoid tiny zones.
Place stops by eye, a little beyond the zone in normal conditions, and wider on gold, oil and in volatile news conditions. Use tighter stops only if your spread is minimal.

When the entry zone sits at a higher-timeframe zone's proximal line, put the stop about halfway into the higher-timeframe zone, not below all of it. Do not expect very old zones to hold. Update your chart every week with any zones you missed. Map out the all-time high (and its supply) before starting the new homework range.

Only ONE of the three is needed. A zone does not need two or all three.

passages.t: There was a demand zone further back that barely qualified, and it was the latest zone. Price pushed down and removed that demand.

passages.t: Choosing the supply: many students would pick one area as the zone, but in his opinion a different move away was 'just a little bit better', so that is the supply.

passages.h: Walkthrough 1: picking the supply that removed demand, and anchoring the first downtrend line
passages.t: Drawing it from the wick across the whole area would be too big, so he uses only two candles as the basing.

passages.h: Walkthrough 1: picking the supply that removed demand, and anchoring the first downtrend line
passages.t: That supply is valid because it did rule number one: it removed an opposing area of demand.

passages.h: Walkthrough 1: picking the supply that removed demand, and anchoring the first downtrend line
passages.t: As price pushed down it made a clear valley, a peak and a lower low, so there will be a trendline.

passages.h: Walkthrough 1: picking the supply that removed demand, and anchoring the first downtrend line
passages.t: Trendline drawing: attach it from the top of the move (before the drop) to the top of the peak. Doing that cut through some candles at the top, so he moved the line to the next highest point where it no longer cuts candles. After that small adjustment it is still attached to the peak and cuts nothing.

passages.h: Walkthrough 1: picking the supply that removed demand, and anchoring the first downtrend line
passages.t: He says it is 'almost too sideways' for him, but there is enough angle for a peak and valley, so it stays.

passages.h: Walkthrough 1: picking the supply that removed demand, and anchoring the first downtrend line
passages.t: Trendline removal: the line is removed only by the candle that closes above it with its full body and wick. An earlier candle came very close but only touched the line with its wick, so that did not remove it.

passages.h: Walkthrough 1: picking the supply that removed demand, and anchoring the first downtrend line
passages.t: The demand zone that removed this trendline had already been tested before it actually became a zone (before it removed anything), so it would not have been a trading setup.

passages.h: Walkthrough 2: the next trendline, a tested supply, and a demand he would not take
passages.t: Another clear valley, peak and lower low, so another new trendline, drawn from the recent peak to the new peak. It is close to too horizontal, but it looks fine.

passages.h: Walkthrough 2: the next trendline, a tested supply, and a demand he would not take
passages.t: If it had been too horizontal, he would go back to the original starting point and draw from there down to the new peak instead.

passages.h: Walkthrough 2: the next trendline, a tested supply, and a demand he would not take
passages.t: Price pushed down and removed a heavily tested area of demand. Looking up for the supply, the only candidate is one explosive move away.

passages.h: Walkthrough 2: the next trendline, a tested supply, and a demand he would not take
passages.t: Like before, that supply was already hit before it became a zone (before it removed anything). He explains that this is why you often see him draw a zone 'after the fact': nothing was removed yet, but it is still the supply even though it was tested.

passages.h: Walkthrough 2: the next trendline, a tested supply, and a demand he would not take
passages.t: Price then pushed and removed the trendline. Explaining the removal: the line was respected once, then removed when neither the wick nor the body touched it, with the whole candle sitting above the line.

passages.h: Walkthrough 2: the next trendline, a tested supply, and a demand he would not take
passages.t: The zone that removed it was a small drop-base-rally with one explosive candle. 'Not the best zone, but what a trade.' It qualified as a trading setup, and it won big.

passages.h: Walkthrough 2: the next trendline, a tested supply, and a demand he would not take
passages.t: He is honest that he would not have taken it. The move away is good, but he would like to see another leg up proving there is more demand there.

passages.h: Trend without a trendline (the arrow with no line)
passages.t: After price hit that zone it broke a higher high, and there was a clear peak and valley, so there is clearly some sort of trend.

passages.h: Trend without a trendline (the arrow with no line)
passages.t: But the trendline you would draw is so horizontal that it is 'completely irrelevant'. If a student draws it on homework that is reasonable, but he will not be looking for it.

passages.h: Trend without a trendline (the arrow with no line)
passages.t: This is why, on his chart link, you sometimes see an up arrow (trend) with no trendline drawn: there is a trend, but no usable trendline.

passages.h: Walkthrough 3: rally-base-rally demand and the 'second explosive move' preference
passages.t: Price pushed up and removed the supply. It was removed by a rally-base-rally demand with a pretty decent move away, and that was a trade.

passages.h: Walkthrough 3: rally-base-rally demand and the 'second explosive move' preference
passages.t: The move away on another zone was actually better, but what he likes more about this zone is the continued move to the upside after it.

passages.h: Walkthrough 3: rally-base-rally demand and the 'second explosive move' preference
passages.t: Drawing on the chart: the first candle after the basing must ALWAYS be an explosive move. That is required for both versions he drew.

passages.h: Walkthrough 3: rally-base-rally demand and the 'second explosive move' preference
passages.t: Version A (preferred): basing, explosive candle, then ANOTHER explosive move. 'It really tells me there's a lot of demand here.'

passages.h: Walkthrough 3: rally-base-rally demand and the 'second explosive move' preference
passages.t: Version B (qualifies, less preferred): basing, explosive candle, then a bunch of basing candles, then another explosive move. There is demand, but it 'kind of based out'. Both qualify, but he much prefers version A for a high-quality setup.

passages.h: Old zones, liquidity traps, and keeping two trendlines
passages.t: A zone on the chart had been removed long ago. Zones from that long ago he no longer expects to hold.

passages.h: Old zones, liquidity traps, and keeping two trendlines
passages.t: There would have been a nice liquidity trap there. If price had pulled back right away, hit the zone and reacted off the liquidity, he would 'take that zone all day'. Students may mark that liquidity on their chart if they want.

passages.h: Old zones, liquidity traps, and keeping two trendlines
passages.t: Momentum versus trendline: he shows a flat line next to a steep one through a clear peak and valley, and says the steep one is momentum and that is a trendline. Draw it from the lowest point possible to the valley.

passages.h: Old zones, liquidity traps, and keeping two trendlines
passages.t: Another quick peak and valley forms (hard to tell), so a second, steeper trendline is drawn.

passages.h: Old zones, liquidity traps, and keeping two trendlines
passages.t: Usually, if the new trendline is as good as the old one, he removes the old one. Here he keeps both, because one is the overall trendline and the other is a temporary, aggressive one.

passages.h: Old zones, liquidity traps, and keeping two trendlines
passages.t: He goes back and removes a supply zone. It is not a setup he would take, but it stays on the chart so you can see what removes it.

passages.h: Walkthrough 4: a barely-qualifying zone and the last supply of the homework
passages.t: With the new trendline in place there is barely a zone: a rally-base-rally. The body of the candle is big enough to count as a move away, but he dislikes the tail-end wick and the overall size of the zone, so it is not a setup he would take.

passages.h: Walkthrough 4: a barely-qualifying zone and the last supply of the homework
passages.t: Last part of the homework: demand removed, trendline removed, and a very obvious area of supply above. There was no immediate pullback, so it was a bit old but 'actually not bad', a nice setup. That zone failed 'pretty miserably', but it is the kind of move away he would take, compared with the weaker one.

passages.h: Walkthrough 4: a barely-qualifying zone and the last supply of the homework
passages.t: Of all the zones, the only ones he would consider taking were that supply and the earlier rally-base-rally demand, which he calls mediocre because he wanted another explosive move. His verdict: the homework was 'actually not as bad as I expected'.

passages.h: Homework marking: trendline anchoring errors (most common mistake)
passages.t: Starting a trendline from a random point is wrong. It must be attached to the most recent peak (downtrend) or valley (uptrend). Even when a random start gives the same signal, it is not the right line.

passages.h: Homework marking: trendline anchoring errors (most common mistake)
passages.t: The only time he does not start at the exact peak is when attaching there would cut through candles. Then he moves to the next point that does not cut through candles. 'Starting it from here doesn't make any sense. Starting it from here, why not up here?'

passages.h: Homework marking: trendline anchoring errors (most common mistake)
passages.t: New peak and valley: draw the new trendline from the most recent peak, not from some random point, as long as it is not too sideways.

passages.h: Homework marking: trendline anchoring errors (most common mistake)
passages.t: Do not draw both an old line and a new line when they share the anchor point you are attaching to. There is only one trendline in that case. A line that ignores the price action between its points is 'not correct at all'.

passages.h: Homework marking: trendline anchoring errors (most common mistake)
passages.t: Almost nobody got the first trendline. Missing it was 'a fatal error': one missed trendline led to one, two, three missed zones, because each zone in the chain depends on what came before. 'That's the importance of the chain analysis.'

passages.h: Homework marking: trendline anchoring errors (most common mistake)
passages.t: Praise: one student properly updated a trendline by attaching it to the peak, not a random point higher up.

Not a demand: there was no explosive move away. A zone must have an explosive move away. Some students drew a zone above or below the right one, or drew one zone instead of the correct one. 'That's the zone, not that one.'
Proximal line: one student was told to move the proximal line up. It makes the zone a little larger, but that is where it belongs.
A wick on the move-away candle does not disqualify it if the body is still big enough. A missed supply with an explosive body caused later zones to be missed.
Ending zones: a zone that was not removed must be extended to the point where it was removed. Do not end it early. This applies to trendlines too ('just want to extend it').
Random zones: 'What did this zone break?' If a zone did not remove a demand/supply, a trendline or an all-time high/low, it does not belong on the chart.

Too big, and inconsistent: if you include all those candles in the zone you cannot ignore one wick. You would have to include everything, and then it is far too large, so draw a tighter zone instead. Gap zones: a student who drew a gap zone was told there is no zone there. No forced zones, which is praised: 'Nothing forced here, love it.'
Session separator: zones after a student's session marker are not counted against them, since they will draw them next week.
Disqualification reasons: when a student said 'basing too large disqualifies', he said it is not the basing. It is that the move away is not amazing and there is no further explosive move.

For a student who seemed new: copy all his zones onto your chart, follow the three rules, watch previous Sunday recordings, and take a trendline lesson. Tighten zones where possible, or make them bigger when they are too small.

passages.h: Data and broker differences (no-gap candles indicator)
passages.t: A student on EURUSD (FXCM) used a 'no gap candles' indicator. On that chart one area is clearly a demand zone, while on his chart the gap makes it look like no zone.

passages.h: Data and broker differences (no-gap candles indicator)
passages.t: He likes the indicator and says he may start using it ('Something to consider'). Based on it, the student should have had that demand.

passages.h: Data and broker differences (no-gap candles indicator)
passages.t: The student's candles looked different from his even on the same broker, and he said he was confused by it. Treat these zones as unresolved.
Homework: January 1992 to January 1993 on the homework chart. First map out the all-time high on your chart, which means you must have that supply zone.
Make it a habit every week to update your chart with any zones you missed (many students did not have a key zone).
There is no Sunday session next week. The Friday forecast still happens. Members whose membership ends can contact him. Homework marking next week may be postponed.
Read Trading in the Zone by Mark Douglas and practise trading psychology. 'Very important.' He will post Daily Market Breakdowns during the week.
He does not measure stops. He places them by eye and does not think measuring matters much.
In normal conditions the stop goes a little beyond the zone. That is a normal stop, not a wide one.
Gold and oil: use a wider stop, because they are volatile and, with the current political news (Trump), 'you never know'.
You can use a tighter stop if you pay little or nothing in spread. He pays spreads and is a swing trader, so a tighter stop does not matter to him.
Give the trade wiggle room. When he first practised day trading 5 to 6 years ago, his zone would be respected and then the spread would stop him out, especially around news.
Toward the end of 2025, zones were respected but trades were barely stopped out because of political headlines. The last month or two has been better, but a slightly wider stop is still sensible.
USDCAD example: a 4-hour demand zone sits right at the proximal line of a daily demand, and there is a weekly demand as well. A normal stop would give the daily zone almost no wiggle room.
Do not put the stop all the way below the daily zone either: 'you might as well just take the whole daily zone'.
Middle ground: put the stop about halfway into the daily zone, so the daily gets a chance to test half of it. The whole trade could still fail.
Summary: not every stop loss is the same. There is a normal stop, one that is too tight, one that is right for the market conditions, and a bigger one when a higher-timeframe zone is underneath.

passages.h: Q&A: zone sizes and immediate returns to the zone
passages.t: Try to keep zones a similar size. On gold, his zones are all very similar, though he rarely measures and there are minor differences.

passages.h: Q&A: zone sizes and immediate returns to the zone
passages.t: What he does not want is a tiny zone half the size of the others. 'Too small. Bigger the better', because if you go too small, 'there's zones everywhere'. A slightly smaller zone is fine; a tiny one is not.

passages.h: Q&A: zone sizes and immediate returns to the zone
passages.t: A zone that removes a previous zone, with a good base and a good explosive move away, but where price comes back quickly: you can draw it.

passages.h: Q&A: zone sizes and immediate returns to the zone
passages.t: He does not love it. From six years of experience, he likes price to stay a little away from the zone first. He does not really know why, but it seems to work out better.

passages.h: Q&A: zone sizes and immediate returns to the zone
passages.t: He has seen zones where the very next candle after the stay-away candle hit the zone and price still went to take profit, but it is not his favourite situation.

passages.h: Q&A: zone sizes and immediate returns to the zone
passages.t: He repeats that the best case is an explosive move followed by another explosive move. Only one is required.

passages.t: All three things happened (zone removed, trendline removed, all-time high) but there was no qualifying zone, so nothing is drawn.

passages.h: Chart: [03:00] After the all-time high: the new supply (two basing candles) drawn as a thin red box, extended right, and the first downward trendline from the top.
passages.t: The supply qualifies because it removed the demand below it (rule 1). He only uses the two basing candles; from the wick across the whole area would be too big.

passages.h: Chart: [03:00] After the all-time high: the new supply (two basing candles) drawn as a thin red box, extended right, and the first downward trendline from the top.
passages.t: The line first cut through candles at the top, so he slid it to the next highest point where it touches without cutting.

passages.h: Chart: [03:36] Same chart: an arrow points at the candle whose wick only touched the downtrend line.
passages.t: A wick touch does not remove a trendline. It is removed only by the later candle that closes above it with full body and wick.

passages.h: Chart: [05:24] Next leg: the tested demand is removed and an arrow marks the only supply candidate, one explosive move away, with the second downtrend line running through the peaks.
passages.t: This supply was already hit before it removed anything, which is why he often draws a zone "after the fact".

passages.h: Chart: [06:00] Two arrows: one at the candle that broke the trendline (whole candle above it), one at the small drop-base-rally demand underneath that removed it.
passages.t: "Not the best zone, but what a trade." It qualified as a setup and won big. He would not have taken it: he wanted a second leg up proving more demand.

passages.h: Chart: [07:48] Two arrows on the rally-base-rally demand (green box) that removed the supply above it.
passages.t: This is a trade. Another zone had a bigger single move away, but he prefers this one for the continued move up after it.

passages.h: Chart: [09:00] His sketch of the two versions: left, basing + explosive candle + another explosive candle; right, basing + explosive candle + a row of small basing candles + another explosive candle.
passages.t: Both qualify (the first candle after the basing must always be explosive). He much prefers the left one: "there's so much demand here". The right one "kind of based out".

passages.h: Chart: [10:12] Momentum vs trendline: from the same low he draws a steep line and a flatter line through the clear peak and valley (a short purple line marks a level at the valley).
passages.t: The steep one is momentum; the trendline is drawn from the lowest point to the valley. He then adds a second, more aggressive line from a quick peak and valley and keeps both: one overall, one temporary.

passages.h: Chart: [12:01] End of the homework section: an arrow at the supply (red box) at the top, after the demand and the trendline were removed.
passages.t: A bit old but "actually not bad", the kind of move away he would take, even though it failed "pretty miserably".

passages.h: Chart: [12:01] End of the homework section: an arrow at the supply (red box) at the top, after the demand and the trendline were removed.
passages.t: Of all the zones, he would only have considered this supply and the earlier rally-base-rally demand.

passages.h: Chart: [14:25] Marking a student (Hans): on the EURUSD 1D he draws the new downtrend line from the most recent peak, an arrow pointing at that peak.
passages.t: After a new peak and valley, do not start the line from a random point. Attach it to the most recent peak.

passages.h: Chart: [14:25] Marking a student (Hans): on the EURUSD 1D he draws the new downtrend line from the most recent peak, an arrow pointing at that peak.
passages.t: The student missed the earlier line, which led to the missed zones further down the chain.

passages.h: Chart: [17:25] A student's EURUSD 1D (FXCM) chart with the area circled where the candles do not look like his.
passages.t: Same broker, different-looking candles: he says he is confused by it. Treat those zones as unresolved.

passages.h: Chart: [31:51] Stefano's chart (red "not sure about this" note and an X on the chart): demand good, but a missed supply led to a missed demand lower down.
passages.t: "Picture perfect" apart from one missed zone; one miss costs the zones that depend on it.

passages.h: Chart: [35:27] Stop-loss Q&A on XAUUSD 1h (OANDA): a 1h supply between about 4,029.47 and 4,043.36 with a short-position box; he circles the stop area above the zone and draws the expected drop.
passages.t: Normal conditions: stop a little beyond the zone, placed by eye, not measured. Gold and oil: wider stops, especially in headline-driven conditions.

passages.h: Chart: [37:15] USDCAD 4h (OANDA): the 4h demand sits on the daily demand (cloned onto the 4h chart); the long-position box and his sketched path dip into the zone and then rally.
passages.t: A normal stop gives the daily zone almost no room; below the whole daily you might as well trade the daily. Middle ground: stop about halfway into the daily zone. The whole trade could still fail.

passages.h: Chart: [40:15] Sketch on gold 1h for a student question: a zone box with the explosive candles leaving it and later candles below.
passages.t: It still counts as a zone, but it is not his favourite. He prefers price to stay away from the zone for a while; the best case is an explosive move followed by another explosive move.

passages.h: Chart: Homework chart (not named; EURUSD FXCM per a student's chart), homework timeframe not stated
passages.t: Supply drawn from a two-candle basing after price removed the latest (barely qualified) demand Why: Rule 1: it removed an opposing demand. He chose the slightly better move away, and a wick-to-wick zone would have been too big, so he used only two basing candles. Result: Valid supply, kept on the chart. It led to a downtrend line from the valley, peak and lower low.
Demand zone that removed the first downtrend line Why: It removed the trendline, but the zone had already been tested before it qualified. Result: Not a trading setup.

Supply above the removed, heavily tested demand (single explosive move away) Why: It is the only supply candidate, but it was hit before it removed anything, which is why it was drawn 'after the fact'. Result: Valid zone, not a trading setup.

Small drop-base-rally demand with one explosive candle, which removed the second downtrend line Why: It qualified as a trading setup. He would not have taken it: he wanted another leg up to prove more demand. Result: Big winning trade. He was honest that he would have skipped it.

Higher high after a clear peak and valley, but the trendline is almost flat Why: There is a trend, but the line is irrelevant. He marks the trend with an arrow and draws no line. Result: Up arrow, no trendline.

Rally-base-rally demand that removed supply, followed by a continued move up Why: Another zone had the better move away, but he likes the continued explosive move after this one, which shows strong demand. Result: Counted as a trade.

Old zone that was removed long ago, with a liquidity trap Why: Old zones are not expected to hold. With an immediate pullback into the zone plus the liquidity he would 'take that zone all day'. Result: No immediate pullback, so no trade.
Rally-base-rally that barely qualifies Why: The body is big enough for a move away, but he dislikes the tail-end wick and the zone's size. Result: Not a setup he would take.

Obvious supply after demand and the trendline were removed (last zone of the homework) Why: A good move away and a nice setup, a little old since there was no immediate pullback. Result: The zone failed 'pretty miserably', but it was a zone he would take.

Stop loss in normal conditions, a little beyond the zone Why: Gold and oil are volatile, and political headlines make them riskier, so use a wider stop. Gold zones are also shown as an example of similar-size zones. Result: Illustration only.

passages.h: Chart: USDCAD 4H entry inside daily demand (weekly demand too)
passages.t: 4-hour demand at the proximal line of a daily demand Why: A normal stop gives the daily zone no wiggle room. A stop below the whole daily means you might as well trade the daily. The middle ground is a stop about halfway into the daily zone. Result: Live example of a wider stop. The outcome was not given, and he said the entire trade could fail.

Q: Can you touch on how to choose a stop loss realistically? A: He places stops by eye, not by measurement. Normal conditions: a little beyond the zone. Gold and oil: wider, because they are volatile and political headlines (Trump) make moves unpredictable. With minimal or zero spread you can go tighter. He pays spreads and swing trades, so it does not matter to him.

Always give the trade wiggle room: when he practised day trading 5 to 6 years ago, the spread stopped him out of zones that were respected, especially around news. In late 2025 many zones held but just stopped people out. When the entry zone (for example a USDCAD 4H demand) sits at the proximal line of a higher-timeframe zone (daily, with a weekly too), put the stop about halfway into the daily zone.
Not below the whole daily, or you might as well trade the daily itself, and not a normal tight stop, which gives the daily no room. Not every stop is the same.

Q: I noticed the zones are the same size. Should they be? A: Yes. Try to keep zones a similar size. His gold zones are all similar, though he rarely measures. Do not draw tiny zones half the size of the others. 'Too small. Bigger the better', because small zones mean zones everywhere. Slightly smaller is fine.

Q: Would you draw a zone that removes a previous zone, with a good base and a good explosive move away, if price comes back to it quickly? A: Yes, you can draw it, but he does not love it. In his six years he has found it works better when price stays a little away from the zone. He does not know exactly why.

He has seen the next candle after the stay-away candle hit the zone and still reach take profit, but it is not his favourite situation. The best case is an explosive move followed by another explosive move, though only one is required.

Q: A student noted that 'basing a little too large disqualifies' a zone. A: He agreed it was not a good zone, but said the basing was not the problem. The move away was not amazing and there was no further explosive move.

Starting a trendline from a random point instead of the most recent peak or valley. Missing one trendline, which then causes several missed zones down the chain. Drawing a trendline that ignores the price action between its points. Drawing both an old and a new trendline from the same anchor. Drawing zones without an explosive move away.

Drawing random zones that removed nothing (no zone, trendline or all-time high/low broken). Drawing zones far too big, or ignoring one wick while including the other candles. Ending a zone or trendline before it was actually removed. Drawing the wrong one of two nearby candidate zones. Putting the proximal line in the wrong place to keep the zone small. Drawing gap zones that are not zones.
Treating a wick on the move-away candle as disqualifying when the body is big enough. Treating a zone tested before it qualified as a trade.
Taking a qualifying but weak zone with one move away and no further explosive leg (he would skip it). Using a stop so tight that the spread or a news spike stops you out while the zone holds.

Putting the stop below the whole higher-timeframe zone, which defeats the point of the lower-timeframe entry. Drawing tiny zones much smaller than the rest. Not updating the chart with missed zones each week.
Did this zone remove an opposing zone, remove a trendline or make an all-time high/low? Is the first candle after the basing explosive (the body counts even with a wick)?

Is there a second explosive move after the first, rather than more basing? (higher quality) Was the zone tested before it qualified? If yes, it is not a trade. Did price stay away from the zone for a while before returning? Is the zone a similar size to my other zones, not too big and not tiny?

Is the proximal line in the correct place, with all wicks of the included candles inside the zone? Is my trendline attached to the most recent peak or valley without cutting candles? Is the trendline too horizontal? If so, use the original start point or just an arrow. Was the trendline removed by a full candle close beyond it, not just a wick? Are zones and trendlines extended up to the candle that removed them?

Is the zone very old? If so, do not expect it to hold. Is there a higher-timeframe zone right behind my entry zone? If so, place the stop about halfway into it. Is this gold, oil or a volatile news period? If so, use a wider stop. Is my stop giving the trade enough wiggle room for my spread?

“We only need one of these three things to be accomplished.” “Not the best zone, but what a trade from that area of demand.” “I'll always be honest.” “That's momentum. That is a trend line.” “It really tells me there's a lot of demand here.” “Missing that trend line was a fatal error.” “We don't start trendlines from random points.” “What did this zone break?” “Nothing forced here, love it.”
“Too small. Bigger the better.” “You might as well just take the whole daily zone.” “Not every stop loss is gonna be the same.”
A stated preference within qualifying zones: a second explosive move straight after the first explosive candle beats basing again before the next move. Both qualify, but the first is higher quality.
Zones tested before they qualified (before removing anything) are still drawn as the zone, which is why he draws zones 'after the fact', but they are never trading setups.

Trendline anchoring: a new trendline must start from the most recent peak or valley, never from a random point. If it is too horizontal, go back to the original starting point. Never draw two lines from the same anchor.
Keeping two trendlines at once (an overall line plus a temporary, aggressive one), versus usually replacing the old line when the new one is equally good.
The cost of a missed trendline in chain analysis: one missed line led to three missed zones down the chain.
Stop placement by eye, not measured, and wider on gold and oil and during political-news volatility (late 2025), with tighter stops only for traders with minimal spread.
A higher-timeframe stop rule: when the entry zone sits at the proximal line of a daily zone, put the stop about halfway into the daily zone, neither a normal stop nor below the whole daily.
Honest trade selection: a winning, qualifying zone he still would not take because there was no further leg; a zone with a bad tail-end wick or size is skipped.
Old zones removed long ago are not expected to hold. Liquidity traps can be marked, and an immediate pullback into the zone plus liquidity is a setup he likes.
Price returning right after the stay-away candle is allowed but not favoured. In his experience zones work better when price stays away a while.
A no-gap candles indicator can reveal zones that broker gaps hide. He is considering using it.
Homework procedure: map the all-time high and its supply first, copy his zones, update missed zones weekly, and zones after your session separator are not marked.

Draw a zone only if it broke a zone, a line, or a record. Imagine a tug of war. One team pulls the rope past a line on the ground. That pull was strong, so we remember where it started. A soft little tug that moved nothing? We forget it. On a chart we only mark the spots where a strong pull broke something.
A zone is like a player who scored a goal. We only write down players who scored: they beat the other team (opposing zone), broke the fence (trendline), or set a new record (all-time high or low).
Draw a zone only if it removed an opposing zone, removed a trendline, or made an all-time high or low.
Trendlines start at the most recent peak or valley and never cut through candles. Only a full candle beyond the line removes it.
The best zone: basing, an explosive candle, then another explosive candle. The stop goes a little beyond the zone, wider when a bigger zone sits behind it.

passages.h: Step: A zone must do a job
passages.t: In chain analysis we only draw a zone if it did one job: it removed an opposing zone, it removed a trendline, or it made an all-time high or low. One job is enough. If nothing did a job, we draw nothing.
Price fell to a valley, bounced to a lower peak, then broke below the valley. That lower low is the signal: now there is a downtrend line to draw.

passages.h: Step: Anchor at the top, touch the peak
passages.t: Draw from the highest point to the most recent peak, never from a random spot. If the line would cut through candles, slide it to the next highest point that cuts nothing.

passages.h: Step: A wick touch is not a removal
passages.t: The explosive candle pokes the line, but part of it still touches. The line is only removed by the first candle that sits fully above it, body and wick.

passages.h: Step: The demand that removed the line
passages.t: Go to where the move started: the little basing candles. Box them. The first candle out must be explosive, and here a second explosive candle follows. Kevin loves that: it shows a lot of demand.

passages.h: Step: Stop a little beyond the zone
passages.t: When price comes back, the stop goes a little beyond the zone, placed by eye. Give the trade wiggle room. Wider on gold, oil and news-heavy weeks.
What are the 3 jobs that let you draw a zone? - Remove an opposing zone, remove a trendline, or make an all-time high/low. One is enough.
What does a downtrend line need before you draw it? - A valley, a peak and then a lower low.
Where does a new trendline start? - At the most recent peak (downtrend) or valley (uptrend), never a random point.
The line cuts through candles. Now what? - Move to the next highest (or lowest) point that cuts nothing.
When is a trendline removed? - When a candle sits fully beyond it, body and wick. A wick touch does not count. What must the first candle after the basing be? - Explosive. Every time.
What is the best-quality zone shape? - Basing, an explosive candle, then another explosive candle.
Where does the stop go when a higher-timeframe zone sits under your zone? - About halfway into the higher-timeframe zone.
One missed trendline costs what? - Often one, two, three missed zones further down the chain.
Kevin returns from vacation, reviews his only trade of the week (a USDCAD 4-hour demand trade closed in profit after the 4-hour trendline broke) and encourages students after a volatile, losing week.

He continues the EURUSD daily chain analysis, drawing only zones that remove an opposing zone, remove a trendline or make an all-time high, and walks through trendline updates, overextended trendlines that must be ended, a near-horizontal line that does not count, and a tricky demand where the basing formed inside the respected supply.

He then marks every student's homework, repeatedly correcting basing-candle 'zones' that accomplish nothing, extended zones, unattached lines, wrong timeframes and unreadable screenshots, and becomes strict: homework that does not follow the instructions will not be marked.
He closes by setting next week's homework (treat a broken-data high as an all-time high) and explaining that every rule-based strategy has obvious yes, obvious no and gray-area cases.
Only draw zones that remove an opposing zone, remove a trendline, or make an all-time high/low - one is enough.
A removed zone or trendline does not automatically create a zone; there must be an explosive move away.
Require peak, valley and a higher high (uptrend) or lower low (downtrend) before drawing a trendline.

Do not let a trendline cut through candles; if it cuts a wick, attach to the next highest/lowest point. End an overextended trendline (no pullback) roughly halfway; never extend it. Do not draw near-horizontal trendlines; a trendline needs a visible angle.
For a demand that removes a supply, the basing must form while the supply is respected (below it); if basing or a wick sits above the supply, there is no zone.
Treat a large candle with wicks on both top and bottom as a basing candle, not an explosive move.

The candle after the zone must be the explosive move; if another basing candle follows, the zone moves to that later basing. Do not combine two separate sections of basing into one zone. Include the basing wick in the zone unless it is massive. End and mark zones when removed; never extend removed zones across the chart. Copy all of his previous zones and trendlines each week so the chain continues.
Submit homework on the correct chart and timeframe (daily) with a clear, readable layout. Attach trendlines and zone lines exactly to the highs/lows (magnet tool).
Treat the broken-data high on EURUSD as an all-time high for next week's homework, marked with a horizontal ray.

passages.t: In the Sunday meetings we are only drawing zones that remove one of three things: an opposing zone, a trendline, or make an all-time high (or low). It does not have to be all three - just one of them.

passages.h: Chain analysis recap: what qualifies a zone to be drawn

passages.h: Chain analysis recap: what qualifies a zone to be drawn

passages.h: Drawing and updating trendlines on the EURUSD daily
passages.t: Three things are required for a trendline: peak, valley, and a lower low (downtrend) or higher high (uptrend). If no new low is made, there is simply no trendline.

passages.h: Drawing and updating trendlines on the EURUSD daily
passages.t: Draw from the highest point possible to the highest point possible of the second touchpoint (downtrend); for an uptrend from the lows.

passages.h: Drawing and updating trendlines on the EURUSD daily
passages.t: When a new peak, valley and higher high forms, the earlier trendline becomes irrelevant and you update to a new line from the most recent valley.

passages.h: Drawing and updating trendlines on the EURUSD daily
passages.t: If the line from the lowest point of the valley cuts through a wick, do not use it; go to the next highest point instead so the line does not cut through candles.

passages.h: Drawing and updating trendlines on the EURUSD daily
passages.t: The odd time a trendline will cut through a candle; leave it until price makes a new all-time high, then adjust it.

passages.h: Drawing and updating trendlines on the EURUSD daily
passages.t: When price shoots up too aggressively with no pullback (overextended), end the trendline - do not keep extending it. There is no specific end point; stop it roughly halfway, which shows you recognised there is no more trendline there.

passages.h: Drawing and updating trendlines on the EURUSD daily
passages.t: You can use the channel tool attached to the peak to see visually how overextended price got, but it is not required.

passages.h: Drawing and updating trendlines on the EURUSD daily
passages.t: Ending overextended trendlines is what he wants to see in homework: it tells him you are paying attention.

passages.h: Tricky demand zone: basing inside a respected supply
passages.t: Price pushed up and got only a small minor reaction off an older supply; he expected more of a move, but it did not hold.

passages.h: Tricky demand zone: basing inside a respected supply
passages.t: Use the remove tool and extend the supply to where it was removed; he did not need the Fibonacci tool there because the removal was obvious.

passages.h: Tricky demand zone: basing inside a respected supply
passages.t: The demand that removed it is valid because the supply was respected, price created the basing candle under/at it, and then an explosive move away removed the supply.

passages.h: Tricky demand zone: basing inside a respected supply
passages.t: If the basing candle (or even a wick) was sitting above the supply, the basing was created after the supply was already removed, and there would be no zone.

passages.h: Tricky demand zone: basing inside a respected supply
passages.t: The move away barely qualifies as explosive - not the best zone. Price reacted off it twice, but it would not have been a trade for him: the demand was already removed and the pullback was too aggressive. He calls it a tricky one and will not give students a hard time if they missed it.

passages.h: No-zone areas, borderline peaks and the near-horizontal line
passages.t: At the new all-time high there is no zone in his opinion: the move away is not good enough, and wicks on both the top and bottom of the candle show it is a basing candle.

passages.h: No-zone areas, borderline peaks and the near-horizontal line
passages.t: A small peak and valley there is borderline; the big explosive candle makes him uncomfortable drawing a trendline. If you drew it he will not mark you down heavily, but he would not have it. No demand there means no supply after it in the chain.

passages.h: No-zone areas, borderline peaks and the near-horizontal line
passages.t: A valley, peak and lower low that produces an almost horizontal line is not a trendline - it is closer to momentum. We want a nice angle on the trendline. There is no angle measurement for this; it is visual and takes time to learn.

passages.h: No-zone areas, borderline peaks and the near-horizontal line
passages.t: When the low is removed in such a case, his chart may show a downward arrow but no trendline, meaning a downtrend with no trendline.

passages.h: No-zone areas, borderline peaks and the near-horizontal line
passages.t: After demand was removed he looked for a supply above that removed it; there was none, so the chain ends there ('that's just the way the cookie crumbles').

passages.h: No-zone areas, borderline peaks and the near-horizontal line
passages.t: He briefly tried TradingView's 'no gaps' chart setting because a student used it; he did not like it (many small gaps he cannot see) and removed it for now - even with it there was still no explosive move away at that high.

passages.t: Final part of the homework: valley, blatant peak, lower low gives the last trendline, then it ended at the session marker. The blacked-out weird price action at the end is to be skipped; just mark the zone below as removed.
Most students extended overextended trendlines - those need to end, just like the earlier one.
Almost everyone drew a borderline demand candle he would not have: large but with wicks at the top and bottom, so it is a basing candle. If it had a bit more body he would accept it.
Because of that one extra zone, the rest of the chain shifted; he still gives credit: 'if that was correct, that would be correct, and that would be correct'.
Students are getting good at spotting the 'little boo-boo basing candles' and not forcing zones.
Homework on the wrong timeframe (e.g. 1-hour instead of daily) or wrong chart cannot be marked; he can change the broker but not the timeframe. It has to be on the daily.
Blacked-out or blurry screenshots where wicks and timeframe are not visible are unmarkable; copy his chart layout for a clear visual.

A first-time submission drew zones that accomplished nothing, a trendline without a lower low, an extended trendline, and missed a blatant explosive zone; he recommends watching previous Sunday meetings.

Candle size alone does not make a move away: two candles of almost the same size can differ - a full-bodied candle with almost no wicks is explosive, while a large candle with big wicks top and bottom is still a basing candle, just a large one.

Lesson 3 (drawing zones): a drop-base-rally that was technically one but he would not consider demand; a rally-base-drop acceptable despite a wick because the body was big enough; one 'zone' was way off - basing candle, non-explosive move.
Daily trainer / 1-hour supply: the top zone was good; a move away that barely qualified looked fine.

Lesson 4 (multi-timeframe): a 4-hour zone in the right place but far too big - the student combined two separate sections of basing (two basing candles, then two more above). Do not combine them; draw only the basing next to the explosive move. The correct zone was well respected.
A student extending removed zones and not drawing opposing zones: he refused to mark it fully - zones are not extended; it makes charts too messy.
Momentum line correctly identified; the student's trendline logic was right but he would have attached it to the clear high that was removed, and the line was not attached properly.

Multiple timeframe analysis homework: the area was right but the student did not include the distal line at the basing candle; draw from the basing candle. Trend vs momentum homework: momentum line and trendline both correct.
A good example student copied all old zones, ended zones when removed, and had no zones cutting through - 'he just followed the instructions'.
Trendlines must be attached exactly (unattached lines are concerning); zone lines must be attached to the high.

A student in another group (who trades differently) drew a non-explosive demand that removed nothing: 'if that's your explosive move, there are demand zones everywhere'. We only look for explosive moves.
No higher high (or lower low) means no trendline - he corrected an experienced student and another student for this multiple times.
Do not ignore a blatant peak, valley and lower low and draw a line where no lower low was made.
When a zone is drawn at a candle, the next candle must be the explosive move. If a basing candle comes after it and then the explosive move, the zone is drawn at that later basing.
Drawing the zone at a basing-candle move away is saying that candle is the explosive move, which it is not; the supply belongs where the explosive move starts.
If it was a zone, do not cut through the wick of the basing - include the wick unless it is massive.

Students who keep drawing zones that accomplish nothing should put the three rules at the top of their chart, as one student does. Charts done on a phone change the angles, so trendlines are harder to judge.
There is no real winner; the 'winner' idea is just for fun and something to strive for. The closest this week was a student who got both ended trendlines and the hidden demand.

Follow the instructions: copy all of his old zones, old trendlines and new trendlines; only draw zones that remove an opposing zone, remove a trendline or break an all-time high; delete/end zones when removed. Homework that does not follow the instructions will not be marked.
He will happily work with anyone who struggles to understand zones; what he will not work with is people who do not follow simple instructions.
EURUSD daily from January onwards; the dark section with broken data (no wicks, the data did not cooperate) is skipped.

Any strategy has obvious no's (clearly not a zone) and obvious yes's (clearly a zone), and gray areas in between that are 50-50.
This applies to zones and trendlines: sometimes a move-away candle is very close, or a peak barely looks like a peak.

passages.t: Every rule-based strategy has obvious yes, obvious no, and 50-50 cases in between, for zones and for trendlines.
4-hour area of demand trade Why: Trade managed while on vacation; managed against the 4-hour trendline Result: Stopped out in profit after the 4-hour trendline broke

Supply zone that removed both a trendline and a demand (double whammy) Why: Followed the rule: removed an opposing zone and a trendline with an explosive move Result: Valid zone in the chain; later removed
Trendline removed through small basing candles Why: No explosive move away, only 'little boo-boo basing candles' Result: No zone drawn

Uptrend trendline update after peak, valley, higher high Why: Line from the lowest valley point cut through a wick, so it was attached to the next highest point; price then overextended Result: Trendline updated then ended roughly halfway; not extended

Demand that removed an older supply Why: Supply respected, basing formed beneath it, then explosive move removed it; move away barely qualified Result: Valid (tricky) zone; reacted twice but not a trade for him - demand already removed and pullback too aggressive
Candle at new all-time high Why: Wicks on top and bottom = basing candle; move away not good enough Result: No zone; most students drew it incorrectly
Valley, peak, lower low forming a near-horizontal line Why: Too horizontal - closer to momentum; no nice angle Result: No trendline; downtrend marked with a downward arrow only
Search for supply that removed a demand Why: No explosive supply above; tested 'no gaps' setting, still no explosive move Result: No zone; chain ends

Zone combining two sections of basing Why: Explosive move correct, but zone too big from merging two basing sections Result: Zone should be only the basing next to the explosive move; that zone was well respected

Q: I was doing a lot of market structure / Dow theory (break of structure) and I see you use trendlines. Should I keep both? A: We do not trade break of structure here, so it is irrelevant to this group. He advises doing trendlines exactly the way the group does them, since his system is winning. You can use break of structure in your own analysis, but he will have no opinion on it because he does not use it. He recommends only looking at peaks and valleys and not worrying about the other stuff.

Q: Can you elaborate what 'it doesn't mean a zone on its own' means? A: If there is a rally-base-rally with a good enough explosive candle, but nothing was removed by it (no opposing zone, no trendline), we do not draw the zone. On his EURUSD chart every zone exists because it removed an opposing zone or a trendline. We only draw zones that accomplish something.

Q: What tool do you use for zones - can I still use the magnet tool? A: It does not matter which tool (Fibonacci or rectangle); the magnet tool works with either. His Fibonacci settings: one colour, levels 0 and 1, background not too dark, prices on, text centre and middle; he posted a screenshot in the chat.
Q: (A student argued a zone would not be an ideal trading situation.) A: Correct that it would not be ideal to trade, but it is still a zone.
Q: How do I review trendlines again / get better? A: Watch the Sunday meetings - go to the Sunday Meeting section and watch 4 or 5 of them; that is your best bet.
Q: Should I re-share my homework link after fixing it? A: No, as long as it is the same link he will look at it after the meeting.

Drawing zones off basing-candle moves that accomplish nothing (remove no zone, no trendline). Extending overextended trendlines instead of ending them. Drawing a trendline without a new higher high or lower low. Ignoring a blatant peak, valley and lower low and drawing a line elsewhere. Counting a big but wicky candle as an explosive move. Drawing a near-horizontal line and calling it a trendline.

Extending removed zones, making charts messy and unmarkable. Not copying the previous weeks' zones and trendlines, which breaks the chain. Combining two basing sections into one oversized zone. Not including the basing candle/distal line, or cutting through the basing wick. Trendlines or zones not attached to the highs/lows. Submitting on the wrong timeframe or chart, or as blurry/blacked-out screenshots.
Getting discouraged after a losing week in volatile conditions. Mixing in other methods (break of structure, other groups' looser zone criteria).

Does this zone remove an opposing zone, a trendline, or make an all-time high/low? Is there a genuinely explosive move away (full body, small wicks), not a large wicky basing candle? Is the candle right after the basing the explosive move?

Did the basing form while the removed zone was still respected (not after it was already broken)? Is the zone drawn only around the basing next to the move, with the wick included? For a trendline: peak, valley and a new higher high / lower low present? Does the trendline avoid cutting through any candles and have a real angle? Has price overextended away from the trendline so it should be ended?
Are removed zones ended and old zones/trendlines carried over? Am I on the correct chart and timeframe with a clear layout? Can I manage the trade (internet, availability) - if not, stay out.

“It doesn't have to be all three, just one of these.” “Little boo-boo basing candles.” “Just because a trendline is removed, or a zone is removed, doesn't mean we automatically have a zone.” “We wanna have a nice angle on the trendline.” “If that's your explosive move, then there are demand zones everywhere.” “We're only drawing zones that accomplish something.”
“You can have rules, but sometimes there will be borderlines.” “It's never personal.” “Some weeks are like this, I've had many weeks like that, so don't get discouraged.”
Overextended trendlines are ended roughly halfway (no fixed point) when price shoots away without a pullback; the channel tool attached to the peak can help see it.
When a trendline from the lowest valley point cuts a wick, attach to the next highest point; the odd candle cut is left until a new all-time high, then adjusted.
A near-horizontal line is not a trendline (visual judgment, no angle measurement); such a downtrend is shown with a downward arrow and no trendline.
A large candle with wicks at both top and bottom is still a basing candle, regardless of size; full body with small wicks is what makes it explosive.
Do not combine two separate sections of basing into one zone - draw only the basing adjacent to the explosive move.
If a basing candle follows the zone candle before the explosive move, the zone is drawn at that later basing. Explicit framing of obvious yes / obvious no / gray-area cases in a rule-based strategy.
Homework now strictly enforced: wrong timeframe, unreadable screenshots, extended zones or missing copied zones will not be marked.
Broken price data on EURUSD daily: mark that high with a horizontal ray and treat it as an all-time high for the chain.
His Fibonacci tool settings for zones (one colour, levels 0 and 1, prices on, text centred) and that the magnet tool works with any drawing tool.

He does not use break of structure / Dow theory market structure and has no opinion on it; only peaks and valleys. Practical risk decision: do not take trades you cannot manage (no internet on vacation).

A zone counts only if its pause came before the break. Picture a fence in a yard. A dog sits quietly by the fence, then leaps over it. That dog broke the fence. Now picture a dog that was already on the other side and sat down there. It did not break anything. On a chart, the basing must happen while the fence still stands.
Basing is the runner crouching at the start line. If the runner crouched after the race was already won, that crouch did not win anything.
A removed zone or trendline does not automatically give a zone: there must be an explosive move away from basing.
For a demand that removes a supply, the basing must form below the supply while it is still respected. End overextended trendlines and removed zones. Never stretch them across the chart.
Here is a supply zone. Sellers pushed price down hard from it. It stays on the chart until something removes it.

passages.h: Step: Basing forms UNDER the supply
passages.t: Price comes back, gets pushed away once, and sits in small basing candles below the supply. The supply is still being respected. This order matters.

passages.h: Step: Explosive move removes the supply
passages.t: Then one big candle shoots up through the supply. Because the basing formed while the supply still held, this demand is the one that removed it. Rule 1: it removed an opposing zone.

passages.h: Step: If the basing sat above, no zone
passages.t: If the basing (even a wick) had formed above the supply, the supply was already broken before the basing. Then that basing did not remove anything, and there is no zone.

passages.h: Step: Big candle, big wicks = basing
passages.t: Size alone is not a move away. A full-bodied candle with tiny wicks is explosive. A large candle with big wicks on top and bottom is just a large basing candle. Some cases are gray: rules decide the obvious yes and no.
Does a removed zone always give a new zone? - No. Only if an explosive move away from basing removed it.

Demand removing a supply: where must its basing be? - Below the supply, formed while the supply was still respected. Big candle with big wicks on both ends? - A large basing candle, not an explosive move.
What makes a candle explosive? - A full body with almost no wicks, much bigger than the basing.
Price rockets away from a trendline with no pullback? - End the trendline (roughly halfway). Do not extend it.
What is a "double whammy" zone? - A zone that removed two things at once, like a trendline and a demand.
What are gray areas? - Borderline 50-50 cases between the obvious yes and obvious no. They exist with any rules. Can't manage a trade (no internet)? - Do not take it. Staying out is a decision.

Kevin walks through the EURUSD daily chain-analysis homework, a hard week with almost no clean zones. He uses it to teach when a trendline is removed (a full candle close beyond it), where to anchor and re-anchor trendlines, and why a removed trendline or zone does not always produce a new zone.

He then marks the members' homework: forced zones, basing candles called move aways, missed blatant trendlines, a wick used as a valley, too big a timeframe jump in multiple sequence analysis, and a confirmation trade taken after the higher-timeframe zone broke.

He closes by switching the homework to AUDUSD daily, explaining why zone size is judged by eye at the current zoom rather than measured, and saying when to go for bigger risk-reward trades instead of a fixed 1:1.
Only draw a zone that removes an opposing zone, removes a trendline, or makes an all-time high or low. Keep the chain-analysis rules in an anchored note on your chart.
A downward trendline is removed only by a full candle close above it with neither body nor wick touching the line; for an upward line, the opposite.
A trendline needs a blatant peak, a blatant valley and a lower low (downtrend) or higher high (uptrend).
Draw upward trendlines from the lowest point possible to the valley without cutting through candles. Move the anchor if it cuts one.
After a break with a new peak, valley and higher high, draw the new trendline from the most recent valley.
When updating a trendline, connect the most recent valleys. Go from the very bottom only if the recent valley makes the line too horizontal.
Don't call a lone wick a valley. Attach to a wick only when a valley from proper candles already qualifies there.
Don't remove a trendline for a small break of the channel; remove it only when price falls far out of the channel.
A removed trendline or zone doesn't mean there must be a zone. If nothing qualifies, draw nothing.
When an opposing zone is removed, go find the zone that removed it, and pick the one with the biggest move away. Don't trade tested zones.

The candle right after the proximal line must be explosive. If it's basing, there is no zone. End a zone when it is removed. Don't extend it past removal. Include all the basing candles and their wicks in the zone, and keep the proximal tight. Judge zone size by eye at the zoom you have, and change the zoom if price has run far. If your higher-timeframe zone breaks, the trade is no longer a confirmation trade.

For a 1H entry use daily as the HTF and 1-month as the sequence. Never jump from 3-month to 1H. On macro charts (3-month), skip the chain rules and draw explosive moves away. Use 4H to 15m rather than a 2H chart.
Send clean charts with visible candles and no overlapping boxes. Leave out CHoCH/BOS markings. Look for larger risk-reward when the chance is there instead of a fixed 1:1.

passages.h: The blacked-out anomaly on EURUSD (May 1993 to 1997)

passages.h: The blacked-out anomaly on EURUSD (May 1993 to 1997)

passages.h: The blacked-out anomaly on EURUSD (May 1993 to 1997)

passages.h: First downward trendline: blatant peak and valley vs small ones
passages.t: There was a small peak and valley and a lower low, but that peak and valley was 'almost too small' next to a much larger, blatant peak and valley. A trendline needs a blatant peak, a blatant valley and a lower low (for a downtrend).

passages.h: First downward trendline: blatant peak and valley vs small ones
passages.t: Most members missed this blatant trendline and drew the small 'boo-boo' peaks and valleys instead. He calls those borderline, not way off.

passages.h: First downward trendline: blatant peak and valley vs small ones
