passages.h: Exactly when a trendline is removed
passages.t: Zoomed in: the downward trendline was removed when one specific red candle closed. Every candle before it, even a green one, still touched the line with its body or its wick.

passages.h: Exactly when a trendline is removed
passages.t: Removal needs a full candle close above a downward trendline with neither body nor wick touching it. If the wick comes back down and touches the line, it is not removed. An upward trendline is the exact opposite: a full close below it without touching.

passages.h: Exactly when a trendline is removed
passages.t: Upward example: a green candle and a red candle both still touched the line. The candle after them closed fully below without touching, and that one removed it.

passages.h: A removed trendline does not guarantee a zone
passages.t: After that trendline broke, the only candidate was a small rally-base-rally that was 'very close'.

passages.h: A removed trendline does not guarantee a zone
passages.t: He doesn't usually measure zones ('it's more of a look'), but price was far from the reference zones, so he measured: the candidate was about 215 pips, compared with the move-away candle of an older zone. Result: 'it's not even close', so no zone.

passages.h: A removed trendline does not guarantee a zone
passages.t: 'Just because… a trendline's removed… doesn't mean we're always gonna have a zone.' If nothing qualifies, leave it.

passages.h: Borderline trendline, old tested zone and the supply that removed it
passages.t: A second trendline with two smaller peaks and valleys does qualify, in his opinion, though it is very close. No update to that line until another peak and valley forms.

passages.h: Borderline trendline, old tested zone and the supply that removed it
passages.t: A very old demand zone below had already been tested, and 'we don't trade at tested zones'.

passages.h: Borderline trendline, old tested zone and the supply that removed it
passages.t: He extended that zone with the remove tool to show where it was removed. In daily analysis you don't have to extend zones all the way back, because it takes too long (he often updates charts on the go). For homework he recommends it because it makes things easier to see.

passages.h: Borderline trendline, old tested zone and the supply that removed it
passages.t: Rule 1 in action: the opposing zone was removed, so go up and find the supply that removed it.

passages.h: Borderline trendline, old tested zone and the supply that removed it
passages.t: Candidates: one with too small a move-away candle; one at about 129; one at about 145. He chose the one with 'the biggest move away' and said others could be justified. He admitted he was 'struggling' and would not give anyone a hard time.

passages.h: Borderline trendline, old tested zone and the supply that removed it
passages.t: Going back to the earlier trendline: it was respected several times, then one candle closed without touching it, and in a real trade that would be the break.
Draw from the lowest point possible, without cutting through candles, to the second touch point at the valley.
If the line from the absolute lowest point cuts through a candle, adjust the bottom anchor until it no longer cuts through.
After the break: blatant peak, valley and a higher high ('we always need that higher high'), so draw the new trendline from the most recent valley.
A demand zone removed here produced no demand, because nothing qualified as the demand that removed the supply.

Re-anchoring on update: normally connect the most recent peaks and valleys (previous valley to the new valley). Skip the recent valley and go from the very bottom only when using it would make the line too horizontal.
Several members drew from the lowest point to the new valley when it wasn't needed. That is 'not totally wrong', but it isn't how he does it here.

passages.h: EURUSD dropped as a homework chart
passages.t: Almost no clean zones: 'just another bad week of homework'. Even his own single zone felt forced.

passages.h: EURUSD dropped as a homework chart
passages.t: His note: EURUSD is only good up to about 1990 for this homework. Price action after that was 'complete junk' (the current EURUSD daily is fine).

passages.h: EURUSD dropped as a homework chart
passages.t: He says this week tested whether members could avoid forcing zones. He gave a lot of grace on borderline calls.
Basing candle almost the same size as the move away = not explosive. That near-equal size is 'the dead giveaway'.
For every zone ask 'what did this zone accomplish?' / 'what did this remove?' If it removed nothing, don't draw it.
Creating a new low does not equal a zone. 'Just because that's a low doesn't mean there's demand.' Don't say three zones removed one zone. Follow the chain analysis, one zone at a time.
Choppiness doesn't matter for a zone. A zone fails because the moves aren't explosive, not because price was choppy.
The next candle out from the proximal line must be an explosive move. If it's basing, basing, basing, there is no zone.
'Explosive' is relative to the basing. A zone can barely qualify if it's explosive compared with its basing. A big wick tells him a candle is basing, not a move away.

Include the wicks of the basing when drawing (for example, a supply drawn without its wick is wrong). Draw the proximal tight to the body. Basing does not have to be tight and well structured. Include all the basing candles.
End a zone when it is removed. Extending it past removal is 'one of my biggest pet peeves'. He wouldn't trade a zone that is very large because of a big wick.
A member who drew zones on almost every basing candle was told to rewatch the full YouTube course and get back to basics ('I'm just being brutally honest').
Drawing zones because price reacts to an area hurts your edge. 'The hard part is identifying boo-boo zones.' His favourite type of zone is a clean drop-base-drop with a single basing candle.

passages.h: Homework marking: trendline mistakes, wicks as valleys, channel lenience
passages.t: Extend trendlines. Several members ended a valid line too early. Lines that just go sideways are not trendlines. 'If we just got one more peak up, for sure.'

passages.h: Homework marking: trendline mistakes, wicks as valleys, channel lenience
passages.t: Pick the better valley as the reference point for an updated line. A technical valley isn't enough when a clearer one is there.

passages.h: Homework marking: trendline mistakes, wicks as valleys, channel lenience
passages.t: A massive wick alone is not a valley. If price is only making momentum lines and one wick sticks out, he won't call that wick a valley.

passages.h: Homework marking: trendline mistakes, wicks as valleys, channel lenience
passages.t: He attaches to a wick only when a valley built from proper candles already qualifies there and the wick is its extreme.

passages.h: Homework marking: trendline mistakes, wicks as valleys, channel lenience
passages.t: Channel lenience: a small break of the lower channel line doesn't remove the trendline, as long as price comes back to test or re-enters the channel. Only when price falls 'way, way out' of the channel does the line go (and there is probably an updated line by then).

passages.h: Homework marking: trendline mistakes, wicks as valleys, channel lenience
passages.t: A member said 'no trendline because it's a range'. He disagreed: there was clearly a trendline. Don't map out random highs and lows for this homework.

passages.h: Homework marking: chart hygiene and other methods
passages.t: Charts you send must be clean: no overlapping blue and red boxes, and the candle details must be visible. 'I can't judge anything off of that.'

passages.h: Homework marking: chart hygiene and other methods
passages.t: Get rid of CHoCH and break-of-structure markings for this homework. 'This is supply and demand, we don't use that.' Fine if you do it on your own. If you're on the wrong timeframe or chart, he can't mark the homework. Don't use the 2-hour: go 4-hour to 15-minute.

passages.h: Multiple timeframe and multiple sequence corrections
passages.t: MTF: the member's daily demand was right, but it broke. Once your higher-timeframe zone breaks, the trade on your entry timeframe (1H) is no longer a confirmation trade. You can still trade the zones, but not as confirmation.

passages.h: Multiple timeframe and multiple sequence corrections
passages.t: The member's 1H 'demand' had a great move away, but drawn properly it was huge because of the wick, so he wouldn't call it a zone.

passages.h: Multiple timeframe and multiple sequence corrections
passages.t: MSA: going from a 3-month chart down to a 1-hour is 'way too crazy of a jump'. For a 1H entry, the HTF is the daily and the sequence above the daily is the 1-month.

passages.h: Multiple timeframe and multiple sequence corrections
passages.t: On macro charts like the 3-month, he mostly ignores the chain rules (opposing zone and so on) because the timeframe is so long, and just draws explosive moves away.

passages.h: Multiple timeframe and multiple sequence corrections
passages.t: Daily and 1H zones in that example were in the right area but drawn too big. Tighter is better, even if that means you might not get filled.

passages.h: Multiple timeframe and multiple sequence corrections
passages.t: Trend trading: a downtrend on the daily was recognised correctly, but the marked 'supply zones' were all basing candles.

Zones form when price breaks all-time highs or lows, not any high or low. Mark the all-time highs and lows as you go so you can spot them.

No supply zones before that point. The homework period starts around January 1993 (he extended it back slightly from December 1992). Price action in the 90s may need a bit more lenience on what qualifies. He plans to cycle through charts over the coming months and come back to EURUSD later.

passages.h: Zone size depends on the zoom, and risk-reward flexibility
passages.t: Gold example: after price shot up so far, old zones look tiny and don't look explosive at the current zoom. At the zoom of that time they barely qualified.

passages.h: Zone size depends on the zoom, and risk-reward flexibility
passages.t: That's why he doesn't measure zones: depending on the price action, zones look smaller or bigger, so it's a visual judgment at the zoom you have. Sometimes you need to change the zoom to judge a zone. Oil weekly is another chart where a huge move distorts the zoom.

passages.h: Zone size depends on the zoom, and risk-reward flexibility
passages.t: Don't always aim for 1:1. Spot chances for larger risk-reward. Those are 'your account boosters' (a 3-4% trade really boosts the account).

passages.h: Zone size depends on the zoom, and risk-reward flexibility
passages.t: He used to believe in a fixed risk-reward (1:1, 2:1, 3:1) and says that leaves money on the table. Recent example: many 1:1 trades lately, but on AUD he saw a possible 3:1 (it didn't work out).

passages.h: Zone size depends on the zoom, and risk-reward flexibility
passages.t: These chances don't come often. He refers to his YouTube 'Set & Forget' video for those situations.

passages.h: Chart: [10:12] Arrow at the supply that was removed, with the upward trendline under the rally.
passages.t: "There's no demand here" that removed that supply, so nothing is drawn. Even his one zone this week felt forced.

passages.h: Chart: [16:09] A student's chart: arrow at an orange supply drawn on a good-looking move away.
passages.t: "Fair enough, that's an explosive move away ... but what did this remove?" If it removed nothing, do not draw it.

passages.t: A small break of the lower channel line does not remove the trendline if price comes back to test or re-enters the channel. Only a clear move far outside ends it.

passages.h: Chart: [28:04] A student's labelled chart ("WILL NOT TRADE. MOVE AWAY NOT GOOD ENOUGH", "WILL NOT TRADE. MOVE AWAY CANDLE TOO CLOSE") with CHoCH / break-of-structure markings.
passages.t: The zones were all borderline, which is fair this week. Remove the CHoCH and BOS markings for this homework: "this is supply and demand".

passages.t: Do not jump from a 3-month chart to a 1h entry. For a 1h entry the higher timeframe is the daily, and above the daily the 1-month.

passages.t: The daily and 1h zones were in the right place but too big; tighter is better even if you might not get filled.

passages.t: Going from A to B is not enough. "We need an explosive move, not little boo-boo basing candles."

passages.t: A massive wick on its own is not a valley. He attaches to a wick only when a valley built from candles already qualifies there.

passages.t: At the zoom of that time they barely qualified. That is why he judges zone size by eye at the right zoom, not by measuring.

First downward trendline after the blacked-out 1993-1997 period, anchored at the highest visible point Why: A blatant peak, blatant valley and lower low (the small peak/valley nearby was too small). The start point is a judgment call because of the anomaly. Result: Valid trendline. Removed when a red candle closed fully above it without touching.

Rally-base-rally candidate right after the downward trendline broke Why: Looked close. He measured it (about 215) against an older zone's move-away candle and it was not even close in size. Result: No zone. A removed trendline doesn't always produce one.

Old tested demand removed, then a search for the supply that removed it (candidates around 129 and 145) Why: Rule 1: opposing zone removed. He chose the supply with the biggest move away and admitted others could be justified. Result: Supply drawn, but borderline and 'almost forced'. The old demand was not tradable anyway because it had been tested.

Upward trendline from the lowest point, adjusted so it doesn't cut a candle, then broken and redrawn Why: The break came on the first candle that closed fully below without touching. A blatant peak, valley and higher high followed, so the new line starts from the most recent valley. Result: Trendline removed. New trendline from the recent valley. No demand had removed the related supply.

passages.h: Chart: Member chart (unspecified) Daily HTF / 1H entry
passages.t: Daily demand with a 1H demand taken as a confirmation trade Why: The daily demand had broken, so it was no longer a confirmation trade. The 1H zone was huge because of a wick. Result: Not a valid confirmation setup. He wouldn't take a zone like that.

Multiple sequence analysis jumping from 3-month to 1H Why: Too big a jump. For a 1H entry the sequence is daily (HTF) then 1-month. On macro charts, just draw explosive moves away. Result: Right area, but zones too big. Should have used the 1-month.

passages.h: Chart: Gold (and oil weekly) Higher timeframe
passages.t: Old zones look non-explosive after a huge rally Why: The current zoom shrinks old moves. At the zoom of that time they barely qualified as explosive. Result: Judge zone size by eye at the right zoom, not by measuring.

Kevin spotted a chance for about a 3:1 instead of his usual 1:1 Why: Bigger risk-reward chances are account boosters, and it is worth spotting when they're available. Result: Didn't work out, but he says looking for these trades is right.
Q: On the last homework on zones, would that have been a continuation trend, not a drop-base? A: He didn't understand what 'continuation trend' meant and gave no further answer.
Q: Trend line versus momentum: is this a momentum line and that a trendline? A: Yes, that one is momentum and the other is a trendline. There is also another trendline the student missed.
Q: Can this be classified as basing? A: Absolutely. Basing doesn't have to be tight and well structured. Include all the basing candles in the zone.
Q: I drew the zones in the middle, but they don't seem good, right? A: Correct, those weren't good, and leaving them out was completely fine.

Q: Which chart should the next homework use? A: Members suggested AUDUSD and noted it hadn't been done yet. He checked USDCAD and AUDUSD and chose AUDUSD daily on FXCM, because EURUSD after about 1990 has been junk. He thought about a weekly chart but said that would change the timeframes.

Q: Struggling with how the zoom changes how zones look? A: Yes, it's tough. The chart rescales after huge moves (gold, oil weekly), so old zones look smaller. Judge visually at the zoom of the time. It's simple as long as there aren't insanely big moves.

Q: Shouldn't you just take 1:1 trades? A: Not always. Spot chances for larger risk-reward, because those are account boosters (a 3-4% trade really helps). A fixed risk-reward leaves money on the table. He's had many 1:1 trades lately but saw a possible 3:1 on AUD. See his Set & Forget video on YouTube.

Forcing zones on a chart with no clean ones. Drawing zones that removed nothing ('what did this zone accomplish?'). Treating a new low or high as a zone. Claiming several zones removed one zone. Calling a basing candle almost as big as the move away explosive. Calling a run of basing candles a move away. Leaving the basing wick out of the zone. Drawing zones too big.

Extending a zone past the point where it was removed. Missing the blatant peak/valley trendline while drawing small boo-boo ones. Ending a valid trendline too early instead of extending it. Drawing sideways lines as trendlines. Re-anchoring an updated trendline from the lowest point when the recent valley was fine. Using a lone wick as a valley. Treating a wick that still touches the line as a trendline break.

Removing a trendline just because price slightly broke the channel. Saying 'no trendline because it's a range' when a clear trendline exists. Counting a trade as confirmation after the higher-timeframe zone broke. Jumping from a 3-month chart to a 1H entry. Using a 2H chart. Cluttered screenshots with overlapping boxes and unreadable candles. Mixing CHoCH/BOS markings into supply and demand homework.

Doing homework on the wrong chart or timeframe. Measuring zone size in pips across very different price levels instead of judging at the right zoom. Always settling for a fixed 1:1 and leaving money on the table.

Did this zone remove an opposing zone, remove a trendline, or make an all-time high or low? Is the next candle out from the proximal line explosive compared with the basing? Is the basing clearly smaller than the move away? Are all the basing candles and their wicks included, with the proximal tight? Is the zone untested? Has the zone been ended where it was removed?

Is the zone size similar to nearby zones at a sensible zoom? Is the trendline built on a blatant peak, blatant valley and a higher high or lower low? Does the trendline avoid cutting through any candle? Did a candle close fully beyond the trendline without touching it?

If updating, is it anchored to the most recent valley (unless that makes it too horizontal)? Is the valley built from proper candles, not just a wick? Is price still roughly within the trendline's channel? Is my higher-timeframe zone still intact, so this is a confirmation trade? Is my timeframe sequence sensible (e.g. 1H / daily / monthly)? Is a larger risk-reward than 1:1 realistically available here?

“Just because… a trendline's removed… doesn't mean we're always gonna have a zone.” “We need a full close above a downward trend line for it to be removed.” “We always need that higher high, too.” “What did this zone accomplish?” “Creating a new low does not equal a zone.” “Little boo-boo peaks and valleys.” “It's one of my biggest pet peeves when people continue it.” “Choppiness doesn't really matter for a zone.”
“The hard part is identifying boo-boo zones.” “Those are your account boosters.” “You're leaving money on the table. You really are.” “Not trying to be rude, I'm just being brutally honest.”
Channel lenience: a small break of the channel doesn't remove the trendline if price comes back to test it. Earlier lessons only said price trading beyond the channel makes the line irrelevant.
A lone wick is not a valley. Attach to a wick only when a valley from proper candles already qualifies.
Re-anchor updated lines through the most recent valleys. Skip back to the bottom only when the recent valley makes the line too horizontal.
Once the higher-timeframe zone breaks, an entry-timeframe trade is no longer a confirmation trade (you can still trade the zone).
Multiple sequence analysis: never jump from 3-month to 1H. For a 1H entry the sequence is daily then 1-month. On macro charts (3-month), skip the chain rules and draw explosive moves away.

Measuring is a fallback: when price is far from the reference zones he measures a candidate (about 215) against a known zone's move-away candle. Otherwise size is judged by eye at the right zoom, because huge rallies (gold, oil weekly) shrink old zones. Don't use a 2H chart; use 4H to 15m.
Risk-reward philosophy: no fixed 1:1. Look for 3:1-type account boosters when the chance is there (3-4% account gains).

Data anomalies: black out unreadable stretches and treat the first high or low after them as an all-time high or low, for homework only. Chart hygiene for submissions: clean screenshots, visible candles, no CHoCH/BOS markings.
Homework notes: EURUSD is only usable up to about 1990. New homework is AUDUSD daily (FXCM) from about January 1993, and the 90s may need a bit more lenience.

More zone pitfalls: a new low is not a zone; don't say several zones removed one zone; choppiness doesn't disqualify a zone, a missing explosive move does; basing doesn't need to be tight; his favourite zone is a single-candle drop-base-drop.

A line breaks only when a whole candle steps fully off it. Think of a balance beam. If your toe still touches the beam, you have not fallen off. You only fell when your whole body is on the floor. A trendline is the beam: a candle that still touches it has not broken it yet.
Breaking a trendline is like leaving a swimming pool. One foot on the ladder is still in the pool. Only when both feet are on the ground are you out.

A trendline is removed only by a full candle beyond it, with no body or wick touching. A removed trendline or zone does not guarantee a zone. If nothing explosive did it, draw nothing. Re-anchor updated lines on the most recent valleys. A lone wick is not a valley.

passages.h: Step: Draw from the lowest point
passages.t: Uptrend line: start at the lowest point and run to the valley. If it cuts through a candle, move the anchor until it does not. A blatant valley, not a tiny wiggle.
Candles start leaning on the line. As long as any body or wick still touches it, the line is still alive.
This candle closed fully below the line without touching it. That is the exact moment the line is removed. For a downtrend line it is the mirror: fully above.

passages.h: Step: No explosive move = no zone
passages.t: Look at what broke it: tiny drifting candles, no explosive move. So there is no zone. A removed trendline does not mean we must have a zone. If nothing qualifies, leave it.

passages.h: Step: Ask: what did it accomplish?
passages.t: For every zone ask "what did this remove?" A new low is not a zone. A choppy area is not the reason a zone fails; weak moves are. Do not force zones on a chart that has none.
When is a downtrend line removed? - A candle sits fully above it, body and wick not touching.
When is an uptrend line removed? - A candle sits fully below it, body and wick not touching. Trendline removed but only small candles broke it? - No zone. Leave it.
Is a lone long wick a valley? - No. Only use a wick when real candles already form a valley there.
Updated uptrend line connects what? - The most recent valleys (previous valley to new valley). Do we trade tested zones? - No. "We don't trade at tested zones."

Higher-timeframe zone broke. Is your entry still a confirmation trade? - No. You can trade the zone, but not as confirmation. Always take 1:1? - No. Spot bigger risk-reward chances: they are your account boosters.

Kevin starts the session by going back over the core zone concept from the Discord learning materials. He covers basing (sometimes only one candle, and occasionally none you can see), the explosive move away, the stay-away space as his main measure of zone quality, and trendline versus momentum. He admits the method is about 95% objective.

He then does the homework on a brand-new daily chart, where the first visible high and low are treated as all-time highs/lows. He draws each zone using the most recent basing section, compares candle sizes in pips (94, 102 vs 80) to settle borderline moves away, rejects a borderline trendline, and ends an overextended trendline instead of extending it. Most of the session is marking students' homework.

The same mistakes keep coming up: zones that are just basing candles, zones drawn too small or too big, momentum lines drawn as trendlines, trendlines with no lower low or higher high, trendlines not attached or started from a random point, and zones ended when tested instead of when removed. The next homework is January 1994 to January 1995.
Students must copy his corrected zones exactly (the distal line matters most), submit the chart on the daily timeframe, and map out every all-time high with a horizontal line.
Only draw zones that remove an opposing zone, remove a trendline, or make an all-time high/low.
On a fresh chart, treat the first visible high and low as the all-time high and all-time low.
Treat every high that price breaks as an all-time high. It does not have to be an obvious peak.
Require an explosive move away. A distance covered by small basing candles is not a move away.
Basing can be one candle. If a massive drop is followed directly by a massive rally, act as if there is basing and draw a zone similar in size to your previous zones.
Judge zone quality by the space between the stay-away candle and the proximal line. The bigger the space, the better. A zone with a small space is still drawn (drawable) but not traded (tradable).
When the basing has separate sections, use the most recent section only. Do not combine them. Include all the basing candles that are grouped together in the zone, not just two.
Keep zones a similar size to your other zones. Slightly bigger is fine. Never really tiny. Include the wick in the zone.
Extend a zone until it is removed, not until it is tested. Then mark it with the remove tool where it was removed.
If something is removed without an explosive move away, there is no zone and the analysis ends.
A trendline needs a blatant peak and valley plus a higher high (uptrend) or a lower low (downtrend).

Draw an uptrend line from the lowest point possible to the valley, and a downtrend line from the highest point to the peak, never from a random spot. Trendlines must not cut through wicks. Adjust them so they don't. Attach the trendline to the valley or peak. No floating lines and no wick poking through. A trendline is removed by a full candle close beyond it.
When price gets very overextended from a trendline, end the trendline. Do not continue it.

When a move away is borderline, draw the zone to see it and compare it with your other zones. Measuring in pips is fine as a baseline. Submit homework on the daily timeframe and leave the saved chart there.
After each session, copy his corrections exactly, especially the distal lines, so the chain analysis matches. Map all-time highs with a perfectly horizontal trendline tool.

The Sunday sessions are where you learn the strategy more in depth through chain analysis. He cannot make a video lesson for every single explanation, so many answers to members' questions are in these meetings.
Watch the daily breakdowns and the Sunday meetings. Members want his breakdowns because they are accurate, but the point of the group is to learn the strategy yourself.
He points students to the 'learning material' section in the Discord. It holds the core concept of a zone and the trendline material.

passages.h: Recap: basing, including single-candle and 'invisible' basing
passages.t: A zone starts with basing. The basing candles are not always 3. It can be just 1 candle. Rare case: a massive red candle down (clearly explosive) followed immediately by a massive green candle up, with no basing candle in between. Act as if there is basing there and draw the zone a similar size to your previous zones. He says this is more nuanced and is the kind of situation the Sunday meetings are for.

passages.h: Recap: basing, including single-candle and 'invisible' basing
passages.t: The move away must be explosive. A move that covers the same distance but is made of tiny 'boo-boo basing candles' is not a move away, so it is not a zone.

passages.h: Recap: stay-away candle and the space that grades a zone
passages.t: Next comes the stay-away candle: price stays away from the proximal line. The stay-away candle creates the space between itself and the proximal line.

passages.h: Recap: stay-away candle and the space that grades a zone
passages.t: That space is pretty much how he judges how good a zone is. The bigger the space, the better the zone.

passages.h: Recap: stay-away candle and the space that grades a zone
passages.t: He loves an explosive move followed by another explosive move. It is preferred, not required.

passages.h: Recap: stay-away candle and the space that grades a zone
passages.t: If a wick comes all the way back and only just misses the proximal line, it is still a zone. This goes back to Lesson 1, drawable vs tradable: a zone with a small space is still drawn, but it is not traded. It is drawn so that, when price comes back, you can see which zone removes it.

passages.h: Recap: trendline vs momentum, and how objective the method is
passages.t: A steep move with no significant pullbacks is momentum. A trendline needs a blatant peak and valley.

passages.h: Recap: trendline vs momentum, and how objective the method is
passages.t: Technically every little wiggle is a peak and valley. What he needs is a significant peak and valley that is extremely obvious.

passages.h: Recap: trendline vs momentum, and how objective the method is
passages.t: A viewer on his channel commented that it seems too subjective. He says it is about 95% objective with a little subjectivity, and that you cannot make something like this 100% objective.

passages.h: Recap: trendline vs momentum, and how objective the method is
passages.t: There is no measurement for a move away. One reason it cannot be fully objective: crazy moves on gold or oil change the zoom of the chart, so you cannot measure moves away consistently. With experience you learn to recognise good moves away. Some are very obvious and some are tricky, and that is okay.

passages.h: Recap: trendline vs momentum, and how objective the method is
passages.t: As long as you are not drawing little boo-boo basing candles as the move away, you should be able to spot moves away.

passages.h: Chain analysis rules and starting a fresh chart
passages.t: Only draw zones that (1) remove an opposing zone, (2) remove a trendline, or (3) make an all-time high or low. If you ask why he doesn't have a zone, it is because it didn't fit the chain analysis.

passages.h: Chain analysis rules and starting a fresh chart
passages.t: This homework starts on a fresh chart. Earlier price action exists but can't be used. Like an axiom, treat the first high as the all-time high and the first low as the all-time low, because you have to start somewhere.

passages.h: Chain analysis rules and starting a fresh chart
passages.t: An all-time high doesn't have to be an obvious peak that price rallied down from. Every wick and high that price breaks above is an all-time high. So a zone can qualify by removing a high that nobody would call an obvious peak.

passages.h: Chain analysis rules and starting a fresh chart
passages.t: Just because something (zone, trendline or all-time high) was removed does not mean there is a zone. If no explosive move away removed it (only basing candles), the analysis simply ends there.

passages.h: Chain analysis rules and starting a fresh chart
passages.t: Do not end a zone when it is tested. Keep extending it until it is removed, then mark it with the remove tool (the remove box goes where it was removed).

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 1: first supply and demand zones (daily)
passages.t: First zone: the starting all-time high was removed by an explosive move. 'Not the best zone, I will admit, but it is an explosive move.'

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 1: first supply and demand zones (daily)
passages.t: The basing had two sections: one before the explosive move and one after. He does not combine them because the zone would be too big. He uses the most recent basing section.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 1: first supply and demand zones (daily)
passages.t: The next all-time high: he found no demand that removed it. The candles were all boo-boo basing candles. One got close to a move away but was not big enough compared with the others, so there is no zone and the analysis ends.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 1: first supply and demand zones (daily)
passages.t: Price came back to the earlier zone and gave a nice trade. The zone was kept until it was removed, which happened on an 'objectively explosive' move away.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 1: first supply and demand zones (daily)
passages.t: Sizing that zone: his first draw was too big, so he tightened it to a similar size to the others. He cloned a previous zone to compare. Going a bit bigger is fine (for example if it was tested), but never make it really tiny. Tiny zones mean zones everywhere.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 2: borderline trendlines and a strong supply
passages.t: He judged one possible trendline 'not a good enough peak and valley', calling it borderline. He judged another close one good enough and drew it, though he usually doesn't like one drawn off wicks. Both were borderline, and it didn't matter because no zone came from them.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 2: borderline trendlines and a strong supply
passages.t: Trendline drawing: go from the lowest point possible to the valley. If the line cuts through a wick, adjust it, because trendlines don't cut through wicks.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 2: borderline trendlines and a strong supply
passages.t: A demand zone was removed, but no explosive move did the removing, only basing candles. So he does not just mark the low and call it a zone.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 2: borderline trendlines and a strong supply
passages.t: Rule 2 (trendline removed = zone): here the trendline broke but there was no zone, because there was no explosive move. The last supply drawn removed 2 demand zones and an all-time low: 'Pretty strong zone.'

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 2: borderline trendlines and a strong supply
passages.t: That supply later failed. He says it was most likely because the zone was so old and there was no liquidity trap before it.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 2: borderline trendlines and a strong supply
passages.t: A new all-time low formed with a blatant valley and peak, much better than the borderline one. It is probably more of a weekly trendline but still looks fine on the daily. He drew it from the highest point to the peak, the next touch point.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 2: borderline trendlines and a strong supply
passages.t: He contrasts very obvious trendlines ('boom, boom, boom'), borderline ones, and plain momentum, which he does not want to see.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 3: measuring borderline moves away and ending an overextended trendline
passages.t: The all-time high was removed (rule 3), with an explosive move away compared with the price action before it. The basing was two candles. The zone was already removed, so he used the remove tool at the removal point rather than extending it.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 3: measuring borderline moves away and ending an overextended trendline
passages.t: For Sunday sessions he sometimes measures. A candidate move away measured 94 pips. It was close and borderline, so he drew it to see how it looked, compared it with the other zones, and kept it on the chart.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 3: measuring borderline moves away and ending an overextended trendline
passages.t: He admits he probably misses zones in his real trading sometimes by judging them too small: 'I'm not worried about missing a trade. I am not.'

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 3: measuring borderline moves away and ending an overextended trendline
passages.t: That zone removed the downward trendline. The trendline counts as removed when a candle closes fully above it.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 3: measuring borderline moves away and ending an overextended trendline
passages.t: Another candidate demand: the overall candle including the wick measured 102 pips, but the green move-away candle was only about 80. Not good enough, so no demand zone. 'Kind of a close one there, I wouldn't be surprised if somebody had that.'

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 3: measuring borderline moves away and ending an overextended trendline
passages.t: A blatant peak and valley plus a higher high gives a trendline. Without the high being removed (for example price only pushes up partway and drops), there is no trendline, even with a great valley.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 3: measuring borderline moves away and ending an overextended trendline
passages.t: Price then got very overextended above that trendline. You could check it with the channel tool, but it was obvious. So he does not continue the trendline. He ends it, and it becomes irrelevant.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 3: measuring borderline moves away and ending an overextended trendline
passages.t: Ending the line on the chart says 'I recognise there was a trendline, and I recognise price got too overextended.' The exact end point doesn't matter as long as you don't continue it.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 3: measuring borderline moves away and ending an overextended trendline
passages.t: Reflection: because the first three or four zones on a fresh chart had very strong moves away, it is easy to get too caught up in needing an extremely explosive move. The later borderline zone does qualify.
Most common: zones drawn too small. Include all the basing candles that are grouped together, not just two of them. Some zones were too big. 'Get rid of, like, a quarter of that.'

Drawing zones on boo-boo basing candles: 'Every candle I see on this chart is a basing candle.' A zone drawn on a basing candle with no stay-away candle is not a demand zone. If you can't tell what an explosive move away is, go back and watch his free full course on YouTube.
Using too much basing: where the basing isn't all together, he would use single-candle basing for the explosive move.

Misidentifying the move away: the candle right after the basing must be the explosive move. If it isn't, the zone is somewhere else, at the actual explosive move. Ignoring the wick: the zone has to use the wick.

Ending zones when they are tested or used: 'Just because it's used doesn't mean we end it.' Extend each zone to where it was removed so he can see your work. Ending a zone early makes it look as if it was drawn randomly.
Small zones change the removal point. If you draw a zone too small, it gets removed earlier than it should, which corrupts the chain.
On a very zoomed-out chart, moves away are hard to judge. Zoomed in, some would probably qualify.
A student measured the zone against the move away from basing before an explosive move. The move was slightly bigger, so no zone. 'It is very close… it's not way off.'
Drawing momentum lines as trendlines. A student had 4 correct trendlines but too many momentum lines, so that is what to work on.

A downward trendline drawn where there is no lower low after the peak is not a trendline. You need a lower low (or higher high), not just a peak and valley. One student also said a zone removed that line. That would have been correct if it had been a trendline.

Trendlines not attached: the line must touch the valley or peak. Zoomed in, even his won't be perfectly attached, but it can't be floating, and a wick must not poke through the line. 'Take pride in our work.'
Wrong starting point: start from the highest point (for a downtrend), not a random spot. The wrong start changes the angle, and that made a student miss a zone later.
A trendline started too far in misses earlier peaks and valleys. Redo sloppy trendlines and don't extend lines past where they belong.
Sideways price action is not a trendline. 'Just one more peak down like that and I would agree.' He praised students who drew the trendline and then ended it once price was overextended.
He admits a student may have found a valid trendline he missed: 'I'm not even gonna say you're wrong… I probably missed that one.'
Submit your homework chart on the DAILY timeframe and leave it there when you save it. He cannot switch to your timeframe, so 4-hour submissions cannot be marked.
Fix chart sharing issues. One chart wouldn't open. Another used a data indicator with no wicks, which can't be used anyway.
The 'winner' of best homework is just for fun. There is no prize, and having the worst homework doesn't matter. That's why you're there.
Struggling with what an explosive move away is is fine and is why the group exists. Not following instructions is what frustrates him and feels like wasted time.

passages.h: Corrections and next homework (Jan 1994 to Jan 1995)
passages.t: Copy his homework exactly after the session and make every correction, because later zones will reference these ones. The chain analysis has to stay the same for everyone.

passages.h: Corrections and next homework (Jan 1994 to Jan 1995)
passages.t: Many students had the borderline zone he rejected. Remove it. It was close, but he doesn't have it.

passages.h: Corrections and next homework (Jan 1994 to Jan 1995)
passages.t: Add the supply he has if you are missing it, and redraw it his way. The proximal line doesn't matter much (try to keep it similar). The distal line matters, because it decides exactly when the zone was removed. Next homework: January 1994 to January 1995.

passages.h: Corrections and next homework (Jan 1994 to Jan 1995)
passages.t: Use the trendline tool, make it perfectly horizontal, and map out every all-time high in the new section. Remember that an all-time high doesn't have to be an obvious one.

passages.h: Corrections and next homework (Jan 1994 to Jan 1995)
passages.t: Next week he will first check that the corrected supply is drawn exactly his way and the rejected zone is removed.

passages.h: Corrections and next homework (Jan 1994 to Jan 1995)
passages.t: He measured moves away this week to set a baseline zone size, and plans to do this whenever a new homework chart starts.
It is August. If trading is not going great, that is the reality, because summer is usually not the best time to trade. See you in the daily market breakdowns during the week.

passages.t: The rare no-basing case: an explosive drop then an explosive rally. Act as if there is basing there and draw the zone a similar size to your other zones.

passages.t: A steep move with no real pullbacks is momentum. A trendline needs a significant, obvious peak and valley, then the higher high.

passages.t: The starting all-time high was removed by an explosive move. The basing had two sections; he uses only the most recent one so the zone is not too big.

passages.h: Chart: [06:27] Sketch on the chart: price stepping up through small highs to a horizontal line at the top.
passages.t: An all-time high does not have to be an obvious peak. Every wick or high that price breaks above is an all-time high.

passages.t: Not big enough next to the real moves away; everything else is boo-boo basing. No demand removed that high, so the analysis ends there.

passages.h: Chart: [11:18] Two small arrows at a close peak and valley that he decides is good enough for a trendline.

passages.h: Chart: [12:54] Arrow at the move under the red supply that removed two demand zones and an all-time low.
passages.t: "Pretty strong zone", yet it later failed, most likely because it was very old with no liquidity trap before it.

passages.t: The zone was already removed, so he places the remove box where it was removed rather than extending it.

passages.t: Close, so he compared it with the other zones and kept it. That zone removed the downtrend line on a full close above it.

passages.t: "Just because it's used doesn't mean we end it." Extend each zone to where it was removed. Zones drawn too small get removed too early and break the chain.

passages.h: Chart: Homework chart (daily, fresh start of new section) Daily
passages.t: Supply zone after the starting all-time high was removed by an explosive move; basing split into two sections Why: Treat first visible high as all-time high (axiom). Use only the most recent basing section so the zone isn't too big. 'Not the best zone, but it is an explosive move.' Result: Zone drawn; later tested and removed by an objectively explosive move away

All-time high removed but only by boo-boo basing candles Why: A removal without an explosive move away does not create a zone; one candidate was close but smaller than the other moves away Result: No zone; chain analysis ends there

Zone that removed the earlier zone, sized against prior zones Why: First draft too big; cloned a previous zone to compare and tightened to similar size; bigger acceptable, tiny never Result: Drawn slightly larger than prior zone; price had given a nice trade off the earlier zone

Two borderline possible trendlines Why: One 'not a good enough peak and valley'; the other close enough though drawn off wicks Result: First rejected, second drawn; irrelevant since no zone formed from either
Supply that removed 2 demand zones and an all-time low Why: Multiple removals = pretty strong zone Result: Later failed, most likely because it was so old and had no liquidity trap before it

passages.h: Chart: Homework chart Daily (likely weekly trendline)
passages.t: New all-time low with blatant valley and peak -> downward trendline Why: Draw from highest point to the peak (next touch point); much better than the borderline one Result: Trendline later removed by a full candle close above it

Demand after all-time high removed; candidate move away measured 94 pips Why: Borderline; drew it to see, compared to other zones Result: Kept on the chart; this zone removed the downward trendline and an area of supply
Candidate demand: total candle incl. wick 102 pips vs green move-away candle ~80 pips Why: Move away not big enough relative to the basing Result: No demand zone (close; some students had it)

Upward trendline: blatant peak, valley, and higher high; price then rallied far above Why: Price got so overextended (channel tool optional, obvious visually) that the trendline is irrelevant Result: Trendline ended, not extended
Student drew a trendline and many zones Why: Not a trendline, though overall trend looks up; most zones were on basing candles Result: Told to stop drawing basing-candle 'moves away'

Q: How big does a move away have to be, and how do you measure it? (a comment on his channel said it seems too subjective) A: There's no measurement. It is about 95% objective with a little subjectivity, which is just reality. You can't make it 100% objective, partly because big moves on gold or oil change the chart's zoom, so a consistent measurement isn't possible. Don't treat boo-boo basing candles as a move away.
Some moves away are very obvious and some are tricky. With experience you learn which are good. At the start of a new homework chart he will measure a few in pips to set a baseline.

Q: (Student homework) Is this basing, before the explosive move away, a zone? A: He measured the move away against it on his other screen. The move was a little bigger, so he wouldn't have that zone, but it was very close and not way off.
Q: (Student) Why did you draw this zone? A: The student explained it removed a supply further up the chart. He hadn't noticed because he was zoomed in down below, so he'll cover it next week.

Q: Any questions before we go? A: The chat was quiet and there were no questions. He repeated that he'll check next week that the corrected supply is drawn exactly his way and the rejected zone is removed.
Drawing zones on boo-boo basing candles with no explosive move away. Calling a basing candle with no stay-away candle a demand zone.
Drawing zones too small: only part of the basing group. This gives zones everywhere and earlier false removals. Drawing zones too big by including too much basing or combining two basing sections.

Picking the wrong candle as the move away. The candle after the basing must be the explosive one. Ignoring the wick when drawing the zone. Ending a zone when it was tested or used instead of when it was removed. Drawing momentum lines as trendlines. Drawing a trendline from a peak and valley with no lower low or higher high. Calling sideways price action a trendline.

Trendlines not attached to the valley or peak, or wicks poking through the line. Starting a trendline from a random point. The angle comes out wrong and later zones get missed. Continuing a trendline after price got overextended.

Getting too caught up in needing an extremely explosive move after seeing a few very strong zones. Marking the low and calling it a zone after a removal that had no explosive move. Submitting homework on the 4-hour timeframe, or as a chart that can't be opened. Not making the corrections he asked for, such as keeping a zone he told you to remove. Very old zones with no liquidity trap before them can fail.
Did this zone remove an opposing zone, a trendline, or an all-time high/low? Is the move away explosive compared with the basing and the surrounding candles, and not made of small basing candles?
Is there a stay-away candle, and how big is the space to the proximal line (tradable or drawable only)?

Am I using only the most recent basing section and including all of its candles and wicks? Is the zone a similar size to my other zones? Is the zone extended until it was actually removed? For a trendline: blatant peak and valley, plus a higher high or lower low?

Does the trendline start at the lowest or highest point, touch the valley or peak, and not cut any wicks? Has price got overextended from the trendline, so it should be ended? If the call is borderline: did I draw it and compare it with other zones, or measure it? Is the zone very old with no liquidity trap before it (higher failure risk)? Is it summer or August (low-odds conditions)?

“The bigger the space, the better the zone.” “It's, like, 95% objective.” “Just because we remove an opposing zone, trend line, or all-time high, doesn't mean we have a zone.” “We don't end the zone when it was tested, unless it was removed.” “If you make the zone really tiny, then we have zones everywhere.” “I'm not worried about missing a trade. I am not.” “He's speaking to me through the charts.”
“Just because it's used doesn't mean we end it.” “It's the distal line that matters.” “Summer is not usually the best.”

Single-candle or 'invisible' basing: after a massive drop straight into a massive rally, act as if there is basing and size the zone like your previous zones. When basing has two sections, use the most recent section only. Never combine them.
On a fresh chart, treat the first visible high and low as all-time high and low 'like an axiom'.
He measures moves away in pips at the start of a new homework chart to set a baseline (94 pips kept; 102-pip candle vs ~80-pip move away rejected), while saying there is no fixed measurement.
Explicit 95% objective / 5% subjective admission. Gold and oil moves change the chart zoom, which is why moves away cannot be measured objectively.

A strong supply that removed 2 demand zones and an all-time low still failed, most likely because it was very old and had no liquidity trap before it. Small zones corrupt the chain: a zone drawn too small gets 'removed' too early.
A wrong trendline start point changes the angle and leads to missed zones further down the chain.

Homework protocol: daily timeframe only, copy his corrections exactly (the distal line decides when a zone is removed), map all-time highs with a horizontal line. Next section is Jan 1994 to Jan 1995. He accepts missing zones in live trading: 'I'm not worried about missing a trade.'

Pause, jump, stay away: the bigger the gap, the better the zone. A frog sits still on a lily pad. Then it jumps far. Then it lands well away and does not hop back right away. The far landing leaves a big gap. A frog that jumps and plops back next to its pad did not really go anywhere.
The basing is the frog sitting, the explosive candle is the jump, and the stay-away candle is where it lands. The water between is the space that tells you how strong the jump was.
Basing can be one candle. If there are two basing sections, use only the most recent one. Grade the zone by the space between the stay-away candle and the proximal line.
Keep a zone until it is removed, not when it is tested. Every high price breaks is an all-time high.

passages.h: Step: Basing can be just one candle
passages.t: A zone starts with basing: small pause candles. It does not need three. One candle is enough. Here is a first little group of basing.
Price nudges up a bit and pauses again. Now there are two basing sections. Do not glue them together: the zone would be too big.
One big full-bodied candle blasts away. This is the bank footprint. Use only the MOST RECENT basing section, right next to the explosive candle, and include all its wicks.

passages.h: Step: Stay-away candle and the space
passages.t: Next, a stay-away candle keeps price away from the proximal line. The space between them is how Kevin grades a zone: bigger space, better zone. Tiny space means drawable but not tradable.
When price comes back and touches the zone, it is tested, not removed. Keep extending the zone until it is actually removed. Ending it early makes it look random.

Minimum basing candles? - One. Basing can be a single candle. Two basing sections before the move? - Use only the most recent one. Do not combine. What grades a zone? - The space between the stay-away candle and the proximal line. Small space zone? - Drawable, not tradable. Keep it to see what removes it.
Massive drop then massive rally, no basing? - Act as if basing is there; draw a zone similar in size to your others. Tested vs removed? - Tested: keep extending. Removed: end it with the remove tool.
Which highs are all-time highs? - Every high that price breaks above, not just obvious peaks.
Which line matters most when copying his zones? - The distal line: it decides exactly when the zone is removed.

Kevin opens with a mini lesson for new members on the four things a zone needs (basing, an explosive move-away, a stay-away candle and the space between the stay-away candle and the proximal line) and what makes a trendline (obvious peak, obvious valley and a new high or low).

He then walks through the chain analysis on the daily homework chart, showing that a trendline is only removed when a candle fully closes beyond it, that overextended trendlines should be ended rather than extended, and that a removal does not automatically give a new zone.

Along the way he explains his normal stop distance, why a zone broken by a few pips might still not have been a loss, and how a large wick on the move-away candle is fine if the body is big enough. In the homework review the main theme is students drawing trendlines that are too large, which makes them miss the recent peaks and valleys and the zones that follow, plus zones drawn too wide.

The session ends with a long off-topic talk on mindset, self-improvement, lowering expenses and keeping your 9-to-5, a note on 12-month stock zones, and the new homework: January 1995 to January 1996.

A zone needs four things: basing, an explosive move-away candle, a stay-away candle, and space between the stay-away candle and the proximal line. Don't draw a zone until the stay-away candle has closed. If there is no basing but the move away is aggressive, draw the basing in yourself.
Make sure the first candle out of the basing is explosive. Little boo-boo candles are not a move away.
Rate zone strength by the space between the stay-away candle and the proximal line. More space is better. Keep drawable-but-untradable zones on the chart to see what removes them.
Draw a zone only if it removes an opposing zone, removes a trendline, or makes an all-time (not just any) high or low. A removal does not guarantee a new zone. If nothing qualifies, draw nothing.
A trendline needs an obvious peak, an obvious valley, and a new high (uptrend) or new low (downtrend).
An uptrend line is removed only by a full candle close below it, and a downtrend line only by a full close above it.

Attach a new trendline to the most recent peak and valley. Don't draw huge trendlines that skip recent structure. End a trendline once price becomes too overextended from it. Don't extend it. When a zone is removed, extend it close to the removal point.

Draw a zone at a similar size to the other zones. Use the single basing candle before the explosive move rather than combining many basing candles. When an obvious explosive move is next to a weaker one, draw the more obvious one. A long wick on the move-away candle is fine if the body is still big enough. Enter at the zone or just a little before it.

Keep the stop at least his normal visible distance beyond the zone. Go wider in volatile conditions. Don't draw momentum lines in the chain-analysis homework. Only trendlines. Do homework on the daily chart and copy his zones exactly, or it won't be marked. Don't zoom in too far when looking for zones.

passages.h: Mini lesson: the four things a zone needs
passages.t: Thing 1 is basing. About 98% of the time there are basing candles. It can be 1 candle or 3. He prefers 1 to 3, and his favourite is a single-candle basing zone (he points to a recent single-candle basing trade that worked very well).

passages.h: Mini lesson: the four things a zone needs
passages.t: The rare exception has no basing: a massive red candle down followed straight away by another aggressive move up. Because the move away is aggressive, you still have a zone, and you simply draw the basing in yourself.

passages.h: Mini lesson: the four things a zone needs
passages.t: Thing 2 is the move-away candle or candles. All you really need is one explosive candle. One big candle is different from a series of little 'boo-boo basing candles'. Little boo-boo candles are not a move away.

passages.h: Mini lesson: the four things a zone needs
passages.t: After the first explosive candle, little boo-boo basing candles are fine. The best case is basing, an explosive move away, then another explosive move away. The most important part is the explosive move away from the basing.

passages.h: Mini lesson: the four things a zone needs
passages.t: Thing 3 is the stay-away candle. It can be a basing candle, but he prefers it to be explosive and to carry another explosive move. A boo-boo candle is acceptable.

passages.h: Mini lesson: the four things a zone needs
passages.t: Thing 4 is the space between the stay-away candle and where you draw the proximal line. You get the space automatically once the stay-away candle closes.

passages.h: Mini lesson: the four things a zone needs
passages.t: You do NOT have the zone yet after just basing plus a move away. He does not draw it until the stay-away candle has closed and the next candle has started forming. Only then does the zone exist.

passages.h: Mini lesson: the four things a zone needs
passages.t: The strength of the zone depends on how much space there is between the stay-away candle and the zone. More space is better. A tiny space is a drawable zone but not really a tradable zone (as in the first video lesson).

passages.h: Mini lesson: the four things a zone needs
passages.t: Drawable-but-not-tradable zones are still kept on the chart because he wants to see what removes them for the chain analysis.
A trendline must be very obvious. He admits that is subjective and says it gets easier the more Sunday sessions you attend.
An uptrend line needs a very obvious peak, then a very obvious valley, then a higher high. If after the peak and valley price fails to make a new high, there is no trendline. 'It's that simple.'
Steady moves without that structure are momentum. 'There's momentum everywhere. There's trend lines not everywhere.' Trendlines are harder to get. He uses trendlines 'as kind of like a guide'.
In the chain analysis you draw all removed zones, all fresh zones, all trendlines, and map all the all-time highs.

Rules (shown top right of the chart): every zone he draws, in homework and in his own chart link, either (1) removes an opposing zone, (2) removes a trendline, or (3) makes an all-time high or low. It must be an all-time high or low, not just any high or low.
He shows examples from earlier in the chart: two zones that qualified because they removed an all-time high, and a supply that removed a demand (rule 1).
Last week's trendline ended where price 'just blasted off'. He did not extend it because it got too overextended. In your homework he wants trendlines to end when they get too overextended.

When a zone is removed, extend it to roughly where it was removed. Leaving it short or running it far past the removal candle is 'laziness'. It does not have to be exactly on it, but it has to be close.

passages.h: Walkthrough part 1: the far-away demand and a downtrend line
passages.t: A supply was removed. Under rule 1 he looked for the zone that removed it. 'Just because a zone is removed doesn't mean we're gonna have a zone.'

passages.h: Walkthrough part 1: the far-away demand and a downtrend line
passages.t: He checked a small area close by against the older zones and decided it was not good enough. The zone that removed the supply was quite far down: a demand area. He wrapped the lines around it at a similar size to earlier zones. It was a little smaller, but 'there's no perfection here'.

passages.h: Walkthrough part 1: the far-away demand and a downtrend line
passages.t: Then he found a very obvious peak, a very obvious valley and a lower low, so a downtrend line was drawn.

passages.h: Walkthrough part 1: the far-away demand and a downtrend line
passages.t: Timing of removal: the trendline was not removed when the first candle poked through it. It was removed when a later candle fully closed beyond it. For a downward trendline you need a full close above it, and for an upward trendline a full close below it.

passages.h: Walkthrough part 1: the far-away demand and a downtrend line
passages.t: He gives a live example: the weekly DXY trendline was not removed earlier when price only pushed into it. It was removed this past week with a full close below it.

passages.h: Walkthrough part 2: single-candle basing demand, stop placement and a broken zone
passages.t: The trendline was removed (rule 2). He then looked at the explosive move away and drew a single-candle basing demand. It was just barely broken afterwards.

passages.h: Walkthrough part 2: single-candle basing demand, stop placement and a broken zone
passages.t: Trading view: you probably would still have been in this trade. With a stop that tight you might have been stopped out by the spread.

passages.h: Walkthrough part 2: single-candle basing demand, stop placement and a broken zone
passages.t: Entry: he enters at the zone or just a little before it, and 'most always' just a little before.

passages.h: Walkthrough part 2: single-candle basing demand, stop placement and a broken zone
passages.t: Stop: he showed a normal stop sitting a visible distance beyond the zone and said his stops are 'pretty much always gonna be that far from the zone' at minimum. In volatile conditions (Trump 'on a tirade', a war in Iran) a wider stop makes sense.

passages.h: Walkthrough part 2: single-candle basing demand, stop placement and a broken zone
passages.t: A zone being broken does not mean the trade lost. It is not ideal, but with his normal stop this one would not have been a loss unless the spread blew out. The odd stop-out from spread happens, especially on day-trading timeframes. He showed the stop only, not a take-profit.

passages.h: Walkthrough part 3: no zone after the next removal, and an uptrend line that was ended
passages.t: After that demand was removed (rule 1), he found no qualifying zone. 'I know a lot of you are probably thinking that's a zone.' Checked against the other zones, the move away was not good enough.

passages.h: Walkthrough part 3: no zone after the next removal, and an uptrend line that was ended
passages.t: A peak, a valley and a higher high gave an uptrend line, attached to the next lowest point.

passages.h: Walkthrough part 3: no zone after the next removal, and an uptrend line that was ended
passages.t: Price got a bit overextended. He put a channel tool on it, attached to the peak, to check, and said 'it's actually not bad'. He still keeps the line on the chart but does not extend it. In homework he wants it ending around that area, or slightly earlier. 'I just don't want to see it continued.'

passages.h: Walkthrough part 3: no zone after the next removal, and an uptrend line that was ended
passages.t: An all-time high followed, but no zone removed it, so nothing was drawn. A second all-time high also had nothing he felt comfortable drawing. 'Just because a zone is removed, or a trend line is removed, does not automatically mean that we have a new zone formed.'

passages.h: Walkthrough part 4: the hidden small supply and the big-wick supply
passages.t: A blatant peak, a valley and a higher high gave another uptrend line. There was a small zone that was 'very difficult to spot'. He zoomed in, compared it with the other zones and found an explosive move away. It was not a great zone and he probably would not have traded it.

passages.h: Walkthrough part 4: the hidden small supply and the big-wick supply
passages.t: It was an odd situation: there was a stay-away candle as needed, then price shot straight back up into the zone. If you block out what follows, it was setting up nicely (explosive move, stay-away candle, another leg). It was 'still a great trade, but nothing that I would have taken personally'. He double-checks for missed trendlines: 'Sometimes I'll miss stuff... I'm not perfect.'

passages.h: Walkthrough part 4: the hidden small supply and the big-wick supply
passages.t: A supply then removed an all-time high and a demand, with a very obvious explosive move away but a long wick. 'Just because it's a large move away, doesn't make... an explosive move away.' It still qualifies because the body is big enough overall compared with the wick.

passages.h: Walkthrough part 4: the hidden small supply and the big-wick supply
passages.t: Drawing it was tricky: there was an overall basing area and a little single-candle basing inside it. He drew it out to a point that keeps it a similar size to the other zones rather than making it really tiny. This supply is a zone for two reasons: it removed an opposing zone and an all-time high.

passages.h: Walkthrough part 4: the hidden small supply and the big-wick supply
passages.t: After that price is at all-time highs. Each little push up is a new all-time high, and there are no more zones, so the chain ends.

passages.h: Walkthrough part 4: the hidden small supply and the big-wick supply
passages.t: Week summary: 4 zones. It was a great 'combination week' that tested spotting zones, trendlines, and not forcing zones that were close.

The biggest theme: students drew huge trendlines. On a daily chart these are most likely weekly trendlines. Being too zoomed-out means you ignore all the trendlines in between, and those recent ones are what give the zones in the chain.
'We're only really trying to draw the most recent one.' He wants the most recent peak and valley, not too big.
One student's trendline was anchored so that after the second touch point price needed a new high, which it never made, so the line was incorrect.
Another student was 'ignoring that valley'. The correct line runs from the most recent peak through the most recent valley. Don't draw momentum lines on the homework. Only trendlines.
A trendline drawn where there is no new high after the peak and valley is 'a big no-no... Where is the new high?'
Make sure your trendline is attached to the correct point (he admits he sometimes gets this wrong too). Ending trendlines when overextended was praised when students did it.

passages.h: Homework review: zones, missed items and logistics
passages.t: The second theme was zones drawn too big from combining too many basing candles. Use the single candle before the explosive move. Some students' zones were only slightly large, and he called that nitpicking. Weak move-away zones were removed. A boo-boo basing candle is not a supply level. When an obvious explosive move sits close to a weaker one, draw the more obvious one.

passages.h: Homework review: zones, missed items and logistics
passages.t: If your homework drew a zone differently, change it to how he drew it so everyone has the same chain analysis next week.

passages.h: Homework review: zones, missed items and logistics
passages.t: Grace was given on the very hard-to-spot small supply and on a borderline zone that 'could go both ways'.

passages.h: Homework review: zones, missed items and logistics
passages.t: For new people he wants all-time highs marked on the chart, even if an experienced student already knew it was an all-time-high move.

passages.h: Homework review: zones, missed items and logistics
passages.t: If a student's earlier zone was wrong, he still marks the later work as if it were correct, because it follows the student's own chain.

passages.h: Homework review: zones, missed items and logistics
passages.t: You must be on the daily chart, or he cannot mark it. A submission that did not copy the old zones was not marked: 'I will not be marking a homework that does not follow the rules.'

passages.h: Homework review: zones, missed items and logistics
passages.t: For other lesson homework (multiple sequence analysis, trend trading), label the timeframe. The recurring problem was zones far too big.

passages.h: Homework review: zones, missed items and logistics
passages.t: The best homework went to the student with only one mistake (the hard demand at the start), who nailed the trendlines and ended them correctly.

A YouTube comment said a 'big move away' is too subjective. He agrees there is some subjectivity, and two people's chain analyses may differ by one item depending on zoom, but most students got the important zones, so 'not really at the end of the day'.
Zoom level matters: don't zoom in too much, because then every zone looks like a large move.

A student flagged Friday's all-pairs news (the Jackson Hole Symposium). He says it will probably affect everything, so Friday might not be a great day to trade. Don't let world events and politics distract you. Focus on your life and on trading.

12-month (yearly) stock zones: there are few options and he is waiting on one that could take years to return. One example was about 100% from a 12-month zone to supply over about 13 years. One stock he bought went up 150% in a day. His 3M purchase at a 12-month zone worked out and paid a dividend on the way up. 'This is building wealth.' He made a TradingView scanner for these but it did not save.

Have a great job so you can afford to take risks like long-term investing. He recommends How to Win Friends and Influence People to help you get a better job. Too much news and information confuses and distracts people (he agreed with a student).

Keep improving: read, give yourself a classical education (rhetoric, logic, grammar), learn philosophy, and don't outsource all your thinking to AI. Use it to help you understand things, not to replace thinking.

Lower expenses: buy meat on sale and freeze it, own DVDs instead of paying for subscriptions. Don't chase the next new thing, and don't care if people think you're weird. Think generationally, not just about spending everything in retirement.
Roughly 15% of your time for pleasure is his rough figure. The rest goes to learning and improving.
To a student who wants to quit their 9-to-5 by trading: don't think you can give it up in the next year or two. Focus on a good 9-to-5, save money, and lower expenses. It's a long journey.
The goal for the group is profitability, but also improving in life. You need a good income so you can trade your own capital.
Chain analysis on the daily chart, January 1995 to January 1996. Map out the all-time high, and carry over his zones exactly the way he drew them.
It is 'pretty much a fresh chart' with lots of trendlines and quite a few zones. 'It's gonna be a good challenge.'
[00:40-04:30] Zone recap diagrams: no-basing case, single explosive candle vs small candles, and the peak / valley / higher-high trendline.

[05:00-15:30] Homework on AUDUSD 1D (FXCM), 1994: the far-away demand, a downtrend line removed on a full close, his single-candle demand trade with the position tool, a rejected candidate, uptrend lines, the hidden small supply and the big-wick supply. [16:00-30:00] Student homework (trendlines too wide, zones too big) and lesson homework.
[40:00-46:00] Forex Factory calendar (Jackson Hole) and 12-month stock zones on 4-pane stock layouts (for example ALB and MRNA).

The homework chart is AUDUSD 1D from FXCM (around 1994), not an unnamed market. Clarified: the single-candle demand example uses TradingView's long-position tool, which shows a target as well as the stop: stop 0.00525 (52.5 pips, 0.741%), target 0.01682 (168.2 pips), risk/reward 3.2. He said he was showing it for the stop, not claiming that target.

passages.h: Chart: [01:00] The labelled zone diagram with the no-basing case drawn beside it: a big red candle, then a big green candle, with a box drawn where the basing would be.
passages.t: About 98% of the time there is basing. In the rare case with none, the move is aggressive enough that you draw the basing in yourself.

passages.h: Chart: [02:00] Sketch: two small basing candles, one tall explosive candle, then the next candle above.
passages.t: One aggressive candle is the move away, not a run of small "boo-boo" candles. Best case: basing, explosive, explosive again; small candles after the first explosive one are fine.

passages.h: Chart: [05:01] The chain so far on AUDUSD 1D (FXCM): "Treating as ATH" / "Treating as ATL" lines, the earlier zones, and last week's trendline ended where price "just blasted off".
passages.t: End trendlines once they are too overextended. Extend each removed zone to roughly where it was removed: not short, not far past it.

passages.h: Chart: [07:02] An arrow down to the demand that removed the supply, quite a way below the nearby candidate he rejected.
passages.t: The nearby area did not hold up against the older zones. He wraps the far demand at a similar size to the earlier zones.

passages.h: Chart: [09:02] Horizontal marks above the demand while answering "do we care how close or far the zone is?"
passages.t: Typically the zone that removed something is fairly close. If it were all the way down, he would probably just end the analysis: a feel, not a measurement.

passages.h: Chart: [10:03] AUDUSD 1D, April 1994: long-position tool on the single-candle demand. Stop 0.00525 (52.5 pips, 0.741%), target 0.01682 (168.2 pips), risk/reward 3.2.
passages.t: He enters at the zone or "most always" just a little before. The stop sits a visible distance beyond the zone, the minimum he uses; wider in volatile news conditions.

passages.h: Chart: [10:03] AUDUSD 1D, April 1994: long-position tool on the single-candle demand. Stop 0.00525 (52.5 pips, 0.741%), target 0.01682 (168.2 pips), risk/reward 3.2.
passages.t: The zone was just barely broken, but with that stop the trade would not have lost unless the spread blew out.

passages.h: Chart: [11:03] A circle on the candle many would call a zone after that demand was removed.
passages.t: "I know a lot of you are probably thinking that's a zone." Compared with the other zones the move away is not good enough.

passages.h: Chart: [17:05] A student's chart: his zig-zag over the recent peak and valley that the student's wide trendline skipped.
passages.t: "You're ignoring that peak and valley." Drawing too wide misses the recent peaks and valleys, and with them the zones.

passages.h: Chart: [18:05] Same student: circles on the hard-to-spot small supply and on a candle that is not a good enough move away.
passages.t: Grace for everyone on the hidden supply. A line anchored so that price then needed a new high it never made is incorrect.

passages.h: Chart: [20:06] El Chapo's chart with his note: "Good move away but I don't like how price quickly came back to test the zone"; Kevin circles the zone.
passages.t: He agrees it would not have been a great setup; include all the basing when drawing it. "Probably your best work yet."

passages.h: Chart: [24:07] Multiple-sequence homework from a student: a large green box labelled "4H consequences Zone".
passages.t: Right area, but the zones are way too big. Draw the little single-candle basing before the move, and label each timeframe.

passages.h: Chart: Homework chart (daily, chain analysis; market not named) Daily
passages.t: Supply removed; demand found far below Why: A nearby candidate was checked against older zones and was not good enough. The real zone that removed the supply was a demand quite far down, drawn at a similar size to earlier zones. Far, but not too far. Result: Drawn as a zone (rule 1: removed an opposing zone).

passages.h: Chart: Homework chart (daily, chain analysis; market not named) Daily
passages.t: Downtrend line: obvious peak, obvious valley, lower low Why: Meets the trendline rules. Removal counted only when a candle fully closed above it, not when the first candle poked through. Result: Trendline drawn and later removed on the full close.
Weekly uptrend line Why: Earlier pushes into the line did not remove it. A full weekly close below it this past week did. Result: Trendline now removed.

passages.h: Chart: Homework chart (daily, chain analysis; market not named) Daily
passages.t: Single-candle basing demand after the trendline removal Why: Explosive move away from a single basing candle (rule 2). Price later just barely broke the zone. Result: Zone counted as broken. As a trade, with his normal stop distance beyond the zone it would probably not have been a loss unless the spread spiked.

passages.h: Chart: Homework chart (daily, chain analysis; market not named) Daily
passages.t: Candidate zone after the demand was removed Why: Many students would call it a zone, but compared with the other zones the move away was not good enough. Result: No zone drawn.

passages.h: Chart: Homework chart (daily, chain analysis; market not named) Daily
passages.t: Uptrend line: peak, valley, higher high, attached to the next lowest point Why: Price became somewhat overextended (checked with a channel tool attached to the peak). Result: Line kept but ended, not extended.
