passages.h: Chart: Homework chart (daily, chain analysis; market not named) Daily
passages.t: Two all-time highs with no removing zone Why: No zone he felt comfortable drawing. Result: Nothing drawn. A removal does not automatically mean a new zone.

passages.h: Chart: Homework chart (daily, chain analysis; market not named) Daily
passages.t: Small, hard-to-spot supply after an uptrend line Why: Explosive move away when zoomed in, with a stay-away candle, but price shot straight back into it. Not a great zone. Result: Drawn as a zone. It played out well, but he would not have taken it personally.

passages.h: Chart: Homework chart (daily, chain analysis; market not named) Daily
passages.t: Supply with a long wick on the move-away candle Why: The body was still big enough compared with the wick, so it qualifies. Drawn from the overall basing out to a size similar to the other zones, not just the tiny single candle. Result: Zone for two reasons: removed a demand and an all-time high. After that, only new all-time highs and the chain ends.

Long-term buys at 12-month demand zones Why: Rare setups that take a long time to play out. Used to build wealth (one with a dividend on the way up). Result: Example of about 100% over about 13 years; one stock up 150% in a day; his 3M buy worked out.

Q: Do we care how close or far the zone that removed something is? A: Yes, closer is better. Typically he wants it reasonably near. The demand in this walkthrough was getting far but not too far. He has no way to measure it. If the zone that removed it were all the way further down, he would not draw it and would just end the analysis. It's a feel thing with some subjectivity, and it's unlikely to be that far anyway.
Q: Is it better to zoom in really close to spot all the zones? A: No. If you zoom in too much, every zone looks like a large move. Missing the small, hard supply this week was understandable.
Q: (Student note) Trendlines have been weak for me recently. A: He agreed. Overall it was very good work, nothing too detrimental. Keep it up.

Q: There's all-pairs news on Friday (Jackson Hole Symposium). What do you think? A: He looked it up: central bank leaders meeting about long-term economic issues and possible shifts. It will probably affect everything, so Friday might not be a great day to trade. Don't let the news itself distract you.

Q: I'm learning to trade so I can give up my 9-to-5. A: Don't think you can give up your 9-to-5 in the next year or two. Focus on having a good 9-to-5, save money, lower your expenses. It's a long journey, but he believes you can do it.
Q: Have you read Surrounded by Idiots? A: No. He looked it up, found it interesting and may add it to his list.

Drawing trendlines too large (really weekly lines on the daily), which misses recent peaks and valleys and the zones they lead to. Anchoring a trendline so no new high or low follows the second touch point. Drawing a trendline where there is no new high or low after the peak and valley. Ignoring the most recent valley or peak when attaching a trendline. Extending a trendline after price has become overextended.

Drawing a zone before the stay-away candle has closed. Treating boo-boo basing candles as an explosive move away. Drawing zones too big by combining too many basing candles. Assuming every removal or all-time high gives a new zone (forcing zones). Calling a trendline removed when a candle only pokes through, before a full close. Stop loss too tight, right at the zone, so spread spikes take you out.

Assuming a broken zone always means a losing trade. Being lazy about where removed zones end. Zooming in so far that every move looks explosive. Drawing momentum lines on the homework. Wrong timeframe or not copying the previous zones in homework. Not labelling the timeframe on lesson homework. Trading big all-pairs news days such as Jackson Hole without caution.
Expecting to quit a 9-to-5 within a year or two of learning to trade.
Is there basing (or an aggressive reversal where I can draw the basing in)? Is the first candle out of the basing explosive, not boo-boo candles? Has the stay-away candle closed?
How much space is there between the stay-away candle and the proximal line? Tradable, or just drawable?

Did this zone remove an opposing zone, remove a trendline, or make an all-time high or low? Is the removing zone reasonably close, not extremely far away? If there is a long wick on the move-away candle, is the body still big enough?
Is the zone a similar size to my other zones (single candle before the move, not too many basing candles)?

Is my trendline built from the most recent obvious peak and valley, with a new high or low after it? Has the trendline actually been removed by a full candle close beyond it? Is the trendline overextended and so should be ended?

Is my entry at or just before the zone, with the stop at least my normal distance beyond it (wider if conditions are volatile)? Is there major all-pairs news (e.g. Jackson Hole) this day? Am I on the daily chart with his zones copied (homework)?

“My favorite one is a single candle basing zone.” “We're not looking for little boo-boo basin candles, we're looking for one aggressive move-away candle.” “The bigger the space between the stay-away candle, the better.” “There's momentum everywhere. There's trend lines not everywhere.” “Just because a zone is removed doesn't mean we're gonna have a zone.” “For an upper trend line, we need a full close below it.”

“I don't want to see this, that's laziness.” “Just because the zone is broken doesn't mean that the trade wouldn't have worked.” “Just because it's a large move away, doesn't make... an explosive move away.” “There's no perfection here.” “We're only really trying to draw the most recent one.” “Where is the new high?” “It's so easy to be better than the average person.” “Focus on having a good 9-5.”

An explicit four-part zone definition: basing, explosive move away, stay-away candle, and the space between the stay-away candle and the proximal line, with zone strength measured by that space. The zone does not exist until the stay-away candle closes.
No-basing exception: after an aggressive reversal with no basing, draw the basing in yourself.
'Boo-boo basing candles' named: small candles that do not count as the move away, though they are fine after the first explosive candle.
Trendline removal timing: a full candle close beyond the line (below for uptrend, above for downtrend), shown on the live weekly DXY.
Use a channel tool attached to the peak to judge whether a trendline is overextended, then end it rather than extend it.

A zone just barely broken can still be a non-losing trade when the stop sits his normal distance beyond the zone. Spread spikes are the main risk with tight stops, especially on day-trading timeframes.
How close the removing zone should be: closer is better, judged by feel. If it is extremely far away, end the analysis.
A large wick on the move-away candle is fine if the body is big enough. In a tricky basing area, size the zone to match the other zones.

The homework's main error: trendlines drawn too large (weekly-sized on the daily) skip the recent trendlines and so the zones in the chain. Don't over-zoom when looking for zones, or every move looks explosive.
12-month stock zones for wealth building (100% over about 13 years, a 150% day, 3M with a dividend).
Career advice: keep a good 9-to-5, lower expenses, and don't expect to go full-time within a year or two.

A zone has four parts: sit, jump, stay away, and a gap. Think of a rocket. First it sits on the pad. Then whoosh, it blasts off. Then it keeps flying and does not fall back down. The empty sky between the rocket and the pad shows how strong the launch was. We only say "launch!" once the rocket has really left.
Basing is the rocket on the pad, the explosive candle is the blast-off, the stay-away candle is the rocket still climbing, and the space is the sky under it.
A zone needs basing, an explosive move away, a stay-away candle and space. It does not exist until the stay-away candle closes.
Only a full candle close beyond a trendline removes it. Use the most recent trendline, not a huge one.
Enter at or just before the zone; keep a normal stop beyond it. A broken zone is not always a loss.
Thing 1: basing. Usually 1 to 3 small candles. Kevin's favourite is a single basing candle, like this one.
Thing 2: one explosive candle straight out of the basing. A run of little "boo-boo" candles covering the same distance does not count.
Thing 3: the stay-away candle. It stays away from where the zone will be. While it is still forming, we do NOT have a zone yet.

passages.h: Step: 4. The space: now the zone exists
passages.t: Thing 4: the space between the stay-away candle and the proximal line. Once the stay-away candle has closed and the next candle starts, the zone exists. More space means a stronger zone.

passages.h: Step: Entry and a normal stop
passages.t: Enter at the zone or just a little before it. Keep the stop at least a normal visible distance beyond the zone; wider when the news is wild. A zone broken by a few pips is not always a losing trade.

The 4 things a zone needs? - Basing, explosive move away, stay-away candle, space to the proximal line. When does the zone exist? - After the stay-away candle closes and the next candle starts. Kevin's favourite basing? - A single basing candle. Tiny space under the stay-away candle? - Drawable, not tradable. No basing but an aggressive reversal? - Draw the basing in yourself.

Where does Kevin enter? - At the zone or just a little before it. Huge trendline on the daily? - Probably a weekly line. Draw the most recent one. Zoom in very close to find zones? - No. Zoomed in too much, every move looks explosive.
Kevin walks through the chain-analysis homework on the daily chart from January 1995 to January 1996, a week he calls tricky because of the many trendlines.

He repeats the three rules for drawing a zone (it removes an opposing zone, removes a trendline, or makes an all-time high/low) and gives a detailed trendline lesson: obvious peak and valley plus a break of the prior low/high, never cutting through wicks, ending overextended lines, updating the line after a new high or low, and counting a trendline as removed only on a full candle close beyond it.

He adds a new clarification: for a zone to be the one that removed a downward trendline, its basing candle must be at or below the trendline. He then marks each student's homework, flags zones that 'accomplished nothing', wrong timeframes and redrawn zones that were never on his charts, and says he is debating a future rule for zones with two explosive moves away.
He closes by saying a swing trader's stop should be wider when a higher timeframe zone is in control, and by explaining why economic data and fundamentals hardly matter for 1:1 to 3:1 swing trades.
Only draw a zone that removes an opposing zone, removes a trendline, or makes an all-time high/low. For every zone you draw, ask: what did it remove?
Draw a trendline only with an obvious peak and valley AND a break of the prior low (downtrend) or high (uptrend).
Anchor from the highest (or lowest) point possible; if the line cuts through wicks or candles, move to the next highest (or lowest) point. End a trendline when price gets overextended away from it.
A trendline is removed only when a candle closes fully beyond it with no wick or body touching; until then extend it.

Let the trendline cut through candles until price breaks it or makes a new high/low; then draw the updated trendline. After a new lower low, draw the updated downward trendline from the recent peak. When a trendline is removed, a zone MIGHT exist; basing candles alone do not qualify.
A demand counts as removing a downward trendline only if its basing candle is at or below the line (for supply and an upward trendline, at or above).
When a zone is removed, look for the opposing zone that removed it; there usually is one, but not always.

When candidates are close, measure the move away; the first one that qualifies goes in the chain analysis. Keep zone sizes similar to your other zones (trim if needed; body to body is fine). Copy his chain analysis exactly each week and delete zones not on his charts. Do homework on the daily FXCM chart. Keep the rules on an anchored note on your chart.
Use a wider stop when a higher timeframe zone is in control; use a tighter stop for momentum trades. All-time highs and lows count on any timeframe.
Sunday livestream for August 30th; Kevin mentions a second child is coming soon and accepts he may miss some trades because of it.

The homework is the chain analysis: if a zone you expected is missing from his chart, it is because it did not fit the chain analysis. Chain analysis = mark out all the zones and trendlines, and the zones that remove them.
Recap of last week: a demand drawn because it removed a trendline, a supply drawn because it removed a trendline, and a demand drawn because it removed a supply and made an all-time high.

The three rules: only draw a zone that (1) removes an opposing zone, (2) removes a trendline, or (3) makes an all-time high or low. If it does none of these, do not draw it. Every time you draw a zone, ask yourself: what did it remove?
This week's range: January 1995 to January 1996. He warns it is tricky with many trendlines and says seasoned members sometimes catch things he missed.

passages.h: Trendline 1: highest point, no cutting through wicks, ending an overextended line
passages.t: First he spots a valley, a peak and a lower low, which gives a downward trendline. For a trendline in either direction you need an OBVIOUS peak and valley, not tiny peaks and valleys, plus a higher high (uptrend) or lower low (downtrend). An obvious peak and valley with no break of the low is not a trendline. Draw from the highest point possible to the peak.

passages.h: Trendline 1: highest point, no cutting through wicks, ending an overextended line
passages.t: Zoomed in, the line from the very highest point cut through candles (wicks stuck above it). We do not want that, so adjust to the next highest point possible. Most of the time it has to be adjusted because of the angle change.

passages.h: Trendline 1: highest point, no cutting through wicks, ending an overextended line
passages.t: Live, he does not try point after point; with experience he can see right away where the anchor goes.

passages.h: Trendline 1: highest point, no cutting through wicks, ending an overextended line
passages.t: This trendline became way overextended (price pushed far away from it), so he simply ends the trendline there.

passages.h: Trendline 2 and identifying the supply that removed the demand
passages.t: A second obvious peak and valley gives another trendline, drawn from the previous peak to that peak. He admits it can be a bit subjective and 'not 100% perfect, as close as we can get it'.

passages.h: Trendline 2 and identifying the supply that removed the demand
passages.t: A demand zone was respected and then removed, so by rule 1 he has to find the supply that removed it. There will not always be one, but most of the time there is.

passages.h: Trendline 2 and identifying the supply that removed the demand
passages.t: Nothing stood out. He compared a few small candidate zones by their moves away; he usually judges by eye, but when it is close he measures: 74 pips (to the body), 63, 93 for the whole wick, 85.

passages.h: Trendline 2 and identifying the supply that removed the demand
passages.t: His pick for the supply that removed the demand is the zone higher up, with the better move away.

passages.h: Trendline 2 and identifying the supply that removed the demand
passages.t: Drawable vs tradable (he refers back to video lesson 1): he would not trade that supply. A lower candidate that is not in the chain analysis had a much better move away, followed by a second explosive move away, and he would take that trade 'all day'. He admits that is partly hindsight.

passages.h: Trendline 2 and identifying the supply that removed the demand
passages.t: He would never really take the drawn supply: he does not like how close the stay-away candle is.

passages.h: No demand from basing candles below the downward trendline
passages.t: A downward trendline was removed. Rule 2 says when a trendline is removed we MIGHT have a zone, and the keyword is might.

passages.h: No demand from basing candles below the downward trendline
passages.t: No demand here: every candle below that trendline is a 'boo-boo' basing candle. None meets the minimum requirement for a zone. Even he gets confused here, so he sets it up as a trendline lesson.

passages.h: Trendline lesson: picking the right peaks and checking with a channel
passages.t: After the lower move there are many small peaks and valleys. He finds the recent obvious peak, valley and lower low, and draws the trendline peak to peak.

passages.h: Trendline lesson: picking the right peaks and checking with a channel
passages.t: He puts a channel tool on the trendline as a check: price sold off but hovered around the bottom of the channel, which is OK.

passages.h: Trendline lesson: picking the right peaks and checking with a channel
passages.t: What he does not want to see is a massive sell-off away from the line, which tells him price pushed far away from the trendline. The earlier trendline got so overextended that he ended it.

passages.h: Trendline lesson: picking the right peaks and checking with a channel
passages.t: Another trendline: peak and lower low, drawn from the highest point possible to the peak, cutting through no wicks; a clean line.

passages.h: Trendline lesson: picking the right peaks and checking with a channel
passages.t: No zone was drawn at a very explosive move here because it removed nothing (no zone, no trendline), so it is not in the chain analysis.

passages.h: Possible future rule: two explosive moves in a row
passages.t: From a pattern he has seen over 7 years, he is debating a rule for zones that remove nothing but have an extremely obvious explosive candle followed by another one.

passages.h: Possible future rule: two explosive moves in a row
passages.t: He does not know how to qualify it yet. His idea: a move away about 4 to 5 times the size of the basing. The example zone moved away about 5 times the size of its basing.

passages.h: Possible future rule: two explosive moves in a row
passages.t: He does not like changing his rules, but when you see patterns it makes sense. A student said such zones worked for them; Kevin agrees they work out quite a bit but says, for now, they do not follow the rules. Status: not a rule yet. Do not add these zones to the chain analysis.

passages.h: The demand that removed the trendlines: basing at or below the line
passages.t: Both trendlines were removed, and there were no zones above them before, so none afterwards either. When a trendline is removed there is a zone; he sees the obvious explosive move away.

passages.h: The demand that removed the trendlines: basing at or below the line
passages.t: Key clarification: for a DOWNWARD trendline, the basing candle of the move away must be AT or BELOW the trendline for that zone to count as the one that removed it.

passages.h: The demand that removed the trendlines: basing at or below the line
passages.t: If the whole basing candle sat above the trendline, that basing and move away did not remove the trendline. Here the basing candle is at the line; even if the line only touches its wick, it counts. So this demand removed trendline 1 and trendline 2.

passages.h: The demand that removed the trendlines: basing at or below the line
passages.t: Zone size: he trims it slightly so it is similar to the sizes of his other zones. Body to body is also fine.

passages.h: When a trendline is removed: full candle close
passages.t: A trendline is removed only when a candle closes fully beyond it, with no wick or body touching the line. Extend the line until then.

passages.h: When a trendline is removed: full candle close
passages.t: Example: one candle's wick still touched the line, so the line was removed on the next candle, which closed fully above with nothing touching.

passages.h: When a trendline is removed: full candle close
passages.t: A later upward trendline: a very obvious peak and valley ('everybody is seeing this peak and valley'), drawn from the lowest point possible. A touch that does not close beyond is a RESPECT of the trendline, not a removal.

passages.h: Updated trendlines after a new high or low
passages.t: We do not cut through candles when drawing, but we let the trendline cut through candles until price either breaks it or makes a new high.

passages.h: Updated trendlines after a new high or low
passages.t: Once a new high is made, you do not just move the line there. Draw the updated trendline from the next valley, if a properly drawn line can be made.

passages.h: Updated trendlines after a new high or low
passages.t: The trendline he wants to see on charts is the updated one. You may keep both, and he does not mind seeing the old one, but the updated one is required.

passages.h: Updated trendlines after a new high or low
passages.t: Later, a downward trendline that was fully respected (wicks and bodies kept touching it) had to be extended, not removed, until a candle closed beyond it.

passages.h: Updated trendlines after a new high or low
passages.t: A student pointed out a new lower low that needed an updated trendline from the recent peak (peak, valley, peak, lower low). Kevin had missed it: 'Trendlines can get a little bit confusing.'

passages.h: Older zone trade and the next demand (measuring a close call)
passages.t: Back at the zone, there was a quick 1:1 off it; he calls it 'a nice little one-to-one' because it is an older zone.

passages.h: Older zone trade and the next demand (measuring a close call)
passages.t: That zone was then removed, so he finds the demand that removed it and measures to check the bare minimum: about 85, then 84 total. It qualifies.

passages.h: Older zone trade and the next demand (measuring a close call)
passages.t: A lower demand made more sense and was the better zone. In real trading you could have both, but the qualifying one goes in the chain analysis. No supply removed that demand, and no supply removed that trendline.

passages.h: Older zone trade and the next demand (measuring a close call)
passages.t: In real trading, if a supply removes and the qualifying zone is mediocre while a very obvious zone sits lower in a better location, you can trade the better one. For the chain analysis, only the zone that qualified first counts.

passages.h: Older zone trade and the next demand (measuring a close call)
passages.t: Many students drew the better zone. He accepts it, but they must delete it for next week to keep the chain analysis consistent.

Ask what each zone accomplished: 'You have your rules, start following them.' Keep the rules on your chart (an anchored note at the top) and check every zone against them. Do not map out every low and high; it does not matter for this analysis.
A zone drawn too big ignores the peaks and valleys inside it; the basing candle defines where the zone actually is.
Do not label basing candles as the zone: the zone is at the basing before the explosive move away. Mark zones as removed when they are removed; do not keep extending them.
Copy his chain analysis exactly each week. Do not carry forward zones that were not on his charts last week. Use the daily FXCM chart. He cannot mark homework done on the 1-hour chart.
A very long trendline is allowed, but it usually skips the peaks and valleys in between. Use the recent valid peak unless the line would become almost horizontal.

A student redrew a trendline from a later peak; that is wrong while the angle from the recent peak is still good. Only if the recent peak were low and the line very horizontal would you do that. Calling an obvious peak and valley 'too flat' is not a reason to skip a trendline. Do not draw a zone from a 'boo-boo' basing candle with no real move away.

One student stopped extending a zone because a new trendline formed: correct. Close call between two supplies: the upper one wins. Both candles are about the same size, but the lower one has a wick at the bottom, which makes it more of a basing candle.
Measured example: candle sizes 203 vs 182 vs 225 ('close enough'), with an older body at 151.

passages.h: All-time highs on any timeframe and the zoom effect
passages.t: A student shared a case with a daily demand (removed an all-time high) and a 1-hour zone (removed a supply). An all-time high is not only on the daily chart; it can be on any timeframe.

passages.h: All-time highs on any timeframe and the zoom effect
passages.t: Next week's homework: January 1996 to January 1997. There is an all-time high to map (rule 3), so there will be a zone.

passages.h: All-time highs on any timeframe and the zoom effect
passages.t: He admits a zone he skipped last week was probably a zone, but he keeps it out for consistency.

passages.h: All-time highs on any timeframe and the zoom effect
passages.t: A student asked if he is gradually changing the measurement. He explains the zoom effect: after an insanely explosive move (gold, oil), the chart scrunches up and earlier good zones look like small basing candles. That is why he does not like relying on measuring. He has used his method for years and it works, so he will not change it.

passages.h: Stops with a higher-timeframe zone in control
passages.t: A student was stopped out on a Euro trade with a tight stop. He had said in his breakdown to use a wider stop because a daily demand sat there.

passages.h: Stops with a higher-timeframe zone in control
passages.t: The wider stop was not because of NFP. It was because a higher timeframe zone was in control, so you give the trade more wiggle room.

passages.h: Stops with a higher-timeframe zone in control
passages.t: Price could still blast through the daily demand, but why not give yourself more room? 'You guys gotta listen.' For a momentum trade, a wide stop does not make much sense.

passages.h: Economic data, fundamentals and time away from the charts
passages.t: He does not follow the release schedule; as a swing trader it matters less to him. Day traders definitely need to know when data comes out.

passages.h: Economic data, fundamentals and time away from the charts
passages.t: Exception: if he is short, price is moving up toward his stop and NFP is coming, closing the trade beforehand might be a decent idea. But the move is 50-50 either way.

passages.h: Economic data, fundamentals and time away from the charts
passages.t: 'Your 2-to-1 trade will not be affected by the economics.' Fundamentals matter more for larger risk-reward trades on higher timeframes.

passages.h: Economic data, fundamentals and time away from the charts
passages.t: Fundamentals may tell you where price ought to be, but not that it will get there or go in a straight line. You can still get a 1:1 off a supply.

passages.h: Economic data, fundamentals and time away from the charts
passages.t: He does not say fundamentals do not matter. He says fundamentals content is an endless source of material for content creators.

passages.h: Economic data, fundamentals and time away from the charts
passages.t: Mindset: spend long sessions on the charts (even 10 hours) to recognise patterns, but also step away; you do not want to be on the charts 100% of the time.

[01:00-14:30] Homework on AUDUSD 1D (FXCM), 1995: recap of last week's zones, the downtrend line slid off the wicks and ended, measured supply candidates, no demand under the broken line, the channel check, the very explosive move that removed nothing, the demand at the line that removed both trendlines, and the updated uptrend line.
[15:00-43:00] Student homework (light and dark themes), with "ATH" marked and notes such as "too flat". [44:30-50:40] Market layouts: WTI, gold and EURUSD multi-timeframe (OANDA).
The homework chart is AUDUSD 1D from FXCM (January 1995 to January 1996), not an unnamed chart.

passages.h: Chart: [01:28] AUDUSD 1D recap of last week: circles on the demand that removed a trendline, the supply that removed a trendline, and the demand that removed a supply and made an all-time high.
passages.t: Every zone on the chart answers "what did it remove?"

passages.h: Chart: [02:56] The first downtrend line from the top, slid down to the next highest point so wicks do not poke above it.
passages.t: An obvious peak and valley plus a lower low. From the highest point it cut through candles, so it moves to the next highest point. Then price got way overextended, so the line simply ends.

passages.h: Chart: [05:08] Measuring candidate supplies: the TradingView measure tool on a small move away near the top of the chart.
passages.t: He usually judges by eye; when it is close he measures (74, 63, 93 with the wick, 85) and takes the one with the better move away.

passages.h: Chart: [07:20] A long arrow along the candles under the removed downtrend line.
passages.t: Rule 2 says there MIGHT be a zone. Every candle below that line is a small basing candle, so there is no demand.

passages.h: Chart: [08:04] Channel tool on the new downtrend line; his curve shows price hovering at the bottom of the channel.
passages.t: Hovering around the channel bottom is fine. A massive sell-off away from the line is what makes it overextended.

passages.h: Chart: [08:48] Circles on the recent peak, valley, peak and lower low used to draw the trendline peak to peak.
passages.t: Among many small swings, pick the recent obvious peak and valley that led to a lower low.

passages.h: Chart: [09:32] A mark at a very explosive move that removed nothing.
passages.t: He is debating a future rule for moves away about 4 to 5 times the basing, followed by another explosive candle. Not a rule yet: do not add these to the chain.

passages.h: Chart: [12:28] An arrow at the candle that finally closed above the downtrend line, above the green demand.
passages.t: The earlier candle's wick still touched the line, so the line goes on the next candle with nothing touching.

passages.h: Chart: [12:28] An arrow at the candle that finally closed above the downtrend line, above the green demand.
passages.t: The basing of that demand sat at the line (touching its wick counts), so this demand removed both downtrend lines.

passages.h: Chart: [13:12] Sketch of the updated uptrend line: after a new high, draw from the next valley.
passages.t: Let the old line cut through candles until it breaks or a new high forms; then the updated line is the one he wants to see.

passages.h: Chart: [19:48] A student's chart: two downtrend lines and a circle at the demand sitting right at the line.
passages.t: "That was a zone." When the basing is at the downtrend line, that demand still counts as the one that removed it.

passages.h: Chart: [30:48] A student's AUDUSD 1D with "ATH" marked and the note "Did not draw this trendline because it was to Flat for a trendline"; Kevin circles the supply.
passages.t: "What do you mean, too flat? It's an obvious peak and valley." Flatness is not a reason to skip a line with a clear peak and valley.

passages.h: Chart: [33:00] A student's chart: a question mark under a zone that did not accomplish anything, and an arrow up and away.
passages.t: "Highly recommend you having the rules, because you drew a zone that did not accomplish anything."

passages.h: Chart: Homework chart (daily FXCM, Jan 1995 to Jan 1996) Daily
passages.t: Downward trendline drawn from the highest point to the peak, then adjusted Why: The original line cut through wicks, so he moved it to the next highest point. Price later got overextended from the line. Result: Trendline adjusted, then ended where it became overextended

Supply that removed a respected demand; choosing between candidates Why: Weak options measured at 74/63/93/85 pips. The upper zone with the better move away qualified. A lower zone (not in the chain) had a better move away plus a second explosive move away. Result: Upper supply drawn but not tradable (stay-away candle too close). He would trade the lower one 'all day', partly in hindsight.
Downward trendline removed, with only basing candles below it Why: Rule 2 says a zone MIGHT exist. All candles were boo-boo basing candles below minimum requirements. Result: No demand drawn

Explosive demand removing two downward trendlines Why: The basing candle sat at the trendline (the line touched its wick). It must be at or below the line for a downward trendline. The line was removed when a later candle closed fully above with nothing touching it. Result: Demand drawn as removing trendlines 1 and 2, trimmed to a similar size to his other zones
Older zone retested Why: Older zone Result: Quick 1:1, then the zone was removed

Demand that removed the older supply; close call between two demands Why: The upper demand measured about 84-85, the bare minimum, so it qualified first. The lower demand was better located and better quality. Result: Upper one goes in the chain analysis. You can trade the lower one in real trading. Students must delete the lower one for consistency.
Daily demand from removing an all-time high, with a 1H zone from removing a supply Why: An all-time high can be on any timeframe Result: Shared as a valid example

passages.h: Chart: EUR (Euro) Swing, with daily demand below
passages.t: Long with a tight stop Why: He advised a wider stop because a daily demand was in control. It was not about NFP. Result: A student with a tight stop was stopped out

Q: A student said zones with two explosive moves worked for them but they stopped drawing them because they do not follow the rules. A: He agrees those zones work out quite a bit. He is debating a rule, roughly a move away 4 to 5 times the basing size, but for now they are not in the chain analysis.

Q: A student pointed out a missed updated trendline after a new lower low. A: He agreed: draw the updated line from the recent peak (peak, valley, peak, lower low). He thanked the student and said trendlines can get confusing.
Q: A student noted a daily demand that removed an all-time high and a 1H zone that removed a supply. A: Correct. All-time highs are not only on the daily; they can be on any timeframe.
Q: A student wrote 'too flat' as the reason for skipping a trendline. A: He did not understand it. It was an obvious peak and valley, so the trendline should be drawn.

Q: Are you gradually changing the measurement of zones? A: No. After insanely explosive moves (gold, oil), the chart scrunches up and earlier good zones look like small basing candles: the zoom effect. That is why he dislikes relying on measuring. His method has worked for years, so he will not change it.

Q: Was the wider stop on the Euro trade because of NFP (this Friday)? A: No. It was wider because a higher timeframe (daily) zone was in control, to give more wiggle room. He does not follow the data schedule as a swing trader. Day traders must. He might close a trade before NFP if price is already moving toward his stop, but it is 50-50.
Drawing zones that accomplished nothing (removed nothing). Mapping out every high and low.

Drawing zones too big, which ignores the inner peaks and valleys and the real basing candle. Drawing a zone on boo-boo basing candles with no real move away. Treating basing candles as the zone instead of the basing before the explosive move. Not marking a removed zone as removed (keeping it extended). Carrying forward zones that were never in his chain analysis. Working on the wrong timeframe (1H instead of daily).
Trendlines that cut through candles or wicks. Missing updated trendlines after a new high or low. Drawing trendlines too large and skipping the obvious peaks and valleys in between.

Re-anchoring a trendline to a later peak while the angle from the recent peak is still good. Missing the zone that removed a trendline when its basing sits right at the line. Using a tight stop when a daily zone is in control. Not listening to the trade breakdowns. Letting economic data and fundamentals drive 1:1 to 3:1 swing trades. Spending 100% of your time on the charts without stepping away.

What did this zone remove: an opposing zone, a trendline, or an all-time high/low? Is there an obvious peak and valley plus a break of the low or high? Does the trendline cut through any wicks or candles? Has the trendline become overextended, so it should be ended? Has a candle closed fully beyond the trendline with nothing touching it? Was a new high or low made, so I need an updated trendline?

Is the zone's basing candle at or below the downward trendline (at or above an upward one)? Is the move away explosive enough, or is this just basing candles? Is the zone similar in size to my other zones? Drawable or tradable: is the stay-away candle too close, and is the move away weak? Am I on the daily FXCM chart with his previous chain analysis copied exactly?
Is a higher timeframe zone in control, so I should use a wider stop?
“Removes an opposing zone, removes a trend line, or makes an all-time high or low. It's really that simple.” “You have to ask yourself, what did it remove?” “Not little boo-boo peaks and valleys.”

“We don't cut through the trend lines, but we let the trend line cut through the candles until we either break it, or until we make a new high.” “We need a full candle close, no wicks, no bodies touching it.” “Keyword, might.” “Trendlines can get a little bit confusing.” “I don't like changing my rules, but when you see patterns, it kind of makes sense.” “You have your rules, start following them.”
“You guys gotta listen to me.” “Your 2-to-1 trade will not be affected by the economics.” “Stepping away also can help.”
The chain-analysis homework method: draw only zones that remove an opposing zone, remove a trendline, or make an all-time high/low, and log what removed what.
New precision rule: a zone removes a downward trendline only if its basing candle is at or below the line (touching the wick counts).
Trendline removal requires a full candle close beyond the line with no wick or body touching (applying the zone 'tested' close logic to trendlines).
Using a channel tool to judge whether price is overextended from a trendline, and ending overextended lines.
Proposed (not adopted) rule: zones with two explosive moves in a row, a move away about 4 to 5 times the basing size, even if they remove nothing.
In close calls between zones, the first one to qualify goes in the chain analysis, but you may trade the better-located zone in real trading. All-time highs and lows count on any timeframe.
The zoom effect after huge moves makes earlier zones look like basing candles, which is why he dislikes measuring.
Stop width: wider when a higher timeframe zone is in control, not because of news; tight for momentum trades.
Fundamentals and economic data barely matter for 1:1 to 3:1 swing trades; consider closing a trade before NFP only if price is already moving toward your stop.

The jump must start below the fence to break it. A kid jumps over a fence and knocks it down. We say that kid broke the fence. But if another kid was already standing on the far side and jumped, that jump did not break anything. The fence was already down.
The downtrend line is a fence. The basing candles are the kid crouching. The crouch must be at or below the fence for the jump to be the one that broke it.
A demand removes a downtrend line only if its basing is at or below the line (supply mirror for uptrend lines).
Touching the line is respect. Only a full close beyond it is removal. After a new lower low, update the line from the recent peak.
When candidates are close, the first one that qualifies goes in the chain. Wider stop when a higher-timeframe zone is in control.

passages.h: Step: Obvious peak, valley, lower low
passages.t: You need an OBVIOUS peak and valley, not tiny ones, plus a break of the low. Draw from the highest point possible to the peak. If it cuts wicks, move to the next highest point.

passages.h: Step: Basing at or below the line
passages.t: Price pauses in basing candles. They sit at or below the downtrend line. That is the key check: for this zone to be the one that removed the line, its basing must be at or below it.

passages.h: Step: Touch = respect, full close = removal
passages.t: A candle touching the line is respecting it, so keep extending. The line is removed only by a candle that closes fully above, with nothing touching.

passages.h: Step: So this demand removed the line
passages.t: The explosive move came from basing at the line, and it removed the trendline. Rule 2: this demand goes in the chain. Trim it to a size similar to your other zones.

passages.h: Step: If the basing were fully above...
passages.t: If the whole basing sat above the line, the line was already broken. That basing and move away did not remove it. Always ask: what did it remove?

Basing vs downtrend line: where must it be to count? - At or below the line (a wick touch counts). Touch without a close beyond? - Respect. Keep extending the line. New lower low after a downtrend line? - Draw the updated line from the most recent peak.

Can a trendline cut candles while you wait? - Yes, until price breaks it or makes a new high/low. Then update it. Close call between two zones? - Measure; the first that qualifies goes in the chain. Higher-timeframe zone in control? - Use a wider stop.
Do 1:1 to 3:1 swing trades depend on economic data? - Hardly. Fundamentals matter more for big targets on higher timeframes. Question for every zone? - "What did it remove?"
Kevin opens after a losing week by reminding students that bad weeks and months are normal and that the 'turn $5 into $500k' picture sold by fake gurus is false.

He finishes the daily chain analysis (Aussie, January 1996 to January 1997) using his three zone rules, showing a trendline-removal demand, an all-time-high supply, a borderline trendline, a demand rejected for having no stay-away candle, and a 10 out of 10 single-candle demand that was spiked through by a news-driven emotional wick.

He defines an emotional wick precisely: a zone is only kept through an emotional wick when only the wick pierces it; if the body closes beyond, it is removed, and if you keep a zone through an emotional wick you extend it and the next supply/demand is taken from there. He explains that being stopped by news on a day-trading chart is your fault, while on a daily swing chart it is out of your control.

The homework review hammers three recurring errors: trendlines started from a random point instead of the most recent peak and valley, trendlines that are too large (weekly-sized) and miss the ones in between, and missing zones because all-time highs were not mapped; plus zones whose first candle out is a basing candle, 50% wick candles drawn as zones, lines not attached (use the magnet tool), and zones that removed nothing. New homework: January 1997 to January 1998.
Only draw chain zones that follow one of the three rules (opposing zone removed, trendline removed, all-time high/low).

Draw a trendline-removal zone only if the trendline touches the basing candles before the explosive move away. Require a stay-away candle that does not touch the zone. Make the candle after the proximal line an explosive candle, never a basing candle. Draw a trendline only after a peak, a valley and a new high/lower low.

Start trendlines from the most recent peak and valley; readjust when a newer peak, valley and new extreme form. Use two points for a trendline, not three. Leave weekly-sized trendlines on the weekly chart; do not draw them on the daily. Prefer a valley formed by candle bodies over one formed only by a wick.
Keep a zone through an emotional wick only if just the wick pierces it; remove it if the body closes beyond, even barely.
Extend a zone through an emotional wick, and take the next opposing zone from the nearest explosive move to the removed zone. Do not draw 50% (huge-wick) candles as zones.

Include adjacent basing candles in the same group if it does not make the zone too big compared to other zones. Map out all-time highs and lows before doing the chain. Copy all previous analysis and correct your zones to match his before the next homework.
Use the magnet tool so zones and trendlines are actually attached; hold Shift for straight horizontal lines. Do not extend zones all the way across the chart.
Know when economic data is released; do not leave day-trading orders at zones into known news.
It was not a good trading week; as he said at the end of the forecast video, these weeks can happen.

Beginners think bad weeks cannot happen because fake gurus advertise trading as turning $5 into $500 grand. That is nonsense, so when a bad week or a bad month comes you must not panic - get that idea out of your head. (Personal chat about a tornado near his home; no trading content.)

passages.h: Chain analysis recap: the three rules
passages.t: Homework period reviewed: daily chart (Aussie), January 1996 to January 1997. For new members: in the chain analysis we only draw zones that follow one of the three rules written on the top right of his chart.

passages.h: Chain analysis recap: the three rules
passages.t: Rule 2: when a trendline is removed, we have a zone. Rule 3: when price makes an all-time high, we have a zone. The other rule used in the chain is that an opposing zone was removed.

passages.h: Chain analysis recap: the three rules
passages.t: Definition repeated: a zone is basing, an explosive move away, a stay-away candle, and space between the stay-away candle and the zone.

passages.h: Walkthrough 1: demand from a trendline removal
passages.t: The last part of the previous chain was a trendline; it is removed, giving a demand zone. The trendline touches both basing candles before the explosive move away, so the demand is valid. If the line were a little lower and did not touch the basing candle, he would not draw the zone - it is that simple. He drew the zone a little big but said it is fine.

passages.h: Walkthrough 2: all-time high supply and a too-large trendline
passages.t: Price made an all-time high, so by rule 3 there is a zone (supply) there. Many students probably wanted to draw a long trendline there. It is technically correct but really big - on a daily chart it is probably a weekly trendline, so he does not draw it.

passages.h: Walkthrough 2: all-time high supply and a too-large trendline
passages.t: The all-time high was removed by an area of demand that looks 'somewhat decent' but is not his favourite and not one he would trade: the move away is barely explosive enough; he wanted another explosive candle.

passages.h: Walkthrough 2: all-time high supply and a too-large trendline
passages.t: There is a demand near the all-time high area that is 'close but just not good enough': the basing barely qualifies and the move away does not.

Determining whether a peak and valley are good enough is sometimes borderline: 'when we have rules, there's gonna be times where it's borderline.' He drew it to see what it looked like and accepted it.
He compared two similar-looking valleys: one was formed only by a wick, the other by actual candles (bodies). The one formed by actual candles makes the better valley, so that trendline was kept.
A trendline needs three things: a peak, a valley, and a lower low (for a downtrend; higher high for an uptrend).

When a new peak, valley and lower low form, the trendline is readjusted to the newer ones. You could have both lines on the chart; he removed the older one, but the newer one is what he wanted to see.
The resulting demand was removed - not surprising because it was very poor quality - leaving a supply zone with an objectively explosive candle (looked better the more he zoomed in).

passages.h: Walkthrough 4: no demand because there is no stay-away candle
passages.t: After the supply removed the opposing demand, he looked for a demand and found nothing that represents demand.

passages.h: Walkthrough 4: no demand because there is no stay-away candle
passages.t: One almost qualified, but drawn that tight it was too small. Drawn at a proper size there is basing and an explosive move but no stay-away candle.

passages.h: Walkthrough 4: no demand because there is no stay-away candle
passages.t: The stay-away candle means price stayed away from the zone. The stay-away candle cannot touch the zone, or it is not a stay-away candle.

passages.h: Walkthrough 4: no demand because there is no stay-away candle
passages.t: Next, a blatant peak, valley and lower low gave another trendline, which was removed by an area of demand that also removed the all-time high.

passages.h: TradingView tip: Shift for straight lines
passages.t: When drawing all-time highs it is hard to get the line perfectly flat. Hold Shift while drawing to get a straight (horizontal) line; it also snaps to a 45-degree angle or a vertical line.

passages.h: Walkthrough 5: the 10/10 demand and the emotional wick
passages.t: A single-candle basing demand that removed an all-time high, with clean basing and an amazing move away: 'a 10 out of 10 zone'. He would take that trade all day, every day.

passages.h: Walkthrough 5: the 10/10 demand and the emotional wick
passages.t: Price spiked straight through it as if it was not there, most likely due to a news event or economic data on the Aussie or, more likely, the US dollar. That can happen.

passages.h: Walkthrough 5: the 10/10 demand and the emotional wick
passages.t: He compared its location to a current 4-hour S&P zone near an all-time high; the S&P zone is good but this one is better.

passages.h: Walkthrough 5: the 10/10 demand and the emotional wick
passages.t: Answering what an emotional candle is: this obvious, massive wick through the zone is an emotional wick.

passages.h: Walkthrough 5: the 10/10 demand and the emotional wick
passages.t: Because it was only a wick, he did not end the zone there; he extended it. The zone was respected afterwards and price pushed up - a pattern he noticed doing the chain analysis, which is why he extends zones through emotional wicks. Later a candle broke the zone with its body, so the zone was removed.

passages.h: Walkthrough 5: the 10/10 demand and the emotional wick
passages.t: Precise rule: an emotional wick only counts (zone not removed) when it is just the wick. Even if the wick is enormous, if the body closes beyond the zone, even barely, the zone is removed.

passages.h: Walkthrough 5: the 10/10 demand and the emotional wick
passages.t: A new supply was created after that and gave a nice move. Drawn tight it is too small, so he drew it a bit bigger; another zone could also be a bit bigger. You would still be stopped out by the emotional wick, 100%, but the zone is not removed.

passages.h: News and fault: day trading vs swing trading
passages.t: On a 1-minute (day trading) chart, if you know inflation data is coming out on the dollar and you leave an order at the zone and get wicked out, that is your fault for placing the trade knowing news was due.

passages.h: News and fault: day trading vs swing trading
passages.t: On a daily (swing) chart with a daily limit order, especially when price is far away, this would not bother him much and is not really your fault - it is out of your control.

passages.h: News and fault: day trading vs swing trading
passages.t: That is why the Sunday forecast starts with when economic data comes out: not to predict the data, but to know when it is released so you do not get hit by an emotional wick.

A student's zone was reasonable but he would include another basing candle from the same group: it does not make the zone much bigger and gives more wiggle room. Including a far-away basing candle would make the zone too big compared to the other zones, so do not.

You must change your zones to match his exactly (e.g. move the distal line) before next week's homework, because a different zone changes the later chain - 'an absolute must'. All zones must be on your charts to get the same chain.
Lines that are not actually attached to the candles: use the magnet tool and wrap the lines around the basing properly. Include the wick at the top/bottom of the zone when it belongs to the basing.
A supply drawn on a candle with a massive wick is a 50% candle; he does not really draw 50% candles as zones. He recommends the 50% candle indicator to show them.
When you extend a zone through an emotional wick, the next zone (e.g. the supply) is the one nearest to the removed demand - the nearest explosive move away - not an earlier one.

A zone the student pointed at was not demand because the first candle out was a basing candle, not an explosive move away. The candle right after the proximal line must be explosive; if it is a basing candle, redraw the zone so the explosive candle follows it. A 'larger basing candle' is still a basing candle; it does not qualify as the move away.
A 5-minute demand had an explosive move but very small space between the stay-away candle and the zone, so it is not really a tradable zone.
A bearish zone 'technically qualifies' but is not good; you want a decent amount of space from the stay-away candle to where the zone is drawn.
Only the zone that broke the opposing zone is the zone by rule; any other is 'just an extra one'. Do not extend zones all the way across the chart - it makes it too messy.
Every zone must accomplish something: ask 'what did it remove?' If nothing, it is not a chain zone.

A student who did not copy the previous weeks' work missed zones; you must copy all previous analysis and follow the instructions (do not submit homework screenshots, only draw the zones/move points).
Most common error this week: many students started the trendline from the same random point. A trendline is drawn from the most recent peak and valley, not from a point that is not a valley.

Even when a student's line ended up as the same line, the concept was wrong: draw from the most recent peak and valley; when a new peak and valley form, go from those. Touching three points does not matter - we only use two.
He does sometimes attach a line to a less obvious point, but only when there is no proper valley/peak to attach to (e.g. attach to the next lowest point). That did not apply here.

A peak and valley without a new high (uptrend) or lower low (downtrend) after it is not a trendline: 'a trend line could have the best peak and valley, but if we do not break that opposing high, there is no trend line'. No trendline means no zone from it.

Too-large trendlines: a weekly-sized line on a daily chart makes you miss all the trendlines (and zones) in between. If it is the only one available it is reasonable, but a weekly trendline stays on the weekly.
Zooming: if you are too zoomed out you miss peaks and valleys in between; too zoomed in and you can miss a trendline (he admitted missing one a student found).
A trendline that is only slightly overextended is still fine (close to too large but valid).
Momentum line (blue) vs trendline (black): a student's momentum line was correct but the trendline too big.

passages.h: Homework review: map the all-time highs
passages.t: Several students missed zones simply because they did not mark the all-time high/low; one missed zone then made them miss the next zone in the chain.

passages.h: Homework review: map the all-time highs
passages.t: 'Map out the all-time highs, and then the chain will most likely be correct.' He recommends having all-time highs mapped before starting.

passages.h: Homework review: map the all-time highs
passages.t: A student asked about an all-time low; he found one was very close and marked it with a horizontal ray.

passages.h: Homework review: map the all-time highs
passages.t: Praise went to work where trendlines, demand and supply were all correct with only one missed trendline.
He will add rules and possibly a copy of his chain analysis exactly as he did it to clear things up.
Next homework: January 1997 to January 1998, with all previous zones drawn exactly as his.
No student questions were asked; he hopes for a better trading week and asks students to stay positive.

[04:00-13:00] Homework on AUDUSD 1D (FXCM), 1996: demand whose basing touches the downtrend line, the all-time-high demand, wick vs candle valleys, a missing stay-away candle, the 10/10 single-candle demand, its emotional wick, the body-close rule, and the new supply.
[14:00-44:00] Student homework, including the "By rules, this is SZ" chart and repeated trendline start-point corrections.
[44:00] A student's EURUSD sketch labelled SUPPLY / DEMAND, then the next homework instructions in Discord.
The homework chart is AUDUSD 1D from FXCM (the notes call it "Aussie" daily); the 10/10 demand that removed the all-time high is in late 1996.

passages.h: Chart: [04:41] AUDUSD 1D: circles on the two basing candles that the downtrend line still touches, and the explosive move up out of them; the demand (green) is drawn there.
passages.t: The line touches both basing candles before the move away, so this demand removed it. If the line sat a little lower and missed the basing, he would not draw the zone.

passages.h: Chart: [05:21] A circle on the demand that removed the all-time high.
passages.t: Rule 3 zone, "somewhat decent" but not one he would trade: the move away is barely explosive and he wanted another explosive move.

passages.h: Chart: [05:21] A circle on the demand that removed the all-time high.
passages.t: The very long line many would draw here is probably a weekly trendline on a daily chart, so he leaves it out.

passages.h: Chart: [06:01] Small circles on two similar valleys: one formed only by a wick, the other by candle bodies.
passages.t: The valley made of actual candles is the better anchor, so that trendline stays.

passages.h: Chart: [07:21] A tall loop at the candle that came straight back into the would-be demand.
passages.t: Drawn at a proper size there is basing and an explosive move but no stay-away candle. "The stay-away candle can't touch the zone, or else it's not a stay-away candle."

passages.h: Chart: [10:02] The all-time-high line circled flat across the chart, and a loop around the single-candle basing demand below the spike that broke it.
passages.t: "A 10 out of 10 zone": it removed an all-time high, clean basing, amazing move away. He would take it all day. Tip: hold Shift in TradingView to draw a perfectly horizontal all-time-high line.

passages.h: Chart: [10:42] Zoomed in: the massive wick that spiked straight through that demand.
passages.t: An emotional wick, likely from news on the Aussie or the US dollar. Only a wick, so the zone is not ended; it was respected afterwards.

passages.h: Chart: [11:22] His drawn example: a red candle body extended to close just below the zone, with the wick stretched far down.
passages.t: If the body closes beyond the zone, even barely, the zone is removed, however big the wick. Emotional wicks only count when it is just the wick. You would still be stopped out by the wick; the zone just is not removed.

passages.h: Chart: [12:42] The new supply (red) drawn after the demand was finally removed.
passages.t: Drawn tight it would be too small, so he draws it a bit bigger. It gave a nice move down.

passages.h: Chart: [16:43] A student's chart (Hans, then the next student): his curve and circle at the trendline start point he questions.
passages.t: Many students started the line from the same random point. Draw it from the most recent peak and valley.

passages.h: Chart: [36:07] A student's AUDUSD 1D with "ATH" and notes: "By rules, this is SZ" on the upper supply and "more preferable cause of emotional wick" on the lower one.
passages.t: "By rule, this is supply zone ... it's the only one that broke that supply. This is just an extra one."

passages.h: Chart: [40:48] A student's chart marked up with a circle, an X and his line under the lows.
passages.t: "What did it remove? Nothing." The trendline also needs to be extended, and the missing all-time high cost the student a zone.

passages.h: Chart: [42:49] A student's chart: his line showing where the trendline should run, crossing out the student's start point.
passages.t: "Since you didn't map the all-time high, you missed that demand." Map the all-time highs first and the chain will most likely be correct.

Demand zone from a trendline removal Why: The trendline touches both basing candles before the explosive move away (rule 2). If the line did not touch the basing candle there would be no zone. Result: Drawn as a valid chain demand (slightly big but fine).

All-time high supply Why: Rule 3: an all-time high gives a zone. A long trendline here was technically correct but weekly-sized, so not drawn on the daily. Result: All-time high later removed by a barely-explosive demand he would not trade.

Borderline trendline Why: Peak/valley borderline; valley formed by actual candles preferred over a wick-only valley. Readjusted when a newer peak, valley and lower low formed. Result: Trendline kept; its demand was very poor and got removed, leaving a supply.

Potential demand after supply removed opposing demand Why: Drawn tight it is too small; drawn properly there is basing and explosive move but no stay-away candle (next candle touches the zone). Result: Not a zone.

Single-candle basing demand that removed an all-time high Why: Clean basing, amazing move away - 10/10, take it all day every day. Result: Spiked through by a news-driven emotional wick (stop hit), but only the wick pierced so the zone was extended; it was respected and pushed up, then later removed by a body close. A new supply formed afterwards with a nice move.
Zone near an all-time high Why: Mentioned as similar location to the 10/10 Aussie demand. Result: Good zone, but the Aussie example is better.
Demand zone Why: Explosive move but very small space between stay-away candle and zone. Result: Not really tradable; would likely not have filled if drawn properly.

Q: What is an emotional candle? A: An obvious, massive wick through a zone, usually from news or economic data. If only the wick goes through, the zone is not removed - you extend it, and it is often respected afterwards. If the body closes beyond the zone, even barely and even with a huge wick, the zone is removed. You still get stopped out by the wick.

Q: Would we still be stopped out by the emotional wick? A: Yes, 100%. You would be stopped out, but the zone is not removed. On a daily swing chart it is out of your control; on a day-trading chart with known news coming, placing the trade is your fault - that is why the forecast lists economic data release times.
Q: Is there an all-time low here? A: He did not think so at first, then saw it was very close and marked it with a horizontal ray.

Q: (Homework) Is a peak and valley alone enough for a trendline? A: No. You need a peak, a valley, and then the opposing high (or low) broken. Without the new high/low there is no trendline and therefore no zone from it.

Q: (Homework) Why can't I start the trendline from this point? A: Because it is not a valley. Trendlines go from the most recent peak and valley. He only attaches to another point when there is no proper peak/valley available.

Believing bad weeks or months should not happen. Starting trendlines from a random point that is not a valley. Drawing trendlines too large (weekly-sized on daily) and missing those in between. Drawing a trendline with a peak and valley but no new high/low. Not mapping all-time highs, which cascades into missing later zones. Calling a basing candle (or larger basing candle) the explosive move away.
Drawing zones with no stay-away candle or tiny space between stay-away candle and zone. Drawing zones too small or too big. Drawing a 50% huge-wick candle as a zone.

Ending a zone at an emotional wick instead of extending it; or keeping a zone when the body closed through. Drawing zones that removed nothing. Lines not attached to candles; not using the magnet tool. Not copying previous weeks' analysis or not correcting zones to match his. Extending zones all the way across the chart. Day trading into known news releases with orders at zones.
Being too zoomed out or too zoomed in and missing peaks/valleys.
Are all-time highs/lows mapped? Which of the three rules created this zone, and what did it remove?
Is there basing, an explosive first candle out of the zone, a stay-away candle that does not touch the zone, and decent space?
Is the zone sized reasonably compared with other zones (including adjacent basing candles)?

Is the trendline from the most recent peak and valley, with a confirmed new high/low, and not weekly-sized? For a trendline-removal zone, does the trendline touch the basing candles? Was the zone pierced by only a wick (extend) or did a body close beyond (remove)? Is the zone a 50% wick candle? Is there economic news due while my day-trading order sits at the zone? Are lines snapped with the magnet tool?

“These weeks can happen.” “When we have rules, there's gonna be times where it's borderline.” “The stay-away candle can't touch the zone, or else it's not a stay-away candle.” “This is a 10 out of 10 zone.” “Emotional wicks only count when it's just the wick.” “You would be stopped out, but we're not removing the zone.”

“A trend line could have the best peak and valley, but if we do not break that opposing high, there is no trend line.” “Map out the all-time highs, and then the chain will most likely be correct.” “What did it remove? Nothing.”
Precise emotional-wick rule: only a wick-only pierce keeps a zone; any body close beyond, however small and however big the wick, removes it.
Zones kept through an emotional wick are extended, and the next opposing zone is taken from the nearest explosive move to the removed zone.
Fault framework for news spikes: day-trading chart with known news = your fault; daily swing limit order = out of your control.
Stay-away candle defined strictly: it cannot touch the zone; a zone drawn at proper size with a touching next candle is not a zone.
Trendline-removal zones require the trendline to touch the basing candles before the explosive move. Wick-only valleys are weaker than body-formed valleys when judging borderline trendlines.
Trendline start must be the most recent peak and valley; only use another point when no proper peak/valley exists.

Weekly-sized trendlines stay on the weekly chart; drawing them on the daily makes you miss the chain. Mapping all-time highs/lows first is the single fix for most cascading chain misses. TradingView tip: hold Shift for perfectly horizontal (or 45-degree/vertical) lines.
Include extra basing candles from the same group if it does not oversize the zone (more wiggle room).

A scary spike that pops back does not break the zone. You poke a balloon with your finger. It dents in deep, then pops back to its shape. It did not burst. But if the balloon pops, it is gone. A zone is the balloon: a wick that dents it and springs back is just a scare. A body that closes through it pops it.
An emotional wick is like a sneeze in class: very loud, very quick, and then everything goes back to normal.
Emotional wick: only the wick pierces, so the zone stays (but your stop is still hit). A body close beyond removes it.
The stay-away candle must not touch the zone. A trendline-removal zone needs the line to touch its basing.
Start trendlines from the most recent peak and valley, keep them daily-sized, and map all-time highs first.
Single-candle basing, an amazing explosive move and a stay-away candle far from the zone. Kevin would take this "all day, every day".
Price drifts back toward the zone. News is coming out: inflation data on the dollar.
A giant wick spikes straight through the zone, then the candle body closes back up. That huge, news-driven wick is an emotional wick. Your stop would be hit, 100%.

passages.h: Step: Only the wick? Keep the zone
passages.t: Because ONLY the wick went through, the zone is not removed. Extend it. If the body had closed beyond the zone, even barely, it would be removed.

Price respects the zone and pushes up. That pattern is why Kevin extends zones through emotional wicks. On a daily swing chart this is out of your control; on a 1-minute chart into known news, it is your fault.

What is an emotional wick? - An obvious, massive (usually news) wick through a zone where the body stays out. Emotional wick: zone removed? - No. Extend it. But your stop is still hit. Body closes beyond the zone, even barely? - Removed. Can the stay-away candle touch the zone? - No. Then it is not a stay-away candle.

Trendline-removal zone check? - The line must touch the basing candles before the explosive move. Trendline start point? - The most recent peak and valley. Use two points, not three. Weekly-sized line on the daily? - Leave it on the weekly. It hides the lines in between. Draw a flat all-time-high line in TradingView? - Hold Shift while drawing.

Kevin recaps the three zone-qualifying rules (removes an opposing zone, removes a trendline, makes an all-time high/low), what a zone is (basing, explosive move away, stay-away candle with space to the proximal line) and his trendline rules (blatant peak and valley plus a higher high / lower low, attached to candles, never cutting through them).

He then walks through the daily chain analysis from January 1997, showing how to draw a zone that has no basing, how to handle very large basing groups, why some removals produce no new zone, when a daily trendline is really a weekly one, how to update a trendline from the previous peak, and why overextended trendlines are ended rather than extended.

In the homework review two students scored a first-ever 100%, and he corrects common errors: trendlines drawn on the top, zones not attached to candles, distal lines in random places, zones shrunk to fake a stay-away gap, and oversized 'higher-timeframe' trendlines that hide the ones in between.
He finishes with a short all-time-low lesson (every new low is an all-time low, so a series of drop-base-drops each forms a zone) and sets the Jan 1998 to Jan 1999 homework.
Qualify every zone by at least one rule: removes an opposing zone, removes a trendline, or makes an all-time high/low.
Require basing, an explosive move away and a stay-away candle with space to the proximal line.
Draw an uptrend line only after a blatant peak and valley followed by a higher high (inverse for downtrend). Attach trendlines to candles and never cut through candles or wicks.
Draw uptrend lines on the lows and downtrend lines on the highs - never on the top of an uptrend.
Count a trendline as removed only when a candle closes fully beyond it (body and wick not touching).

Do not draw a zone whose basing touches a trendline until the stay-away candle closes fully beyond that trendline. End zones and trendlines where they were removed or became irrelevant; never extend them. End an overextended trendline (check with the channel tool) instead of extending it.
Update a trendline from the recent peak; if that makes no sense, use the previous peak and valley.
Start trendlines only from a real previous peak at its highest point, not from random points or manipulation.

For a zone without basing, put the distal at the extreme and copy the size of your other zones. Exclude a basing candle with an outsized wick from a large basing group. Copy the size of properly drawn zones; don't shrink a zone to create a stay-away gap. Include wicks and all relevant basing candles in the zone. Ignore emotional wicks for removal; a normal wick through a zone does remove it.

Exclude daily lines that are so large they are really weekly trendlines from daily chain analysis. If you draw two zones for one removal, add a note saying which is the qualifying zone. Do homework on the daily chart and copy his previous chain analysis first.
Treat every new low (or high) as an all-time low (high); each drop-base-drop beyond it is a zone.

passages.h: Recap: the 3 zone-qualifying rules (anchored note on the chart)
passages.t: He keeps the three rules as an anchored note in the top right of the homework chart so they stay visible wherever he scrolls.

passages.h: Recap: the 3 zone-qualifying rules (anchored note on the chart)
passages.t: Rule 1: did the zone remove an opposing zone? (and did that opposing zone itself remove an opposing zone - the chain). Rule 2: did it remove a trendline? Rule 3 (the rarer one): did it make an all-time high or low? You only need ONE of the three, not all three.

passages.h: Recap: the 3 zone-qualifying rules (anchored note on the chart)
passages.t: Example from last week's homework: a zone that broke no zone and no trendline, but broke an all-time high, so it qualified under rule 3.

passages.h: Recap: what a zone is (basing, explosive move away, stay-away candle)
passages.t: Zones won't always be as clean as the textbook example in the Discord learning material. Needs basing candle(s) and a move-away candle that must be explosive - measured from the proximal line, the candle leaving the zone must be explosive, not 'little boo-boo basing candles on the way out'.

passages.h: Recap: what a zone is (basing, explosive move away, stay-away candle)
passages.t: A move from A to B made of small basing-like candles is not the same as an explosive move.

passages.h: Recap: what a zone is (basing, explosive move away, stay-away candle)
passages.t: Stay-away candle: the candle that stays away from where the zone would be drawn, which naturally leaves a space between the stay-away candle and the proximal line.

passages.h: Recap: what a zone is (basing, explosive move away, stay-away candle)
passages.t: The smaller that space (e.g. a wick reaching down close to the proximal), the worse the zone - not great, but he still draws it (drawable vs tradable, video lesson 1). He does not measure the space; it is visual and comes with the Sunday work over time.

passages.h: Recap: what a zone is (basing, explosive move away, stay-away candle)
passages.t: Preferred (optimal, not required): basing, an explosive move away, then ANOTHER explosive move away - two explosive candles show a lot of demand. Basing, one explosive candle then a pullback is also fine.
Everything is a peak and valley; what he wants is a blatant, obvious valley that everybody would see as a valley. Shallow ones are momentum.

Uptrend line: a peak, an obvious valley, and then a HIGHER HIGH above that peak. If price approaches the high and sells off without breaking it, there is no trendline. Downtrend line is the inverse: peak, obvious valley, then a lower low. Trendlines are attached to candles and never cut through candles. Rally-base-rally names etc. don't really matter for this exercise.

passages.h: Homework instructions and the January 1997 supply
passages.t: Last week covered Jan 1996 to Jan 1997; your chart must contain all the zones and trendlines he corrected. The first thing he checks is whether you followed instructions and copied his chain analysis - otherwise you can't see what removed what. Doing badly is fine; not copying his zones upsets him.

passages.h: Homework instructions and the January 1997 supply
passages.t: Last zone was a supply that qualified by rule 1 (removed an opposing demand). A huge wick there was just an emotional wick (look at the size), not the removal; the demand was cleanly removed when a body closed below it.

passages.h: Homework instructions and the January 1997 supply
passages.t: A body close is not always required: a normal-sized wick (candle not small, wick not massive) breaking a zone also removes it.

passages.h: Homework instructions and the January 1997 supply
passages.t: There was also a trendline he forgot to draw (a member caught it) - rule 2, trendline removed, with an explosive move and basing.

passages.h: Homework instructions and the January 1997 supply
passages.t: The basing there was very large. He excluded one candle with a big wick and used only the 3 other basing candles; if that wick had been smaller he would include all three/four.

passages.h: Homework instructions and the January 1997 supply
passages.t: The zone was respected, then removed; he ends the zone where it was removed instead of extending it - that is how you keep a clean chart.

passages.h: Homework instructions and the January 1997 supply
passages.t: Some students drew a trendline on a nearby peak/valley; for him it was close but not a good enough valley.

passages.h: Homework instructions and the January 1997 supply
passages.t: The trendline is continued right to the candle that removed it: it was officially removed only when a candle closed fully below it (body and wick not touching). That trendline touched both basing candles and even the explosive candle, so he would not draw the zone until the stay-away candle closed fully below the trendline.

passages.h: Large basing groups: two ways to draw, risk-reward trade-off
passages.t: After the zone was removed his eye went straight to the explosive candle; the full basing behind it was too big for him.

passages.h: Large basing groups: two ways to draw, risk-reward trade-off
passages.t: You can draw the whole big basing area if you really want to trade that big, but your risk-reward will be much worse; you get less chance of being stopped out. 'There's no free lunch.' For chain analysis we do not draw it that big.

passages.h: Large basing groups: two ways to draw, risk-reward trade-off
passages.t: There were two groups of basing (a cluster plus one candle); he drew it around the relevant group.

passages.h: Large basing groups: two ways to draw, risk-reward trade-off
passages.t: Not a great zone; he would not have traded it - not terrible, just not one he'd personally take. It was later removed.

passages.h: Large basing groups: two ways to draw, risk-reward trade-off
passages.t: Removal with no new zone: an opposing zone being removed does not mean a zone removed it. Nothing there resembled supply.

passages.h: Large basing groups: two ways to draw, risk-reward trade-off
passages.t: A candle bigger than the others can still be a basing candle - just a larger basing candle.

passages.h: Daily vs weekly trendlines and overextended trendlines
passages.t: A clear low was removed, and many students wanted a large trendline. On a daily chart that line is massive compared with normal daily trendlines, so it is most likely a weekly downward trendline. He won't include it in the chain analysis, but it's 'not really wrong'. A proper daily trendline: good enough valley, peak, lower low.

passages.h: Daily vs weekly trendlines and overextended trendlines
passages.t: Price then got very overextended, making the trendline basically irrelevant; updated trendlines follow.

passages.h: Daily vs weekly trendlines and overextended trendlines
passages.t: He wants that trendline on your chart but ENDED there, not extended. Extending it tells him you don't understand that it became irrelevant.

passages.h: Daily vs weekly trendlines and overextended trendlines
passages.t: Old zones: he removed some very old zones. 'We don't expect these to hold.' One was respected once, but he's not surprised an old zone with no real liquidity trap fails; he doesn't like trading older zones.

passages.h: Drawing a supply zone that has no basing
passages.t: A rare case: a supply with essentially no basing, just a huge explosive move, but you still want a zone there.

passages.h: Drawing a supply zone that has no basing
