passages.t: How: go to the very top (the extreme) - that is the distal line - then look at the other zones on your chart and draw it a similar size. It was an older zone, so it is tracked for much later. Students mostly got this one right; he was impressed since there's no basing.

passages.h: Trendline from the highest point of the previous peak; trendline updates
passages.t: With a very obvious peak and valley and a lower low, take the highest possible point at the previous peak and draw to the next touch - rule 2 trendline. That trendline was removed, but nothing resembled demand, so no zone. Updated trendline after a new peak and valley: normally draw it from the RECENT peak.

passages.h: Trendline from the highest point of the previous peak; trendline updates
passages.t: If drawing from the recent peak makes no sense (the line would not work), use the previous peak and valley instead. If another previous peak sat higher, attach to that.

passages.h: Trendline from the highest point of the previous peak; trendline updates
passages.t: Later in the same chart a new peak, valley and lower low did allow drawing from the recent peak - no need to go up to the older one. Again highest point possible.

passages.h: Trendline from the highest point of the previous peak; trendline updates
passages.t: That line also got overextended: he uses the channel tool to show price is no longer staying within the channel, so it is ended, not extended.

passages.h: Trendline from the highest point of the previous peak; trendline updates
passages.t: A trendline must start from a real previous peak, not from some random point (unless that point was part of a trendline before). Manipulation spikes are not peaks.

passages.h: Almost-zones: no stay-away candle, too-small zones
passages.t: An almost-zone: basing and an explosive move away, but no stay-away candle - price pushed straight back and wicked into it. So no supply there, and nothing above either. Again, a removed zone does not guarantee a new zone. Price 'falling off a cliff' = very difficult trading conditions.

passages.h: Almost-zones: no stay-away candle, too-small zones
passages.t: A small potential supply at the end: if drawn it would be too small; you don't want to draw zones too small. He compared it against other zones and decided it did qualify - very poor quality, not a trade he would take, even though it 'worked beautifully'.

passages.h: Almost-zones: no stay-away candle, too-small zones
passages.t: The red line is the all-time low. Very poor quality zones are drawn only to map them for the future and see what removes them, not because we want to trade them.
Missing one zone often makes you miss the next zone in the chain (missed supply -> missed demand).
If you draw a second, safer zone in a real trading situation because the qualifying one is very poor, that makes sense - but put a note saying which one is the zone and why you're drawing the other.
Distal lines must be based on the candles; zones placed with a random distal 'don't make any sense'.
Boo-boo basing candles are not zones; a very wicky area is not demand/supply; a weak move away or tiny zone is not a zone.
Include the basing candles and include the wick in the zone (an example: including the wick would have avoided being stopped out).

We do NOT draw trendlines on the top: uptrend lines go on the bottom (lows), downtrend lines on the top (highs). A line across the top of an uptrend is a momentum line. Zones must be attached to the candles.

A clear big wick means it is not a supply zone - if that wick were part of a basing candle body it would be, but it's just a larger basing candle. End zones where they end; don't extend a zone past the candle that broke it. Don't cut through wicks with trendlines; oversized trendlines are wrong.

Shrinking a zone so there is a gap to the stay-away candle is not how we do it - copy the size of a properly drawn zone (he measured 88 and copied it; at the same size the candle touches, so no zone). He admits he's been guilty of it.
Don't combine two separate sets of basing inside one larger basing area - draw just the relevant set. No trendline where price never broke to a lower low.

Huge trendlines are higher-timeframe lines; focusing on them makes you miss all the daily ones in between - a bad habit. Homework must be on the daily timeframe; homework on the 1 hour chart cannot be marked.

passages.h: Weird zones: explosive move after lots of basing; drawable vs tradable
passages.t: Example where the explosive move comes after a long run of basing candles: he doesn't want to exclude the basing, so he may draw the zone at the explosive move but tuck the stop underneath all the basing - his best idea for a trading situation; he hasn't fully figured out the best way. It looks like breaking the rules but isn't. Remember which candle is the explosive move - the basing is not the move away.

passages.h: Weird zones: explosive move after lots of basing; drawable vs tradable
passages.t: Drawable but not tradable example: basing and move away fine, but very small space between the stay-away candle and the proximal line. He'd draw it, not trade it, even though it worked beautifully. A very good tradable zone: one he would 'risk my hard-earned capital off all day'.

passages.h: Weird zones: explosive move after lots of basing; drawable vs tradable
passages.t: If you can't draw a zone without making it too small, and making it bigger removes the stay-away candle, and drawing from lower makes the basing bigger than the move away, it is not a zone. When the move away is the same but there's a clear pinpoint of basing, it is a zone.

passages.h: Weird zones: explosive move after lots of basing; drawable vs tradable
passages.t: A very poor weekly zone drawn oddly because it was too large to draw normally - a one-off anomaly.

passages.h: Trades, drawdowns and his Euro stop-out
passages.t: A student went 4 for 4 following his analysis; he congratulates but warns: expect a drawdown.

passages.h: Trades, drawdowns and his Euro stop-out
passages.t: He doesn't give signals ('that's illegal'); in daily breakdown videos he points out good zones where you can look for confirmation trades.

passages.h: Trades, drawdowns and his Euro stop-out
passages.t: His EUR trade was stopped out, likely by the spread at news time; he believes his stop was wider than the zone; he got over it quickly.
Every candle making a new low is an all-time low; it doesn't have to be an obvious valley - every wick that makes a new low counts.
So when price breaks the all-time low and keeps going drop-base-drop, drop-base-drop, each one is a zone (rule 3), even without breaking an obvious low.
Copying his chart: do it manually (two monitors, or watch his chart on your phone while drawing on desktop); a member noted you can make a copy of the chart from the Sunday Meeting drop-down.
Homework: Jan 1, 1998 to Jan 1, 1999 on the daily, monitor all the lows; some trendlines this week.
Two students got 100% - the first perfect homework ever. 8 or 7 out of 10 is still doing good.
[01:20-04:30] Recap slides: the labelled zone diagram (basing, move-away, stay-away, space to the proximal line) and the labelled peak / valley / higher-high trendline diagram.

[05:30-17:40] Chain analysis on AUDUSD 1D (FXCM): emotional wick vs real removal, the trendline that touched the basing and explosive candles, an overextended daily line ended early, a supply drawn from the top with no basing, trendline updates from the previous and then the recent peak, an almost-supply with no stay-away candle, and a borderline small supply.
[19:00-52:00] Student homework on the same AUDUSD 1D chart, plus a few student charts on other pairs. [53:30-55:30] All-time-low sketch, then the next homework posted in Discord.

The homework chart in this session is AUDUSD 1D from FXCM (shown in the chart header), not an unnamed "homework chart". The note on the chart says the last homework was EURUSD, which was only good back to 1990.

passages.h: Chart: [01:38] His labelled zone diagram from the learning material: basing candles inside the zone box (proximal line on top, distal line at the bottom), the move-away candle, the stay-away candle, and a red arrow for the space between the stay-away candle and the proximal line.
passages.t: The candle leaving the proximal line must be explosive, not small "boo-boo" basing candles on the way out. The smaller the space under the stay-away candle, the worse the zone.

passages.h: Chart: [04:07] Labelled trendline diagram: "Peak", "Valley" and "Higher High" marked on an uptrend, with the line attached under the valley.
passages.t: An uptrend line needs a peak, an obvious valley, and then a higher high above that peak. Approaching the high and selling off is no trendline.

passages.h: Chart: [05:45] AUDUSD 1D: the huge wick he circles is an emotional wick, not the removal; the supply (red box, extended right) removed the demand when a body closed below it.
passages.t: A body close is not always required: a normal-sized wick breaking a zone also removes it. A massive one-off wick does not.

passages.h: Chart: [08:13] Arrow at the candle that officially removed the trendline: the line still touched both basing candles and the explosive candle before it.
passages.t: He does not draw that zone until the stay-away candle closes fully below the line (no body or wick touching).

passages.h: Chart: [12:20] A long arrow along the fall away from the daily downtrend line: price got so overextended that the line became irrelevant.
passages.t: Keep that line on the chart but end it there. Extending it tells him you did not see it became irrelevant. Very old zones are removed with the remove tool; he does not expect them to hold.

passages.h: Chart: [13:10] The supply with no basing: a box drawn from the very top of the huge explosive move (red, extended right), sized like his other zones.
passages.t: With no clear basing, put the distal line at the extreme and copy the size of your other zones. It is an older zone, tracked for much later.

passages.h: Chart: [14:49] Sketch on the chart of a hypothetical peak and valley, with the updated downtrend line drawn from that recent peak.
passages.t: Normally the updated line starts at the recent peak. Here the real recent peak did not make sense for a line, so he used the previous peak and valley.

passages.h: Chart: [15:38] An almost-supply (red box) with the candle that came straight back circled.
passages.t: Basing and an explosive move away, but no stay-away candle: price pushed back in and wicked it. No supply there. A removed zone does not guarantee a new zone.

passages.h: Chart: [16:27] The recent peak circled: a new peak, valley and lower low, so this time the updated line starts from the recent peak (highest point possible).
passages.t: This line also gets overextended; he uses the channel tool to show price leaving the channel, so it is ended, not extended.

passages.h: Chart: [17:17] A small possible supply circled near the end of the homework range, just above the green demand.
passages.t: If drawn it would be very small. "You don't want to draw it too small." He compares it with his other zones before deciding.

passages.h: Chart: [36:13] A student's chart: a long run of basing candles, then the explosive candle, with a green demand drawn under it.
passages.t: In a trading situation he would draw the zone at the explosive move but tuck the stop under all the basing. The basing is not the move away.

passages.h: Chart: [40:20] A student's AUDUSD 1D homework with his handwritten score on it: the first perfect homework.
passages.t: Two students got 100% this week, a first. 7 or 8 out of 10 is still doing well.

passages.h: Chart: [51:02] A student's chart with "ATL" marked at the bottom; he circles where a downtrend line was drawn without a lower low.
passages.t: "Certainly not a trend line here, as we did not even break a lower low."

passages.h: Chart: [54:20] Sketch on a blank chart: "ATL" with a horizontal line and price breaking below it in steps.
passages.t: Once the all-time low breaks, every drop-base-drop that makes a new low is a zone (rule 3), even without breaking an obvious valley.

passages.h: Chart: Homework chart (daily chain analysis) Daily
passages.t: Supply removing a demand (rule 1), Jan 1997 Why: Huge wick was an emotional wick; removal confirmed by body close below the demand Result: Valid supply carried into this week's chain

Zone after trendline removal with large basing (rule 2) Why: Excluded the big-wick candle, used 3 basing candles; zone drawn only after the stay-away candle closed fully below the trendline Result: Respected, then removed; zone ended at removal candle
Wide two-group basing zone Why: Drawing the whole basing gives worse R:R but fewer stop-outs; drawn around the relevant group Result: Not a great zone, he would not trade it; later removed
Large downward trendline Why: Too massive for a daily line, likely a weekly trendline Result: Excluded from chain analysis (not wrong)
Daily downtrend line then overextension Why: Price got overextended, trendline irrelevant Result: Keep it but end it; do not extend
Supply with no basing, huge explosive move Why: Distal at the very top, size copied from other zones Result: Valid old zone, tracked for later
Trendline update where recent peak makes no sense Why: Used previous peak and valley instead Result: Trendline updated correctly
Almost-supply: basing + explosive move but no stay-away Why: Price pushed back and wicked into it Result: Not a zone
Small poor-quality supply near all-time low Why: Compared to other zones; it qualifies, but very poor Result: Drawn for mapping only; 'worked beautifully' but not a trade he'd take
Zone trade Why: Stop probably wider than the zone; news time spread Result: Stopped out, likely by spread

Q: Can you show an example of a drawable zone? A: The one down below is drawable, not really tradable, not the best. Whereas another zone is very good - he'd risk his hard-earned capital off it all day. Another drawable-not-tradable example: basing and move away fine, but the space between the stay-away candle and the proximal line is very small; he'd draw it, not trade it, even though it worked beautifully.

Q: How do you follow him (a student who went 4/4)? A: Probably by watching his daily breakdowns and using his chart analysis. He doesn't give signals and never will (illegal); he points out good zones to look for confirmation trades. Expect a drawdown.

Q: How can I copy your setups/chart? A: Manually: have his chart open (second monitor or phone) and redraw each zone. A member said you can make a copy from the Sunday Meeting drop-down; he'll try it, but manual seems best.

Not copying his previous chain analysis into your homework. Assuming a removed zone always has a new zone that removed it. Calling it a zone without a stay-away candle (price wicked straight back in). Drawing trendlines on the top of an uptrend (that's a momentum line). Extending zones and trendlines past where they ended or became overextended.

Drawing massive higher-timeframe trendlines on the daily and missing the trendlines in between. Shrinking a zone to fake a gap to the stay-away candle. Random distal lines not based on candles; zones not attached to candles. Drawing boo-boo basing candles or wicky areas as zones. Excluding the wick from a zone (gets you stopped out). Combining two separate sets of basing into one oversized zone.

Starting a trendline from a random point or a manipulation spike. Drawing a trendline where price never broke a lower low / higher high. Drawing zones too small. Trading very old zones that are unlikely to hold. Trading drawable-only zones with little space to the stay-away candle. Doing homework on the 1 hour chart instead of daily. Expecting a winning streak to continue - expect a drawdown.
Ignoring spreads around news times.

Does the zone meet at least one of the 3 rules? Basing identified, move away explosive, stay-away candle present with visible space? Is the zone attached to candles, wick included, similar size to my other zones? If basing touches a trendline, has a candle closed fully beyond the trendline?

Is the trendline from a real peak, blatant valley, with a higher high / lower low, on the correct side? Is the trendline overextended (outside the channel)? Then end it. Is the trendline so large it's really a higher-timeframe line? Is the zone old with little liquidity? Drawable or tradable? Is the risk-reward acceptable given the zone size? Is it news time - can the spread hit my stop?

“You don't need all three, you just need one.” “We don't want little boo-boo basing candles on the way out.” “We end it where it was ended, and that's how we keep a clean chart.” “There's pros and cons to everything, there's no free lunch.”

“Just because we have a zone removed, does not mean we will have an actual area of demand.” “We don't draw trend lines on the top.” “I'll risk my hard-earned capital off a zone like that all day.” “Just because we draw it doesn't mean we're looking to trade.” “Expect a drawdown.” “I don't give signals, never will give signals.”
How to draw a zone with no basing at all: distal at the extreme, size copied from other zones.
Trendline updates: use the recent peak normally, fall back to the previous peak when the recent one makes no sense; start only from real previous peaks, not manipulation spikes.
A daily trendline that is too massive is really a weekly line - leave it out of daily chain analysis; obsessing over big lines makes you miss the daily ones.
Don't draw a zone whose basing touches a trendline until the stay-away candle closes fully beyond the line. Explicit: trendlines are never drawn on the top of an uptrend.

Large basing: drawing the whole base trades worse R:R for fewer stop-outs ('no free lunch'); alternative of drawing at the explosive move but tucking the stop under all the basing. Exclude a single big-wick candle from a basing group; don't combine two basing sets. Shrinking a zone to manufacture a stay-away gap is wrong - copy standard zone size. Optimal demand has two explosive move-away candles.
Not-a-zone test: if the zone is too small, enlarging kills the stay-away, and lowering makes basing bigger than the move away.
All-time low clarification: every new low counts, so successive drop-base-drops are each zones. Note your choice when drawing two zones for one removal.

No pause? Draw the zone at the tip, same size as the others. A ball is thrown hard at a wall and bounces right back. It never stopped, but we know exactly where it hit: the very tip. We mark the wall there, and we make the mark the same size as our other marks.
Like a cookie cutter: every zone uses the same size cutter. When there is no basing, you press the cutter right at the tip of the move.

No basing: distal at the extreme of the move, height copied from your other zones. Uptrend lines go on the lows, downtrend lines on the highs. End overextended lines; daily lines that are huge are really weekly.
Every new low is an all-time low. A normal wick through a zone removes it; only an emotional wick does not.

passages.h: Step: A normal supply for size
passages.t: Here is a normal supply zone: basing, explosive drop, stay-away candle. Remember its size. We will copy it.
Later, price rallies with one huge candle.

passages.h: Step: ...then a huge drop, no basing
passages.t: Straight away a huge drop. There is no basing candle between them. Rare, but you still want a zone here.

passages.h: Step: Distal at the very top, copy the size
passages.t: Put the distal line at the very top (the extreme). Then make the zone a similar size to your other zones. Do not shrink zones to fake a gap to the stay-away candle.

passages.h: Step: Every new high or low counts
passages.t: Every candle that makes a new low is an all-time low, not only obvious valleys. So when price breaks the all-time low and keeps going drop-base-drop, each one is a zone (rule 3).

Zone with no basing: where is the distal? - At the extreme of the move (the very top or bottom). Zone with no basing: how tall? - Similar to your other zones. Which side does an uptrend line go? - The lows. Downtrend lines go on the highs. Normal wick through a zone? - Removes it. Only an emotional wick does not. Which lows are all-time lows? - Every candle that makes a new low.

Big-wick candle in a big basing group? - Leave it out; use the other basing candles. Two zones drawn for one removal? - Add a note saying which one is the qualifying zone. Winning streak (4 for 4)? - Expect a drawdown.

Kevin walks through a quiet week of the chain analysis on the daily chart. Most of the new price was at all-time lows (rule 3), but only three zones qualified because almost everything in between was small basing candles, not explosive moves away.

The main lessons were patience (don't force zones), drawing zones that include all the basing candles, and keeping trendlines strict: an obvious peak and valley followed by a lower low or higher high, ended when an updated line appears or when it gets overextended. He then marks the students' homework.

The most common mistakes were trendlines with no lower low, missed updated trendlines, forced zones and badly drawn zones. He also answers a question on removals across timeframes: removal only counts on the exact same timeframe.

Draw a zone only if it removes an opposing zone, removes a trendline, or makes an all-time high/low. One is enough. Don't force zones. If nothing in a stretch shows an explosive move away, draw nothing.
Don't call a bigger-than-usual basing candle an explosive move away. Judge it against real explosive moves. An explosive candle that removed nothing is not a zone.
When the basing candles are close, include all of them in the zone. Only tighten it if the basing gets crazy.

Put the distal at the bottom wick of the basing for demand (top wick for supply), using the magnet tool. Put the proximal right against where the explosive move away starts. Include the wick. Don't cut through it when drawing a zone.
If the candle after your drawn zone is a basing candle, it is not a zone. Move the zone to where the explosive move away begins.

A downtrend line needs a starting point, an obvious valley, a peak, then a lower low. An uptrend line needs an obvious peak, valley, then a higher high. Use only very obvious peaks and valleys. Small ones are momentum. A trendline must not cut through candles. Adjust the anchor point if needed.

When a newer peak and valley forms, draw the updated trendline and end the old one, which is now invalid. End a trendline that has become overextended. Don't draw one massive trendline that skips the valid trendlines in between. Judge zone and trendline removals only on the same timeframe. Use the actual all-time low/high when marking it.
End a removed zone at the point it was removed (shorten it only for chart cleanliness). Submit homework on the daily chart, as a proper screenshot.
Watch the daily breakdowns and check his chart link before asking whether something is a zone.

passages.h: Opening: purpose of the Sunday session and psychology
passages.t: Sunday sessions are where they dive into the 'meat' of the system: the rules, trendlines, what a zone is. Video lessons, daily breakdowns and forecasts sit alongside them.

passages.h: Opening: purpose of the Sunday session and psychology
passages.t: The chain analysis moves one year at a time. Some weeks are great for lessons and some are not; this one is a weak week, and that is just how it is.

passages.h: Opening: purpose of the Sunday session and psychology
passages.t: Reminder for new members: only draw zones that qualify under one of the three rules (remove a zone, remove a trendline, or make an all-time high/low). One rule is enough, not all three.

passages.h: Opening: purpose of the Sunday session and psychology
passages.t: This week is mostly rule 3. Once price trades at these levels, everything is an all-time low. Clear the old zones off the chart as you go.

passages.h: Opening: purpose of the Sunday session and psychology
passages.t: The last zone carried over was a very poor-quality supply. It is drawable, not tradable. He would not take it, even though it worked out fantastically, and he refuses to claim afterwards that he would have.

passages.h: Opening: purpose of the Sunday session and psychology
passages.t: 'The best zones can fail, and the worst zones could work.' He passes on good trades and takes bad ones, which is why trading psychology matters so much.

passages.h: Opening: purpose of the Sunday session and psychology
passages.t: You can have the best strategy in the world, with a good win rate or good overall risk-reward, and still fail without the psychology. Everyone struggles with it, him included. He recommends his podcast episodes for this.

passages.h: Zone 1: supply that removed demand plus an all-time low
passages.t: Rule 1 reminder: an opposing zone being removed only sometimes gives a zone. A zone, trendline or all-time low being removed does not guarantee one.

passages.h: Zone 1: supply that removed demand plus an all-time low
passages.t: Here a demand zone was removed AND an all-time low was made, a 'double whammy'. He immediately spotted the supply above.

passages.h: Zone 1: supply that removed demand plus an all-time low
passages.t: He ended the removed zone's line short of the exact removal point to keep the chart clean, because a new zone was being drawn there. Normally you end it right where it was removed.

passages.h: Zone 1: supply that removed demand plus an all-time low
passages.t: He rated this supply as decent: nice basing and a good move away. It was a little better than the old poor supply, which price came straight back to. With this one, price stayed away for a while.

passages.h: Zone 2: demand that removed two supplies, and how to draw it
passages.t: Anyone in the group for a month should see it: a great explosive move away with two basing candles. It removed two opposing supply zones.

passages.h: Zone 2: demand that removed two supplies, and how to draw it
passages.t: Because the two basing candles are close together, and using both doesn't make the zone massive or tiny, use BOTH. Don't draw the zone off only one candle.

passages.h: Zone 2: demand that removed two supplies, and how to draw it
passages.t: Distal: go all the way to the bottom wick, using the magnet tool. Proximal: put it right up against where the explosive move away started.

passages.h: Zone 2: demand that removed two supplies, and how to draw it
passages.t: The zone later failed, most likely because it was against the downtrend you see when you zoom out. Trends and trendlines are vital. Spotting supply and demand zones alone is not enough.

passages.h: Zone 2: demand that removed two supplies, and how to draw it
passages.t: The push up after it was momentum, not a trendline. A trendline needs very obvious peaks and valleys, not 'little boo-boo' peaks and valleys.

passages.h: Downtrend lines: updating, ending and overextension
passages.t: After a low was removed, an obvious peak and valley appeared, followed by a lower low. You need that lower low after the peak and valley. That gave a valid downtrend line.

passages.h: Downtrend lines: updating, ending and overextension
passages.t: Don't keep extending one trendline forever, especially once a new peak and valley forms. Here the next one was 'pretty much a peak and valley', so the line was updated to go from the new point.

passages.h: Downtrend lines: updating, ending and overextension
passages.t: Homework expectation: both trendlines on the chart, the original ended and the updated one drawn.

passages.h: Downtrend lines: updating, ending and overextension
passages.t: Extended, the line got hugely overextended as price was pushed down. It is fine to have it in real trading. Once it is that overextended, end it by marking that it got too extended.

passages.h: Downtrend lines: updating, ending and overextension
passages.t: Two reasons a trendline ends here: (1) an updated trendline replaces it, which makes the old one invalid; (2) it got too overextended.

passages.h: Big basing candles vs explosive moves: don't force zones
passages.t: Above the demand there was no supply at all, just small basing candles. The confusing part: a candle that is bigger than the tiny ones around it is still a basing candle, just a bigger one. Compared with its neighbours it looks explosive, but it isn't the kind of explosive move he means.

passages.h: Big basing candles vs explosive moves: don't force zones
passages.t: He doesn't usually measure anything. Judging an explosive move is a feel you build over time by taking part in these meetings.

passages.h: Big basing candles vs explosive moves: don't force zones
passages.t: Many all-time lows were made in this stretch and none of them showed demand or supply. Main lesson: be patient and don't just draw any zone.

passages.h: Big basing candles vs explosive moves: don't force zones
passages.t: One nice explosive candle removed nothing (rules 1-3), so it is not a zone. Ask what it removed.

passages.h: Big basing candles vs explosive moves: don't force zones
passages.t: A small drop-base-drop looked like a zone but wasn't, because the move-away candle wasn't good enough. Without the wick, as a full red body, it probably would have been a zone.

passages.h: Momentum vs trendline; not cutting through candles
passages.t: Valley, peak and lower low: a trendline. Small steps with no obvious valleys: momentum. Compare the two. Draw from the most recent peak to the new peak.

passages.h: Momentum vs trendline; not cutting through candles
passages.t: Don't anchor from the highest older peak if the line would cut through candles. A trendline must not cut through candles. There are extreme exceptions, but he won't cover them yet.

passages.h: Momentum vs trendline; not cutting through candles
passages.t: An uptrend line was also needed: peak, valley, higher high. Then another peak, valley and higher high appeared, so it had to be updated.

passages.h: Momentum vs trendline; not cutting through candles
passages.t: The straight update would have cut through candles, so he adjusted the anchor. His line can therefore start where there is no peak or valley, because the real peak and valley is elsewhere and the line was moved to avoid candles. The older line ended, and he wants it ended on your charts. He marked an all-time low early so it is ready for a later homework.

passages.h: Zone 3: demand from a removed trendline, and old zones
passages.t: Rule 2: a trendline was removed, giving an extremely obvious demand zone. Unfortunately the zone got very old. When price finally returned it got at most a tiny reaction and then failed. That is the issue with older zones.

passages.h: Zone 3: demand from a removed trendline, and old zones
passages.t: Ideally you wait for a pullback into a zone like this, but there wasn't one. You won't always get a pullback entry; accepting that is part of trading psychology.

passages.h: Zone 3: demand from a removed trendline, and old zones
passages.t: Another example: a peak and valley that is only momentum compared with real trendline structure.

passages.h: Zone 3: demand from a removed trendline, and old zones
passages.t: Week recap: only three zones. The test was not forcing poor-quality zones and keeping trendlines updated and correct.
Some weeks test whether you can identify every one of many zones, which is tricky. Some weeks are heavily about trendlines.
Some weeks, like this one, are about not forcing zones. Each week depends on how the charts played out. He doesn't only grade the zones you draw. He also checks that you didn't force any zones.
A student got all three zones but missed an updated trendline that needed to end the old one.

A borderline trendline idea: it was only a wick. If those candles had been bodies he would agree, but because it's just a wick he doesn't really see a trendline. He gave grace because it was close and 'too wicky'.
The repeated error: a trendline with NO lower low after the peak. That is not a trendline. If price had then broken that low, it would have been correct.
Several students got the demand right but for a bad reason: they said it removed an invalid trendline. He still grades the rest of your chain as if your trendline were right.
Another student drew a peak and valley with no higher high. Remember: peak, valley, higher high.

Trendline recipe as he repeated it: starting point, peak, a valley deep enough to be extremely obvious, then a break of the high where your peak is (higher high). Downtrend: starting point, valley, peak, lower low. No lower low means no trendline.

He suspects people are overcomplicating trendlines and considers them easier than identifying zones. The rules are in the Discord learning material. Nobody, or maybe one person, got both of the tricky trendlines.

passages.h: Homework review: zone drawing and forced zones
passages.t: Forced zone: a move away the same size as the surrounding basing candles. If you draw that zone you would also have to draw others like it, which shows it isn't a zone.

passages.h: Homework review: zone drawing and forced zones
passages.t: Attach trendlines properly. Not perfectly attached is tolerable when doing quick after-the-fact analysis, but live it must actually be attached. Zones not attached to the highest wick: you must go up to the proximal line properly. Don't cut through the wick when drawing a zone. Include the wick.

passages.h: Homework review: zone drawing and forced zones
passages.t: Big tip: if you draw your zone and the next candle is a basing candle, it is not a zone. The zone belongs where the explosive move away actually starts.

passages.h: Homework review: zone drawing and forced zones
passages.t: Include all the basing candles when they are close together. If a wick reached far down he would draw it differently. A frequent error was zones that were too tiny because they ignored one of the basing candles. Only tighten the zone if the basing gets crazy.

passages.h: Homework review: zone drawing and forced zones
passages.t: Your distal line must have a reason, such as the lowest wick of the basing. A distal placed at a random point makes no sense. When drawing an all-time low, use the actual all-time low.

passages.h: Homework review: zone drawing and forced zones
passages.t: Removal check: one student drew two zones that each removed one. Zoomed in, the earlier zone was fully respected by the basing, so only one zone counted. It would only remove it if part of the basing wicked above it.

passages.h: Homework review: zone drawing and forced zones
passages.t: A zone that is way too big compared with the others: if it had removed supply, he would still draw it big and accept that it's massive. That can happen sometimes.

passages.h: Homework logistics and using his resources
passages.t: Homework must be on the DAILY chart. Submissions on the wrong timeframe (one on 1H) could not be marked.

passages.h: Homework logistics and using his resources
passages.t: Send real screenshots (get a screenshot app), not sideways photos taken on another device.

passages.h: Homework logistics and using his resources
passages.t: Members in the chat ask about zones that his daily breakdown and chart link already answer. Watch the breakdowns: that is why he makes them. Asking why something is not a zone is fair.

passages.h: Homework logistics and using his resources
passages.t: You may have your own rule (e.g. drawing an amazing move away that removed nothing), but his chart link shows what qualifies under his rules. A borderline example a member raised was not on his chart.

passages.h: Homework logistics and using his resources
passages.t: He is hard on students who did well before because he cares. If he didn't, he would just say try again next week.

passages.h: Homework logistics and using his resources
passages.t: He recommends watching previous meetings for trendlines; they cover it better than a short video, though he may make one.
Next homework: January 1999 to January 2000. The chart starts clean with no zones needing removal, and it is mostly about trendlines.

No pip-measurement rule for trendlines (e.g. 'if the depth is 168 pips it's a trendline'). Pip values differ between pairs, so it's visual. That is why he gives grace on borderline cases: 'We are not robots, we are humans.'
Classic rule: the trendline must be as obvious as possible, super obvious peak-valley, peak-valley. Don't draw one massive trendline that ignores the smaller valid trendlines in between.
Grace is given on subjective wick-or-valley calls, but NOT on trendlines that break the basic rule (no lower low), unless it's your very first time.
Market note: the dollar looks strong. The current hiccup is most likely the start of a pullback after a long strong run.
A student asked if an opposite zone can be removed by a zone on a different timeframe. No. Everything happens on the exact same timeframe.
A one-minute zone will not remove a monthly zone. Zone removal and trendline removal are judged on the same chart and timeframe. If you trade the 5-minute, look for removals only on the 5-minute.

[01:30-13:10] Homework on AUDUSD 1D (FXCM) near the all-time lows: the poor supply carried over, the double-whammy supply, the two-candle demand, an overextended downtrend line ended, big basing candles that are not moves away, momentum vs trendline, an updated uptrend line, and the rule-2 demand.
[14:30-44:10] Student homework on the same chart (light and dark themes), with his trendline recipes sketched at 32:00-33:10. [45:00] DXY multi-timeframe layout for the market note.
The homework chart is AUDUSD 1D from FXCM (header on every frame), not an unnamed "homework chart". The bottom-right note on it says the last homework was EURUSD (only good back to 1990).

passages.h: Chart: [01:58] AUDUSD 1D: he circles the carried-over, very poor-quality supply that price came straight back to.
passages.t: Drawable, not tradable. It worked, but he would not have taken it: "the best zones can fail, and the worst zones could work."

passages.h: Chart: [03:56] The new supply above (removed a demand and made an all-time low) and, below it, the demand built off two close basing candles before a great explosive move.
passages.t: Use both basing candles when they are close and the zone stays a normal size: distal at the lowest wick (magnet tool), proximal where the move away starts. This demand removed two supplies, but later failed against the bigger downtrend.

passages.h: Chart: [06:34] The downtrend line extended out with his hand-drawn path of price falling far away from it.
passages.t: Two reasons a line ends: an updated line replaces it, or it got too overextended. Keep both lines on the homework, the old one ended.

passages.h: Chart: [07:14] An arrow at a candle that looks big next to its tiny neighbours.
passages.t: It is still a basing candle, just a bigger one. Compared in context it looks explosive, but it is not the explosive move he means. No supply above this demand.

passages.h: Chart: [08:32] A long loop around a steady, step-like decline into new all-time lows.
passages.t: Valley, peak and lower low exist, but with no obvious valleys this is momentum, not a trendline. Many all-time lows here and none of them show a zone: be patient.

passages.h: Chart: [13:09] Circles on the obvious peaks and valleys of the real trendlines vs a steep straight line with no clear valleys, with the rule-2 demand (green) further right.
passages.t: "Look at the difference between this peak and valley ... compared to something like that, which is momentum."

passages.h: Chart: [21:42] Zoomed in on a student's two zones: the circle shows the older zone was fully respected by the basing.
passages.t: Only one zone counts. It would remove the older one only if part of the basing wicked above it.

passages.h: Chart: [22:21] A student's borderline trendline: circles on the wick-only point.
passages.t: "If that was body, that'd be fine", but it is too wicky to call a trendline. Close, so he gives grace.

passages.h: Chart: [32:13] Sketch: starting point, peak, a deep obvious valley, then the break of the peak (higher high).
passages.t: Uptrend line recipe. If the high is not broken, there is no trendline.

passages.h: Chart: [32:52] On a student chart: starting point, valley, peak circled, and a horizontal line at the valley that price never broke.
passages.t: Downtrend recipe: starting point, valley, peak, lower low. "No lower low" means no trendline.

passages.h: Chart: [36:10] Dark-theme student chart: a yellow X over a trendline and a very large purple zone.
passages.t: The zone is way too big, though if it had removed a supply he would draw it big too and accept it. The line is "not a trend line", but close.

passages.h: Chart: [44:03] Back on AUDUSD 1D: a black line drawn down into the green demand while he explains which lines get grace and which "blatantly" break the lower-low rule.
passages.t: Grace for subjective wick-or-valley calls, not for lines that break the lower-low rule (unless it is your first time).

passages.h: Chart: [45:22] DXY 4-pane (1W, 4h, 1D, 1h): green arrow on the 4h, supply above on the 1D.
passages.t: Market note: the dollar has been strong; the current hiccup is most likely the start of a pullback.
Carried-over very poor-quality supply Why: Drawable, not tradable: poor quality. Result: Worked out fantastically, but he would still not take it. The best zones can fail and the worst can work.

Supply that removed a demand zone and made an all-time low (rules 1 and 3) Why: Nice basing, good move away, price stayed away for a while. Better than the prior poor supply, which price came straight back to. Result: Drawn as a valid zone; it removed the demand and made an all-time low.

Demand off two basing candles with a great explosive move away, removing two supplies Why: Use both close basing candles: distal at the bottom wick (magnet tool), proximal against the start of the move away. Result: Failed, most likely because it was against the larger downtrend.

Downtrend line: peak, valley, lower low; then updated to a newer peak/valley Why: An updated line invalidates the old one. The extended line became overextended, so it was ended. Result: Both lines expected on homework; old one ended.

Larger basing candles and a drop-base-drop among many all-time lows Why: Bigger-than-normal basing candles aren't explosive moves. One explosive candle removed nothing. The DBD's move-away candle had a wick and wasn't a full red body. Result: No zones drawn: don't force zones.

Uptrend line: peak, valley, higher high, then updated after another higher high Why: The straight update would have cut through candles, so the anchor was adjusted. Result: Old line ended; updated line drawn from an adjusted point.

Demand that removed a trendline (rule 2) Why: Extremely obvious demand, but it became very old with no pullback entry. Result: At most a tiny reaction when finally retested, then failed. That is the issue with old zones.

Q: Can an opposite zone be removed by a zone on a different timeframe? A: No. Everything is on the exact same timeframe. A one-minute zone will not remove a monthly zone, technically speaking or not, because they don't switch timeframes. Zone removed, trendline removed, it's all on the same chart and timeframe. If you trade the 5-minute chart and look for removed zones, look only on the 5-minute.

Q: (A student asked for a dedicated lesson on trendlines.) A: He can, but recommends watching previous meetings, where trendlines come up all the time; that's better than a little video lesson. It's simple: you need a good enough peak and valley, and you attach it like that. There are some more details, but he thinks trendlines are easier than identifying a zone.
Q: (A student whose homework slipped asked how to get back on track.) A: Do what you did last week. He's hard on you because he cares.

Trading drawable-only, poor-quality zones, or claiming afterwards you'd have taken one that worked. Forcing zones from larger-than-normal basing candles. Drawing a zone off an explosive candle that removed nothing. Drawing a trendline with no lower low (or no higher high) after the peak and valley. Using wick-only peaks or valleys as trendline structure ('too wicky'). Calling momentum a trendline.

Missing the updated trendline and not ending the old one. Extending a trendline forever even when it is overextended. Drawing a trendline that cuts through candles. Drawing a zone off only one basing candle, so it's too tiny. Cutting through the wick, or not attaching the zone to the highest/lowest wick. Placing the distal line at an arbitrary point. Drawing a zone where the next candle is still basing.

Assuming a zone removed another when the basing actually respected it (zoom in). Marking an all-time low that isn't the real all-time low. Getting a zone right for the wrong reason (removal of an invalid trendline). Trading zones against the larger trend. Waiting on very old zones and expecting them to hold. Submitting homework on the wrong timeframe (e.g. 1H) or as sideways photos.
Not watching the daily breakdowns or checking the chart link. Measuring trendline depth in pips instead of judging visually. Drawing one massive trendline that ignores the ones in between.
Did this zone remove an opposing zone, remove a trendline, or make a real all-time high/low?
Is the move away truly explosive compared with real explosive moves, and not just a larger basing candle? Is the next candle after my zone a move-away candle, not another basing candle?

Have I included all the close basing candles, with the distal at the extreme wick and the proximal against the move away? Does my trendline have an obvious peak and valley AND a higher high or lower low? Does the trendline avoid cutting through candles? Is there a newer peak and valley that means I should update the line and end the old one? Has the trendline become overextended and needs ending?
Am I judging every removal on the same timeframe? Is the zone against the larger trend, or very old? Have I checked the daily breakdown or chart link for this zone?
“The best zones can fail, and the worst zones could work.” “There's trades where they're great, and I don't take them. There's trades that are bad, and I take.”

“You think you can just spot supply and demand zones and trade that, you are certainly mistaken.” “We're not just gonna force a zone.” “If you draw your zone, and the next candle is a basin candle, that is not a zone.” “Peak, valley, higher high.” “We are not robots, we are humans.” “If I didn't care, I wouldn't be hard on you.” “A one-minute zone will not remove a monthly zone.”
Quick zone test: if the candle right after your drawn zone is a basing candle, it is not a zone. Relocate it to where the explosive move begins.
A larger-than-normal basing candle is still a basing candle. 'Explosive' is judged against real explosive moves, by feel, not measurement.
Explicit two reasons to end a trendline: an updated trendline (makes the old one invalid) or overextension. Both should be shown on the homework.
An adjusted trendline anchor can sit where there's no peak or valley, because it was moved to avoid cutting candles.
Wick-only peaks or valleys are 'too wicky' for trendline structure. As bodies they'd count, and borderline wick cases get grace.
No pip-depth rule for trendlines because pip values differ between pairs. Don't draw a massive trendline that skips the ones in between.
Grading policy: the chain is graded as if your (wrong) trendline were right, so you can get a zone right for a wrong reason. Grace on subjective calls, none on the missing lower low/higher high.
Removal check by zooming in: a zone only removes an earlier one if the basing actually wicked past it.
Removals (zone or trendline) only count on the exact same timeframe. A 1-minute zone never removes a monthly zone. An oversized zone that qualifies is still drawn big and accepted as massive.
Homework logistics: daily chart only, proper screenshots, use the daily breakdowns and chart link.
Homework weeks vary in focus (many zones / trendlines / not forcing zones). This week was 'don't force zones'.

No big jump? No zone. Waiting is part of the game. You are fishing. Little fish nibble all day, but you wait for the big one. If you pull up every nibble, you catch nothing worth keeping. On the chart, small candles are the nibbles. We wait for the big explosive jump. A bigger nibble is still a nibble. Only the big tug on the line is the fish.
Do not force zones. A bigger-than-usual basing candle is still a basing candle, and an explosive candle that removed nothing is not a zone.
Include all close basing candles: distal at the extreme wick, proximal where the explosive move starts.
End a trendline when an updated one forms or when price overextends. Judge all removals on the same timeframe.

passages.h: Step: Lots of lows, few zones
passages.t: Price keeps making new lows. Many candles here are just basing candles, some a bit bigger than their neighbours. A bigger basing candle is still a basing candle. Be patient: do not force zones.

passages.h: Step: Downtrend line: valley, peak, lower low
passages.t: Starting point, an obvious valley, a peak, then a lower low. No lower low, no trendline. Draw it so it does not cut through candles.
A candle closes fully above the line. Rule 2: a trendline was removed, so now look for the zone that did it.

passages.h: Step: Use BOTH close basing candles
passages.t: Two basing candles sit close together. Using both does not make the zone massive or tiny, so use both. Distal at the bottom wick (magnet tool). Proximal right where the explosive move starts.

passages.h: Step: Next candle basing? Wrong place
passages.t: Big tip: if the candle right after your zone is another basing candle, it is not the zone. The zone sits directly before the explosive candle. And judge every removal on the same timeframe.

Week with almost no zones? - The test is to not force zones. Draw nothing if nothing qualifies. Bigger basing candle among tiny ones? - Still a basing candle. Two basing candles close together? - Use both. Tighten only if the basing gets crazy.
Next candle after your zone is basing? - Wrong place. Move the zone to right before the explosive candle.
Can a lower timeframe zone remove a higher timeframe zone? - No. Removals are judged on the same timeframe. When does a trendline end? - When an updated line forms, or when price overextends.
Did a zone remove an earlier zone? - Only if its basing actually went past it. Zoom in to check.
"The best zones can fail, and..." - "...the worst zones could work." That is why psychology matters.

Kevin opened with the learning path (free S&D course, then private video lessons, then Sunday sessions) and walked through this week's daily chain-analysis homework, where the only zones drawn are ones that remove an opposing zone, remove a trendline, or make an all-time high/low.

He hammered the trendline anatomy (peak, valley, then a higher high / lower low), drawing from the lowest/highest point possible without cutting candles, avoiding overly large trendlines when smaller ones exist in between, and 'ending' a trendline once price overextends.

He measured borderline moves away in pips to separate drawable from tradable zones, then marked every student's chart, correcting momentum mistaken for trendlines, zones that accomplished nothing, zones drawn too small, and normal wicks mistaken for emotional wicks.

He then explained the parallel channel tool (50% line = golden zone vs overextended zone and how it affects trade management and counter-trend odds) and answered questions on watchlists, day-trading timeframes, trading after losses, win rate vs R:R, and how to get market direction (higher timeframe plus one).
Only draw zones that remove an opposing zone, remove a trendline, or make an all-time high/low.
Draw a trendline only after a clear peak, valley and a higher high (uptrend) or lower low (downtrend).

Draw uptrend lines from the lowest point possible to the valley; downtrend lines from the highest point possible to the peak. Never cut through candles with a trendline; move the anchor point instead.

Do not draw large trendlines when smaller valid trendlines exist in between; keep one trendline at a time. End (stop extending) a trendline once price becomes heavily overextended from it. Consider a trendline removed only when a candle fully closes (body and wick) beyond it. Include all basing candles in the zone when they are close together. End the distal line at the wick; do not end the zone randomly.

Do not trade a zone that is tricky to draw; if you have to ask whether the move away is good enough, avoid it. Measure and compare to older zones when a move away is questionable. A zone needs a stay-away candle when drawn at normal size. Do not shrink a zone to make its move away look valid.

Treat a normal-sized wick through a zone as a removal; only a clearly exaggerated wick is emotional. Remove a supply zone when price peaks above it. Do not map out every high and low. Submit homework as a chart link, on the daily chart. Draw the trendline first, then apply the channel tool to the next valley/peak.
Prefer trades between the trendline and the channel's 50% line; trade beyond 50% only with more aggressive management. Day traders: keep 4-5 instruments max and use one entry timeframe.
Take the next valid setup after a loss unless you know your emotions are compromised; then step away.
Get direction from the timeframe above your entry, then add one more (higher timeframe plus one).
Attendance has dropped (maybe school is back); sessions are recorded, but he deletes ones older than about 2 months because of storage limits, so the last ~5 are available.
Recommended path for new traders: (1) watch the full free S&D course on YouTube, (2) watch the private video lessons, (3) watch and participate in the Sunday sessions, and watch old ones too.
If you already understand what a zone is (and that 'little basing candles' are not the zones we want) you can skip the free course, but he still recommends it.
The Sunday sessions are the most important factor, but you cannot really understand them without the full course and the private lessons first.

passages.t: Task: mark all zones that remove opposing zones, trendlines (and all-time highs/lows) on the daily homework chart, continuing from last week's demand and upward trendline.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 1: trendline anatomy and large trendlines
passages.t: He saw a large trendline but did not draw it because a smaller trendline exists in between; draw larger trendlines only if there are no trendlines in between, which is often not the case.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 1: trendline anatomy and large trendlines
passages.t: A trendline needs a blatantly obvious peak and valley followed by a higher high (uptrend). If price fails to break the high, there is no trendline.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 1: trendline anatomy and large trendlines
passages.t: Upward trendline: draw from the lowest point possible to the next lowest point in the valley. If a wick would be cut through, attach the line to a different point instead; we never cut through candles.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 1: trendline anatomy and large trendlines
passages.t: Example of what is NOT a trendline: a valley and peak with no lower low after it (some students drew this last week). Remove the missing lower low and you would have the trendline.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 1: trendline anatomy and large trendlines
passages.t: Only one trendline at a time is really kept; drawing too many/too large ones makes you miss the relevant one.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 2: basing candles, measuring borderline moves away
passages.t: He pointed out an obvious small basing candle, then bigger basing candles, then a candle that is neither a basing candle nor a good enough explosive move away; that is not what we want. What we want is a very clear explosive move away; zones like that are 'never a question'.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 2: basing candles, measuring borderline moves away
passages.t: For a close supply call (a student asked) he measured: the reference move was 112 pips and he looked for at least 112 pips on the candidate; it qualified, so he drew it, but called it 'not a great zone' - drawable, not tradable.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 2: basing candles, measuring borderline moves away
passages.t: On his real trading charts, if a zone is that close and needs measuring, he usually just does not draw it; he only measures for the homework's sake.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 2: basing candles, measuring borderline moves away
passages.t: Chart zoom changes perception: zoomed out, only extremely obvious moves look explosive; zoomed in, zones look beautiful everywhere. It is nuanced and somewhat subjective.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 2: basing candles, measuring borderline moves away
passages.t: Key distinction: for a tricky zone the question is 'is it drawable?'; for an obvious zone the question is 'is it tradable?'. Tricky-to-draw zones are never really tradable - if you do not know if it is a good move away, avoid it. Nothing wrong with measuring and comparing to your older zones when it is questionable.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 2: basing candles, measuring borderline moves away
passages.t: Second borderline supply after a supply was removed: body measured 82, from bottom of body to wick top 102; the wick at the top made him nervous. Comparison measures were 108 and 115. He drew it but felt he was 'forcing zones'; definitely not a trade he would take, and price blasted right through it.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 3: overextended trendlines, removal, drawing the zone
passages.t: New uptrend trendline with obvious peak, valley and higher high, but price became very overextended above it, making the trendline essentially irrelevant.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 3: overextended trendlines, removal, drawing the zone
passages.t: He wants students to have that trendline but end it around that point (no specific point) - not extend it, because extending it says it is still relevant. If price had stayed around the trendline it would stay relevant. Extending the overextended trendline would also make you miss the next trendline.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 3: overextended trendlines, removal, drawing the zone
passages.t: He started a trendline from the actual low, but it would have cut through candles, so he started it at another point; that is why his trendline start points sometimes look random but are not.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 3: overextended trendlines, removal, drawing the zone
passages.t: A trendline is not removed until a candle has a full close, body AND wick, below an upward trendline (or above a downward trendline). The explosive move candles that still touched the line did not remove it. When drawing the resulting demand zone, include all of the basing candles.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 3: overextended trendlines, removal, drawing the zone
passages.t: Would he take that trade? Probably yes: pretty good zone, not his favourite, better than the earlier two borderline zones; what he really wants is the zone with a very nice move away. It produced a nice trade.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 4: downtrend lines and the end of the chart
passages.t: Downtrend line: blatant peak, valley and lower low; draw from the highest point possible to the peak.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 4: downtrend lines and the end of the chart
passages.t: That trendline was removed not by the first candle poking through but by the candle that fully closed above it, full body and wick.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 4: downtrend lines and the end of the chart
passages.t: Rule 2 (trendline removed) gives a zone 'not always': if everything is just basing candles with no qualifying move, there is no zone and the analysis just ends.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 4: downtrend lines and the end of the chart
passages.t: Out of the borderline zones, if you traded all of them: loss, loss, winner, and you could be in profit depending on target - but he personally would only have traded the one good zone.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 4: downtrend lines and the end of the chart
passages.t: A later candidate had a decent move away candle, but when drawn similar in size to the other zones there was no stay-away candle, so no zone.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 4: downtrend lines and the end of the chart
passages.t: A final borderline peak/valley trendline: he would not draw it but gives grace if students did.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough part 4: downtrend lines and the end of the chart
passages.t: He admitted he completely forgot to draw an obvious zone that a student found - 'just one that I simply forgot to draw'.

passages.h: Purpose of chain analysis and next week's homework
passages.t: Chain analysis: only draw zones that (1) remove an opposing zone, (2) remove a trendline, or (3) make an all-time high or low. If you draw a zone that removed nothing, ask: what did it remove? Nothing.

passages.h: Purpose of chain analysis and next week's homework
passages.t: Zones are kept on the chart to see what removes them, so every zone shows its work: this demand removed this trendline, this supply removed this demand, etc. This is what he does on his chart link.

passages.h: Purpose of chain analysis and next week's homework
passages.t: Next week's homework: from January 2000 to January 2001 (at the very end he said '1999 to 2000', likely a slip). You must have the existing zone and the all-time low on your chart because of rule 3. He expects next week's chart to have few zones.

passages.h: Purpose of chain analysis and next week's homework
passages.t: New members overwhelmed by needing previous zones: put a vertical line at the start and end dates, copy his zones from his chart link in Discord, add the all-time low, then draw all trendlines. You will struggle at first and that is fine.
Zones should usually be drawn a bit larger, including all the basing candles when they are close together. Pick the more blatant peak and valley when two candidates are close.
Trendlines with a wrong start point can create a zone that should not exist; start from the correct lowest/highest point. A student on the 1-minute chart: homework must be on the daily chart.
Wicks: a supply with a big wick is worse, especially when a better supply exists above - choose the better one. Too-small moves away, forced zones: delete them. 'Too horizontal to be a trendline.'

A student kept drawing random zones that followed none of the 3 rules and mapping every single high and low; 'we do not map out every single high and low'. He will be hard on repeat mistakes to hold students accountable, but first-timers get leniency.
A zone should be removed when price peaks above it (supply) - one student did not remove it.

Momentum is not a trendline: a move up with tiny peaks and valleys is just momentum; the peak and valley we look for are the obvious swings. Distal line: do not randomly end the zone; include the wick (end the distal at the wick).
Homework must be submitted as a chart link (so he can zoom in), not a screenshot; screenshots are only for the video-lesson homework. Watch the welcome video on how to submit.
Very thick distal/proximal lines make charts hard to mark; messy dots/indicators should be removed.
Liked when students 'ended' overextended trendlines - shows they recognise it got overextended. If one candidate barely qualifies, a smaller one next to it certainly does not.
The higher high concept is 'very, very simple': the peak and valley can look identical, but you need the higher high.
Big-mistake student summary: trendlines too large, wrong start points, zones that accomplished nothing, moves away not good enough - needs a complete reset.

passages.h: Emotional wick vs normal wick; drawing zones too small
passages.t: A student kept a zone alive because of what they thought was an emotional wick. It was just a normal-sized wick: larger than nearby wicks but the overall candle and wick were normal, so it is a normal break and the zone is removed.

passages.h: Emotional wick vs normal wick; drawing zones too small
passages.t: An emotional wick would be a much larger, exaggerated wick (he sketched it); then it would be a different story.

passages.h: Emotional wick vs normal wick; drawing zones too small
passages.t: Drawing a zone too small makes the move away look good enough; drawn at proper size, the move away becomes much worse. Do not shrink zones to justify the stay-away candle. When you draw zones super tiny, a lot of zones become zones that aren't.

passages.h: Channel tool (parallel channel on a trendline)
passages.t: First draw the trendline normally; the channel tool is not used to draw the trendline. Place the channel on the trendline, then drag the opposite side to the valley after the peak (downtrend) - roughly, it does not have to be perfect.

passages.h: Channel tool (parallel channel on a trendline)
passages.t: Downward trendline: anything below the 50% mark of the channel is overextended - you can still trade there but he does not love it. Between the downward trendline and the 50% mark is the optimal area to trade.

passages.h: Channel tool (parallel channel on a trendline)
passages.t: Upward trendline example (S&P 500): between the trendline and the 50% line is the 'golden area'; once price breaks above the 50% mark it is the 'danger zone' - price can still go up, but it is less likely.

passages.h: Channel tool (parallel channel on a trendline)
passages.t: Trading in the golden area: less aggressive trade management. Trading in the overextended area: allowed, but be more aggressive with trade management.

passages.h: Channel tool (parallel channel on a trendline)
passages.t: Counter-trend: an entry-timeframe supply zone in the overextended area (especially way above the channel) is more likely to work than an entry-timeframe supply inside the golden area where we want longs.
No pairs strictly to avoid, but cross pairs are generally junk and whippy, especially yen crosses. As a swing trader he has a large watchlist; silver is on it only because a zone is near.

Day traders: stick to 4-5 instruments max, e.g. gold, S&P, the euro, the yen, maybe GBP/USD and the Aussie; definitely the euro. If one instrument (e.g. USD/JPY) has nothing for a couple of weeks, swap another in.
Good idea: a larger general basket plus a weekly watchlist picked from it based on trends, opportunities and his forecast, in separate columns.

passages.h: Q&A: chart questions, trading after losses, win rate
passages.t: A student asked why he did not mark a recent rally-base-rally zone: that zone did not remove anything; the zone he has is the one that removed the supply.

passages.h: Q&A: chart questions, trading after losses, win rate
passages.t: After a losing trade: if the next setup follows the rules, take it. But if you know two losses in a row will make you do stupid things, step away - and work on yourself so you can take the next setup. Two losses (down 2%) should not affect you.

passages.h: Q&A: chart questions, trading after losses, win rate
passages.t: Win rate: risk-to-reward and win rate are correlated; larger R:R targets mean a lower win rate. To raise win rate, target lower R:R and trade good zones. Be specific when asking: which supply, which chart, which timeframe.

passages.h: Q&A: chart questions, trading after losses, win rate
passages.t: BTC 15-minute supply: some supply there but he does not love zones that just peak up and drop like that.

passages.h: Q&A: use his chart link, day-trading timeframes, direction
passages.t: Many members never use his chart link or daily breakdown video - that is the core of the membership; even day traders should use his zones.

passages.h: Q&A: use his chart link, day-trading timeframes, direction
passages.t: Day-trading example (USD/CAD): no zones or trendlines on the lower timeframe means nothing to trade; wait until price hits his H4 zone, then go to your 15-minute for day-trading longs. He swing trades entering on H4 and H1. New traders should stick to ONE entry timeframe.

passages.h: Q&A: use his chart link, day-trading timeframes, direction
passages.t: Stay off the 1-minute (its higher timeframe would be the 15-minute, which he does not analyse). Use the 5-minute with his H1 charts as the guide, or the 15-minute with his H4 as the guide. Pick one, not both.

passages.h: Q&A: use his chart link, day-trading timeframes, direction
passages.t: A student using daily, 1H and 5M: fine. Avoid the 15-minute unless a 15M zone sits right next to your 5M zone - then take the 15M zone because it is that close.

passages.h: Q&A: use his chart link, day-trading timeframes, direction
passages.t: His own early mistake 6-7 years ago: trying to day trade and swing trade while entering on 5M, 15M, H4 and H1 at once - extremely confusing and overwhelming. You really need a computer to trade; he dislikes trading on a phone.

passages.h: Q&A: use his chart link, day-trading timeframes, direction
passages.t: Direction depends on your entry timeframe: entering on 5M, direction comes from H1; once mastered add the daily ('higher timeframe plus one' / multiple sequence analysis). Example: H1 uptrend line means look for 5M longs, but at a daily supply expect the H1 trendline to break.

passages.h: Q&A: use his chart link, day-trading timeframes, direction
passages.t: A 1-minute trader does not need the daily; he, entering on H4/H1, uses daily, weekly and monthly.

passages.t: An uptrend line needs a blatant peak and valley and then a higher high. "If we fail to break this high, then we do not have a trend line."

passages.t: Several students drew this last week. Without the lower low there is no downtrend line.
