passages.t: He drew them, but "I kind of feel like I'm forcing zones": drawable, definitely not tradable. On his real charts a zone that needs measuring usually is not drawn.

passages.h: Chart: [17:38] A student's chart: his sketch of the more blatant peak and valley for the trendline.
passages.t: When two candidates are close, use the more obvious peak and valley. Include all the basing candles and draw zones a bit larger.

passages.h: Chart: [23:12] A student's chart with a big loop around a cluster of small zones.
passages.t: "It just seems like you're kind of forcing some zones here ... These are all just a little too small."

passages.h: Chart: [26:54] A student's chart: a circle at a missed trendline and his line showing where it should run.
passages.t: The missed trendline made the student miss the supply. Two other zones followed none of the three rules.

passages.h: Chart: [35:16] A student's note "Emotional wick, can we ignore it?" with the wick circled at the red supply.
passages.t: Not emotional: bigger than the nearby wicks, but a normal-sized candle and wick, so it is a normal break and the zone is removed. Do not shrink a zone to make the move away or the stay-away gap look good.

passages.h: Chart: [42:41] His sketch over a student chart: the large trendline vs the smaller swings with their own trendline in between.
passages.t: Draw a large trendline only if there are none in between. "Absolutely no trend line here. Did not make a higher high."

passages.h: Chart: [49:11] Channel tool on a downward trendline (XAUUSD 1h, OANDA): the channel is placed on the trendline and its other side dragged to the valley.
passages.t: Draw the trendline first; the channel does not draw it. Below the 50% mark is overextended: tradable, but he does not love it.

passages.h: Chart: [51:02] SPX500USD 1W (OANDA): an upward channel on the trendline, with his marks near the upper half.
passages.t: Between the trendline and the 50% line is the "golden area" (less aggressive management). Above 50% is the danger zone: price can still rise but less likely, so manage more aggressively.

passages.h: Chart: [51:02] SPX500USD 1W (OANDA): an upward channel on the trendline, with his marks near the upper half.
passages.t: Counter-trend, a supply far above the channel is more likely to work than one inside the golden area.

passages.h: Chart: [63:06] DXY 4-pane (1W, 4h, 1D, 1h): he circles the 1h trend while answering which timeframe gives direction.
passages.t: Direction comes from the timeframe above your entry (5m entry, 1h direction); add the daily once that is mastered ("higher timeframe plus one").

Large trendline vs smaller trendline in between Why: A smaller valid trendline (peak, valley, higher high) exists inside the large one, so the large one is not drawn. Result: Only the smaller trendline kept; drawing the large one makes you miss zones.

Borderline supply zone (student asked) Why: Reference move measured 112 pips; needed at least 112 pips; it qualified. Result: Drawn as drawable but not tradable; on real charts he would skip such a zone.

Borderline supply after a supply was removed, with a top wick Why: Body 82, body-bottom to wick 102 vs comparisons 108/115; wick made him nervous; felt like forcing. Result: Drawn for chain analysis only, not a trade; price blasted right through it.

Uptrend line that became overextended Why: Valid peak/valley/higher high, but price ran far from it, making it irrelevant. Result: Keep the line but end it; extending would also hide the next trendline.

Demand zone from a trendline removal Why: Trendline removed only when a candle fully closed (body and wick) beyond it; zone includes all basing candles. Result: Pretty good zone he would probably take; produced a nice trade.
Downtrend line removal followed by basing only Why: Rule 2 does not always give a zone; only basing candles, no explosive move. Result: No zone; analysis ends there.
Candidate zone with decent move away but no stay-away candle Why: Drawn at a size similar to the other zones, there is no stay-away candle. Result: Not a zone.
Zone kept because of a supposed emotional wick Why: The wick was normal-sized relative to the candle; an emotional wick is much larger. Result: Zone should be removed.
Zone drawn very small to make the move away look good Why: At proper size the move away is much weaker. Result: Not a valid zone; do not shrink zones.

Channel tool on an upward trendline Why: Price between trendline and 50% line = golden area for longs; above 50% = danger/overextended. Result: Trade in the golden area with normal management; overextended area allowed with more aggressive management; counter-trend supply more likely to work when overextended.

passages.h: Chart: USD/CAD Lower TF (5M/15M) with his H4
passages.t: Day-trading plan Why: No zones or trendlines on the lower timeframe; wait for price to reach his H4 zone. Result: Then drop to the 15-minute and look for day-trading longs.
Student-identified supply Why: There is some supply, but he dislikes zones that just peak up and drop. Result: Not bad, not loved.
Direction for 5M entries Why: H1 uptrend line means look for 5M longs; but price at a daily supply means the H1 trendline may break. Result: Higher timeframe plus one.
Q: Are the old Sunday sessions available? A: Yes, but he deletes ones older than about 2 months because he refuses to pay for unlimited storage; the last ~5 are always available.

Q: Is this close supply zone valid? A: It is close; on real charts he would just not draw it. For homework he measured: 112 pips reference, needed at least 112; it qualified, so draw it, but it is not a great zone - drawable not tradable.

Q: As a new member I'm overwhelmed since zones depend on removing previous zones. A: Put vertical lines at Jan 2000 and Jan 2001, copy his zones from his chart link in Discord (you just need the existing zone and the all-time low), then draw all the trendlines. You will struggle at first, that is fine and why the meetings exist.
Q: Should I make a new account just for this community / trading? A: Yes, just open a blank chart; the welcome video explains how to submit homework properly.
Q: No candle closed yet beyond the trendline (student note)? A: Exactly - great observation; the trendline is removed only by a full close.

Q: How do you use the channel tool? A: Draw your trendline first. Put the channel on the trendline and drag the other side to the valley after the peak (roughly). For a downtrend, below the 50% mark is overextended (tradable but not loved); between trendline and 50% is optimal. For an uptrend, between trendline and 50% is the golden area; above 50% is the danger zone - trade it with more aggressive management.
Counter-trend zones are more likely to work in the overextended area than in the golden area.
Q: Can we all speak with each other on mic? A: Yes if you have a question; he does not want to talk for no reason.

Q: How do I know which pairs to trade and avoid? A: No pairs to strictly avoid, but cross pairs (especially yen crosses) are whippy junk. Swing traders can have a big watchlist; day traders 4-5 max (gold, S&P, euro, yen, maybe GBP/USD, Aussie). Keep a large general basket and pick a weekly watchlist from it based on trends and opportunities.
Q: Why didn't you mark the recent zone that blew off that rally-base-rally? A: Because that zone did not remove anything; the zone he has is the one that removed the supply.

Q: If you have a losing trade, would you still take the next setup? A: If it follows the rules, yes, 100%. But if you know two losses in a row will make you do stupid things, step away, and work on your emotional control so you can take it. Two losses is only down 2%.
Q: How can I improve my win rate? A: Vague question; R:R and win rate are correlated. Larger R:R means lower win rate, so look for lower R:R and trade good zones.
Q: BTC, there's supply? A: Be specific (which chart, timeframe, where). On the 15-minute there is some supply but he does not love zones that just peak up and drop.

Q: As a day trader, what timeframes should I use? A: He enters on H4 and H1 as a swing trader, but a newer trader should stick to one. Avoid the 1-minute. Use the 5-minute with his H1 charts as the guide, or the 15-minute with his H4 as the guide. Pick one.
Q: It's difficult to track on the phone. A: If you are going to be a trader you need a computer; he generally does not like trading on his phone.

Q: As a day trader I use daily, 1H and 5M - OK? A: Yes. Avoid the 15-minute, unless a 15M zone is right next to your 5M zone; then take the 15M zone. Stick to one entry timeframe - his own early mistake was trading many timeframes and styles at once.

Q: What timeframe gives a clear market direction? A: Depends on your entry timeframe. Entering on 5M, direction is from H1; once mastered, add the daily (higher timeframe plus one / multiple sequence analysis). If you trade the 1-minute you do not need the daily; he uses daily, weekly and monthly because he enters on H4/H1.

Drawing a trendline from a peak and valley without a higher high / lower low. Calling momentum (small zigzags) a trendline. Drawing overly large trendlines and missing the ones in between. Drawing too many trendlines at once. Starting a trendline from the wrong point, creating zones that should not exist. Extending an overextended trendline as if still relevant.

Treating a trendline as removed before a full body-and-wick close beyond it. Drawing zones that accomplished nothing (random zones). Mapping out every single high and low. Forcing zones with too-small moves away. Drawing zones too small to justify the move away / stay-away candle. Drawing zones too small in general instead of including all basing candles. Ending the distal line before the wick.

Mistaking a normal wick for an emotional wick and keeping a removed zone. Not removing a zone after price peaks above it. Picking the zone with a big wick when a better one exists above. Trading borderline, drawable-only zones. Doing homework on the wrong timeframe (1-minute instead of daily). Submitting homework as a screenshot; thick lines and cluttered dots. Repeating the same mistakes week after week.

Trading several entry timeframes and both day and swing trading at once. Trading on the 1-minute as a beginner. Large watchlists for day trading; trading whippy yen cross pairs. Asking vague questions without chart, timeframe and location. Not using his chart link and daily breakdown video. Trading after losses when emotionally compromised.
Does this zone remove an opposing zone, a trendline, or make an all-time high/low? Is the move away clearly explosive, or would I need to measure it? If measuring, treat it as drawable only.
Is there a stay-away candle with the zone drawn at proper size, including all basing candles and the wick?

Is the trendline built on peak, valley and a higher high / lower low, from the extreme point, not cutting candles? Is there a smaller trendline in between that makes a large one invalid? Has the trendline been removed by a full body-and-wick close?

Is price overextended from the trendline (beyond the channel's 50%)? If so, manage more aggressively. Was any wick through the zone truly emotional or just normal? Is the instrument on my small watchlist and am I on my one entry timeframe? What does the timeframe above my entry (plus one more) say about direction? Am I emotionally fit to take this after recent losses?

“If it's tricky to draw, if you don't really know if it's a good move away, I would avoid it.” “We're not trying to cut through candles.” “We need the higher high.” “We do not map out every single high and low.” “When you draw it that small, a lot of zones become zones that aren't.” “Why is this a zone? Oh, trend line was removed.” “You're down 2%, big deal.” “Pick one, don't do both.”
“I kind of feel like I'm forcing zones at this point.”
Channel tool explained: draw trendline first, project channel to the next swing; between trendline and 50% = golden/optimal area, beyond 50% = overextended/danger zone.

Trade management tied to the channel: less aggressive inside the golden area, more aggressive when trading in the overextended area; counter-trend entry-TF zones more likely to work when overextended beyond the channel.
Concrete pip measuring of borderline moves away (112 pips reference; 82/102 vs 108/115) and the rule that zones needing measurement are drawable, not tradable; on real charts he simply skips them.

Emotional wick vs normal wick distinction: a proportionally normal wick through a zone removes it. Do not shrink zones to justify the move away/stay-away candle. Chart zoom/price action scale makes moves away look different; explosiveness is relative. Learning path: free course, private lessons, then Sunday sessions.
Day-trading setup: 4-5 instruments (gold, S&P, euro, yen, GBP/USD, Aussie), large basket plus weekly watchlist, yen crosses whippy.

Timeframe pairings for using his charts: 5M entry with his H1, or 15M entry with his H4; avoid 1M; use 15M zone only if right next to the 5M zone. Direction = timeframe above entry plus one; 1M traders do not need the daily. Win rate vs R:R correlation; trading after two losses only if emotionally in control. Next homework: January 2000 to January 2001 with the all-time low marked.

Trade near the road; far from it is the danger zone. A road has a white line down the middle and a ditch on the side. Driving near the line is safe and easy. Driving way out by the ditch, you can still move, but you must be very careful. A trendline is the road. The channel shows where the safe half ends.
The 50% line is like the edge of the playground. Inside, play normally. Outside, a grown-up keeps a closer eye on you.
Draw the trendline first, then the channel to the peak: line to 50% is the golden area, beyond 50% is overextended. If you must measure a move away to accept it, it is drawable only, not tradable.
A normal-sized wick through a zone removes it; only an exaggerated wick is emotional. Never shrink a zone to fit.
Peak, valley, then a higher high: a valid uptrend line, from the lowest point possible to the valley without cutting candles.
Put the channel tool on the trendline and drag the other side to the peak. It does not have to be perfect.

passages.h: Step: Golden area vs danger zone
passages.t: Between the trendline and the 50% line is the golden area: the best place to trade with the trend. Above 50% is the danger zone: price can still go up, but it is less likely.
Price blasts far above the channel. The trendline is now basically irrelevant. End it around there; extending it says it still matters, and you would miss the next trendline.

Trading in the golden area: normal management. Trading in the overextended area: allowed, but manage more aggressively. A counter-trend supply up here is more likely to work than one inside the golden area.

Golden area? - Between the trendline and the channel's 50% line. Above the 50% line (uptrend)? - Overextended / danger zone: manage more aggressively. Counter-trend zone odds? - Better in the overextended area than in the golden area. Had to measure the move away? - Drawable, not tradable.

Normal wick vs emotional wick? - Normal-sized wick = removal. Only an exaggerated wick is emotional. Learning path? - Free S&D course, then private lessons, then Sunday sessions. How many instruments for day trading? - 4-5 max. Avoid whippy yen crosses. Win rate vs risk-reward? - Linked: bigger targets mean a lower win rate.

Kevin reviewed the AUDUSD daily chain-analysis homework (the stretch ending around 2000-2001), where the only zones allowed are ones that remove an opposing zone, remove a trendline, or make an all-time high/low.

He walked through how to anchor a trendline from the highest point possible and lower it so it never cuts through candles, where a trendline is removed (a full wick-and-body close beyond it), and when to keep extending one after price overextends.

Because the price action that week was very borderline, he said he would be more lenient on moves away and gave students grace on close calls, then marked each student's chart, repeatedly correcting momentum mistaken for trend and lines with no lower low/higher high.

He answered questions on zones that remove nothing, which timeframes he trades (H1 and H4 with daily/weekly as higher timeframes) and whether trendlines are drawn on every timeframe, set next week's homework (Jan 2001 to Jan 2002, all-time low must be marked), asked for feedback on the homework format, and closed with a short review of students' trade screenshots.

Only draw homework zones that remove an opposing zone, remove a trendline, or make an all-time high/low. Treat only a true all-time high/low as a zone source, not any minor high/low. End a removed zone at the point of removal; do not extend it. After a zone is removed, look for the opposing zone that removed it. Be able to say what every zone on your chart removed.
Anchor a trendline from the highest (or lowest) point possible to the next peak (valley). Never let a trendline cut through candles; move the anchor to the next highest point instead.

Require starting point, peak, valley, higher high for an up trendline (inverse, with a lower low, for a down trendline). Make the trendline actually touch its anchor points. Consider a trendline removed only when a candle closes fully beyond it, wick and body. Stop a trendline where it was removed; do not continue it.

Keep extending a trendline after an overextension if price immediately pushes back into it and respects it. Mark every new all-time low; each new low is an all-time low. Avoid drawing very large trendlines unless the middle ones are too borderline. Draw trendlines and zones the same way on every timeframe. Stick to one entry timeframe if you are new. Place the distal line where the basing is, never at a random level.
Submit each timeframe's chart separately, set to the correct timeframe, not as images. Show the zone in trade-review screenshots; send two screenshots if the zone is far back.
The homework is 'chain analysis': find which zones removed which zones and trendlines, following the chain across the chart.

Only three kinds of zones go on the homework chart: a zone that removes an opposing zone, a zone that removes a trendline, or a zone that makes an all-time high or low. All-time high or low means exactly that, not any little high or low.
You can trade differently if you want, but for the homework you must follow these rules; if you are not going to follow them, maybe don't submit the homework.
First-week students not understanding it is completely reasonable; the frustration is with students on their fourth submission still drawing a zone that removed nothing.
He is not saying this is the only way to trade; it is simply what the homework is testing.
Last week's homework ran from January 2000 (the red line) forward, which meant the prior zone had to be properly drawn already.

A larger downward trendline was valid. Many students drew a steeper one, which he called too momentum-like: close, not super wrong, but not the one.
The valid line had a very good peak, a very obvious valley and, more importantly, the lower low. Anchor the trendline from the highest point possible to the next peak.
If the line from the highest point cuts through candles, you do not keep it; we never cut through candles for a trendline. Lower it to the next highest point.
He can often tell in advance that a given anchor will cut through candles and skip straight to the anchor that will not.
Structure for an upward trendline: starting point, peak, valley, higher high. A downward trendline is the inverse: starting point, valley, peak, lower low.
If there is no lower low (downtrend) or higher high (uptrend), it is not a trendline, no matter how the line is drawn.
A trendline must actually touch the price points it is drawn from; one student's line was not even touching.
Usually do not draw very large trendlines, because then you are usually skipping trendlines in the middle; but in this homework the large one was required because the middle ones were too borderline.

passages.h: Borderline zones and leniency on moves away

passages.h: All-time low as a zone source

The correct answer had exactly two trendlines and three zones on the chart. Most common miss: the large trendline coming in, which was the necessary one; missing it caused students to miss downstream zones.
Most common wrong line: a steeper line that was 'way too much like momentum' and not a trend.
A zone whose wick is almost the same size as its candle is close to not being a zone; to him it is a very large basing candle. If the wick were half the size he would accept it.
One student had a zone that removed the low, which he also had, but it also removed that demand; always note every removal.

A drop-base-rally shape built on a single basing candle was correctly identified as DBR but was not an area of demand. 'Biggest explosive move' is not enough when a wick negates it. A trendline drawn where price never made a new low is very incorrect.
Peak-to-peak line where the first point is not a peak and there is no lower low: incorrect, and any zone justified by removing it is therefore not a zone.
'What did this zone accomplish?' If it removed nothing, it does not belong on the homework chart. Not marking the all-time low caused students to miss the zone that formed there.
He gave grace on close trendlines and borderline zones: 'it's never gonna be like, oh, you're wrong' when it is not out of left field. One student had no forced zones, which he praised.
