Q: Is the trend removal on the higher timeframe and the zone on the lower timeframe? A: No, everything is on the same timeframe. It has nothing to do with timeframes; price is fractal, so it doesn't make much difference.

Q: How important are 'proven' zones, i.e. zones that don't remove opposing zones? A: He wouldn't use them. But if a move is very obvious, e.g. a huge explosive move that didn't remove anything, he doesn't see an issue with drawing it.

Q: What timeframe do you use most for entering and looking for zones? A: H1 and H4, those are the zones he trades. His layout: H1 with the daily as its higher timeframe, H4 with the weekly as its higher timeframe; if the daily isn't showing much he looks at the weekly, so they work in flow and in sequence. He recommends sticking to one entry timeframe, especially if new; he can handle two after 7 years.

Q: Do we draw trendlines on both timeframes? A: Trendlines are drawn on any timeframe. Trendlines, zones, everything he does on the H1 he does on the daily exactly the same way, whether 1 minute or 1 month.

Q: A student found the submission confusing (sent a daily chart with H1/H4 zones on it). A: Very easy: make sure the chart is on the correct timeframe (the daily for this homework) and hit save. If you have H1 and H4 zones, send those charts separately or he cannot see or mark them.

Q: Suggestion: interactive analysis where everyone annotates the chart, or posting finished trades for review. A: Interactive annotation has been tried and never works (nobody participates or it's laggy). Going over trade reviews is a good idea; he may start next week with trade reviews and lessons from them.
Drawing a zone that removed nothing on the chain-analysis homework. Drawing a steep, momentum-like line as a trendline.
Drawing a trendline with no lower low (or higher high), or from a point that is not a peak. Missing the large necessary trendline and thereby missing downstream zones.
Calling the explosive candle the trendline removal instead of the first full wick-and-body close beyond it. Continuing a trendline after it has been removed.
Ending a trendline too early after a brief overextension that price immediately reclaimed. Trendline not touching its anchor points or cutting through candles.

Treating a candle with a wick almost the size of the candle as a zone (it is a large basing candle). Calling a single basing candle a demand zone just because the shape is drop-base-rally. Not marking the all-time low, so the zone there is missed. Combining separate sections of basing candles into one zone. Wrong zoom level making moves away look stronger or weaker than they are.

Sending a daily chart when the zones are on H1/H4, or submitting homework as images or on the wrong timeframe. Drawing the distal line randomly away from the basing. Posting trade screenshots where the zone can't be seen.

Does this zone remove an opposing zone, remove a trendline, or make an all-time high/low? Can I name exactly what this zone removed? Is this a trend (clear peak, valley, lower low/higher high) or momentum?

Is my trendline anchored at the highest/lowest point possible without cutting through candles? Does the line touch its anchors? Has any candle closed fully (wick and body) beyond the trendline? If so, end it there. If price overextended past the line, did it immediately push back and respect it? Is the all-time high/low marked? Is the wick so big relative to the candle that this is just a large basing candle?
Is the zone drawn on a single clear basing section, with the distal at the basing? Is my zoom appropriate when judging the move away? Is the chart on the correct timeframe before saving/submitting?
“We only have zones on our charts that remove an opposing zone, removes a trend line, or makes an all-time high or low.” “We're never really going to cut through candles for a trendline.”

“When we have a trend line removed, we don't continue the trend line, we end it where it was removed.” “Every time you break a new low, that's an all-time low, 100%.” “A trend line looks like this. Peak, valley, lower low, removed.”
“Doesn't matter if I was trading the 1 minute or the 1 month, it would be the same thing.”
“There's objectivity, but sometimes there is some subjectivity, so we have to accept that.” “Make sure you show the zone.”
Formal chain-analysis homework rule set: only zones that remove an opposing zone, remove a trendline, or make an all-time high/low; every new low below an all-time low is itself an all-time low.
Trendline removal defined precisely as the first candle with a full wick-and-body close beyond the line (not the explosive candle), and the line is ended there.

Trendline anchoring: start from the highest point possible and lower to the next highest point when the line would cut through candles; must touch anchors; explicit four-point structure (start, peak, valley, higher high / inverse).
Keep extending a trendline after an overextension if price immediately pushes back into and respects it.
Avoid very large trendlines because they skip middle ones, except when the middle ones are too borderline.
He does not measure moves away; zoom level changes whether candles look like basing, and he is now more lenient on borderline moves away.
A candle whose wick is nearly the candle's size is a large basing candle, not a zone; a DBR shape on one basing candle is not demand.
Explicit layout: H1 paired with daily, H4 paired with weekly, falling back to weekly when daily is uninformative; new traders should use one entry timeframe.
Zones that remove nothing: generally not used, but a very obvious huge move can still be drawn.
Homework/trade-review submission standards (separate timeframes, correct timeframe, not images, zone visible, send both screenshots).

Start the line at the top, slide it down until it cuts nothing. Imagine laying a ruler across the tops of some blocks. If the ruler pokes into a block, it is not lying right. You lower one end until it only touches the tops. Then the ruler is right.
A trendline is a rope over the tops of hills. The rope can touch the hilltops, but it can never go through a hill.
Anchor from the highest point possible; if the line cuts candles, lower it to the next highest point.
A trendline is removed by the first full wick-and-body close beyond it, not by the explosive candle.
An all-time low is only a potential zone. A wick almost the size of its candle means a large basing candle.
A downtrend line needs a starting point, a valley, a peak and, most importantly, a lower low. No lower low, no trendline, however you draw it.
Start from the highest point possible to the next peak. But look: this line cuts through a candle. We never cut through candles.
Lower the anchor to the next highest point that cuts nothing. That is why his start points sometimes look random. They are not.
The explosive candle pierces the line, but it still touches. The removal is the first candle whose wick AND body sit fully above. End the line there.
The demand that removed the line: distal line at the basing wick, never at a random level. Every zone must have a name for what it removed.

Line from the highest point cuts candles? - Lower the anchor to the next highest point. Does the explosive candle remove the line? - Not if it still touches. The first full wick-and-body close beyond does. After removal, do you continue the line? - No. End it where it was removed. Brief overextension that is reclaimed at once? - Keep extending the line.

Wick nearly the size of the candle? - A large basing candle, not a zone. Every new wick below the all-time low? - A new all-time low: a potential zone, not a guaranteed one. Where does the distal line go? - At the basing, never at a random level.
Momentum-like steep line? - Not the trendline. Look for the obvious peak, valley and lower low.

Kevin re-explained the zone recipe for new members and stressed that the space between the stay-away candle and the proximal line is what tells him whether a zone is good or poor. He then walked the homework chain from January 01 to January 02 (an all-time low with no valid demand, trendline drawing and removal on a full candle close, a supply widened on its proximal side, and a trendline break with no zone).

He marked every student's homework, pointing out common faults: distal lines not attached to the wick, zones drawn too small, and momentum lines drawn as trendlines. For the first time he went through the Discord trade-review channel.
He set the rules for posting reviews (show the zone and the reaction, no dollar amounts) and judged each trade on zone quality, the trendline, how old the zone was, the stop width and the trend.

Grade every zone by the space between the stay-away candle and the proximal line. Large space = good zone, minimal space = poor zone. Draw poor-space zones for the chain analysis, but do not trade them.
Count the move away only if it is a single explosive candle, not a run of small candles or two candles that look like one. Use 1 to 3 basing candles, of any colour.
Only draw zones in the Sunday analysis that remove an opposing zone, remove a trendline, or make an all-time high or low.
After an all-time low or high, a removed zone or a removed trendline, check the closest explosive candle first.
Never shrink a zone to create space. Draw it at a similar size to nearby zones and then judge it.
Draw a trendline only after an obvious peak, an obvious valley and a broken high (or a lower low).
Treat a trendline as removed only when the first candle closes fully beyond it (body and wick). Touching does not count.
If a zone drawn wick to wick is much smaller than nearby zones and it has two basing sections, widen only the proximal side a little. Don't swallow the other basing.
A trendline or zone break without a qualifying zone produces no zone. End the chain there. Attach the distal line to the wick of the basing candle.
Draw the zone on the single basing candle when the base is one candle; don't include the neighbouring candle.
Remove trendlines that are overextended and irrelevant, and do not trade zones that depend on them. Avoid very tight stops; use wider stops in these market conditions.

Post trade reviews showing the zone and the reaction (two screenshots if needed), with no dollar amounts, only percentages. Put questions in the questions channel, not in trade review. Submit homework with the right chart and timeframe visible.

passages.h: Opening and new format for Sunday sessions
passages.t: Some homework weeks have lots of zones and some, like last week, are mostly about not forcing zones. Learning when NOT to draw a zone matters just as much.

passages.h: Opening and new format for Sunday sessions
passages.t: He wants new things in these sessions, so from now on he will go through the Discord trade-review channel every Sunday.

passages.h: Opening and new format for Sunday sessions
passages.t: Keep the trade-review channel simple, clean and clear so it can be reviewed live. Questions belong in the questions channel, not in trade review.

passages.h: Opening and new format for Sunday sessions
passages.t: A student asked about a EURUSD H1 'green candle that failed'. His answer: he does not see a candle as failing. A candle is just a candle.

passages.h: Zone recipe recap for new members
passages.t: A zone has four required parts, but parts 3 and 4 are linked, so you really only need three. Get those three and you have all four.

passages.h: Zone recipe recap for new members
passages.t: 1) Basing candles: small candles, found everywhere on a chart. You need 1 to 3, and they can be any colour (a basing candle in a demand zone can be green).

passages.h: Zone recipe recap for new members
passages.t: 2) Move-away candle: it must be explosive. He gives no measurement on purpose, because when price gets very overextended the moves away start to look smaller. You learn to judge it over time, and there is some subjectivity.

passages.h: Zone recipe recap for new members
passages.t: The move away must be one explosive candle that covers the distance. If price got there through a series of little basing candles, it does not count. 3) Stay-away candle: it stays away from the proximal line.

passages.h: Zone recipe recap for new members
passages.t: 4) Space between the stay-away candle and the proximal line. A stay-away candle automatically gives you this space.

passages.h: The space between the stay-away candle is the quality grade
passages.t: How he judges a zone as good or bad: by the space between the stay-away candle and the proximal line.

passages.h: The space between the stay-away candle is the quality grade
passages.t: EURUSD H1 example: single-candle basing ('my favorite'), a very obvious explosive move away, a stay-away candle and a large space. It is a very good zone and the trade worked.

passages.h: The space between the stay-away candle is the quality grade
passages.t: On the same chart, a second zone had very little space. It was not the best zone, so that trade was 'completely avoidable'. It failed completely.

passages.h: The space between the stay-away candle is the quality grade
passages.t: A third zone had decent space and was a pretty good zone. It gave about a 1:1, or break-even, depending on the R:R target.

passages.h: The space between the stay-away candle is the quality grade
passages.t: So the three examples were a great, a poor and a pretty good zone, and the results matched the space: 'it's no coincidence'.

passages.h: The space between the stay-away candle is the quality grade
passages.t: Poor-space zones are still drawn (drawable versus tradable) so you can follow what removes them in the chain analysis. They are just not traded.

passages.h: The space between the stay-away candle is the quality grade
passages.t: Stops: don't use a very tight stop, in these market conditions or in general. Even a sensible stop can be taken out by the spread; that happened to him on EURUSD a couple of weeks ago.

passages.h: Trendline recap and the three Sunday-analysis rules
passages.t: A trendline needs an obvious peak and valley, not small ones, and then a higher high (or a lower low for a downward line).

passages.h: Trendline recap and the three Sunday-analysis rules
passages.t: In the Sunday analysis, only draw zones that do one of three things: remove an opposing zone, remove a trendline, or make an all-time high or low. It must be an ALL-TIME high or low, not just any high or low.

passages.h: Trendline recap and the three Sunday-analysis rules
passages.t: He is being a little more lenient on moves away this time. In some market conditions moves away are huge, and then people only look for moves that big, when smaller explosive ones are fine too.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough, January 01 to January 02 (chain analysis)
passages.t: An earlier zone was valid because it removed the downward trendline. Price reacted nicely (maybe a 1:1) and then removed that zone.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough, January 01 to January 02 (chain analysis)
passages.t: He spotted a single-candle-basing supply right away and kept it a similar size to the previous zones (by eye, not measured). He would not have liked trading it: price took so long to come back that the zone was old, and old zones are usually not the best to trade.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough, January 01 to January 02 (chain analysis)
passages.t: All-time low: under rule 3 this suggests a zone, but not every time ('this is a tricky one'). He looked for explosive candles and started with the one closest to the all-time low. When the trigger is an all-time low, a removed zone or a removed trendline, the candidate is always the closest one to it.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough, January 01 to January 02 (chain analysis)
passages.t: Drawn at a similar size to the other zones, the nearest candidate had almost no space and no stay-away candle, so it is not a zone. The next candidate was the same, so they left the zone above as it was and did not force a demand.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough, January 01 to January 02 (chain analysis)
passages.t: A student suggested drawing it very small to create space. His answer: 'we're not gonna make zones smaller just to fit.'

passages.h: Homework walkthrough, January 01 to January 02 (chain analysis)
passages.t: He marked the all-time low with a horizontal ray. There was an obvious peak and valley there, but no high was broken afterwards, so there is no trendline. If a high had been broken, there would definitely be one.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough, January 01 to January 02 (chain analysis)
passages.t: Upper trendline: peak, valley, and then the high above the valley was broken, so it is valid. Draw it from the lowest point of the valley. If that cuts through candles, adjust it to the next point.

passages.h: Homework walkthrough, January 01 to January 02 (chain analysis)
passages.t: Downward trendline: obvious peak, valley and a lower low, drawn from the highest point. It is borderline 'almost too horizontal', but he kept it. Any more push down would have made it irrelevant.

passages.h: When the trendline was removed, and the zone that removed it
passages.t: A trendline is NOT removed when candles merely touch it. Here a red candle and even the green explosive candle were still touching the line.

passages.h: When the trendline was removed, and the zone that removed it
passages.t: It is removed only when the first candle closes fully above it (body and wick) for a downward line, or fully below it for an upward line. If a wick still touches the line, it is not removed until a candle closes clear of it. Then you find the zone that removed it. Here it was a zone that 'just barely' qualified.

passages.h: When the trendline was removed, and the zone that removed it
passages.t: Later, a supply zone 'very obviously' removed the zone and the upper trendline, and it gave a beautiful little trade.

passages.h: Drawing a supply larger on the proximal side
passages.t: Drawn wick to wick, that supply was only about half the size of the earlier zone (he cloned the zone to compare them).

passages.h: Drawing a supply larger on the proximal side
passages.t: He did not stretch it over all of the earlier basing, because there were two different sections of basing.

passages.h: Drawing a supply larger on the proximal side
passages.t: Instead he made it 'just a little bit bigger' on the proximal side so it matches the size of nearby zones. That is why you sometimes see him widen a zone; there are examples in the Weekly Forex Forecast.

passages.h: Drawing a supply larger on the proximal side
passages.t: He would trade that supply on appearance alone: the space under the stay-away candle was good. Price reacted and removed it, and right away there was a demand below with an explosive move away.

passages.h: A trendline break with no zone
passages.t: There was a peak and valley, so there was a trendline, and it broke. But no supply removed it.

passages.h: A trendline break with no zone
passages.t: 'Just because a trend line breaks or a zone breaks doesn't mean we just automatically have a zone.' In that case the chain ends there.

passages.h: Homework marking: borderline calls and subjectivity
passages.t: 'Nothing is personal in this homework.' If he is hard on someone, it is because he cares. Zones and trendlines that were close got a 'borderline'. Borderline means it could go either way, so it is not marked wrong. 'Nothing is going to be 100%' and trading will be a little subjective.

passages.h: Homework marking: borderline calls and subjectivity
passages.t: What made him nervous about one borderline zone was the wick. If that part had been bodies (more basing candles) it would have been obvious. A wick there makes it less certain.

passages.h: Homework marking: borderline calls and subjectivity
passages.t: What he does not want to see is lines nowhere near a trendline being called trendlines. That is 'way wrong'.

passages.h: Homework marking: borderline calls and subjectivity
passages.t: Missing one trendline can cascade and make you miss the zones and trendlines that follow in the chain.

passages.h: Homework marking: borderline calls and subjectivity
passages.t: He admitted he had missed an obvious trendline himself because he was too focused on another part of the chart. 'I'm not perfect.' A student had caught it, and everyone should add it to their charts.

passages.h: Homework marking: borderline calls and subjectivity
passages.t: He found one homework zone drawn over an extra candle. The zone must be drawn on the single basing candle only.

Distal line not attached to the candle (a 'random distal line'). The distal line must sit on the wick. Getting this wrong made one student miss the next zone in the chain. Zones drawn too small. Make them bigger so they match the size of nearby zones. Basing that is too big means it is not a zone.

Trendlines drawn with no lower low (or higher high). 'If you draw trend lines like this, they're literally everywhere on the chart.' After the peak and valley, a new high (or low) must form. Momentum drawn as trendlines. 'This is momentum.' Focus on the larger peaks and valleys. A basing candle labelled as a zone ('that's a basing candle, not a zone').
Two zones drawn at one all-time low with no reason, and zones not extended until the candle that actually removes them. Moves away that are not explosive enough.

In a multiple-timeframe homework (EURUSD daily demand plus H1 zones), the daily demand was good. One H1 zone was rejected because the move away was not explosive. The other H1 zone, with nice single-candle basing, was fine.
Submission problems: wrong chart, wrong timeframe, links that would not open, and no visible timeframe or symbol all mean he cannot mark the work. He will not chase anyone for homework.
He praised a student who marked peaks, valleys and higher highs, because it shows they are applying the rules. He called it a good tip for new traders.

Chain from January 2002 to January 2003. Make sure the supply zone from this session is on your chart and drawn properly (proximal widened as shown). That is the first thing he will check. New members can start with the lesson homework; doing both is better.
Show both the zone and the trade. If the zone is far from the reaction, post two screenshots, one of the zone and one of the reaction.
A screenshot of only the result, a 5-minute entry with no context, or a risk-reward tool covering the zone cannot be judged.
A student pointed out that people mostly post wins. He agreed and asked everyone to show the full analysis. Don't tag him with a chart and no question; he won't answer it.

Never post dollar amounts, even on a demo account. Post percentages. Dollar amounts can make people feel bad: the same trade might make $30 for one person and $300 for another. Percentage is what matters, and it is in the rules.
A trade after a trendline removal, with nice basing and a very explosive move away, was a great trade. It was entered halfway into the zone, which happened to work.
Entering halfway through the zone is not banned. It gives a higher R:R when it works, but you get filled less often and miss trades. 'There's no free lunch.' A break-even on a good zone is fine.

A EURGBP quick 1:1 had a pullback too quick for his liking, but it worked. The trade was with the trend, so a bigger R:R was technically possible. With price that overextended, he liked the aggressive management.
A full take-profit trade had the zone on a basing candle. The proper zone was lower, and that would still have been a trade.
For a set & forget zone, he would have drawn only the single basing candle instead of the whole large area.

A confirmation trade had a good upper trendline but large basing. When the basing is almost the size of the move-away candle, 'it's kind of our sign to kind of stay away'. It removed the trendline, and if you are convinced by the higher timeframe it was a nice confirmation trade.

USDCHF 3:1 was a great trade. The box the student called 'liquidity' was not obvious liquidity, just a random box. AUDUSD liquidity trap: a decent zone that he liked. Natural gas gap zone: a decent trade, but not his favourite setup.

A 15-minute set & forget loss: the trendline was really horizontal price action with no real peak (first mistake). The supply only just qualified, and it was old. The zone 'move away' was two green candles that look like one move but are not, so it was not explosive. Looking at the overall move instead of the single candle is a mistake he makes too.
Several trades won from zones with no explosive move away, or from basing candles. He was glad they worked but said they were not zones, and he 'wouldn't be doing my job' if he didn't say so.
A 1:2 trade was too zoomed in and had no explosive move away. It also did not remove any demand, so it was not supply.
Lost trade: the trendline was way overextended and basically irrelevant, so the supply it depended on was not valid either. The zone itself was not terrible, but the loss was avoidable.
Rally-base-rally confirmation zone with beautiful basing and move away, and price staying far away: 'as good as it's gonna get'.
A break-even on EUR and a 1:6 (1.26) on EURJPY with a wider stop were a great example of why wider stops are often better, especially in these market conditions.
US100 H1 zone: he did not love one wick, but it was a pretty good trade and a fine loss for that market. On another trade the only thing against it was the higher timeframes.
A wicked-out trade was counter-trend against very strong USDCAD momentum, which is why he preferred the long. 'Break-even, win, loss' over a week is completely reasonable.

Being stopped out again and again by a tight stop: use a wider stop loss. A student said that cutting 75% of their pairs, keeping swing trading in the background and checking charts at most once a day had improved their results. He agreed it is not stupid at all. You can backtest on any timeframe you like. Gold had a nice confirmation-trading setup for the week ahead.
'If you lose, don't let it frustrate you. It's the reality of trading.'
[02:00-07:30] Zone diagram (3/3 gives 4/4, the space circled), then EURUSD 1h (OANDA) with three zones graded by the space under the stay-away candle.

[08:30-17:30] Homework on AUDUSD 1D (FXCM): all-time low candidates with no space, a peak and valley with no higher high, upper and downward trendlines, the supply widened on the proximal side, and a trendline break with no zone. [18:00-34:00] Student homework (light and dark themes).
[35:40-56:00] First trade-review segment from the Discord channel, then gold and USDCAD multi-timeframe layouts.
The homework chart is AUDUSD 1D from FXCM ("Jan 01 to Jan 02" means January 2001 to January 2002), not an unnamed homework chart.

passages.h: Chart: [02:26] The labelled zone diagram with "3/3" and "4/4" written beside it.
passages.t: Four parts, but the stay-away candle and the space are linked: get basing, an explosive move away and a stay-away candle (3 of 3) and the space comes with it (4 of 4). Basing is 1 to 3 candles of any colour.

passages.h: Chart: [04:52] Same diagram with the stay-away candle and the space under it circled.
passages.t: A stay-away candle automatically gives you the space. That space is how he grades a zone.

passages.h: Chart: [05:41] EURUSD 1h (OANDA): three zones drawn as orange boxes; a blue bar marks the large space between the first zone and its stay-away candle.
passages.t: The first zone: single-candle basing, a very obvious explosive move, a big space. A very good zone, and it worked.

passages.h: Chart: [07:19] Same chart: an arrow to the zone with very little space, which failed completely.
passages.t: Great, poor and pretty good zones, and the results matched the space: "it's no coincidence". Poor-space zones are drawn, not traded.

passages.h: Chart: [08:57] AUDUSD 1D homework: a long arrow up to the all-time low area, where rule 3 means there might be a zone.
passages.t: He is more lenient on moves away now: in some conditions moves away are huge, and then smaller explosive ones look wrong when they are fine.

passages.h: Chart: [09:45] The zone that removed the downtrend line (green) and the single-candle-basing supply above it.
passages.t: The supply is kept a similar size to the earlier zones by eye. Not his favourite trade: price took so long to return that the zone was old.

passages.h: Chart: [10:34] Three arrows at the explosive candles below, checked in order starting with the one closest to the all-time low.
passages.t: Drawn at a similar size, the candidates had no stay-away candle and no space, so no zone. "We're not gonna make zones smaller just to fit."

passages.h: Chart: [12:12] All-time low ray, with small circles on an obvious peak and valley.
passages.t: No high was broken after the valley, so no trendline. If a high had broken, there would definitely be one.

passages.h: Chart: [13:50] The upper trendline (peak, valley, then the high broken) and a hand-drawn downtrend line across the peaks.
passages.t: Draw from the lowest point of the valley; if that cuts candles, slide to the next point. The downtrend line is "almost too horizontal" but qualifies.

passages.h: Chart: [17:05] The supply drawn a bit bigger on the proximal side, the demand below it, and the later trendline break with no supply.
passages.t: Wick to wick the supply was about half the size of earlier zones, so he widened the proximal side rather than stretching it over separate basing. "Just because a trend line breaks ... doesn't mean we just automatically have a zone."

passages.h: Chart: [24:24] A student's dark-theme chart with the note "I don't know with this fib, I think it could be both of these zones ..." and a missed demand.
passages.t: The zone had a random distal line not attached to the wicks, which made the student miss the next zone.

passages.h: Chart: [39:03] Trade review: EURGBP 4-pane (1W, 4h, 1D, 1h, OANDA) with red down arrows on the weekly and daily.
passages.t: A quick 1:1 with the trend. The pullback was too quick for his liking, but with price that overextended he liked the aggressive management.

passages.h: Chart: [41:30] Sketch on a blank EURGBP 1h: a zone on the left and a long path out to a reaction far to the right.
passages.t: If the zone and the reaction do not fit in one screenshot, post one of the zone and one of the reaction.

passages.h: Chart: [48:49] A student's trade post with dollar amounts; he writes "30$" and "300" over it.
passages.t: Post percentages, never dollar amounts: the same trade can be $30 for one person and $300 for another.

Demand with single-candle basing, a very explosive move away and a large space under the stay-away candle Why: Big space between the stay-away candle and the proximal line = great zone Result: Good trade
Zone with very little space between the stay-away candle and the proximal line Why: Poor quality. Drawable, not tradable Result: Failed completely; he called it avoidable
Zone with moderate space Why: Pretty good zone Result: About 1:1 or break-even depending on the R:R target

passages.h: Chart: Homework chart (Jan 01 to Jan 02) homework timeframe
passages.t: Candidate demands at an all-time low Why: Drawn at a similar size, they had no stay-away candle and no space. Shrinking them to create space is not allowed Result: No zone. The zone above stays

passages.h: Chart: Homework chart (Jan 01 to Jan 02) homework timeframe
passages.t: Downward trendline (borderline flat) removed by the first full close above it, and the zone that removed it Why: Candles touching the line did not remove it; only the full body-and-wick close did. The zone just barely qualified Result: Valid chain link

passages.h: Chart: Homework chart (Jan 01 to Jan 02) homework timeframe
passages.t: Supply that removed the zone and the upper trendline, widened on the proximal side Why: Wick to wick it was half the size of the other zones. It had two basing sections, so he widened it only a little. It had good space Result: Beautiful little trade, later removed by a demand

passages.h: Chart: Homework chart (Jan 01 to Jan 02) homework timeframe
passages.t: Trendline break Why: No supply removed it Result: No zone; the chain stops

passages.h: Chart: EURUSD daily / H1 (student MTA homework) D / H1
passages.t: Daily demand with H1 zones Why: The daily move away is obvious. One H1 move away was not explosive; the other had single-candle basing Result: One H1 zone rejected, one accepted
With-trend zone, quick pullback Why: Pullback too quick for him; price overextended so aggressive management was fine Result: Quick 1:1 win

Confirmation trade after upper trendline removal, large basing Why: Basing almost the size of the move away is a sign to stay away; acceptable if the higher timeframe is convincing Result: Win; 'pretty good job'
Good zone with a 'liquidity' box Why: Good trade; the liquidity box was not obvious Result: 3:1 win
Liquidity trap zone Why: Decent zone Result: Win
Gap zone Why: Decent but not his favourite setup Result: Win

Supply off a flat 'trendline' Why: The trendline was horizontal with no peak. The zone barely qualified and was old. The move away was two candles, not one explosive candle Result: Loss; not a great setup
Supply depending on an overextended trendline Why: The trendline was irrelevant, so the supply was not valid, even though the zone looked fine Result: Loss; avoidable
Rally-base-rally confirmation zone Why: Beautiful basing and move away, and price went further away Result: 1:1 win; 'as good as it's gonna get'
Two trades, one with a wider stop Why: Wider stops survive these market conditions Result: Break-even and a 1:6
H1 zone with one wick he didn't love Why: Pretty good trade for that market Result: Loss; 'a fine loss'
Counter-trend short against strong momentum Why: Counter-trend; he preferred the long Result: Wicked out

Q: Can you share tips on the EURUSD H1 green candle that failed? A: He does not see a candle as failing; a candle is just a candle. The zone involved was not a good zone, because the stay-away candle left very little space.
Q: Why not draw the all-time-low demand very small so it has space? A: We do not make zones smaller just to fit. Drawn at a similar size, it has no space and no stay-away candle, so it is not a zone.
Q: Isn't that downward trendline too horizontal? A: It is close and borderline. Any more push down would make it irrelevant, but in his opinion it still qualifies.
Q: My chain this week is totally wrong. A: That's okay.
Q: Can you check a specific pair at the end? A: He doesn't like turning the session into a forecast, but said to remind him at the end.

Q: Why do you not recommend entering halfway through the zone? A: He is not really against it. There are pros and cons and no free lunch: your R:R is higher when the zone works, but you get filled less, so you win fewer trades and miss some.
Q: My base is only one candle; is that allowed? A: A base is not limited to one candle. It can be one to as many as you want; he prefers one to three, up to five.

Q: A student summarised the strategy: good basing, an explosive move away, a stay-away candle, a trendline needs an obvious peak and valley, and a zone must remove an opposing zone. A: A pretty good, accurate representation.
Q: Do we have to do the homework on the AUD pair, or can we start with the lessons? A: Start with the lessons; doing both is better.
Q: What should I do if I keep getting knocked out by a tight stop loss? A: Use a wider stop loss.
Q: If I backtest on the daily timeframe, is it good for all timeframes? A: He wasn't sure what was meant, but you can backtest on any timeframe you like. Send follow-ups in text on Discord.
Q: When are the Sunday meetings? A: Around 9:30 a.m. Eastern Time.

Trading zones with minimal space under the stay-away candle. Treating a run of small candles, or two consecutive candles, as one explosive move away. Calling a basing candle a zone. Shrinking a zone so that it appears to have space. Drawing trendlines with no higher high or lower low. They end up everywhere on the chart. Drawing momentum as a trendline. Treating horizontal price action as a trendline.

Removing a trendline when a candle only touches it or a wick crosses it. Distal lines not attached to the wick. Zones drawn too small compared with nearby zones. Assuming every trendline or zone break gives a zone. Trading old zones that price took a long time to return to. Keeping an overextended trendline and trading the supply that depends on it. Taking a zone whose basing is almost the size of the move away.

Stops that are too tight and get taken out by the spread. Counter-trend trades against very strong momentum. Hyper-zooming into lower timeframes and calling random structures zones. Labelling random boxes as liquidity. Posting only wins, only results, or screenshots where the R:R tool hides the zone. Posting dollar amounts. Submitting homework with the wrong chart or timeframe, or a link that won't open.
Missing one trendline, which makes you miss the zones that follow in the chain.

Are there 1 to 3 small basing candles? Is the move away a single explosive candle? Is there a stay-away candle, and how big is the space under it? Is the zone drawn at a similar size to nearby zones, with the distal line on the wick? Did it remove an opposing zone, remove a trendline, or make an all-time high or low? Is it the closest explosive candle to that event?

Was the trendline really removed by a full body-and-wick close? Is the trendline built from an obvious peak and valley plus a higher high or lower low? Is it too horizontal or overextended? Is the basing small compared with the move away? How old is the zone? Is the trade with the trend, not against strong momentum? Is the stop wide enough to survive the spread and current conditions?

“We have to learn when to not draw a zone as well.” “A candle is just a candle.” “The space between the stay-away candle and the zone is what really tells me if it's a good zone or not.” “It's still drawable versus tradable.” “We're not gonna make zones smaller just to fit.”

“Just because a trend line breaks or a zone breaks doesn't mean we just automatically have a zone.” “Nothing is going to be 100%.” “There's no free lunch.” “I wouldn't be doing my job if I didn't say that.” “If you lose, don't let it frustrate you. It's the reality of trading.”
The size of the space between the stay-away candle and the proximal line is the main quality grade (great, poor or pretty good, with live EURUSD H1 results), not just a yes/no requirement.
After an all-time low or high, a removed zone or a removed trendline, check the closest explosive candle first.

Widen a zone slightly on the proximal side when wick to wick is about half the size of nearby zones and there are two separate basing sections. Old zones that price takes a long time to return to are usually not the best to trade. A basing almost the size of the move away is a sign to stay away.

Two consecutive candles that look like one move are not an explosive move away; judge the single candle, not the overall move. A wick, rather than bodies, in the basing area makes a borderline zone less certain.
Borderline calls on zones and trendlines are explicitly not marked wrong; some subjectivity is accepted. Entering halfway through the zone gives a higher R:R but fewer fills.
Wider stops are often better in current conditions; very tight stops get taken out by the spread.
New Sunday format: trade-review rules (zone plus reaction screenshots, no dollar amounts, questions elsewhere). Homework chain continues from January 2002 to January 2003.

The bigger the gap under the stay-away candle, the better the zone. Three kids jump off a step. The first lands far away: great jump. The second lands right next to the step: hardly a jump. The third lands at a good distance: pretty good. You can tell how good each jump was just by the gap.
The space is like the score on a test. Big space, top marks. Tiny space, you still write it down, but you do not bet on it.
Grade every zone by the space between the stay-away candle and the proximal line. Never shrink a zone to make space. If it is too small next to other zones, widen the proximal side a little.
After an all-time low, a removed zone or a removed trendline, check the closest explosive candle first.
Single-candle basing, a very obvious explosive move and a stay-away candle far away. Big space between them.
Price comes back and launches. A great zone, a good trade.
Same recipe, but the stay-away candle's wick reaches almost back to the proximal line. Very little space. Drawable, not tradable.
Price comes back and breaks straight through. That trade was "completely avoidable".
Decent space between the stay-away candle and the zone. A pretty good zone.
Great, poor and pretty good, and the results matched the space. That space is how Kevin grades a zone. Poor-space zones are still drawn to see what removes them, just not traded.

What grades a zone? - The space between the stay-away candle and the proximal line. Minimal space? - Poor zone: draw it, don't trade it. How many basing candles, what colour? - 1 to 3 (up to 5), any colour.

Two candles that look like one move? - Not an explosive move away. It must be one explosive candle. Zone too small vs neighbours, two basing sections? - Widen the proximal side slightly. Trigger happened (ATL, removal)? - Check the closest explosive candle first.
Trade review rules? - Show zone and reaction, percentages only, questions in the questions channel. Keep getting stopped by a tight stop? - Use a wider stop.

After a tough trading week, Kevin re-teaches the trendline concept (obvious peak and valley plus a break of the pivot high/low) and when he does NOT follow the chain-analysis drawing rules: confirmation off a very convincing higher-timeframe zone, and macro charts (1 month and up).

He then walks the AUDUSD daily chain analysis from January 2002 to January 2003, showing how to attach a trendline without cutting candles, how to update a trendline from the most recent valley, how to end overextended trendlines and removed zones, and how to size zones consistently.

Homework reviews focus on missed trendlines and missed updated trendlines, and trade reviews cover zones drawn too large for the timeframe, the 'third zone in a range' warning, overextended markets and a 10/10 NASDAQ zone that still failed. Homework for next week is AUDUSD daily on FXCM, January 2003 to January 2004.
Draw a trendline only after an obvious peak and valley AND a break of the prior pivot high (uptrend) or low (downtrend). Judge trendline peaks/valleys visually; do not draw borderline ones.
Only draw zones that remove an opposing zone, remove a trendline or make an all-time high/low.
Break that rule only for confirmation off a very convincing HTF zone, or on macro charts (1 month and up).
A trendline is removed only when a candle closes fully beyond it, body and wick not touching the line.
Attach the trendline at the lowest/highest point; if it cuts candles, move to the next point that doesn't.

When an updated trendline forms, end the old one and start the new one from the most recent valley/peak. End an overextended trendline instead of extending it. End a removed zone exactly where it was removed; do not extend it.

Keep zone sizes consistent; enlarge a too-small zone slightly, don't make it needlessly large. Do not draw momentum lines. Draw missed zones on your chart anyway so you can see what removes them. Copy his zones exactly before starting the next homework period. Do homework on AUDUSD, FXCM, daily, and leave it saved on the daily. Manage aggressively when entering in an overextended market.
Draw zones to fit the timeframe you are trading.

passages.h: Opening: a tough week is normal
passages.t: Last week was a very tough trading week for him too, after a little over 7 years of trading.

passages.h: Opening: a tough week is normal
passages.t: If you struggled, don't worry: keep taking the setups. Weeks like this happen a few times a year; it is the nature of the beast.

passages.h: Opening: a tough week is normal
passages.t: The plan for the session: trendlines (a member asked about them), homework review, then trade reviews from the Discord.
A steep move with small peaks and valleys is momentum, not a trendline. A trendline needs an OBVIOUS, deep peak and valley.

He does not measure the peak/valley depth. A member measured it (about 50%) and that may be reasonable, but for him it is purely visual: it saves time and is accurate enough. You can build a measuring system if you want.
An obvious valley alone is not enough. After the obvious valley, price must break the pivot high that came before it (uptrend). Then it is a trendline. Downtrend line: valley, peak, then a lower low.
Example: obvious peak, obvious valley, broke the high after the valley - trendline drawn from the valley to the next touch.
Borderline cases exist: a peak, valley and lower low that are close but not as obvious - he does not draw it. Without measuring, the odd one may not be 100% right, but it is good enough.
There is no single video for adjusting trendlines because every situation differs; that is why the Sunday meetings, homework and chain analysis exist.

passages.h: When to draw zones, and the only two exceptions
passages.t: Only draw a zone when it does one of three things: removes an opposing zone, removes a trendline, or makes an all-time high/low.

passages.h: When to draw zones, and the only two exceptions
passages.t: Exception 1 - confirmation, but only when he is very convinced by the higher-timeframe zone (a very good zone with a great move away, not a barely qualifiable one).

passages.h: When to draw zones, and the only two exceptions
passages.t: Why: often price makes one massive aggressive candle into the HTF zone with no trendline and no opposing zones to remove. The entry-timeframe zone that forms at the HTF zone cannot remove anything because the pullback was too aggressive, so he accepts it if it has a good move away.

passages.h: When to draw zones, and the only two exceptions
passages.t: Exception 2 - macro charts (1 month and up: 1M, 3M, 6M, 12M). Zones are harder to get there, so any explosive move is valuable whether or not it did one of the three things. Even in these cases he still much prefers to follow the rules.

passages.h: AUDUSD daily walkthrough part 1 (Jan 2002 - Jan 2003): trendline removal and zone sizing
passages.t: A trendline was removed by a supply zone. Compare move-aways: one decent, one great; the trade off it was maybe break-even.

passages.h: AUDUSD daily walkthrough part 1 (Jan 2002 - Jan 2003): trendline removal and zone sizing
passages.t: That supply qualified because it removed the trendline (rule 2). The trendline was removed when the candle CLOSED fully below it, body and wick - not by the earlier candle.

passages.h: AUDUSD daily walkthrough part 1 (Jan 2002 - Jan 2003): trendline removal and zone sizing
passages.t: That supply was then removed by a demand zone. Drawn wick to body it is far too small; wick to wick looks decent compared with the other zone sizes - slightly smaller but not too small.

passages.h: AUDUSD daily walkthrough part 1 (Jan 2002 - Jan 2003): trendline removal and zone sizing
passages.t: If a zone is too small for his liking, just make it a little bigger. In a safer situation you can draw it up to where it was tested later, but he did not do that here.

passages.h: AUDUSD daily walkthrough part 1 (Jan 2002 - Jan 2003): trendline removal and zone sizing
passages.t: Zoomed out there is a larger trendline, but with the channel tool you can see price got very overextended from it, so he does not use it (having it is understandable).

passages.h: AUDUSD daily walkthrough part 1 (Jan 2002 - Jan 2003): trendline removal and zone sizing
passages.t: Explosive moves that removed nothing are not zones - 'what did it accomplish? Nothing.' That is momentum.

passages.h: Part 2: attaching the trendline without cutting candles
passages.t: A good-enough peak and valley appears, so a trendline is drawn from that valley. Attach to the lowest point of the valley first. Here that line cut through candles, so keep the second point and move to the next lowest point that does not cut through candles.

passages.h: Part 2: attaching the trendline without cutting candles
passages.t: A trendline start that looks random is not random: it is the lowest point possible, adjusted so it does not cut through candles. Extend the trendline up to where it was removed and no further.

passages.h: Part 2: attaching the trendline without cutting candles
passages.t: A zone that was respected then broken: delete it with the remove tool and END it where it was removed - do not extend it past that. Extending makes charts sloppy.

passages.h: Part 2: attaching the trendline without cutting candles
passages.t: Then find the zone that removed it: small candles are not good enough; the standout explosive candle, on par with the other explosive moves used, is the zone. Not a coincidence. It was an older zone, so trading it would have made him a little nervous.

Price broke above a high after an obvious valley, so there is a new, updated trendline. When there is an updated trendline, END the old one around that point (he had extended it thinking it was the only one).
Do not start the new line from the bottom again. Start from the MOST RECENT valley: the old line's second touchpoint becomes the first point of the new line.
The new trendline was removed by the first candle that did not touch the line with body or wick - he first picked the wrong candle and corrected himself; candles still touching the line do not count.

The massive explosive candle there is the demand/supply zone (large zone). Not his favourite: explosive move and stay-away candle present, but little space between the stay-away candle and the zone. Still a nice trade, and price pulled back to another zone too - a great year for daily zones on the Aussie.

passages.h: Part 4: downtrend line at the exact top, tricky basing
passages.t: Obvious valley, obvious peak, lower low: a downtrend line from the highest point. He expected it to cut through a candle; it only touched (did not cut through), so starting at the exact top was correct. If the wick were slightly bigger he would have moved the start point.

passages.h: Part 4: downtrend line at the exact top, tricky basing
passages.t: Reference zone sizes: stick to similar sizes across the chart - don't draw one far larger than needed.

passages.h: Part 4: downtrend line at the exact top, tricky basing
passages.t: Trendline removed when a candle closed above it (not the earlier candle). The explosive move signals demand.

passages.h: Part 4: downtrend line at the exact top, tricky basing
passages.t: Drawing is tricky with many basing candles: drawing it huge makes no sense when you don't have to, one candle is too small, so use both green basing candles and leave out the red one.

passages.h: Part 5: multiple updated trendlines and overextension
passages.t: Another obvious peak, valley and higher high gives a trendline (you may use a wick he does not love).

passages.h: Part 5: multiple updated trendlines and overextension
passages.t: That trendline was removed but no supply removed it, so the chain analysis just ends there.

passages.h: Part 5: multiple updated trendlines and overextension
passages.t: Another peak and valley formed, so draw a new trendline from the most recent valley; then yet another peak and valley gave another update from the newest valley. This is where trendlines get tricky. The newest trendline got very overextended, so do not continue it; just end it there.

passages.h: Part 5: multiple updated trendlines and overextension
passages.t: An already-tested supply being removed is no surprise. It was removed by an obvious single-candle-basing demand - his favourite kind - with nice spacing and an explosive move away.
Most common error: missing updated trendlines and the trendlines after them, which then makes you miss the zones that remove them. Borderline trendlines drawn by students got grace; it is either-or.
Only end a trendline when there is a new (updated) trendline; when there is one, end/delete the old one about 95% of the time. Do not draw momentum lines at all.
If you missed a zone, you still have to put it on your chart, because you need to see what removes it later.
A student drew two zones where only one removed the opposing zone; the other removed nothing.
A student's demand was right but for the wrong reason: it removed a different supply than the one they marked - fix the chain.
A technically correct trendline that did not affect the chain analysis does not need to be drawn.
Overextended trendline means price got so far from the line that it becomes irrelevant; you want price trading in the range of the line.
Homework on the wrong chart (1H, 15m, ICE) cannot be marked. It must be AUDUSD, FXCM broker, daily chart, saved on the daily before the meeting.
AUDUSD one-day chart, FXCM, from January 2003 to January 2004. First copy his zones onto your chart EXACTLY as he drew them so your distal lines match his and you can see what removed what.

You may use the chart for anything during the week, but before the meeting it must be saved on the daily AUDUSD FXCM chart. He is hard on the instructions because he cares and wants paying members to participate.

passages.h: Trade reviews: what he liked and disliked
passages.t: 1H supply in a bearish daily: in the daily breakdown he had a bad feeling - in tight price action where one zone is removed then another, the third zone more often than not fails because price is ranging. That is how he avoided the loss.

passages.h: Trade reviews: what he liked and disliked
passages.t: The same market was overextended, so even if taken, use aggressive trade management; a far target is chasing. A 15m zone without an explosive move: only the lower gap zone was the trade.

passages.h: Trade reviews: what he liked and disliked
passages.t: USDCAD 1R: great trade, but he prefers the entry just a little before the proximal line, giving wiggle room below, rather than far above.

passages.h: Trade reviews: what he liked and disliked
passages.t: Gold 1H/5m 1:3: good trade, but the line drawn was not a trendline because the low was not broken after the peak.

passages.h: Trade reviews: what he liked and disliked
passages.t: EURUSD loss: buying 5m demand while very overextended is risky; a 1H or 4H zone is better because a 1H turnaround means more than a 5m one. Basing candle as big as the move-away candle and a small gap - not a great zone.

passages.h: Trade reviews: what he liked and disliked
passages.t: 5m demand drawn including all basing candles: really a 15m or 1H zone on a 5m chart - not wrong, but the wrong timeframe; a smaller single-candle-basing zone would have been its own nice trade. CADJPY loss: good trade with liquidity, move away could be better - just a loss.

passages.h: Trade reviews: what he liked and disliked
passages.t: 15m winner off an old zone with no reaction at the liquidity: he would not have taken it unless it was a 4H set-and-forget.

passages.h: Trade reviews: what he liked and disliked
passages.t: S&P 1H and NASDAQ 4H all-time-high zone: removed the trendline, liquidity, great basing, great move away - a 10/10 zone that failed. Don't get frustrated; it happens. Trading an entire daily zone on NASDAQ is fine - a great trade too.
This week tests your emotions. Usually the week after a bad week is decent, but nothing is guaranteed.

Post trade reviews in the trade review channel; questions about them go in the questions channel to keep things clean. He will try to do trade reviews every Sunday because there is a lot to learn from them.
[01:00-05:50] Momentum vs trendline sketch and his note on the two exceptions to the drawing rules.

[07:00-20:30] Homework on AUDUSD 1D (FXCM), 2002: supply that removed a trendline, the wick-to-wick demand, the slid trendline start, a zone ended where it broke, updated trendlines from the most recent valley, the removal candle, an overextended line ended, and the single-candle demand. [21:00-37:00] Student homework (light and dark themes).
[37:30-48:50] Trade reviews from the Discord channel (USDCAD, gold, EURUSD, CADJPY, AUDCAD, NASDAQ).

passages.h: Chart: [01:24] Sketch on a blank chart: left, a steep climb with tiny peaks and valleys (momentum); right, a deep obvious peak and valley, then a break above the peak.
passages.t: The left one has peaks and valleys too, just not obvious and deep. He judges this visually, not by measuring. An obvious valley is not enough: price must then break the high before it.

passages.h: Chart: [05:39] AUDUSD 1D with his note "1. Confirmation in HTF ZONE When convinced by my HTF".
passages.t: The two times he draws zones outside the three rules: (1) confirmation inside a higher-timeframe zone he is convinced by, (2) macro charts (1 month and up). He still prefers the rules.

passages.h: Chart: [07:47] The supply that removed the uptrend line, with his curve tracing the move up into it.
passages.t: Rule 2 zone. The line was removed by the candle that closed fully below it, body and wick. "Move away here is decent, move away here is great."

passages.h: Chart: [08:29] The demand that removed that supply, drawn wick to wick (green).
passages.t: Wick to body would be far too small; wick to wick is a little smaller than the other zones but fine. If a zone looks too small, make it a little bigger.

passages.h: Chart: [10:37] A circle at the valley where the uptrend line starts, and an arrow along the line.
passages.t: From the lowest point the line cut through candles, so he keeps the second point and moves to the next lowest point. The start is not random.

passages.h: Chart: [11:19] The supply that price respected and then broke, ended with the remove tool where it was removed.
passages.t: Do not end a zone early or extend it past its removal: "I have seen many guys have sloppy-looking charts like that."

passages.h: Chart: [13:26] His curve from the old line's second touch point down to the most recent valley.
passages.t: Updated trendline: do not start from the bottom again. The old line's second touch point becomes the new line's first point; end the old line there.

passages.h: Chart: [14:09] A steep red line next to the black trendline from the recent valley.
passages.t: "That's momentum. It's completely different." The trendline has an obvious valley and a higher high.

passages.h: Chart: [14:51] The updated uptrend line where it was removed, with the large explosive candle below.
passages.t: He first picked the wrong candle: the removal is the first candle that does not touch the line with body or wick.

passages.h: Chart: [14:51] The updated uptrend line where it was removed, with the large explosive candle below.
passages.t: The big explosive candle gives a large zone; explosive move and stay-away candle are there but the space is small.

passages.h: Chart: [19:06] Circles at the most recent valley and the next touch for yet another updated uptrend line.
passages.t: Each new peak, valley and higher high means a new line from the newest valley: "this is where the trend lines get a little bit tricky."

passages.h: Chart: [19:49] The newest line, overextended, ended; the already-tested supply removed; the single-candle-basing demand below.
passages.t: An overextended line is ended, not continued. The demand is "single candle basing, absolutely love this zone".

passages.h: Chart: [40:20] Trade review: a student's gold 1h chart (OANDA) with a 1h supply at about 4,205 to 4,225, a demand at about 4,137 to 4,146, and a diagonal line drawn across the lows.
passages.t: A good 1:3 trade off the 1h supply, but the line is not a trendline: "we didn't break the low after the peak."
Supply that removed a trendline Why: Qualified by rule 2 (trendline removed on the full close below the line). Move away decent, not great. Result: Maybe break-even trade.
Demand that removed that supply, drawn wick to wick Why: Wick to body too small; wick to wick similar to other zone sizes; enlarge slightly if too small. Result: Valid zone in the chain.

Older standout explosive candle that removed a respected zone Why: Small candles not good enough; the explosive candle matches the other explosive moves. Result: Valid but old, would have made him nervous.

Large zone after the updated trendline was removed Why: Removed on the first candle not touching the line; explosive move and stay-away present, but little space. Result: Nice trade; pullback to another zone too.
Demand with several basing candles after a downtrend line removal Why: Use both green basing candles, exclude the red one; avoid an oversized zone. Result: Drawn as the zone.
Single-candle-basing demand removing tested supply Why: His favourite basing, nice spacing, explosive move away, removed supply. Result: Valid demand.
1H supply after previous demand taken out Why: Third zone in tight ranging price after two zones removed tends to fail; also overextended. Result: He avoided it; aggressive management if taken.
Demand, entry well above proximal Why: Great trade, but he enters just before the proximal for wiggle room. Result: 1R win.
1H supply in control, demand removed Why: Line drawn was not a trendline (low not broken after peak); supply not the best. Result: 1:3 win.
Gap demand while overextended Why: Day-trading timeframes while overextended is risky; basing candle the size of the move-away; small gap. Result: Loss.
Large demand including all basing candles Why: Really a 15m/1H zone on a 5m chart; smaller single-candle zone was its own trade. Result: 2.34R win.
Zone with liquidity Why: As good as it gets for liquidity; move away could be better. Result: Stop loss hit - good trade, just a loss.
Old supply, no reaction at the liquidity Why: Would only be better as a 4H set-and-forget. Result: 1:2 win, he would not have taken it.
All-time-high supply that removed the trendline Why: Liquidity, great basing, great move away: 10/10. Result: Failed - it happens.
Uptrend weekly, wide entry Why: Wide entries sometimes play out well. Result: 1:3.4 win.
Q: Was that a downside trendline? A: Yes - valley, peak and a lower low, so it would have been a downward trendline. He agreed after checking.

Q: What is an overextended trendline? A: When price gets too far away from the trendline, which makes it pretty much irrelevant. You want price trading in the range of the line; when it runs far away (check with the channel tool), end the line.
Q: Should I end the old trendline here? A: Don't end a trendline unless there is a new one. When there is an updated trendline, end the original one (about 95% of the time).
Q: Why is this explosive move not a zone? A: Because it accomplished nothing - it did not remove an opposing zone, a trendline or make an all-time high. That is momentum.
Q: How do I get the homework right? A: Go to AUDUSD, make sure the broker is FXCM and the chart is daily, and save it on the daily before the meeting. Message him if you need help.

Treating momentum (small peaks and valleys) as a trendline. Drawing a trendline after an obvious valley without the pivot high being broken. Missing updated trendlines, which cascades into missing the zones after them. Starting an updated trendline from the original bottom instead of the most recent valley. Picking a candle that still touches the trendline as the removal candle.

Extending removed zones or overextended trendlines across the chart (sloppy charts). Drawing zones that removed nothing. Drawing a 15m/1H-sized zone on a 5m chart. Entering far above the proximal line instead of just before it. Trading the third zone in tight ranging price after two zones were removed. Chasing overextended markets with 5m entries. Taking zones whose basing candle is as big as the move-away candle.
Doing homework on the wrong broker or timeframe. Getting frustrated when a 10/10 zone fails.

Is there an obvious peak and valley and was the pivot broken? Is there a newer trendline that replaces the old one? Does the trendline cut through any candles? Is price overextended from the trendline (channel tool)?

Did this zone remove a zone, a trendline or make an all-time high (or is it a valid exception)? Is the zone sized consistently and for the right timeframe? Is there space between the stay-away candle and the zone? Is this the third zone in a tight range after two removals? Is the market overextended, requiring aggressive management? Did the old zone get a reaction at the liquidity?

“We will get weeks like this a few times a year. It's the nature of the beast.” “This is not a trend line. This is momentum.” “What did it accomplish? Nothing. That's why we don't have them.” “I'm not choosing a random spot here to draw my trend line.” “Single candle basings are my favorite.” “This is like a 10 out of 10 zone. And it failed.” “I'm your teacher. I gotta be hard on you guys, and that's because I care.”

The two explicit exceptions to the 'remove a zone / trendline / all-time high' drawing rule: confirmation off a very convincing HTF zone after an aggressive one-candle pullback, and macro charts (1M, 3M, 6M, 12M) where any explosive move counts.
Trendline validity explicitly needs the pivot high (or low) BEFORE the obvious valley (peak) to be broken; he judges depth visually, no 50% measure.

Updated trendlines: end the old line (about 95% of the time) and start the new one from the most recent valley - the old second touchpoint becomes the new first point. End removed zones exactly where they were removed; extending them is sloppy.
Third zone in tight ranging price after two removals tends to fail - his reason for skipping a 1H supply.
A zone drawn including all basing candles on a 5m chart is really a 15m/1H zone - match zone size to the timeframe.
A 1H/4H turnaround means more than a 5m one when the market is overextended; enter just before the proximal for wiggle room.
Missed zones must still be drawn so later removals can be tracked; technically correct trendlines that don't affect the chain need not be drawn.

When a new step forms, move the handrail up to it. You climb stairs holding a handrail. When you reach a new landing, you grab the next rail that starts there. You do not walk back to the bottom to grab the first rail again. Trendlines work the same way: each new valley starts the new line.
The old line's second touch is like the landing between two staircases: the end of one rail and the start of the next.
A trendline needs an obvious peak and valley AND a break of the pivot before it. Small steps are momentum.
Updated line: start from the most recent valley (the old second touch) and end the old line.
Only two exceptions to the drawing rules: confirmation off a very convincing HTF zone, and macro charts (1 month and up).

passages.h: Step: Obvious valley is not enough
passages.t: A steep move with small peaks and valleys is momentum. A trendline needs an obvious, deep peak and valley.
After the obvious valley, price must break the pivot high before it. Now it is a trendline: from the lowest point to the valley, not cutting candles.
Price pulls back to a new, higher valley. Keep the line for now.

The high breaks again, so there is an updated trendline. Do not start from the bottom again: the old line's second touch (the most recent valley before) becomes the first point of the new line. End the old one.

passages.h: Step: Only end a line when there is a new one
passages.t: About 95% of the time, when an updated line forms, end or delete the old one. Do not end a trendline unless there is a new one, or price overextends far from it.
Momentum vs trendline? - Small steps = momentum. Obvious deep peak and valley + pivot break = trendline. Updated line starts where? - The most recent valley (the old line's second touch).
When do you end the old line? - When an updated line forms (about 95% of the time), or when it overextends.

Exception 1 to the drawing rules? - Confirmation off a very convincing higher-timeframe zone. Exception 2? - Macro charts (1M, 3M, 6M, 12M): any explosive move counts. Third zone in a tight range? - More often than not fails. Entering in an overextended market? - Manage aggressively; a far target is chasing. Where to place the entry? - Just a little before the proximal line.
After another rough October week, Kevin walks the AUDUSD daily chain analysis from January 2003 to January 2004.

The theme is not forcing zones: a demand candidate fails because, sized like his other zones, its stay-away candle touches the proximal line; two trendlines and a supply are removed with no zone at all; a supply that removed a trendline is drawn but was never a trade because it only qualified on that close.

He re-teaches attaching a trendline off a wick, checks overextension with the channel tool (a little overextended but hovering is fine), and shows the removal candle again. The homework review centres on trendlines: wick-only valleys, lines too large (weekly), momentum lines, unattached lines, a trendline extension that no student made, and when to start a line from the top.

Trade reviews stress matching the target to the higher timeframe (1:1 against it, 3:1 with it, 5:1 plus only with an HTF trendline AND an HTF zone in control), no break-of-structure confirmation, and basing as big as the move away. Next homework is AUDUSD daily on FXCM, January 2004 to January 2005. He may miss next week's meeting.
Only draw zones that remove an opposing zone, remove a trendline or make an all-time high/low.
A removed zone or trendline does not guarantee a zone: if no explosive move removed it, draw nothing.
Size a zone like the other zones on the chart; if at that size the stay-away candle touches the proximal line, it is not a zone. Do not combine two separate sets of basing into one zone.
A trendline needs a blatant peak, a blatant valley and a higher high (uptrend) or lower low (downtrend).

Attach the trendline at the lowest point, then adjust it so it does not cut through a wick. Valleys and peaks need candle bodies, not just one wick. Start a trendline from the top only when a line from the bottom would be too horizontal.
Keep a slightly overextended trendline if price keeps hovering around it; end it when price takes off.
A trendline is removed only by a candle that closes beyond it with body and wick clear of the line.
A zone that qualified only on a later close was not a trade before that close; draw it, don't count it as a trade. Do not draw very large (weekly-sized) trendlines on the daily homework.
The first candle of a zone's move away must be explosive; three ordinary candles are not an imbalance. Basing about the same size as the move away is not a zone.

Against the higher timeframe target 1:1; with it look for about 3:1; look for 5:1 plus only with an HTF trendline and an HTF zone in control. Target 1:1 on older zones. Do not use break of structure as confirmation. Leave the homework saved on AUDUSD, FXCM, daily.

passages.h: Where the analysis ends: garbage price action
passages.t: It reminds him of the USDCAD daily right now, one of the worst charts he has seen: since the trendline broke it is straight up, straight down, no explosive moves.
A valley without enough body is not a trendline ('little boo-boo trend line'). He wants bodies in the valleys, not a line resting on one wick here and one wick there.
Even if the valley had bodies, the line would start from the lowest point, not partway up.
Extending a line that got very overextended (and was not a trendline anyway) is a mistake; it becomes irrelevant.
Starting a trendline from up top is something he does only when a line from the bottom would be too horizontal. With a fair enough angle, start from the bottom.
Many students drew a very large trendline. It is not wrong, but it represents a weekly chart; he would not draw it. Close calls like this are borderline, not 'way off'.

Not a single student extended the one trendline that needed extending. It was a close call, but price kept coming back to it. A little overextended and hovering is fine; if price takes off, end the line. Missing that extension cost students the supply that removed it.

A valley and a peak without a lower low after them is not a downtrend line. Lines that are 'too momentum-y' are not trendlines. Attach your trendlines; a student's lines were floating, not attached. When a trendline is wrong, delete and fix everything after it.
Good: most students did not force zones in the empty areas. 'What did this remove?' A zone that accomplished nothing should not be on the chart: you have your rules, so follow them.
A student asked whether a 3-candle move can be an imbalance: no. The initial candle has to be the explosive move away; three ordinary candles are not enough. No 'little boo-boo basing candle zones'.

Demand candidate under a broken older supply Why: Too large over all basing (two sets), too small on one candle; at normal size the stay-away candle touches the proximal. Result: Not a zone; left off the chart.

Uptrend line from the recent valley Why: Blatant peak, valley and higher high; attached off the lowest red wick so it doesn't cut it; channel shows only slight overextension. Result: Kept and extended to its removal.
Tested supply removed Why: Nothing that looks like demand; the nearest candidate is basing, not a move away. Result: No zone.
Two downtrend lines removed Why: Removed on full closes above; no demand at the removal. Result: No zones.
Supply that removed the old uptrend line Why: Drawn even though tested; only qualified on the close below the line. Result: A zone but not a trade.
Demand at about 0.6447 to 0.6508 Why: Removed a downtrend line and an opposing supply. Result: No pullback; broken years later (2008).
Daily demand in control, H1 confirmation trades Why: Sideways, so no trend: about 3:1 target, not the high. Result: He broke even on both; some members won.
H1 demand that removed a trendline, daily bearish Why: Line drawn was not a trendline but the real one gives the same zone; 1:1 against the daily. Result: 1:1 win with a wide stop.
H1 demand that removed several supplies, daily bullish Why: With the trend, so a larger target; zone drawn larger than his. Result: 3:1 win.
H1 zone with a 5m break-of-structure entry Why: Not how they confirm; weird zone. Result: 1:1 win.
Demand with basing the size of the move away Why: Not a demand. Result: Win, but he would not count it.
Older zone after a liquidity trap Why: Older zone, so 1:1 only. Result: 1:1 win.
Single-candle-basing zone, daily supply above, wider stop Why: Great zone; wide position for a lower R:R target. Result: 1:2R win.
Zone that removed a trendline, with a wick and a quick return Why: Technically qualifies, low quality. Result: Win; he would not have traded it.
Trade after ignoring a daily demand removal (wick read as emotional) Why: The wick was on par; the demand was removed. Result: Loss, probably because of that.
Q: Is a peak and valley the same as a higher high? A: No. A peak and valley is an obvious, blatant peak and valley. Higher highs and higher lows are any little higher high; that is momentum.
Q: The 50% candle, not a CP? A: He wasn't sure what was meant; 50% candles can be part of a CP zone, yes.
Q: Can these 3 candles be considered an imbalance? A: No. It doesn't matter if it's 3 candles: the initial candle has to be an explosive move away.
Q: Do you have a video on chain analysis? A: No. That is what all the Sunday meetings are about: go to the Sunday Meeting tab and watch as many as you can.

Q: I didn't remove the daily demand when you did, because I saw the wick as emotional. A: Be careful: the wick is pretty much on par, just a little bigger. The demand was removed there, and the loss was probably due to that.
Q: How do I share the homework correctly? A: Open AUDUSD daily, copy the chart link, post it in the homework tab, and leave it on the daily (not the 1 hour or 15 minute).

Forcing a zone after every removal. Enlarging a too-small zone without checking that the stay-away candle still stays away. Combining two sets of basing candles. Drawing momentum lines as trendlines. Drawing trendlines on wick-only valleys. Starting a trendline partway up instead of from the lowest point. Not extending a trendline that was only slightly overextended. Extending a very overextended line.

Drawing downtrend lines without a lower low. Leaving trendlines unattached. Drawing zones that removed nothing. Calling three ordinary candles an imbalance. Little basing-candle zones and basing as big as the move away. Drawing a lower-timeframe zone far too large. Ignoring a removal because the wick looked emotional. Homework on the 15-minute chart. Low-detail screenshots and showing dollar amounts.
Following gurus who never seem to lose.

Did an explosive move actually remove the zone or trendline, or is there nothing to draw? Sized like the other zones, does the stay-away candle still stay away from the proximal? Am I combining two sets of basing?

Is the trendline built on obvious peaks and valleys with bodies, plus a higher high or lower low? Does the trendline cut through a wick, and is it attached? Would a line from the bottom be too horizontal (only then start from the top)? Is price only slightly overextended and hovering, or has it taken off? Did this zone qualify before the entry, or only on a later close? Is the basing smaller than the move away?
Am I trading with or against the higher timeframe, and does my target match? Is this an older zone (target 1:1)?
“Just because we have a zone removed, or a trend line removed, doesn't mean we have a zone.” “We're not gonna force any zones here.”

“Everything is technically a peak and valley. What we're looking for is these obvious peaks and valleys.” “We gotta have bodies in it as well.” “Whenever I see price action like this, it bums me out. It's absolute garbage.”

“Aggressive with trade management on this one, less aggressive with trade management on this one. That's what separates the beginners from the pros.” “We do not look for break of structure for confirmation.”

The size test for a candidate zone: enlarge it to the chart's normal zone size and check the stay-away candle; if it now touches the proximal line, there is no zone. Do not combine two separate sets of basing into one zone. Removals without an explosive move give no zone at all: rule 2 does not force a zone.

Trendline valleys need bodies, not a single wick; start from the top only when the line from the bottom would be too horizontal. A slightly overextended trendline that price keeps hovering around is kept and extended.
Target ladder by the higher timeframe: 1:1 against it, about 3:1 with it, 5:1 plus only with both an HTF trendline and an HTF zone in control.
Wider stop and entry with a bigger position for lower risk-reward targets; tighter stops for larger risk-reward situations.
