Raja's first filter: you never trade every supply and demand level, only strong zones. A zone is strong in two ways: (1) a CP (continuation, drop-base-drop or rally-base-rally) level whose leg-out closes beyond the opposite zone, or (2) an 'arrival zone' whose leg-out both crosses the trendline and removes the opposite zone.

On his EURUSD monthly chart he marks both: the 2014 drop-base-drop supply that broke the old demand, and the 2017 low demand whose rally crossed the descending trendline. Fresh strong zones are the only ones he trades 'set and forget' with limit orders.

Trade only strong zones; skip weak ones or treat them with the confirmation rule. A zone is strong when its leg-out closes beyond the opposite zone. Arrival zone = the move away crosses the trendline AND removes the opposite zone. Set and forget (limit order) is allowed only on fresh strong / arrival zones. Stop exactly at the distal line on daily zones; 3-4 pips beyond it on H4.
Removing one opposite zone (plus the trendline cross) is enough to make an arrival zone.
When price falls it leaves many supply levels. Most are not worth trading; you pick only the strong ones.
Strong zones can be traded; weak zones cannot be traded the same way (they need the confirmation rule, see the next lesson). There are two kinds of strong zone.

passages.h: Strong zone type 1: the CP level that removes the opposite zone
passages.t: When price drops it forms a CP (drop-base-drop) supply. If that zone's leg-out closes below the opposite (earlier) demand, the supply becomes a strong zone.

passages.h: Strong zone type 1: the CP level that removes the opposite zone
passages.t: He says 'CP or PCP' here. His basics class (Urdu course recording 1) defines it: a PCP is a CP level, or any departure, that removed the opposite zone; a plain CP is just a pause on the way to the destination. So a strong CP zone is a PCP.

passages.h: Strong zone type 1: the CP level that removes the opposite zone
passages.t: Why it is strong: price used that base to take out the opposing demand, which shows real sellers there.

passages.h: Strong zone type 1: the CP level that removes the opposite zone
passages.t: On the chart he boxes the whole basing area of the CP level as one rectangle, from the base highs (distal) to the base lows (proximal), and extends it to the right until price returns. Only a fresh strong zone can be traded set and forget.

passages.h: Strong zone type 2: the arrival zone
passages.t: An 'arrival zone' is a zone whose move away (a) crosses the trendline and (b) removes the opposite zone.

passages.h: Strong zone type 2: the arrival zone
passages.t: His EURUSD monthly example (11:04): a red descending trendline runs from the 2016 high down to the 2017 low. The demand box sits at that 2017 low, and the rally out of it crosses the line and removes the supply in its way. That demand is the arrival zone, and he bought it.

passages.h: Strong zone type 2: the arrival zone
passages.t: Arrival zones usually form at the peak or valley (the swing high or low). A CP level can also be an arrival zone, but not always.

EURUSD monthly (02:29): one box on the base of the 2014 drop. That drop closed below the earlier demand, so the supply 'took' the demand and became strong. Price returned to the box in early 2018, respected it and dropped. That was a set-and-forget sell limit.
A second, higher EURUSD case: the demand was removed by a supply, the supply became strong, and price reversed from it again.

Arrival example (EURUSD monthly, 11:04-11:18): the bottom box is the arrival demand (trendline crossed + supply removed). Price rallied from it into the top strong supply, dropped again, and is now moving between the two strong zones.

Set and forget means placing a buy limit or sell limit order at the zone and leaving it. Only two kinds of zone get this treatment: a strong (CP that removed the opposite zone) zone and an arrival zone, both on the first touch.

passages.h: From the Urdu recordings: entry, stop and arrival details
passages.t: Entry, stop, target (course 1 and 2): the proximal line is the limit entry, the distal line is the stop, and the take profit is the proximal line of the opposite zone. Wait for price to come back to the zone; do not jump in as it leaves (Feb 2025 class).

passages.h: From the Urdu recordings: entry, stop and arrival details
passages.t: Stop placement (course 2, 05:43): on a daily zone the stop goes exactly at the distal line, because a daily stop is already big (about 40 pips minimum, depending on the pair). On H4 put it 3-4 pips beyond the distal line. Market makers watch the daily and above and hunt the stops below that.

passages.h: From the Urdu recordings: entry, stop and arrival details
passages.t: One opposite zone is enough for an arrival zone: breaking the first opposite zone already breaks the structure (course 2, 11:23). Two removed zones is the separate direction-change rule.

passages.h: From the Urdu recordings: entry, stop and arrival details
passages.t: After an arrival zone the market usually does not reverse quickly; it runs first and comes back later. Market makers trade from one arrival zone to the other, while retail trades the lower timeframe in between (course 2, 12:00).

passages.h: From the Urdu recordings: entry, stop and arrival details
passages.t: A strong zone against the higher-timeframe direction gives one entry and is then removed; an arrival zone can give two or three entries (course 2, 34:00).

passages.h: From the Urdu recordings: entry, stop and arrival details
passages.t: If a supply hits a demand but cannot break it, both are weak and price will come back to break one of them. If the demand later breaks the supply, the demand becomes the strong zone and the supply the weak one (Feb 2025 class, 18:15).

Strong zone type 1: a drop-base-drop (CP) supply whose leg-out closes below the old demand. A fresh one gets a sell limit at the proximal line.
Strong zone type 2, the arrival zone: one leg-out crosses the trendline and removes the last demand. It usually forms at the peak.
His EURUSD monthly read: the drop-base-drop supply removed the old demand (strong CP zone); the 2017 low demand crossed the trendline and removed the last supply (arrival zone).

Trading every supply and demand level a falling or rising market leaves behind. Using set and forget on zones that never removed an opposite zone. Entering as price leaves the zone instead of waiting for it to return.

Did this zone's move away remove (close beyond) an opposite zone? Did it also cross the trendline (arrival zone)? Is it fresh (not touched since it formed)? If all yes: limit order at the proximal line, stop beyond the distal line.

“We cannot use all supply and demand levels; we only choose the strong zone for the trade.” “Arrival means: crossed the trendline plus removed the opposite zone.” “Set and forget means buy limit order and sell limit order.”
“Market makers trade between two arrival zones; retail trades the low time frame in between.”
Kevin also requires a zone to be 'qualified' (it removes an opposing zone or a trendline). Raja splits this into two named types: CP strong zone and arrival zone (trendline AND opposite zone).
Seiden does not count a DBD/RBR base as a real zone. Raja trades CP (continuation) levels as strong zones when they remove the opposite zone.
Raja links the order type to zone strength: limit orders only for fresh strong or arrival zones. Seiden decides with an odds-enhancer score.
PCP, as defined in his Urdu basics class: any CP that removed the opposite zone. That settles the 'CP or PCP' wording in this lesson.

Trade only the strong zones: the ones that knocked out the opposite zone. Two teams play tug of war over a line on the ground. Lots of kids pull for a moment and then let go, so those spots mean nothing. But one team pulled so hard that the other team fell over the line. That spot shows where the strong team stands. Raja only trades spots like that.
A strong zone is the team that pulled the other team over the line. A weak zone is a team that pulled a bit and then stopped.

Price leaves many zones. Raja trades only strong ones. Strong = the move away closed beyond the opposite zone. Arrival = it also crossed the trendline. Only a fresh strong or arrival zone gets set and forget (a limit order you leave alone).
Price rose, paused and rose again. That pause is a demand zone. Raja draws it over the whole basing candles, wick to wick. Markets leave many zones like this, and most are not worth trading.

passages.h: Step: A drop-base-drop: the CP level
passages.t: Price turned down, paused for three small candles and kept dropping. A pause in the middle of a move is a CP (continuation) level. Here it is a CP supply.

passages.h: Step: The leg-out removes the demand
passages.t: Watch the drop leave the CP supply. A candle closes below the old demand. The supply has removed the opposite zone, so real sellers are sitting there. That makes it a strong zone.
The zone is strong and fresh (not touched yet). Raja puts a sell limit at the proximal line (the bottom of a supply), a stop beyond the distal line (the top), and walks away.

passages.h: Step: First touch: price respects it
passages.t: Price comes back for the first time, fills the sell limit and drops away. The strong zone did its job.
Which zones does Raja trade? - Only strong zones. Most zones are skipped. Strong zone (type 1)? - A CP zone whose move away closed beyond the opposite zone.

Arrival zone (type 2)? - Its move away crossed the trendline AND removed the opposite zone. Where do arrival zones usually form? - At the peak: the swing high or swing low. Set and forget means? - A buy limit or sell limit order left at the zone.
Which zones get set and forget? - Only fresh strong zones and fresh arrival zones, on the first touch. Where does the limit order go? - At the proximal line. Stop beyond the distal line.

Every zone that is not fresh and strong is treated as weak and traded only with the confirmation rule. To confirm, drop to a lower timeframe inside the higher-timeframe zone and wait for price to cross that timeframe's trendline and remove the last opposite zone. Then trade the new CP or valley/peak zone that did it.

His charts show this on GBPJPY (monthly demand retested twice, confirmed on H4) and CHFJPY (weekly supply retested). The weak types he names are retested, inheritance, flip and overlap zones. He says most S&D traders lose because they only know set and forget.

A retested zone is always considered weak; use confirmation only. Confirmation = on a lower timeframe, the trendline is crossed AND the last opposite zone is removed. Then trade the new CP or valley/peak zone. Monthly zone: touch 1 set and forget, touches 2-3 confirmation, touch 4 expect a break. Daily/weekly zone: touch 1 set and forget, touch 2 confirmation, touch 3 risky.

Inheritance, flip and overlap zones get confirmation only. Confirmation can also be: price returns into the zone and closes back across the proximal line; enter there with the stop beyond the zone. A flip area without a clean zone is confirmation only.
The first touch of a fresh strong zone can be set and forget. The second touch is a retest: no set and forget, only confirmation.
Monthly zones: 1st touch set and forget, 2nd confirmation, 3rd confirmation, and the 4th touch usually breaks the zone.
Daily and weekly zones: 1st set and forget, 2nd confirmation, and the 3rd is risky (price can break it). Trade it only if confirmation appears.
A retest on the higher timeframe often shows as a long wick ('wicky candle') into the zone.

If the zone is on the monthly or weekly chart, go down to the weekly, daily or H4 chart. On the lower timeframe price is still falling into the demand and making new supply levels. Wait for it to (1) cross the lower-timeframe trendline and (2) remove the last opposite supply zone.
Before that break, price usually creates a new CP level or a valley (or peak) level. That new zone removed the supply, so it is strong: you can use it with a limit order and hold.

GBPJPY: the screenshot he sent students says: 'waiting for confirmation coz GJ already retested 2 times, so technically we can't use set and forget rules here but we can use confirmation rules ... ' On H4 price crossed the trendline and removed the last supply; the new demand held and the move ran about 600-800 pips. On the monthly it only shows as a wick into the purple demand box.

CHFJPY weekly (the captions only say 'CHF'; the chart header reads CHFJPY): a red supply box that had already been used. He waited: trendline crossed, last demand removed by a supply, price respected that supply and dropped about 400 pips. Price is back at the box now, so it again gets confirmation only.
Two supply zones at a top: #1 crossed the trendline but could NOT remove the demand below; #2 then removed that demand. #2 is the strong zone.

#1 'gave all its power' to create #2. He calls #1 an inheritance zone. It is weak, even though it sits on the peak (high-curve area). On his EURUSD board (13:56) he numbers the two boxes 1 and 2 and writes about 10% beside the weak one.

In his estimate an inheritance zone has about a 10% chance of holding and a 90% chance of breaking. Price may hit it once, give a confirmation the second time, and break it the third time. When it breaks, price often breaks the top supply as well.
His 15:38 sketch: a rising market making higher highs; each peak supply is a flag in price-action terms. Inheritance zones are found mostly at these higher highs and lower lows.

EURUSD (16:05-16:43): a demand that could not remove the previous supply was weak. Price removed it, and the new supply that did so became strong. On the weekly he expects a dip to the weekly demand before buying.
A broken resistance becomes support (and the reverse). In S&D he calls these flip areas or flip zones: a zigzag area where price can reverse.
Price often forms a CP level near the old support or resistance. You can trade that CP, but a flip zone uses the confirmation rule.

In plain words (live session, Mar 27): price makes a higher low, and each new leg comes back to the previous higher-low area, so resistance becomes support and back again. On a clean chart price keeps hitting the same area. If no proper zone sits at the flip, use confirmation only; otherwise the lower timeframe gives a zone at the next area.
If a supply forms inside an old demand area (or a demand inside an old supply area), it is an overlap zone. Overlap is a weak area: confirmation only, never set and forget.
Set and forget: strong zone (removed the opposite zone) and arrival zone (crossed the trendline and removed the opposite zone).
Confirmation rule: weak zones, retested zones, inheritance zones, flip areas and overlap zones.
An intraday trader who can sit at the screen may apply confirmation even on strong zones. He calls confirmation 'safe trading'.

passages.h: From the live sessions: confirmation and weak zones
passages.t: The simple form of confirmation on a weak zone (Feb 18): the market must properly leave the zone, come back, and only then do you trade it.

passages.h: From the live sessions: confirmation and weak zones
passages.t: A second kind of confirmation without going lower (Apr 7 and Apr 30): let price come into the zone; when it turns and crosses back over the proximal line (upward for a demand, downward for a supply), enter at market with the stop beyond the zone. The stop is a little bigger than a limit order's, but it is much safer, and if you can watch the screen you do not miss the trade.

passages.h: From the live sessions: confirmation and weak zones
passages.t: Meshing marks a zone as tested (Feb 18): if price pokes a few pips through a zone and chops there, it is no longer fresh. The market usually taps a zone 1, 2, 3, 4 times while meshing and then crosses it.

passages.h: From the live sessions: confirmation and weak zones
passages.t: Overlap in practice: a demand with strong imbalance is still weak if it was built inside a supply level (2022 meeting); a CP supply on a descending trendline that sits on an old demand is an overlap (Apr 7). The student admitted most of his mistakes came from overlap zones.

passages.h: From the live sessions: confirmation and weak zones
passages.t: During news (Apr 30) the market mostly respects valleys, while CP and PCP levels get blown through. Thick base candles take longer to break, even when the zone is only an overlap (course 4).

[04:28-07:28] GBPJPY monthly board sketch: a monthly box on top and one at the bottom. Price falls into the bottom box; inside it a small H4 zigzag crosses its trendline (marked x) and the trade goes back up. He circles '90' for the 90% of traders who only use set and forget.
[07:50-08:52] Opens WhatsApp and shows the GBPJPY monthly screenshot he sent students: purple demand box with the 'waiting for confirmation' note.

[09:03-09:59] GBPJPY monthly then H4: the H4 V-bottom inside the monthly box, the trendline cross and the run higher. [10:36-10:41] Back on the monthly, the whole H4 move is just a wick into the box. [11:04-11:18] EURUSD monthly with the arrival zone (see the previous lesson).
[13:56] EURUSD board: zones 1 and 2 at the top, with the weaker inheritance zone crossed out and marked about 10%. [15:38] Higher-high zigzag sketch (flags) to show where inheritance zones form.
[16:05-16:43] EURUSD monthly and weekly: weak demand removed, new strong supply, dip to weekly demand expected.
[20:24-21:18] CHFJPY weekly screenshot (red supply box) and the CHFJPY monthly and daily charts: retested zone, confirmation only.

passages.h: Chart: [06:28] Board sketch on GBPJPY monthly: top and bottom monthly boxes
passages.t: Price falls from the top box into the bottom box. Inside the bottom box the lower timeframe crosses its trendline: that is the confirmation.

passages.h: Chart: [07:28] Same sketch finished: the H4 zigzag, the x at the break, circled 90
passages.t: 90% of S&D traders lose because they only use set and forget. The second touch of a monthly zone is a retest, so he waits for confirmation.

passages.h: Chart: [08:25] The GBPJPY monthly screenshot he sent students
passages.t: Purple demand box at the bottom; his note: already retested 2 times, so confirmation rules only. 'First let market leave this area, then we can safe trading.'

passages.h: Chart: [09:03] GBPJPY monthly with the demand box
passages.t: The zone had already been used twice, so no limit order.

passages.h: Chart: [09:59] GBPJPY H4 inside the monthly box
passages.t: H4 forms a V-bottom, crosses its trendline and removes the last supply. The new demand that did it is bought; the move ran about 600-800 pips.
On the monthly the whole H4 confirmation only shows as a wick into the box.

passages.h: Chart: [13:56] EURUSD board: zones 1 and 2 at the peak
passages.t: Zone 1 crossed the trendline but did not remove the demand; zone 2 did. Zone 1 is the inheritance zone: about 10% hold, 90% break.
Each peak in a rising market is a flag in price-action terms. Inheritance zones form mostly at these peaks.
A demand that could not remove the previous supply was weak and was broken. The supply that broke it is now the strong zone.
He expects price to dip to the weekly demand before buying (about 90% in his words).

passages.h: Chart: [20:50] CHFJPY weekly screenshot: red supply box, price back at it
passages.t: A retested zone: he told students he was still waiting for confirmation. Earlier the confirmation (trendline cross + demand removed) gave about 400 pips.
The lower timeframe where the confirmation would appear.

passages.h: Chart: [17:35] USDPLN daily (live session, Mar 27): boxes at the earlier areas price keeps coming back to along the descending trendline
passages.t: Flip area: the previous higher low or lower high gets revisited each leg. No clean zone at the flip: confirmation only.
Retest count on a daily or weekly zone: 1st touch set and forget, 2nd confirmation, 3rd risky. Monthly zones get one more confirmation touch before they usually break.
GBPJPY as he showed it: the monthly demand had been touched twice, so he waited for H4 to cross its trendline and remove the last supply, then bought the new demand.
Inheritance zone: supply #1 crossed the line but left the demand standing. #2 removed it, so #2 is strong and #1 is weak, even though it is on the peak.
Overlap zone (a supply formed inside an old demand) and flip zone (old resistance acting as support): both are weak areas for the confirmation rule.

Using only set and forget: he blames this for '90% of S&D traders' losses'. Treating an inheritance zone at the peak as strong because of where it sits. Setting a limit order on a supply that formed inside an old demand (overlap). Treating a zone that price has already poked through and meshed in as fresh.

How many times has this zone been touched (and on what timeframe)? Is it an inheritance, flip or overlap zone? If weak: on the LTF, has price crossed the trendline? Has the last opposite LTF zone been removed? Trade the new CP / valley (peak) zone that did the removing. Has price already poked into this zone and meshed there (then it is tested)?
“First time we can use set and forget, but the second time it is a retested zone.” “Retested zone is always considered as a weak zone.” “Confirmation is actually safe trading.”
Kevin also separates set-and-forget zones from confirmation zones and has two confirmation entry methods. Raja's confirmation is specifically 'LTF trendline crossed + last opposite zone removed'.
Seiden counts touches as an odds enhancer (fresh is best). Raja gives fixed counts per timeframe (monthly 4th touch breaks, daily/weekly 3rd touch risky).
'Inheritance zone' is Raja's own term. Neither Kevin nor Seiden name a weak peak zone that 'gave its power' to a later zone.
The overlap zone (a zone born inside an opposite zone) is similar to the Rulebook's flip / void discussions, but Raja simply says: confirmation only.

Weak zones need proof first: line crossed, last opposite zone removed. A bridge held a heavy truck once. The next day it has cracks, so you do not just drive over it. You send a small car first and watch. If the small car makes it across safely, then you go. Raja does the same with a zone that has been used before.
A retested zone is a cracked bridge. The confirmation rule is the small test car you send across first.

First touch of a fresh strong zone: set and forget. Any retest is weak. Confirmation: on a lower timeframe, the trendline is crossed AND the last opposite zone is removed. Weak types get confirmation only: retested, inheritance, flip and overlap zones.
This demand made a strong move up. On the first touch a buy limit worked and price bounced. That was the zone's fresh, set and forget trade.

passages.h: Step: Touch 2 is a retest, so it is weak
passages.t: Price comes back a second time. Raja says a retested zone is always weak. No limit order now. On a daily or weekly zone the third touch is risky, and on a monthly zone the fourth touch usually breaks it.

passages.h: Step: Zoom in to the lower timeframe
passages.t: Drop to a lower timeframe inside the zone. Price is still falling: it follows a down trendline and leaves supply levels. The last one is the zone to watch.
A rally closes above the trendline and then closes above the last supply. That is the confirmation. The new demand that did it removed the opposite zone, so it is strong.
Now a buy limit goes on the new strong demand, stop under it. On the higher timeframe all of this looks like one wick into the zone.

Is a retested zone strong or weak? - Always weak. Confirmation only. Monthly zone touch count? - 1st set and forget, 2nd and 3rd confirmation, 4th usually breaks. Daily / weekly touch count? - 1st set and forget, 2nd confirmation, 3rd risky.
Confirmation rule? - On a lower timeframe: trendline crossed AND last opposite zone removed.

Inheritance zone? - A peak zone that crossed the line but could not remove the opposite zone. Weak. Overlap zone? - A zone born inside an old opposite zone. Weak, confirmation only. Flip zone? - Old resistance turned support (or the reverse). Confirmation only.

Raja's rule for when a timeframe has really turned. Price must cross that timeframe's trendline AND remove two opposite zones. One removed zone may only be a pullback. With two removed, direction has changed on that timeframe and price heads for the higher-timeframe strong or arrival zone.
His board shows it both ways (an up leg losing two demands, a down leg losing two supplies), and his gold trade shows the entry: the valley demand after the downtrend line was crossed.

Direction change on a timeframe = trendline crossed + TWO opposite zones removed. One opposite zone removed is not yet a direction change. After a change, target the HTF strong or arrival zone in the new direction. Enter on the retest at the new CP level or peak/valley level.
Open trade against the move: first opposite zone gone -> stop behind the second; second gone -> close.
Setting: two HTF strong or arrival zones, one above and one below. On the lower timeframe price is trending and following its trendline.

On his board the up leg leaves a stack of demand boxes along the uptrend line. At the top, price crosses the line and removes the two highest demands (he crosses them out). The down leg then leaves supply boxes, and at the bottom price removes two of those and turns up.
If price crosses the trendline and removes one opposite zone, that is 'perfect' but not enough.

If it crosses the trendline and removes the #1 AND #2 opposite zones, direction has changed on that particular timeframe. Target: price then usually goes to the opposite HTF strong zone or arrival zone.
EURUSD weekly (02:11): price removed two demand levels and then turned down. It later hit an arrival zone (crossed the trendline + removed the opposite zone) that is a monthly zone.
When only one demand is removed and a second demand is still below, there is still a chance for longs. If the second is removed, the next target is the zone below.

Gold daily 2018 (05:19): he drew the downtrend line from the high, a supply box across the base and a small demand box at the valley. He placed a buy limit on that valley demand. Price retested it two or three times, then crossed the line and removed supply #1 and #2. He shared the trade (Instagram post at 05:43) and was still holding it.
Student Q: 'Do you trade only when two zones are removed?' Yes: wait for two removals, then expect the move.
Wait for a retest. Price usually makes two pushes (one removing each zone). The retest usually comes at a CP level or a peak/valley level, which is where you enter.
In the gold trade the entry zone was the valley demand at the low, under the supply that was later removed.

passages.h: From the live sessions and Urdu recordings
passages.t: A trendline cross and a direction change are two different things (Feb 10). Direction changes only with the cross plus two opposite zones removed. If price crosses and even closes beyond the line but does not remove the opposite zone, it goes back (Mar 5): supply and demand is the main thing, the trendline is a tool for direction and safety.

passages.h: From the live sessions and Urdu recordings
passages.t: One opposite zone removed with the trendline crossed is still the same trend. When the second goes too, the old trendline is finished and you stop using it (course 3, 01:05).

passages.h: From the live sessions and Urdu recordings
passages.t: Where the new move goes: back to where the move started, the opposite higher-timeframe arrival zone (course 3, 01:45; Feb 10). When the market crosses an ascending trendline it usually goes to the zone on the descending side, not to the nearby CP (Feb 10).

passages.h: From the live sessions and Urdu recordings
passages.t: Every timeframe has its own direction (Feb 10). His example: NZDCHF M5 crossed its trendline and removed two opposite zones, so M5 headed up to the H1 zone (or else the H4 one), with low-curve buys and the TP there. He also showed EURNZD monthly, GBPCAD H4 and NOKSEK daily (likely in that order).

passages.h: From the live sessions and Urdu recordings
passages.t: Risk rule for an open trade (Feb 10): when the first opposite zone breaks, move the stop behind the second; when the second breaks, close at a loss, because price is now heading back to where it started. The student had held a trade hoping for the HTF zone and gave back about 200 pips of profit. Course 3 says the same: most S&D traders lose here, and news can remove the reversal zone you are hoping for.

passages.h: From the live sessions and Urdu recordings
passages.t: Gold (course 3): on the weekly the trendline was crossed and the opposite zone removed (arrival zone); the first supply broke, then the second, and a new bullish trendline started. His own gold buy was retested once and twice before the break.

[00:00-01:30] XAUUSD monthly, then a board drawing over it: HTF box on top and bottom, an uptrend line with demand boxes, the top two crossed out, the drop, two supplies at the bottom right, and the rally that removes them. [02:11] EURUSD weekly: the 2018 turn after two demands were removed.
[02:43-04:37] XAUUSD daily and weekly: the move up after the turn and the weekly demand box (the arrival area) that was retested.

[04:49-05:19] XAUUSD daily 2018: downtrend line, supply box and the valley demand box he bought. [05:43-05:53] His Instagram post of the same gold trade, with the trendlines and the box. [06:27-07:18] Quick look at EURSEK, GBPSGD and GBPTRY daily charts before the next topic.
The chart he uses as a canvas for the rule.

passages.h: Chart: [01:30] Board: trendline crossed + two opposite zones removed
passages.t: Up leg: demand boxes along the uptrend line; the top two are crossed out when price breaks down. Down leg: two supply boxes at the bottom right are removed by the rally. The HTF boxes at top and bottom are the targets.
Price removed demand #1 and #2 and then turned down toward the monthly arrival zone.
The trend after the change: price runs toward the HTF zone.

passages.h: Chart: [03:42] XAUUSD daily with a box at the breakout
passages.t: The retest area: a weekly-timeframe zone (an arrival-type zone) that price came back to.

passages.h: Chart: [04:14] XAUUSD weekly with the demand box
passages.t: The weekly zone price retested before rallying.
The fall into the 2018 low that he bought.

passages.h: Chart: [05:19] XAUUSD daily 2018: downtrend line, supply box, valley demand
passages.t: He bought the valley demand with a buy limit. Price retested it 2-3 times, then crossed the line and removed supply #1 and #2.

passages.h: Chart: [05:43] His Instagram post of the gold trade
passages.t: Same setup shared with students: trendlines and the entry box.
The rising line under the lows and the box where he entered.

passages.h: Chart: [04:00] XAUUSD daily (Urdu course 3): the descending trendline crossed out of the base boxes, then the rally
passages.t: Trendline crossed, first and then second opposite zone removed: the trendline changed. The new move runs toward the opposite HTF zone.
His board, redrawn: the up leg loses demand #1 and #2 (direction turns down), the down leg loses supply #1 and #2 (turns up). Targets are the HTF zones.
Gold daily 2018: downtrend line, valley demand bought with a buy limit, retests, then the supply above is removed and the trade runs.
Calling a reversal after only one opposite zone is removed. Selling or buying against the move before the second zone has gone.
Holding the old-direction trade after two opposite zones are removed, hoping the HTF zone will save it.

Which timeframe am I judging? Has its trendline been crossed (on a close)? How many opposite zones have been removed: one or two? Where is the next HTF strong / arrival zone (the target)? Is there a retest CP / peak-valley zone to enter?

“If market removes the second zone, it means market just changed their direction on this particular time frame.” “We wait for the market to remove the two demand levels, then the market can drop.” “Trendline cross and direction change are two different things.”
Kevin's 'qualification' needs one opposing zone or a trendline to be removed. Raja's direction change needs the trendline AND two opposite zones.
Seiden says trends start and end at S/D levels and does not count zones removed. Raja's two-zone count is a concrete, mechanical trend-change test.

A turn is real only after the line breaks and two opposite zones fall. A river flows downhill. One day you see a little water splash back up a rock. That is not the river turning, it is just a splash. But if the water climbs over two rocks in a row, the river really is flowing a new way. Raja waits for that second rock. One removed zone is a splash. Two removed zones is the river changing course.
Direction changes on a timeframe when price crosses its trendline AND removes two opposite zones. One removed zone may only be a pullback.
After the change, enter on the retest (CP or peak/valley zone) and target the HTF strong or arrival zone.

passages.h: Step: An uptrend and its line
passages.t: Price is rising along its trendline and leaves two demand zones on the way: #2 lower and #1 higher. Far below sits an HTF strong demand.

passages.h: Step: The line is crossed on a close
passages.t: A big candle closes below the trendline. That is the first condition, but it is not enough on its own.

passages.h: Step: Zone #1 removed: maybe a pullback
passages.t: Price closes below demand #1. Raja calls this good, but still not a change. Demand #2 is below, so buyers still have a chance.
After a small pause (a CP supply), price closes below demand #2 too. Line crossed plus two zones removed: direction has changed on this timeframe.

passages.h: Step: Sell the retest, aim for the HTF zone
passages.t: Price usually makes two pushes and then retests. The retest comes at the CP level. Sell there, with the target at the HTF strong demand below.

Direction change rule? - Trendline crossed + TWO opposite zones removed. Only one zone removed means? - Maybe just a pullback. Not a change yet. Target after a change? - The HTF strong or arrival zone in the new direction.
Where is the entry after a change? - On the retest, at the new CP level or peak/valley level. Which timeframe changed? - Only the one whose line and two zones broke.

Between two HTF (monthly/weekly) strong zones, the top 0-25% is the high curve (sellers only) and the bottom 0-25% is the low curve (buyers only). On his gold chart the curve lines are drawn from the proximal line of the supply box to the proximal line of the demand box (the red lines at 25%, 50% and 75%). Use lower-timeframe demand only in the low curve and supply only in the high curve.
A trendline break counts only on a candle close. Trail the stop to each new fresh zone, because price may turn before the TP.
Map the high curve and low curve between two HTF strong zones (0-25% bands, 50% line). Buy only in the low curve and sell only in the high curve; ignore LTF zones on the wrong side.

A trendline is crossed only when a candle closes beyond it (wait for the next candle to open). Trail the stop to each new fresh zone; drop a fixed TP when the target zone is weak. Close the position if price removes two opposite zones against you. A demand in the high curve, or a supply in the low curve, is not tradable. Draw the trendline through the two latest valleys/peaks and do not keep redrawing it.
Treat the 4th touch of a trendline as a likely break.
Take the two HTF strong or arrival zones (monthly or weekly) above and below price. On his board (08:22) these are two boxes with a line across the middle.

Mark the 50% line in the middle and the 25% lines near each zone. On XAUUSD daily his red lines sit at about 1221, 1255 and 1298, i.e. 25/50/75% of the space between the demand box top (about 1175) and the supply box bottom (about 1335). So the curve is measured proximal to proximal.
You can use a Fibonacci retracement to measure it, but he prefers to draw it manually ('I do not trust indicator things').

High curve (top 0-25%) is for sellers only; low curve (bottom 0-25%) is for buyers only. On the lower timeframe, demand levels near the HTF supply (in the high curve) must not be used. Suppliers sit there ('market makers sit there') and you can lose money. Likewise, do not use supplies in the low curve.
In the low curve, wait for a very good opportunity, especially a daily demand level, and buy.

Gold (daily, 12:25): the monthly supply box was tested three times (2016, 2017, 2018) and broke on the fourth (2019). Before that break price dipped from the supply to the 50% line, and he bought from the 50% area.

passages.h: Trailing the stop to fresh zones
passages.t: Price does not have to reach the opposite zone or the TP; it can turn before it. So after buying, each time a new fresh demand forms he moves the stop loss to that new zone.

passages.h: Trailing the stop to fresh zones
passages.t: If price is near the high curve and the top zone is weak, he removes the fixed TP and keeps trailing. If the stop is hit, he still closes with good pips; if price removes the top zone, he holds long term. If price removes two opposite zones against your position, close it.

passages.h: When is the trendline really crossed?
passages.t: The cross must be by a candle that closes beyond the line: an engulfing / departure candle, i.e. a big bullish (or bearish) candle.

passages.h: When is the trendline really crossed?
passages.t: Price often makes a fake signal: it pierces the line, leaves a wick, and closes back on the original side.

passages.h: When is the trendline really crossed?
passages.t: So always wait for the close, and for the next candle to start. Only then can you say price can change direction and head for the opposite level.

passages.h: When is the trendline really crossed?
passages.t: For a bearish break the candle must close below the trendline. Then use any fresh zone for the trade.

Monthly (16:05): he bought from one arrival zone (the 2017 low) and plans to sell from the top arrival zone (the 2018 high box), which is the TP. The monthly arrival supply is the box where price crossed the red rising trendline and removed the demand.

Weekly (16:35-18:08): price is still about 500 pips from that TP and needs buyer power. There is a weekly demand box and a rising trendline below, so a dip to the weekly demand and a buy from there is likely (he calls the return a realignment).
Daily (17:22): one daily demand has been removed so far; the next target below is the weekly demand.

A student was stopped out selling a 4H zone (18:46). Raja: that supply formed inside a previous demand, so it was an overlap / weak area and not a clear zone. The H4 supply box higher up was the better sell-limit area. For an intraday trader he suggests a first TP about 60 pips away, then holding the rest.

passages.h: Curve and trendline-close details from the live sessions
passages.t: Draw the curve with the Fibonacci retracement, 0 to 100 with the 50% line (Feb 10, on XAUUSD monthly and daily); hand-drawn lines work too.

passages.h: Curve and trendline-close details from the live sessions
passages.t: Buyers may buy up to the 50% line (course 3 says even the 75% area, likely), but a demand found in the high curve cannot be used: price can drop at any time without reaching the supply. The same holds for a supply in the low curve.

passages.h: Curve and trendline-close details from the live sessions
passages.t: Nested curves (Feb 10, GBPNZD): the daily can sit in the weekly's low curve (a daily buy area) while the weekly sits in the monthly's high curve. Then wait for a break before trading the bigger move.

passages.h: Curve and trendline-close details from the live sessions
passages.t: Gold daily (Feb 10): a zone usually breaks on the 4th tap, but here the 4th visit went to the 50% line first and then entered: that area was for selling, not buying.

passages.h: Curve and trendline-close details from the live sessions
passages.t: HTF supply already hit once or twice: do not buy a lower-timeframe demand under it. Let the lower timeframe remove the HTF zone first; then its new zone is strong and usable (course 3, 16:09).

passages.h: Curve and trendline-close details from the live sessions
passages.t: The trendline-close rule in full (Feb 10, low-TF class): a long, full OHLC candle must close beyond the line. Small candles drifting through are a fake signal. A big candle that has crossed but not yet closed can still leave a long wick and reverse. Even after a full close, if a demand sits right below, no sell limit: wait for that demand to break or take a confirmation entry.

passages.h: Curve and trendline-close details from the live sessions
passages.t: Sideways crosses with small candles: wait for one big candle; if price simply runs far, the cross is clear anyway (Feb 18). A wick-only poke through the line does not matter unless price closes back inside the departure (Jun 25).

Draw it through the two most recent valleys (uptrend) or peaks (downtrend) (low-TF class; Feb 10). Do not keep redrawing it with every new swing; keep the old one, and add an aggressive line only for impulses (Feb 10).
Draw a new trendline only after the new low or high has formed (Jun 25). Do not over-draw; use what is easy for you (course 5).

Touches: the 1st, 2nd and 3rd touch of a trendline are fine; the 4th is very risky and usually breaks it (Mar 5, Mar 13). A line tested 3, 4, 5 times is very weak: direction can change any time, so wait for a new valley (Jun 25).
The best demand sits just above the trendline. A zone 25-30 pips away from the line often gets broken when price comes down to hit the trendline (Jun 25).
[07:18-08:22] GBPTRY daily, then GBPTRY monthly as a blank canvas: two boxes (top and bottom) and a line across the middle for the 50%.
[12:25-12:27] XAUUSD daily: monthly supply box above, demand box below, and three red lines at 25/50/75%. Price tested the supply three times, dipped to the 50% line, then broke out.

[13:04-13:41] XAUUSD monthly: the same two boxes on the monthly candles and the 2019-2020 breakout. [15:05] XAUUSD monthly zoomed out: the range is a small part of the larger trend. [16:05] EURUSD monthly: supply box at the 2018 high and the red trendline it broke.

[16:35-18:08] EURUSD weekly and daily: weekly demand box, rising trendline, daily supply on top and the long vertical measure to the weekly demand. [18:46] EURUSD H4: the clean supply box above and the small overlap box the student sold.
The pair he uses to start the curve topic.

passages.h: Chart: [08:22] Board: two HTF boxes and the middle line
passages.t: Top box and bottom box are the HTF strong zones; the line is the 50%. Top 0-25% for sellers, bottom 0-25% for buyers.

passages.h: Chart: [12:25] XAUUSD daily with monthly boxes and red curve lines
passages.t: Red lines at about 1221 / 1255 / 1298 = 25 / 50 / 75% between the box edges. The supply held three tests and broke on the fourth; he bought the dip to 50%.
The demand box at the 2016/2018 lows marks the low curve.

passages.h: Chart: [13:05] XAUUSD monthly with the same boxes
passages.t: On the monthly the range is clear: supply above, demand below, curve lines between.
Only demand levels are used in the low curve and only supply levels in the high curve.
After the break, the old range sits under a strong trend.

passages.h: Chart: [16:05] EURUSD monthly: arrival supply box and red trendline
passages.t: Monthly TP: the top arrival zone. He bought the bottom arrival zone.

passages.h: Chart: [16:35] EURUSD weekly: demand box and rising trendline
passages.t: About 500 pips still to the monthly TP; buyers are needed, so a dip to this weekly demand is likely.
Daily supply on top, weekly demand below, and the vertical box measuring the room.

passages.h: Chart: [18:08] EURUSD weekly with the daily zones
passages.t: Two trendlines: the steep one is already crossed, the slower one still holds.

passages.h: Chart: [18:46] EURUSD H4: the student's sell
passages.t: The small box formed inside the previous demand: overlap, so it failed. The supply box above was the better sell-limit area; first TP about 60 pips.

passages.h: Chart: [32:01] XAUUSD monthly (live session, Feb 10): supply and demand boxes with the Fibonacci lines between them
passages.t: High curve = sell entries only; low curve = buy entries only. Here the 4th visit went to the 50% area first: that area was for sellers.
Curve between the two HTF zones, measured proximal to proximal like his red lines on gold: sell only in the top 25%, buy only in the bottom 25%; he bought the dip to 50%.
A trendline cross counts only on a close. A wick through the line is a fake signal; a big engulfing candle closing beyond it is a valid break.
EURUSD Q&A top-down: monthly TP at the arrival supply, weekly demand below, daily shows a dip toward the weekly demand before the buy.
The student's stopped-out sell: a supply born inside an old demand (overlap). The clean H4 supply above was the better sell limit.

Buying LTF demand right under HTF supply (high curve). Treating a wick through the trendline as a break. Leaving a static stop when fresh zones keep forming behind the trade. Selling a trendline cross while a demand sits right under the closing candle. Redrawing the trendline after every swing.

What are the two HTF strong zones bounding price? Is price in the high curve, the low curve or the middle? Is my LTF zone on the correct side of the curve? Did the trendline break on a candle close? Where is the next fresh zone to trail my stop to? How many times has this trendline been touched (4th touch = likely break)?

“High curve is for sellers, and from the low curve 0 to 25% area is for the buyers.” “We always wait: let the market close above, and then the next candle start.” “I change my stop loss with the new fresh zone.”

Kevin and Seiden both use a 'curve' (Kevin: golden area up to the 50%, best at 33% or less; Seiden: buy low on the curve). Raja's version is 0-25% bands at each end, drawn between two HTF strong or arrival zones.
Raja drops the fixed TP and trails to fresh zones when the target is weak. The Rulebook's default is to hold to the opposing HTF zone.
His close-based trendline-break rule (wait for the next candle) is stricter than a touch or wick break.

Buy near the floor, sell near the ceiling, and trust only closes. Picture a room with a hard floor and a hard ceiling. A ball thrown near the ceiling is about to come down, and a ball near the floor is about to bounce up. So you catch balls going up only near the floor. Raja splits the room into a top quarter for sellers and a bottom quarter for buyers.
The two HTF zones are the floor and the ceiling. The low curve is the trampoline at the bottom; the high curve is the low roof at the top.

Between two HTF strong zones: top 0-25% is the high curve (sellers only), bottom 0-25% is the low curve (buyers only). A trendline is crossed only when a candle closes beyond it. A wick is a fake signal. Trail the stop to each new fresh zone, because price may turn before the TP.

passages.h: Step: Two HTF zones frame the map
passages.t: Find the two monthly or weekly strong zones above and below price. Everything happens between them.
Mark the 50% line in the middle and a 25% band at each end. Raja draws it by hand; he does not trust indicators. Top band: high curve, sellers only. Bottom band: low curve, buyers only.

passages.h: Step: Skip demand in the high curve
passages.t: Price rallies into the high curve and leaves a small demand. Raja does not use it: sellers sit near the HTF supply. Price soon drops right through it.

passages.h: Step: Buy demand in the low curve
passages.t: Price falls into the low curve and builds a fresh demand. This is the buyers' area. This is where he buys.

passages.h: Step: Trail the stop to fresh zones
passages.t: Each time a new fresh demand forms, move the stop under it. Price may not reach the far target, so the trail locks in pips. If two opposite zones get removed against you, close.

High curve? - Top 0-25% between two HTF strong zones. Sellers only. Low curve? - Bottom 0-25% between two HTF strong zones. Buyers only. Fib or by hand? - By hand. He does not trust indicators. When is a trendline crossed? - When a candle closes beyond it and the next candle starts. A wick through the line is... - A fake signal. Trailing stop rule? - Move the stop to each new fresh zone.
Target zone is weak? - Drop the fixed TP and keep trailing.

Price moving with the trendline is the impulse: big departure candles, fast and easy to trade. Moving against it is the correction: small base candles, fake signals, risky. On H4 and below, trade only impulses. On the monthly, weekly and daily you may also trade corrections. A zone's purpose is to reach its target.
Once the target has been reached, the zone will hold for only one or two candles on its next test and then break. 5x the previous correction.
On H4 or lower, trade only with-trend impulses. Trade corrections only on monthly, weekly or daily, and do not hold them long.

Once a zone's target is achieved, expect its next test to hold only briefly and then break; use confirmation. A demand that removed no supply is weak; use confirmation only. Use the 2.5x impulse-to-correction ratio as a rough exhaustion guide. With no zone above to target, project the impulse as 100% + 100% + 50% of the correction.
On correction trades take profit before the target zone, and close if the LTF trendline crosses back.

With a descending HTF trendline, the moves down along it are impulses. The pullbacks up ('the market needs the power of the buyers') are corrections. In price action this is a counter-trend move. Impulses print strong imbalance / departure / engulfing candles and move fast.
Corrections print small, tiny base candles and fake signals. Even near a strong or arrival zone, market makers make fake signals there.
Trading the impulse side is easy: when price crosses the trendline and removes two opposite zones, trade with it.
Corrections are risky; price does not have to reach the opposite zone. Use them only on the monthly, weekly or daily, where the candles carry 'good volume'.

Scenario 1: a supply removed the demand, so it is strong. Sell limit there. Its purpose is to drop and hit the target (the demand or the descending trendline). Once that target is achieved, the supply's job is done. On a reverse it will likely break, because it is now a retested zone and it lies against the trend. Use confirmation only, or wait and buy a fresh demand.

Scenario 2: a supply formed and price dropped to the target without retesting it. On the reverse, price hits the zone once, maybe gives one or two candles, and then breaks it. You can still sell limit, but do not hold long term.
Example: a strong demand (removed a supply) was bought with a buy limit. Price reached the supply target. On the way back the demand gave one candle of respect and then broke.
If the monthly and weekly are dropping and you have a strong daily demand: expect one hit, then a break after one or two candles.
A demand that did not remove any supply is weak; a demand formed inside a supply area is an overlap. Use confirmation only, or a lower timeframe. He also calls this a flip zone in this lesson.
Example: price moved up but did not remove the supply, so the demand was weak and price later dropped through it.

With the trend, an impulse is often about 2.5 times the size of the correction before it. If price removes one supply and there is no second one to target, project the move instead (Feb 18 session): measure the correction from the last higher high down to its low; the impulse usually travels 100% of it, another 100%, then half, i.e. 250%. The '1.5x' heard in the English recording was likely this same projection.
After roughly 2.5x, price usually starts correcting again.
On H4 and below, catch only impulses. When price drops in an uptrend, do not sell; wait for it to reach the trendline or demand, then buy.
Selling a correction risks price forming a new, more aggressive trendline and running away.

H4 example: the impulse leg paid about 159 pips; buying the correction would have paid about 26 pips, and another correction trade only about 28 pips. Low-timeframe traders lose because they do not understand impulse vs correction.
Find the trend on the high timeframe, then find the zones on the low timeframe and trade with that trend.

passages.h: From the live sessions and Urdu recordings
passages.t: How to recognise an impulse (course 4): (1) a structure break and (2) a strong move with big departure candles. Corrections print small candles, sometimes one or two big ones when the demand is far away.

passages.h: From the live sessions and Urdu recordings
passages.t: Market makers avoid building strong zones on the correction side, because they need to break them easily later. A strong zone on the correction gets tapped again and again, meshes, and breaks around the 4th time (Feb 18).

passages.h: From the live sessions and Urdu recordings
passages.t: Correction trade targets (Feb 18; course 4): the target is the demand, or the trendline if that is closer. Price often turns before the demand (market makers close their sells, retail sells near the low, then a sharp rally; common in crypto), so take profit before it. Use the 3x profit levels and close when price crosses the third, because it is now in the buying area.

passages.h: From the live sessions and Urdu recordings
passages.t: When the lower timeframe crosses its trendline against your correction trade, close it: the HTF impulse comes back fast and hurts (course 4, 15:20).

passages.h: From the live sessions and Urdu recordings
passages.t: Pip comparison on H4 (course 4, 21:13): the impulse legs paid about 200, 90 and 80 pips; the correction sells about 44, 5 and 37. Follow the newest trendline on any timeframe; the market may build a new, more aggressive line instead of returning to the old one.

passages.h: From the live sessions and Urdu recordings
passages.t: The zone that already did its job (Feb 18 drawing): a strong supply formed after the trendline was crossed, but price fell to the target without touching it. If a CP level sits near the peak, prefer it (market makers hunt the stops at the peak, test it, then drop); if the CP is far away with a gap, the nearer supply gets used.

passages.h: From the live sessions and Urdu recordings
passages.t: Once the target has been hit, the supply is tapped once more and broken on the second visit.

passages.h: From the live sessions and Urdu recordings
passages.t: Strong daily zone against the HTF (Feb 18; 2022 meeting): the market taps it first, which makes it weak, and breaks it the second time. With the HTF trend behind it, a strong daily zone drops at once with speed: that is the impulse.

passages.h: From the live sessions and Urdu recordings
passages.t: Pair selection by structure (Feb 18): first, pairs moving in clear impulse and correction with a clear monthly/weekly direction (they give wow trades); second, pairs clear on the daily that are in a correction with the target below; third, pairs zig-zagging on the HTF without a clear direction, traded only on H1/H4.

passages.h: Chart: [02:44] GBPAUD monthly used as a board (live session, Feb 18): impulse and correction along the trendline
passages.t: Measure the correction; the impulse runs about 100% + 100% + 50% of it. Impulse legs: big, fast candles. Corrections: small ones.

passages.h: Chart: [09:30] Same board, second scenario: stacked CP boxes near the peak and the supply that reached its target without a retest
passages.t: A CP near the peak is preferred; a far one with a gap is skipped for the nearer supply. Target already hit: tapped once more, broken on the second visit.
Impulses (with the descending trendline) are big departure candles; corrections are slow strings of small base candles.
Rough guide: the with-trend impulse often runs about 2.5x the prior correction before price corrects again.
A strong demand did its job when price reached the target. On the return it holds for 1-2 candles and then breaks.

Selling small corrections on low timeframes against the HTF trend. Holding a counter-trend trade long term after the zone already reached its target. Expecting a weak or overlap demand to hold. Holding a correction trade for the exact demand; price often turns before it.

Is this trade with the impulse or against it (correction)? If it is a correction: am I on the monthly, weekly or daily? Has this zone already reached its target? Did the zone remove an opposite zone (strong) or not (weak)? How big is the impulse vs the last correction (about 2.5x)?
“When market follows the trendline, market will move fast.” “The main purpose of the supply level: market drops and hits the target.” “Try to catch impulses.” “A good trader catches impulses.”
Kevin contrasts trend with momentum and trades only with trends. Raja allows HTF correction trades but forbids them on H4 and below.
The 'zone purpose / target achieved' idea (a zone weakens once it has reached its target) is not stated as a rule by Kevin or Seiden. The 2.5x impulse-to-correction ratio is unique to Raja.

Ride the big fast moves; be careful with the slow ones going back. Think of a kid riding a bike down a hill. Going down is fast and easy: that is the impulse. Pushing the bike back up a bit is slow and tiring: that is the correction. Raja rides the downhill part. And once a zone has sent price to its goal, it is a tired helper and will not hold for long.
Impulse = rolling downhill with the trendline. Correction = pushing the bike back up against it.
Impulse = with the trendline, big fast candles. Correction = against it, small slow candles and fake signals.
On H4 and below, trade only impulses. Corrections only on monthly, weekly or daily, and not for long.
A zone's purpose is to reach its target. After that, its next test holds 1-2 candles and then breaks.
Price falls along a descending trendline with big, fast candles. That is the impulse. It is fast and easy to trade.
Now price pushes back up with small, slow candles. The market needs buyers' power to do it. This correction is full of fake signals.
The next impulse runs about 2.5 times the size of the correction before it. After about 2.5x, price usually starts to correct again.

passages.h: Step: A strong demand reaches its target
passages.t: A demand forms and its rally removes the supply, so it is strong. On a daily chart you could buy it, short term. Price reaches its target: the descending trendline. The zone's job is done.

passages.h: Step: Job done: one candle, then a break
passages.t: The impulse comes back down to the demand. It holds for one candle, then breaks. It is now a retested zone that lies against the trend.

Impulse? - A move with the trendline: big, fast departure candles. Correction? - A move against the trendline: small slow candles and fake signals. H4 and below? - Trade only impulses. Where may you trade corrections? - Monthly, weekly or daily only, and not long term.
Zone purpose? - To reach its target. After that, its next test holds 1-2 candles and breaks. Impulse size guide? - About 2.5x the prior correction.

Price moves in waves: bullish and bearish momentums. Analysis is done on the monthly or weekly chart for direction, but entries are taken on lower-timeframe zones nested inside the HTF zone. That nested entry area is the 'location area', which keeps the stop small. A good trader enters only where momentum and location come together.
Use monthly/weekly for direction, but enter on a nested lower-timeframe zone (the location).

Pick the smallest valid zone nested inside the HTF zone to minimise the stop and maximise reward. Inside the HTF zone use only fresh LTF zones; skip retested ones. Enter where momentum (zone created, then retested) and location coincide. Inside the location area pick the strongest zone; if all are weak, use the top one. Below H4 add 5-10 pips to the stop.
On a line chart, a trending market moves in waves. Each up wave is a bullish momentum and each down wave a bearish momentum.

Example: price is rising from a weekly demand; on H4 that is bullish momentum. When H4 crosses its trendline, the bullish momentum is finished and a bearish one starts. On the HTF this is just price retesting the fresh demand it created. He also defines momentum as: price created a zone, then came back to it.
He shares analysis on the monthly or weekly, but entries go on H1, H4 or daily. The HTF chart is for direction.
A monthly supply might need a 1000-pip stop, which is too risky. A weekly zone might need 500 pips, which is better. Go further to the daily, and inside the daily find the H4 zone.
That smallest zone inside the bigger ones is the location area, also called nested zones. Inside an HTF zone you find many nested LTF candles and zones, and that is where market makers decide.
Analogy: country > city (he is in Islamabad) > town > street > home. The home is the location, where the stop loss goes.

Example: a monthly supply with a stop of 500+ pips. Inside it he found the weekly, daily and then an H4 strong zone (removed areas, arrival-type). That H4 zone was entered with about a 50-pip stop, and the trade ran about 1900 pips.
Rule for the monthly: use the zone before the gap (likely the zone at the start of the gap/departure).
Latest example: in the second monthly zone he found a weekly zone. Inside the weekly, the daily had two retested zones and one fresh zone. Only the fresh one was used for the sell.

A good trader takes entries only when momentum and location come together: price created the zone (momentum), then came back to it in the location area. When they line up, the moves are large (he cites 4000-5000 pip moves on the HTF).
Q: if price never comes back to the first zone? Let it go and use any new fresh zone. And once price hits the target, the zone's main purpose is finished.
To judge a trader, look at their charts: if they trade momentum plus location, they are a good trader.

passages.h: Location in practice (live sessions and Urdu recordings)
passages.t: Stops shrink as you drill down: monthly about 1,000 pips, weekly 500, daily 200, H4 100 or 50 (course 4). The 2022 class gives about 700, 300, 150, 70 and 50.

passages.h: Location in practice (live sessions and Urdu recordings)
passages.t: EURUSD (course 4): monthly supply, weekly zone, then a fresh daily/H4 strong zone with about a 56-pip stop; the drop gave about 1,900 pips. In a second example he skipped the broken and retested zones and used the fresh one: about an 83-pip stop (likely) and a drop of about 1,700 pips.

passages.h: Location in practice (live sessions and Urdu recordings)
passages.t: EURUSD (Feb 18): monthly to weekly to daily, then the H4 zone that broke the opposite zone, about a 60-pip stop against a 900-pip move. In the newer area the weekly had only one zone, and the daily had a broken weak zone, a used strong one and tested ones, so only the fresh location zone was left: about a 66-pip stop. Sometimes the location is missed.

passages.h: Location in practice (live sessions and Urdu recordings)
passages.t: Several zones inside the location area (course 5, 26:20; Feb 18): take the strongest one, with the best departure candles that removed the opposite zone. Usually that is the lower daily zone for a supply and the upper one for a demand, unless its departure is weak. If all are weak, use the top one. Below H4, add 5-10 pips to the stop.

passages.h: Location in practice (live sessions and Urdu recordings)
passages.t: If the location zone is not fresh, wait for a new fresh one and use it (2022 class). Plain momentum is when a zone is made but price leaves without coming back to it.

passages.h: Location in practice (live sessions and Urdu recordings)
passages.t: Momentum (Feb 18): impulse and correction make two momentums, buy and sell, and market makers trade them. A fresh weekly candle is bullish momentum for the lower timeframes until price reaches the weekly demand, or the trendline is crossed and two opposite zones are removed.

passages.h: Location in practice (live sessions and Urdu recordings)
passages.t: His own swing style (Apr 30): weekly location areas, stops of 300-600 pips, a focus on valleys and peaks; sometimes 3-4 trades a month, sometimes one.

passages.h: Chart: [24:03] Boxes inside boxes on GBPCHF monthly (2022 class): monthly, weekly, daily, H4
passages.t: Nested zones: the smallest box inside the bigger ones is the location. Minimum stop, maximum profit.
Location area: monthly > weekly > daily > H4. The nested H4 zone gives a ~50-pip stop instead of ~1000.
Momentum + location: the zone is created (momentum leaves), price returns to the fresh location zone, then the move is fast.
Trading the monthly zone directly with a 1000-pip stop. Waiting forever for a missed zone instead of using the next fresh one.

What is the HTF (monthly/weekly) direction? Which weekly zone sits inside the monthly zone, which daily inside the weekly, which H4 inside the daily? Is the nested zone fresh? Did price create the zone and is it now returning to it (momentum + location)? Stop size acceptable?
“We always use the entries on low time frame, but we check the chart on high time frame for the direction.” “A good trader always takes entry when location and momentum come together.”

Kevin and Seiden both refine HTF zones into LTF zones (Rulebook: refine big zones / three-TF check). Raja calls the refined entry the 'location area' and requires momentum (a return to the zone) at that location.
Raja's 'momentum' means the waves of the line chart. In Kevin's course 'momentum' is a steep, unsustainable move he avoids. Same word, different meaning.

Big chart for direction, tiny zone inside it for the entry. If a friend says "come to my house", you need more than the country name. You need the city, then the town, then the street, then the house. Raja does the same with zones. The monthly zone is the country and only tells the direction. The small zone hidden inside it is the house, and that is where the stop goes.
Country > city > town > street > home. The home is the location area.
Use monthly or weekly for direction; enter on a nested lower-timeframe zone inside the HTF zone.
The smallest fresh zone inside the big one is the location area: a small stop and a big reward. A good trader enters only where momentum (zone made, then revisited) and location meet.

passages.h: Step: Direction from the big chart
passages.t: A wide monthly supply sent price down hard. It tells us the direction: sell. But a stop above this wide zone would be huge.

passages.h: Step: Momentum: price left and comes back
passages.t: Price made the zone and moved away. Now it is coming back to it. That return is what Raja calls momentum.

passages.h: Step: Find the home inside the city
passages.t: Inside the big zone, price builds a tiny base and drops a little. That small zone, nested inside the monthly one, is the location area.
A stop above the monthly zone is far away. A stop above the nested zone is tiny. Same idea, much less risk. Raja once used a ~50-pip stop instead of ~1000.

passages.h: Step: Momentum + location = a fast move
passages.t: Price taps the nested zone and falls fast. When momentum and location come together, the moves are large.

HTF chart is for? - Direction only. Location area? - The smallest fresh zone nested inside the HTF zone. Why nest zones? - Small stop, big reward. Raja's momentum? - Price made a zone, then came back to it (the waves of the chart). Best entries? - Where momentum and location come together. The nesting analogy? - Country > city > town > street > home.

Trade only when the profit margin to the opposite zone is about 3x the stop (2x is still acceptable; 1x is a sideways market, so skip). Three rules for swing traders: take direction from daily or higher only; follow pips, not money; and always use a small lot size, risking only profit, not your deposit.
Require about 3:1 room to the opposite zone; 2:1 is the minimum; 1:1 means no trade. Direction only from monthly, weekly or daily. Follow pips (zone to zone), not money.

Start at 0.01 lots; increase only after building a profit cushion, so losses come from profit. Risk at most 1-2% per trade and at most two positions per zone. Take profit 5-10 pips before the opposite zone. The held position's stop stays at the zone (not breakeven) until new fresh zones form.
From a demand to the opposite supply (or the reverse), measure the room in multiples of the stop.
3x profit margin is good. 2x can still be traded. 1x cannot be traded; he calls that a sideways market.
Zoomed in: with a 1x margin the stop is bigger than the profit margin, which is not a good idea.

passages.h: Rule 1: direction from daily or higher
passages.t: Do not look below the daily for direction; use monthly, weekly or daily. If you take direction from H1, you are ready to lose money.

passages.h: Rule 1: direction from daily or higher
passages.t: Entries can be on any timeframe, even 5 minutes, but direction must follow monthly, weekly or daily.

passages.h: Rule 2: follow the pips, not the money
passages.t: If you chase money you drift to the 5-minute chart and big lot sizes. Instead follow the pips: when price removes the second supply, the next zone is the target, and those are the pips to catch.

passages.h: Rule 3: always a small lot size
passages.t: Most traders lose by using big lots on low timeframes. With $100, trade 0.01 lots and first make $50. That $50 is the backup ('margin equity backup money'). Then 0.02-0.03 lots are fine, and a stop-out should come out of that profit, not your deposit.

passages.h: Rule 3: always a small lot size
passages.t: With $1000, still use 0.01 until you have made at least $100 and can control your emotions. Big lots mean fear and aggression: you keep reopening MT4 and close positions early.

passages.h: From the live sessions: lot size, two positions, stops and targets
passages.t: Risk per trade: 1-2% at most (course 4). Other methods risk 3-10%. Three rules that save the account (Feb 25): never ignore the HTF, even when trading M5 (if the monthly/weekly have a long wow trade and the LTF is shorting, wait for the demand); keep positions small; follow pips, not money (pick the pair with about 1,000 pips of room over one with 100).

passages.h: From the live sessions: lot size, two positions, stops and targets
passages.t: He tells the same story in several sessions: a student with a large account (the figure varies between sessions) kept losing with random lot sizes and wide stops, traded 0.01 lots for months to learn what pips mean (EURUSD 200 pips is about 20 USD at 0.01), then scaled up slowly and became profitable.

passages.h: From the live sessions: lot size, two positions, stops and targets
passages.t: Step-up plan (Feb 25 board '1000 / 0.01 / 200 / 0.10'): with 100-1,000 USD trade 0.01 until you have made 100-200 USD, then step up to 0.10. Losses and stop hunts come out of that cushion, never out of the deposit.

passages.h: From the live sessions: lot size, two positions, stops and targets
passages.t: Two positions per zone (Feb 25, Mar 13, Jun 25, course 5): split one size into two at the same price (0.04 becomes 2 x 0.02). Close one at the near target or when the LTF trendline crosses into a correction; hold the other. Re-enter two at the next zone. At most two positions per zone; four stacked positions is a fake trader (course 4).

passages.h: From the live sessions: lot size, two positions, stops and targets
passages.t: The held position's stop stays at the original (HTF/daily) zone, not at breakeven, because breakeven gets hunted. As new fresh H4 zones and CP levels form, move it there; near the target move it behind the last demand (Mar 13). Once the H1 trendline has been tested 4-5 times, trail on H1 instead of giving back H4 swings (Jun 25).

passages.h: From the live sessions: lot size, two positions, stops and targets
passages.t: Stop distance (Mar 5, Mar 27): keep it 10-15 pips beyond the zone on H4/daily; small brokers widen the spread to hunt tight stops.

passages.h: From the live sessions: lot size, two positions, stops and targets
passages.t: Take profit (Apr 2025 class; Apr 30): 5-10 pips before the opposite zone, not at it, because the market often turns early or makes a new valley/peak. Close and re-enter if it comes back. An LTF entry targets the HTF zone (H1 entry, daily target); lock the stop into profit as new zones form.

passages.h: From the live sessions: lot size, two positions, stops and targets
passages.t: No revenge trading (course 4): after a loss stop for the day and come back fresh; revenge flips get caught when price returns to the zone.

passages.h: From the live sessions: lot size, two positions, stops and targets
passages.t: Pair priority (Feb 25): (a) pairs with a wow trade; (b) pairs in sequence; (c) pairs that already moved on the monthly/weekly and left a long wick on the open candle: wait for the retracement and buy from below to fill it; (d) pairs sideways between an HTF supply and demand: trade them only on the LTF until they break.

passages.h: Chart: [33:39] His sizing note on CADJPY monthly (2022 class): '100 / 0.01 / 50'
passages.t: With 100 USD trade 0.01 and make 50 USD first. Then trade bigger out of that profit; the deposit stays as backup.
Profit margin: room to the opposite zone measured against the stop. 3x is good, 2x acceptable, 1x is a sideways market, so skip it.

Trading when the stop is larger than the room to the next zone. Taking direction from H1 or lower. Using big lots on low timeframes and then reacting emotionally. Moving the stop to breakeven too early (it gets hunted). Revenge trading after a loss. Stacking four positions on one zone.

Room to the nearest opposite zone >= 2x (ideally 3x) the stop? Is direction taken from daily or higher? Am I targeting the next zone (pips) rather than a money amount? Is the lot size small enough that a loss comes from profit, not the deposit? Two half-size positions instead of one? Which one closes at the near target?

“Three-time profit margin is good, two-time we can use, but one time we cannot.” “You must follow the pips; don't follow the money.” “If you take a big lot size, you cannot control your emotional level.” “Small positions, small losses.”
Matches the Rulebook's profit-margin rule (Kevin about 3:1, 2:1 accepted). Raja adds that 1:1 means a sideways market.
The 'risk only profit money' lot-size plan (0.01 until a cushion is built) is specific to Raja; the PDFs do not give account-size rules like this.

Only play when you can win about three times what you risk. A game at the fair costs one sticker to play. If the prize is three stickers, it is worth a try. If the prize is one sticker, why play at all? Raja measures the room to the next zone against his stop. He also plays with a tiny bag of stickers until he has won some extra.
The stop is the price of the ticket. The room to the opposite zone is the prize. Three tickets of prize is good; one is a waste.

Room to the opposite zone: 3x the stop is good, 2x is OK, 1x is a sideways market, so skip. Take direction from daily or higher only. Follow pips (zone to zone), not money. Always a small lot. Start at 0.01 and only risk money you have already made.

passages.h: Step: Find the zone and the opposite zone
passages.t: You have a demand to buy from. Above it sits the nearest opposite zone: a supply. That supply is the end of your room.
Entry at the top of the demand, stop under the bottom. That distance is one unit of risk.
Now measure from the entry up to the supply. Here the room is about 3.34x the stop. Raja wants about 3x.
If the supply sat just one stop away, the profit would be no bigger than the risk. He calls that a sideways market and does not trade it.
Price runs from zone to zone. Those are the pips to catch. Do not chase a money amount on the 5-minute chart with big lots.

Good profit margin? - 3x the stop. 2x is still OK. 1x profit margin? - Sideways market. No trade. Direction timeframe? - Daily or higher only. Entry timeframe? - Any, even 5 minutes, but it must follow the HTF direction. Pips or money? - Follow the pips: zone to zone. Starting lot size? - 0.01, until a profit cushion is built.

Sequence: when the monthly and weekly point the same way, trade the daily in that direction using new fresh CP or peak/valley zones. Realignment: when the daily has run, crossed its trendline and removed two opposite zones, wait for price to return to the higher-timeframe area where a weekly zone and a daily zone sit together, and enter on that daily zone.
The Urdu recordings and live sessions add the full realignment chain (H4 to daily, daily to weekly, weekly to monthly), the 'never trade sideways' rule and when sequence zones go out of trendline.

Sequence: HTF (monthly + weekly) agree, so trade fresh daily zones in that direction. Realignment: after a daily trendline cross + two opposite zones removed, wait for the return to the weekly + daily confluence and enter on the daily zone. Use a realignment area once; after it is retested, do not reuse it. Never trade a sideways market; skip pairs stuck between zones.
Realignment chain: H4 cross -> daily zone; daily cross -> weekly zone; weekly cross -> monthly zone.
Once the trendline is crossed, the sequence zones are out of trendline: switch to the HTF realignment zone.
If the monthly is dropping and the weekly is dropping, sell on the daily, using a new CP level or peak level. If the monthly and weekly are rising, buy on the daily.
Same with weekly up and daily up: use the daily fresh zones for the trade. He calls this 'sequence' (the captions also say 'sequence number'; likely just 'sequence').
When the daily has already moved, crosses its trendline and removes the two opposite zones, price is going back to check the alignment area on the higher timeframe.
The alignment (realignment) area is where a weekly strong zone and a daily strong zone come together: a daily zone inside or next to the weekly zone.
Enter on the daily zone near the weekly zone. Do not use the daily zones that were just removed. Use a timeframe one step bigger than your entry timeframe for the area.
EURUSD example: price crossed the daily trendline and removed two opposite zones, then went back to the weekly zone (the high-curve area), where a daily zone sat inside it. That was the trade.
After the realignment area has been retested once, he does not use it again. If there is another weekly + daily pair further on, price can react there again.

passages.h: Sequence in detail (Urdu recordings and live sessions)
passages.t: Three market states (Apr 2025 class): up, down and sideways. Never trade sideways; emotions are hardest there and 99% of traders lose. Sideways is what the market does while it is realigning, so skip pairs stuck there.

passages.h: Sequence in detail (Urdu recordings and live sessions)
passages.t: Sequence = trading each new zone below (or above) the trendline, one after another, before the HTF target is hit. His drawing (low-TF class): H4 dropping from H4 supplies, a CP on H1, and on M15/M30 the market making and using supplies below its trendline. Every pair in the world is in sequence on some timeframe.

passages.h: Sequence in detail (Urdu recordings and live sessions)
