passages.t: Timeframe sets (course 2; low-TF class): monthly + weekly for direction, daily + H4 for entries; daily + H4 down means sell H1 supplies below the trendline; H4 + H1 means trade M15. For most trades go no lower than H1.

passages.h: Sequence in detail (Urdu recordings and live sessions)
passages.t: Prefer zones near peaks; after about three CPs the market usually reverses (2022 class). After 3-4 CPs, rest the pair and look at another (course 2).

passages.h: Sequence in detail (Urdu recordings and live sessions)
passages.t: To cross the trendline the market first builds gaps and stacked zones; it rarely crosses in one go (2022 class). Once it has crossed, the sequence zones are out of trendline: stop using them and use the higher zone instead (low-TF class, EURUSD daily 2019).

The chain (low-TF class; course 5; Apr 2025 class): when H4 crosses its trendline, the market realigns with the daily zone; a daily cross goes to the weekly zone; a weekly cross goes to the monthly, even to the 6-month or yearly candle's zone. On the low timeframes: an M5 cross heads for the H1 zone, and when M15 breaks it realigns with H1.

After the LTF crosses and removes the opposite zone, stop using the LTF zones and use the H4/H1 zone: that is where the market realigns and what it respects (low-TF class). He calls this the most important low-timeframe rule; follow it and you rarely take a loss, even scalping.

How to spot the area (Apr 2025 class): two trendlines, and the realignment area is where they point; it is often visible directly on the weekly. Most of the time the realignment area is also the arrival zone, especially H1/H4 coming into a daily strong zone (course 5).
Even after a cross, a demand right next to the line blocks selling until it breaks (low-TF class).

A realignment area can be tapped again. HTF zones survive more taps (monthly/H4 3-4, while an H1 zone usually breaks on the 2nd), but once tapped use confirmation (Apr 2025 class). If the weekly realignment CP is weak: always confirmation, never set and forget (Feb 25).
Do not panic-close when a small trendline breaks: it only realigns with the next timeframe; lock profit once it moves (Apr 2025 class).
After a big HTF candle, do not buy on top of it (Feb 25, AUDNZD): the market retraces to the daily realignment area first, then fills the candle from there.
A student's loss (course 5): he sold the first drop (the left shoulder) with an H1 confirmation and was stopped out; that sell sat inside a demand level, so it was never valid.

passages.h: Chart: [00:39] Sequence drawing on GBPSGD monthly used as a board (low-TF class): supplies used one after another under the falling line, the target demand below
passages.t: Each new supply below the trendline gets used in turn. Once the trendline is crossed, those zones are out of trendline.

passages.h: Chart: [40:14] Realignment board on EURUSD monthly (Apr 2025 class): stacked daily, weekly and monthly zones
passages.t: Daily crosses its trendline -> realigns with the weekly zone. Weekly crosses -> realigns with the monthly.

passages.h: Chart: [20:06] Sequence drawing on GBPSGD monthly (live session, Feb 25): the daily zigzag along a rising trendline
passages.t: Monthly and weekly up: trade each new daily zone along the trendline. Highest win chances when the sequence is clear.
Realignment: the daily crosses its trendline and removes two zones, then returns to where a daily zone sits inside the weekly strong demand. Buy there.

Re-using the daily zones that were just removed. Re-using a realignment area after it has been retested. Trading a sideways (realigning) market. Buying on top of a just-formed big HTF candle. Closing in panic when a small trendline breaks.

Are the monthly and weekly in sequence (same direction)? Has the daily crossed its trendline and removed two opposite zones? Is there a daily zone inside or next to a weekly strong zone? Has that realignment area already been used? Is the market sideways? Then skip it. Which HTF zone will this LTF trendline cross realign with?
“When two time frames come together, a weekly strong zone and a daily strong zone, we use it for the trade.” “Market will reverse back to realign with the high time frame.”
“Whenever the low time frame crosses its trendline, it goes to the high time frame realignment area.”
Close to the Rulebook's three-timeframe check (the HTF of the HTF for the curve). Raja names the weekly + daily confluence the 'realignment area' and triggers it with his two-zone direction change.
Neither Kevin nor Seiden ties the HTF return to 'trendline crossed + two zones removed' on the lower timeframe.

When the daily wanders off, wait for it to come home to the weekly. A puppy runs ahead of its owner on a walk. After a while the leash pulls it back to the owner's side. Then they walk on together. The daily chart is the puppy and the weekly chart is the owner. Raja buys when the puppy comes back to the owner's feet.
Sequence = owner and puppy walking the same way. Realignment = the puppy coming back to the owner's feet.

Sequence: monthly and weekly agree, so trade fresh daily zones in that direction. Realignment: after the daily crosses its line and removes two zones, wait for the return to where a weekly and a daily zone sit together. Never reuse the removed daily zones. Use a realignment area only once.

passages.h: Step: Sequence: the big charts agree
passages.t: Monthly and weekly both point up. A weekly strong demand sits below, and a daily zone sits right next to it.
The daily rallies along its trendline and leaves more daily demands on the way.

passages.h: Step: Line crossed, two zones removed
passages.t: The daily closes below its trendline and removes two daily demands. Price is now going back to check the higher timeframe.

passages.h: Step: Back to the realignment area
passages.t: The removed daily zones are not used. Price returns to where the daily zone sits next to the weekly strong demand. That meeting point is the realignment area.

passages.h: Step: Price realigns with the big chart
passages.t: Price bounces from the realignment area and moves with the weekly direction again. After this retest, Raja does not use this area again.

Sequence? - Monthly and weekly agree; trade fresh daily zones that way. Realignment trigger? - Daily crosses its trendline and removes two opposite zones. Realignment area? - Where a weekly strong zone and a daily strong zone sit together. Entry in the area? - On the daily zone near the weekly zone. Reuse the area? - No. Once retested, it is done.

A live Q&A where Raja walks through GBPJPY, EURCZK, USDCAD, GBPNZD, SGDJPY, AUDCAD, SEKJPY and the SPA35 index top-down. The monthly is used only to find direction and the target (the opposite strong zone) and to count the pips left. Then he steps down to weekly, daily, H4 and H1 to find a fresh strong zone (one that removed the opposite zone).
When the monthly and weekly disagree, he waits for the retracement to complete and for confirmation.

Find the monthly target and count the pips before anything else. Use the monthly only for direction; trade on lower timeframes. Skip a zone that sits inside an opposite zone. If a timeframe already took its entry, go one timeframe lower for a fresh zone.
If the monthly and weekly disagree, wait for the retracement to finish and for confirmation.
Monthly: identify the target and count the remaining pips with the measure tool (e.g. 700+, 800, 1000 pips). If there is room, go lower.
Weekly: check whether there are still pips to the target and which zones exist. Skip a zone that already sits inside an opposite supply level.
Daily: if the daily has already taken its entry ('already touched'), do not look at it any more and go to H4.
H4 / H1: find a strong zone (one that removed the opposite zone). Wait for a retracement into it, especially after a big move. If the market creates a new zone, use the fresh one.
The first TP is the nearest opposing level; he also checks whether the trendline is still unbroken, which points to the further target.

GBPJPY (00:02-02:02): monthly supply lines above with about 700+ pips of room. The daily demand box was already used, so he goes to H4: price had left the H4 demand with departure candles and a new H4 demand (box) formed. First TP is the nearest level (about 160 pips). His H4 trendlines (dotted) are not crossed, so the bullish move is still intact.

EURCZK (02:49-05:02): monthly top zone and bottom zone with price in the curve to sell; about 800-900 pips to the bottom zone. The weekly has only one zone, used as the TP. The daily already moved away from its supply zones. On H1 he deletes the clutter and keeps only the box that removed the opposite demand; he waits for a retracement into it to sell.

USDCAD (05:33-06:53): dropping from the top, target the weekly demand line about 200+ pips away. The weekly zone above is skipped because it sits inside a supply level. The daily already took its trade, so he waits for H4 to remove the daily demand and then sells the H4 supply box (drawn under two dotted downtrend lines).
GBPNZD monthly (07:51): technically long, but the demand box is a retested zone and price still follows the trendline, so he waits for a proper daily trendline cross and confirmation.
SGDJPY weekly (08:52): price left the monthly demand; the target is the supply box above, about 200-400 pips away, so long.
AUDCAD monthly (09:22-10:22): the trendline was crossed out of the big demand box, so price targets the supply box above. The top box removed the opposite demand: a strong CP-level zone.

SPA35 daily (11:22-12:30): already in the low curve, a buy area. Fake signals both ways, but price should reach the top supply. His green drawing circles gap #1 and gap #2 in the crash leg (likely unfilled gaps), the nearest target, and the downtrend line that has been crossed.
Monthly and weekly disagree: wait for the retracement to complete and for a proper trendline cross on the daily. If the zone is a retested zone, wait for confirmation.
If the monthly trend is up but candles alternate, use the weekly strong zone for the trade.
When to apply the two-opposite-zones rule: on that particular timeframe. For example, if the weekly removes two opposite zones, price will head to the monthly strong zone.

[00:02] GBPJPY monthly: two black supply lines above, measure line to the target. [00:32-02:02] GBPJPY daily box, then H4 boxes and dotted trendlines; measure 53 / 469 to the next level. [02:19] Deletes old objects on EURCZK so only the fresh drawing remains.
[02:49-04:49] EURCZK monthly, weekly, daily, H4, H1 with boxes at each level and the measure to the bottom zone.

[05:33-06:53] USDCAD weekly, then H4 with the target line, the H4 supply box and two downtrend lines. [07:51] GBPNZD monthly: demand box and rising trendline (retested zone: wait). [08:22-08:52] GBPTRY weekly and SGDJPY weekly with the target supply box.
[09:22-10:52] AUDCAD monthly (big demand box, crossed trendline, top supply box) and SEKJPY monthly.

[11:22-12:30] SPA35 daily: draws in green the circles on the gaps, the downtrend line and the rising line, with the demand box at the breakout. [13:30] Soybeans weekly: 'similar pair', next target above.

passages.h: Chart: [00:02] GBPJPY monthly with target lines and measure
passages.t: Step 1: the monthly target and the pips left (700+).
The daily already took its entry, so he does not use it again.

passages.h: Chart: [01:02] GBPJPY H4: new demand after the departure
passages.t: Use the fresh H4 zone; first TP is the nearest level.

passages.h: Chart: [02:02] GBPJPY H4 with trendlines and the measure
passages.t: The dotted trendlines are not crossed: still bullish.

passages.h: Chart: [02:49] EURCZK monthly: top and bottom zones
passages.t: Price is in the curve to sell; about 800-900 pips to the bottom zone.
Only one weekly zone below: it is the TP.

passages.h: Chart: [03:49] EURCZK daily with two supply boxes
passages.t: Price already left these zones: drop to H4/H1.
Only the box that removed the opposite demand is strong. Wait for the retracement, then sell.

passages.h: Chart: [05:33] USDCAD weekly with the target line
passages.t: Target about 200+ pips below.

passages.h: Chart: [06:53] USDCAD H4 supply box and two downtrend lines
passages.t: Daily already used: wait for H4 to remove the daily demand, then sell the H4 supply.

passages.h: Chart: [07:51] GBPNZD monthly: retested demand and trendline
passages.t: Monthly and weekly disagree: wait for the retracement and a daily trendline cross.

passages.h: Chart: [08:52] SGDJPY weekly with the target supply
passages.t: Price left the monthly demand: target the opposite zone, 200-400 pips.

passages.h: Chart: [09:22] AUDCAD monthly big demand box
passages.t: Trendline crossed from the demand: target the supply above.

passages.h: Chart: [10:22] AUDCAD monthly: top supply and crossed trendlines
passages.t: If the weekly removes two opposite zones, price heads to this monthly strong zone.

passages.h: Chart: [11:22] SPA35 daily: demand box in the low curve
passages.t: A buy area: price is in the low curve.

passages.h: Chart: [12:00] SPA35 daily: his green drawing
passages.t: Circles on gap #1 and gap #2, the downtrend line crossed, and the rising line from the low. Target: the top supply box.
EURCZK funnel: monthly target and pip count, daily already used, H1 strong supply that removed the opposite demand, sold after a retracement.
USDCAD: weekly demand is the target; the daily zone was used, so he waits for H4 to remove the daily demand and sells the H4 supply.
SPA35 daily: low-curve buy using his clues (gap #1, gap #2, nearest target, crossed downtrend line).
Raja's top-down funnel: monthly direction and target, weekly room and curve, daily freshness, then an H4/H1 strong zone for entry and stop.
Trading straight off the monthly chart. Using a daily zone that has already been touched. Entering when the HTFs conflict instead of waiting.

Monthly target identified and pips counted? Weekly zone valid (not inside an opposite zone)? Daily already touched? Then go to H4/H1. Entry zone strong (removed the opposite zone) and fresh? Do the HTFs agree? If not, wait.
“Monthly we only use for direction.” “First of all we identify the target and then we can trade.” “If you identify the direction, you can easily trade on low time frame.”
Same top-down idea as Kevin and Seiden. Raja's order is 'target and pip count first', and he drops a timeframe whenever the current one already took its entry.
He uses 'gaps' on the monthly as clues to the target (likely departure gaps); the PDFs do not use gaps this way.

First find where price is going and how far. Then find the door. Before a trip, you first pick the town you are going to and check how far it is. Only then do you pick which road and which bus stop. Raja does the same. The monthly chart shows the target and the pips left. Then he walks down the timeframes until he finds a fresh, strong door to go through.
The monthly is the map with the destination. The H4 or H1 zone is the bus stop where you get on.

Monthly first: find the target (the opposite strong zone) and count the pips left. Step down weekly, daily, H4, H1. Skip zones inside an opposite zone or already touched. If monthly and weekly disagree, wait for the retracement and for confirmation.
The monthly supply points down. The opposite strong zone below is the target. Raja always finds the target first.
From the supply down to the target there are about 46 points of room on this chart. Raja counts these pips before anything else. There is room, so it is worth going lower to look for an entry.
A daily supply removed a demand, so it was strong, but it has already been touched. Raja says: if the daily already took its entry, stop looking at it and go to H4.

passages.h: Step: Go lower: a fresh H4 zone
passages.t: On H4, price leaves a new fresh supply. That is the one to sell, with a stop just above it.

passages.h: Step: Ride it to the target
passages.t: Price taps the fresh H4 zone and travels down to the monthly target. Direction from the monthly, entry from the low timeframe.

First job on the monthly? - Find the target and count the pips left. Monthly chart is for? - Direction only. Never the entry. Daily zone already touched? - Go one timeframe lower for a fresh zone. Zone inside an opposite zone? - Skip it. Monthly and weekly disagree? - Wait for the retracement and for confirmation.
Two-zone rule on the weekly? - If the weekly removes two opposite zones, price heads for the monthly strong zone.

Raja's 'wow trade' is the open run of pips between one zone and the next. There are two versions. (1) A zone removes the nearest opposite zone, so price is drawn to the next zone of that type. (2) Price breaks a trendline with a big candle, so the room from the break to the next opposite zone is a wow trade area, traded on the lower timeframe.

On his charts every lower high (or higher low) gets its own trendline, so a cross of the newest line targets the zone at its origin and a cross of the next, older line targets the zone above (or below) that. A wow trade can come in two parts, from the first zone to the second. He never sells while price still sits in a demand (or buys in a supply): that zone must first be removed by a candle close.
A zone that removes the nearest opposite zone makes the next zone of that type the target; the pips between them are the wow trade area.
On the lower timeframe, a proper trendline cross (a big candle closing beyond it) starts a wow trade from the break to the next opposite zone.
Never sell while price sits in a demand, or buy while it sits in a supply: wait until that zone is removed (or price reaches the opposite zone).

A zone counts as removed only by a candle close beyond it; a wick through it is a fake signal. Use monthly / weekly for direction only; take entries on the daily and lower timeframes. If an opposite zone sits near the trendline, the zone has priority over the trendline. Skip setups with little room to the next zone; choose pairs with good pips.
Part 2 of a wow trade starts only when the zone at the end of part 1 is removed. The first wow area (after the first zone breaks) is smaller than the second; hold one position for the second.

passages.h: Version 1: zone to zone ("extension of pips")
passages.t: Example: two supply levels, supply #1 above and supply #2 below. A demand forms underneath and its rally removes supply #2.

passages.h: Version 1: zone to zone ("extension of pips")
passages.t: Because the market already removed that supply, the next target is supply #1. Price may come back and retest the demand first, or go straight to supply #1 without a retest.

passages.h: Version 1: zone to zone ("extension of pips")
passages.t: The room between supply #2 and supply #1 is the wow trade area; he also calls it the 'extension of pips'.

passages.h: Version 1: zone to zone ("extension of pips")
passages.t: The same works downwards: if price removes the first demand it will go to the second demand. From the first demand to the second is the wow trade area.

Example: demands #1 and #2 below and an ascending trendline. When price crosses the ascending trendline, the area from there down to the next zone is a wow trade: there is no zone in between to stop it, so you can sell on the lower timeframe.

The cross has to be proper: a big candle (he says an 'OCL' candle, likely a full-bodied open-to-close candle) closing beyond the trendline. A line that is only touched or barely crossed does not count; price is still 'meshing' (chopping) there.
If price then also removes demand #1, the run from demand #1 to demand #2 is the second wow trade area. He splits it into part 1 and part 2.
In the lower timeframe price still makes 'ups and downs' (retracements, fake signals) inside the wow trade area, but overall it travels to fill the area and hit the next zone.

Each swing gets its own trendline. On his EURUSD daily (13:00-15:38) he draws a supply box at every lower high and a separate descending line from each of those highs. A close above the newest line targets the supply at that line's origin; when that supply is retested once and broken on the second attempt, the next, older line and the supply above it become the target. That is what he means by 'the next target is the previous trendline' area.

He draws the lines as steep dotted lines along the impulse legs (NZDJPY daily at 04:01, USDRUB daily at 08:56, FRA40 monthly at 10:29, US2000 daily at 18:08). A broader, slower line is often drawn next to the steep one: the steep one breaks first and starts the first wow trade; the broader one is the 'different trendline' that starts the next.

passages.h: Do not trade into an opposite zone
passages.t: If the trendline is crossed but price is already sitting in a demand, do not sell yet. Wait for the market to remove that demand (or to reach a supply), then sell on the lower timeframe 'without any hesitation'.

passages.h: Do not trade into an opposite zone
passages.t: If price is still far above the demand when the trendline breaks, you can sell straight away on the lower timeframe because the demand is far.

passages.h: Do not trade into an opposite zone
passages.t: Buying works the same way: while price still follows a descending trendline you cannot buy; let it cross the trendline first.

passages.h: Do not trade into an opposite zone
passages.t: When an opposite zone sits near the trendline, the zone matters more than the trendline: focus on the zone and let it be removed first.

passages.h: Do not trade into an opposite zone
passages.t: A demand already retested once or twice is a weak area: buying there needs the confirmation rule.

passages.h: Do not trade into an opposite zone
passages.t: On his USDCAD daily (19:18) the box is drawn exactly where price is consolidating after the rally: price is sitting in that demand, so even with the trend line crossed he says 'remove demand or hit the supply' first.

A zone is removed when a candle closes beyond it; he points to a demand where one candle closed below and the next big candle also closed below (20:45-21:15). Only then is the run to the next zone a wow trade.
A spike that only hits the stop losses with a wick and reverses back is a fake signal. He sees this mostly on Fridays because of low volume.
News-driven markets (he mentions COVID headlines) also produce these fakes, so he waits for the proper removal before selling.
Monthly and weekly analysis is for direction, not a promise that price hits a level. It tells you in which direction to look for strong zones on the daily and lower timeframes.
Daily supply and demand levels can be traded on their own; you do not have to go to the monthly every time. Inside a wow trade, H4 or H1 entries are fine if risk management is proper.

Measure the pips in the wow trade area (his examples: about 370 pips for part 1 and about 1,200 pips for part 2 on EURUSD; 'almost 3,112' pips on EURMXN daily, a pair that 'moves a lot'). On his GBPUSD monthly (28:46) he passes: the demand had already been retested twice and there were only about 100 pips to the next resistance, so the trade is not worth it. Choose pairs that show good pips.

Order of checks in his words: first the trendline, then the zone (fresh zones). Base candidates that are only a few candles of chop (the small boxes under price on EURZAR at 25:17) are 'not properly zones', so they are weak and do not stop a wow trade.

His GBPMXN daily (31:01-31:46) shows the layout: three demand boxes stacked under a steep rally, one steep ascending trendline and one broader one. Selling from the top, part 1 runs to the nearest demand and part 2 to the next one only if the first is removed. If you sold at the top and your target was the end of part 1, close there.

If you held, move your stop loss down. If the market then removes the next zone, you can sell again for part 2; otherwise you keep the old position and close it at the first target. The take profit is the next zone along the straight line of the trend.

passages.h: From the Urdu recordings and live sessions
passages.t: Two wow areas (course 5): the first, smaller one opens when the first zone breaks; the second, bigger one when the next zone goes. EURUSD daily: from the big black candle through the trendline down to the weak demand was about 300+ pips (area 1); the next zone below added about 1,100 (about 1,400-1,500 in all). Hold one position for the second area.

passages.h: From the Urdu recordings and live sessions
passages.t: On the lower timeframe the same holds even if it is only 10 pips: from the trendline break to the demand level is a wow area (course 5, EURUSD H4).

passages.h: From the Urdu recordings and live sessions
passages.t: With a clear wow area you could even buy blindly and price would follow within days (course 2). His three 'blind entry' places (Mar 27): a wow trade, a fresh arrival zone, and a zone near the trendline that has not been tapped a 4th time. Such zones are rare.

passages.h: From the Urdu recordings and live sessions
passages.t: Never ignore the wow trade on any timeframe (low-TF part 2): if an H1 supply breaks, the run goes to the trendline; there, go to M15 and wait for the cross and the opposite-zone removal before the next trade.

passages.h: From the Urdu recordings and live sessions
passages.t: A wow trade on a clean HTF valley/peak structure is the first-priority pair (Apr 2025 class). With no supply above to target, use the 250% impulse projection (Feb 18).

passages.h: From the Urdu recordings and live sessions
passages.t: A heavily tested demand area: when it finally breaks, everything down to the next demand is sell pips (course 2).

passages.h: Chart: [17:04] WOW drawing on EURMXN monthly (Urdu course 5): supply I on top, supply II below, and a rally that breaks II
passages.t: Once II is removed, I is the target either way (retest first or straight up). The pips in between are the extension of pips.
Version 1: the demand's rally closes above supply #2, so supply #1 becomes the target. The gap between them is the wow trade area ('extension of pips'), with the TP at supply #1's proximal line.

His NZDJPY daily (04:01), redrawn: a box at the origin of the drop (supply) and at the low (demand), with a steep dotted trendline along the sell-off. Once the lower timeframe closes above that line, the whole room up to the last supply is the wow trade area.

His GBPMXN daily (31:46), redrawn: three demand boxes stacked under a steep rally, with two ascending trendlines. The steep line breaks first. Part 1 runs to demand #1; part 2 runs to demand #2 only after #1 is removed by a close.
No sell while price is still sitting in a demand. Wait for a candle close below it (a wick through, e.g. on a quiet Friday, does not count).
Selling right after a trendline break while price is already inside a demand. Treating a wick through a zone (often on a low-volume Friday) as a removal.

Calling a trendline broken when price is still 'meshing' around it without a full-bodied close. Reading a monthly / weekly level as a guaranteed target instead of a direction. Buying a demand that has already been retested twice without confirmation. Taking a trade with only ~100 pips to the next resistance.

Which zone was just removed, and where is the next zone of the same type? How many pips is the wow trade area? Is it worth it? Has the lower-timeframe trendline been crossed by a big candle close? Is price currently inside an opposite zone? If yes, wait for its removal. Was the last zone removed by a close, not just a wick? Is this part 1 or part 2? Where is the stop moved if holding?
Does the monthly / weekly direction agree?
“When market crosses the trend line, we can say the wow trade can start.” “Let the market remove this demand, then we can sell.” “Remove the demand or hit the supply.”

Kevin's course has the same chain idea (a zone that removed an opposing zone, then targeting the next level); 'wow trade' and 'extension of pips' are Raja's own names for the room between the removed zone and the next one.
Raja starts a lower-timeframe sell campaign from a trendline cross alone, as long as no opposite zone is in the way. Kevin's confirmation entry needs the trendline AND an opposing zone removed.
Splitting the move into part 1 / part 2 (re-entering only after the intermediate zone is removed) is not in Kevin's or Seiden's material.
His removal test (a candle close beyond, not a wick, and be wary of low-volume Fridays) matches the course rulebook's 'removed = a close beyond the distal'.
Seiden judges targets by profit margin to the opposing level; Raja expresses the same thing as counting the pips in the wow trade area and skipping pairs with small room.

When a zone is knocked out, price rides the empty road to the next one. Picture a road with two gates. A truck smashes through the first gate. Now nothing stops it until the second gate further on. That empty stretch of road is free distance. Raja calls it the wow trade: good pips with nothing in the way. The wow trade area is the open road between a smashed gate and the next gate.
Version 1: a zone removes the nearest opposite zone, so price heads to the next zone of that type. The gap is the wow trade area.
Version 2: a big candle closes beyond the LTF trendline, so price can run to the next opposite zone.
Never sell while price sits in a demand (or buy in a supply). First that zone must be removed by a close.
Price fell and left two supplies: #1 higher up and #2 lower down.
A demand forms at the bottom and its rally closes above supply #2. A wick would not count; this is a real close.
Supply #2 is gone, so the next target is supply #1. The open room between them is the wow trade area, also called the extension of pips. TP at the bottom of supply #1.

passages.h: Step: Trade it on a lower timeframe
passages.t: Use the high timeframe to find these pips and take the entry on a lower timeframe. Price may retest first or go straight there. Here it travels up to supply #1.

Wow trade? - The open run of pips from a removed zone to the next zone. Another name for it? - The extension of pips. Version 2 trigger? - A big full-bodied candle closing beyond the LTF trendline. When is a zone removed? - When a candle closes beyond it. Wicks do not count. Line crossed but price in a demand? - Do not sell yet. Wait for the demand to be removed.
Zone near the trendline? - The zone has priority over the line. Part 2 of a wow trade starts when? - Only after the zone at the end of part 1 is removed.

Not every fresh zone can be traded. Raja uses only strong zones for pending orders, and there are three kinds: the simple strong zone (its move removed the opposite zone), the wow trade zone, and the arrival zone (it crossed the trendline AND removed the opposite zone). A zone whose move failed to remove the opposite zone is weak and gets no set & forget order. He also defines impulse vs correction relative to the trendline.
Use pending (limit) orders only on strong zones: simple strong, wow trade, and arrival zones.
A zone is strong when its move removed the opposite zone; if it failed to remove it, it is weak. First touch of a strong zone = set & forget.
Arrival zone = crosses the trendline AND removes the opposite zone; only the trendline cross = inheritance zone (weak).
High timeframe for direction and pips, low timeframe for the entry (small stop, big target).
Trades with the trendline are impulse / trend trades; against it, they are short-term corrections.
Among fresh zones there are three types where you can put a buy limit or sell limit order (set & forget). Everything else is weak.
Simple strong zone: a supply forms, its drop removes a demand. Because it removed the opposite zone, that supply becomes strong: use a sell limit order.

Weak zone: the supply's drop failed to remove the demand below. That supply is technically weak: no set & forget, because the market can break it. In that picture the demand (which held) is the stronger zone.
Simple strong zones are found mostly on CP levels (continuation bases) and sometimes on valleys and peaks (reversal bases).
His short rule: whichever zone removed the opposite zone becomes the strong zone, and the market mostly respects strong areas.
On the whiteboard (01:04) he draws it as a supply box at the top, candles dropping through a demand box lower down, and the sell limit box placed back at the supply.
Candle strength when drawing (08:14-08:58): he sketches several base shapes. A single candle followed directly by the drop is risky and he does not use it; the base has to be a proper basing area.

On EURUSD monthly (08:45-09:20) a demand that 'could not reach' the supply above it is weak; the fresh supply that formed next and dropped through those demands became the strong zone, and the market respected it on the retest.
On the first return to a strong zone, always use set & forget. When the market wants to break a zone it taps it once and breaks it on a later visit.
Example: monthly and weekly are dropping and you have a strong daily demand. Price may tap it with one candle and then drop through it on the next candles. It will not break on the first tap.
Use the high timeframe to identify the pips (the run from the removed zone to the next zone), then take the entry on the low timeframe.
The high timeframe is for direction only, never for entries: the stop would be too big. Forex rule: small stop loss, maximum profit.
Example: supply #1 at the top, supply #2 lower. Price drops, forms a demand, and that demand removes supply #2. The next target is supply #1. Price may retest the demand first or jump straight there.
He says if you understand wow trades you can make money even without deep supply & demand knowledge. 'Wow' just means good pips.

On EURUSD monthly (14:30) he measures from the strong supply down to the next demand: 'almost 1,000 pips' of sell pips. Until price reaches that target you can keep using strong zones on the lower timeframe that sit on the right side of the trendline.
His 'arrival zone' (transcribed as 'arrival' / 'rival') has two rules. Rule 1: the move crosses the trendline. Rule 2: it removes the opposite zone (the last supply, for a demand).
If price only crosses the trendline but does not remove the opposite zone, the zone is an inheritance zone, which is weak (covered in part II).

Example: price drops from top to bottom making supplies. A demand forms; its rally first crosses the descending trendline, then removes the last supply. That demand is an arrival zone and the market will respect it when it comes back.
Market makers use arrival zones for their entries, especially on the monthly and weekly. They work on every timeframe, from 1 minute to monthly. He calls arrival zones the most important zones.

Chart examples: EURUSD monthly (16:11) shows the rally crossing a small descending line and closing above the last supply, so that demand is the arrival zone; EURUSD daily (17:01) shows the mirror case, a large supply at the top whose drop crossed the ascending line and removed the demand.
He shows the same pattern on USDCNH monthly, then M1 and M5 (18:13-18:58), to make the point that arrival zones work on every timeframe.

Two trendline types: ascending (drawn along the lows going up) and descending. On his charts the descending line runs from the major top through the following peaks (EURUSD monthly, 11:06-12:06). A descending line is confirmed once price has crossed the ascending one and made two new lower highs and lows (likely).
Moves with the trendline are impulses (trend trading). Moves against the high-timeframe trendline are corrections (counter-trades).

Trading against the HTF trendline means trading the correction side: example, the market was dropping, a demand on the correction side removed a supply and became strong. Price tapped it, ran to the TP (the supply level), and later the down-trend removed that demand. Hold long only with the trend; correction trades are short-term.

We have no control over the market; we read the old data to predict the future. He claims supply & demand repeats with about 98% probability (his number) if the rules are followed. Other methods 'work under' supply & demand.
When news comes out, the market creates new fresh supply and demand; knowing the rules tells you which ones are good or bad. He does not use indicators: they are slow, the market is fast.

19:37-19:39 EURUSD M15 and H4: supply boxes under a descending trendline that the market respected.

passages.t: Why the market respected it: the zone removed the opposite zone.

passages.t: About 1,000 sell pips: the wow trade from the removed zone to the next one.

passages.t: The demand whose rally crossed the line and removed the supply is an arrival zone.

passages.t: Mirror case: the supply's drop crossed the line and removed the demand.

passages.t: The rules apply from 1 minute to monthly.

passages.t: The strong supplies on the right side of the trendline were respected.

Same supply, two outcomes. Left: its drop closes below the demand, so the supply is strong (sell limit, set & forget). Right: the drop fails to remove the demand, so the supply is weak (no set & forget).
Redrawn from his '(2) WOW' sketch (04:33): supply #1 at the top, supply #2 lower (he circles it), demand at the bottom. The demand's rally removes #2 and the zigzag fills the box up to #1.

His EURUSD monthly (08:03-16:15), redrawn: the box at the base of the drop is strong because the drop removed the demands below it. A descending trendline runs through the peaks, and each rally back is a correction that taps the supply and fails.
Arrival zone: the demand's rally (1) crosses the descending trendline and (2) removes the last supply. With only rule 1 it would be an inheritance zone.

Putting limit orders on every fresh zone instead of only strong ones. Trading a supply whose drop failed to remove the demand below as if it were strong. Entering on the high timeframe and carrying a huge stop loss. Holding a correction-side trade as if it were a trend trade.
Calling a zone an arrival zone when it only broke the trendline (that is an inheritance zone).

Did this zone's move remove an opposite zone? (strong / weak) Is it a simple strong zone, a wow trade zone or an arrival zone? For an arrival zone: trendline crossed? Opposite (last) zone removed? Is this the first touch? (set & forget) Otherwise use confirmation. Am I trading with the trendline (impulse) or against it (correction)? Is the entry on a low timeframe with a small stop?
“Whichever zone removed the opposite zone, that zone becomes a strong zone.” “High time frame we only use for direction, not for entries.” “Wow means good pips.”

Kevin's 'chain / qualification' rule (a zone qualifies if its move removed an opposing zone or trendline) is the core of Raja's 'strong zone'. Raja turns it into a strict gate: only strong zones get pending orders.
Both mentors use 'arrival zone' for a zone that broke a trendline and took out an opposing zone. Raja adds the 'inheritance zone' (trendline broken, opposite zone not removed) as its weak twin.
Seiden's freshness rule (the first return is best) matches Raja's 'first time always set & forget'.
Raja's 98% figure is his claim, not a tested statistic; neither PDF course gives such a number.

Only three kinds of fresh zone earn a pending order. Everything else is weak. At a school race, many kids say they are fast. The teacher only believes the ones who actually beat someone. One kid beat a rival: strong. One kid beat a rival and also jumped the fence on the way: that is the arrival kid, the best of all. A kid who only jumped the fence but beat nobody is just showing off.
Strong = beat a rival. Arrival = jumped the fence AND beat a rival. Only jumped the fence = inheritance (weak).
Pending orders only on three strong types: simple strong zone, wow trade zone and arrival zone.
Arrival = crossed the trendline AND removed the opposite zone. Only crossed the line = inheritance zone, weak.
First touch of a strong zone = set and forget. Trade with the trendline to hold; corrections are short-term.
Price falls along a descending trendline and leaves supplies on the way down.

passages.h: Step: A demand forms at the bottom
passages.t: Price pauses at the low and builds a demand. Is it strong or weak? Its leg-out will tell us.

passages.h: Step: Rule 1: it crosses the trendline
passages.t: The rally closes above the descending trendline. That is rule 1. With only this, the zone would be an inheritance zone.

passages.h: Step: Rule 2: it removes the last supply
passages.t: The rally also closes above the last supply. Both rules on one leg-out: this demand is an arrival zone. Raja calls these the most important zones.

passages.h: Step: First touch: set and forget
passages.t: On the first return, a buy limit at the top of the arrival zone, stop under it, target the next supply. Price respects it.

Three strong zone types? - Simple strong zone, wow trade zone, arrival zone. Simple strong zone? - Its move removed the opposite zone. Found mostly on CP levels. Arrival zone rules? - 1: crosses the trendline. 2: removes the opposite zone. Only rule 1 met? - Inheritance zone. Weak. First touch of a strong zone? - Set and forget. Indicators? - Not used. They are slow; the market is fast.

The second half of the strong-zones session. Raja explains how many times a zone can be used (1st touch set & forget, 2nd and 3rd only with confirmation, the 4th usually breaks), what confirmation means (apply the arrival-zone rules on a lower timeframe), and the weak zone types that need confirmation: inheritance, overlap, flip, out-of-trendline, tested and plain weak zones. Total: 3 strong + 6 weak = 9 zone types.

1st touch set & forget; 2nd and 3rd touch confirmation only; expect the 4th to break. Confirmation = on a lower timeframe, the trendline is crossed AND the last opposite zone is removed; then use that new strong LTF zone. Confirmation timeframes: monthly/weekly -> daily/H4; daily -> H1; H1 -> 15m/5m/1m. No confirmation = no trade; move to an easier pair.
Inheritance, overlap, flip, out-of-trendline, tested and plain weak zones get confirmation only, never a blind limit order.
A zone formed inside an old opposite zone (no gap) is an overlap zone and weak, even if it removed a zone.
A daily zone without an H1 confirmation is skipped; wait for it to be removed and trade the new zone.

passages.h: How many times a zone can be used
passages.t: First touch: set & forget. Second touch: only if the market gives you confirmation. Third touch: again only with confirmation. Fourth time: expect the market to break the zone. The same count applies to strong and arrival zones that have already been tested.

Confirmation = the same rules as the arrival zone, applied on a lower timeframe. Example: a tested monthly supply. Go to the daily or H4. Price was rising there along an ascending trendline. Wait for the lower timeframe to cross the trendline AND remove the last demand. The supply that did this on the lower timeframe is now strong; put a set & forget order on it.
On a high timeframe this looks like one long candle into the zone and then the next candle dropping.
Timeframe pairs: monthly / weekly trades confirm on the daily or H4; daily trades confirm on H1; H1 trades confirm on 15m, 5m or 1m.

If the market gives no confirmation, do not trade that pair. Move on and look for the easiest pairs, not hard ones. Traders think they will miss the entry; you only trade when the market gives you a 'safe pass' (likely: a clear signal). He calls confirmation the main key of forex trading.

On the EURJPY monthly (21:43) he sketches both views side by side: a box with a few big candles reaching into it (the HTF view), and a zigzag climbing along a trendline into the same box (the LTF view where the cross and the removal happen).

A tested monthly arrival area (23:20-23:34: a wide demand box at the bottom of the GBPJPY monthly with a smaller box inside it where price based). On H4 (24:22): price crossed the descending trendline (rule 1) and removed the last supply (rule 2); the green demand box that did it became the strong H4 zone.
Price came back, triggered the entry and gave about 800 pips; the measuring tool on his H4 chart shows the run.
He chose the zone that removed the opposite zone, not simply the lowest one; the lowest one was an inheritance zone.

Daily example (25:27): the same green demand on GBPJPY daily, under a steep descending line. A supply removed by a demand made that demand strong; while rising, price removed another supply, giving a second entry on the new demand.

If price crosses the trendline but cannot remove the opposite zone (because that opposite zone was removed by a CP level or another strong area), the previous top supply becomes an inheritance zone, not an arrival zone.
Example A: supplies #1 (top) and #2. #2 removed the demand, so it is strong: sell limit there, set & forget. #1 at the top is an inheritance zone, technically weak: use confirmation only.
Market makers create fake signals too: next to arrival zones they also leave inheritance zones. It is your job to tell them apart.

Why still watch the top zone: market makers can lose power when price reaches a high-timeframe supply, so they may sell there. The technical rule is to sell from the top only if the market gives confirmation; otherwise wait for a strong zone that removes something.

Same picture as Example A, with one difference: no gap between the supply and the demand. The supply was created inside the area of an old demand (or a demand inside an old supply). That is an overlap zone: technically weak, even though it removed a zone.
Most supply & demand traders lose money here: they think the zone is strong because it removed something, but the market does not respect it.

Gold example (XAUUSD monthly, 32:52): a long green demand box from the earlier range, and the supply the student wanted to sell drawn inside that old demand area. He told him to use confirmation; the market ignored the supply and rallied through, toward 3k as he expected.
Price moves in a zigzag. A broken resistance becomes support: other methods call it higher highs and higher lows, distribution and accumulation; in supply & demand it is the flip zone.
The CP level found at the flip area is weak because it overlaps the previous supply. Zoom out and you will see it was an overlap.

Bitcoin example (BTCUSD weekly, 35:28): a demand box at the bottom, a flip box in the middle where old resistance became support, a horizontal line at the top and a steep ascending trendline. The middle area had overlaps; one level only showed as a CP level on a lower timeframe. He expects the next pullback to land in an overlap zone.
Patterns like flags, double tops / bottoms and head and shoulders are other names for the same behaviour. Just focus on strong zones (limit order) and treat tested zones with confirmation.
You trade with the trend. If a zone was missed and is still fresh, but the market has since crossed the major trendline, use confirmation there.
Reason: the major trendline is no longer bullish (it is now bearish), so the zone is 'out of trendline'. Out-of-trendline zones never get set & forget.
Strong (pending order, set & forget): simple strong zone (removed the opposite zone), wow trade zone, arrival zone.

Weak (confirmation only): weak zone that removed nothing, inheritance zone, flip zone, out-of-trendline zone, overlap zone, tested / retested zone. On every zone, first decide whether it is strong or weak. Weak means confirmation.

passages.h: More on touches and confirmation (Urdu recordings and live sessions)
passages.t: Daily zone: look for the confirmation on H1. If H1 gives no entry, let the zone be removed and trade the new opposite zone instead (course 2, 43:14).

passages.h: More on touches and confirmation (Urdu recordings and live sessions)
passages.t: Higher timeframes follow the rules more and can give repeated confirmations; lower timeframes make more fakes (tap once, remove the next time) (course 2). HTF zones survive more taps: an H1 zone often breaks on the 2nd tap, a monthly or H4 zone can hold 3-4 if HTF pressure is there (Apr 2025 class). Mar 5 in short: 1st, 2nd and 3rd touch fine, the 4th very risky.

passages.h: More on touches and confirmation (Urdu recordings and live sessions)
passages.t: When the HTF is heading the other way (or its zone is weak), any strong LTF zone gets retested once, moves a little, and is broken on the 2nd or 3rd visit (2022 meeting).

passages.h: More on touches and confirmation (Urdu recordings and live sessions)
passages.t: A confirmation needs a proper close beyond the zone, not just a rejection (2022 meeting). Even one pip beyond counts as broken (Feb 2025 class, likely).

passages.h: More on touches and confirmation (Urdu recordings and live sessions)
passages.t: The confirmation trade happens inside the HTF candle: the LTF crosses and removes the zone while the monthly shows only a wick, so take it on the spot on the LTF or the pips are lost (course 2, 35:58; Feb 2025 class).

21:43 EURJPY monthly sketch: a supply box with big HTF candles reaching it, and the LTF zigzag rising along a trendline into the box. Confirmation = the LTF crosses the line and removes the last demand.
22:36-23:34 GBPJPY monthly: a wide demand box at the lows (the tested arrival area) and a smaller box inside it where he looks for the entry.

24:22-24:52 GBPJPY H4: the green demand that crossed the descending line and removed the last supply; the measuring tool shows the run of about 800 pips. He picks this zone, not the lowest base (the inheritance zone).
25:27-26:16 GBPJPY daily: the same demand on the daily, the steep descending line, and the later range sitting on the box.
27:49-32:06 GBPJPY monthly again with the box and his marks: the tested monthly zone is traded only through LTF confirmation.
28:15-31:00 Examples A and B (inheritance, overlap) are explained verbally; no chart frame of that drawing was captured.
32:52 XAUUSD monthly: an old demand box with a supply drawn inside it. The overlap supply failed and gold rallied through it.
35:28-36:49 BTCUSD weekly: demand box, flip box, top line and a steep ascending line. Flip areas are overlap zones: confirmation only.
38:36 BCHUSD weekly: a demand box under price. Crypto was still stuck on the monthly; buy limits go only on strong zones.

passages.h: Chart: [21:43] EURJPY monthly: confirmation sketch, big HTF candles into a supply box and the LTF zigzag along a trendline
passages.t: Tested zone: no set & forget. Go to daily / H4 and wait for the trendline cross plus the last demand removed. On the HTF this shows only as a long candle into the zone and the next candle dropping.

passages.h: Chart: [23:20] GBPJPY monthly: a wide demand box at the lows with a smaller box inside
passages.t: This is the tested monthly arrival area; the smaller box is where he looks for LTF confirmation.

passages.h: Chart: [24:22] GBPJPY H4: green demand box under a descending trendline, with the measuring tool
passages.t: Rule 1: trendline crossed. Rule 2: last supply removed. The demand that did it is strong. The entry triggered and gave about 800 pips.

passages.h: Chart: [24:52] GBPJPY H4: the outline of the same demand zone after the move
passages.t: He uses the zone that removed the opposite zone, not the lowest base (that one is an inheritance zone).

passages.h: Chart: [25:27] GBPJPY daily: the same demand on the daily chart with the descending line
passages.t: The same arrival pattern is visible on the daily; a second demand while rising gave a second entry.

passages.h: Chart: [27:49] GBPJPY monthly: the demand box at the lows with his marks
passages.t: Monthly / weekly trades confirm on daily or H4.

passages.h: Chart: [32:52] XAUUSD monthly: a supply drawn inside an old demand area (overlap)
passages.t: The supply removed zones but sat inside an old demand: overlap, weak. The market ignored it and gold rallied through.

passages.h: Chart: [35:28] BTCUSD weekly: demand box, flip box, top line and a steep ascending line
passages.t: Old resistance turned support is a flip area; it overlaps older zones, so confirmation only.

passages.h: Chart: [38:36] BCHUSD weekly: a demand box under price
passages.t: Buy limit only on a strong zone; weak zones need confirmation.

Confirmation as he sketched it on the EURJPY monthly (21:43). On the HTF it is only a long candle into the tested supply and then a drop. On the LTF, price crosses its ascending trendline and removes the last demand, and that new LTF supply gets the set & forget order.

His GBPJPY H4 (24:22-24:52), redrawn: the demand whose rally crossed the descending trendline and closed above the last supply is the arrival zone. The retest triggered the buy and the move ran about 800 pips. The deeper base is an inheritance zone.
Example A: a gap between supply #2 and the demand it removed makes it strong. Example B: the supply is built inside an old demand (no gap), so it is an overlap zone and weak.
Raja's nine zone types: three strong (pending order) and six weak (confirmation).
Using set & forget on a zone that has already been tested. Trading an overlap zone because it 'removed' something.
Picking the lowest (inheritance) demand instead of the one that removed the opposite zone. Forcing a trade when the lower timeframe gives no confirmation.
Using a set & forget order on a still-fresh zone after the major trendline has turned against it. Taking a rejection wick as confirmation instead of waiting for a close.

How many times has this zone been touched? Strong or weak? If weak, which kind (inheritance / overlap / flip / out of trendline / tested / plain weak)? Is there a gap between this zone and the zone it removed? For confirmation: which lower timeframe? Trendline crossed? Last opposite zone removed? Is the major trendline still on my side? No confirmation: did I move on to another pair?
“Confirmation is the main key of the Forex trading.” “You can only trade when the market gives you a safe pass.” “First check: that is a strong zone or a weak zone.”

Raja's confirmation (lower-timeframe trendline cross + opposite zone removed) is the same as Kevin's confirmation entry. His use of it for 2nd and 3rd touches is a firmer touch-count rule than Kevin's.
Seiden treats a broken zone as a possible flip only with conditions. Raja flags every flip area as weak because it overlaps an older zone, so confirmation only.
'Inheritance zone' and 'overlap zone' are Raja's names; neither PDF course defines them. The overlap idea is close to the course rulebook's 'look left' check for an older zone under the base.
'Out-of-trendline zone' (a fresh zone that ends up against the major trendline) has no counterpart in Kevin's or Seiden's material.
Kevin voids zones after deep penetration; Raja allows up to three uses (the 2nd and 3rd with confirmation).

Every zone is strong or weak. Weak ones must prove themselves first. A rubber band stretches fine the first time. The second and third time you test it gently before you trust it. The fourth time it usually snaps. Zones are the same. Raja also warns about fake strong zones: some look tough but were born inside an old zone, like a band that was already frayed.
Touch 1 = new rubber band. Touch 2 and 3 = test it gently. Touch 4 = it snaps.
1st touch set and forget; 2nd and 3rd only with confirmation; expect the 4th to break. Confirmation = the arrival rules on a lower timeframe: line crossed AND last opposite zone removed.
9 types: 3 strong (pending order) and 6 weak (inheritance, overlap, flip, out-of-trendline, tested, plain weak).
At the peak, supply #1 drops and closes below the rising trendline. Rule 1 of an arrival zone is met.
The drop stops above the demand. Rule 2 is not met. So #1 is not an arrival zone; it is an inheritance zone.
Price bounces, builds supply #2 and drops again. This time a candle closes below the demand. #2 removed the opposite zone, so #2 is strong. #1 gave its power to #2.

passages.h: Step: Sell limit on #2, confirmation on #1
passages.t: Put a set and forget sell limit on #2. #1 at the top gets confirmation only: market makers leave inheritance zones next to arrival zones as traps.

passages.h: Step: The strong zone is respected
passages.t: Price taps #2 and drops. Same picture, two zones, two very different treatments.

Touch rules? - 1st set and forget, 2nd and 3rd confirmation, 4th usually breaks. Confirmation? - Arrival rules on a lower timeframe: line crossed + last opposite zone removed. Confirm a daily trade on? - H1.
Overlap zone? - Born inside an old opposite zone (no gap). Weak even if it removed a zone.
Out-of-trendline zone? - A fresh zone after the major trendline turned against it. Confirmation only. How many zone types? - 9: 3 strong, 6 weak. No confirmation? - No trade. Move to an easier pair.

In a Q&A call Raja walks through the board he shared with students, applied to every pair: (1) pick the timeframe you follow (the HTF is for finding the wow trade; monthly direction, entries on daily / H4), (2) risk management, meaning a profit margin of 1:3, or at least 1:2, (3) the market condition, ranging or trending, (4) the market you trade (equity, bonds, stocks, cryptos) matched to your account, (5) the entry (pullback, breakout, and the flip area he explains as the third; the board also lists news), (6) the stop, placed away from the market structure, and (7) the target: fixed TP, trailing stop or swing management by moving the stop zone to zone.
He finishes with quick reviews of US oil (Brent on screen), GBPJPY, AUDCAD, USDCAD and AUDJPY.
Fix one direction timeframe per trade and judge pips on that timeframe; enter on a lower one.

Minimum profit margin 2x the stop; prefer 3x. If the margin is smaller than the stop, skip. Hold long only in trending conditions; trade ranges short-term. Match the instrument to your equity: no BTC, bonds or US30 on a $100 account.

Entries: a pullback limit on a strong zone; a breakout via H1 demand above the H1 trendline (short-term); the flip area with confirmation (long-term). No structure (meshing) = no trade. Swing management: move the stop to the second-latest zone, keeping one zone as a buffer. Practise on a cent or demo account until your trades have been reviewed. Keep XAUUSD off the low timeframes; use XAUAUD there.

His board reads: 'HIGH TF = WOW' and 'MONTHLY -> ENTRY DAILY / H4'. Decide which timeframe you follow (monthly, weekly, daily or H4) and be strict with it. This is for direction; entries are always on the low timeframe.
Focus on that timeframe's pips: monthly trader -> monthly pips; daily / weekly trader -> daily / weekly pips. The main reason to use the high timeframe is to identify the wow trade.

The board shows the two ratios as 1:3 and 1:2. You need a profit margin of 3x the stop (he says 'three time'), or at least 2x. Then both the supply and demand levels are usable. Measure on the high timeframe how many pips are left, then trade those pips.
If the supply and demand are close together and the profit margin is smaller than the stop loss, it is not a good idea to trade.

On NZDCHF daily (04:07) he marks the demand price is sitting in (weak, wait for its removal) and counts 25% / 50% of the move to show a 2x margin; on the next screen (04:50) a supply box sits right above a demand box: the margin is smaller than the stop, so no trade.
He sketches the first case in red on NZDCHF daily (06:09): a demand box and the candles that rallied from it, then price dropping back toward the demand while the trendline still points up.
Ranging (correction) example: price respected a demand and moved up, now drops back towards the demand while the trendline still points up. Price is retracing to the trendline.
Another range: after the entry price goes sideways (one candle up, one down) and even crosses the trendline. That is also ranging.
If the market already moved up and crossed the trendline with a demand below, you can sell on the lower timeframe down to that previous demand (trading the range / pullback).
Trending: price respects the demand and the demand sits above the trendline, so you trade with the trend.
In a range you cannot hold long term; only trend trades are held. In a trend you can hold for very good pips.

passages.h: 4. Market: equity and what you trade
passages.t: The board's step 4 is 'MARKET: equity, bonds, stocks, cryptos'. Check your equity first. With $100 you cannot trade bonds and you should not trade Bitcoin (big moves, big spread); even with $1,000 he advises against Bitcoin.

passages.h: 4. Market: equity and what you trade
passages.t: His broker (transcribed 'paper stone', likely Pepperstone) has a 0.10 minimum size on some instruments (as he describes it), which is too big for small accounts on volatile markets.

passages.h: 4. Market: equity and what you trade
passages.t: Ethereum is acceptable. Smaller coins with small spreads (Solana, Dogecoin, ADA) are tradeable even on $100. AVAX moves a lot. Indices: US30 is risky for a $100 account; he names GER30 (likely) and NAS as easier.

passages.h: 4. Market: equity and what you trade
passages.t: Currencies: almost any pair is fine at 0.01 lots, but be careful with pairs that move a lot (e.g. USDMXN).

passages.h: 4. Market: equity and what you trade
passages.t: Do not fix yourself to one or two pairs (e.g. only gold); most traders lose that way. As an S&D trader pick whichever pair is easiest at the moment and in a trend.

The board lists 'Pullbacks, Breakout, News'. In the call he explains three entries: pullback, breakout and the flip area; news is listed on the board but not explained. Pullback: a buy limit order on a strong zone.

Breakout: when a high-timeframe supply is removed, price can run to the next one, often about 2.5x the size of the correction (his rule of thumb, 'not essential'). Do not lose those pips: go to H1 and buy H1 demands above the H1 trendline. This is for the short term.
Flip area: when H1 then crosses its trendline, wait for the pullback into the flip area (on daily or H4) and buy there with confirmation. This is for holding long term.
Remember: a flip area is a weak (overlap) zone; use the buy limit only when it has been broken properly. The best areas are always valleys and peaks.
A wow trade can be traded several times: breakout entry, then the flip entry, each time targeting the daily CP (likely: the next continuation zone / TP).

passages.h: 6. Stop: away from the market structure
passages.t: The board's step 6 is 'STOP: AWAY Market Structure': the stop belongs beyond the structure that has to break for the idea to be wrong, which is why he follows the structure of impulses and corrections.

passages.h: 6. Stop: away from the market structure
passages.t: Follow the structure of impulses and corrections. While price respects a buying structure (impulse side) you can buy on the low timeframe.

passages.h: 6. Stop: away from the market structure
passages.t: When price starts 'meshing' (chopping without shape) there is no structure: wait. If the daily already moved a lot, wait for it to drop back to the trendline, or for the structure to break and a new one to form.

passages.h: 6. Stop: away from the market structure
passages.t: A zone already tested with the market still meshing there: you cannot know whether to buy, so stay out.

passages.h: 7. Targets: fixed TP, trailing stop, swing
passages.t: The board's step 7 is 'TARGETS: fixed, trailing stop'. Example (23:02): NZDCHF monthly with a steep purple descending trendline; from a strong supply the fixed TP is the opposite zone. Fixed TP: from a strong supply, put the TP at the opposite zone.

passages.h: 7. Targets: fixed TP, trailing stop, swing
passages.t: If the opposite zone is weak but far from your entry, you can hold. When price reaches the high curve area (likely: the overbought top of the high-timeframe range, where sellers sit), move your stop loss up.

passages.h: 7. Targets: fixed TP, trailing stop, swing
passages.t: Trailing stop: if you cannot watch the screen, measure the distance to the demand (e.g. 120 pips) and set a trailing stop of that size. If the market reverses 120 pips it closes; if it removes the supply above, the stop keeps following. Use it after the weak opposite zone is removed.

passages.h: 7. Targets: fixed TP, trailing stop, swing
passages.t: Swing: an H1 zone you entered from becomes an H4 zone after a few candles, then a daily, then a weekly one. After two more demands form, move your stop to the second-latest zone, because a reversal needs a trendline cross, one zone removed and then a second zone removed. The first zone is left as a buffer.

US oil (Brent on screen, 28:56-29:56): monthly box at the highs and H4 with two descending lines, a supply box at the top and demand boxes below. Still in monthly / weekly demand; the first TP is the current structure; for more, wait for the supply above to break, then buy the fresh demand.

GBPJPY (30:56-31:56): daily below a steep descending line with a box (supply), monthly stuck in a supply box at the highs, and the daily is sideways. Wait for H1 to cross its trendline and for the structure to break, then sell on H1 only.
AUDCAD: in a weak monthly supply. For a sell, the daily must cross the trendline and break the structure; buys only with confirmation; ranging, so wait.
USDCAD (32:56-33:44): H4 sold off then rallied; a horizontal line marks where the new H4 demand is forming. Monthly demand, weekly respected: wait for that fresh demand, then buy.

AUDJPY (34:44): monthly up and the daily above its trendline. H1 crossed its descending line and he marks a box below, but there is no H4 zone yet and H1 is meshing, so leave it. On another pair, H4 supply vs H1 buy: short-term trade only.

Brokers: he prefers Australian-regulated brokers, Pepperstone first (Razor account), then IC Markets (course 2; Apr 2025 class; Mar 5). Avoid small local brokers: they can widen spreads or print fake candles to hunt stops. If a stop is hunted, compare with TradingView and claim it back (Mar 5).
Each broker's server time shapes the candles differently, so analyse and trade on your own broker's chart (Apr 7).

Practise on a cent account before going live: a 10-20 USD deposit shows as roughly 1,000-2,000 cents and 0.01 lot risks almost nothing. It feels more real than a demo, though spreads are higher (Mar 5).
Not live yet: finish the sessions, practise 3-4 weeks and have him review your trades first (Feb 25, Mar 5, Apr 2025 class).

Timing: Tuesday to Thursday are best for the LTF; Monday's open and Friday's close are volatile (Apr 30). The NFP release on Friday jumps the market (low-TF part 2). Crypto often retraces at the weekend and resumes on Monday evening (Jun 25).

Gold on the low timeframes is full of fakes (high spread, many small traders). For LTF gold he uses XAUAUD, which moves more cleanly in steps (Mar 5, Apr 7, Jun 25). Stocks and indices: stay on the daily and above (Feb 18, Apr 7).
He does not use bots or indicators (Mar 13). The EMA 5/15 crossover he once showed was only for a struggling student; supply and demand is enough (Apr 2025 class).
