His seven-step board, redrawn: 1 Time frames (the HTF finds the wow trade; monthly direction, entry on daily / H4), 2 Risk management 1:3 or at least 1:2, 3 Conditions, 4 Market, 5 Entries (pullbacks, breakout, news), 6 Stop away from the market structure, 7 Targets (fixed or trailing).
Step 2: room from the entry to the opposite zone must be 2-3x the stop. Zones too close together means skip.
Step 5, three entries: a pullback limit on a strong zone; a breakout (HTF supply removed, buy H1 demands above the H1 trendline); a flip area with confirmation after the H1 trendline break.
Step 7, swing management: an H1 entry zone grows into an H4 / daily zone. Move the stop under the second-latest demand, keeping one zone as a buffer.

Trading when supply and demand are so close that the reward is smaller than the stop. Trading Bitcoin or US30 with a tiny account. Marrying one instrument (e.g. only gold). Holding a range trade as if it were a trend trade. Using a buy limit on a flip / overlap area without confirmation. Trading a meshing market with no structure. Trading XAUUSD on M1-M15. Going live before finishing the sessions.

1. Which timeframe am I following for direction? Is there a wow trade on it? 2. Profit margin to the opposite zone: 1:3? At least 1:2? 3. Is the market ranging or trending? (hold only in a trend) 4. Does this market suit my equity and lot size? 5. Which entry: pullback, breakout or flip area?
6. Is the stop away from the market structure? Is there a clear structure, or is price meshing? 7. Target: fixed TP, trailing stop or swing stop moves?
“You need at least three time or two time reward.” “Don't fix with the one or two pairs.” “For the long term we can only trade with the trend.”
Raja's 2-3x margin is close to Kevin's and Seiden's profit-margin / R-multiple filters; Seiden's run-out ≥ 3x zone height is a different measure.
Picking the instrument by account size (no BTC, US30 or bonds on $100; small-spread coins OK) is new; the PDFs do not cover broker or instrument limits.
His breakout entry (buy H1 demands above the H1 trendline after an HTF supply is removed) is similar to Kevin's breakout idea; Seiden prefers waiting for the return to the origin.
The ~2.5x 'impulse vs correction' rule of thumb is Raja's own heuristic, not from either course.

Swing stop management (move to the second-latest zone because a reversal needs a trendline cross + two zones removed) applies his reversal rule; Kevin trails behind new demand/supply in a similar way. Trailing-stop sizing by the pip distance to the demand is new.

Seven quick checks before every trade, like a pilot before take-off. A pilot never just jumps in and flies. She checks the fuel, the weather, the runway and the wings, one by one. Raja checks seven things on every pair. Timeframe, profit room, trend or range, account size, entry type, structure and exit plan. If one check fails, the plane stays on the ground.
The seven steps are a pilot's pre-flight checklist. One red light and you do not take off.
Fix your direction timeframe; demand 2-3x room to the opposite zone; hold only in a trend.
Match the instrument to your equity. Pick an entry: pullback, breakout or flip area (with confirmation).
No structure (meshing) = no trade. Swing exit: stop under the second-latest zone, one zone kept as a buffer.
Pick the timeframe you follow for direction. Then measure: from the demand to the opposite zone there is far more than 3x the stop. Step 2 passes.
Price respects the demand and keeps rising, so it is trending: you may hold. The pair suits a small account at 0.01 lots. Entry type: a pullback buy limit on a strong zone.
Price keeps making impulses up and small pauses. That is a clear buying structure. If it started meshing, he would wait.

passages.h: Step: Step 7: swing stop, one zone as buffer
passages.t: Two new demands have formed. Move the stop under the second-latest one (zone 1), not the latest. A reversal needs a line cross, one zone removed, then a second, so one zone stays as a buffer.

passages.h: Step: Keep stepping the stop up
passages.t: Zone 3 forms. Now the second-latest is zone 2, so the stop moves under zone 2. Price reaches the opposite zone.
Step 1? - Pick the timeframe you follow for direction. Enter lower. Step 2? - Profit margin at least 2x, ideally 3x the stop. Step 3? - Ranging or trending? Hold only in a trend.

Step 5: three entries? - Pullback limit, breakout (H1 demand above the H1 line), flip area with confirmation. Step 6: meshing? - No structure = no trade. Step 7: swing stop? - Under the second-latest zone, keeping one zone as a buffer. Marry one pair? - No. Pick whichever pair is easiest and trending.

A live review across forex pairs, indices and crypto. The routine: read direction and the target on the monthly / weekly, check the daily trendline and zones, then go to the 15-minute chart for a fresh zone and use the 5-minute only as confirmation. A trendline counts as broken only when a big departure candle closes beyond it; small candles drifting across do not count. Zones built from long, lengthy candles are not basing zones.
Direction and target come from monthly / weekly; never enter from them. Entry on a fresh 15m zone on the correct side of the trendline; 5m only for confirmation.

A trendline break needs a big departure candle closing beyond it; small candles drifting across do not count. Do not buy into a supply that has not been removed; wait for its removal (or sell it). Long, lengthy candles are not a base. If the supply above is removed, look only for buys. Use the LTF only when the HTF gives no entry; stop at M15 once you have a zone. No zone on the LTF = no trade.
Monthly: is price above or below the trendline, and is it in a monthly demand or supply? This gives the direction and whether there are 'buy pips' or 'sell pips'.

Weekly / daily: is there a zone? Has the daily crossed its trendline? With no supply above and the daily pushing up, the market can move up more. 15 minute: use the fresh demand (for a buy) above the trendline. This is the entry chart.
5 minute: confirmation, used as a backup when you found the trade on the 15m. He prefers 15m because it is easy to read; 1m is risky and gives poor signals.
His summary: find the target from the high timeframe, use the low timeframe for the entry.
A change of direction needs a proper departure candle: a big candle that closes below (or above) the trendline. If a lot of small candles cross the trendline without a departure candle, wait.
Once the departure candle has closed beyond the line, the market can drop any time and you have a new zone for the trade.
He combines three things for a stronger signal: price crosses the zone, crosses the trendline, and removes the opposite zone.
A pair in monthly demand but below the monthly trendline: the weekly had no demand, the daily was crossing its trendline with no supply above, so he looked for a 15m fresh demand to buy.

AUDJPY (likely): pushing up on the monthly but below the weekly trendline. Better to wait for the supply to be removed before buying; with no buy pips he would rather wait for a sell after a full departure candle on the 15m.

CADJPY: the daily was heading into a supply that is still below the trendline, so sell from that fresh supply. A student who sold got stopped out because the H4 supply was an overlap zone with a demand there. Long, lengthy candles are not considered basing; only the real base is a zone.

Bitcoin: the student bought the last demand; Raja told him to move the stop up and hold. Bitcoin cash was near demand; DOT was in the low curve area (likely: near the bottom of the HTF range), so wait for the demand.

US30 / NAS100 / UK100 / US500 / US2000: US30 was in the high curve area with a once-tested (weak) zone. UK100 was stuck in a weak supply (confirmation only). US2000 sat in weekly demand and had crossed the trendline ('90% chance for the buy'). USDJPY: up on the weekly, the daily zone weak; trade the H1 / H4 zone.
EURCHF: the monthly had already dropped a lot; use a 15m demand above the trendline for a buy.
A pair where the supply had been removed: only buys, no sells. A demand retested many times can break.
NZDCAD on 5m: already in demand; to drop it must break that demand first, so hold the long from the only zone.
USDCNH: removed one demand and respected the second; the zone was not great but it was the lower-timeframe zone that held.
Pairs driven by market makers tend to go into profit after a few hours or days if the direction is right.
He expects Bitcoin to reach 100k because of the halving (transcribed 'heavily'), which halves new supply (his view, not a rule of the method).
Set & forget on a strong zone; confirmation on 1m is risky, so prefer 15m with 5m confirmation. Practice makes perfect: it looks simple when he explains it and harder on your own chart.

passages.h: Three low-timeframe styles (low-TF class part 2, live session Mar 5)
passages.t: Use the LTF only when the HTF gives nothing. Style 1, missed HTF entry: if the daily/H4 entry was taken or missed, drop to H1 and trade its zone on the trendline; if H1 is tested too, go to M15/M30. Stop at M15 once you have a zone; do not go down to M5 (Mar 5).

passages.h: Three low-timeframe styles (low-TF class part 2, live session Mar 5)
passages.t: Style 2: a fixed chain H1 -> M15 -> M5 with the entry on M5 (Mar 5). Or: you know an H1 demand will break, so sell the pips to the next demand on the LTF after its trendline cross (low-TF part 2).

passages.h: Three low-timeframe styles (low-TF class part 2, live session Mar 5)
passages.t: Style 3: flip areas on an M15 line chart. Each structure break makes the last low or high a flip area; trade the zones near them, preferring the one that broke its last low/high over a CP in between. It works on the HTF too, but the stop gets too big.

passages.h: Three low-timeframe styles (low-TF class part 2, live session Mar 5)
passages.t: Do not trade corrections on the LTF: it builds aggressive new trendlines in the impulses. A correction sell might pay 2 pips while the impulse pays 600-700 (Mar 5). The realignment area is where the M15 and M5 zones coincide.

passages.h: Three low-timeframe styles (low-TF class part 2, live session Mar 5)
passages.t: On the LTF the market can reverse within one candle: no zone, no trade (low-TF part 2). About 90% of LTF moves fake (stop hunts); the HTF needs big news to hunt stops (Jun 25).

passages.h: Three low-timeframe styles (low-TF class part 2, live session Mar 5)
passages.t: Market makers rarely look below the daily; swing traders and retail watch H4, so more entries form on H4. If H4 is missed, M15 keeps giving entries because the market runs in sequence (low-TF part 2).

passages.h: Three low-timeframe styles (low-TF class part 2, live session Mar 5)
passages.t: Missed-entry formula (Jun 25): if price starts dropping early and breaks its LTF trendline, sell directly; the stop is close. After a big candle beyond the departure, wait for a long-wick retrace and buy directly on the LTF: the market fills the wick.

passages.h: Chart: [14:36] AUDUSD M15 line chart (low-TF part 2): the flip area box after the structure break
passages.t: Each break of the last low/high makes a new flip area. Prefer the zone that broke the last low/high over a CP in between.
Left: small candles drift across the line, so it is not a proper break. Right: one full-bodied departure candle closes beyond the trendline, so the break is real.
Raja's top-down routine: monthly / weekly direction, daily / H4 trendline and zones, 15m fresh zone for the entry, 5m confirmation.

Taking a trendline break on a series of small candles. Using the 1m chart for confirmation. Selling from an H4 supply that overlaps a demand (it gets run over). Not moving the stop once the trade has moved off the last demand. Buying in the high curve area from a zone already tested once. Selling corrections on M5/M15. Going down to M1/M5 when M15 already has a zone.

Monthly / weekly: direction, buy pips or sell pips, which zone is the target? Daily / H4: trendline crossed? Is price sitting inside an opposite zone? Did a big departure candle close beyond the trendline? 15m: is there a fresh zone on the correct side of the trendline? Need 5m confirmation? (weak or tested zone) Is the zone a real base, not long lengthy candles? Any overlap?
“You find the target from the high time frame, use the low time frame for the entry.” “Wait for a proper departure candle that closes below the trend line.” “Practice makes perfect.”
Kevin's departure (leg-out) strength is about the move away from a base; Raja uses 'departure candle' for the candle that breaks the trendline. Same quality idea, applied to the trendline break.
The fixed 15m entry / 5m confirmation pairing is Raja's preference; Kevin's confirmation pairs depend on the trading timeframe.
'High curve / low curve area' matches the curve location (buy low, sell high in the HTF range) in Kevin's and Seiden's material.
Removing a long-candle range as 'not a base' matches the course's basing-candle definition (body < 50% of range).

A real break needs one big candle closing through the line. A fence keeps the sheep in the field. A few lambs squeeze their heads through the gaps and pull back. That is not an escape. Then one big ram smashes right through and keeps going. That is a real break, and now the flock can follow.
Small candles drifting across the line are lambs poking their heads through. The departure candle is the ram smashing the fence.
Direction and target from monthly/weekly; entry on a fresh 15m zone; 5m only as confirmation.
A trendline is broken only by a big departure candle closing beyond it. Small drifting candles do not count. Long, lengthy candles are not a base. Do not buy into a supply that has not been removed.
Price is falling along a descending trendline with lower highs.

passages.h: Step: Small candles drift across: no break
passages.t: A string of small candles creeps across the line. There is no departure candle, so Raja waits. Soon price falls back.
Now one big, full-bodied candle closes well above the line. That is a proper departure candle. Direction can change.

passages.h: Step: A fresh 15m demand above the line
passages.t: Right after the break, price builds a small fresh demand above the line. On the 15m this is the entry zone. Use the 5m only as a backup confirmation.

passages.h: Step: Target from the HTF, entry from the LTF
passages.t: Price retests the fresh demand and moves up. Find the target from the high timeframe; use the low timeframe for the entry.

Departure candle? - A big full-bodied candle that closes beyond the trendline. Small candles drifting across? - Not a break. Wait. Entry chart? - 15 minute. 5 minute only as confirmation. 1 minute for confirmation? - Risky. Poor signals. Long, lengthy candles? - Not a base. Supply above removed? - Look only for buys.
Raja's Urdu basics class (course 1, about 44 min), with points from the first class of a 2025 group (Feb 28). Price moves between higher-timeframe supply and demand because market makers trade it.

A zone is a base (1-6 small candles) followed by a departure that travels at least twice the base's size; the box runs from the wick to the thick body, the proximal line is the entry, the distal line the stop, and the opposite zone's proximal line the target. Zones come in two families: valleys/peaks (reversal) and CP levels (continuation); a CP that removed the opposite zone is a PCP. Trade fresh and original zones with the trend; retested zones are weaker.

Proximal line = entry, distal line = stop, opposite zone's proximal line = target. A zone needs a departure of at least twice the base size, and the departure candle must have closed. Demand: bottom wick to thick body; supply: top wick to thick body. 1-6 base candles; more than 6 = weak; never a single doji. Use the zone before a gap, not the gap.
Trade fresh and original zones with the trend; prefer valleys and peaks for reversals. After three CPs, do not trade the next CP.
He spent about eight years on S&D after 10-12 other methods. S&D works because market makers use it; retail uses Elliott waves, Gann or plain price action.
Milk-shop analogy: when demand is bigger than supply the price goes up (you pay double for the last packets); when there is too much supply about to expire it is sold cheap and the price drops.
The market moves between higher-timeframe (monthly) supply and demand: the supply's target is the demand and the other way round. Lower-timeframe valleys, peaks and trades happen in between.
Follow the daily, weekly and monthly (market makers do not look below the daily). Practise the HTF first to read direction; entries can then be on any timeframe, even M5.

passages.h: The box: entry, stop and target
passages.t: Supply on top, demand at the bottom. The proximal line is the limit entry (buy limit at the top of a demand, sell limit at the bottom of a supply); the distal line is the stop; the take profit is the proximal line of the opposite zone.

passages.h: The box: entry, stop and target
passages.t: Never sell into a falling market 'on execution', even on a 1,000-pip day: wait for price to reach the zone. Trade only from a zone, even if you wait a month.

passages.h: The box: entry, stop and target
passages.t: Price often tests only the thick body, but sometimes runs to the distal line and reverses: hold until the distal line is crossed. A broken zone usually drops a lot.

passages.h: The box: entry, stop and target
passages.t: Follow pips, not money: the same rules with 10 USD or 100,000; small size, grow the account.
Big candles are departure candles (any big or engulfing candle); small ones are base candles, like a wall's foundation. Colour does not matter (course 2; Feb 2025 class).
The departure must travel at least twice the base area away. No departure, no zone. Wait for the departure candle to close (beyond 50% of the base area) before drawing.
Draw a demand from the bottom wick to the thick body and ignore the top wick; a supply from the top wick to the body.
Leg-in candles must be in or near the base area; the leg-out leaves it. Ignore far wicks on the low timeframes.
Base count: 1-6 candles inside the box range is tradable; more than 6 is a weak zone. Three stair-stepping candles (each opening and closing above the last) are weak; one or two are fine.

Base shapes: the hammer is the most common; a marubozu (no wicks) shows strong imbalance; a doji is weak and its wick gets filled, so never trade a single doji; an extended range candle that fills the departure area can still be drawn; for an engulfing supply take the top wick and the thick body.

passages.h: Two families: valleys/peaks and CP levels
passages.t: Valleys and peaks: a V shape is a demand (drop-base-rally), an inverted V a supply (rally-base-drop). This is where reversals happen, so prefer them (Feb 2025 class).

passages.h: Two families: valleys/peaks and CP levels
passages.t: CP = continuation pattern: drop-base-drop or rally-base-rally. Like a bus stopping at a station to refuel on the way to its destination: the trend continues. After three CPs do not trade the next one; mostly the market retraces or reverses.

passages.h: Two families: valleys/peaks and CP levels
passages.t: PCP: a CP (or just a departure) that removes the opposite zone; any CP formed after removing the opposite zone is also a PCP. A plain CP is just a zone formed on the way to the destination. Every timeframe, even M1, has its own valleys and peaks (AUDUSD monthly example).
Weekend news (for example a military strike) can open Monday with a gap. Gaps always get filled, even after a year (Bitcoin weekly examples). Use the zone before the gap, not the gap itself.

passages.h: Fresh, original, retested and multiple zones
passages.t: Fresh = drop, base, reverse, and not revisited since (check the right side of the chart). Retested = revisited. Original = a zone formed by itself, with no prior zone behind it.

passages.h: Fresh, original, retested and multiple zones
passages.t: Multiple zones ('hierarchy'): zone 1 is strong but retested; zone 2 formed because of zone 1's impact; zone 3 from zone 2's impact (fresh); zone 4 formed by itself (original). Trade fresh and original zones; retested zones are usable on the monthly/daily, but strong zones are preferred.

passages.h: Fresh, original, retested and multiple zones
passages.t: You cannot trade every zone, only strong ones (the next lessons). S&D works with the trend: trade fresh zones along the trendline; when the trendline is crossed a bearish market becomes bullish and you start buying.

passages.h: Why it works: market makers vs retail
passages.t: Market makers (banks, big firms) make fake signals: retail sells on the LTF, makers buy, retail is stopped out, revenge-buys, and makers drop it again. That is how CP levels form. Trade with the market makers, not against them. Retail is retail whether the account is 1 USD or 100,000.

passages.h: Chart: [03:51] AUDUSD monthly as a board: supply box (S) on top, demand box (D) at the bottom
passages.t: Proximal line = entry, distal line = stop. Target = the opposite zone's proximal line.

passages.h: Chart: [10:00] Topic 1: valleys (V) and peaks (inverted V)
passages.t: V = drop-base-rally demand; inverted V = rally-base-drop supply. The other family is the CP (continuation) level.

passages.h: Chart: [22:58] EURUSD monthly as a board: base-candle shapes drawn as boxes
passages.t: Hammer, marubozu, doji, extended range candle, engulfing. Never trade a single doji: its wick gets filled.

passages.h: Chart: [32:13] Bitcoin monthly: multiple zones (the hierarchy) under the price
passages.t: Zones formed from an earlier zone's impact vs an original zone formed by itself. Trade fresh and original zones.

Selling into a falling market without a zone. Drawing a zone before the departure candle has closed. Treating a base of more than six candles, or a single doji, as a good zone. Trading the gap zone instead of the zone before the gap. Judging a base by candle colour.

Is there a clear base (1-6 candles) and a departure of at least 2x its size? Has the departure candle closed? Box drawn from the wick to the thick body, ignoring the far wick? Valley/peak or CP? Did it remove the opposite zone (PCP)? Fresh, original or retested? Is there a gap? Then use the zone before it. Entry at proximal, stop at distal, target at the opposite proximal line?
“Trade only with a zone, even if you have to wait a month.” “Market makers use supply and demand; that is why it is accurate.” “Follow the pips, not the money.”
The 2x departure rule and the 1-6 base-candle count are close to the course rulebook's basing definition; Raja adds that more than six candles or three stair-steps make a zone weak.
'Original' zone (formed by itself, no zone behind it) and the zone 'hierarchy' are his own terms.
PCP (a CP that removed the opposite zone) is his name for what Kevin calls a qualified continuation zone. Gap rule (gaps always fill; use the zone before the gap) is not in the PDFs.

Raja's first weekly 1:1 session with you (58 min). He answers one question: on which zones do you place buy/sell limit (set and forget) orders? Only on fresh strong zones (the leg-out removed the opposite zone) and arrival zones (the leg-out crossed the trendline AND removed the opposite zone), inside a wow-trade area and with the higher-timeframe trend.

Everything else - tested, retested, overlap, flip, inheritance and out-of-trendline zones, plus zones that did not remove anything - is weak and is traded only with lower-timeframe confirmation, or not at all.

He also adds price-action rules he uses alongside supply and demand: long wicks get filled, do not trade while price is 'meshing' between a supply and a demand, and in weak situations prefer the zone nearest the trendline.
Limit (set and forget) orders only on FRESH strong zones and arrival zones. Strong zone = its leg-out removed the opposite zone.
Arrival zone = leg-out crossed the trendline AND removed the opposite zone; usually at a valley or peak. Crossed the trendline but did not remove the opposite zone = inheritance zone = weak.
Tested and retested zones are weak: 1st touch set and forget, 2nd touch confirmation only.
Confirmation = trendline cross + opposite zone removed, one timeframe lower (H1 -> M15, M15 -> M5).
A supply formed inside or next to a demand (overlap) is weak, even if it removed something.

After the trendline is crossed, the old trend CP levels are weak; trade only fresh zones in the new direction. No wow area identified = no trade. Do not trade a strong zone against an opposite higher-timeframe zone sitting next to it. Long wicks get filled. Market meshing between a supply and a demand = no trade. In weak setups with stacked CPs, the zone nearest the trendline is the one respected.

Trade with the trend. Supply and demand works when you trade in the direction the market is going; in an uptrend you keep buying the zones that form above the trendline, in a downtrend you sell the supplies along the trendline.
Higher timeframe first. Market makers look at the high timeframes and hunt stop losses on the low ones, so read the HTF before going lower. He starts students on the HTF for that reason.

Only fresh zones. A tested zone is always a weak area: the second time price comes to it, it is going there to break it, not to respect it. Tested and retested zones are both weak. You still do not skip the entry - you use confirmation there.

Step 1 - strong zone: a zone whose move removed the opposite zone (a supply whose drop broke the demand below, or a demand whose rally broke the supply above). He says the market respects such a zone about 98 percent of the time.
Condition on the strong zone: do not trade it against the higher timeframe. If a daily strong supply sits right next to a monthly demand, price will tap the supply and remove it rather than drop.

Step 2 - wow trade (extension of pips): when a zone is removed, price is drawn to the next zone of the same type. Everything between the broken supply and the next supply is buy pips (and between a broken demand and the next demand, sell pips). Either price retests and enters from the new zone, or it goes straight; in both cases it goes to the target. Without an identified wow area you do not trade at all, because the direction is unknown.

In the wow area you go to the lower timeframe and keep trading with the trendline. Pips you "lose" on one timeframe while waiting for the break are picked up by trading the lower timeframe inside the same buying area.

Step 3 - arrival zone: two rules. (1) Price crosses the trendline, (2) the same move removes the opposite zone. Arrival zones are usually found at valleys and peaks (swing lows and highs). The market respects them.
Trendlines: an ascending trendline joins at least two higher lows; when it is crossed, a descending trendline is drawn across at least two lower highs (peaks). Both exist on low and high timeframes.

How many times can a zone be traded? First touch: set and forget (limit order). Second touch: you do not know whether the market is going to break it, so go to a lower timeframe (weekly, daily or H4, depending on the zone) and wait for confirmation. On a monthly zone that means: on the daily/H4 price crosses the trendline and removes the opposite zone; then enter, with the stop at that supply or above it (likely).
Confirmation timeframe: one step below the zone. A zone seen on H1 is confirmed on M15; a zone on M15 is confirmed on M5.

An arrival zone is hard to break on the first test. If the market wants to break it, it tests it twice, comes to the extreme point, and then breaks it. Multiple zones keep forming along the way and you trade them in that sequence.

The nine zone types (his board at 50:27): strong side = strong zone, wow trade, arrival zone (three, of which two - strong and arrival - get limit orders). Weak side = (1) zone that did not remove the opposite zone, (2) tested, (3) retested, (4) overlap, (5) flip, (6) inheritance and out-of-trendline zones. Weak zones are the reason people fail with supply and demand.

passages.h: The weak zones, one by one
passages.t: Plain weak zone: the supply could not break the demand (or the demand could not break the supply). When price returns it will try hard to remove it. Wait to see whether it breaks; do not jump in.

passages.h: The weak zones, one by one
passages.t: Inheritance zone (41:44-44:18): a zone whose move crossed the trendline but did NOT remove the opposite zone; the zone below it (number 2) is the one that removed it. Zone 1 inherits from zone 2. Price taps zone 2, it becomes weak, price then breaks zone 2 and goes for zone 1 too, forming a V shape. He says market makers build these on purpose so they look like arrival zones but are fake.

passages.h: The weak zones, one by one
passages.t: Rule: a zone that only crossed the trendline is weak; only trendline cross PLUS opposite zone removed is strong.

passages.h: The weak zones, one by one
passages.t: Overlap zone (44:20-46:20): a demand and a supply that form right next to or inside each other (no gap between them). Such a supply is weak even if it removed the opposite zone. Most supply-and-demand losses come from people trading overlap zones.

passages.h: The weak zones, one by one
passages.t: His old example (gold, from a session with another student, "Ankit", likely): the student expected a drop from a supply; Raja said price would break it because the supply formed inside a demand level - and it did.

passages.h: The weak zones, one by one
passages.t: Flip zone (47:54-49:00): where a broken resistance becomes support (or support becomes resistance) as the market zig-zags in impulse and correction. Overlap zones are usually found at flip areas. Use confirmation there.

passages.h: The weak zones, one by one
passages.t: Out-of-trendline zones (49:04-49:45): once the market crosses the trendline, the CP levels of the old trend automatically become weak and the market breaks them easily. If the trend has changed (price coming down), look only at fresh supplies.

passages.h: The weak zones, one by one
passages.t: In weak situations, prefer the zone nearest the trendline: when price has run away and left a gap above the first CP, the next pullback will not come back to the far CP; it will respect the CP closest to the trendline. To reach the far one it would have to cross the trendline first. This is for weak scenarios only; on strong zones you simply place the order.
Long wicks get filled. Whenever the market makes a long wick, it later comes back to fill it; you do not need supply and demand for that. A long wick is a signal of where the market is going next.

Gold (07:51-10:13): the daily shows a long upper wick that price is filling (dropping). The weekly/monthly also show the wick above, so long term gold should go up again and hit about 6,600 USD (likely, he says "chhe-sath sau"). Before that he expects the drop to cross the trendline and reach the proper strong area lower down (about 3,600 USD said; his blue daily box sits around 3,250-3,500).

Meshing: sometimes the market keeps a supply above and a demand in between and just chops between them, up and down. Do not trade during that. Gold is in this state now (stop-loss hunting on the low timeframe); if it breaks structure on the low timeframe, a new zone forms and then you buy.
Three CPs, then the fourth: as discussed in an earlier session, after three CP (rally-base-rally) levels the market tries to build a fourth, and then it reverses, making a new valley/peak.

Base-candle box (29:02, your question): if the next candle already covers the base candle area, it is still valid. With one very long base candle, box only its body, otherwise the zone becomes too big. With small base candles, take the whole group including wicks in one box (he adds this applies on the lower timeframes; meaning of the HTF remark unclear).

Wick or close for a break (22:14, your question): a cross of the zone line by 5-10 pips counts even if it is only a wick (likely). For trendline crosses the signal sometimes comes from a wick and sometimes from the body, but wicks can give fake signals; his next session covers that rule.

BTCUSD daily/H4/monthly (10:52-12:07): a demand the market has not broken yet. Rule: forget a supply or demand only once the market has crossed it. Market makers hunt the stops of other methods.

Hand drawings on BTCUSD monthly (15:27-18:21): (1) strong zone - supply that broke the demand; (2) "WOW" - broken supply, buy pips to the next supply; (3) arrival zone - descending trendline crossed (T) and opposite zone removed (Opp).

EURUSD monthly (19:11-21:24): the 2014 rally-drop-base-drop CP supply removed two demands below it (one a V-shaped valley), so it is a strong supply; a later fresh supply removed another demand and became strong too. A CP that formed as an overlap is weak. A later demand removed the opposite CP supply, became strong, tested, entered and rallied; a tested zone was then removed on the second visit.

GBPJPY monthly (21:28-22:50): two demands broken by one CP supply = strong; price entered and dropped. Another area became strong because its move broke the opposite level, and price entered and went up.

USDCNH monthly (23:01-24:10, transcript reads "USD-CNH", chart confirms USDCNH): a demand rallied and broke the supply, then the market respected that demand. Once the trendline changes, think sell, with that strong demand as the target. A second demand is not strong: price hunted stops below it and meshed - a kind of overlap zone. Use confirmation on the tested one.

EURUSD/GBPJPY monthly wow (24:20-25:40): one demand broke, the next demand below is the target, everything between is sell pips; same for supplies upward. A tested supply in between will simply break, so the next supply is the target.

Monthly arrival examples (30:33-33:13): GBPJPY monthly - price crossed the descending trendline and removed the opposite zone; the demand that did it is an arrival zone, tapped once, twice, and broken on the third visit (it was weak by then). USDCNH monthly demand at the bottom: trendline crossed, opposite zone removed, respected; he expects USD weakness from here.

GBPJPY confirmation, March 2020 (35:12-39:40): monthly zone tested twice (recoloured as tested). On H4: descending trendline crossed, opposite strong supply removed by the demand = arrival zone; the move gave about 700-800 pips. On the daily the same pattern: trendline crossed, supply removed by the demand, about 1,000 pips, then a further supply removed = second trade.
Step by step, each strong zone that removed the opposite zone is respected, even on M1, M5 or M15.

Drawn examples A and B on GBPJPY monthly (41:27-42:02): two stacked zones on a rising trendline. You answered that zone 2 is strong in both (it is the one that broke the opposite zone) - correct. Zone 1 on top is the inheritance zone.

You said you have been marking zones since you started supply and demand but are not yet profitable. His fix: stop treating every zone as tradable. Identify only strong zones and arrival zones for limit orders, use confirmation on weak ones, and practise this every day for the week.
Buying a zone just because it crossed the trendline. That alone is an inheritance zone (weak, often a market-maker trap); it also has to remove the opposite zone.
Expecting a drop from a supply that formed inside a demand (the overlap example from another student). Overlap zones break; most S&D losses come from them.
Placing a limit order on a zone the second time. Second touch = confirmation on the lower timeframe, never set and forget.
Trading gold now. It is meshing and stop-hunting on the low timeframe; there is no clear direction, so no trade until structure breaks and a new zone forms.

Taking a trade without an identified wow area. If you do not know where price is being drawn, the trade is just a stop-loss hunt waiting to happen. Using indicators: he tells you not to; S&D zones and trendlines only.
Your clarifying questions he confirmed: the same rules apply on small timeframes (yes, exactly the same); after a trend change you look only at fresh supply (yes).

Most of this repeats "Strong Zones I: strong vs weak, wow trade and arrival zones" and "Strong Zones II: tested zones, confirmation, inheritance, overlap and flip zones" (same 3 strong + 6 weak scheme). New or sharper here:
A higher-timeframe veto on strong zones: a daily strong supply next to a monthly demand will be removed, not respected. Not stated this explicitly in "Strong Zones: CP Zones and Arrival Zones".
Explicit confirmation timeframe mapping: H1 zone -> M15 confirmation, M15 -> M5 (the "Live Pair Review" lesson used M15 entries with M5 confirmation; here it is a general one-step-down rule).
"Nearest the trendline" tie-breaker for weak scenarios when several CPs are stacked with a gap - not in the course lessons.
Long-wick-fill rule and the "meshing = no trade" rule are new price-action filters on top of S&D.
Inheritance zones described as deliberate market-maker fakes of arrival zones, and overlap zones as the main source of S&D losses; overlap zones are said to form at flip areas.

Arrival zone breaking pattern: two tests, then the extreme point, then the break on the third visit (compare the 1st/2nd/3rd/4th-touch rule in "Strong Zones II", where the 4th touch usually breaks - here a monthly arrival zone broke on the 3rd).
Base-candle box rule (body-only for one long base candle, whole group with wicks for small candles) is new detail.

“A tested zone is always considered a weak area - the second time, the market is going there to break it, not to respect it.” “If you do not have the wow trade area identified, you cannot take any trade.” “Most of the losses people make in supply and demand come from trading overlap zones.”
“Whether it is one minute, five minutes or fifteen minutes, a strong zone that broke the opposite zone is what the market respects.”

HTF veto: a lower-timeframe strong zone next to an opposite higher-timeframe zone gets removed. Confirmation one timeframe lower (H1 -> M15, M15 -> M5). Nearest-the-trendline tie-breaker for weak scenarios. Long-wick-fill and meshing (no trade) price-action filters.
Inheritance zones as market-maker fakes; overlap zones form at flip areas and cause most losses. Monthly arrival zone broke on the third visit (two tests, extreme point, break).

A 62-minute 1:1 that is mostly a live review on his MT4 charts (BTCUSD, ETHUSD, US30, XAUGBP, XAGAUD, GBPNOK) plus Q&A. The recurring idea: the real zone is the one nearest the trendline, and no trade is taken until the trendline is crossed.

He gives the 1st-2nd-3rd-touch rule (the 4th is very risky), two ways to use the low timeframe (only when the HTF gives nothing, or a fixed H1-M15-M5 chain, never trading corrections), says the trendline is only a tool while supply and demand removal decides, and explains stop hunts by small brokers and why to practise on a cent account first.

The zone nearest the trendline is the real zone. No trade until the trendline is crossed. 1st-3rd touch fine; the 4th touch is very risky. Use the LTF only when the HTF gives nothing; stop at M15 once you have a zone. Never trade corrections on the LTF. Supply and demand close together and used = sideways: lower timeframe only, or wait. Stop 10-12 pips beyond the zone with small brokers.

The real zone is the one nearest the trendline, not one in the middle; check how much space is left. A lower zone that broke nothing will still get touched if it sits along the trendline. Take a trade only after the trendline is crossed.

On a demand buy, split into two small positions: take profit on the first early and hold the second while the LTF does not cross the trendline. For sells, go deeper, near the trendline / location area.
Touches: the 1st, 2nd and 3rd are fine; the 4th is very risky because momentum is likely to break. A level touched 3-4 times is weak and will be broken.

Stacked zones: prefer the one with strong imbalance; the weak one next to it will turn into a flip area. That strong zone gets set and forget, on ETH too. Once a trendline is crossed, the zone above (or below) it is automatically weak.
When supply and demand are close together and both have been used, the market is sideways: trade it only on a lower timeframe, or wait for the major zone to break and a new trendline to form.

Trendline cross with a close beyond it, but the opposite zone was not removed: price goes back. Supply and demand is the main thing; the trendline is only a tool for direction and safety. Choose what can give a wow trade.

Low timeframe, way 1: use it only when the HTF gives nothing. If the H4 entry was taken or is tested, drop to H1 and trade its trendline zone; if H1 is tested too, go to M15/M30, and stop there once you have a zone.

Low timeframe, way 2: a fixed chain H1 -> M15 -> M5 with the entry on M5. Do not trade corrections there: the LTF builds aggressive new trendlines in impulses, and a correction sell might pay 2 pips while the impulse pays 600-700. The realignment area is where the M15 and M5 zones coincide.
Second method: wait for the trendline cross plus a structure break, then trade the LTF zones below (or above) the trendline as the market retests them.

BTCUSD daily (00:00-03:07): technically a sell, but use confirmation here. The daily is on its 3rd touch; a drop from here goes to about 65k (likely). If the trendline is crossed it can pass 100k (likely) within a candle or two. Extend the trendline to find the TP. Long term (monthly): buy and leave it.

ETHUSD weekly (05:00): a lot of space, so it fills slowly with meshing. Take the TP from the weekly trendline; lifting from the monthly, about 2,600-2,700 (likely) is easy, then meshing and later a drop to the weekly demand box around 1,400-1,500. On a buy, close at about 400-500 USD profit.
US30 H4 (06:12): a sell he gave a student dropped and is filling the long wick (NAS100 sell too). It may drop more because there is no strong HTF zone to realign with; only a tested zone.

BTCUSD weekly (08:25): technically BTC should come to the weekly zone (the box around 40k). Price fills, meshes, then drops. He calls a visit to about 40k (likely) a once-in-ten-years buying chance (his strong personal view, not a rule).
XAUGBP H4 (09:46): no HTF zone and heading down. On the LTF it crossed the trendline; the first TP is the lower box. Not a great zone, but the new supply under the trendline can be used for shorts.

XAUAUD / XAGAUD (10:30-13:56): XAUAUD is the oldest gold pair; it moves straight with few glitches and a big range. XAGAUD: the lower area is not strong because it did not close past the opposite zone; on M15 the supply under the trendline gives a sell.

GBPNOK H4 (18:46-21:40): both supply and demand already used, so sideways. A strong weekly zone means no trade until it breaks; the daily still follows its trendline. Wait for the daily cross, then the sell pips come. Keep it on the watchlist with a sell bias, confirmation only.

Stops hit on the LTF when the spread widens: broker practice. Small brokers can widen spreads or print fake candles to hunt stops (sometimes not visible on TradingView). Put the stop 10-12 pips beyond the zone; if hunted, compare with TradingView and claim the money back. Use Pepperstone or IC Markets, not local brokers.
COT reports: the weekly CFTC report helps medium/bank traders, more for shares than forex; he stopped using it because it comes late. Supply and demand sits above it.
FOMO, entering early or late: in the coming sessions you practise and he reviews your trades on screen. A mentor's job is to fix psychology and behaviour and to discuss upcoming news.

Starting live: not yet; practise on a cent account first (a 10-20 USD deposit shows as about 2,000 cents; 0.01 lot risks almost nothing; higher spread, but it feels real). Trade 0.01, build the habit, then go live small with Pepperstone or IC Markets.

Which zone is nearest the trendline? Has the trendline been crossed, and was the opposite zone removed? Which touch is this (4th = very risky)? Does the HTF give an entry? If not, which LTF way am I using? Am I trading the impulse, not a correction?
“The real zone is the one near the trendline.” “The trendline is only a tool; supply and demand is the main thing.” “Avoid corrections and you become a good trader.”
Two explicit ways to use the LTF (only when the HTF gives nothing, or a fixed H1-M15-M5 chain).
The trendline is a tool, not a rule: a close beyond it without an opposite zone removed goes back. Stacked zones: the weak neighbour of a strong-imbalance zone becomes a flip area.

The lessons: wait for price to come to the zone, because rushed entries lose; a clean zone takes 5-7 candles to leave; on a correction trade, close or tighten once price crosses the location area's 50/25% lines; news first makes a wick that gets filled later; a trendline touched three times usually breaks on the 4th; and with two positions, close one when the H1 trendline crosses and keep the other's stop at the original zone, not at breakeven.

Wait for price to come to the zone; never rush the entry. On correction trades, tighten or close once price crosses the location area's 50/25% line. A trendline touched three times usually breaks on the 4th. News makes a wick first; expect it to be filled.
Two positions: close one at the H1 trendline cross; the held one's stop stays at the zone, not breakeven.

Correction trades are fine, but close before the TP: take the location area and mark its 50% and 25% levels. Once price crosses that line, either move the stop up to the last LTF supply (H4 -> H1) and drop the TP, or close, because the market will now look for the other side.
A clean zone with good departures takes time to leave (5-7 candles, with fake signals to shake people out). A small departure is 1-2 candles. Wait for the zone.
Wait for the zone: price always retraces, it just takes time. If you rushed in, go to the LTF, close when its trendline crosses, and re-enter lower.
Two small positions: close one in profit, hold the other, and re-enter if price comes back, so you never miss the entry.
News rule: a fundamental event first makes a wick (imbalance) and forex investors fill it later. Old glitch wicks were filled too.
A trendline touched three times usually breaks on the 4th. After the trendline cross and a zone break, sell from fresh H4/H1 zones.

Direct (market) entries: the stop goes at the zone (below the demand); the risk is acceptable because you are buying near the proximal line. In MT4 you can drag the order line to create the stop or the TP.

Two positions, the follow-up: close one when the H1 trendline crosses and the opposite zones break, and re-enter on the retest. Keep the held one's stop at the original HTF/daily zone, not at breakeven (breakeven gets hunted). As price forms new fresh H4 zones and CPs, move it there; near the TP move it behind the last demand. A stop-hunt wick below a zone (ETH) is not a break: no trade until a clear full break.
AUDJPY (likely): your sell from the daily targeting the daily demand, plus a short on the correction.

GBPJPY / AUDJPY (his Instagram post): the monthly zone broke, so a wow trade started; the next HTF zone is far, so about 250 more pips are likely. The weekly may retrace first; the correction length tends to repeat (measured move).

EURUSD monthly: sell. A single long-wick candle (doji / pin bar) will likely be broken; the weekly demand will likely break (big gap), then short on the daily. Once price crosses it, the next demand becomes strong and you trade it inside the trendline.

GBPJPY weekly: the supply is weak (it did not break the demand); the daily one was strong. If price comes back you get a trade; otherwise let it break and buy the new fresh demand. The current demand is not strong, so confirmation only. Later: the daily zone is about to break, then the weekly becomes a very good zone.

Crude oil: your H4 buy near the trendline. Oil must break the weak zone above (meshing now); overall bias up.

EURGBP: technically should rise from the strong area; the H1 trendline crossed with a long candle, so wait for the M15/M30 cross and buy directly.
UK100: sell, the demand below is weak. US30: monthly/weekly/daily zones are weak, CP levels without a zone break. AUDCAD: monthly strong area, wait for the wow trade.
Exness and Pepperstone show different candles; spread spikes hunt tight stops. Put the stop a few pips further and use a smaller size.
Bots: he prefers manual trading. Prop firms: practise first and check the firm is trustworthy.

A 34-minute live review, pair by pair (gold, ETHUSD, the JPY crosses, AUDNZD, USDPLN, SGDJPY, GBPMXN, silver, NAS100).

He explains flip zones (the previous higher low revisited each leg), when to prefer the P (peak/valley) over a CP next to it, keeps repeating that the market prefers the zone nearest the trendline, tells you not to place your stop near the trendline when the base is big, and lists the only three places for a blind entry: a wow trade, a fresh arrival zone, and a zone near the trendline that has not been tapped a 4th time.
Prefer the P over a CP right next to it; use the CP when it formed below with a gap. The market prefers the zone nearest the trendline.

Blind entries only at: a wow trade, a fresh arrival zone, a near-trendline zone not tapped a 4th time. Stops 10-15 pips beyond H4/daily zones, not at the trendline. Flip area without a clean zone = confirmation only.

Flip zone: the market makes a higher low, and the previous higher-low area gets revisited each leg (resistance becomes support and back). On a clean chart it keeps hitting the same zone. If there is no zone at the flip, use confirmation; the LTF gives a zone at the next one.
Stops: below H4/daily zones keep the stop 10-15 pips beyond the zone. Do not put it near the trendline when the base is big (your AUDJPY/CHFJPY stop was hit for that reason).
P vs CP: if a CP sits right next to the P (peak/valley) with no gap, prefer the P; if the CP formed below with a gap, always use the CP.
The market prefers the zone nearest the trendline; to reach a further one it must make another candle across. A new supply forming near the trendline gets hit, not the far upper one.
Out of trendline: when the market goes out of the trendline, makes a demand and respects it, that demand is still a weak zone.

The three blind-entry places: a wow trade, a fresh arrival zone, and a zone near the trendline that has not been tapped a 4th time. They are rare; an HTF wow trade has a high chance of being respected.
A 'dusty' (congested) zone that meshes for hours is not tradable on the HTF; a sell is clear only on the LTF, with limited pips.
Correlation: USD-base pairs rising while USD-quote pairs fall is correlation (he will send a sheet). Gold no longer moves inversely to JPY; it moves against the dollar index on the LTF.
For a new trend, wait for the demand first; when price goes up, the zone and the new trendline form automatically.

Gold H4: still under the trendline, so it can drop any time and will fill the wick. It will not go straight to the upper supply: it taps the middle one, traps entries, then drops (around the 3,300 area, likely).

ETHUSD (the transcript says 'Euro'; the chart is ETHUSD): structure broken and two opposite zones removed on the LTF, about 700 pips. If this weak demand breaks too, sell from the supply under the trendline.

CHFJPY: monthly up, weekly demand tested again; congested and meshing, sell only on the LTF. CADJPY H4: trendline crossed, reached the weekly arrival zone (likely), try selling. GBPJPY: meshing for hours, wait for the break, then a long-term short.

AUDNZD H4: structure and trendline broken; it comes down then goes up. Buy if the structure breaks up; if the demand breaks, sell. It did not touch the flip zone you expected: a new zone formed nearer the trendline.
USDPLN daily: started a flip area, so direction changed on this timeframe (USD pairs up). Flip-area trades are confirmation only unless the zone is strong and clear.
SGDJPY: rising while the other JPY pairs drop; monthly/weekly up, a valid daily demand already triggered, nothing on H4.
GBPMXN daily: structure almost broken at the last HTF supply; on a close above it he would close his own long-term sell and expect a new trendline.
Silver daily: monthly up, a great weekly trendline; let it fill down to the 59-60 area first. Once the trendline breaks there is no strong zone until about 110 (his view).
NAS100: straight down; it always pulls back on the daily, so the entry will not be missed.

A 52-minute analysis session: he starts on his MT4 (NAS100, gold, silver, USDJPY, oil) and then reviews your TradingView analysis (AUDCAD, AUDCHF, AUDJPY, EURUSD, AUDNZD, CADJPY).

Main points: a new zone out of the trendline is not usable, while an M30 zone that removed the opposite zone inside the trendline is; when an H1 and an M30 zone are the same area the market is realigning; after a sharp move into an HTF zone the market leaves a long wick, retraces, then fills it, so trade the fill; and there are two kinds of confirmation, the LTF trendline cross plus removal, or price closing back across the proximal line. He also tells you to keep XAUUSD off the low timeframes for now and use XAUAUD.

A zone out of the trendline is not usable; one that removed the opposite zone inside the trendline is. When the H1 and M30 zones coincide, the market is realigning. After a sharp move into an HTF zone, wait for the long wick and trade the fill. Confirmation = LTF trendline cross + removal, or a close back across the proximal line. No HTF zone: go to the LTF and follow the trendline the candles respect.
Trade on your own broker's chart.
Weak zones sometimes reverse too, but prefer the zone nearest the trendline; otherwise the market makes a new zone, breaks, and you use that one.

A new demand that is out of the trendline is not usable. An M30 supply that removed the opposite zone and is still inside the trendline is usable, even set and forget (better on demo first). When the H1 and M30 zones are the same area, the market is simply realigning.
A full departure candle must properly cross and close beyond the trendline before you consider buys; a long wick below may form a CP and a new trendline, but that would be an overlap zone.
Supply and demand close together = the market is just imbalancing back and forth; buy only after a break (gold). Long wicks get filled first, then the market decides (silver H4).
Two opposite zones removed = direction change; until then only sells or trailing (USDJPY), and wait for the daily confirmation before buying.

Entering early out of emotion: however strong the imbalance, when price hits an HTF zone it makes a long wick, retraces, and later fills it. Trade the fill. You can place two entries, one closed short term and one held long term.

Two kinds of confirmation: (1) the LTF trendline cross plus the opposite zone removed; (2) at a daily demand, price checks the location, comes back and crosses the proximal line upward: buy directly with the stop below the zone (the LTF has already changed direction). If you can sit at the screen you will not miss the trade.
No HTF zone: go to the LTF and follow the trendline the candles respect. Normally go daily -> H4 for the last demand; if H4 has nothing, go to H1. A fake trendline cross with no departure is weak.
Each broker's server time shapes the candles differently: trade on your own broker's chart.

Precise entries (like a student in the group): sit at the screen, wait for a zone to break (wow trade), then buy the LTF zone that forms on the pullback. On the LTF do not over-prefer CPs; use the broken higher high and buy its return (support/resistance style).

Markets: S&D works on any market, including Indian stocks, but do not go below the daily on stocks. USDTRY is HTF only. XAUUSD fakes a lot on the LTF (high spread, now tied to oil and war news); use XAUAUD for LTF gold. All US indices follow Nasdaq.

NAS100 H1: already reached the supply; it will tap, retrace a little and leave a long wick. That supply is not strong: overlap-type, still inside the demand level and under the trendline. A proper close above the trendline would bring the upper zone into play.
Oil: inside supply after a news jump; the daily zone is still valid (the supply broke on the zoom-in). A good buy zone if it reverses; otherwise it makes a CP.

AUDCAD 3-month/monthly (your chart): the trendline was crossed only slightly. The supply is strong because it broke the demand, and this CP removed the previous two supplies; wait for the forming supply to break before the CP/demand becomes valid. On the daily it is meshing: a break of the demand means sell, a break of the other side buy.

AUDCHF H4 (the transcript says 'Swiss franc'; the chart is AUDCHF): you marked the supply nearest the trendline, which is correct; wait for an LTF trendline cross. On H1/M30 a demand with a supply above leaves buy pips; a buy limit there gives about 1:4 (likely).
AUDJPY weekly: trendline crossed but the demand not broken; one zone gone, and if the second breaks it goes short; otherwise buy on the LTF.
EURUSD daily: zone tested twice, so confirmation: go to H1, let the big H1 structure break and sell when it drops. Keep the set-and-forget order you already placed; it may mesh a bit first.
AUDNZD H4/daily: the right buying area, now going up. H4 showed a fake trendline cross with no departure (weak); on M15 the war conditions mean stop hunts, so let a new zone form.
Daily CP on a descending trendline sitting on an old demand: overlap, weak. You said that is exactly where your mistakes come from.
CADJPY: realigning with demand; monthly strong zone, weekly supply. Wait for the daily confirmation under the trendline. EURGBP: in supply, no buys until it breaks.

Entering early before the wick fill. Trading an overlap CP on a descending trendline. Trading XAUUSD on the low timeframes in news-driven conditions. Using a new zone that is out of the trendline.

Is the zone inside the trendline and did it remove the opposite zone? Do the H1 and M30 zones coincide (realignment)? Has the long wick formed? Am I trading the fill? Which confirmation am I using: LTF cross or proximal-line close? Is this an overlap zone?
“However strong the imbalance, when it hits a high time frame zone it makes a long wick and later fills it.” “If there is no high time frame zone, go to the low time frame and follow the trendline.”

Second confirmation type: a close back across the proximal line, without going to a lower timeframe. H1 and M30 zones coinciding = realignment. Long-wick fill as the entry after a sharp move into an HTF zone.
A 46-minute review of your TradingView charts (AUDJPY, GBPJPY, AUDCAD, SoFi, Disney, Alibaba) after a look at his MT5 (NAS100/US30, oil, BTC).

A level counts as broken only when a full candle closes through it; in news the market respects valleys while CP and PCP levels get blown through; a flip zone needs a prior trendline cross; overlap zones are confirmation only; an LTF entry always targets the HTF zone, with half booked early and the rest run with the stop locked; and confirmation can be taken without a lower timeframe by waiting for price to cross back over the proximal line.

A level is broken only by a full candle close through it. News: valleys hold; CP/PCP levels get blown through. No flip zone without a prior trendline cross. LTF entry -> HTF target; book half, lock the stop on the rest. Overlap zones: confirmation only. TP before the supply, not at it.
Broken means a full candle closing through the level; a big candle closing above says it can go up. Until then, wait.

Strong zones take time to break; a weekly demand can be a good buy-limit zone even if the market is not testing it, while the daily keeps building continuation CPs (NAS100/US30). During news the market mostly respects valleys; CP and PCP levels get blown through.
Flip zone: only if the trendline had been crossed and price dropped first. Until then the zone is simply the one price can drop from.

First exit: an LTF entry always targets the HTF zone (H1 entry, daily target). Lock the stop into profit as new zones form. Booking 50% and running the rest is right; he takes two positions per zone, one closed at the near target and one held.
An overlap zone ahead: the market will likely take the liquidity and drop; overlap zones only with confirmation (an LTF trendline cross).
A fresh strong zone on a correction: the first time a correction trade is fine; the second time the market tries hard to break it.

Which valley to use: the one where the move restarted, with the previous demand. A zone above an ascending trendline gets respected. A zone retested 2-3 times is weak and may break even on the first drop.

Direction change and targets: if support breaks, wait for the first supply and demand to break (two opposite zones = direction change), then go to H4 for the next zone; first TP there, then the daily target.
Do not put the TP right at a supply; close before it, because sometimes the market makes a new valley/peak and turns. When a new CP forms, move the stop there.

Confirmation without the LTF: let price come to the proximal line; when it rotates and crosses back over it, enter (for a sell: no sell limit, take the entry after it crosses back down). Slightly bigger stop, much safer.
Volume profile: fine if it helps you; he only reads long wicks and long candles as low volume / fast moves. A demand inside a proper zone acts as a magnet.
Keep the chart clean: with too many lines you cannot read the candles. Stock entries 10-15 points below the line, depending on the spread (likely).

Oil: the monthly supply broke, so it will not stop easily; the only valid zone is the daily one (H4 shows the same area). Brent is still inside supply and should come down to the demand, but strong zones take time.
BTC/ETH: trendline with a zone below; if crossed, ETH could go to about 1,500 USD (likely). For now good support.
AUDJPY (your trade): a correction trade from the weekly demand after confirmation, about 400 pips, and a second entry on the trendline cross. On the LTF just keep a stop above the high.

GBPJPY: another student bought the H4 demand; it hit exactly that demand and then dropped on news. It tapped and left a wick, so GJ will likely fill the wick: a good second entry. Monthly and weekly are still buy (trendline not crossed); this is a correction.
EURUSD / GBPUSD: still inside supply, out of trendline: let price come and take a sell confirmation; at a peak a drop is likely.
AUDCAD: crossed, two zones broken; the CP there is an overlap, so not a tradable zone; confirmation on M15.

SoFi (your stock): the area in the way is not strong (out of trendline, tapped once), so it will break. Disney: bounced off the monthly demand; let it drop more before buying. Your other target sits under a supply that did not remove the previous zone, so the second visit should remove it.
Alibaba monthly: removed the previous zone the first time, so it looks bullish; above the trendline, a good zone; meshing now, likely up.

Calling a flip zone before the trendline has been crossed. Trading an overlap CP without confirmation. Putting the TP exactly at the supply. A chart cluttered with lines.

Did a full candle close through the level? Is news due? (valleys hold, CPs fail) Has the trendline been crossed before I call this a flip? Is the zone ahead an overlap? Where is the HTF target? Half booked, stop locked?
“We trade zone to zone.” “Low time frame entry, the target is always the high time frame zone.”
News behaviour: valleys hold while CP/PCP levels get blown through. A flip zone exists only after a trendline cross. Confirmation by a close back across the proximal line, with no lower timeframe.
A 49-minute review: Raja's MT5 first (gold, GBPJPY, EURUSD), then your pending orders and swing trades (GBPAUD, EURSGD, GBPCAD, CHFSGD, Solana, NAS100, soybeans, USDCHF, the dollar index, stocks).

He approves limit orders placed on strong zones near the trendline, says a zone 25-30 pips away from the trendline often breaks, a trendline tested 3-5 times is very weak, a trendline crossed only by a wick does not count unless price closes back inside the departure, and gives a missed-entry formula.
On management: two positions, close one at the trendline cross, trail the other on H1 once the H1 trendline has been tested 4-5 times, and stop trading gold on the low timeframes.

Limit orders on strong zones near the trendline; a zone 25-30 pips away often breaks. A trendline tested 3-5 times is very weak; wait for a new valley. A wick-only trendline cross does not count unless price closes back inside the departure. Missed entry: on an early LTF trendline break, enter directly with a close stop.
Trail on H1 once the H1 trendline has been tested 4-5 times; close one of two positions at the trendline cross. No XAUUSD on the low timeframes; use XAUAUD.
Use the zone near the trendline; if the market keeps meshing around a supply, trade it only on confirmation. Wait for the H4/daily confirmation, then take it on M15 once it crosses.
A trendline tested 3, 4, 5 times is very weak: direction can change any time, so wait for a new valley and use it.
The best zone sits just above the trendline (for a demand); a zone 25-30 pips off the trendline often gets broken when price comes to hit the trendline.
Long base or wick candles: look for location at long wicks, the market tries to fill them. The market often crosses the trendline with a wick only; do not worry unless it closes inside the departure.
Missed-entry formula: if price starts dropping early and breaks its LTF trendline, sell directly; the stop is close.
If a strong zone's trendline gets crossed, the setup is not invalid; it becomes a confirmation trade (NAS100).

Draw the new trendline only after the new low has formed. A long wick often means continuation, maybe with a retrace on the next candle. Gaps are rare on Pepperstone, but when they appear the market fills them.

Holding a swing: if the target is not reached by next week, go to the LTF and trail. Big news can hit at the weekly open, so lock profit before the weekend. On H4 you give back profit; once the H1 trendline has been tested 4-5 times, move the stop to H1. Two small positions: close one at the trendline cross, keep one, re-add in the zone.
With HTF swings you sometimes wait a week; watching 6-7 such pairs at a time gives 3-4 profitable trades.
Do not trade only gold: XAUUSD is full of fake signals from small traders. He trades XAUAUD for cleaner moves. On the LTF about 90% of moves fake; the HTF needs big fundamental news to hunt stops.
After a big candle beyond the departure, wait for a long-wick retrace and buy directly on the LTF; the market fills the wick (more next session).

Gold weekly: a normal retracement; the monthly zone is far below, the weekly fresh area about 3,600 (likely) at a CP level is where to close sells. The daily made a new zone near the trendline without crossing it, so he expects a fresh sell from there.
GBPJPY daily: an ideal buy area near the trendline, but no realignment yet; it must break this level and that zone first. He has not given anyone a buy (too risky).
A weekly demand that was strong has been tapped: if it breaks, sell (EURUSD and GBP dropping); if you are in a buy, close it there because the second attempt is the break.

Your GBPAUD buy limit (likely GBPAUD): a clear, perfect buy area; he would place it there too; it may bounce, so use confirmation. Your EURSGD sell limit on the H4 strong area near the trendline: correct; SGD follows USD, so when EURUSD sells from the daily, sell this too. GBPCAD: the daily area is right. CHFSGD: placed after it broke two 'walls' (demands): good.

Solana: down confirmed; the nearest supply is the next short. This demand is weak (a fake signal): its job was to remove the inheritance zone, and the overlap zone is already gone, so it likely goes lower; a CP should form on M15/M5 to drop from.
NAS100: your sell limit on the H4 strong zone that removed two demands; price not there yet.
Soybeans monthly: your planned daily buy had too few pips. On the HTF the demand is broken and a strong supply sits near the trendline: a sell limit there pays well if it goes into impulse.

USDCHF: crossed all supplies; the lower daily demand near the trendline is more likely; confirmation on H4 or a limit on the lower one. The dollar index the same: use the lower daily zone near the trendline for the buy.
Your earlier analysis with no location (impulse and correction will chop, then drop): move the zone a bit higher; even if broken, it drops from there.

Stocks (OKLO, SEZL weekly): demand tested once, second tap as the retracement entry; you took TP1 at the supply, closed half, and are running the rest to TP2. Good: focus on the HTF and trade with its direction.
GBPSEK: daily demand, impulse and correction; the weekly is at a higher low and correcting toward the demand. A new zone near the trendline on the daily: wait for the retracement.

Trading only gold. Rushing gold entries on the low timeframes (stops hunted). Planning a trade with too few pips when the HTF offers a bigger setup. Going into the weekend without locking profit.

Is my zone right at the trendline (not 25-30 pips away)? How many times has the trendline been tested? Did price close back inside the departure, or was it only a wick? Two positions? Which one closes at the trendline cross? Is it the weekend? Profit locked?
“If the trendline gets crossed it is not invalid; it becomes a confirmation trade.” “Trade what is clear.”

Zone distance from the trendline: 25-30 pips away tends to break. A wick-only trendline cross is ignored unless price closes inside the departure. Trailing switch: move to H1 once its trendline has been tested 4-5 times.

XLT class notes that turn level quality into a score: strength of the move away, reward-to-risk, big picture, how many times price has returned, time at the level and the arrival. Each factor gets 0-2 (or 0-1) points, and the total decides whether you use a limit order, a confirmation entry or no trade. Time of day (the first hour) is an extra odds enhancer for short-term traders.

Score every level on six factors: strength (0-2), reward/risk (0-2), big picture (0-2), retracement count (0-2), time at level (0-1), arrival (0-1). Total 9-10: limit entry allowed; total 8: confirmation entry only; under 7: no trade.

Require at least 3:1 to the nearest opposing level (e.g. 20 cents risk needs 60 cents of room). First return = 2 points, second = 1, third = 0. Check the daily chart for trend and big-picture levels even for intraday trades. Prefer setups that meet entry in the first 45-60 minutes of the session.
How price left the level tells you how far out of balance supply and demand were there: a fast exit means a large imbalance.
The job is to find the levels where supply and demand are most out of balance; the speed of departure is the biggest clue.
Strongest (2) = one or two very large candles leaving the level; strong (1) = a steady run of mid-size candles; weak (0) = a choppy, overlapping drift with mixed colours.
Measure how far price travelled from the level before it came back: that is the initial profit margin.
When buying at demand, find the nearest supply. Example: risking 20 cents, the nearest supply must be 60 cents or more away, otherwise skip.
Scoring in the diagrams: 3:1 or better to target 1 = 2 points, 2:1 = 1 point, 1:1 = 0 points. Levels are everywhere; only take the best ones.
Even though most of Sam's trades are intraday, he checks the daily chart for two things: the bigger trend (which side to be on) and where the big-picture supply and demand levels are.
Do not short just above a big-picture demand level; you only know it is there from the higher timeframe.
Shorting on a lower timeframe inside a big downtrend scores 2; shorting inside a bigger uptrend close to big-picture support scores 0 or 1.
The first return to a level is the highest-probability entry: first time = 2, second time = 1, third time = 0.
It is motion into mass: the mass is the stack of unfilled orders, and each visit removes some of it.
Chopping-tree analogy: every swing of the axe removes wood, so the more swings, the more likely price goes through.
Where the imbalance is greatest, price spends the least time - only a few candles. Long time at a level means equilibrium, which is not where you want to trade.
Do not fix a magic candle count: the count changes with timeframe. Compare time spent at this level with time at other levels on the same chart.

Arrival: price should come back to the level cleanly, without new resistance forming before a buy or new support forming before a sell. A strong arrival usually means a strong departure from the level.
Score 9 or 10: a limit order is acceptable. Score 8: use a confirmation entry. Below 7: no trade (the notes list 7 next to 'no trade if less than 7').

Time of day: setups that meet entry in the first 45-60 minutes of the session are usually the best; afternoons are weaker because by then orders are processed and supply and demand are back near balance.
If you do not know what you are doing, do not trade the open; if you do, the open is when most money moves between accounts.

'Strength at Origin of Move' panel: demand row shows 2 = two or three tall green candles leaving almost vertically, 1 = a staircase of five medium green candles, 0 = a long mixed red/green drift upward. Supply row mirrors it with red candles.

'Reward to Risk Ratio' panel: each box shows a V-shaped line chart, an entry line on the basing candle, a stop just beyond it, and target 1 at the first opposing level. Strongest box marks 1 unit of risk vs 3 of reward, strong 1 vs 2, weak 1 vs 1. Supply boxes are the same upside down with the stop above.

'Retracement' panel: buy zone (demand) and sell zone (supply) drawn as two horizontal lines under or above a big candle. 'Strongest = 2' shows a yellow tag '1st time to level'; 'Strong = 1' has a blue '1st' bubble where price already touched and a tag '2nd time to level'; 'Weak = 0' shows '1st' and '2nd' bubbles and a '3rd time to level' tag.

passages.h: Chart: Score-sheet diagram 'Strength at Origin of Move': demand (top row) and supply (bottom row) departures graded Strongest = 2, Strong = 1, Weak = 0.
passages.t: Strongest = 2: one or two very large candles leave the level - the biggest imbalance. Strong = 1: a steady staircase of mid-size candles in one direction.

passages.h: Chart: Score-sheet diagram 'Strength at Origin of Move': demand (top row) and supply (bottom row) departures graded Strongest = 2, Strong = 1, Weak = 0.
passages.t: Weak = 0: overlapping candles of mixed colour drifting away - little imbalance, low odds on the return.

passages.h: Chart: Score-sheet diagram 'Reward to Risk Ratio': entry on the basing candle, stop just beyond it, target 1 at the first opposing level; 3:1 = 2 points, 2:1 = 1, 1:1 = 0 (supply row mirrored).
passages.t: Measure risk from entry to stop, and reward from entry to the first opposing level (target 1), not to a hoped-for extreme.

passages.h: Chart: Score-sheet diagram 'Reward to Risk Ratio': entry on the basing candle, stop just beyond it, target 1 at the first opposing level; 3:1 = 2 points, 2:1 = 1, 1:1 = 0 (supply row mirrored).
passages.t: Only 3:1 or better earns the full 2 points; a 1:1 setup scores zero even if the zone looks clean.

passages.h: Chart: Score-sheet diagram 'Reward to Risk Ratio': entry on the basing candle, stop just beyond it, target 1 at the first opposing level; 3:1 = 2 points, 2:1 = 1, 1:1 = 0 (supply row mirrored).
passages.t: The supply row is the same picture upside down: stop above, entry at the zone, target 1 below.

passages.h: Chart: Score-sheet diagram 'Retracement': buy/sell zones with the 1st, 2nd and 3rd time price returns to the level (Strongest = 2, Strong = 1, Weak = 0).
passages.t: The first return to a fresh zone is the highest-probability entry (2 points). Each previous touch (blue numbered circles) has already filled orders at the level, lowering the score to 1 and then 0. By the third visit the zone is likely to break - motion into mass removes the mass.
Score the departure: one or two large candles out of a small base = 2, a steady run of mid-size candles = 1, a choppy overlapping drift = 0.
Retracement score: 1st return to the zone = 2 points, 2nd = 1, 3rd = 0. Each touch removes unfilled orders until the level gives way.

Treating a level with lots of candles as strong - textbooks say more time = stronger, Sam says the opposite. Fixing a specific basing-candle number regardless of timeframe. Shorting just above a big-picture demand level because only the small chart was checked. Trading the third or later return to a level as if it were fresh. Trading the open without knowing how to read levels.
Strength of departure scored (2 = one or two large candles). Nearest opposing level is at least 3x the stop distance away.

Daily trend and big-picture levels checked; not shorting into HTF demand or buying into HTF supply. This is the first return to the level. Few candles at the level compared with other levels on the same chart. No new opposing level formed on the way back. Total score 9-10 for a limit order, 8 for confirmation, otherwise skip.
“The more quickly they move, the more out of balance they are.” “Every swing removes some of the mass.” “Morning is the golden opportunity.”
A numeric 10-point score with explicit cut-offs (9-10 limit, 8 confirmation, under 7 skip); Kevin grades zones by qualifiers but not with this point table.

Reward/risk is itself a zone-quality factor (2/1/0 for 3:1/2:1/1:1), not only a trade filter. Freshness scored in steps (1st/2nd/3rd visit) rather than tested vs untested only. 'Arrival' factor: no new opposing levels on the way back into the zone. Time-of-day enhancer: first 45-60 minutes after the open.

Give every zone a score out of ten. Only trade the high scores. Imagine a teacher grading a test with six questions about a zone. Did price leave fast, is there room to the next wall, and does the big chart agree? Is this the first visit, did price stay only a short time, and did it come back cleanly? Add the points: 9 or 10 means you can wait with a buy order, 8 means wait for proof, and under 7 means skip it.
It is like rating a lemonade stand before you invest: busy line, good price, nobody else on the street, first day open. Six ticks and you buy in; a few ticks and you walk past.

A fast exit from a level means a big imbalance. Speed is the biggest clue. Score six things: strength, reward to risk, big picture, how many returns, time at level, arrival. 9-10 = limit order, 8 = confirmation entry, below that = no trade.

passages.h: Step: Strength of the move away (0-2)
passages.t: Price paused for two small candles, then left with two very large green candles. One or two big candles leaving a level is the strongest exit, so this scores 2 points.

Price spent only two candles at the level before it left. Where the imbalance is greatest, price spends the least time. Few candles compared with other levels on this chart scores 1 point. Box the base: highest body on top, lowest wick on the bottom.

Look to your left for the nearest supply. Entry sits on the top line of demand, the stop goes just under the bottom line, and the first target is that supply. The room is many times the stop, well over 3:1, so 2 more points.

passages.h: Step: First return and a clean arrival (2 + 1)
