passages.t: Price now comes back for the first time, in a straight drop with no new support forming on the way. First visit scores 2, clean arrival scores 1. Add the big picture and the total is 9 or 10: a limit order is allowed.
The waiting buy order fills on the first touch and price runs to the supply above. We never knew it would work; we only stacked the odds with an objective score.

Strongest exit from a level scores? - 2 points: one or two very large candles leaving the level. Retracement points for 1st, 2nd, 3rd return? - 2, 1, 0. Score 9-10 allows which entry? - A limit order at the level. Score 8 means? - Use a confirmation entry. Minimum reward to risk to target 1? - 3:1 (20 cents risk needs 60 cents of room). Long time at a level means? - Equilibrium, which is not where you want to trade.
Best time of day for short-term setups? - The first 45-60 minutes of the session.

Class notes covering the rally-base-drop / drop-base-rally definitions, how to join trends with little risk, Weinstein's four market stages, top-down analysis, not cutting through candles, and the three entry types. Most space goes to how confirmation entries are run mechanically with a trigger price and a stop price.

Supply = rally-base-drop; demand = drop-base-rally. Uptrend: buy pullbacks to demand. Downtrend: sell rallies to supply. Range: do both at the edges. Analyse monthly -> weekly -> daily -> hourly -> 5-minute before trading.
Pick the entry type from the score: strongest levels with limit orders, weaker ones with confirmation.

Confirmation uses a fixed rule (e.g. 0.01/0.05/0.10 beyond the level); skip if it ruins reward/risk. If the stop price trades before the confirmation entry, cancel the trade. A 2-candle base on 240-minute: refine on 60-minute; 3-6 candles is the ideal base size.

Supply forms as rally-base-drop; demand forms as drop-base-rally. In an uptrend buy pullbacks to a quality demand level; in a downtrend short rallies into supply; in a sideways market sell rallies into supply and buy pullbacks into demand.
The more often price returns to a level and gets a chance to trade there, the more likely the level breaks (it turns).

passages.h: Four stages of the market (Stan Weinstein, 'Secrets for Profiting in Bull and Bear Markets')
passages.t: Stage 1: a trading range after a sell-off, read with a 30-week moving average; institutions accumulate while the public sells in pain. Stage 2: uptrend - prices rise, then range again.

passages.h: Four stages of the market (Stan Weinstein, 'Secrets for Profiting in Bull and Bear Markets')
passages.t: Stage 3 (end of 2007 example): a violent range where institutions sell high to the public, using upgrades and hype so they can unload. Stage 4: an ugly decline.
Work down from the big picture: monthly, weekly, daily, hourly and 5-minute. Two reasons: know where you are relative to big-picture support/resistance, and know the bigger trend.
If price cannot rally to test supply, it has no choice but to go back down and test the next demand; if it breaks up, look further left for the next level.
Do not cut through candles when drawing levels - you want the supply/demand equation as it really traded.
Most problems blamed on stops or targets are really entry problems; knowing where the turning points are is everything.
Three entry types: limit, confirmation and breakout. Which one to use comes from the odds-enhancer sheet, especially strength of the move.
Confirmation entry: let price enter the level and buy as it leaves; if price goes through the level, cancel.
Many XLT members never take confirmation entries because they only take the strongest setups.
Set a rule for confirmation - e.g. 0.01, 0.05 or 0.10 outside the level, or a trigger inside it. Any rule is fine as long as it is a fixed rule; if the rule kills the reward/risk, skip the trade.
Mechanics: once the trigger is hit, the entry order becomes active. If entry fills first, you are in with your stop; if the stop price is hit before the entry, cancel and never get in.

passages.h: Time at level and turning points
passages.t: Rule of thumb: if a base is just two candles on the 240-minute chart, drop to a smaller timeframe such as 60 minutes to find the base.

passages.h: Time at level and turning points
passages.t: Three to six candles is probably the best base on any timeframe, but the key is still a fast exit from the level - no fast exit, no interest.

passages.h: Time at level and turning points
passages.t: There are only two reasons for a turn: at a top sellers outnumber buyers (or buyers simply leave), at a bottom buyers outnumber sellers.
No chart images on these pages - text notes only.
The two reversal zones: a small base between a rally and a drop is supply (RBD); a base between a drop and a rally is demand (DBR). Proximal = edge nearest price, distal = far edge.
Confirmation entry: wait for price to enter the zone and print a reaction candle, buy above that candle, stop under the distal line; cancel if the stop trades first.

Drawing support and resistance lines that cut through candles. Blaming targets or stops when the real problem is a poor entry. Having no fixed confirmation rule and deciding by feel. Entering a confirmation trade after the stop level already traded.

Top-down done from monthly to entry timeframe. Stage of the market identified (accumulation, uptrend, distribution, decline). Base found on a timeframe where it shows 3-6 candles. Entry type chosen from the score. Confirmation rule written down before the trade (trigger and offset). Cancel plan if stop price trades before entry.
“Understanding where the turning points are is everything.” “More important is that you have a rule and make it rule based.”
Weinstein four-stage cycle with a 30-week MA as market-phase context; Kevin uses pure price action. Breakout entry listed as one of three standard entries.
Confirmation entry defined as a fixed price offset / trigger with a cancel-if-stop-first rule, rather than candle-pattern confirmation on a lower timeframe.
Explicit refine rule: a 2-candle 240-minute base is redrawn on 60-minute; 3-6 candles ideal.

Pick your entry type by the score, and follow a fixed confirmation rule. Supply is a pause between a rally and a drop; demand is a pause between a drop and a rally. Before you trade, you look from the monthly chart down to the 5-minute chart. For the very best levels you just leave a buy order waiting. For weaker levels you let price step into the zone first and only buy as it leaves. If price runs through your stop before your entry fills, you cancel and never get in.
A confirmation entry is like waiting for the bus doors to open before you step forward. If the bus drives past without stopping, you simply do not get on.
Supply = rally-base-drop, demand = drop-base-rally. Draw them without cutting through candles. Work top down: monthly, weekly, daily, hourly, 5-minute.
Confirmation entry: price enters the zone, you buy as it leaves; if the stop trades first, cancel.
Price dropped, paused, then rallied hard. That pause is a drop-base-rally demand level. The best bases show about three to six candles on the timeframe you use.

passages.h: Step: Draw it without cutting candles
passages.t: Wrap the base with two lines: the highest body on top and the lowest wick on the bottom. Do not slice through candles; you want the area where the buying really happened.
This level scored only 8, so we do not leave a limit order. We wait for price to trade into the zone and print a reaction candle.

passages.h: Step: Trigger above the reaction candle
passages.t: Our fixed rule: buy 0.10 above the high of the reaction candle, stop under the bottom line. Once the trigger trades, the order is live. If the stop had traded first, we would cancel.
The next candle trades above the trigger and price rallies away. The rule did the work, not a feeling.
Supply forms as? - Rally-base-drop. Demand forms as? - Drop-base-rally. Three entry types? - Limit, confirmation and breakout.

Confirmation entry in one line? - Let price enter the level, buy as it leaves; cancel if the stop trades first. Ideal base size? - About 3-6 candles on the timeframe you use. Real cause of most stop and target problems? - A poor entry.

Defines 'profit margin' as the distance from your entry level to the opposing supply or demand level and makes it the key go/no-go factor: look to your left and require at least 3:1 to the first target. Trading ideas show how a strong initial move away marks a good level, and how buyers chasing after an advance into supply are the people to sell to.
Before any entry, look left for the opposing level and measure the profit margin. Initial profit margin must be at least 3x the stop (3:1 to target 1).
Short supply levels that were left with a strong initial decline; buy demand left with a strong rally.
A level badly placed on the higher-timeframe curve is a day trade only, not a swing trade.
Profit margin = the objectively measured distance between the supply (resistance) level and the demand (support) level.
There are only two entry types - the pullback entry and the breakout entry - and both depend on having a profit margin.
Look to your left: before buying make sure supply is far above; before shorting make sure demand is far below.
Sam's minimum: the initial profit margin must be at least 3 times the stop (3:1 to the first target). Price often goes well beyond, but 3:1 gets the trade started in your favour.
Business analogy: a losing trader buys inventory at $4.00 (supply) without research and then finds the market will only pay $3.00 (demand).
A strong initial decline from a supply level suggests a large imbalance, so price will likely fall fast on the first revisit.
A level can have a strong move out but still be badly placed on the bigger supply/demand curve - then it is a day-trade bounce, not a swing trade. A very large level is not always a good thing.
Buyers buying after a large advance and at a level where supply exceeds demand are not consistently profitable traders - take the other side.

OTA graphic 'Entries: First Pullback / Breakout': left side shows a red/green base between two green lines, a rally to a high (red line), then a pullback into the top green line with an arrow labelled 'Low Risk Entry' and a circled 'Profit Zone' between entry and the red supply line.
Right side shows a drop from a red supply band into a green base, a breakout candle above the base marked 'Low Risk Entry', and the circled profit zone up to the red lines.

10-Year Note futures (intraday, 9/20-9/23): supply drawn between about 109'03 and 109'08 (two red lines) at a small base after the opening candles; price then fell hard in several large red candles to about 108'12. It has since climbed back to 108'30.5, just under the zone. The drop from the zone to the low is the initial profit margin, more than 3:1, so short in the supply area.

S&P E-mini (daily, late Aug-early Oct): demand drawn about 1485-1500 (green lines) under a small base before one tall green candle up to roughly 1540; last price 1534.25. Strong move out, but the level sits badly on the bigger curve: fine for a day-trade bounce, not a swing entry.

Newell Rubbermaid NWL (daily, Jun-Sep): wide supply band about 29.1-29.9 drawn across a long June-July range, followed by a large drop to about 24.5 in August. In September price rallied straight back into the band with tall green candles and no basing (28.83). Large level and only average volume, so a watch idea: buyers here are buying after a big advance into supply.

Goldman Sachs GS (daily, Jul-Sep): supply about 219-222 (red lines) at the July top, a long decline to about 160, then a steady recovery. A circle marks large green candles and gap-ups near 190-205 after the advance (last 209.98) - the novice buyers. Plan: sell to them if price reaches the supply level.

passages.h: Chart: OTA slide 'Entries: First Pullback / Breakout': left - base between two green lines, rally to a red supply line, pullback into the base = Low Risk Entry; right - drop into a base under two red lines, entry as price breaks up from the base. Circled 'Profit Zone' up to supply in both.
passages.t: Both entries are taken at demand, close to the protective stop. The profit zone is the room between entry and the next supply line - that is the profit margin to measure before entering.

passages.h: Chart: OTA slide 'Entries: First Pullback / Breakout': left - base between two green lines, rally to a red supply line, pullback into the base = Low Risk Entry; right - drop into a base under two red lines, entry as price breaks up from the base. Circled 'Profit Zone' up to supply in both.
passages.t: First pullback: wait for price to come back to the fresh base after the rally; breakout: enter as price leaves the base.

passages.h: Chart: 10-Year Note futures, intraday (9/20-9/23): supply about 109'03-109'08 (two red lines) at a small base, a hard drop in large red candles to about 108'14, and a slow climb back to 108'30.5 just under the zone.
passages.t: The fast, large-candle drop out of the base marks a strong imbalance at the supply zone. Distance from the zone to the low is the initial profit margin on a short at the first return.

passages.h: Chart: 10-Year Note futures, intraday (9/20-9/23): supply about 109'03-109'08 (two red lines) at a small base, a hard drop in large red candles to about 108'14, and a slow climb back to 108'30.5 just under the zone.
passages.t: The return is slow and overlapping - buyers drifting up into supply, the people a short sells to.

passages.h: Chart: S&P E-mini, daily (late Aug-early Oct): demand about 1485-1500 (green lines) under a small base, then one tall green candle to about 1540 (last 1534.25).
passages.t: One very large candle out of a small base = strongest departure. Even a strong level must be judged on the bigger curve: here it is fine for a day-trade bounce but too high for a swing entry. Look left for the nearest supply before deciding the trade has enough profit margin.

passages.h: Chart: Newell Rubbermaid NWL, daily (Jun-Sep): wide supply about 29.0-29.9 (red lines) across the June-July range, a drop to about 24.5 in August, then tall green candles straight back into the zone (28.83).
passages.t: Price rallied into supply with big green candles and no basing - novice buyers buying after an advance.

passages.h: Chart: Newell Rubbermaid NWL, daily (Jun-Sep): wide supply about 29.0-29.9 (red lines) across the June-July range, a drop to about 24.5 in August, then tall green candles straight back into the zone (28.83).
passages.t: A wide zone means a wider stop; it was kept as a watch idea rather than a full-size trade. The opposing demand near 25 defines the profit margin for a short from the zone.

passages.h: Chart: Goldman Sachs GS, daily (Jul-Sep): supply about 219-222 (red lines) at the July top, a decline to about 160, then a recovery; the circle marks large green candles and gap-ups near 190-205 (last 209.98).
passages.t: The circled big green candles are late buyers chasing the advance - the people to sell to.

passages.h: Chart: Goldman Sachs GS, daily (Jul-Sep): supply about 219-222 (red lines) at the July top, a decline to about 160, then a recovery; the circle marks large green candles and gap-ups near 190-205 (last 209.98).
passages.t: The plan is a short only if price reaches the red supply lines, not in the middle of the move. Profit margin is large: the whole decline from 220 to 160 sits below the zone.
Profit margin: entry at the demand proximal line, stop beyond the distal line, first target at the nearest supply to the left. Require 3:1 or better.
Who you trade against: buyers who chase large green candles and gaps after a long advance, right into an old supply zone, are the people to sell to.

Entering without checking how far the opposing level is. Buying after a large advance and into supply (the novice buyer). Assuming a large-range level is automatically strong. Swing trading a level that is badly placed on the big-picture curve.

Opposing level found to the left and distance measured. Profit margin at least 3:1 to the first target. Strong initial move out of the level. Level is well placed on the bigger picture if this is a swing trade. Price is returning after a run (others are chasing) and this is the first visit.
“All you have to do is look to your left.” “The initial profit margin must be at least 3 times the stop.”
'Profit margin' framed as the distance between opposing zones measured before entry; Kevin uses 3:1 too but Seiden makes it the main pass/fail filter for both pullback and breakout entries.
Distinguishes levels good for a day-trade bounce but not a swing because of curve location.

Before buying, look left: is there room to the next wall? A shop owner buys toys for $4 and hopes to sell them for more. If nobody will pay more than $3, he loses money no matter how good the toys are. In trading, the space from your entry to the opposing level is your profit margin. Seiden only trades when that space is at least three times his stop.
It is like checking a parking spot before you drive in: if the wall is right in front of your bumper, you cannot go anywhere.

Profit margin = distance from your entry level to the opposing supply or demand. Look to your left. Require at least 3:1 to the first target. Buyers who chase after a big advance into supply are the people to sell to.
Price dropped, paused for two candles, and left with two big green candles. A strong initial move away suggests a big imbalance. Box the base as demand.
Before buying, find the nearest supply above. Here it is the small base at the top, where price turned down.
Entry on the top demand line, stop just under the bottom line, target at the supply. The room is many times the stop, far more than 3:1, so the trade is allowed.
On the first pullback the order fills and price climbs to the opposing supply. The 3:1 rule got the trade started in our favour.

Profit margin? - Distance from your entry level to the opposing level. Minimum initial profit margin? - 3 times the stop (3:1 to target 1). Before buying, look where? - To your left, for the nearest supply.

Two entry types that both need a profit margin? - The pullback entry and the breakout entry. Strong level in a bad big-picture spot? - Day-trade bounce only, not a swing. Is a very large level always good? - No. A wide level means a wide stop.

Follow-up on a 30-year bond supply level from the previous letter that triggered right away and paid about 3:1 on the first day. The lesson: level quality is judged mainly by how price first left the level - strong exit means large imbalance, slow drift means a smaller one. Trading ideas cover the Russell, SMH and silver.

Judge a level mainly by the strength of the original move away from it. Trade the first pullback to the level, with the stop just beyond it. Use sector ETF levels to time trades in that sector's stocks. Size for the contract value (Russell: $100 per point) and keep risk low.

One of the most important features of a quality level is how price originally left it. A strong move away from an area of apparent equilibrium happens because there is a large supply/demand imbalance there. If price slowly drifts away, the level can still be traded, but the imbalance is smaller. The higher the imbalance, the higher the probability the trade works.

passages.h: Using a sector chart as a guide
passages.t: The distance between an unvisited supply level above and an unvisited demand level below is the profit margin.

passages.h: Using a sector chart as a guide
passages.t: An ETF chart such as SMH can be traded directly and also used as a guide for the sector's stocks (XLNX, NVLS, KLAC, NSM).

30-Year Bond futures (intraday, 9/6-9/14): rally from about 111 28/32 to 114, a topping range, then a drop and a small base around 113 12/32-113 18/32 marked with red lines and the label 'Last weeks supply level (sell short)'. Price fell from it to about 112 16/32, rallied back into the zone, and was rejected with a tall red candle (now 112 27/32) - the trade that paid about 3:1.

Russell futures ER2 (intraday, 9/5-9/17): supply labelled about 795-802 (red lines) at a small base right after a drop from about 810; price then gapped and fell to about 767 on 9/10 and has recovered to 789.30 just under the zone. Strong initial decline = strong imbalance; short-term shorts there. Note Russell is $100 per point per contract.

SMH semiconductor ETF (daily, Apr-Sep): demand labelled about 34.2-34.9 at an April base before a strong rally; supply labelled about 37.8-38.3 at a small September base below a lower high. Price is 37.14, and the large gap between the two unvisited levels is circled and labelled 'Profit Margin'.

Silver futures (daily, late Jul-Sep): supply about 13.00-13.20 (red, top base) followed by a collapse to about 11.50; demand about 11.85-12.15 (green) at a late-August base before a rally to 12.745. Buy the first pullback to demand with a protective sell stop just below the level; it is well placed on the curve and has a decent profit margin.

passages.h: Chart: 30-Year Bond futures, intraday (9/6-9/14): 'Last weeks supply level (sell short)' about 113 10/32-113 17/32 (red lines) at a small base after the drop from 114; price fell to 112 16/32, rallied straight back into the zone and was rejected with a tall red candle.
passages.t: The short from last week's letter triggered on the first return and paid about 3:1 on the first day.

passages.h: Chart: 30-Year Bond futures, intraday (9/6-9/14): 'Last weeks supply level (sell short)' about 113 10/32-113 17/32 (red lines) at a small base after the drop from 114; price fell to 112 16/32, rallied straight back into the zone and was rejected with a tall red candle.
passages.t: Entry at the proximal line, stop just above the distal line - a tiny stop compared with the drop that followed.

passages.h: Chart: 30-Year Bond futures, intraday (9/6-9/14): 'Last weeks supply level (sell short)' about 113 10/32-113 17/32 (red lines) at a small base after the drop from 114; price fell to 112 16/32, rallied straight back into the zone and was rejected with a tall red candle.
passages.t: Why it worked: price had left that base fast, so a large imbalance (unfilled sell orders) was still waiting.

passages.h: Chart: Russell 2000 futures ER2, intraday (9/5-9/17): 'Supply' about 795.5-802 (red lines) at a small base after the drop from about 810, a gap down to about 767 on 9/10, and a recovery to 789.30 just under the zone.
passages.t: Strong initial decline (including a gap) away from the base = strong supply. Short-term short on the first return to the zone, stop above the distal line.

passages.h: Chart: Russell 2000 futures ER2, intraday (9/5-9/17): 'Supply' about 795.5-802 (red lines) at a small base after the drop from about 810, a gap down to about 767 on 9/10, and a recovery to 789.30 just under the zone.
passages.t: Note the contract size: Russell points are worth $100, so position size must match the stop.

passages.h: Chart: SMH semiconductor ETF, daily (Apr-Sep): demand about 34.2-34.9 at the April base, supply about 37.8-38.3 at a small September base; price 37.14 with the gap between the two levels circled as 'Profit Margin'.
passages.t: Two unvisited opposing levels define the trade: sell supply, buy demand. The circled gap between them is the profit margin for either trade. A sector ETF like SMH can also be used as a guide for its component stocks.

passages.h: Chart: Silver futures, daily (late Jul-Sep): supply about 13.00-13.20 (red lines) at the top base, a collapse to about 11.50, demand about 11.85-12.15 (green lines) at a late-August base, then a rally to 12.745.
passages.t: Buy the first pullback into the green demand with a protective sell stop just under it. Target the red supply above - the profit margin between the two levels is several times the risk. The demand base sits low on the bigger curve after a collapse, which raises the odds.
Level quality: a base followed by one or two large candles away shows a large imbalance (high odds on the first return); a slow overlapping drift shows a small one.
Treating a level that price slowly drifted away from as equal to one with a violent departure. Ignoring contract size in fast markets.

Departure from the level was strong, not a slow drift. Level is unvisited. Opposing unvisited level gives a large profit margin. Stop just beyond the zone. Position size fits the contract's point value.
“The higher the imbalance at the level, the higher the probability of the trade working out well.”
Using a sector ETF's zones as a guide for individual stocks in that sector. Distinguishes 'slow drift' levels as tradeable but lower-odds, rather than invalid.

Judge a level by how fast price first ran away from it. Picture a quiet room that suddenly empties because someone shouts "free ice cream outside!" The faster everyone runs, the bigger the prize must be. When price leaves a level with one or two huge candles, a big pile of orders was there. When price just drifts away, the pile was small.
A fast exit is like a rocket launch; a slow drift is like a balloon floating off. Both leave, but only the rocket shows real power.

How price first left a level is one of its most important features. Strong exit = large imbalance = higher odds. Slow drift = smaller imbalance. Trade the first pullback with the stop just beyond the zone.
Price rallied and then paused for three small candles. It looks like balance, but we cannot know yet.
Two tall red candles leave the pause. A strong move away from apparent balance only happens when supply hugely outweighed demand. Box the pause as supply.
Price rallies back for the first time. Sell at the bottom line, stop just above the top line. The stop is tiny compared with the drop that left the zone.
The unfilled sell orders were still waiting. Price turned at the zone and fell toward the demand below, like the bond trade that paid about 3:1 on the first day.

Most important feature of a quality level? - How price originally left it. Strong exit means? - A large imbalance, so higher odds. Slow drift away means? - A smaller imbalance; tradeable but lower odds. Which pullback do you trade? - The first one, stop just beyond the zone.
Why check contract size? - Fast markets with big point values (Russell $100/point) need smaller size.

Explains why Sam focuses on turning points instead of joining trends late or buying breakouts: the turning-point trader earns his money from late trend-followers and breakout buyers. The QQQQ supply short shows how entering at the level gives a stop very close to entry and a maximal profit margin. He also argues for price-only analysis because indicators lag.

Enter at the pre-planned level, not after the move has started. Prefer the lowest-risk entry at the zone over extra confirmation lower down. Check the monthly chart for big supply/demand before taking longer-term trades. Use price as the primary input; treat lagging indicators as secondary.
When you buy, many others must buy after you at higher prices for you to profit; when you short, others must sell after you lower.
The trader who picks turning points with simple supply/demand rules usually takes money from those who enter trends late and from breakout traders who buy after buying and sell after selling.
Entering at the pre-determined turning point gives a short entry very close to the protective stop and far from demand targets.
The longer you wait and let price drop before shorting, the more risk rises and the profit margin shrinks. Prefer a low-risk entry at supply over lots of confirmation.
Always check supply and demand on a big-picture chart (e.g. monthly) to put things in perspective.
If price has not been able to even reach a big supply level, there is plenty of supply there and a turn lower is likely before any break through.
Use price alone: all influences on price are already reflected in price, and anything added (e.g. a moving average) lags, which adds risk. Indicators can be used, but there is a right and wrong way.

QQQQ (intraday, 7/23-9/7): supply about 50.00-50.30 (red lines) from the late-July top, after which price fell to about 45 on 8/16. Price rallied back and the 'Short Entry' label sits at the first touch of 50.00 on 9/5; price then fell about $2 and gapped down toward 48 (now 49.12). 'Supply Level' is labelled at the left origin.

NASDAQ futures NQ (monthly, 2001-2007): supply level drawn about 2,100-2,250 at the start of the chart; a circle marks the sharp drop out of it in 2002 down to about 1,100. Price has climbed back for years to about 2,025 but has never re-entered the zone - lots of supply waits there, so long-term low-risk buys are lower.

30-Year Bond futures (intraday, 8/24-9/13): demand (support) about 110 24/32-111 at a late-August base before the rally; supply (resistance) about 113 4/32-113 8/32 at a small base after the top near 114. Price sits at 112 22/32 between them and the circled gap is labelled 'Profit Margin' - both levels to be traded the first time price revisits them.

passages.h: Chart: QQQQ, intraday (7/23-9/7): 'Supply Level' about 50.00-50.30 (red lines) at the late-July top, a fall to about 45 on 8/16, then a rally back; 'Short Entry' at the first touch of 50.00 on 9/5, followed by a $2 drop and gap down toward 48 (now 49.12).
passages.t: Shorting at the first touch of the zone put the stop only cents away above 50.30. The trend follower who bought the rally and the breakout buyer at the highs were on the other side.

passages.h: Chart: QQQQ, intraday (7/23-9/7): 'Supply Level' about 50.00-50.30 (red lines) at the late-July top, a fall to about 45 on 8/16, then a rally back; 'Short Entry' at the first touch of 50.00 on 9/5, followed by a $2 drop and gap down toward 48 (now 49.12).
passages.t: Entering at the turning point maximises the profit margin; entering after confirmation lower down gives part of it away.

passages.h: Chart: NASDAQ futures NQ, monthly (2001-2007): supply level about 2,100-2,250 (red lines) at the start, a circled sharp drop in 2002 down to about 1,100, and a multi-year climb back to about 2,025 without re-entering the zone.
passages.t: The big-picture chart shows where large supply still waits - price has never returned to that zone. Long-term buying near that level is low odds; it is where a turn is likely. Always check the monthly chart before longer-term trades.

passages.h: Chart: 30-Year Bond futures, intraday (8/24-9/13): demand (support) about 110 24/32-111 at the late-August base, supply (resistance) about 113 4/32-113 8/32 at a small base after the 114 top; price 112 22/32 with the gap between them circled as 'Profit Margin'.
passages.t: Both levels are tradable: short supply, buy demand, each with a stop just beyond the zone. The space between the levels is the profit margin for each trade. Price-only analysis: no indicator is needed to locate either level.
Turning points vs late entries: the trader who buys demand and sells supply is paid by the trend follower and the breakout buyer who enter late, far from support, into supply.

Joining a trend well after it is under way. Buying breakouts after a period of buying. Waiting for lots of confirmation, which increases risk and cuts reward. Relying on lagging indicators for entry decisions.

Entry is at the level, not after a run away from it. Stop is close (just beyond the zone). Profit margin to the opposing level is still large. Monthly/weekly picture does not put a big opposing level close by.
“The longer you wait and let prices decline before selling short, the more risk is increasing.” “Any and all influences on price are reflected in price.”
Explicit argument that the zone trader's profit comes from late trend-followers and breakout traders.
Monthly-chart zone that price has never re-entered used as a reason to expect a turn there.

Sell at the turning point, not after the drop has started. If you buy something, someone must later pay you more for it. The late buyer who jumps in after a long rise is the one who pays you. Seiden plans his turning points in advance and waits there. The longer you wait for proof, the further price has already moved and the less is left for you.
It is like catching a ball at the top of its throw: right at the top it is easy and close. Chase it after it falls and you miss most of the catch.
Turning-point traders are paid by late trend followers and breakout buyers. Entering at the level gives a tiny stop and the biggest profit margin. Use price only; indicators lag and add risk.

passages.h: Step: Mark the turning point first
passages.t: Price rallied, paused, then fell hard. The pause is supply. We mark it before price returns.
Price rallies back for weeks. Trend followers and breakout buyers jump in near the top, right into supply.

passages.h: Step: Short at the first touch
passages.t: Our short sits at the bottom line, with the stop just above the top line. Stop very close, targets far away.
Someone who waits for the drop to "confirm" sells much lower. Their stop is far away and their room to the target is small. Prefer the low-risk entry at the level.
Where do you enter a short? - At the pre-planned supply level, not after the drop starts. What happens if you wait to short? - Risk rises and the profit margin shrinks.

Why check the monthly chart? - To see big supply and demand that frames all smaller trades. Main input for decisions? - Price. Indicators lag. Two people on the wrong side at a top? - The late trend follower and the breakout buyer.

Sam credits his success to having mechanical rules based on supply and demand and actually following them. A mentoring student's AAPL day-trade short shows the method: find a supply and demand pair with a good profit margin, short at supply before the big red candle and cover at demand. Trading ideas in QQQQ, CEPH and EUR/USD repeat the first-revisit rule.

Find the supply/demand pair first; only trade if the profit margin between them is ideal. Short at supply before the big red candle forms; do not chase lower. Exit at the opposing demand level. Only trade the first revisit of a level.
Two reasons for Sam's success: a mechanical, objective rule set based on supply and demand, and learning to actually follow those rules.
Most mentoring time is spent identifying true supply and demand in any market and timeframe.
He first found a demand and supply pair with an ideal profit margin, then shorted right at supply and covered at demand.
The low-risk entry matters more than the gain: shorting at supply, before a big red candle, puts you first in line, close to the buy stop and far from demand.
The more you let price drop before shorting, the higher the risk and the lower the reward, so do not wait.
Nobody knows for sure a level will turn; we only stack the odds with objective information.
The buyer he sold to made the two novice mistakes: buying after a move up, and buying where supply was already known to exceed demand.
Levels are zones, areas to buy and sell, not single lines. Take positions the first time price revisits: risk is lowest and reward highest; each further pullback lowers the probability.

3. 9 at the morning base. 'Sold short' arrow at the first return into supply near 133; a circle shows the drop and 'Covered' arrow at the demand line; the space between them is labelled 'Profit Margin'.

QQQQ ETF (intraday, 7/23-early Sep): supply about 50.0-50.3 (red lines) at the left; a small demand zone (green lines) about 48.8-49.0 near the current price of 49.35 after the late-August rally. Both are the nearest levels to trade on first revisit.

CEPH (intraday, 7/23-early Sep): 'Resistance (supply)' about 78-80 at the top-left base, then a dramatic decline including a gap to about 69. Price has climbed steadily back to about 75.5 and is nearing the zone - plan to short the first revisit, selling to buyers who buy after an advance.

EUR/USD cash forex (intraday, 9/3-9/4): supply about 1.3610-1.3627 (red lines) at a sideways base after a fall from 1.3650, followed by a strong drop with large red candles to about 1.3555 (now 1.35691). Day traders can short the first return intraday.

passages.h: Chart: AAPL day trade (OTA student trade, intraday 8/28-8/29): 'Resistance (supply)' about 132.7-133.2 at a small base before the free-fall to about 127.3; next day 'Support (demand)' about 131.5-131.9 forms after the gap up, price rallies into supply, 'sold short' at the zone and 'Covered' at demand; the gap is labelled 'Profit Margin'.
passages.t: The student found a supply/demand pair first, then measured the profit margin between them.

passages.h: Chart: AAPL day trade (OTA student trade, intraday 8/28-8/29): 'Resistance (supply)' about 132.7-133.2 at a small base before the free-fall to about 127.3; next day 'Support (demand)' about 131.5-131.9 forms after the gap up, price rallies into supply, 'sold short' at the zone and 'Covered' at demand; the gap is labelled 'Profit Margin'.
passages.t: Short entered at supply before the big red candle - first in line, stop right above the zone. Cover at the opposing demand rather than hoping for more: the plan was set before entry.

passages.h: Chart: QQQQ, intraday (7/23-early Sep): supply about 49.9-50.3 (red lines) at the top left; a small demand zone (green lines) about 48.8-49.0 near the current price of 49.33 after the late-August rally.
passages.t: Mark the nearest supply above and nearest demand below; both are first-revisit trades. The trade with more room to the opposing level is the better one. Rules decide the entry: no change of plan once price reaches a level.

passages.h: Chart: CEPH, intraday (7/23-early Sep): 'Resistance (supply)' about 78-80 at the top-left base, a dramatic decline including a gap to about 69, then a steady climb back toward the zone.
passages.t: Plan: short the first revisit of the supply, selling to buyers who buy after an advance. A gap in the departure shows a strong imbalance at the level. The slow, steady rally back is not a reason to doubt the zone - it is how novices arrive.

passages.h: Chart: EUR/USD cash forex, intraday (9/3-9/4): supply about 1.3610-1.3627 (red lines) at a sideways base after the fall from 1.3650, then a strong drop with large red candles to about 1.3555 (now 1.35691).
passages.t: The base (drop-base-drop) is supply because price left it with large red candles. Day traders can short the first intraday return to the zone with a stop above 1.3627. The size of the decline shows the profit margin available on that return.
Supply/demand pair: short at the first revisit of supply (stop just above it) and cover at the proximal line of the demand below - the room between them is the profit margin.

Waiting for a large red candle before shorting. Being impressed by the gain instead of the low-risk entry. Buying after a move up and into known supply. Trading second or third pullbacks into the same zone.

Supply and demand pair identified with a large profit margin. First revisit of the entry zone. Entry placed at the zone, stop just beyond. Target = opposing zone. Rules written down and followed without changes.
“It is one thing to have rules and another thing to actually follow rules.” “It allows us to be first in line at the right time.”
Day-trade framework of shorting supply and covering exactly at the next demand (zone-to-zone targeting) shown on a real student trade.

Find a supply and demand pair, short one, cover at the other. A student found a supply level above and a demand level below with lots of space between them. He sold at supply before the big red candle came and bought back at demand. The gain was nice, but the real lesson was the low-risk entry. Having rules is one thing; following them every time is the hard part.
It is like a ball bouncing between the ceiling and the floor: you catch it at the ceiling and let go at the floor.
Find the supply/demand pair first; trade only if the space between them is large. Enter at the level before the big candle; do not chase. Levels are zones. Trade the first revisit only.
A small base, then a free fall. That base is supply: resistance where sellers beat buyers.
Later a new base forms low down and price rallies. That is demand. Now we have a pair, with a big profit margin between them.

passages.h: Step: Short at supply, first in line
passages.t: Price rallies back into supply for the first time. Sell at the bottom line, stop just above. We are first in line, before any big red candle.
Price falls and we buy back at the demand line, exactly as planned before entry.

Two reasons for Seiden's success? - Mechanical supply/demand rules, and actually following them. Where is the target on a short at supply? - The opposing demand level. Which revisit do you trade? - The first one. Levels are lines or zones? - Zones: areas to buy and sell. What matters more than the gain? - The low-risk entry.

A short list of day-trading rules: trade only at supply or demand, use two entry types (breakout and first pullback), mark one supply and one demand level per market each day on a larger intraday timeframe, demand 3:1 to target 1, pre-set entry/stop/targets, and ignore news and lagging indicators. Trading ideas show a Russell cluster, EUR/GBP and the 10-year note.

Enter only at a supply or demand level. Use only two entries: first pullback or breakout. Each day mark one supply and one demand per market on a larger intraday timeframe. Minimum 3:1 profit zone to the first target. Set entry, stop and targets before price arrives. Level must be fresh (unvisited) for either entry type.
Only enter when price is at a support (demand) or resistance (supply) level, at any time of day or night. Two types of entries: breakouts and first pullbacks.

Each day, mark one demand and one supply level per market on a larger intraday timeframe, and always know where the market sits in the larger picture. Only trade opportunities with at least a 3:1 profit zone to the first target. Pre-plan and pre-set entry, stop and target(s).
Do not get fooled by news, lagging indicators or subjective information - all influences are reflected in price.
Emotion will have day traders buying and selling at the wrong time, so self-control to follow rules is essential.
The first pullback entry is lower risk and higher reward, though many people are uncomfortable with it; breakouts are fine when done properly.
Two conditions: the level must be fresh (price has not revisited it), and the profit zone must be significant - there must be room to move after you enter.
A cluster of trading that looks like equilibrium becomes supply once price declines from it; the decline can only mean supply exceeded demand.

Entries graphic (First Pullback vs Breakout) repeated: first pullback buys the return to the top of the demand base after a rally; breakout buys the candle closing above a base that formed after a drop; both show a circled 'Profit Zone' up to the red supply lines.

Russell 2000 futures (intraday, 8/28-8/29): after a drop from about 795, a long cluster around 776-782 is circled; price then broke down to about 769.90. The circled cluster is the first supply level above - short the first rally back into it.

Euro/Pound cash forex (intraday, 8/29): supply about 0.6788-0.6795 (red lines) at a small top base, then a dramatic slide to about 0.6765; price has stabilised and found demand, now 0.67725. Very active non-dollar pair, called ideal.

10-Year Note futures (intraday, 8/24-8/30): demand (green lines) about 108'22-108'27 at a 8/27 base, followed by a strong rally and a gap to about 109'24 (now 109'18.5). Nearest demand below price; buy the first revisit.

passages.h: Chart: OTA slide 'Entries: First Pullback / Breakout' (repeated): low-risk entry at the base after a rally (left) or as price breaks up out of a base (right), with the profit zone up to the red supply line.
passages.t: These are the only two entry types in the rules: breakout and first pullback. Both entries are at demand, so the stop is close. The profit zone must be at least 3x the risk to target 1.

passages.h: Chart: Russell 2000 futures, intraday (8/28-8/29): after a drop from about 795, a long cluster around 776-782 is circled; price then broke down to about 769.90.
passages.t: The circled cluster is the first supply level above price after the breakdown. Short the first rally back into it.

passages.h: Chart: Russell 2000 futures, intraday (8/28-8/29): after a drop from about 795, a long cluster around 776-782 is circled; price then broke down to about 769.90.
passages.t: Long time at a level means it was near balance while it formed - the breakdown shows sellers won.

passages.h: Chart: Euro/Pound cash forex, intraday (8/29): supply about 0.6788-0.6795 (red lines) at a small top base, a dramatic slide to about 0.6765, then price stabilising at 0.67725.
passages.t: Small base, dramatic departure = high-quality supply. Mark one supply and one demand per market each day on a larger intraday timeframe. Very active non-dollar pairs work with the same rules.

passages.h: Chart: 10-Year Note futures, intraday (8/24-8/30): demand about 108'22-108'27 (green lines) at the 8/27 base, a strong rally and gap to about 109'24 (now 109'18.5).
passages.t: Nearest demand below price - buy the first revisit. The strong rally away from the base confirms the imbalance. Pre-set entry, stop and target before price arrives.
The two entries: the first pullback into a fresh demand zone, and the breakout as price leaves a base. Both need room (profit zone) up to the next supply line.

Trading in the middle, away from any level. Being moved by news, lagging indicators or opinions. Entering a breakout with no room before the next level. Making decisions in real time instead of pre-setting orders.

Price is at a marked supply or demand level. Level is fresh. Entry type is first pullback or breakout. At least 3:1 to target 1. Entry, stop and target pre-set. No news-based or indicator-based reason for the trade.
“Price is all we need.” “There must be room for price to move after you enter.”
Breakout entries are one of the two standard entries (Kevin's notes mention breakout trades only occasionally).
Routine of marking only one supply and one demand per market per day from a larger intraday timeframe.

Only trade at a fresh level, with room to run, planned in advance. Seiden's day-trading rules fit on a napkin. Only enter at supply or demand, never in the middle. Use just two entries: the first pullback or the breakout. Each day mark one supply and one demand per market on a bigger intraday chart. Pre-set your entry, stop and target, and ignore the news.
It is like fishing only at the spots where you know the fish gather, with your rod set up before you leave home.
Enter only at a supply or demand level. Never in the middle. Two entries: first pullback and breakout. Both need a fresh level and room to move. Pre-set entry, stop and target. Need 3:1 to target 1.
On a larger intraday chart, mark today's demand: the base price left with big green candles.
Then mark the supply above, where price turned down. That is the target and the other edge.
The level is fresh: price has not been back yet. There is far more than 3:1 of room. Pre-set the buy at the top line, the stop below the zone, the target at supply.
Price returns, fills the order and runs to the target. No news, no indicator, just price at a level.
Where are you allowed to enter? - Only at a supply or demand level. Two entry types? - First pullback and breakout.

Two conditions for either entry? - The level is fresh, and there is a significant profit zone. Minimum room to target 1? - 3:1. When do you set entry, stop and target? - Before price arrives. News, tips and lagging indicators? - Ignore them; price is all we need.

With volatility high, Sam explains why price alone is enough: all news, reports, tips, upgrades and indicators pass through each person's belief system into a buy or sell action at a price. Trading ideas show a daily Dow demand level formed by a gap, intraday Dow and QQQQ supply levels, and a USD/JPY swing short.

Base decisions on price and supply/demand levels, not on the information that moved perceptions. Wait for price to reach the level; do not buy a falling market above demand. Size every position to a fixed percentage of capital at risk. Distant but well-placed levels are swing trades with large profit margins.

passages.h: Any and all influences on price are reflected in price
passages.t: Earnings, news, financial statements, Fed announcements, economic reports, terror alerts, tips, brokers, upgrades/downgrades, analyst opinions and technical indicators all become thoughts and perceptions.

passages.h: Any and all influences on price are reflected in price
passages.t: Everyone filters the same information through their own belief system, so perceptions differ.

passages.h: Any and all influences on price are reflected in price
passages.t: Perceptions lead to action, and in markets action is only buying or selling at a specific price - so price is all the consistently profitable trader needs. Adding other information distorts what is real according to supply and demand.
At a demand level after a decline, sellers are selling after a decline and where demand exceeds supply - buy from them.
At a supply level after a rally, buyers are buying after a rally and where supply exceeds demand - sell to them. In high volatility a supply level that seems far away can be reached quickly.
Always size positions so you only risk the percentage of capital you are comfortable with.

Diagram 'Any and all influences on price are reflected in price': a list (earnings report, news, income statement, balance sheet, Fed announcement, economic report, terrorist alert/attack, trading/investing tip, broker, upgrade/downgrade, analyst opinion, technical indicators) braces into 'Thoughts and Perceptions', which braces into 'ACTION: Buy or Sell'.

DOW Mini CBOT futures (daily, Apr-Aug, with volume): demand (green lines) about 12,900-12,990 at a two-candle base in late April, which then gapped up and trended to the all-time high near 14,000. Price has dropped to 13,237 with rising volume; no buying until price reaches the demand lines.

DOW Mini intraday (8/9-8/13, with volume): supply about 13,480-13,550 (red lines) at a small base, followed by a steep drop in large red candles to about 13,110. Price is back near 13,245; day traders short the zone if volatility brings price there.

QQQQ intraday (8/9-8/13, with volume): supply about 48.12-48.33 (red lines) at a small base after an opening drop; price then fell to about 46.7 and is at 47.38. Shorting opportunity for traders who do not trade futures.

USD/JPY cash forex (daily, Jul-Aug): supply about 121.65-122.6 (red lines) at a mid-July base after a tall red candle from about 123.4; a sharp slide followed to about 117.2 (now 118.207). Far from price but well placed on the big-picture curve - swing short with a very large profit margin.

passages.h: Chart: Diagram 'Any and all influences on price are reflected in price': earnings, news, statements, Fed, economic reports, terror alerts, tips, brokers, upgrades/downgrades, analyst opinions and technical indicators feed 'Thoughts and Perceptions', which become ACTION - Buy or Sell.
passages.t: Every influence ends up as a buy or sell order at a price. So the chart already contains the news; price is the only data you need. Indicators are just one more input to people's beliefs, and they lag price.

passages.h: Chart: DOW Mini CBOT futures, daily (Apr-Aug, with volume): demand about 12,900-12,990 (green lines) at a two-candle base in late April that gapped up; trend to near 14,000, now dropped to 13,237 on rising volume.
passages.t: A gap out of a small base marks strong demand. No buying until price reaches the green lines - the middle of the move is not a level. Rising volume on the decline is not a reason to buy early.

passages.h: Chart: DOW Mini, intraday (8/9-8/13, with volume): supply about 13,480-13,550 (red lines) at a small base, followed by a steep drop in large red candles to about 13,110; price back near 13,245.
passages.t: Small base and large red candles away = strong supply. Day traders short the zone if volatility brings price back to it. The drop from the base shows the profit margin.

passages.h: Chart: QQQQ, intraday (8/9-8/13, with volume): supply about 48.12-48.33 (red lines) at a small base after an opening drop; price fell to about 46.7 and is at 47.38.
passages.t: Same supply logic in the ETF for traders who do not trade futures. Short at the first return, stop above the upper red line. Compare the zone with the Dow chart: the same supply shows up across related markets.

passages.h: Chart: USD/JPY cash forex, daily (Jul-Aug): supply about 121.65-122.6 (red lines) at a mid-July base after a tall red candle from about 123.4, then a sharp slide to about 117.2 (now 118.207).
passages.t: Far from price, but well placed high on the big-picture curve. A swing short from the zone has a very large profit margin down to the 117 area. Fresh daily supply after a strong departure - patience until price returns.
Any and all influences pass through beliefs and become a buy or sell order at a price - so supply and demand on the chart already contain them.
Assuming everyone interprets news the same way you do. Letting news or tips drive buy/sell decisions. Buying in a decline before demand is reached.
Trade reason is a price level, not news or a tip. Level formed with a strong departure (gap or large candles). Price has actually reached the level. Position size within your max risk percent.
“Price is all the consistently profitable trader and investor needs to focus on.” “Any and all influences on price are reflected in price.”
A gap away from a base counts as the strongest form of departure for a demand level. Belief-system model (information -> perception -> action) as the reason to ignore news.

All the news ends up as buy or sell orders. Just read price. Earnings, the Fed, tips, upgrades and indicators all go into people's heads. Each person sees the same news through their own beliefs, so everyone reacts differently. But in the end every reaction is only one thing: a buy or a sell at a price. So the price chart already holds all the news, and that is all a consistent trader needs.
Like many streams flowing into one lake: you do not need to study every stream, just look at the water level of the lake.
Any and all influences on price are reflected in price. A gap away from a small base is the strongest kind of departure. Wait for price to reach the level; the middle of a fall is not a level.
News, reports and opinions turn into thoughts, then into actions: buy or sell at a price. That is why the chart is enough.

passages.h: Step: A gap out of the base
passages.t: After a two-candle base, price gapped up and trended higher. A gap away from a base shows buyers swamped sellers there. Box the base as demand.

passages.h: Step: The fall is not a buy yet
passages.t: Price drops, maybe on scary news and rising volume. In the middle of the fall there is no level, so we do not buy early.
Only when price reaches the demand lines do we buy, with the stop below the zone. Price turns up from the level.

Where do all influences on price end up? - In price, as buy or sell orders. Why ignore news and tips? - They distort what supply and demand show; price already has them. Strongest departure from a base? - A gap away from it. Price is falling toward demand. When do you buy? - Only when it reaches the demand lines. Position size rule? - Risk only the fixed percent of capital you are comfortable with.

Applies the A-B-C logic to futures: A is a pause that looks like equilibrium, B is the move away that proves A was out of balance, C is the first return and the low-risk entry. Trading ideas give exact zones, entries and stops for the S&P E-mini, Canadian dollar and crude oil shorts, which are taken as swing trades because they sit high on the curve.

Level = pause (A) + strong move away (B); entry on the first return (C). Let price trade into the zone, enter as it leaves the zone (just below supply / just above demand). Stop just beyond the zone (e.g. S&P supply 1465-1471.50 -> stop 1472). Levels high/low on the big-picture curve: manage as swing trades. Use the tight entry-to-stop distance to size up while risking little.

passages.h: The A-B-C logic of a level
passages.t: A: temporary price stability that looks like supply/demand equilibrium. B: the rally (or drop) away from A; it proves A was really a level where demand (or supply) greatly exceeded the other side. News that comes with B adds nothing that price is not already telling you.

passages.h: The A-B-C logic of a level
passages.t: C: the first revisit of A, where price meets a level of large imbalance - the low-risk, high-reward entry. A dramatic B suggests a similar reaction at C.

passages.h: Entry and stop mechanics from the trading ideas
passages.t: Let price trade into the supply level and then short if and when it declines from the level (a confirmation-style entry just under the zone). Place the stop just above the supply level.

passages.h: Entry and stop mechanics from the trading ideas
passages.t: The closer the entry to the stop, the larger the position you can hold while risking very little capital.

passages.h: Entry and stop mechanics from the trading ideas
passages.t: Levels high on the big-picture curve have huge profit margins, so treat them as swing trades rather than day trades. Sam trades over 30 futures markets with a mechanical rule set.

S&P demand example (intraday, 4/20-4/25): A = small flat base about 1479.5-1481.5 (green lines); B = bracketed rally to about 1494; C = a sharp drop on 4/24 back into the zone (about 1480) that reversed immediately; price then rallied to 1502.50.

S&P supply example (intraday, 9:30-13:30): A = base about 1452.7-1454 (red lines) at the open; B = bracketed drop to about 1447.5; price ranged back up and C = the first revisit near 1453 around 12:00-12:30, after which it fell to about 1446.

S&P E-mini CME (intraday, 7/30-8/6): 'Supply' arrow at a small base; zone 1465-1471.50 (red lines). Sharp decline to 1443.25 followed. Plan: let price rally into the zone and short as it declines from it (about 1464 or higher), stop 1472; demand lower near 1430.

Canadian Dollar CME futures (intraday, 8/4-8/5): huge green spike from about .9470 to .9530, then a base about .9500-.9511 (red lines) and a drop to .9469. Zone .9500-.9515, entry about .9495-.9498 as price declines from it, stop .9517. High on the curve plus dramatic drop = swing trade.

Crude oil NYMEX (intraday, 8/2-8/5): after a range near 77, price dropped through a small base around 75.75-76.15 (red lines) to 75.20. Zone 75.85-76.30, entry about 75.80-75.85 on decline from the level, stop 76.35. High on the curve, so swing rather than day trade.

passages.h: Chart: S&P, intraday (4/20-4/25): A = small flat base about 1479.5-1481.5 (green lines), B = bracketed rally to about 1494, C = a sharp drop back into the zone on 4/24 that reversed immediately; price then rallied to 1502.50.
passages.t: A looks like equilibrium while it forms; only the move B proves it was out of balance. C is the first return - the low-risk buy with the stop just below the lower green line. The sharp drop into C is novice selling into demand.

passages.h: Chart: S&P, intraday (9:30-13:30): A = base about 1452.7-1454 (red lines) at the open, B = bracketed drop to about 1447.5, C = first revisit near 1453 around 12:00-12:30, after which price fell to about 1446.
passages.t: Same A-B-C logic at supply: base, strong decline, first return. Short at the lower red line with the stop above the upper one.

passages.h: Chart: S&P, intraday (9:30-13:30): A = base about 1452.7-1454 (red lines) at the open, B = bracketed drop to about 1447.5, C = first revisit near 1453 around 12:00-12:30, after which price fell to about 1446.
passages.t: The slow rally into C contrasts with the fast drop out of A - the imbalance is still there.

passages.h: Chart: S&P E-mini CME, intraday (7/30-8/6): 'Supply' arrow at a small base, zone about 1465-1471.50 (red lines), followed by a sharp decline to 1443.25.
passages.t: Plan: let price rally into the zone and short as it declines from it (about 1464 or higher), stop 1472. Demand lower near 1430 is the opposing level. High on the curve plus a dramatic drop - treated as a swing trade.

passages.h: Chart: Canadian Dollar CME futures, intraday (8/4-8/5): a huge green spike from about .9470 to .9530, a base about .9500-.9511 (red lines), then a drop to .9469.
passages.t: Rally-base-drop: the base after the spike is supply. Zone .9500-.9515, entry about .9495-.9498 as price declines from it, stop .9517. High on the curve plus a dramatic drop = swing trade.

passages.h: Chart: Crude oil NYMEX, intraday (8/2-8/5): after a range near 77, price dropped through a small base around 75.75-76.15 (red lines) to 75.20.
passages.t: Drop-base-drop: the small base inside the decline is supply. Zone 75.85-76.30, entry about 75.80-75.85 on the decline from the level, stop 76.35. High on the curve, so a swing rather than a day trade.
A-B-C at demand (S&P example): small base A, rally B, first return C = buy at the proximal line, stop below the distal line.
A-B-C at supply (futures shorts): base A, drop B, rally back to C; sell as price declines from the zone with the stop just above the distal line.
Believing the news explains the move rather than the imbalance. Shorting far below supply after the drop is under way. Day trading a level that offers a swing-size profit margin.

A (pause) and B (strong departure) identified. This is C, the first return. Entry just outside the zone in the trade direction after price trades in. Stop just beyond the far side of the zone. Curve location checked: day trade or swing trade. Position size computed from entry-to-stop distance.

“News and everything else that accompanies the price action does not offer any benefit that price is not already telling us.” “The closer our entry is to our stop, the larger the position size we can have.”

A-B-C labelling for every zone (pause, departure, first return). Entry placed a few ticks outside the zone after price trades into it (e.g. S&P 1464 under a 1465-1471.50 zone) - a hybrid between limit and confirmation. Curve location decides whether a trade is managed as a day trade or a swing trade.

A is the pause, B the escape, C the first return to buy. At A price rests quietly, like a car at a red light. At B it races away, which proves the light was hiding a lot of power. At C price comes back to A for the first time, and that is where we act. A big, dramatic B usually means a strong reaction at C.
Like a spring: A is the spring pressed down, B is it shooting up, and C is when you press it back to the same spot and it shoots up again.

A = a pause that looks like balance. B = the strong move away that proves it was not. C = the first return to A: the low-risk, high-reward entry. A tight entry-to-stop distance lets you size up while risking little.
Price pauses with small candles. It looks like supply and demand are in balance. We cannot tell yet.
Price rallies hard away from A. That proves demand greatly exceeded supply at A. Any news that came with it adds nothing price is not already telling us.
Price drops straight back into A for the first time. The sellers here are selling into a level of large imbalance.

passages.h: Step: Enter at C, stop beyond A
passages.t: Buy at the top line of A, stop just under the bottom line. A dramatic B suggests a similar reaction at C, and price rallies.
A in A-B-C? - A pause that looks like balance. B in A-B-C? - The strong move away that proves A was out of balance. C in A-B-C? - The first return to A: the entry.

Where is the futures short entry? - A few ticks under the supply zone after price trades into it. Stop on a supply short? - Just above the zone (e.g. zone to 1471.50, stop 1472). Level high on the curve? - Manage it as a swing trade.

A Disney swing short shows the A-B-C logic on a daily chart, and introduces moving-average crosses as a guide: the first return to the point where averages crossed often holds supply or demand. Trading ideas give semiconductor shorts (SMH as a guide, NVLS with exact entry/stop/objective) and an IBM demand buy.
Short the first revisit of a base that was followed by a steep decline (and vice versa for demand).

A moving-average cross can mark the origin of a level; extend it right and wait for the first return. Prefer stock trades when the sector ETF is at a matching level. Write every idea as entry zone, stop just beyond, and initial profit objective.
Area A was stable, then a steep decline B followed, so A had more supply than demand. The first revisit of A means buyers buying after an advance and into supply - be the seller to them.
The two moving averages crossed at the origin of the imbalance; this happens most of the time and has to, if you think about it.
After meeting entry, price fell to the first target. The trade was planned on objective, mechanical rules.
The first time price revisits a moving-average cross, there is often supply or demand in that area. When averages cross, extend a line to the right and wait for price to come back to it.
Used correctly, averages are guides to true support and resistance, not the textbook definitions.

Use SMH's supply as a guide: short semiconductor stocks if the sector rallies into its level. Highest-probability when both the stock and its sector ETF reach supply together. NVLS: short 31.00-31.35, stop 31.46, initial profit objective 1.50-3.00.
IBM (strong during the market decline): buy 108.10-109.10, stop 107.75, initial objective 3.00-6.00.

Walt Disney DIS daily 'Before': supply A about 35.2-35.9 (two red lines) at a small base, bracket B shows the steep drop to about 33.4, a circle marks where the two moving averages (grey and pink) cross right at the zone, and C (dashed box) marks the expected first revisit at the right edge.
DIS daily 'After': price came back into the red lines in July, stalled, and then dropped in tall red candles toward about 33.9 - the first target.
SMH (intraday, 7/23-7/30): supply about 39.10-39.45 (red lines) at a 7/24-7/25 base, then a steady slide to 37.73.
NVLS (intraday, 7/23-7/30): 'Resistance (supply)' about 31.00-31.30 at a small base before a big red drop; price slid to 28.62. Short 31.00-31.35, stop 31.46.
IBM (daily, Jul-Aug): 'Support (demand)' about 108-109.7 (green lines) at a mid-July base of small candles, followed by a gap up to about 118 (now 115.62). Buy 108.10-109.10, stop 107.75.

passages.h: Chart: Walt Disney DIS, daily 'Before': supply A about 35.2-35.9 (red lines) at a small base, bracket B the steep drop to about 33.4, a circle where the two moving averages cross at the zone, and C (dashed box) the expected first revisit.
passages.t: A-B-C on a daily chart: base, strong departure, wait for the first return. The moving-average cross right at the zone adds weight to the supply. C is planned in advance - the order waits at the zone.

passages.h: Chart: DIS daily 'After': price came back into the red lines (about 35.2-35.85) in July, stalled, then dropped in tall red candles toward about 33.9 - the first target.
passages.t: The planned first revisit (C) held exactly as expected. Short at the lower red line, stop above the upper one, target the prior low area. Patience paid: the trade only existed because the level was marked weeks earlier.

passages.h: Chart: SMH, intraday (7/23-7/30): supply about 39.10-39.45 (red lines) at a 7/24-7/25 base, then a steady slide to 37.73.
passages.t: SMH is used as a guide for semiconductor shorts. Base after a pop, then a decline - supply above price. When the sector ETF has supply overhead, look for the same setup in its stocks.

passages.h: Chart: NVLS, intraday (7/23-7/30): 'Resistance (supply)' about 31.00-31.30 at a small base before a big red drop; price slid to 28.62.
passages.t: Exact plan: short 31.00-31.35, stop 31.46. Large red candle out of the base = strong supply. The stock confirms what the SMH sector chart shows.

passages.h: Chart: IBM, daily (Jul-Aug): 'Support (demand)' about 108-109.7 (green lines) at a mid-July base of small candles, followed by a gap up to about 118 (now 115.62).
passages.t: Exact plan: buy 108.10-109.10, stop 107.75. A gap away from a base of small candles marks strong demand. Large profit margin back up to the 118 area.
Disney idea in a diagram: supply base A where the moving averages cross, a strong drop B, and the first return C as the low-risk short.
Using textbook support/resistance definitions instead of imbalance origins. Buying because a moving average 'turned up' at a level where supply exceeds demand.
Base followed by steep move away identified. First revisit only. Sector ETF also at a level in the same direction (bonus). Entry range, stop and initial objective written before the open.
“When moving averages cross, simply extend a trend line to the right and wait for price to come back to that level.”
Moving-average crosses used as a locator for zone origins; Kevin trades with no indicators. Sector ETF + stock confluence as a probability booster.
Profit objective given as a dollar range (e.g. 1.50-3.00) rather than the next zone alone.

Base, steep drop, first return: sell there. Moving-average crosses can point to it. Disney's price sat still for a while at A, then fell steeply at B. That told Seiden sellers had swamped buyers at A. He waited weeks for the first return to A and sold to the buyers who bought after the rally. The two moving averages had crossed right at that spot, which happens at the origin of many moves.
Like a crossroads where two roads meet: the place they crossed is a good spot to wait for traffic to come back.

Short the first revisit of a base that was followed by a steep decline. Where moving averages cross, extend a line right and wait for price to return. Odds are highest when the stock and its sector ETF reach supply together.
Price was stable at A. It looked like nothing was happening.
A steep drop followed, so A had more supply than demand. The moving averages crossed right at this origin. Mark the zone and extend it to the right.

passages.h: Step: C: wait for the first revisit
passages.t: Price rallies back. Buyers here buy after an advance and into supply. Plan the short: entry at the bottom line, stop just above, first target the prior low.
Price stalls at the zone and drops toward the first target. The trade only existed because the level was marked weeks earlier.

Disney short in three letters? - A base, B steep drop, C first revisit = short. Moving-average cross use? - Extend a line right; the first return often holds supply or demand. Sector confluence? - Stock and its sector ETF at the same kind of level raises odds. Full trade plan format? - Entry range, stop just beyond, initial profit objective. Textbook support or imbalance origin? - Imbalance origin.

A new-year checklist of questions every trader should answer before risking money - plan, discretion, objectivity, quantifying supply and demand, and reviewing results. Market review shows why a support level that has been revisited many times is getting weaker, and uses the 200-day moving average as trend context.
Have a written plan with no discretion left in it. Use objective supply/demand analysis instead of lagging indicators. Review average win, average loss and win rate regularly.
Avoid buying a support that has been revisited many times; prefer the unvisited origin below. Short resistance when the 200 MA slopes down (trend filter).
Do you have a trading plan, and do you stick to it? Is there discretion in your plan? Discretion means unanswered questions; turn them into rules. Is your analysis objective or partly subjective?
Can you quantify supply and demand, or do you rely on a lagging indicator that leads to high-risk, low-reward trades? Have you reviewed your results - average win vs average loss and win percentage?
As an educator: do not trade until these are handled. The novice trader almost always funds the consistently profitable one.
Each revisit of a support level lets more of the waiting buyers fill, so the support gets weaker, not stronger. The better buy is at the origin of the demand that has not been revisited yet.
A down-sloping 200 MA confirms a downtrend, which makes shorting at resistance acceptable.
Long-unvisited demand below a falling market can be used to time longer-term buys in that sector.

SPY (S&P ETF, weekly, 2006-2008): 'Support 1' about 137 drawn from a small base during the 2006 rally; price has come back to it several times (wicks touching in 2007). 'Support 2' about 129-132 (two green lines) at the earlier origin of the rally, still unvisited, with the rising 200 MA reaching it around 129. Price is 144.93.

QQQQ (NASDAQ ETF, intraday, 12/11-12/20): 'Resistance' about 51.10-51.55 (red lines) at a 12/13-12/14 base after a fall from about 52.7, with a down-sloping 200 MA running through the zone. A dramatic drop to about 49.2 followed; price is 49.92. Swing and day traders can short the range.

XLF (Financial Service ETF, weekly, 2003-2008): 'Support' about 25.0-26.2 (green lines) from the 2003 base at the start of the multi-year uptrend; the 200 MA rises below the trend. Price has fallen fast from about 38 to about 29, below the 200 MA, toward the unvisited demand.

passages.h: Chart: SPY (S&P ETF, weekly, 2006-2008): 'Support 1' about 137 drawn from a small base during the 2006 rally and revisited several times in 2007; 'Support 2' about 129-132 (two green lines) at the earlier origin of the rally, still unvisited, with the rising 200 MA reaching it around 129.
passages.t: Support 1 has been touched many times - each visit removed demand, so it is weakening. Support 2 is fresh and coincides with the 200 MA - the higher-quality demand. Ask the checklist questions before trading either level.

passages.h: Chart: QQQQ (NASDAQ ETF, intraday, 12/11-12/20): 'Resistance' about 51.10-51.55 (red lines) at a 12/13-12/14 base after a fall from about 52.7, with a down-sloping 200 MA running through the zone; a dramatic drop to about 49.2 followed (now 49.92).
passages.t: A down-sloping 200 MA confirms the downtrend, so shorting resistance is with the trend. Swing and day traders can short the first return to the range. The dramatic drop away from the base shows the imbalance.

passages.h: Chart: XLF (Financial Service ETF, weekly, 2003-2008): 'Support' about 25.0-26.2 (green lines) from the 2003 base at the start of the multi-year uptrend; price has fallen fast from about 38 to about 29, below the 200 MA, toward the unvisited demand.
passages.t: An old, never-revisited demand level is waiting below price. Price below a falling 200 MA - wait for the level instead of buying the decline. Sets up the 'Trading and Time' lesson that follows.
Repeated tests weaken a support level; a fresh, unvisited level below - especially where a rising 200 MA meets it - is the better demand.
Starting the year by increasing size without fixing process. Trading with discretionary, subjective decisions. Thinking repeated tests make support stronger. Rushing back into thin holiday markets.

Written trading plan exists and is being followed. No discretionary decisions left in the plan. Level is the unvisited origin, not a level touched several times. Trend context (e.g. 200 MA slope) agrees with direction. Results reviewed: average win/loss and win rate.
“It is best to turn those questions into RULES.” “Support is getting weaker, not stronger.”
200 MA used as a trend filter and as confluence at a demand origin; Kevin uses no indicators. Review of average win/average loss and win rate as a pre-trading requirement.

Support gets weaker every time price comes back to it, not stronger. Imagine a bowl of candy for buyers at one price. Each time price comes back, some buyers take their candy and leave. After a few visits the bowl is nearly empty, so price falls right through. Seiden prefers a fresh level below that nobody has touched yet. He also asks five questions before every year of trading: plan, discretion, objectivity, measuring supply and demand, and reviewing results.
Like a sandcastle wall hit by waves: every wave takes a bit of sand until the wall falls.
Each revisit fills more waiting buyers, so tested support weakens. The better buy is the unvisited origin below.
Turn every open question in your plan into a rule; review average win, average loss and win rate.
There are two demand levels: Support 2 at the origin of the whole rally, and Support 1 higher up.

passages.h: Step: Support 1 gets tested again and again
passages.t: Price comes back to Support 1 three times. Each bounce is smaller, because each visit filled more of the waiting buy orders.
On the next visit there are not enough buyers left and price breaks through.
Support 2 has never been revisited. That is the higher-quality demand. Buy at its top line with the stop below.

Repeated tests make support...? - Weaker: each test fills more waiting buyers. Better demand to buy? - The unvisited origin of the move. What should discretion become? - Rules. Three stats to review? - Average win, average loss, win percentage. Who funds the consistent trader? - The novice trader, almost always.

The XLF reached a demand level from 2003 and gained $2 in two days; Sam explains trade management and answers whether a level that old can matter. Markets are always in one of three states, and old levels are often better because price returning to them is far from equilibrium, giving large profit margins.
Once in profit, move the stop to breakeven and take some or all near the next opposing level.
Do not discard a level because it is old; old untouched levels often offer the biggest profit margins. Trade only when price is far from equilibrium.
After a $2 gain in two days you can move the stop to breakeven and consider taking some or all off near the nearby supply (the circled area).
The gain is nice, but the low-risk entry is the key point - getting gains is one thing, getting them with the lowest possible risk is another.
Demand exceeds supply: competition to buy, prices rise. Supply exceeds demand: competition to sell, prices fall.
Equilibrium: everyone can trade as much as they want; moving away from it increases competition, which forces price back. At equilibrium there is little or no opportunity.
A demand level from 2003 is not less relevant than one from last week; old levels usually produce better trades.
When price comes back to a level from long ago it is far from equilibrium, so the level is ideally placed on the curve with a large profit margin.
They are not the same buyers from 2003 - it is pure supply and demand: lower prices attract more buyers, higher prices attract more sellers.
Not every cluster is a level and not every high or low is a level; it takes objective rules.

XLF (Financial Service Sector ETF, weekly, 2003-2008): 'Demand (support)' about 25.0-26.0 at the 2003 base. Price rose to about 38 in 2007 and then crashed; an arrow labelled 'Low Risk High Reward Buying Opportunity' points to the touch of the zone near 26 in early 2008. A small circle near 29 marks nearby supply where profits can be taken; price is 27.41.

Stick-figure supply/demand curve: red sellers grow in number with price (3 at 40, 7 at 50, 14 at 60) and green buyers grow as price falls (3 at 30, 7 at 20, 13 at 10). It is a chart with time removed, showing the number of willing buyers and sellers at each price.
