passages.h: Chart: XLF (Financial Service Sector ETF, weekly, 2004-2008): 'Demand (support)' about 25-26 (green lines) from the 2003 base; price collapsed from about 38 to 27.41, and the arrow marks the 'Low Risk High Reward Buying Opportunity' at the zone.
passages.t: The demand level is years old but untouched - price returning there is far from equilibrium.

passages.h: Chart: XLF (Financial Service Sector ETF, weekly, 2004-2008): 'Demand (support)' about 25-26 (green lines) from the 2003 base; price collapsed from about 38 to 27.41, and the arrow marks the 'Low Risk High Reward Buying Opportunity' at the zone.
passages.t: Buy at the proximal line with a stop under the distal line: small risk, large profit margin. Price gained about $2 in two days after reaching the level.

passages.h: Chart: Stick-figure supply/demand curve: red sellers grow with price (3 at 40, 7 at 50, 14 at 60) and green buyers grow as price falls (3 at 30, 7 at 20, 13 at 10).
passages.t: It is a chart with time removed: the number of willing buyers and sellers at each price. The further price moves from equilibrium, the more the other side outnumbers it. Old levels far from current price are where the imbalance is greatest.
The supply/demand curve: willing sellers grow as price rises and willing buyers grow as it falls. The further price is from equilibrium, the bigger the imbalance.
XLF lesson: a demand level from 2003 that price had never revisited. When price finally returns, it is far from equilibrium, so the reaction and the profit margin are large.
Judging the trade by the gain instead of the entry risk. Ignoring old higher-timeframe levels as irrelevant. Trading in equilibrium where there is no opportunity.

Level is unvisited, regardless of its age. Price is far from equilibrium (good curve location). Exit plan: breakeven stop after a solid move, partials at the next supply. Opposing level marked for profit taking.
“At equilibrium, there is little to no trading opportunity.” “Obtaining them with the lowest possible risk is another story.”

Explicit claim that older untouched levels tend to give better trades than recent ones. Market-states model (demand > supply, supply > demand, equilibrium) and the time-removed supply/demand curve picture.

An old, untouched level is often the best level of all. A market can be in three moods: more buyers, more sellers, or balance. In balance nothing much happens. When price comes back to a level from years ago, it has travelled very far from balance, so the reaction can be big. It is not the same people from years ago; lower prices simply attract more buyers.
Like a rubber band: the further you stretch it from the middle, the harder it snaps back.

Three states: demand > supply, supply > demand, equilibrium. No opportunity at equilibrium. Old untouched levels are far from equilibrium, so they offer big profit margins. Once in profit, move the stop to breakeven and take some near the next supply.
Long ago, price based here and rallied hard. That demand was never revisited.
Price climbs for a long time and then crashes. By the time it returns to the old level, it is very far from where buyers and sellers balanced.

passages.h: Step: Low risk, high reward buy
passages.t: Buy at the top of the old zone, stop under the bottom. Small risk, very large room.
After a solid gain, move the stop to breakeven and consider taking some or all profit near the nearby supply. Getting gains is one thing; getting them with the lowest risk is another.
Three states of a market? - Demand > supply, supply > demand, equilibrium. Opportunity at equilibrium? - Little to none.
Why are old levels often better? - Price returning to them is far from equilibrium: big profit margin.
Supply/demand curve picture? - A chart with time removed: willing buyers and sellers at each price. After a solid move in your favour? - Stop to breakeven, partials at the next supply.

Profitable trading means finding the novice trader and taking the other side. Novices make two mistakes: they buy after buying and sell after selling, and they buy into supply and sell into demand. Sam walks through a chart where a range breaks, a rally on above-average volume returns to the range, and a confirmation candle gives the short, then tells his CME pit story.

Only short when the buyer on the other side is buying after a rally and into supply (and ideally in a downtrend); reverse for longs. Trade the first rally into a broken range/supply area, before its supply is absorbed.
Confirmation variant: enter below the low of the body of the candle that reacted at the level. Do not short after selling is already under way.
Buying after a period of buying (late, high risk) and selling after a period of selling. Buying into resistance (supply) and selling into support (demand) - always a low-odds trade.
In the pit story the novice was also buying in a market whose average price was falling (downtrend), making the odds even worse.
Focus on what the masses do wrong; Plato and Aristotle found the right answers by finding every way to fail first.
A: what books call sideways trading - really a period where supply and demand were in balance.
B: a candle that closes below the range; it can only do that because there was too much supply at A. Shorting after the selling is under way is late and high risk.
C: the novice buyers - buying after a rally, on above-average volume, into an area we already know has too much supply; first rally into the area, so none of the supply is absorbed.
D: the close of this candle is the confirmation; the entry is on E, below the low of D's body. This happens every day and is the essence of a turn in price.
Sam started on the CME floor handling order flow, with no screen charts for his first year.
A successful floor trader had him watch a newer trader desperately bidding after a long rise, then sold to him; the market fell minutes later.
His friend's whole approach: turns happen when the novice has entered, so find the novice and take the other side consistently.
Sam then worked out what that looks like on a price chart; indicators (e.g. a CCI piece) can show the same idea.
Emotion, not intellect, drives most human behaviour; emotional decisions lead to high-risk, low-reward trades.

OTA intraday chart with volume (11:00-16:00): A = a range drawn with a red top line and green bottom line; B = a long red candle breaking below the green line around 14:00 on rising volume. Price bounces; a red line extends from the broken range low as supply.

C = a tall green candle rallying back to that line on above-average volume (circled bar labelled 'Above Average Volume'); D = the candle at the line whose close confirms; E = the entry below D's body low, after which price slid to the close.

passages.h: Chart: OTA intraday chart with volume (11:00-16:00): A = range (red top line, green bottom line); B = long red candle breaking below the range low around 14:00; C = tall green candle rallying back to the broken low (red line) on above-average volume; D = confirmation candle; E = short entry; price then declines.
passages.t: After the break, the old range low becomes supply. C is the novice: buying after a rally, into supply, in a falling market - with heavy volume. Short below the D confirmation candle with the stop above C; target the B low and lower.
Range A breaks at B; the broken low becomes supply. C rallies back into it on above-average volume (novices buying after a rally into supply), D is the confirmation candle, E the short.
Buying after a period of buying, or selling after a period of selling. Buying into supply / selling into demand. Trading against the bigger trend. Making decisions based on emotion.

Price arrives after a strong run in the opposite direction (others are chasing). Price is at an unabsorbed supply/demand area (first visit). Bigger trend agrees with your side. If using confirmation: wait for the reaction candle and enter beyond its body.
“All we have to do is consistently find the novice trader.” “Find the novice trader and take the other side of his trade consistently.”
Confirmation entry defined as entry beyond the body low of the reaction candle at the level.
Above-average volume on the rally into supply used as evidence of novice buying; Kevin does not use volume. Broken-range low used as the supply level (range breakdown and retest).

Find the novice trader making a mistake, and take the other side. On the trading floor, an older trader showed young Sam a newer trader begging to buy after a long rise. The old pro sold to him, and minutes later the market fell. Novices make two mistakes: they buy after buying (late), and they buy into supply. Find that person on the chart and do the opposite.
Like a game of musical chairs: the novice runs for a chair after the music has already stopped.

Mistake 1: buying after a period of buying (or selling after selling). Mistake 2: buying into supply (or selling into demand). Confirmation variant: enter beyond the body of the reaction candle at the level.
Price moves sideways. Books call it a range; really supply and demand were roughly in balance.
A long red candle closes below the range. It can only do that because there was too much supply at A. Selling now would be late. The broken range low becomes supply.
Tall green candles rally back to the line on above-average volume. These buyers buy after a rally, into supply, in a falling market. That is the novice.

passages.h: Step: D and E: confirm and enter
passages.t: Candle D reacts at the line and closes lower; that close is the confirmation. Enter on E, below the low of D's body, with the stop above C. Price slides away.

Whose side do you take? - The opposite side of the novice trader. Novice mistake 1? - Buying after a period of buying (selling after selling). Novice mistake 2? - Buying into supply (selling into demand). After a range breaks down, the old low becomes? - Supply. Confirmation entry here? - Beyond the body low of the reaction candle at the level.
What makes the novice even more wrong? - Trading against the bigger trend.

A student in an options class bought RIMM puts when RIMM had run more than $8 from the morning low into the prior days' highs (resistance) with CCI overbought and a possible double top. He sold the puts the next day at the double bottom for a large gain; Sam stresses the low-risk entry, not the profit.

Sell to buyers who buy after a large advance and at resistance; buy from sellers who sell after a decline and at support. The prior days' highs/lows act as supply/demand for intraday trades. Take profits at the opposing level (here the double-bottom support). Keep risk small because any level can fail.
RIMM was flying, up over $8.00 from the morning low, and rallied into the prior days' highs, which are resistance.
The buyer there was buying after a large move up and at resistance - a novice. CCI was very overbought and a double top was possible.
The student took the other side with puts: bought them very cheap when they were about to get expensive and sold them expensive when they were about to get cheap.

Price could have gone higher and stopped him out; that is why risk stays low. The low-risk entry is the only reason he could enjoy the gain. He did the same trade in two other stocks at about the same time.
Most people who trade fail; simply do the opposite of what they do, when they do it, which is visible on a chart.
When someone buys after a significant advance and at resistance, consider selling to them; when someone sells after a decline and at support, consider buying from them.
Learning the rules is easy; emotion makes applying them one of the hardest things you will do.
The answers are in the trader on the other side of the trade, not in what the student did.
Do not trade in class; if you do, only when risk is low, reward is high and odds are in your favour.

OTA RIMM chart (intraday, 1/17-1/23, CCI panel below): a 'Double Top' circle near 91-92 on 1/17 and a second circle at the same height on 1/22 after the rally; text box 'Student bought PUT options on RIMM expecting a decline'.

Between them a 'Double Bottom' around 82 is circled (1/22 low and 1/23 low); text box 'Student sells his PUT options for a big profit because price has hit his target and turns into a double bottom'. CCI is circled above +100 at the second top.
Account screenshot: bought 10 puts (two fills of 5) at 6.50 on 01/22/08 around 13:16 for -6,517.49, sold 10 at 11.00 on 01/23/08 at 11:22 for +10,982.34 (about $4,465 gain).

passages.h: Chart: OTA RIMM chart (intraday, 1/17-1/23, CCI panel): 'Double Top' circles near 91-92 on 1/17 and 1/22; student bought puts at the second top after an $8 run from the morning low; 'Double Bottom' circles around 82 (1/22 low and 1/23 low) where he sold the puts; CCI overbought circled.
passages.t: The entry was at the prior days' highs (resistance) after a big rally - the novice was buying there. The exit was planned at the prior low (demand), where the double bottom formed.

passages.h: Chart: OTA RIMM chart (intraday, 1/17-1/23, CCI panel): 'Double Top' circles near 91-92 on 1/17 and 1/22; student bought puts at the second top after an $8 run from the morning low; 'Double Bottom' circles around 82 (1/22 low and 1/23 low) where he sold the puts; CCI overbought circled.
passages.t: The low-risk entry, not the size of the profit, is the lesson; CCI only supported the read.
RIMM trade: after an $8 run from the morning low into the prior highs (a possible double top), short via puts; take profit at the prior low where a double bottom forms.
Being impressed by the gain instead of the low-risk entry. Letting emotion override easy-to-learn rules. Trading personal accounts during class without a plan.

Price arrived after a large run (others chasing). Price is at prior highs/lows or a marked level. Target is the next opposing level. Risk defined and small; instrument choice (stock/options) fits the plan.
“Emotion will make applying the rules one of the hardest things you will ever attempt to do.” “The real key is to focus on the trader who was on the other side.”
Using options (buying puts) to express a supply-zone short. Prior days' highs treated as resistance on intraday charts; CCI overbought as supporting evidence (Kevin uses no indicators).

Sell to the buyer who chases a huge run into the old highs. A stock flew up more than $8 in one morning, straight into the highs of the days before. Anyone buying there was buying after a huge rise and right at resistance. A student bought put options to take the other side, cheap when they were about to get expensive. He sold them the next day at the old low, where a double bottom formed.
It is like buying an umbrella on a sunny day when it is cheap, and selling it when it starts to rain.

Sell to buyers after a large advance at resistance; buy from sellers after a decline at support. The prior days' highs and lows act as supply and demand. The low-risk entry is the lesson, not the size of the profit.
Mark the prior days' high (resistance) and low (support).
Price runs up hard into the prior highs. The buyer here is buying after a large move up and at resistance: a novice. A possible double top is forming.
The student bought puts at the second top. Risk stays small: if price kept going up, the loss would be limited.

passages.h: Step: Exit at the opposing level
passages.t: Price falls back to the prior low, where a double bottom forms. That was the planned target, so he takes profit.

Buyer after a big run into resistance is? - A novice: sell to him. Seller after a decline at support is? - A novice: buy from him. Prior days' highs on intraday charts? - Supply (resistance). Target for the RIMM puts? - The prior low, where a double bottom formed.
Should you trade your account in class? - Only when risk is low, reward high and odds in your favour.

Conventional chart patterns (triangles, flags, pennants, cup and handle, head and shoulders) all use breakout entries, and whether they work depends entirely on the supply and demand at the levels price breaks into. Before taking a pattern breakout, measure the profit margin to the next opposing level; RIMM, DRYS and EBAY examples compare good and poor margins.

Before any pattern breakout, find the next opposing supply/demand level and measure the profit margin. Skip pattern breakouts that run straight into a nearby opposing level. Do not chase a missed breakout fill. Prefer continuation patterns where price spends little time.
Indicators always do exactly what they are programmed to do; the problem is how traders use them. The same logic applies to chart patterns.

Every common pattern uses a breakout entry; the win or loss depends 100% on the supply/demand at the price levels being broken into. Before pressing buy or sell, check there is room for price to run after you enter.
A picture-perfect pattern can fail badly when the breakout runs straight into a support or resistance level.
Breakout entries are hard to fill well; do not chase price. If you miss the low-risk entry, let it go - there is always another trade.
Continuation patterns (descending triangle, bear pennant) are better when price spends very little time in the pattern.
Chart patterns, indicators, candle patterns and more can all be used; how well you quantify supply and demand decides the outcome.

RIMM intraday (5-minute TradeStation): a 'Descending Triangle' drawn with a falling top line and a flat bottom line after a rally; 'Short Entry' arrow at the break of the bottom line. 'Support - Target 1' is a green line at a prior pullback low below, and 'Support - Target 2' is a lower green line at the earlier base. Plenty of room - about 5:1 reward to risk.

DRYS (TradeStation title shows 60-minute, the text calls it daily; 12/17-12/28): after a steep decline, a small 'Descending Triangle' forms near 75-77; 'Short Entry' at the break of its base around 75. 'Support - Target' is the green line about 71 just below, marked with a double arrow - a much smaller reward-to-risk than RIMM. Price then based and rallied to 82.10.

EBAY 5-minute (12/10-12/11): after a gap up and drift near 34.8-35.0, a tall red candle dropped to about 34.45; a small 'Bear Pennant' formed there and broke lower. 'Support - Target' is the green line at about 33.85 drawn from the prior day's base, and the double arrow shows the decent profit margin from entry.

passages.h: Chart: RIMM, 5-minute: 'Descending Triangle' (falling top line, flat bottom line) after a rally; 'Short Entry' at the break of the bottom line; 'Support - Target 1' at a prior pullback low and 'Support - Target 2' at the earlier base, both reached.
passages.t: A pattern breakout is only worth taking if there is room to the next demand. Here target 1 and target 2 gave a good profit margin from the short entry. The pattern is just an entry trigger; supply and demand decide whether it works.

passages.h: Chart: DRYS, 60-minute (12/17-12/28): after a steep decline a small 'Descending Triangle' near 75-77; 'Short Entry' at the break around 75; 'Support - Target' about 71 just below (double arrow); price hit it and later rallied to 82.
passages.t: The support target sits close to the entry - a much smaller reward-to-risk than the RIMM example. The triangle formed low on the curve after a big decline, near demand. After the target, price turned up strongly - shorting near demand is the novice side.

passages.h: Chart: EBAY, 5-minute (12/10-12/11): after a gap up and drift near 34.8-35.0, a tall red candle drops to about 34.45; a small 'Bear Pennant' forms and breaks lower; 'Support - Target' about 33.85 from the prior day's base (double arrow).
passages.t: The prior day's base is the demand that defines the target. The double arrow shows a decent profit margin from the pennant entry. Measure that margin before taking any pattern breakout.
Descending triangles with the same short entry: one has support far below (good 3:1+ margin), the other has support just under the break (poor margin, skip).
Taking picture-perfect patterns without checking where the next support/resistance is. Chasing breakout entries for a fill. Using every indicator signal without logical rules around it.
Next opposing level located below/above the breakout. Reward to that level is at least 3:1. Price spent little time in the pattern. Entry is fillable without chasing.
“If you miss the low risk entry, let it go. There is always another trade.” “The less time price spends in the pattern, typically the better the outcome.”
Classic chart patterns allowed as entry triggers when filtered by supply/demand room; Kevin's course does not use pattern breakouts. Time-in-pattern rule: shorter consolidation = better continuation.

A chart pattern only works if there is room before the next level. Triangles, flags and head-and-shoulders all use a breakout entry. Whether they win depends on what waits at the prices price breaks into. If the next support is far below, the breakout has room to run. If support sits just under the break, even a perfect-looking pattern is a poor trade.
Like kicking a ball toward a wall: a great kick still goes nowhere if the wall is one step away.

Every common pattern uses a breakout; the outcome depends 100% on the supply and demand it breaks into. Measure the room to the next opposing level before you press the button. Do not chase a missed breakout fill. There is always another trade.
Price makes lower highs against a flat bottom. Classic books call this a short when the bottom line breaks.

passages.h: Step: Where is the next demand?
passages.t: Before shorting, look left for the next demand below. Here it is the base far below, where the earlier rally started.
The break comes. From the short entry to that demand is several times the risk to a stop above the last high. The pattern is just the trigger; supply and demand decide.

passages.h: Step: Price runs to the target
passages.t: Price falls all the way to the demand. A good profit margin made this pattern worth taking.

What entry do all common chart patterns use? - A breakout entry. Before taking a pattern breakout? - Find the next opposing level and measure the profit margin. Missed the low-risk fill? - Let it go. There is always another trade. Time in a continuation pattern? - Less time usually means a better outcome. Pattern breaks right into support? - Skip it.

The opening gap entry is usually Sam's lowest-risk, highest-reward trade of the day. Gaps happen because orders at the open overwhelm the other side, so price opens where supply and demand are out of balance; when a gap opens straight into a supply or demand level, the novice is on the wrong side. A SPY 60-minute chart shows three gap entries in one week.

At the open, check whether price gapped into a marked supply or demand level. Short gap-ups into supply after a rally; buy gap-downs into demand after a decline. Enter near the open (seconds to minutes), when the imbalance is greatest. Skip the open if you cannot yet identify levels objectively.
Gap up = more buy orders at the open than supply at the prior close; gap down = more sell orders than demand.
So at the open price is almost always at an imbalance - opportunity. Trade it back toward balance.
Floor example: with 10 buyers and 5 sellers at a price, price must rise as soon as the 5th seller sells.
The open is not for the novice trader, but it is a great opportunity for the trader who can spot the novice. Entries are usually seconds to minutes after the bell.

Imbalances are greatest at or near the open; by the end of the first hour a lot of novice capital has moved to astute traders. Order flow works as it did 100 years ago, and novices are always present.

Only a losing trader buys a gap up, after a rally, into an objective supply level; only a novice sells a gap down, after a decline, into demand. Do not see candles as red and green pictures; understand what is happening behind them. If you cannot see the novice trader in the market, you probably are the novice.

0 (two black lines) at the 2/14 top. B = 2/19 gap up into that supply at the open (tall oval), then a decline. 3 at the 2/15 base; E = 2/20 gap down into demand at the open (circle), then a rally. 74. Three gap entries in three days, all low risk if taken near the open.

passages.h: Chart: SPY 60-minute (2/11-2/22): supply A about 136.4-137.0 (black lines) at the 2/14 top; B = 2/19 gap up into that supply at the open (oval), then a decline; demand D about 133.9-134.3 at the 2/15 base; E = 2/20 gap down into demand (circle), then a rally; C = 2/21 gap up into supply again, then a decline.
passages.t: Three gap entries in one week, each opening straight into a marked level. Gap up after a rally into supply = short at the open; gap down after a decline into demand = buy. The novice buys the gap up and sells the gap down - take the other side within minutes.
Gap trades: a gap up after a rally that opens inside supply is a short at the open; a gap down after a decline into demand is a buy. Stop just beyond the zone.
Buying a gap up after a rally and into supply. Selling a gap down after a decline and into demand. Reading candles as colours and patterns instead of order flow.

Supply and demand levels marked before the open. Price gapped directly into a level. Gap came after a run in the same direction (novice chasing). Entry within the first minutes; stop just beyond the level.
“If you can't see the novice trader in markets, you likely are the novice trader.” “The open is not for the novice trader.”
Opening gaps into zones as a dedicated setup traded within minutes of the open; Kevin's notes cover session times but not gap fades.
Claim that imbalance is greatest at the open and the first hour is where most profit is made.

When price gaps straight into a level at the open, fade the crowd. At the opening bell, a crowd of orders rushes in. If there are 10 buyers and only 5 sellers, price must jump as soon as the 5th seller sells, and that is a gap. A gap up after a rally that opens right inside supply means late buyers are rushing into sellers. Seiden sells to them within minutes, and buys gaps down into demand the same way.
Like a crowd rushing into a shop at opening time to buy what the shop is about to put on sale.

Gaps happen because orders at the open overwhelm the other side: price opens at an imbalance. Short a gap up after a rally into supply; buy a gap down after a decline into demand. If you cannot see the novice in the market, you probably are the novice.

passages.h: Step: Mark levels before the open
passages.t: Supply A sits at the top base; demand D sits at the base after the drop.
After a rally, price gaps up at the open right into supply A. Only a novice buys a gap up, after a rally, into supply. Sell within minutes of the bell.
Next day price gaps down after a decline straight into demand D. Only a novice sells there. Buy.
Price gaps up into supply A once more and falls. Three gap entries, all at levels marked before the open, all low risk near the open.

Gap up means? - More buy orders at the open than supply at the prior close. Gap up after a rally into supply? - Short it near the open. Gap down after a decline into demand? - Buy it near the open. When are imbalances greatest? - At or near the open (first hour). Can't see the novice? - You are probably the novice.

A macro essay arguing that the nominal Dow and NASDAQ hide large declines once the falling US dollar is factored in, that the dollar is a faith-based currency, and that gold is a better yardstick of value. Sam closes by showing supply and demand on the US Dollar index and the 10-year note with the same A-B logic used for any market.
Analyse any market - currencies, bonds, gold - with the same A (pause) / B (first revisit) supply-demand logic. Use real-value benchmarks rather than nominal prices when judging long-term wealth.
Producers/savers (East Asia, China, Japan, OPEC) vs consumers/borrowers (US government and public); the US borrowed about $2 billion a day and ran a goods deficit over $800 billion in 2006.

Dow 2000 top 11,700 x dollar index 1.24 = 14,508 'GPPP' points; 2007 Dow 13,500 x 0.81 = 10,935, a 25% real decline. NASDAQ 5000 x 1.24 = 6,200 in 2000 vs 2,500 x 0.81 = 2,100 in 2006: a 66% real decline.
The Dow now buys over 30% fewer euros, 35% less milk, 40% less corn or wheat, 65% less silver, 70% less oil and 80% less copper than in 2000.
Since Nixon closed the gold window on 15 August 1971 the dollar is uncollateralised and faith-based.
Think of currencies like companies: the US dollar looks more like Enron than Microsoft; producer/saver currencies are the Microsofts.

Gold held its value: a $20 suit in 1932 vs an ounce over $700 today that still buys a nice suit. Printing money -> inflation -> higher rates -> weak bonds -> weak stocks. Dow/gold ratio fell from 47:1 in 2000 (11,700 / $250) to 19:1 in 2007 (14,000 / $740).

passages.h: Supply and demand on the dollar and bonds
passages.t: Area A: temporary stability that looks like equilibrium; the decline from it shows sellers greatly exceeded buyers.

passages.h: Supply and demand on the dollar and bonds
passages.t: B: the first revisit of A, where price is expected to decline again; a dramatic first decline suggests a similar decline at B.

passages.h: Supply and demand on the dollar and bonds
passages.t: Higher interest rates attract foreign buyers to a currency; falling treasury prices = rising yields (inverse).

passages.h: Supply and demand on the dollar and bonds
passages.t: Everyone with dollars or a mortgage has a reason to read charts of the dollar and the 10-year note objectively.

US Dollar index (daily, Oct 2006-Oct 2007): first A = base about 85.3-85.9 (red lines) followed by a gap and drop to about 82.3; B = the first revisit near 85.4 in early 2007, after which price declined. Second A = base about 82.7-83.4 in April, drop to about 81.3, B = revisit near 83.3 around June, then a slide to about 77.8 (now 78.56).

10-Year Note (daily, Jul-Sep): supply A about 117'00-117'16 (red lines) at a small July base, B = first revisit a few days later, followed by a steady decline to 108'23 (falling prices = rising yields).

US Dollar (daily, Apr-Jul, same period): demand A about 94.2-95.1 (green lines) at a base after a V-shaped low near 93; B = the pullback into the zone, after which price rallied to about 99 as rates rose.

passages.h: Chart: US Dollar index, daily (Oct 2006-Oct 2007): first A = base about 85.3-85.9 (red lines) followed by a gap and drop; B = the first revisit near 85.4 in early 2007, then a decline; second A = base about 82.7-83.4 in April, B = revisit near 83.3 around June, then a slide to about 78.
passages.t: The same A-B logic works on a macro chart: base, strong departure, first revisit. Each revisit of supply produced the next leg of the downtrend. Read the dollar objectively from price, not from the news narrative.

passages.h: Chart: Left: 10-Year Note, daily (Jul-Sep): supply A about 117'00-117'16 (red lines) at a small July base, B = first revisit, then a steady decline to 108'23. Right: US Dollar, daily (Apr-Jul): demand A about 94.2-95.1 (green lines), B = pullback into the zone, then a rally to about 99.
passages.t: Supply in the note and demand in the dollar, both traded at the first revisit (B). Falling note prices mean rising yields - the charts tell the macro story without opinions. A-B works the same for supply and demand.
Dollar index: each base (A) followed by a sharp drop marks supply; the first revisit (B) is the short, and the downtrend steps lower each time.
Judging wealth by nominal index highs while the currency loses value. Trusting media narratives instead of objective supply/demand.
Base A and strong departure identified on the macro chart. First revisit (B) only. Rate/currency relationship considered for FX and bond trades.
“What changed is the purchasing power of a fiat dollar to buy each asset class.” “Even the slightest illusion in the search for truth ensures truth will never be found.”
Intermarket and macro view (dollar index, treasury yields, gold ratio); Kevin's course is purely chart-based per pair.

The same A-B logic reads the dollar, bonds and gold. Seiden argues that stock indexes looked higher only because the dollar lost value, and that gold is a fairer ruler of wealth. But when he reads the dollar itself, he uses the same simple steps as any chart. A is a quiet pause, then a sharp drop proves sellers won. B is the first return to A, where price falls again. The downtrend steps lower each time.
Like going down a staircase: every landing where you paused becomes a step you will not climb back past easily.

A = a pause that looks like balance; a sharp drop from it proves sellers greatly exceeded buyers. B = the first revisit of A, where price is expected to fall again. Read any market objectively from price, not from media stories.
The dollar index pauses at A, then gaps and drops. Sellers greatly exceeded buyers there.
Price climbs back to A for the first time and declines again. A dramatic first drop suggested a similar drop at B.
Lower down, a new pause forms and price drops from it. That is the next supply.

passages.h: Step: Second B, next leg down
passages.t: The first revisit of the second A gives the next short, and the downtrend steps lower again.
A in this lesson? - A pause that looks like balance, left with a sharp drop. B in this lesson? - The first revisit of A.

Does the method change for currencies or bonds? - No. Same supply and demand logic everywhere. Treasury prices vs yields? - They move in opposite directions. Media narrative or chart? - Read the chart objectively.

In an LA stock class, Citigroup upgraded ImClone (IMCL) and the stock gapped up at the open right into a supply level formed by a dramatic decline from 45-46. The class sold to the crowd of upgrade buyers. Morning prep is about 15 minutes: find stocks opening at large imbalances, using upgrade/downgrade lists as one source.

Before the open, list stocks gapping into marked supply or demand (use upgrades/downgrades as a scan source). Fade an upgrade-driven gap up into supply; fade a downgrade-driven gap down into demand. Have the order plan set before the open.

Prep consists of finding stocks opening at price levels where supply and demand are out of balance in a large way and trading them back to balance. Two sources are used; one is the list of morning broker upgrades and downgrades. About 15 minutes of prep each morning; many stocks did the same thing that day.
On 3/7 there was a dramatic decline from the $45-46 area, so there was much more supply there than demand.
On 3/19 Citigroup upgraded the stock to Buy and price opened right into that supply level.
The plan made before the open said sell to anyone buying at that level: only a novice buys after an advance and into supply. Entries at strong imbalances near the open usually move very fast.
Everything else around markets is noise that invites you in at the wrong time and direction; as a trader Sam welcomes it.

IMCL 60-minute (3/6-3/20): 'Resistance (Supply)' between about 44.95 and 45.75 (black lines) at a 3/7 base, followed by a large red drop to about 42.5 and weeks of trading near 42-43.5. On 3/19 a 'Citigroup Upgrade Gap Up' candle opens into the zone (high about 45.2); 'Short Entry' points to the zone, and price then fell in red candles to 43.31.

passages.h: Chart: IMCL 60-minute (3/6-3/20): 'Resistance (Supply)' about 44.95-45.75 (black lines) at a 3/7 base, a large drop to about 42.5 and weeks near 42-43.5; on 3/19 a 'Citigroup Upgrade Gap Up' opens into the zone (high about 45.2), 'Short Entry' there, then price falls to about 43.3.
passages.t: The upgrade brought a crowd of buyers to the open - right into supply formed by a dramatic decline. Short the gap into the zone with the stop above the upper line.

passages.h: Chart: IMCL 60-minute (3/6-3/20): 'Resistance (Supply)' about 44.95-45.75 (black lines) at a 3/7 base, a large drop to about 42.5 and weeks near 42-43.5; on 3/19 a 'Citigroup Upgrade Gap Up' opens into the zone (high about 45.2), 'Short Entry' there, then price falls to about 43.3.
passages.t: Use upgrade/downgrade lists in a 15-minute pre-open scan to find stocks opening at big imbalances.
Morning gap fade: an upgrade gap opens straight into supply formed by a dramatic decline. Short the open with a stop above the zone; target the prior trading range.
Following a big bank's upgrade by buying the gap into supply. Treating news as a reason to enter instead of a source of novice order flow.
15-minute pre-open scan done (gaps, upgrades/downgrades). Gap opens directly into an unvisited level formed by a strong move. Entry, stop and target set before the bell.
“Everything else in and around markets is just noise.” “As a trader, I love it - the more noise the better.”
Broker upgrades/downgrades used as a scanning tool for gaps into zones; Kevin's rule is to avoid trading into news. Fixed 15-minute morning prep routine for stocks.

An upgrade gap into supply brings a crowd of buyers to sell to. A big bank told everyone a stock was a "Buy". The next morning the stock gapped up right into a price where it had crashed from before. That crash showed sellers were waiting there. Seiden's class had planned before the open to sell to anyone buying at that level, and price fell fast.
Like a store announcing a celebrity visit: the crowd rushes in, and the smart shop owner sells them everything at full price.

Prep about 15 minutes before the open: find stocks opening at big imbalances. Upgrade and downgrade lists are a scan source, not a reason to buy or sell. Fade an upgrade gap up into supply; fade a downgrade gap down into demand.

passages.h: Step: Supply from a dramatic decline
passages.t: Price rallied, paused, then fell hard. Much more supply than demand sat in that pause.
Price trades quietly below the zone for weeks. The level waits, untouched.
A bank upgrades the stock and it opens right inside the supply. The pre-open plan says sell to anyone buying here.
Entries at strong imbalances near the open usually move fast. Price drops back toward the old range.

Morning prep length? - About 15 minutes. Upgrade gap into supply? - Fade it: sell. Downgrade gap into demand? - Fade it: buy. Upgrade lists are...? - A scanning source, not a signal. When are orders set? - Before the open.

An essay on illusions: fundamental and news analysis feel real but layering them creates subjective illusions that lead to failure. Beliefs create behaviour and actions; strong news usually creates turns opposite to what the crowd expects because one side exhausts itself into a level. A goose that mechanically flies south each winter is the model for rule-based trading.

Only buy where there is objectively more demand than supply; otherwise no reason to buy, whatever the news. Treat strong news moves into a level as likely exhaustion and reversal points. Follow the rules mechanically, like a goose, without re-debating them each time.

Consistent low-risk profit rules are simple, but layers of illusion hide them. Mastering fundamental/news analysis to get consistent profits is an illusion; it stacks subjective views. Beginners are 'driving from LA to NY trying to reach Mexico' - the path itself is wrong.
Strategies that work do not change with market conditions; believing conditions change is itself an illusion. Beliefs -> behaviour patterns -> actions; decisions are made at the level of beliefs.
Strong news leads to strong emotion. Example: the London bombings made many sell, but once price reached demand (area A, the origin of an earlier rally) and the last seller sold, price rose.
No matter how bad the news is, when the last seller sells at a level with more willing buyers, prices rise.
Strong news creates powerful turns opposite to the majority's expectation because one side exhausts itself into an objective imbalance.
QLGC example: a rally back into an imbalance area came with good earnings, an uptrend and brokerage upgrades, but it was an objective supply level.
The only question: is price at a level with objectively more demand than supply? If not, there is no reason to buy.
The drop from that supply was fast because willing buyers went to zero while sellers were still there. When perceived risk is lowest, actual risk is often highest, and vice versa.
When everything about the company looks good, the price is usually high - and who will buy from you then?
Illusions disguise risk as opportunity and lead to the two mistakes: buying after rising prices and buying where sellers outnumber buyers.
Humans decide by emotion; a goose acts like a machine and flies south each autumn without debate.
Markets are supply and demand at work; opportunity is when the relationship is out of balance. Reality-based traders profit from the illusion-based crowd who buy after them.

Figure 1 (London bombings) and Figure 2 (QLGC supply with upgrades) are referenced, but the images are missing in this PDF - pages 74, 75 and 77 show only blank space with the captions. The text describes Figure 1 as demand A at the origin of a rally and B the bombing-day drop that turned higher at A, and Figure 2 as a labelled supply area that price rallied into on good news and upgrades before dropping fast.
Illusion of the news: strong good news brings the last buyers in, they exhaust themselves into supply, and price turns the opposite way to what the crowd expects.

Layering fundamental opinions and calling it analysis. Selling into demand on bad news, buying into supply on good news. Believing that market conditions change and the strategy must change too. Feeling safe because everyone agrees (comfort in numbers).
Is price at an objective level? If not, no trade regardless of news. Am I joining the crowd after a move? If yes, stop. Am I following the written rule without debate?
“When perceived risk is lowest, actual risk is often highest.” “The many illusions are nothing more than risk disguised as opportunity.”
News is treated as a source of exhaustion into levels (fade it at zones) rather than something to avoid trading around.

News and opinions are illusions. Follow simple rules like a goose. A goose flies south every autumn. It does not read the news or argue with itself; it just goes. People, though, stack up opinions about earnings, upgrades and scary headlines, and then buy high and sell low. When bad news pushes price into demand, the last seller sells and price must rise. When good news pulls price into supply, the last buyer buys and price falls.
Like a goose that flies south without checking the weather report: the rule works every year, so it just follows it.

Only buy where there is objectively more demand than supply; otherwise there is no reason to buy. Strong news into a level often marks the turn, opposite to what the crowd expects. When perceived risk is lowest, actual risk is often highest.

passages.h: Step: Demand at the origin of a rally
passages.t: Price based here and rallied. This area A is demand.
Terrible news hits and people sell hard. Big red candles race down toward A.
At A there are more willing buyers. No matter how bad the news, once the last seller sells, price rises.

passages.h: Step: The turn the crowd did not expect
passages.t: Price rallies away. Strong news created a turn opposite to the majority's view because one side exhausted itself into an objective level.

Bad news pushes price into demand. Then? - Once the last seller sells, price rises. Perceived risk lowest means? - Actual risk is often highest. Do market conditions require a new strategy? - No. Believing they do is an illusion. Why trade like a goose? - Follow the rule mechanically, without re-debating it. Illusions are...? - Risk disguised as opportunity.

Recurring reader questions answered with a daily DIA demand setup. The first answer explains how to draw zone lines: enclose the majority of trading, check two timeframes because wicks and bodies swap between timeframes, and reduce position size if the zone is wide. The second question (how to choose an exact price inside a zone) begins here and its answer continues past page 80.
Draw the zone so the majority of trading in the base sits between the lines. Check the base on two timeframes before fixing the lines.
If the zone is drawn wide (full highs/lows), cut position size to keep risk within limits. Buy the return into a demand cluster that price left upward.
Once price moved above the cluster of trading, that cluster became a significant demand level for a couple of long trades.
Price could only leave that area upward because demand for Dow stocks exceeded supply there.
When price declined back into it, sellers were selling where demand exceeds supply - the novice seller to buy from.

passages.h: Q1: where to draw the lines (opens, closes, wicks?)
passages.t: Make sure the vast majority of trading sits between your two lines. There is no fixed 'include wicks' or 'exclude wicks' answer: change the timeframe and some wicks become bodies and some bodies become wicks.

passages.h: Q1: where to draw the lines (opens, closes, wicks?)
passages.t: Look at the area on two different timeframes to see where most trading happened and draw there. Using the candle highs and lows is fine but often makes a very large stop.

passages.h: Q1: where to draw the lines (opens, closes, wicks?)
passages.t: If you draw the lines around the entire price action (as the student did in this chart), reduce position size so the risk stays inside your maximum.
A reader notes that Sam says true levels are found in bases, pivots and gaps, and asks how to quantify them and where inside a range such as 15.20-15.50 to buy or sell.
The reader lists clues Sam has mentioned: a momentum bar followed by a reversal bar, a slow stochastic cross, and a cross of the +/-100 CCI line. The answer follows after page 80.

DIA daily (TradeStation, Mar-May): after a drop to about 118 in March and a choppy recovery, price formed a cluster in early April; 'Support (Demand)' is drawn about 125.2-127.2 (two black lines) around the whole cluster. Price rose above it, came back twice (circled in late April and early May, both touching about 127) and bounced each time; last price 130.05.

passages.h: Chart: DIA daily (TradeStation, Mar-May): after a drop to about 118 and a choppy recovery, 'Support (Demand)' drawn about 125.2-127.2 (two black lines) around the early-April cluster; price rose above it and came back twice (circled, late April and early May), holding near 127 both times before moving to about 130.
passages.t: The student drew the lines around the whole cluster - a wide zone means a wide stop. Enclose the majority of the trading and check a second timeframe for where bodies and wicks sit. If the zone stays wide, reduce position size so risk stays within your maximum.
Zone lines: enclose the majority of trading in the base (body tops for the proximal, the extreme wick for the distal). If the lines must cover all the price action, the stop is wider, so cut size.
A long daily lower wick hides a base of candle bodies on the 60-minute chart; checking both timeframes gives truer proximal and distal lines.
Applying one fixed wick/body rule on every timeframe. Drawing wide zones and keeping full position size.

Base examined on two timeframes. Lines contain most of the trading in the base. Stop size measured; position size reduced if the zone is wide. Price left the cluster strongly and is returning into it.
“Make sure that the vast majority of trading is between your two lines.” “Some wicks become bodies and some bodies become wicks.”

Kevin's distal line always includes the wick (objective rule); Seiden says no fixed wick rule - enclose the majority of trading, judged across two timeframes. Wide zones handled by cutting position size instead of redrawing the zone smaller.
Mentions slow stochastic and CCI clues for timing entries inside a zone (indicators, which Kevin does not use).

Draw zone lines so most of the trading sits between them. A reader asked: do I draw zones on the candle bodies or the wicks? Seiden says there is no fixed answer, because on another timeframe some wicks become bodies and some bodies become wicks. Look at the base on two timeframes and make sure the vast majority of trading is between your two lines. If your zone ends up wide, keep it but trade a smaller size.
Like drawing a fence around a herd of sheep: you fence in where nearly all of them stand, not the one sheep that wandered off.

Enclose the vast majority of the trading in the base between two lines. Check the base on two timeframes: wicks and bodies swap between them. A wide zone means a wide stop: cut position size so risk stays inside your maximum.
Price falls, trades in a cluster, then rises above it. Price could only leave upward because demand exceeded supply there.
Drawing from the highest high to the lowest low covers every tick, but it makes a very large stop.
Instead, put the top line on the highest body and the bottom line on the lowest wick, so most of the trading is inside. Check a second timeframe to confirm where the bodies really are.
Sellers who sell back into this cluster are selling where demand exceeds supply. Price returns twice and bounces both times.

Zone drawing goal? - The vast majority of trading in the base is between the two lines. Bodies or wicks? - No fixed rule: they swap between timeframes. Check two timeframes. Wide zone? - Keep it, but cut position size. Why does price leave a cluster upward? - Demand exceeded supply there. Seller back into that cluster is? - A novice: buy from him.

Continued from p80: the tail of a reader Q&A. Seiden says not to pick exact turns but to wrap each level in two lines and bet on a turn in that area, buying at the upper demand line with the stop just below the lower line. Any entry trigger is acceptable as long as it fires AT a level.
A second question about market makers 'manipulating' price is answered from his floor experience: institutions push price into known supply to invite the public in, then sell into it.
Mark every level as a zone with two lines, not a single price. Long entry at the upper (proximal) demand line; protective stop just below the lower (distal) line.
Only act on a trigger (reversal candle, CCI extreme, etc.) when it occurs at a supply or demand level. Size the position from the stop distance so the loss stays within your comfort limit.

He did not invent supply and demand; he is repeating Adam Smith and Newton's laws of motion, where the 'mass' is order flow. The same equation has governed price movement for centuries and has not changed.

passages.h: Two lines instead of an exact turning point
passages.t: Picking the exact turning point is hard and adds little profit even if you manage it. Draw two lines around each supply (resistance) and demand (support) level; you are only betting that price turns somewhere in that area.

passages.h: Two lines instead of an exact turning point
passages.t: Long: buy when price reaches the upper demand line; once filled, put the protective sell stop just below the lower demand line. Size the position so the loss, if stopped, is no more than you are comfortable with.
A momentum candle followed by a reversal candle AT a demand or supply level is a valid entry signal. A CCI overbought/oversold reading AT a level is also valid.
Use any signal you like; what matters is that it fires at a price where demand likely exceeds supply (or vice versa).

passages.h: Are market makers just manipulating price?
passages.t: From the trading floor: when large supply sat above the market, institutions bid price up to that level, inviting the public to buy, then dumped a large sell order there, leaving the public on the wrong side.

passages.h: Are market makers just manipulating price?
passages.t: That is not a contradiction of supply and demand; it is how the game is played, and those who understand it best get paid by those who understand it least.

passages.h: Are market makers just manipulating price?
passages.t: The one place an institution cannot hide is the price chart, so candles should be read as footprints of real buyers and sellers, not red and green signals.
The chart this answer refers to is on p80 (previous part); no chart appears on pp81-82.
Two-line demand zone: the base is wrapped by a proximal and a distal line. Buy at the proximal line on the return, stop just below the distal line, target the opposing supply.

Trying to pick the exact tick of a turn. Taking indicator or candle signals away from a level. Believing price is pure manipulation and ignoring what the chart shows. Learning from books written by people who do not trade.

Is the level drawn as a two-line zone? Is my entry at the proximal line and my stop beyond the distal line? Did my trigger fire at the level, not in the middle of nowhere? Is position size based on the stop distance?
“The one place a market maker or institution can't hide is the price chart.” “You're just betting that they will turn in that area.”

Same as Kevin: entry at the proximal line, stop beyond the distal line. Differs: Seiden accepts indicator triggers (CCI overbought/oversold) as long as they fire at a level; Kevin's lessons avoid indicators.

Wrap each level in two lines and bet price turns inside them. Guessing the exact tick where price turns is hard and adds little money even when you get it right. So Seiden draws two lines around each level and simply bets that price turns somewhere in that area. He buys at the upper demand line and puts his stop just under the lower line. Any entry signal is fine, as long as it fires at the level and not in the middle of nowhere.
Like catching a ball with a big basket instead of two fingers: you only need it to land somewhere inside.

A level is a zone with two lines, not a single price. Buy at the upper (proximal) demand line, stop just below the lower (distal) line. Any trigger is fine - reversal candle, CCI extreme - only if it fires AT a level.

passages.h: Step: Two lines around the level
passages.t: Wrap the base in two lines: the proximal line on top, the distal line at the bottom. We are only betting price turns in this area.
Buy when price reaches the upper line. Once filled, the protective stop goes just below the lower line. Size the trade so that loss is one you are comfortable with.

passages.h: Step: A signal AT the level
passages.t: A momentum drop into the zone followed by a reversal candle is a valid signal, because it fires at a price where demand likely exceeds supply.
Big players cannot hide on the price chart. Read candles as footprints of real buyers and sellers. Price rallies to the supply.

How many lines per level? - Two: proximal and distal. Long entry? - At the upper (proximal) demand line. Long stop? - Just below the lower (distal) demand line. Which entry signals are allowed? - Any - as long as it fires at a supply or demand level. Where can institutions not hide? - On the price chart. Whose ideas is this method? - Adam Smith's supply and demand and Newton's laws of motion.

Seiden explains the breakout, the most popular entry at Online Trading Academy, in two forms: the support/resistance breakout and the trend-line breakout. A level that is hit repeatedly with shrinking reactions, and then has price basing right at it, has run out of opposing orders and is likely to break.
A trend-line break shows price has reached a level where the other side is now stronger, and a logical target is the origin of the whole trend.

Breakout setup: repeated tests with progressively shallower reactions, then sideways basing AT the level, then enter on the break. Draw a trend line only once there are two points. Long on a break above a down-trend line; short on a break below an up-trend line. Logical target for a trend-line break: the origin of the move that began the trend. Manage risk first; an entry is only the beginning of the plan.
Read the level left to right: the first pivot high forms because supply greatly exceeds demand; the first drop away is large.
On each later visit some of the resting sell orders are filled, so the drop gets shallower: the equation is moving toward balance.
Tree-chopping analogy: each chop removes mass, so the tree is more likely to fall; in trading the mass is the supply or demand at the level.

On the fourth visit price stops falling and bases sideways under the line: there are no longer more sellers than buyers. That is when you get ready to buy the breakout as a low-risk entry. For shorts, do the mirror image (he jokes: print the page and turn it upside down).

A trend line needs two points before it can be drawn. Downtrend: price falls because it is at levels where supply exceeds demand. Instead of guessing where demand is, wait for the break above the down-trend line; the break shows a level with more willing buyers has been reached.

Uptrend: connect the pivot lows and sell short on the break (breakdown) of the line instead of guessing where supply is. One logical profit target is the origin of the move that started the whole trend.
Stocks, futures, forex, options, trading cards or rare coins: it is all people and price, and a breakout is quantified the same way.
Rookie-card analogy: when the last card offered at the current price sells, price has to rise.
Risk management is the most important part of trading; the entry is only the start of a risk-averse strategy.
TradeStation EURUSD 30-min, 5/14 to 5/15. A horizontal resistance line is drawn at about 1.5485 (labelled 1.54849).

Three small circles mark the touches of the line on 5/14 at about 08:00, 12:00 and 16:00. After a low near 1.5395 around 04:00, the first touch rejects into a dip; the later touches give smaller and smaller pullbacks (to about 1.5465-1.5470). Price then grinds sideways just under the line overnight (about 1.5455-1.5470).
A large green oval on 5/15 near 00:00-02:00 shows price basing right at the line and breaking through; price then runs to about 1.5540-1.5550. The oval is the breakout buy area.

passages.h: Chart 2 (p85): EURUSD 15-min, down-trend line break, long
passages.t: EURUSD 15-min, evening of 5/11 into 5/12. A down-trend line starts at the pivot high of about 1.5483 (labelled 1.54826) at about 20:00 and runs down across the lower highs. Price falls to about 1.5375-1.5385 by 01:00-02:00 on 5/12.

passages.h: Chart 2 (p85): EURUSD 15-min, down-trend line break, long
passages.t: A circle at about 02:30 marks the green candle breaking above the line near 1.5390: the long entry.

passages.h: Chart 2 (p85): EURUSD 15-min, down-trend line break, long
passages.t: A dashed red horizontal line at 1.5483 (the origin of the decline) is the target; a second circle around 09:00 shows price reaching it. Price then continues to about 1.5540.

passages.h: Chart 3 (p86): EURUSD 5-min, up-trend line break, short
passages.t: EURUSD 5-min. A steep up-trend line is drawn from the pivot low at about 1.5567 (02:30) through the rising lows of a rally to about 1.5630 (03:30-03:45).

passages.h: Chart 3 (p86): EURUSD 5-min, up-trend line break, short
passages.t: A narrow oval at about 04:00 marks the red candle breaking below the line near 1.5615-1.5620: the short entry.

passages.h: Chart 3 (p86): EURUSD 5-min, up-trend line break, short
passages.t: A dashed red line at about 1.5567 (the origin of the rally) is the target; a circle at about 05:45 shows price falling back to it before bouncing slightly.

passages.h: Chart: EURUSD 30-min (5/14-5/15): horizontal resistance at 1.54849 tested three times (circles at 08:00, 12:00, 16:00) with shrinking pullbacks, then price bases just under the line overnight and breaks out in the green oval, running to about 1.5540.
passages.t: Read the level left to right: the first rejection is the deepest, later ones are shallower as sell orders are filled.

passages.h: Chart: EURUSD 30-min (5/14-5/15): horizontal resistance at 1.54849 tested three times (circles at 08:00, 12:00, 16:00) with shrinking pullbacks, then price bases just under the line overnight and breaks out in the green oval, running to about 1.5540.
passages.t: The key tell is basing AT the line instead of rejecting from it: sellers there are used up. Entry is the break of the line out of that basing; the stop belongs below the small base.

passages.h: Chart: EURUSD 15-min (5/11-5/12): down-trend line drawn from the 1.54826 pivot high across the lower highs. The circled green candle near 02:30 breaks above the line around 1.5390 (long entry); the dashed line at 1.5483, the origin of the decline, is the target, reached about 09:00.
passages.t: A trend line needs two points; the break shows price has reached a level where buyers now outnumber sellers. Target the origin of the whole move that the trend line contained. No guessing where demand is: the break tells you.

passages.h: Chart: EURUSD 5-min: steep up-trend line from the 1.5567 pivot low (02:30) through the rising lows of a rally to about 1.5630. The circled red candle near 04:00 breaks the line around 1.5617 (short entry); the dashed line at 1.5567, the origin of the rally, is the target, reached about 05:45.
passages.t: Mirror image of the long: short the break of an up-trend line instead of guessing where supply is. Target is again the origin of the move (the dashed line). Stop goes above the swing high just before the break.
Consumed-level breakout: each visit to resistance produces a smaller drop as sell orders are filled; when price bases right under the line, buy the break.
Trend-line break: draw the line through two lower highs, buy the first candle that breaks above it, and target the origin of the decline.

Guessing where a trend will end instead of letting the line break show it. Buying a breakout without seeing evidence that the opposing orders at the level are used up. Thinking breakouts only work in one market or one era.

Have the reactions from the level been shrinking with each visit? Is price now basing at the level instead of rejecting from it? Does my trend line have at least two points? Is the origin of the trend far enough away to justify the trade? Is the stop and position size set before entry?
“With each chop, you are removing mass from the tree.” “They are all just people and price.”

New: a 'consumed level' breakout setup (shrinking reactions, then basing at the level, then buy the break). Kevin's breakout entry is a buy above a supply zone after confirmation at an HTF zone, not this exhaustion pattern.

Differs: Kevin uses a trendline break as confirmation at a zone and stresses full-candle closes; Seiden trades the trend-line break itself as the entry. New: target = origin of the whole trend after a trend-line break.

When a level is used up, price breaks through it. Buy the breakout. Think of chopping a tree. The first chop takes a big chunk, and every chop after removes a bit more wood. Each time price hits resistance, some sellers there get filled, so the drop gets smaller. When price stops dropping and just sits right under the line, the sellers are gone and the tree is about to fall. A broken trend line works the same way: it shows the other side has become stronger.
Like a rookie card for sale: once the last card at today's price is sold, the price has to go up.

Repeated tests with shrinking reactions mean the level's orders are being used up. Basing right AT the level, then the break, is the low-risk breakout buy. Trend-line break: needs two points; target the origin of the whole trend.

passages.h: Step: Read the level left to right
passages.t: The first visit to resistance gives the deepest drop: supply greatly exceeds demand there.
Each later visit fills more sell orders, so the drops get smaller and smaller. The equation is moving toward balance.
Now price stops falling and bases sideways right under the line. There are no longer more sellers than buyers. Get ready to buy the break.
Price breaks through. Enter on the break with the stop below the small base. Risk management comes first: the entry is just the start of the plan.

Shrinking reactions at resistance mean? - The sell orders there are being used up. The key tell before a breakout? - Price bases right at the level instead of rejecting. Tree-chopping analogy? - Each visit removes mass (orders) until the level gives way. Points needed for a trend line? - Two. Target after a trend-line break? - The origin of the move that started the trend.
Most important part of trading? - Risk management; the entry is only the start.

After a London class in the week of 5/19/08 where the class shorted all week, Seiden returns to the question of time at a level. A pivot (price could not stay at the level) shows a large imbalance and is a stronger level than a cluster of sideways trading, where supply and demand were only mildly out of balance. There is a hierarchy of levels, and the greater the imbalance the greater the opportunity.

Rank levels: pivots (price could not stay) above clusters (price stayed a long time). Buy the first pullback into a pivot-low demand area. Expect a cluster level to give way easily, especially after a strong move into it.
The London class traded only the short side because the supply and demand picture said global equities would fall.
He also flags a coming US dollar rally; to short EUR against USD, wait for a short-term rally against the dollar first.
Trading comes down to catching reversals or trading with the trend; for reversals, success depends on your definition of support and resistance.
Ask why price cannot stay at a level. A series of pivot lows with no basing means demand and supply are so out of balance that price cannot remain there: a very strong demand level.
A cluster is a level where price stayed a long time; that means supply and demand were not far out of balance, so the level is weaker.
A cluster can still work as support or resistance, but pivot areas are, by definition, stronger most of the time.

passages.h: Chart (p88): E-mini S&P 60-min (Jun08), pivot A versus cluster B
passages.t: @ES 60-min from 4/21 to 5/30/2008, price range about 1,370-1,440. Area A: two lines at about 1,371 and 1,375 under a series of pivot lows on 4/22-4/24, where price kept spiking down and leaving at once.

passages.h: Chart (p88): E-mini S&P 60-min (Jun08), pivot A versus cluster B
passages.t: Price rallies to about 1,440 by 5/19, then falls. Area B: a box at about 1,392-1,398 around 5/22, a cluster of sideways candles before a further drop.

passages.h: Chart (p88): E-mini S&P 60-min (Jun08), pivot A versus cluster B
passages.t: Area C (oval, 5/23-5/27): the first pullback into demand A around 1,373-1,378; this is the low-risk buy.

passages.h: Chart (p88): E-mini S&P 60-min (Jun08), pivot A versus cluster B
passages.t: Area D (circle, 5/29): price rallies from C straight through cluster B, showing B held little supply. Last price about 1,397.50.

passages.h: Chart: E-mini S&P 60-min (Jun08): A = pivot-low demand at about 1,371-1,375 where price spiked down and left immediately; B = cluster box at about 1,392-1,398 where price lingered. C (oval) is the first pullback into A, the buy; D shows the rally slicing straight through cluster B.
passages.t: Pivot (price could not stay) beats cluster (price stayed): A held, B gave way. The buy is the first return to A, with the stop under the lower line. A cluster is a weak obstacle for the move out of a strong pivot.
Pivot versus cluster: price could not stay at pivot A (big imbalance, strong level), but lingered at cluster B (mild imbalance). The rally from A slices straight through B.
Treating every sideways cluster as strong support or resistance. Fading a strong move at a weak cluster level.
Is my level a pivot where price left quickly, or a cluster where price lingered? Is this the first pullback into the level? If it is a cluster, have I lowered my expectations or skipped it?
“The greater the supply and demand imbalance, the greater the opportunity.” “Price just rallies right through it like a hot knife through butter.”
Similar direction to Kevin's preference for short bases (few basing candles), but Seiden states an explicit 'cluster = weaker level' hierarchy that Kevin's lessons do not.

A spot price could not stay at beats a spot where it sat around. Ask why price could not stay somewhere. At a pivot low, price spiked down and left at once, so buyers hugely outnumbered sellers. At a cluster, price sat around for a long time, so buyers and sellers were only a little out of balance. When a strong move comes out of the pivot, it slices through the cluster like a hot knife through butter.
Like touching a hot stove versus a warm mug: you pull your hand off the stove instantly, but you can hold the mug all day.
Pivot (price could not stay) = big imbalance = strong level. Cluster (price stayed a long time) = mild imbalance = weaker level. Buy the first pullback into the pivot; expect clusters to give way.
Price spikes down and leaves immediately, again and again. It cannot stay here: demand is far greater than supply.
On the way down, price lingers sideways for many candles. Supply and demand were only mildly out of balance here.
Price slips through the cluster easily and falls back toward A.

passages.h: Step: C and D: buy A, slice through B
passages.t: The first pullback into A is the low-risk buy, stop under the lower line. The rally from A cuts straight through the cluster.

Pivot level means? - Price could not stay: big imbalance, strong level. Cluster level means? - Price stayed: mild imbalance, weaker level. Which pullback to buy? - The first pullback into the pivot area. Strong move vs weak cluster? - It slices right through it. Big question to ask at any level? - Why can price not stay here?

Seiden sets out the three principles behind his whole method: price in a free market is a function of supply and demand; all influences on price are reflected in price; and price moves when one of the two competing forces becomes zero at a price. An earthquake analogy and a worked 300-buyers/200-sellers example show that apparent balance is often an imbalance that just needs time to play out.

Base every decision on price; filter out opinion and news. Look for the price where one side is exhausted (the origin of motion). Do not trade at equilibrium; trade the pivots where imbalance is obvious.

A former earthquake scientist asked for help; Seiden told him he already had the tools. Two plates press against each other until a threshold is reached and one overwhelms the other. Buyers and sellers are quantified the same way.

passages.h: Principle 1: price is a function of supply and demand
passages.t: A market is buyers, sellers and a 'widget' (stock, futures, currency, bond). A market is always in one of three states: demand exceeds supply (competition to buy, rising prices; a pivot low on the chart), supply exceeds demand (pivot high), or equilibrium.

passages.h: Principle 1: price is a function of supply and demand
passages.t: At equilibrium there is no competition; moving away from it creates competition that pushes price back. Most candles are at equilibrium, but that is not where you want to trade.

passages.h: Principle 2: all influences are reflected in price
passages.t: News, earnings, analyst opinion and events create different perceptions depending on each person's belief system; people wrongly assume others think like them.

passages.h: Principle 2: all influences are reflected in price
passages.t: Beliefs lead to action (buying or selling), and every action happens at a price, so price is all you need. Adding other information distorts your view.

passages.h: Principle 3: motion starts when one force reaches zero
passages.t: Example: 300 buyers and 200 sellers at $20.50. Price looks stable until the 200th seller sells; then 100 buyers remain with no sellers and price must rise. What looked like equilibrium was an imbalance that took time to play out.
Hand-drawn candles: two red candles falling from about $22.00, a dip to $20.50, then green candles rising back to about $22.00+, a small pullback and another rise.

Under the lows the table reads Sellers 200, 100, 0 and Buyers 300, 200, 100. The circled column (0 sellers, 100 buyers) with an arrow marks the exact candle where the rally begins. Labelled '2 Competing Forces'. Price levels marked $22.00, $21.00 and $20.50.

passages.h: Chart: Hand-drawn diagram '2 Competing Forces': red candles fall from $22.00 to $20.50, then green candles rise back above $22.00. Under the low: Sellers 200, 100, 0 and Buyers 300, 200, 100; the circled column (0 sellers, 100 buyers) marks the candle where the rally starts.
passages.t: Apparent balance at $20.50 was an imbalance (more buyers than sellers) that needed time to play out. Motion starts the moment one side reaches zero. This is what every demand zone is: a price where buyers outnumber sellers.
Two competing forces: at $20.50 there are more buyers than sellers. Price looks stable until the last seller is filled (sellers = 0), then the remaining buyers must pay up.
Assuming others share your beliefs about news. Adding outside information that distorts the supply/demand picture. Mistaking sideways 'balance' for a lack of opportunity.
Is price at a pivot (imbalance) rather than at equilibrium? Am I making this decision from price alone, not from news or opinion? Can I see where one side was exhausted?
“Any and all influences on price are reflected in price.” “It just took a certain amount of time for this unbalanced equation to play out.”
New framing: the three principles, the 'one side becomes zero' idea and the earthquake analogy are not in Kevin's course. Kevin's lessons do not discuss equilibrium as a market state.

Price moves when one side runs out. That is the whole game. At $20.50 there are 300 buyers and 200 sellers. Price looks still while they trade, but it is not balance. When the 200th seller sells, 100 buyers are left with nobody to buy from, so they must pay more and price rises. Like two earth plates pushing until one gives way, the market moves the moment one force reaches zero.
Like a tug of war where one team keeps losing players: the rope stays still until the last one lets go, then it flies.
Price is a function of supply and demand. All influences are reflected in price, so price is all you need. Motion starts when one of the two forces reaches zero at a price.
A market is always in one of three states: more demand (prices rise), more supply (prices fall), or balance. Here sellers are winning and price falls.
Price goes quiet at the low. It looks balanced, but there are 300 buyers and 200 sellers. The sellers are slowly being filled.
The last seller sells. The buyers left must pay up, and price rises. That apparent balance was an imbalance that needed time to play out.

passages.h: Step: Trade the pivot, not the balance
passages.t: Most candles are near equilibrium, which is not where to trade. When price returns to the place where one side ran out, buy there.

Principle 1? - Price in a free market is a function of supply and demand. Principle 2? - All influences on price are reflected in price. Principle 3? - Motion starts when one competing force reaches zero at a price. Pivot low on a chart shows? - Demand exceeded supply.
Earthquake analogy? - Plates push until one overwhelms the other, like buyers and sellers.

Now the XLT instructor for futures and forex, Seiden compares a non-quality support level (a sideways range in the middle of a move) with a quality one (a pivot low that price exploded away from). The S&P gapped straight through the non-quality range but later gapped down into the quality pivot low, which was a buy from novice sellers, with targets at the gap origin and the nearest pivot high.
Reject ranges that sit in the middle of a move (rally-range-rally) as buy levels. Prefer pivot lows that price explodes away from.
Gap down into quality demand: buy; target 1 = origin of the gap, target 2 = nearest pivot high. Always ask who is on the other side of the trade.
'Support' means different things to different people (Fibonacci, moving averages, pivots, clusters).
A sideways range preceded by a rally and followed by a rally sits in the middle of a move; it is not a quality level and price often slices through it.
A pivot low that price explodes away from shows demand greatly exceeds supply: that is quality.

passages.h: Who is selling the gap down?
passages.t: Someone said buying a gap down was high risk. Seiden asks who is selling: a seller AFTER a decline and INTO a level where demand exceeds supply is a novice.

passages.h: Who is selling the gap down?
passages.t: The laws of supply and demand ensure that trader loses over time, so be the buyer. If wrong, the loss is small because risk is low.
Long dollar, short GBP and EUR position trades were working, but it was no longer the time to enter: the dollar was nearing supply and GBP/EUR nearing demand.

passages.h: Chart (p94): E-mini S&P 15-min, non-quality A versus quality C
passages.t: @ES 15-min from 8/8 to 8/14, price about 1,265-1,312. A (non-quality, circled, 8/8): a small sideways range at about 1,281-1,285 after a strong rally from about 1,265 and before a further rally to about 1,310 on 8/11. Two lines extend right. B (arrow, 8/13 open): price opens right into A and falls straight through it.

passages.h: Chart (p94): E-mini S&P 15-min, non-quality A versus quality C
passages.t: C (quality, circled, 8/13): a pivot low at about 1,275-1,279 that price explodes away from to about 1,293.

passages.h: Chart (p94): E-mini S&P 15-min, non-quality A versus quality C
passages.t: D (8/14, arrow): price gaps down into C (lines about 1,275 and 1,279): the buy. Two short red lines mark the targets: the gap origin at about 1,284 and the nearest pivot high at about 1,293. Price then rallies to about 1,299.75.

passages.h: Chart: E-mini S&P 15-min (8/8-8/14): A (non-quality) is a sideways range at about 1,281-1,285 in the middle of a rally; B shows price falling straight through it. C (quality) is a pivot low at about 1,275-1,279 that price exploded from. D: the 8/14 gap down into C is the buy; red lines mark targets at the gap origin (about 1,284) and the nearest pivot high (about 1,293).
passages.t: A mid-move sideways range is not quality support; price sliced through it. Quality = a pivot price left explosively. Gap down into quality demand after a decline: the seller is the novice, be the buyer. Target 1 is the gap origin, target 2 the nearest pivot high.

Non-quality vs quality support: a sideways range in the middle of a rally (A) gets sliced; a pivot low that price exploded from (C) holds. A gap down into C is the buy, targeting the gap origin and the nearest pivot high.
Buying a gap into a non-quality, mid-move range. Selling after a decline into demand (novice action). Calling a gap-down buy 'high risk' without looking at who is selling.

Is the level a pivot with an explosive departure, not a mid-move range? Is the gap taking price INTO demand after a decline? Are targets set at the gap origin and the nearest pivot high? Is the risk small?
“Who is selling on that gap down?” “A consistently profitable trader would never do that.”

Differs: Kevin treats mid-move (RBR/DBD) zones as tradable continuation zones; Seiden rejects this particular mid-move range as non-quality because it was a sideways cluster, not an explosive pivot. New: gap-trade targets (gap origin, then nearest pivot high); Kevin does not trade gaps.

Buy a gap down into a quality pivot, not into a lazy mid-move range. "Support" means different things to different people.
