A sideways range sitting in the middle of a rally is not quality: price often slices right through it. A pivot low that price exploded away from is quality, because demand hugely beat supply there. When price later gaps down into that pivot after a decline, the person selling is the novice, so Seiden buys from him.
Like a trampoline versus a pile of pillows: you bounce hard off the trampoline but sink through the pillows.
A sideways range in the middle of a move is not quality support. Quality = a pivot price exploded away from. Gap down into quality demand: buy. Target 1 = gap origin, target 2 = nearest pivot high.
Price rallies, goes sideways, then rallies again. This range sits in the middle of a move. It is not quality.
When price returns, it falls straight through A. Weak support gives way.
A pivot low forms and price explodes away from it. Demand greatly exceeded supply here. That is quality.

passages.h: Step: D: gap down into C
passages.t: Price gaps down into C. Who is selling? Someone selling after a decline into demand: the novice. Buy, with targets at the gap origin and then the nearest pivot high.

Non-quality support? - A sideways range in the middle of a move. Quality support? - A pivot low price exploded away from. Gap down into quality demand? - Buy from the novice seller. Gap trade target 1? - The origin of the gap. Gap trade target 2? - The nearest pivot high.

New XLT students look at too many things; Seiden strips it back to one idea: focus on price levels price cannot go to or stay at. The S&P 1263-1264 demand was special because price only briefly touched 1262.50 and left, and the revisit a week later was a low-risk buy toward 1270+ from novice sellers.

Draw demand where price could not go to or stay at. Buy the revisit of that demand; first target about 1270 in the example, higher if available. Ask 'who is on the other side of my trade?' at every entry.
A level is important because of what did NOT happen there: price could not go to or past it.
Price did trade to 1262.50 once, but moved higher quickly, which only happens where demand exceeds supply.
1) Focus on price levels price can't go to or stay at. 2) Understand why: think of order flow, buyers and sellers, not red and green candles.
At the revisit, ask who is on the other side. Only a novice sells after a decline and into demand; be the buyer to that seller.

@ES 30-min from 8/18 to 8/29, price about 1,262-1,300. A (shaded oval, 8/19-8/21): after a decline from about 1,300 price repeatedly dips to the 1,263-1,264 band and is pushed back up; two lines at about 1,262 and 1,265. Price rallies to about 1,293 by 8/22, then falls again.
B (shaded oval, 8/26-8/27): the revisit of the same band; this is the buy. Price then rallies to about 1,298 by 8/29. XLT traders targeted 1,270 and higher.

passages.h: Chart: E-mini S&P 30-min (8/18-8/29): oval A shows price repeatedly dipping into the 1,262-1,265 band (lines at about 1,262 and 1,265) and leaving. Price rallies to about 1,293, falls back, and oval B marks the revisit of the same band, the buy, before a rally to about 1,298.
passages.t: The level matters because price could not stay there: it touched 1,262.50 and left. The revisit after a decline is a low-risk buy from novice sellers; XLT targeted 1,270 and higher. Stop goes below the lower line.
A level matters because of what did not happen: price touched the band and could not stay. The revisit after a decline is the low-risk buy from novice sellers.
Processing too much information and too many tools. Reading candles as colours instead of order flow. Selling after a decline into demand.
Did price fail to stay at (or get past) this level before? Is the current move into the level a decline that novices are selling into? Is there room to the first target?
“Focus on price levels where price can't go to or stay at.” “Who is on the other side of your trade?”

Focus on prices that price cannot go to or stay at. New students look at too many things at once. Seiden boils it down to one idea. A level matters because of what did NOT happen there: price touched it and could not stay. That only happens where demand beats supply. When price comes back after a decline, ask who is on the other side: a novice selling into demand. Be his buyer.
Like a floor that is too hot to stand on: every time someone steps there, they jump right back off.
Focus on price levels price cannot go to or stay at. Think in order flow - buyers and sellers - not red and green candles. At every entry ask: who is on the other side of my trade?
After a decline, price dips into the same band again and again but is pushed right back up. It can touch it, but it cannot stay.
Price only leaves that fast where demand exceeds supply. Wrap the band in two lines.
Price rallies, then falls back to the band. The trader selling here sells after a decline and into demand.
Buy at the top line, stop below the bottom line, first target a few points up. Price rallies away.

Thought 1? - Focus on price levels price cannot go to or stay at. Thought 2? - Understand why: order flow, not candle colours. Question at every entry? - Who is on the other side of my trade? Price touches a level and leaves fast means? - Demand exceeds supply there. Where does the stop go on the buy? - Below the bottom line of the band.

One-timeframe active traders are like a one-trick pony and do not make consistent profits. Larger-timeframe levels decide whether small-timeframe setups work and where trends start and end. In late 2008 the Dow, gold and crude all reached monthly demand and bounced, and Seiden ignores the news: he would not have traded any differently without it.

Never trade from one timeframe only. Avoid small-timeframe buys near larger-timeframe supply and sells near larger-timeframe demand. Review weekly and daily (and monthly) supply and demand at least once a week. Expect larger-timeframe trends to start and end at larger-timeframe levels.
He has yet to see anyone make consistent profits using only small timeframes; small plus large timeframes is the recipe.

The best 5-minute buy near larger-timeframe supply is unlikely to work; the best 15-minute sell near larger-timeframe demand is unlikely to work. Larger-timeframe trends begin and end at larger-timeframe supply and demand.

passages.h: Weekly review in the XLT (three reasons)
passages.t: 1) Know where trends are likely to end and begin, so you are first in line when risk/reward is ideal. 2) Know which side of the market has the odds for active trades. 3) Find swing and position trades (e.g. the GBPUSD short from May 2008). Look at weekly and daily charts at least once a week.
The XLT does not trade the news; all influences are already in price. Chasing news on a 5-minute chart just transfers your account to someone else.

DIA monthly, 2004-2009. Demand zone labelled 'Demand' between about 100 and 108, drawn from the 2004-2005 base before the long rally. Price rallies to about 140 in late 2007, then falls hard through 2008.
A shaded circle in late 2008 marks a long lower wick into the top of the zone near 105-108; price bounces to 113.38.
@ZG (100 oz gold) monthly, mid-2006 to 2009. Two lines at about 672 and 748 wrap the 2006-2007 base before the breakout. Gold rallies to about 1,030 in early 2008, then drops.
A shaded circle at about 745-750 (around August 2008) marks the long wick into the top of the zone; price is back at 870.10.
@CL monthly, late 2007 to 2009. Two lines at about 87 and 96 wrap the late-2007/early-2008 base before the rally. Crude rallies to about 145 by July 2008, then falls sharply.
The September 2008 candle wicks down to about 90, inside the zone, and closes near 100.96: a strong bounce from monthly demand.

passages.h: Chart: DIA (Dow ETF) monthly, 2004-2009: demand zone between about 100 and 108 from the 2004-2005 base. After the 2007 peak near 140, the late-2008 candle wicks into the top of the zone (shaded circle) and closes back up near 113.
passages.t: Large-timeframe trends end at large-timeframe demand. On the monthly chart a single long lower wick into the zone is the footprint of big buyers. Short-term sells into this area had poor odds regardless of the news.

passages.h: Chart: Gold futures (@ZG) monthly, mid-2006 to 2009: lines at about 672 and 748 wrap the 2006-2007 base. After the rally to about 1,030, the 2008 sell-off wicks into the top line around 745-750 (shaded circle) and price recovers to 870.
passages.t: Same lesson in a different market: the proximal line of monthly demand stopped the decline. The zone is drawn from the base before the breakout rally.

passages.h: Chart: Crude oil (@CL) monthly, late 2007 to 2009: lines at about 87 and 96 wrap the late-2007/early-2008 base. After the run to about 145, the September 2008 candle wicks down to about 90 inside the zone and closes near 101.
passages.t: Price penetrated into the zone but closed back above it: demand absorbed the selling. Check monthly and weekly levels at least once a week so you know where trends may turn.
Larger-timeframe demand decides the outcome: a monthly base, a long rally, then a hard decline that wicks into the top of the monthly zone and bounces. Small-timeframe sells there have poor odds.
Trading a single small timeframe. Taking a perfect-looking LTF setup straight into HTF opposing supply or demand. Chasing news on a 5-minute chart.

Have I checked weekly and daily levels this week? Is my LTF trade running into an HTF opposing level? Which side of the market does the HTF picture favour? Am I ignoring the news and trading the levels?
“One time frame active traders simply can't compete.” “If we as traders never heard any of it, would we have traded any different? Nope.”
Matches Kevin's top-down HTF approach and weekly chart update habit. Differs on news: Kevin says be aware of news and do not day-trade it; Seiden says ignore it entirely.

Big timeframe levels decide whether small timeframe trades work. A trader who only watches the 5-minute chart is like a one-trick pony. The best small sell signal will usually fail if it sits right on top of big monthly demand. In 2008 the Dow, gold and crude all fell hard into old monthly demand and bounced. Seiden checks weekly and daily charts at least once a week so he knows where big trends are likely to start and end.
Like a small wave meeting a sea wall: no matter how strong the little wave looks, the wall decides.

Larger-timeframe trends begin and end at larger-timeframe supply and demand. Avoid small-timeframe sells into big demand and buys into big supply. Review weekly and daily levels at least once a week; ignore the news.
On the monthly chart, a base launched a long rally. That base is big-picture demand.
Price trends up for years, then falls hard. Small-timeframe traders sell every bounce on the way down.

passages.h: Step: The trend ends at the level
passages.t: One long lower wick pierces the top of the monthly zone and closes back up. Big buyers left their footprint. Short-term sells here had poor odds.
Price bounces from big demand. The news did not matter: without it, Seiden would have traded the same way.
Where do big trends begin and end? - At larger-timeframe supply and demand. Small-TF sell into HTF demand? - Low odds - avoid it.

Weekly review: three reasons? - Where trends end/begin, which side has the odds, find swing trades. One-timeframe trader? - A one-trick pony that cannot compete. Long monthly wick into demand? - Footprint of big buyers.

Trading is gambling, but the one form where you see the cards before betting and choose the size, so you can stack the odds. Seiden lists his odds enhancers for buying a pullback to demand: uptrend, 3:1 profit margin, a quality level (strong rally away, not retested, near HTF demand, pivot low well placed on the curve) and a sharp arrival. Like a casino, keep fixed rules and do not change them after losses.

Buy only pullbacks to demand. Require a profit margin of at least 3:1. Prefer levels with a strong departure, untested, near HTF demand, and low on the curve. Prefer a sharp decline into demand over a stair-step decline. Decide position size after scoring the odds. Never change the rules because of a loss.
Poker, trading and Pepsi buying TV time all put money at risk for an uncertain return. In trading you can decide whether to bet after seeing your cards and the dealer's, and how much to bet.

passages.h: When to buy: a pullback to demand, plus odds enhancers
passages.t: 1) In an uptrend. 2) A profit margin of at least 3:1 (reward/risk). 3) A quality demand level: a) strong rally from demand (big imbalance); b) not retested yet (greatest odds); c) near larger-timeframe demand; d) a pivot low well placed on the larger supply/demand curve.

passages.h: When to buy: a pullback to demand, plus odds enhancers
passages.t: 4) How price gets there: a stair-step decline into demand is a low-odds buy; a sharp drop into demand is a much higher-odds buy. Indicators and oscillators can add further enhancers. Assess the odds first, then decide how much capital to risk.
Casinos lose every day but stay profitable because they never change their rules after a loss.
If you do not have a rule set that stacks the odds, do not trade; you are competing with people who do.
Expect losses; the only certainty is the lack of certainty, so search for better odds, not certainty.
No charts in this article; the odds-enhancer list is text only.
How price arrives matters: a stair-step decline into demand (many small legs and bases) is a low-odds buy; a sharp drop of big red candles into fresh demand is a higher-odds buy.
Trading without a written, odds-stacking rule set. Changing rules emotionally after losses. Searching for certainty instead of better odds.

Is the higher trend up? Is reward at least 3x risk? Was the departure from demand strong? Is the level untested? Is it near HTF demand and low on the curve? Did price arrive with a sharp drop rather than a stair-step? Have I sized the trade after scoring these?
“The one thing that is certain is the lack of certainty.” “Make sure you have a set of rules that stacks the odds in your favor.”
Mostly matches Kevin's zone qualifiers (trend, R:R, strong departure, fresh, HTF alignment, curve).
Differs: 'stair-step' in Kevin's course describes the basing; Seiden applies it to the arrival leg into the zone (stair-step arrival = low odds).

Trading is gambling where you see the cards first. Stack the odds. Poker players and traders both risk money on an unknown result. But in trading you can look at your cards and the dealer's before you bet, and you choose how much to bet. Seiden only buys a pullback to demand when the odds are stacked: uptrend, 3:1 room, a strong fresh level low on the curve, and a sharp drop into it. Like a casino, he never changes the rules after a loss.
Like a casino: it loses some hands every day, but its fixed rules keep the odds on its side, so it wins over time.

Buy pullbacks to demand only when the odds enhancers line up. A sharp drop into demand is a high-odds buy; a stair-step decline is low odds. Score the odds first, then size. Never change the rules after a loss.

passages.h: Step: Uptrend and a quality level
passages.t: The trend is up. Price left this demand with a strong rally, and the level has not been retested. Two enhancers already.
The supply above is far away: well over three times the risk from entry to stop.
Price drops into demand sharply in big red candles, not in a slow stair-step. A sharp arrival is a much higher-odds buy.

passages.h: Step: Bet, then accept the result
passages.t: With the odds stacked we decide size and buy. This time price rallies to supply, but losses will come too, and the rules do not change.
Why is trading "gambling with stacked odds"? - You see the cards before betting and choose the bet size. Minimum profit margin? - 3:1.

Quality demand (4 parts)? - Strong rally out, untested, near HTF demand, pivot low well placed on the curve. Stair-step arrival? - Low-odds buy. Sharp drop into demand? - Higher-odds buy. What never changes after a loss? - The rules.

Seiden gives part of the XLT gap checklist, crossing the trend with gap direction. In a downtrend a gap up into supply is the highest-probability short; in an uptrend a gap down into demand is the highest-probability long. The deciding factor is who is making the biggest mistake.

Downtrend + gap up into supply = highest-odds short. Uptrend + gap down into demand = highest-odds long. Counter-trend gap trades need low risk and a high target. Every gap trade needs low risk and high reward measured on the chart.
Gap up into objective supply: likely the highest-probability trade. Only a novice buys a gap up into supply in a downtrend; sell to them. This gap usually fills very quickly.
Gap down into objective demand: a lower-probability buy in a downtrend. The gap almost always fills, but usually takes longer.
Gap up into supply: consider a short only if risk is low and the target high; not one of the best trades because it is against the trend. It usually fills within the day or soon after.
Gap down into demand: likely the highest-probability trade; only a novice sells a gap down into demand in an uptrend. Usually fills very quickly.
The best gap trade is where the other side is making the biggest mistake. In every scenario, risk must be low and reward high, determined objectively from the chart.
No charts in this article.
Gap-by-trend matrix: the highest-odds gap trades are with the trend into an opposing level, where the other side makes the biggest mistake.
Buying every gap down into demand at the open regardless of trend. Buying a gap up into supply in a downtrend.
What is the trend? Is the gap going INTO supply (up) or INTO demand (down)? Is this the with-trend gap scenario? Is risk low and the target large?
“Identifying who is making the biggest mistake.”
New: Kevin's course does not trade opening gaps; this gap-by-trend matrix has no equivalent.

The best gap trade is where the other side makes the biggest mistake. Seiden crosses two questions: which way is the trend, and which way did price gap? In a downtrend, a gap up into supply is the best short, because the buyer is buying against the trend, after a rally, into sellers. In an uptrend, a gap down into demand is the best buy for the mirror reason. Gaps against the trend can still be traded, but only with low risk and a big target.
Like swimming: swimming with the river current is easy; a gap with the trend into a level lets the current carry your trade.
Downtrend + gap up into supply = highest-probability short. Uptrend + gap down into demand = highest-probability long. Counter-trend gap trades need low risk and a high target.
Price is falling overall: a small rally, then a big drop. The trend is down.
The pause before the big drop is supply.
Price gaps up at the open straight into supply. Only a novice buys a gap up into supply in a downtrend. Sell to him, stop above the zone.
This gap usually fills very quickly and price keeps falling with the trend.

Downtrend + gap up into supply? - Highest-probability short. Uptrend + gap down into demand? - Highest-probability long. Downtrend + gap down into demand? - Lower-probability buy; usually fills, but slower. Uptrend + gap up into supply? - Short only if risk is low and target high. The deciding factor for gaps? - Who is making the biggest mistake.

The Dow found buyers around 8000, a monthly demand area it had bounced from several times since 1998. Seiden uses it to teach an XLT rule: do not buy a support level that has been tested more than once, because each visit uses up more of the resting buy orders. Buy on the first or second revisit only, and be cautious about the Dow until price reaches fresh demand.

Do not buy a support level that has been tested more than once. Buy on the first or second revisit only, with a desirable profit margin. Be cautious at heavily tested levels; wait for fresh demand for low-risk buys.

passages.h: Why repeated tests weaken a level
passages.t: Many books say wait for support to be tested once or twice before buying; Seiden completely disagrees.

passages.h: Why repeated tests weaken a level
passages.t: On the floor, when the stack of buy orders exceeded sell orders, price had to rise once the last seller was filled. That stack is the demand.

passages.h: Why repeated tests weaken a level
passages.t: Each revisit lets more of those buy orders fill, so fewer buyers remain and the chance of breaking lower grows.

passages.h: Why repeated tests weaken a level
passages.t: Depth of penetration into a level is another XLT factor for judging the orders left, but he does not explain it here.
First: quantify supply and demand properly on the chart. Second: buy only the first or second time price revisits the level, and only with a desirable profit margin.

passages.h: Chart (p106): Dow Jones Industrial Average monthly
passages.t: $INDU monthly, 1996 to early 2009, scale about 4,000-14,000. A black box at about 7,000-7,900 marks the demand area from the 1998 consolidation.

passages.h: Chart (p106): Dow Jones Industrial Average monthly
passages.t: Shaded ovals mark the earlier bounces from it: the 1998 dip (about 7,500) and two 2002-2003 lows (about 7,200 and 7,400).

passages.h: Chart (p106): Dow Jones Industrial Average monthly
passages.t: After the 2007 peak near 14,000, price collapses in 2008 to 8,507.26 (low about 8,187), just above the box: the fourth visit to this area.

passages.h: Chart: Dow Jones Industrial Average monthly, 1996 to early 2009: a box at about 7,000-7,900 marks demand from the 1998 consolidation. Shaded ovals mark earlier bounces from it in 1998 and 2002-2003. In late 2008 price collapses from about 14,000 to about 8,190-8,500, approaching the box for the fourth time.
passages.t: Each prior bounce used up some of the resting buy orders. By the fourth visit the level is weak: XLT buys only the first or second revisit. A heavily tested level is a reason for caution, not confidence.
Each test of a demand level fills more of the resting buy orders. By the third and fourth test there are few buyers left and the level is likely to break; buy only the first or second revisit.
Waiting for a level to be tested two or three times before buying. Assuming a level that has held many times will keep holding.
How many times has price returned to this level? Is this the first or second revisit? Is there a desirable profit margin? Is there fresher demand lower down that would be a better buy?
“We make it a rule in XLT NOT to buy at a support level if it has been tested more than once.” “Politely say 'no thanks'.”

Close to Kevin's freshness preference, but Seiden explicitly allows the second revisit, while the repo strategy blocks any tested zone. Depth of penetration is named here without numbers; Kevin's course has a test-depth grid.

Buy only the first or second return to support. Then say "no thanks". Books say wait until support has been tested a couple of times before you trust it. Seiden completely disagrees. On the trading floor he saw that a stack of buy orders is what makes demand, and each time price comes back, more of those orders get filled. After a few visits, few buyers are left and the level is likely to break.
Like a pantry: every trip to it takes some food out. After enough trips, the shelf is empty.

Demand is a stack of resting buy orders; each revisit fills some of them. XLT rule: do not buy a support level that has been tested more than once. Buy the first or second revisit only, with a desirable profit margin.
Price based here and rallied: a demand area, a stack of resting buy orders.
Price comes back three times. Each bounce uses up more of the buyers, and each bounce is weaker.
XLT does not buy a level tested more than once. Politely say "no thanks".
With the buyers used up, price falls straight through. Wait for fresher demand lower down.

What does each revisit do to demand? - Fills more resting buy orders, weakening it. XLT rule on tested support? - Do not buy if tested more than once. Which revisits can you buy? - The first or second. Fourth visit to a level? - Say "no thanks". Another factor for orders left? - Depth of penetration into the level.

Gaps are the most obvious way to spot the novice, and the picture of the ultimate supply and demand imbalance. A NASDAQ gap up after a rally, in a downtrend, into supply was 'the most potent novice trader signal', and the next day was a big down day. Seiden restates four gap rules by trend.

Gap up + downtrend = very high-odds short; gap down + uptrend = very high-odds long. Counter-trend gap trades only with a significant profit margin. Plan gap trades before the open. Check where the opposing level is before entering (room to run).
If you cannot spot the losing trader in a market, it is probably you (like poker). Analysis is done before the open so trades are planned objectively, without emotion.
Buying after a rally, in a downtrend, into supply, and doing it on a gap up stacks every mistake together.
Demand was much lower, so the path of least resistance was down. The goal is not certainty but objectively assessing the odds.
1) Gap up in a downtrend: very high-odds short. 2) Gap up in an uptrend: lower-odds short; can be a buy if there is a significant profit margin. 3) Gap down in an uptrend: very high-odds buy.
4) Gap down in a downtrend: lower-odds buy; sometimes a short if there is a significant profit margin. Before entry, ask who is on the other side and make sure they are making a big mistake.
$COMPX daily from late September to mid-November 2008, price about 1,500-2,300. A clear downtrend from about 2,300 to a low near 1,500 on 10/27.
A horizontal supply line at about 1,780 is drawn from the mid-October highs (around 10/14-10/20).
Price rallies back up; an arrow labelled GAP marks the early-November gap up into that line (shaded small circle at about 1,750-1,780). The next candle is a big red down day to 1,681.64.

passages.h: Chart: NASDAQ Composite daily, late September to mid-November 2008: a downtrend from about 2,300 to about 1,500. A supply line at about 1,780 comes from the mid-October highs. After a rally, the arrowed GAP up in early November runs into that line (shaded circle); the next candle is a big down day to 1,681.64.
passages.t: Buying after a rally, into supply, in a downtrend, on a gap: every novice mistake at once. Gap up in a downtrend is the very high-odds short. Demand was far below, so the path of least resistance was down.
The most potent novice signal: in a downtrend, a rally that gaps up into supply. The gap buyer is buying after buying, into supply, against the trend; the next day is a big down day.
Buying a gap up after a rally into supply in a downtrend. Trading from a conventional TA book instead of reading order flow. Making decisions while the market is moving and emotions are high.

What is the trend, and which way did price gap? Is the gap into supply (for a short) or demand (for a long)? Where is the opposing level, and is the margin large? Who is on the other side, and what mistake are they making?
“If you can't spot the novice, consistent losing trader in a market, it is probably you.” “The picture of the ultimate supply and demand imbalance is a gap.”
New: gap rules are absent from Kevin's course; in a Zoom session Kevin told a student a drawn gap area was not a zone.

A gap is the easiest place to spot the novice trader. In poker, if you cannot spot the losing player at the table, it is probably you. Markets work the same way. A gap is the picture of the ultimate supply and demand imbalance, so it shows the novice clearly. In a downtrend, after a rally, someone buying a gap up into supply has stacked every mistake together, and the next day is often a big down day.
Like someone running into a store just as it closes, paying full price for the last thing on the shelf.

Gap up in a downtrend = very high-odds short; gap down in an uptrend = very high-odds buy. Counter-trend gap trades only with a significant profit margin. Plan gap trades before the open, without emotion.
Price is falling hard. Lower prices, lower highs: the trend is down.
The pause before the drop is supply. Demand is much lower, so the path of least resistance is down.

passages.h: Step: Rally, then GAP up into supply
passages.t: Price rallies and then gaps up straight into supply. The buyer is buying after a rally, into supply, against the trend, on a gap. That is the most potent novice signal.
The next candles fall hard. The goal was never certainty, only objectively stacked odds.

Gap up in a downtrend? - Very high-odds short. Gap up in an uptrend? - Lower-odds short; maybe a buy with a big profit margin. Gap down in an uptrend? - Very high-odds buy. Gap down in a downtrend? - Lower-odds buy; sometimes a short with a big margin. Picture of the ultimate imbalance? - A gap.
Amid 2008 bailout news, Seiden says the XLT rule on a bailout announcement is to find supply and short the stock market. Volatility is simply the distance between demand and supply levels.

A NASDAQ 2-minute short at supply that was also the overnight high, reached by a rally with no demand levels in it, shows why a strong arrival and large profit margin matter, and stock traders should time their trades with S&P and NASDAQ levels.
Short at the proximal (lower) line of supply with the buy stop just above the distal (upper) line.

Require a strong arrival with no demand levels inside the rally; the empty space is your profit margin. Extra confluence when supply lines up with the overnight high. For stocks, map S&P and NASDAQ levels first and time stock entries with them. Trade only a handful of stocks.
Foreclosures, job losses and the $700 billion bailout were not news to the XLT; they had been expected.
XLT rule: each time a country announces a bailout, find supply and short the stock market (stocks or futures). This is his opinion-heavy macro view.
Volatility is high because the distance from demand to supply is large; it will shrink when the levels tighten.

Area A is supply: price could not stay there and left wicks, the footprints of sellers. Confluence: 1,175 was also the overnight (globex) high, which was the high because that is where the supply was.
B is the first revisit; buyers there buy after buying (mistake 1) and at supply (mistake 2). Short at the lower line of the zone, protective buy stop just above the upper line.

The rally into B was built with no demand levels, just big green candles, so once supply was hit price could fall quickly through that empty space to C. That empty space is the profit margin; the XLT requires strong rallies into supply like this.
The largest order imbalance is at or near the open, so that is where high-probability opportunities are. Buyers at B fell for the 'greed' trap; the XLT sets traps rather than falling for them.

passages.h: Stocks: time trades with the indexes
passages.t: Stocks ebb and flow with the broad market; analyse S&P and NASDAQ supply and demand first.

passages.h: Stocks: time trades with the indexes
passages.t: Spend about five minutes on index buy and sell zones, then trade a handful of stocks at most, timed with those levels.

passages.h: Stocks: time trades with the indexes
passages.t: Free-market view: bailouts keep weak banks (cracks in the foundation) in the system; do not expect them to help.

@NQ 2-min from the afternoon of 11/12 into the morning of 11/13, price about 1,148-1,178. A (yellow shaded box, 11/12 about 14:45-15:00): supply between two black lines at about 1,174 and 1,178, where candles left long upper wicks. Price falls overnight to about 1,149 by 9:00 on 11/13.
C (bottom of a gray shaded oval, about 1,154 at 9:15): a run of large green candles with no basing rallies straight up the gray area to B.

B (about 9:30, high about 1,177.50): the first revisit of A; short at the lower line (about 1,174), stop above the upper line (about 1,178). Price then drops back through the gray space to about 1,148.25 by 10:30.

passages.h: Chart: E-mini NASDAQ 2-min (11/12-11/13): A (yellow box) is supply at about 1,174-1,178 where candles left long upper wicks; it is also the overnight high. Price falls to about 1,149, then from C (about 1,154) a run of large green candles with no basing rallies straight to B (high 1,177.50), the first revisit of A. Price then drops back to about 1,148.
passages.t: Short at the lower line (about 1,174), stop just above the upper line (about 1,178). The rally into B left no demand levels behind, so the gray area is empty space: the profit margin. Extra confluence: supply matched the overnight high.

Short at supply A on the first revisit B: sell at the lower (proximal) line, protective buy stop just above the upper line. The rally into B left no demand levels, so the empty space down to C is the profit margin.

Buying after a rally into supply (both novice mistakes at once). Avoiding the open out of fear when it holds the largest imbalance (for experienced traders). Scanning hundreds of stocks instead of starting with the index.

Is the supply zone marked with two lines, with wicks showing sellers? Does it line up with another reference (overnight high)? Did price rally into it fast, with no demand levels left behind? Is the profit margin to the next demand large? For stocks: is the index at a matching level?
“We don't fall for those traps, we set them.” “Candle wicks which are the footprints of sellers.”
New: using the overnight (globex) high as confluence for supply. New: volatility defined as the distance between demand and supply levels.
Arrival quality (no demand levels in the rally) is only partly covered in Kevin's material. New: index-timing for stocks; Kevin's course has no index or correlation filter.

A rally with no stops on the way up can fall just as fast. At area A, candles left long upper wicks: the footprints of sellers. It was also the overnight high, for the same reason. Later, price rallied straight back up with big green candles and no pauses. Those pauses would have been demand; with none, there is empty space below. So when supply is hit, price can fall quickly through that space.
Like an elevator shaft with no floors: once the cable is cut at the top, nothing stops the fall.

Short at the lower (proximal) line of supply, stop just above the upper (distal) line. A rally into supply with no demand levels inside it leaves empty space: that is your profit margin. Volatility is simply the distance between demand and supply levels.
Candles at A leave long upper wicks: price could not stay up there. Those wicks are sellers' footprints. It is also the overnight high.

passages.h: Step: C: a rally with no bases
passages.t: From C, big green candles race straight up with no pauses at all. No pauses means no demand levels were left behind.
Buyers at B buy after buying and at supply. Sell at the lower line, buy stop just above the upper line.
Nothing below holds price up, so it drops back through the space the rally left. That empty space was the profit margin.

Long upper wicks at a level? - Footprints of sellers: supply. Short entry and stop? - Lower line of supply; buy stop just above the upper line. Rally with no demand levels? - Empty space below = profit margin. Volatility is? - The distance between demand and supply levels. Where is the largest order imbalance? - At or near the open. Trap setter or prey? - We set traps, we do not fall for them.

Seiden defines demand as a price where someone is willing and able to buy (where to buy) and supply as where someone is willing and able to sell. A sideways base only looks balanced: the equation was out of balance and needed time to play out. The big move away comes from institutions, because retail lacks the buying power, and where smart money buys is where retail sells.

Treat demand as where to buy and supply as where to sell; ignore other definitions of support and resistance. Read a tight sideways base before a big move as hidden imbalance, not balance. Buy the return to the base the institutions left (B), not the move away.

Support and resistance mean different things to different traders (Fibonacci, pivot lows, rising moving averages); supply and demand have only one definition. Demand = a price at which someone is willing and able to buy = where to buy. Supply = a price at which someone is willing and able to sell = where to sell. Opportunity exists when the supply/demand equation is out of balance.
Institutions profit from retail traders, so it helps to know where institutions buy and sell; price action shows it without expensive software.

Three candles basing sideways look balanced, but the equation was always out of balance; once the last seller sells, price must rise. Retail traders do not have the buying power to cause that rally; institutions do. Where smart money buys is where retail sells, and vice versa.

passages.h: Chart 1 (p115): EURGBP 10-min, supply and demand zones
passages.t: EURGBP 10-min, evening of 10/15 into 10/16, price about 0.7740-0.7815. Supply: two lines at about 0.7776 and 0.7788 around a small base near 23:00, from which price drops sharply in big red candles.

passages.h: Chart 1 (p115): EURGBP 10-min, supply and demand zones
passages.t: Demand: two lines at about 0.7742 and 0.7752 around the base at the low (about 00:00-01:00 on 10/16), from which price rallies.

passages.h: Chart 1 (p115): EURGBP 10-min, supply and demand zones
passages.t: An oval at about 02:00 shows price rallying back into the supply zone and turning down; a circle at about 02:30 shows price dropping back into demand and launching to about 0.7810.
Hand-drawn candles with price labels 1.6300, 1.6200 and 1.6100: a decline, three candles basing just above 1.6100, then a rally back to about 1.6300.

Under the base: Sellers 200, 100, 0 and Buyers 3000, 2000, 1000. The circled column (0 sellers, 1000 buyers) is labelled 'Price must rise (Demand exceeds supply)'. A red box asks 'Whose demand is this?': the answer is institutional, not retail.

EURJPY 15-min, price about 134.9-136.8. Side notes: A = demand exceeds supply (the bank dealer desk has too much to buy at A); B = low-risk, high-reward buy for the astute speculator. A: a demand zone with two lines at about 134.95 and 135.15 at the low around 05:00-06:00.
Price rallies to about 135.8, then pulls back; B is a shaded oval at about 135.15 around 08:00-09:00, the return to the zone.
Price then rallies to about 136.8. Caption: when price reaches a level where demand exceeds supply, price must rise.

passages.h: Chart: EURGBP 10-min (10/15-10/16): supply between about 0.7776 and 0.7788 from a small base at 23:00 that price dropped hard from; demand between about 0.7742 and 0.7752 from the base at the low. The oval at about 02:00 shows price rallying back into supply and turning down; the circle at about 02:30 shows price returning to demand and launching to about 0.7810.
passages.t: Each zone is the base a strong move left from. Price respected both: sell at the supply return, buy at the demand return. Opportunity exists where the equation is out of balance, at the edges, not in the middle.

passages.h: Chart: Hand-drawn diagram 'Whose demand is this?': a decline to three basing candles just above 1.6100, then a rally back to about 1.6300. Under the base: Sellers 200, 100, 0 and Buyers 3000, 2000, 1000; the circled column reads 'Price must rise (Demand exceeds supply)'.
passages.t: The base looks balanced but buyers far outnumber sellers. Only institutions have the size to drive the move away; retail does not. Where smart money buys is where retail sells.

passages.h: Chart: EURJPY 15-min with notes: A is a demand zone at about 134.95-135.15 at the 05:00-06:00 low ('bank dealer desk has too much to buy at A'). Price rallies to about 135.8, then B (gray oval, about 08:00-09:00) returns to the zone: the low-risk, high-reward buy. Price then rallies to about 136.8.
passages.t: Buy the return to the base the institutions left, not the move away. When price reaches a level where demand exceeds supply, price must rise. The stop goes just below the lower line at A.
Whose demand is it? Three quiet basing candles hide an imbalance only institutions can create; the big move away is their footprint. Buy the return to that base (B), where retail is selling.
Believing a sideways base means buyers and sellers are balanced. Paying for software to find institutional orders that the chart already shows. Selling where smart money is buying.
Is there a strong move away that only institutions could cause? Have I marked the base it came from as the zone? Am I buying where retail is selling?
“Where the smart money buys is where retail sells.” “Demand = (Support) = where to buy.”

Demand is where to buy; supply is where to sell. Big players leave the footprints. Support and resistance mean different things to different traders, but supply and demand have one meaning. Demand is a price where someone is willing and able to buy. Three quiet candles may look balanced, but buyers far outnumber sellers there. Only institutions have the buying power to launch the move away, and where smart money buys is where retail sells.
Like a whale under a quiet sea: the surface looks calm, but when it moves, the wave is huge.

Demand = where someone is willing and able to buy = where to buy. Supply = where to sell. A quiet base before a big move hides an imbalance, not balance. Buy the return to the base institutions left; that is where retail is selling.
Price paused, then dropped hard. That pause is supply: a price where someone was willing and able to sell a lot.

passages.h: Step: A base that only looks balanced
passages.t: Three quiet candles at the low look balanced. Underneath, buyers outnumber sellers by far: 3000 buyers to 200 sellers.
The rally away needs huge buying power. Retail does not have it; institutions do. Mark the base as demand.
Price rallies back into supply and turns down, then drops back into demand and launches. Opportunity is at the edges, not in the middle.

Demand = - Where someone is willing and able to buy = where to buy. Supply = - Where someone is willing and able to sell = where to sell. Quiet base before a big move? - A hidden imbalance, not balance. Who drives the move away? - Institutions. Need expensive software to see bank orders? - No. Price action shows them.

From his CME pit days, Seiden learned that turns happen when the novice enters, and that the novice makes two mistakes: buying after a period of buying (or selling after selling) and buying into supply (or selling into demand). On screen, candlesticks show the same emotion. A USDCHF short at a pivot-high supply level illustrates it, followed by his task, tools and three-step analysis: trend, levels, profit margin.

Never buy after a period of buying into supply, nor sell after selling into demand. Enter before others, at levels, with low risk. Run the three-step analysis every time: trend, levels, profit margin. Short the first return to a pivot-high supply level when buyers arrive after an advance.
A successful floor trader had him watch a desperate buyer, then sold to him; minutes later the market fell.
That trader's whole approach was to find the consistent loser and take the other side of his trade.
Emotion, not intellect, drives most decisions, so emotional traders are invited in when risk is high and reward low.

1) Buying after a period of buying, or selling after a period of selling (late, high risk). 2) Buying into supply, or selling into demand (low odds). To profit from a buy, someone must later pay more than you; most traders do the opposite. Studying what losers do wrong is a good way to learn what is right.
Task: 1) objective, anticipatory analysis, entering before others; 2) low-risk entries. Tools: candlesticks (price), proper trend analysis, proper supply and demand analysis.
Analysis step 1: trend of average prices (rising = odds with buyers, falling = odds with sellers). Proper trend analysis is objective anticipation of the next trend.
Step 2: where are support (demand) and resistance (supply)? Entries are at or near support for longs and resistance for shorts.
Step 3: is there a profit margin? For longs, resistance minus support at the time of entry; the reverse for shorts.
Books teach chart patterns that need a bullish picture to buy; seminars teach lagging indicators. Astute traders get interested in buying well before green candles appear.
People buy on good news and sell on bad news; good news does not bring price down to demand, bad news does. The advantage now lies with screen traders who know what to look for.

passages.h: Chart (p122): USDCHF 30-min, short at pivot-high supply
passages.t: USDCHF 30-min from 11/24 to about 12/1, price about 1.1840-1.2210. A: a pivot high on 11/24 with supply wrapped by two lines at about 1.2190 and 1.2205; price immediately collapses to about 1.1925, then to about 1.1840 by 11/25-11/26.

passages.h: Chart (p122): USDCHF 30-min, short at pivot-high supply
passages.t: Price climbs back over several days in a choppy rally, with a sharp spike higher on 11/28.

passages.h: Chart (p122): USDCHF 30-min, short at pivot-high supply
passages.t: B: the candle that spikes into the same zone at about 1.2195 on 11/28. Those buyers are buying after an advance and into supply; the short entry is on candle B. Price then drifts lower to about 1.2105 by the right edge.

passages.h: Chart: USDCHF 30-min (11/24 to about 12/1): A is a pivot high on 11/24 with supply wrapped by lines at about 1.2190-1.2205; price collapses from it to about 1.1840. After a choppy multi-day rally and a spike on 11/28, candle B reaches the same zone at about 1.2195; that is the short. Price then drifts lower to about 1.2105.
passages.t: The buyer at B is buying after an advance AND into supply: both novice mistakes. Short the first return to a pivot-high supply level. Run the three steps: trend, levels, profit margin.
The two novice mistakes on one chart: candle B buys after a period of buying AND into the pivot-high supply A. The astute trader sells to that buyer at the zone.
Buying when everyone else is buying and the picture looks bullish. Relying on lagging indicators and chart-pattern books. Buying on good news; selling on bad news. Letting emotion decide entries.

Is the other side buying after buying, or selling after selling? Are they buying into supply or selling into demand? What is the trend of average prices? Where are the nearest supply and demand? Is the profit margin large enough?
“Turns in the market happen when the novice trader has entered the market.” “An astute trader gets interested in buying well before pretty green candles appear.”
Differs: Seiden defines trend by average prices; Kevin defines it by swing structure and trendlines.
New: the 'two novice mistakes' and 'who is on the other side' framing is not in Kevin's course.

Turns happen when the novice enters. Find his two mistakes. On the trading floor Sam watched a desperate buyer chase price up after a long rise. An experienced trader sold to him, and minutes later the market fell. Candles on a screen show the same emotions. The novice buys after a period of buying, and buys into supply. Seiden runs three steps every time: trend, levels, profit margin.
Like a kid buying the last ice cream at a fair for triple the price: the seller is delighted to take his money.

Mistake 1: buying after buying (late). Mistake 2: buying into supply. Task: objective, anticipatory analysis and low-risk entries before others. Three steps: trend of average prices, where supply and demand are, profit margin.
Average prices are falling. The odds are with the sellers.
A pivot high where price collapsed at once: that is supply. Wrap it in two lines.
After a choppy multi-day rally, candle B spikes into the zone. That buyer buys after an advance and into supply: both mistakes.

passages.h: Step: Step 3: the profit margin and the short
passages.t: There is plenty of room below, back to the lows. Short on B with the stop above the zone. Price drifts lower.

When do turns happen? - When the novice trader has entered. Two novice mistakes? - Buying after buying; buying into supply. Seiden's task? - Objective, anticipatory analysis and low-risk entries. Tools? - Candles, proper trend analysis, proper supply and demand analysis. Profit margin for a long? - Resistance minus support at the time of entry.

We are conditioned from birth to trade wrong; good buys come at the end of downtrends, with bad news and indicators pointing down. Seiden estimates about 80% fail from poor education and 80% of the rest from poor discipline. Two pre-planned XLT trades (NASDAQ and crude oil) and an OCO bracket order show how to remove emotion: enter, stop and target all at once, then walk away.

Mark demand below and supply above before the open. Buy at demand after a decline; take profit (or go short) at the supply above. Place entry, stop and target together as an OCO bracket, then do not touch it. Embrace sharp, bad-news declines into demand as buying opportunities.
If you are invited to buy only after an uptrend, with indicators up and good news, price is probably high.
College finance (good earnings, good management, industry leader, uptrend) points you to buy when price is already high.
Two requirements: a correct understanding of how markets work with a rule-based strategy, and the discipline to follow it.
Roughly 80% fail because they are taught wrong; of the 20% properly educated, about 80% fail on discipline.

Before the US open, mark the demand below and the supply above. At the open, buy from whoever sells after a decline at demand; at the supply above, sell longs or initiate shorts to the buyer making both mistakes.
In the crude trade, price arrived at demand with a severe, big-red-candle decline (probably bad news, indicators falling), which is what makes buying there feel scary but correct.
Seiden does not claim to be free of emotion; his brain is flawed for trading, so he lets the order platform keep emotion out.
OCO (order cancels order): enter the buy at demand, the protective sell stop and the profit-taking sell limit at the same time, then stay hands-off.
This handles emotion and means no need to watch the screen all day. Use it for day, swing and position trades.
@NQ 30-min, 12/16 to 12/18, price about 1,209-1,245. Demand (support): two lines at about 1,209 and 1,216 around the base at 12:00-14:00 on 12/16, before a big rally to about 1,243.
Supply (resistance): lines at about 1,239.5 and 1,245 at the top of that rally; the upper line is labelled 'XLT Profit Target'.
A shaded circle at about 1,215 on the 12/17 open marks 'XLT Buy' after a sharp drop into demand.
Price rallies to the supply zone, where a shaded oval at about 1,240-1,245 (around 13:00) marks the target; price then fades to 1,228.50.
@CL 15-min, 12/9 to 12/10, price about 46.5-50.5. Demand (support): lines at about 46.50 and 46.80 at the 15:00 low on 12/9, from which price climbs to about 48 and then 49.
Supply (resistance) / XLT target: a shaded oval with lines at about 49.0 and 49.3 at the top of the move.
Around 9:00-9:30 on 12/10 price plunges in large red candles all the way back to demand; a shaded oval marks 'XLT Buy' at about 46.80. Price then rockets through the target to about 50.5.

A TradeStation order-bar screenshot with the OCO/OSO drop-down open. Entry options include OCO Breakout, OCO Breakout/Fade Buy, OCO Breakout/Fade Sell, OCO Fade, Single Order Long and Single Order Short.
Highlighted: 'Entry - Single Order - Long' with 'Exit - Bracket - 1 Limit & 1 Stop Level': one buy entry with one profit limit and one protective stop.

passages.h: Chart: E-mini NASDAQ 30-min (12/16-12/18): demand at about 1,209-1,216 from the 12/16 base before a big rally; supply at about 1,239.5-1,245 at the top of that rally, labelled XLT Profit Target. The shaded circle on 12/17 marks the XLT Buy after a sharp drop into demand; price rallies into the supply oval, then fades to 1,228.50.
passages.t: Mark demand below and supply above before the open. Buy at demand after a sharp decline; the profit limit sits at the supply above. Entry, stop and target placed together, then hands off.

passages.h: Chart: Crude oil 15-min (12/9-12/10): demand at about 46.50-46.80 at the 12/9 low; supply/XLT target at about 49.0-49.3 at the top of the move. Around 9:00-9:30 on 12/10 price plunges in big red candles straight back to demand, marked XLT Buy at about 46.80, then rockets through the target to about 50.5.
passages.t: The scary, big-red-candle decline into demand is exactly the high-odds buy. The bracket order removes emotion: the buy, stop and target were set before the plunge.

passages.h: Chart: TradeStation order-bar screenshot with the OCO/OSO menu open: 'Entry - Single Order - Long' is highlighted with the sub-option 'with Exit - Bracket - 1 Limit & 1 Stop Level'.
passages.t: One order places the buy, the profit-taking limit and the protective stop together. When the stop or the limit fills, the other is cancelled automatically (order cancels order). This is the mechanical way to 'set it and forget it'.
Set it and forget it: one OCO bracket places the buy limit at demand, the protective stop below the zone and the profit limit at supply, all before the move, so emotion never touches the trade.
Buying when trend, indicators and news all look good. Relying on willpower instead of order automation to control emotion. Sitting in front of the screen all day managing trades by hand.

Are demand and supply marked before the session? Is the entry at demand after a decline (or at supply after a rally)? Is the stop placed beyond the zone? Is the profit limit at the opposing level? Is everything entered as one bracket order?
“From birth, we are conditioned to trade incorrectly.” “I call this 'set it and forget it' trading.”
Matches Kevin's 'set and forget' idea for zone orders; the explicit OCO bracket and the 80/80 failure estimate are new.

Place entry, stop and target together, then walk away. From birth we learn to buy when things look good, which in markets means buying high. Good buys come at the end of declines, with scary news. That feels terrible, so emotion gets in the way. Seiden's fix is one bracket order: buy at demand, stop below it, profit target at supply, all placed at once. When one exit fills, the other cancels, and he does not touch it.
Like setting the oven timer: you put the cake in, set the timer, and go do something else instead of opening the door every minute.
Mark demand below and supply above before the open. Good buys feel scary: sharp, bad-news declines into demand. OCO bracket: entry, stop and target placed at once. Set it and forget it.
Mark the demand below and the supply above.
Place the buy at the top of demand, the protective stop under it, and the profit limit at supply - all at once, as an OCO bracket.
Price plunges in big red candles, probably on bad news. This is exactly the high-odds buy, and your order is already waiting.
The buy fills, price rallies and the limit at supply fills. The stop order cancels automatically. No screen-watching needed.

When are levels marked? - Before the open. OCO? - Order cancels order: one exit filling cancels the other. Three parts of the bracket? - Entry at demand, stop below, profit limit at supply. How do good buys feel? - Scary: sharp declines and bad news into demand. Works for which trade lengths? - Day, swing and position trades.

Like scam prize letters and infomercial systems, markets transfer money from those who fall for traps to those who set them. Two XLT student trades show it: an S&P short pre-set at 914 supply after a fast breakout rally, and an S&P long in a demand zone sitting just below an obvious 'red line' of old pivot lows, where breakdown sellers sell straight into real demand.
Pre-place shorts at supply that sits above a breakout area; let the breakout rally deliver buyers to you.

Mark obvious pivot-low lines just above your real demand; expect them to break and fuel your entry. Enter close to the protective stop to keep risk small (2-3 points on the S&P examples). Use multiple targets at the opposing levels.
Trap-setters disguise risk as opportunity and pick the weakest prey. Someone truly owning a money-printing system would not sell it to you for $1,900.
A student marked supply up and to the left and pre-placed a short at 914 (supply 914-917). Days later price broke out of the 905 area and rallied strongly straight into 914-917.
An early breakout buyer could profit, but anyone buying after the strong rally and into supply made both mistakes; they thought 914 was value because of the breakout and green candles.
A demand zone formed from an explosive move up; draw it with two black lines and carry it forward.
A red line connects two pivot lows just above the zone: most traders see that as the demand level.

When price falls to the red line, many buy; when it breaks, they turn bearish and sell, straight into the real demand zone. Price then reverses fast. Enter close to the protective stop; turning points let you limit risk properly. If you cannot clearly see the trap on a chart, you are probably the prey.
@ES 20-min (Mar09 contract). A supply box ('Futures XLT - Supply Zone (The Trap)') at about 914-917 is drawn from a sharp drop in the upper left.
Lower, a 'Futures XLT - Demand Zone' box at about 888-893 marks the origin of a later rally.

Price rallies from about 893 up through the 905 area and spikes into the supply box: 'XLT Short Entry - student sets a trap and sells to a novice buyer'. A huge red candle then drops price to the demand box: 'XLT Profit Target Reached'.
Trade box: short 914, stop 917, target 895, risk $300 (3 points x $50 x 2 contracts); result 19 points x $50 x 2 contracts = $1,900 profit.

passages.h: Chart 2 (p132): S&P 5-min, demand zone and the bait
passages.t: @ES 5-min around 12/2, price about 812-850. 'XLT Demand Zone': two black lines at about 812.34 and 815.55 around the low from which price explodes up to about 846.

passages.h: Chart 2 (p132): S&P 5-min, demand zone and the bait
passages.t: A red line at about 817.18 connects two pivot lows just above the zone, labelled 'The Bait - Setting the Trap'.

Weeks later on 1/15, price falls from about 820 through the red line (817.18) into the black-line zone; an arrow marks 'Novice Trader Falls For Trap' where breakdown sellers sell. 'XLT Student Buys' at the zone; price then rallies to about 846.
Trade box: bought 814, stop 812, three targets 821, 827 and 834; risk $300 (2 points x $50 x 3 contracts); 40 total points x $50 = $2,000 profit (printed '$2,00.00').

passages.h: Chart: Futures XLT student trade, E-mini S&P 20-min (Mar09): supply box ('The Trap') at about 914-917 from a sharp drop at upper left; demand box at about 888-893 marks the origin of a later rally. Price rallies through the 905 area into the supply box where the student's pre-placed short fills; one huge red candle drops price to the demand box (target reached). Trade: short 914, stop 917, target 895, 19 points x $50 x 2 = $1,900.
passages.t: Supply up and to the left is where breakout buyers get trapped. The short was placed in advance; the breakout rally delivered the buyers. Risk 3 points to make 19.

passages.h: Chart: E-mini S&P 5-min around 12/2: the XLT demand zone between about 812.34 and 815.55 at the origin of a rally; a red line at about 817.18 just above it connects two pivot lows and is labelled 'The Bait - Setting the Trap'.
passages.t: Most traders see the obvious pivot-low line as support. The real demand is the zone just below it, where the move started. When the bait line breaks, its buyers become sellers into your zone.

passages.h: Chart: E-mini S&P 5-min on 1/15: price falls through the 817.18 bait line into the demand zone (arrow: 'Novice Trader Falls For Trap'); the XLT student buys at 814 with a stop at 812 and targets at 821, 827 and 834. Price rallies to about 848. Result about 40 points on 3 contracts.
passages.t: Enter close to the protective stop: 2 points of risk. The breakdown sellers are selling after a decline into demand. Scale out at several opposing levels.

The bait: an obvious line through two pivot lows sits just above the real demand zone. Novices buy the line, then panic-sell its break straight into the zone, where the trap-setter buys with a tight stop.
The supply trap: shorts are pre-placed at supply up and to the left. A breakout rally delivers late buyers into that supply, and the sell order fills straight into a fast drop to demand.
Buying a strong breakout late, into supply. Buying at an obvious double-pivot-low line and then panic-selling when it breaks. Being unable to see where the trap is.

Is my level the real origin of the move, not the obvious pivot line above it? Is there an obvious 'bait' level that will push novices into my zone? Is my order placed in advance? Is the stop tight and the reward several times the risk?
“If you can't recognize a market trap clearly on a chart, chances are you are still the prey.”
Similar to Kevin's 'liquidity trap' just before a zone; Seiden's version is specific: an obvious pivot-low line just above real demand acts as the bait.

Set traps like the pros; do not be the prey. Scam letters promise prizes and infomercials sell "money machines" - they hide risk inside a shiny opportunity. Markets do the same. Most traders see an obvious line through two lows and buy there. When it breaks, they panic and sell, straight into the real demand zone just below. The trap-setter waits in that zone with a tight stop and buys their panic.
Like cheese on a mousetrap: the obvious line is the cheese, and the real demand underneath is the trap.

The real level is the origin of the explosive move, not the obvious line above it. The obvious pivot line is bait: its break sends novices selling into real demand. Pre-place orders close to the stop; scale out at opposing levels.
Price exploded up from a small base. That base is the real demand zone: two lines, carried forward.
Later, two pivot lows form a neat line just above the zone. Most traders call that line support.

passages.h: Step: The novice falls for it
passages.t: Price drops to the line, people buy, then it breaks and they panic-sell - right into the real demand.
Buy in the zone with a tight stop below. Price reverses fast; take profits at several levels above.

Real level vs obvious line? - Real = origin of the explosive move; obvious line = bait above it. What happens when the bait line breaks? - Its buyers become sellers into the real zone. Student short trade? - Short 914, stop 917, target 895. Student long trade? - Buy 814, stop 812, targets 821, 827, 834. Can't see the trap? - You are probably the prey.

The XLT Momentum Intraday sessions now start 30 minutes before the open so trades are planned in advance. Step one is to find supply, demand and trend in the S&P and NASDAQ; step two is to find stocks whose levels line up with them. On 1/21 the S&P opened under supply, and Google and RIMM supply levels lined up with it, giving fast short trades, with RIMM risking $0.50 to make $1.50.

Begin analysis before the open; plan trades in advance. Mark S&P and NASDAQ supply, demand and trend first. Only trade stocks whose levels line up with the index level. Favour stock levels with a rapid move away. Require about 3:1 (e.g. risk $0.50 to make $1.50).
Sessions start 30 minutes before the stock market opens so students set up day trades ahead of time. Lessons and live trading alternate: learn, trade, learn, trade.

Step 1: mark demand, supply and trend in the governing markets (S&P and NASDAQ). Step 2: scan for stocks whose supply or demand lines up with the index level. Levels with a rapid move away carry very high probability.
When the S&P rallied to its supply, Google rallied hard into its own supply; the short worked fast.
RIMM gave the same setup in a cheaper stock, with demand about $1.50 below the short entry: risk $0.50 to make $1.50 (3:1).

Time stock trades with the index: when the S&P rallies into its supply, look for stocks rallying into their own supply at the same moment and short those with about 3:1 to the demand below.
Trading stocks without checking where the index is relative to its own levels. Waiting until after the open to start analysis.
Is the index at supply or demand right now? Does my stock's level line up with the index level? Did price leave the stock's level rapidly? Is reward at least 3x risk to the opposing level?
“Timing your equity trades with the S&P or NASDAQ supply and demand is the key to high odds trading.”
New: index-to-stock alignment; a possible FX analogue is checking DXY levels, which Kevin only mentions in passing.

Time your stock trades with the S&P and NASDAQ levels. Stocks mostly move with the whole market, like boats on the same tide. So Seiden starts 30 minutes before the open by marking supply, demand and trend on the S&P and NASDAQ. Then he looks for stocks whose own levels line up. When the S&P rallied into supply, Google and RIMM rallied into their supply at the same time, and the shorts worked fast.
Like rowing out only when the tide is going your way: the same strokes take you much further.

Step 1: mark demand, supply and trend in the S&P and NASDAQ. Step 2: trade only stocks whose levels line up with the index level. Favour levels with a rapid move away and about 3:1 to the opposing level.
Before the open, the S&P is rallying toward its own supply. That sets the timing.
This stock has supply where price left with a rapid drop. Mark it, plus the demand below.
The stock rallies into its supply at the same moment the index reaches its supply. Sell, stop above the zone.
Like RIMM: risk about $0.50 to make about $1.50. Price falls to the demand below.

Step 1 of XLT timing? - Mark S&P and NASDAQ supply, demand and trend. Step 2? - Find stocks whose levels line up with the index. When do XLT sessions start? - 30 minutes before the open. RIMM example ratio? - Risk $0.50 to make $1.50 (3:1). Which stock levels to favour? - Ones price left with a rapid move.

Gaps form when demand or supply at the prior close is out of balance. A professional gap goes against the prior move, comes at the start of moves and ignites them: join it on a pullback to the gap's origin. A novice gap goes with the prior move, comes at the end of moves and leads to reversals: fade it at the nearest support or resistance. Both need a significant profit margin.
Pro gap: join on a pullback to the gap origin. Novice gap: fade at the nearest support/resistance. Both only with a significant profit margin. Beginners should not trade the open.
More demand than supply at the prior close: gap higher. More supply than demand: gap lower. The rules for gaps are the same in stocks, futures, forex and options.
Professional gap: after a move, in the opposite direction. It starts and ignites a new move. Action: join it on a pullback to the origin of the gap, if there is a significant profit margin.
Novice gap: after a move, in the same direction. It tends to mark the end of a move. Action: fade it at the nearest support or resistance, if there is a significant profit margin.
After a pro gap down, price often rallies quickly to fill the gap and then continues lower; sell near the origin of the gap.
A novice gap down means someone is selling after a decline and during a gap down, which usually means losses for that seller.
The open is where supply and demand are most out of balance. Trading the open is not for beginners, but once you can quantify supply and demand it is a very good time to trade.

passages.h: Chart: SPY 30-min (2/2-2/12/2009): price support at 81.36 from the 2/2 low; price rallies in steps to about 87.5. 'Pro Gap' (2/10): a gap down after the rally, against it, that starts a slide to about 83. 'Novice Gap' (2/12): a gap down after the decline onto the price-support line at about 81.7; price then rallies.
passages.t: Pro gap = against the prior move; it ignites a new move. Join it on a pullback to its origin. Novice gap = with the prior move into a level; it tends to end the move. Fade it. Both only with a significant profit margin.

Professional gap versus novice gap. A pro gap goes against the prior move and starts a new one: join it on the pullback to its origin. A novice gap goes with the prior move into a level and ends it: fade it.
Selling after a decline and during a gap down (novice gap). Chasing a pro gap instead of waiting for the pullback to its origin. New traders trading the open.

Was there a prior move, and did the gap go with it or against it? Pro gap: am I waiting for the pullback to the gap origin? Novice gap: is there support/resistance to fade from? Is the profit margin significant?
“Gaps represent the ultimate supply and demand imbalance.” “These gaps tend to be found at the end of moves and lead to reversals.”
New: the professional versus novice gap classification has no counterpart in Kevin's course.

Pro gaps start moves; novice gaps end them. A gap happens when the orders at the open overwhelm the other side. A professional gap goes against the prior move: after a rally, price gaps down and a new move starts. A novice gap goes with the prior move: after a decline, price gaps down again into support, and the move ends. Join pro gaps on a pullback to where the gap started; fade novice gaps at the level.
Like a starting gun versus a finish line: the pro gap fires the start, the novice gap crosses the finish.

Pro gap = against the prior move, starts a new one. Join on a pullback to the gap origin. Novice gap = with the prior move, into a level, tends to end it. Fade it. Both only with a significant profit margin. Beginners should not trade the open.
A support line comes from the early low. Then price rallies in steps.
After the rally, price gaps DOWN, against the move. That gap starts a new slide.
After the decline, price gaps down AGAIN, with the move, right onto support. Someone is selling after a decline during a gap down.
The novice gap marks the end of the move. Buy at support; price rallies.

Why do gaps form? - Demand or supply at the prior close is far out of balance. Pro gap? - After a move, against it; starts a new move. Novice gap? - After a move, with it, into a level; ends the move. Trade a pro gap how? - Join on a pullback to the gap origin. Trade a novice gap how? - Fade it at the nearest support or resistance. Same rules in every market? - Yes: stocks, futures, forex, options.

Three student questions. In an uptrend a novice gap is a gap up after a strong rally, while a pro gap is a gap down after a rally, usually at resistance, which ends the uptrend. The best time for active equity traders is the open until about two hours in, with analysis done pre-market. Profit margin is the space between the supply and demand levels; without a significant one there is no trade.

Uptrend: fade a gap up after a strong rally into resistance; join a gap down after a rally at resistance. Active equity window: the open to about two hours in, prepared pre-market. No significant profit margin = no trade.

passages.h: Khoi: pro gap versus novice gap in an uptrend
passages.t: Novice gap in an uptrend: a gap up after a strong rally; professionals do not buy after a strong rise, especially on a gap up.

passages.h: Khoi: pro gap versus novice gap in an uptrend
passages.t: Pro gap in an uptrend: a gap down after a rally, usually at resistance; it ends the uptrend and starts a downtrend.

passages.h: Tom: best time of day for equities
passages.t: At and around the open until about two hours into the day, because that is when supply and demand are most out of balance and direction is most predictable. Quantify levels pre-market and trade the market 'back to balance' at the open.

passages.h: Tom: best time of day for equities
passages.t: New traders should not trade the open; XLT sessions start 30-60 minutes before the open to prepare.

The top shaded area is supply, the bottom is demand; the space between them is the profit margin. The plan was to short at supply and take profit at demand. Two good levels are not enough; there must also be a significant profit margin.

The space between the two boxes is the profit margin: short at the supply box, take profit at the demand box.

passages.h: Chart: QQQQ 30-min (12/9-12/26/2008) with a 10-period moving average: resistance at about 30.45 from the 12/9 high. After an uptrend from about 28.9, the circled 'Pro-Gap' on 12/17 gaps down at resistance, against the rally; the uptrend ends and price trends down to about 29.0.
passages.t: In an uptrend, a gap DOWN after a rally at resistance is the professional gap. It marks the end of the uptrend and the start of a downtrend.

passages.h: Chart: SPY 30-min (10/7-10/16/2008) with a 10-period moving average: resistance lines at about 104.8-106 from the 10/7 highs. After the collapse to about 86 and a sharp uptrend, the circled 'Novice Gap' on 10/14 is a big gap up after the rally straight into resistance; price then falls back to about 88-90.
passages.t: In an uptrend, a gap UP after a strong rally into resistance is the novice gap. Professionals do not buy after a strong rise, especially on a gap up: fade it.

passages.h: Chart: RIMM 5-min (same chart as in 'Market Timing in the XLT Course'): supply box about 51.70-52.05 and demand box about 49.95-50.15; the space between them is the profit margin.
passages.t: Profit margin = distance from the entry zone to the opposing zone. Short at the supply box, take profit at the demand box. Two good levels without a significant margin = no trade.
Profit margin is the space between supply above and demand below. Two good levels are not enough: short at supply and cover at demand only if that space is significant.
Buying a gap up after a strong rally. New traders trading the open. Taking a trade between two levels that are too close together.
Is this gap with or against the prior move? Am I trading within about two hours of the open, with levels already drawn? Is the distance to the opposing level significant?
“Without the presence of a significant profit margin, there is no trading opportunity.”
Differs: Kevin picks one session to trade; Seiden names the open to about two hours in for equities. Profit margin to the opposing zone matches Kevin's R:R-to-opposing-zone idea.

Fade a gap up after a strong rally; demand a real profit margin. In an uptrend, a gap up after a strong rally straight into resistance is a novice gap: pros do not buy after a big rise, especially on a gap. A gap down after a rally at resistance is a pro gap and usually ends the uptrend. For stocks, the best time is the open to about two hours in, with levels drawn before the bell. And whatever the setup, two good levels are not enough: you need real space between them.
Like two goalposts: you need a whole field between them to score, not a step.
Uptrend: gap up after a strong rally into resistance = novice gap; fade it. Best equity window: the open to about two hours in, prepared pre-market. No significant profit margin = no trade.
Price based at the highs and collapsed. That base is resistance (supply).
A sharp uptrend begins from the lows and climbs toward resistance.
Price gaps UP after the strong rally, straight into resistance. Pros do not buy here. Sell, stop above the zone.
Price falls back. The plan was made pre-market and executed near the open.

Uptrend novice gap? - A gap up after a strong rally (into resistance). Uptrend pro gap? - A gap down after a rally at resistance; ends the uptrend. Best equity trading window? - The open to about two hours in. Profit margin? - The space between the supply and demand levels. Two levels too close? - No trade.

The best traders are professional losers. Seiden's three risk tools are protective stops (always stop-market, never stop-limit), proper position size (risk 1% of the account) and keeping losses small. An S&P short at gap supply shows stop placement and trailing the stop above new supply on a smaller timeframe, and a student's stats show a 29% win rate producing +46.79% because losses were small.
Use stop-market orders for protection; never stop-limit. Initial stop just beyond the zone, where the opposing orders sit.

Trail on a smaller timeframe: move the stop beyond each new supply (short) or demand (long) left by a strong candle. Risk a fixed 1% per trade and size from the stop distance. Eliminate big losses; let winners reach pre-planned targets.
Stop-market order: becomes a market order once price passes the stop. Execution is almost guaranteed, the price is not (slippage). Seiden always uses it for protection.

Stop-limit order: becomes a limit order at the stop price; it gives price control but no guaranteed exit. Example: bought at $41.00, stop limit at $40.50, no buyers there, and the loss keeps growing. He never uses it for protection.
Place the initial stop just above where all the sellers are (for a short): just beyond the supply line, where price could not go.
Drop to a smaller timeframe. Each strong decline candle creates new supply at its origin; move the buy stop down to just above that new supply.
If the market is weak it should not rally above these new levels; this protects profit without giving much back. Mirror it for longs.
Account $100,000, max risk 1% = $1,000. Buy at the top of the support zone, stop below the zone. Entry $22.30, stop $21.90, stop size $0.40, so 2,500 shares.
A position-sizing grid keeps you mechanical; you do not want to be 'thinking' while the market moves.
Four outcomes: big win, small win, small loss, big loss. Eliminate the big loss and you can live with the other three.

Student stats (Roth IRA, start of 2009): 952 ticks, profit $13,185.73, 7 wins, 17 losses, avg win $2,528.29, avg loss $265.43, biggest winner $4,369.30, biggest loser $925.50, win rate 29.17%, P/L ratio 9.53, max risk 2% ($827.35), capital $28,182.00 to $41,367.73, net +46.79%. He feels no different about a winning or losing trade; he is executing a profitable plan.

'The Entry' at $22.30 (Buy); 'Protective Stop (the initial risk)' at $21.90; stop size $22.30 - $21.90 = $0.40.
