'XLT Sells Short' at the gap supply line on 3/11 with a 'Protective Buy Stop Market' just above (about 73.9); 'Profit Target - Gap Demand' at about 72.1, the origin of the gap up.
passages.t: Initial stop just beyond the level, as a stop-market order. Target is the opposing level: the origin of the gap up. Gaps leave both supply and demand behind.

passages.h: Chart: SPY 10-min (3/10-3/11): the short entry circled at about 73.6 near the 3/11 high; 'Gap Demand' line at about 72.1. Two circled strong red decline candles (about 10:30 and 11:45); after each, the buy stop moves down to just above the new supply (about 73.45, then about 73.1). Price reaches the gap demand line around 13:30, the profit target.
passages.t: Trail the stop on a smaller timeframe. Each strong decline candle leaves new supply at its origin; move the stop just above it. If the market is truly weak it will not rally back above those levels.

passages.h: Chart: Position-sizing slide: account $100,000, max risk 1% ($1,000). Drawn candles fall to price support between $22.30 and $21.90; entry at $22.30, protective stop at $21.90, stop size $0.40. A grid lists shares by stop size; $0.40 = 2,500 shares is highlighted.
passages.t: Size = maximum dollar risk / stop distance. Buy at the top of the zone, stop below the bottom of the zone. Use a pre-computed grid so you never think about size while the market moves.

Trailing the stop on a smaller timeframe: every strong red candle leaves new supply at its origin. Move the protective buy stop to just above that new supply; a weak market should not rally back through it.
Position size from the stop: risk 1% of a $100,000 account ($1,000). Buy at the top of support $22.30, stop below at $21.90; a $0.40 stop allows 2,500 shares.
Using a stop-limit for protection. Thinking about size while the market is moving instead of using a grid. Needing to be right; letting a loss become big. Judging a system by win rate alone.

Is my stop a stop-market order beyond the zone? Is size = (1% of account) / stop distance? Do I have a rule for trailing the stop on a smaller timeframe? Is the target a pre-planned opposing level? Could this trade produce a big loss? If so, fix it before entry.
“What the best traders have in common, however, is that they are very professional losers.” “As a trader, I NEVER use this order for protection.”
New: stop-market versus stop-limit; for an EA this means a server-side stop that exits at market, never a pending stop-limit exit.

Similar to Kevin's trailing below each new zone, but Seiden specifies a smaller timeframe and the origin of each strong candle. 1% sizing matches Kevin; the student's 2% max risk is above Kevin's norm.

Great traders are professional losers: small losses, fixed size, real stops. The best traders lose often, but they lose small. Seiden uses three tools. A stop-market order that always gets you out, never a stop-limit that might not fill. A position size that risks only 1% of the account. And keeping losses small, so even a 29% win rate made a student +46%. On a winning short, he drops to a smaller timeframe and moves the stop above each new supply left by a strong red candle.
Like a fire exit door that always opens when you push it - not one that opens only if someone is waiting outside.
Protect with stop-market orders; never stop-limit. Size = (1% of account) / stop distance.
Trail on a smaller timeframe: stop just beyond each new supply (or demand) a strong candle leaves.

passages.h: Step: Short at supply, stop-market above
passages.t: Sell at the bottom line of supply. The protective buy stop is a stop-market order just above the top line, where price could not go.
A strong red candle drives price down and leaves a small pause: new supply at its origin. Move the stop to just above it.
Another strong decline, another pause. Move the stop down again. A weak market should not rally back through these levels.
Price reaches the demand target. The trailing stops protected profit without giving much back.

Stop-market vs stop-limit? - Stop-market: exit almost guaranteed. Stop-limit: price control, no guaranteed exit. Max risk per trade? - 1% of the account. Position size formula? - Dollar risk / stop distance. $1,000 risk, $0.40 stop? - 2,500 shares.
How to trail a short? - Smaller timeframe; stop just above each new supply from a strong red candle. Best traders are...? - Very professional losers.

New traders assume bad news means price must fall. On 4/1/2009 the ADP report showed a much bigger drop in jobs than expected, and sellers pushed the NASDAQ straight into a pre-drawn drop-base-rally demand level, from which it rallied hard. Filter the news through the chart: only sell on bad news if price is at supply.

Bad news that pushes price into pre-drawn demand is a buy opportunity. Before selling on bad news, make sure price is at supply, not demand. Draw levels before the news; let the news deliver price to them.
Markets are flooded with conflicting news each morning. Bad news creates perceptions, perceptions create trades, and trades become candles: all influences are reflected in price.
In XLT pre-market sessions, bad news often leads Seiden to look for a low-risk place to buy the S&P or related stocks.
ADP: non-farm private employment fell by 742,000 in March versus an expected 663,000 (February revised to -706,000).
Traders who heard it sold after a drop and into a level where demand exceeded supply: a demand level with a decline-base-rally (pivot low) structure.
Once the last seller sold, price shot higher; the news was the invitation for sellers to take novice action.
@NQ 60-min, 3/27 to 4/2/2009, price about 1,204-1,280. 'XLT Demand': two lines at about 1,204 and 1,214 around the 3/30 low (drop-base-rally) from which price rallied to about 1,252.
Price drifts back down over 3/31-4/1; a gray circle on 4/1 at about 1,214 ('Buying Opportunity') marks the dip into the top of demand on the news. Price then rallies to about 1,279 by 4/2.

passages.h: Chart: E-mini NASDAQ 60-min (3/27-4/2/2009): 'XLT Demand' between about 1,204 and 1,214 around the 3/30 drop-base-rally low. Price rallies to about 1,252, drifts back over 3/31-4/1, and on the bad ADP news dips to about 1,214 (gray circle, 'Buying Opportunity'); price then rallies to about 1,279.
passages.t: Draw the levels before the news; let the news deliver price to them. Sellers on bad news after a decline and into demand are the novice side. Buy at the proximal line, stop below the distal line.
Bad news is the invitation: the demand level (drop-base-rally) is drawn before the report; the news pushes price into its proximal line, novices sell, and the buyer at demand gets paid.
Assuming bad news means price must fall. Selling on bad news after a decline and into demand.
Where is price relative to my pre-drawn levels when the news hits? Is the news pushing price into demand (buy) or supply (sell)? Am I about to sell after a decline into demand?
“Filter your perception of the news through the objective supply and demand equation.”
Differs from Kevin: he says do not day-trade the news and wait for spreads to settle; Seiden actively buys when news drives price into demand. Both agree news should not override a valid setup.

Bad news that pushes price into demand is a buying chance. New traders think bad news means price must fall. One morning a jobs report was much worse than expected, and traders rushed to sell. But they sold after a drop and straight into a demand level Seiden had drawn the day before. Once the last seller sold, price shot higher. The news was simply the invitation for sellers to make a novice move.
Like a storm warning that makes everyone sell their umbrellas cheap - right before it rains.

Draw levels before the news; let the news deliver price to them. Bad news into demand = buy. Only sell on bad news if price is at supply. Filter the news through the objective supply and demand picture.
A drop-base-rally: the base is demand, drawn before any news.
Price drifts lower over a few days. Nothing special yet.
A terrible report hits. Sellers dump after a drop, straight into the top of demand.
Once the last seller sells, buyers take over and price shoots higher.

Bad news into demand? - A buying opportunity. When are levels drawn? - Before the news. Sell on bad news only if...? - Price is at supply. What is the news, really? - An invitation for novices to act. Filter the news through what? - The objective supply and demand equation.

Most trading problems (stops, management) are really poor entries. Seiden's shift in focus: do not scan for bases, which are everywhere; first find the strong momentum move, then follow it back to its origin, where the key supply or demand level will be. Crude oil and Qualcomm charts show the A-B-C-D sequence.
Step 1: find a strong momentum move. Step 2: go to its origin and draw the zone there. Enter on the first revisit of the origin (C). Target the nearest opposing level (D).
Identifying turning points is the most important part of trading; without it you cannot manage risk. Almost every problem traders report is a function of poor entry points.
Most traders look first for area A, the basing. Basing is everywhere, so this leads to many poor levels.

Instead, look first for area B, the strong move; then follow price back to its origin. That is likely the key level. Step 1: identify strong momentum moves. Step 2: find the origin of each move. Buy the revisit at C from a seller making both mistakes; target the opposing level D.

passages.h: Chart: E-mini crude (@QM) 60-min (4/1-4/13/2009) with volume: A is a base of three or four candles at about 47.3-48.0; B (gray oval) the strong rally out of it to about 51.5-52.0; D a supply line at about 52.0. Price declines and C (4/8) is the revisit of A at about 48.0, followed by a rally to D on 4/9.
passages.t: Look for B, the strong move, first; then go to its origin A. Buy the first revisit C; target the opposing level D. Basing alone is everywhere; the strong move away is what makes A special.

passages.h: Chart: Qualcomm 60-min (4/8-4/16/2009): after a rally, A is a small base at the top on 4/9 at about 41.5-41.85; B (gray oval) the strong drop out of it on 4/13; D a demand zone at about 40.1-40.5 around the 4/15 base. C (4/16): price rallies back into A, the short, targeting D.
passages.t: Same process for supply: strong drop B, origin A, revisit C, target D. Short at the proximal (lower) line of A, stop above the upper line.
Look for B (the strong move) first, then follow it back to its origin A and draw the zone there. Buy the first revisit C from the seller making both mistakes and target the opposing level D.
Scanning charts for bases first. Blaming stops or trade management when the real problem is the entry location.
Did I start from a strong momentum move? Is my zone at the origin of that move? Is this the first revisit? Is there an opposing level far enough away for the target?
“Make the FIRST thing you look for area 'B', the STRONG move in price.” “Almost every trading problem... is directly a function of poor entry points.”
Same process as Kevin's 'find the large move away, then go to the origin' from his intro lesson.

Look for the strong move first, then trace it back to where it started. Most trading problems - stops, management - are really bad entries. Many traders hunt for bases, but small pauses are everywhere, so they find lots of poor levels. Seiden flips it: first find B, the strong momentum move. Then follow it back to its origin, A. That is the key level. Buy the first revisit, C, and target the opposing level, D.
Like finding a river by its rushing water, then walking upstream to the spring where it starts.
Almost every trading problem is really a poor entry. Step 1: find a strong momentum move. Step 2: go to its origin. A base, B strong move, C first revisit (entry), D opposing level (target).

passages.h: Step: B first: the strong move
passages.t: Do not start by hunting bases. First find the strong move - this rally of big green candles.

passages.h: Step: A: follow it back to the origin
passages.t: Trace B back to where it started: the base. That is the key level.
Mark the opposing supply above as the target.
Price returns to A for the first time. Buy from the seller making both mistakes; target D.

First thing to look for? - B: the strong move. Where is the key level? - At the origin (A) of the strong move. C? - The first revisit: the entry. D? - The opposing level: the target. Real cause of most trading problems? - Poor entry points.

Cut off: this range covers the start of the article (pp157-160) and it continues in the next part with the sector (XLF) step. Seiden describes his top-down scan (index, then a few large sectors, then a handful of high-volume stocks, all at the same kind of level), ranking candidates by largest profit margin, and why he dropped automated scanners. The S&P step shows an unfilled gap origin acting as demand on 4/21/09.

Scan top-down: index, then sectors, then a handful of stocks. All three layers should be at the same kind of level (all at demand for buys). Rank candidates by profit margin (distance to the opposing level). An unfilled gap origin can act as quality demand.
He started on the CME floor and drew charts by hand with graph paper and coloured pencils, which taught him where significant buyers and sellers were.
For years he wrote daily advisory letters using a top-down scan each afternoon after the close.
Step 1: find demand and supply in the S&P and NASDAQ. If they closed near demand, look for buys the next day.
Step 2: check a few large sectors for ones also near demand; one or two usually set up well with the broad market.
Step 3: look at a handful of high-volume stocks in those sectors that are also near demand.
If more than three or four candidates qualify, choose those with the largest profit margin: at or near demand and farthest from supply.
He tried every scanning product, scrolling hundreds of symbols for hours, and found it made an easy process hard.
Seeing children with coloured pencils in a library reminded him the power was in the old-fashioned analysis; he has not used an automated scanner since.

passages.t: SPY 60-min, 4/6 to 4/23/2009, price about 81.8-87.5. Price bases around 82-83 on 4/7-4/8, then gaps up on 4/9 to about 84.8. A black line labelled 'S&P Fills a Gap' at about 82.8 marks the origin of that unfilled gap. Price rallies to about 87.3 by 4/17, then drops on 4/20.

passages.h: Chart: SPY 60-min (4/6-4/23/2009): price bases around 82-83, then gaps up on 4/9; a line labelled 'S&P Fills a Gap' at about 82.8 marks the origin of that unfilled gap. Price rallies to about 87.3, drops on 4/20, and on 4/21 (arrow) gaps down into the line at about 82.9 before rallying strongly to about 85-86.
passages.t: An unfilled gap origin acts as demand. Step 1 of the scan: the index closed near demand, so look for buys in sectors and stocks. The gap down into it was a with-trend novice gap into demand.
Top-down scan: index, then a sector, then a handful of stocks, all at demand at the same time. Among the candidates, pick the one with the largest profit margin to the supply above.
An unfilled gap origin acts as demand: price bases, gaps up and rallies; when it later gaps down into the origin of that gap, buyers waiting there push it back up.
Spending hours on automated scanners and hundreds of symbols. Picking stocks without checking the index and sector first.

Is the index at demand (or supply)? Is a major sector at the same kind of level? Is the stock at the same kind of level, with high volume? Among candidates, does this one have the largest profit margin?
“I would choose the stocks that had the largest profit margins.”
New: a sector layer and ranking candidates by largest profit margin. Differs: Seiden treats an unfilled gap origin as demand; Kevin told a student a gap area was not a zone.

Scan top down: index, then sector, then a few stocks, all at the same level. Seiden started on the trading floor drawing charts by hand with coloured pencils. Later he tried every automated scanner and found it turned an easy job into hours of scrolling. So he went back to the old way. First, is the S&P near demand? Then, which big sectors are near demand too? Then, which few high-volume stocks in those sectors are near demand, with the most room to supply?
Like checking the weather for the country, then your city, then your street before you plan a picnic.

Top-down scan: index, then a few large sectors, then a handful of stocks. All layers should be at the same kind of level (all at demand for buys). Rank candidates by the largest profit margin. An unfilled gap origin can act as demand.
The S&P based, then gapped up. The origin of that unfilled gap is demand.
Price rallies, then drops back toward the gap origin. The index is getting close to demand - time to look for buys.
Check a few large sectors that are also near demand, then a handful of high-volume stocks in them. Pick those with the largest room to supply.

passages.h: Step: The gap fills into demand
passages.t: Price gaps down into the gap origin and buyers waiting there push it back up strongly.

Top-down scan order? - Index, sectors, a handful of stocks. What must all layers share? - The same kind of level (all at demand for buys). How to rank candidates? - Largest profit margin. Unfilled gap origin? - Can act as quality demand (or supply). Automated scanners? - Dropped; old-fashioned analysis is faster and clearer.

Continued from p157-160: the sector and stock steps of the top-down scan. The financial sector ETF (XLF) had a gap-origin demand level that lined up with the S&P demand, and Bank of America (BAC) had a demand zone created by a strong gap away. On 4/21/09 all three gapped down into their pre-planned demand and rallied; the BAC risk was only $0.15.

Work top-down: index, then 3-4 sectors, then 3 major stocks in the best sector. Take the stock whose demand lines up with the sector and index demand. Grade a level by how strongly price left it; a gap away is a strong departure. Do the analysis the day before and have orders ready before price arrives.
After the index, he checked three or four sectors and found the financial sector ETF had quality demand lining up with the S&P demand.
The gap higher at 'A' shows how much more demand than supply existed at its origin; a return there was likely to rally and lift the stocks in the sector.
Next day the sector opened right into that demand ('B') and rallied all day, just like the S&P.
Of three major bank stocks, BAC had a demand level ('A') made high quality by a strong gap away. The stronger the move away from a level, the larger the imbalance at its origin.
All analysis was done on April 20; on April 21 price gapped down into the pre-planned zone, giving a very low risk, high reward entry. Risk was $0.15 per share.
The sellers at 'B' made the two novice mistakes: selling after a decline and selling into a level where demand exceeds supply. Be the buyer to that seller.

The whole scan took minutes the day before; automated scanners would have taken longer and probably never found BAC. Plan trades in advance and time them with the broad market, whatever your holding period.

Price runs to about 11.2, then on 4/21/09 (arrow, 'B') drops straight into the box (low about 9.4) and closes back up near 10.5. Last price 10.22.

After a 4/15 gap down and recovery to about 11.1, price gaps down on 4/20 and slides to about 8.2; on 4/21 it gaps into the zone at 'B' (arrow) and rallies to about 9.2 by 4/22. Last price 8.41.

passages.h: Chart: XLF daily, Jan to Apr 2009: a small base around 9.2-9.6 gaps higher at A; the grey box wraps that gap origin. On 4/21/09 (B) price drops straight into the box (low about 9.4) and closes back near 10.5.
passages.t: The gap away at A is the proof of a large demand imbalance at the base. The first return (B) is the buy: limit order at the top of the box, stop under its bottom, target the April high near 11.2.

passages.h: Chart: XLF daily, Jan to Apr 2009: a small base around 9.2-9.6 gaps higher at A; the grey box wraps that gap origin. On 4/21/09 (B) price drops straight into the box (low about 9.4) and closes back near 10.5.
passages.t: The sector level matched the S&P demand on the same day, which raised the odds for bank stocks.

passages.h: Chart: BAC 30-min, 4/6 to 4/22/2009: an XLT demand zone (about 6.9-7.1) under the flat base at A, where price gapped to 8.2 and ran to 11.4. On 4/21 price gaps down into the zone at B and rallies to about 9.2.
passages.t: A strong gap away from a base marks a high quality level. Entry at the zone top on the gap down risked only about $0.15 per share. The sellers at B sold after a decline and into demand: the two novice mistakes.
Top-down alignment: the S&P, the financial sector ETF and BAC each had fresh demand at the origin of a strong (gap) move, and all three returned to it on the same morning.
Gap-origin demand: price bases, gaps away (A), and on the first return (B) gaps straight into the zone. Buy at the proximal line, stop under the distal line, target the prior high.
Selling after a decline into a level where demand exceeds supply. Relying on automated scanners instead of a quick rule-based top-down read.

Is the index at demand? Is a sector ETF at a matching demand level? Does the chosen stock have demand at the same time with a strong (gap) departure? Is the plan written the day before with entry and stop?
“The stronger the move away from a price level, the greater the demand and supply imbalance.”
“Planning your trades in advance and timing your trades with the broad market is important.”
New: a sector-ETF layer between index and stock; Kevin's course has no sector step. Differs: a gap origin is treated as quality demand here.

Check the market, then the sector, then the stock. Buy where all three agree. Picture a shopper who first checks if the whole mall is on sale, then the shoe shop, then one pair of shoes. Sam did the same thing with the S&P, the bank sector fund and Bank of America. All three had a spot where price had jumped away with a gap. He wrote his plan the day before. The next morning all three gapped down into those spots, and the buyers there risked only 15 cents a share.
It is like three friends all saying the same restaurant is good. One opinion is a guess; three that agree make a much safer bet.

Scan top-down: index first, then 3-4 sectors, then 3 big stocks in the best sector. A gap away from a base shows a big imbalance. The stronger the move away, the better the level. Do the work the day before, so the orders are ready when price arrives.

passages.h: Step: A base, then a gap away
passages.t: Price dropped, paused for three small candles, then gapped higher and ran. A gap means buyers wanted in so badly that no trading happened in between. That is a large imbalance at the base.
Wrap the base with two lines: the top line on the highest basing body, the bottom line on the lowest basing wick. This is the demand zone we want price to come back to.

passages.h: Step: Line it up with the index and sector
passages.t: Before trusting this stock, check that the S&P and the sector fund also sit just above their own fresh demand. When all three line up, the odds go up a lot. All of this is done the evening before.

passages.h: Step: The gap down is the gift
passages.t: Next morning price gaps down straight into the zone. The people selling here make two novice mistakes: they sell after a decline, and they sell into demand. Our resting buy at the top line is filled from them. The stop sits just under the bottom line, so the risk is tiny.
Price rallies away from the zone, just like the index and the sector did that same morning. Low risk, high reward, and planned in minutes the day before.
Order of the top-down scan? - Index, then 3-4 sectors, then 3 major stocks in the best sector.

What does a gap away from a base tell you? - A large imbalance: much more demand than supply (or the reverse). When was the BAC trade planned? - The day before; orders were ready when price gapped in. BAC risk per share on 4/21/09? - About $0.15.
Two novice mistakes of the gap-down sellers? - Selling after a decline, and selling into demand.

Seiden introduces the XLT 'Odds Enhancers', a rule-based scoring of each supply or demand level out of 10. A student's gold short scored 9 out of 10 and was entered with a limit order and all exits pre-placed. He explains three enhancers (strength of move, profit margin, big picture) and stresses that a larger purpose gives the discipline to wait.

Score every level before trading: strength of move 2, profit margin 2, big picture 2, retracement 2, time at level 1, return 1 (total 10). Profit margin scores full only when reward to the nearest opposing level is at least 3:1. Check the higher timeframe: never short near HTF demand; prefer shorts near HTF supply. Pre-place entry (limit), stop and targets before price arrives.
Trail the stop as targets are hit so a retrace still leaves a profit.
Not every prior turning point is support or resistance; price turns where demand and supply are most out of balance.
The Odds Enhancers are a simple criteria set that steer you to the best levels and help you ignore weak ones. Highest possible score is 10; the score tells you whether to act.
How did price initially leave the area? A fast, strong departure means a big imbalance; a gradual drift means a small one. The gold supply had a fast, strong initial decline, so it scored 2 of 2.
Compare entry-to-stop with entry-to-nearest opposing level (target 1). At least 3:1 reward to risk scored 2 of 2.
The setup was on the hourly chart, so check the larger timeframe's fresh levels. Do not short anywhere near higher-timeframe demand; ideally short close to higher-timeframe supply.
Three more (retracement, time at level, return) are listed but not explained here. Use the formal scoring for a while as a new member, then learn to 'eyeball' the enhancers.
The student risked $1,200 and made $4,100, but the focus should be the mechanical steps, not the money.
A grander vision (more time with family) is what gives the discipline to wait for low risk opportunities.

Gold futures (ZG, 100 oz) 60-min, about 1/6 to 1/12/2009, scale about 827-875. A black 'Supply Zone' box (about 862-870) is drawn around an earlier rally-base-drop top (circled, 'Supply (resistance)'); price dropped sharply from it into the 840s.
Price later rallies back into the box (circled, 'XLT Student sells to a novice buyer') and turns down.
'Target One' circle at about 852 and 'Target Two' circle at about 835 mark the exits; last price about 827.

Scoring panel: market Gold, short, entry 864, stop 870. Max/student scores: strength 2/2, profit margin 2/2, big picture 2/2, retracement 2/1, time at level 1/1, return 1/1; total 10/9. Reward/risk 3:1, limit entry yes, confirmation entry no.
Risk on trade $1,200; reward 12 points on target 1 and 29 points on target 2 at $100 per point x 2 contracts = $4,100 profit.

passages.h: Chart: Gold 60-min slide "Probability Scoring": a supply zone (about 862-870) over a rally-base-drop top; the XLT student sells the return at 864 with a stop at 870, Target One about 852 and Target Two about 835. Score panel: 9 of 10, reward 3:1.
passages.t: Strength of move: the first decline from the zone was fast and large (2 of 2). Profit margin: entry to stop 6 points, entry to first target 12+ points, at least 3:1 (2 of 2).

passages.h: Chart: Gold 60-min slide "Probability Scoring": a supply zone (about 862-870) over a rally-base-drop top; the XLT student sells the return at 864 with a stop at 870, Target One about 852 and Target Two about 835. Score panel: 9 of 10, reward 3:1.
passages.t: Entry was a limit order with stop and both targets pre-placed; risk $1,200, profit $4,100.
Gold 60-min short scored with the Odds Enhancers: a rally-base-drop supply left fast, reward to the first target is 3:1 and the bigger picture agrees, so the zone scores 9 of 10.
Strength of move, the first Odds Enhancer: a fast, wide-range departure from the base scores full points; a slow, overlapping drift away scores nothing.

Treating every prior turning point as support or resistance. Trading because you want to trade rather than because the score is high. Following the herd methods taught in books and seminars (no edge).

Did price leave the zone fast and strong? Is the nearest opposing level at least 3x the stop distance away? Is the higher timeframe supporting the direction (not shorting into HTF demand)? What is the total score out of 10? Are entry, stop and both targets placed before the trade?
“This setup is a 9.” “Those who focus on the realities of markets and price simply get paid from those who don't.”

New: a numeric 10-point score per zone; Kevin grades a zone simply good or bad and lets the HTF decide. New: a minimum 3:1 profit-margin rule; Kevin warns a fixed R:R leaves money on the table. Similar: the big-picture check matches Kevin's HTF zone filter.

Score every level out of ten before you trade it. A student found a supply level in gold where price had dropped away fast. Before selling, he gave the level points: 2 for the fast drop, 2 for lots of room to the next demand, 2 because the bigger chart agreed. A few more checks brought the total to 9 out of 10. So he placed a sell order, a stop and two targets ahead of time, and walked away. Risk was $1,200 and the profit was $4,100.
It is like a report card for a level. You only invite the straight-A students to the party.

Not every old turning point is a level. Score it: strength 2, profit margin 2, big picture 2, retracement 2, time 1, return 1. Profit margin gets full points only at 3:1 or more to the nearest opposing level. A high score earns a limit order with stop and targets placed in advance.
Price rallied, paused for two candles, then fell hard with big red candles. A fast, strong departure means a big imbalance, so this scores the full 2 points. A slow drift away would score zero.
Box the rally-base-drop: bottom line on the lowest basing body, top line on the highest basing wick. This is the zone we will score.
Entry is the bottom line, the stop goes just above the top line. Measure that risk and compare it with the room down to the nearest demand. At least three times the risk scores 2 points.
Check the larger chart. Never short close to higher-timeframe demand; it is best to short near higher-timeframe supply. Here the bigger chart has supply overhead, so 2 more points.

passages.h: Step: Score 9: let the order work
passages.t: Add retracement, time at level and return and the level scores 9 out of 10. The sell, the stop and both targets were all placed before price came back. Price touched the zone and fell to both targets.

Odds Enhancer points (6 items)? - Strength 2, profit margin 2, big picture 2, retracement 2, time at level 1, return 1 = 10. Full profit-margin points need? - At least 3:1 reward to the nearest opposing level.
Big-picture rule for shorts? - Never short near higher-timeframe demand; prefer shorting near HTF supply.
Gold student trade: score, entry, stop? - 9 of 10; short 864, stop 870, targets about 852 and 835.
What gives the discipline to wait? - A bigger purpose than the money, like more time with family.

Your psychological belief system IS your strategy. News, upgrades, earnings and indicators are 'invitations' to buy or sell; a profitable belief system filters them through the real supply and demand picture. BAC was bought at demand on 4/21/09 despite bad CEO news, while the sellers acted on the news.

Filter every piece of news through the supply and demand picture before acting. Bad news that drives price into peak demand is a buy opportunity, not a sell. Good news that drives price into peak supply is a sell opportunity, not a buy.

Market invitations come only from supply and demand; the other kind is everything else (news, earnings, upgrades and downgrades, tips). The first keeps you on reality; the second on everything but reality.
A good earnings report or a buy recommendation does not equal demand; bad news or a downgrade can be a low risk buying opportunity.

Not following rules comes from invitations that do not fit your belief system, causing internal conflict at the moment of action. Even a little illusion in the belief system means truth is never found.
Do not punish yourself for not acting; clean your belief system so it only holds objective information.

passages.h: All influences are reflected in price
passages.t: Every input creates thoughts and perceptions, which lead to an action: buy or sell. So focus on price.

passages.h: All influences are reflected in price
passages.t: Conventional support and resistance (a cluster of trading) is not necessarily true supply and demand; a specific pattern shows peak supply and demand.

passages.h: All influences are reflected in price
passages.t: Two rules: negative news that brings price to peak demand is usually a buy; positive news that brings price to peak supply is usually a sell.
BAC 60-min, 4/8 to 5/8/2009, scale about 6.8-15. Grey 'XLT Demand Zone' (about 6.9-7.1) from 'A' on 4/9, where price jumped from the base to about 8.2 and on to about 11.4.
On 4/21 ('B', arrow) price gaps down into the zone on the CEO's bad credit-quality news and rallies to about 9.
Price then holds 8-9.3 through late April and rallies to about 15 by 5/7; last price 13.05.

A list of inputs (earnings report, news, income statement, balance sheet, Fed announcement, economic report, terrorist alert, trading tip, broker upgrade/downgrade, analyst opinion, technical indicators) feeds 'Thoughts and Perceptions', which feeds 'ACTION: Buy or Sell'.

passages.h: Chart: BAC 60-min, 4/8 to 5/8/2009: the same XLT demand zone (about 6.9-7.1) from A. On 4/21 (B) price gaps into it on bad CEO news, holds 8-9.3 for two weeks, then rallies to about 15.
passages.t: Bad news drove price into peak demand: that was the buy, not a reason to sell. The news sellers acted on an outside invitation; the level was the market invitation. Stop under the zone, first target the 4/14 high near 11.5 and far more was available.

passages.h: Chart: Diagram: earnings, news, statements, Fed, economic reports, tips, upgrades and downgrades, analyst opinion and technical indicators all feed "Thoughts and Perceptions", which lead to "ACTION: Buy or Sell".
passages.t: Every input ends as a buy or sell decision, so all of it is already reflected in price. Filter each invitation through the supply and demand picture before acting.

Every input becomes a buy or sell decision, so filter it through the level: BAC gapped down on bad CEO news straight into pre-planned demand, the sellers acted on the news, the buyers acted on the level.
Selling on bad news after a decline and into demand (the BAC sellers on 4/21). Assuming a cluster of trading is real supply or demand.
Blaming a lack of discipline when the real issue is a belief system that conflicts with the rules.
Is the news pushing price into demand (buy) or supply (sell)? Am I acting on a market invitation or a news invitation? Is my hesitation a belief conflict rather than a rules problem?
“Your psychological belief system IS your trading and/or investing strategy.” “Any and all influences on price are reflected in price.”
Similar: Kevin also says even good news should not override a valid setup. New: the explicit 'news into peak demand = buy' rule and the belief-system framing.

News is only an invitation. The level tells you whether to accept it. One morning the boss of Bank of America gave bad news, and many people sold the stock in a hurry. But the price fell right into a demand level Sam had already marked. He bought from the scared sellers. Two weeks later the stock had almost doubled. The news sellers listened to the headline; the buyers listened to price.
Bad news is like a rainy day at the beach shop: people dump their umbrellas cheap. If you know umbrellas always sell again, rain is your chance to buy.
There are two kinds of invitations: market invitations (supply and demand) and everything else (news, upgrades, tips).
Bad news that pushes price into peak demand is usually a buy. Good news into peak supply is usually a sell.
Discipline problems are belief problems. Clean your beliefs so they hold only objective facts.
Price fell, paused, then gapped up and ran. That base is peak demand: the place where buyers far outnumbered sellers. Box it before any news comes out.
Bad news hits. Price gaps down hard. The headline invites you to sell. But first, filter it: where is price on the supply and demand picture?

passages.h: Step: Filter the news through the level
passages.t: The news pushed price straight into peak demand. That turns the scary headline into a market invitation to buy. Entry on the top line, stop under the bottom line.
Every input, from earnings to tips to indicators, ends as a buy or sell decision. So it is all reflected in price. The news sellers were the fuel; price rallied far away from the zone.

Two kinds of invitations? - Market invitations (supply and demand) and everything else (news, tips, upgrades, indicators). Bad news into peak demand? - Usually a buy. Good news into peak supply? - Usually a sell. Where are all influences on price reflected? - In price itself. Your strategy is really your...? - Psychological belief system.

A follow-up on psychology: success comes from keeping things simple and grounded in unchanging laws. Newton (motion until met by an equal or greater force), Adam Smith (supply over demand means price falls) and Nash (do what is best for yourself and the group, as dolphins herd a bait ball) describe realities that always existed.
In markets, supply and demand is the mass and price movement between levels is the motion.
Base every trade decision on supply and demand; treat other tools as secondary. Expect price to travel from one imbalance level to the next opposing one.

Trading decisions must rest on supply and demand; adding derivatives of that concept is tricky and dangerous. Traders fail because they complicate things and because the mind creates illusion. More indicators, strategies and books do not help; a few basic principles never change.
Newton (1686): an object stays in motion until met by an equal or greater force. Adam Smith: when supply exceeds demand at a price, price declines.
Neither invented these; they challenged mass perception with a reality that existed all along, thanks to a belief system that let them apply core principles widely.
Nash: the best outcome comes when each does what is best for himself and the group; dolphins herding fish into a bait ball and feeding in turns show the same thing.

Supply and demand is Newton's mass; motion is price moving from levels where demand exceeds supply to levels where supply exceeds demand. Theories that try to change these basics are usually proven wrong.
Correction note (p174): last week's article should have said the SELLERS of BAC on 4/21 fell into the trap, not the buyers.
No charts in this article.
Governing dynamics: supply and demand levels are the mass; price movement is the motion from a level where demand exceeds supply to the next level where supply exceeds demand.
Adding more indicators and strategies instead of simplifying. Letting illusion replace observable price reality.
Is my reason for this trade a supply/demand imbalance, not an add-on tool? Where is the next opposing level (where motion should stop)?
“Those who can't keep things simple typically pay those who can.” “You can't change what can't be changed.”

Levels are the walls. Price is the ball bouncing between them. Long ago Newton noticed that a moving thing keeps moving until something big enough stops it. Adam Smith noticed that when there is more supply than demand, the price falls. Nobody invented these rules; they were always true. In the market, supply and demand levels are the heavy walls, and price moving between them is the motion. Keep it that simple and stop piling on extra tools.
Think of a ball rolling between two walls in a hallway. It rolls until it hits a wall, then turns. You only need to know where the walls are.
Base every decision on supply and demand. Extra tools built on top of it add risk and confusion.
Supply and demand are the mass; price moving from one level to the next opposing level is the motion. You cannot change a law that never changes. Simple beats complex.

passages.h: Step: Find the first wall: demand
passages.t: Price dropped, paused, and rallied hard. Demand overwhelmed supply at that base. That is one wall.

passages.h: Step: Find the second wall: supply
passages.t: Price rallied, paused, and fell hard. Supply overwhelmed demand at that base. That is the opposing wall.

Price falls back into demand and turns up. It then travels all the way to the next opposing level, where it stops and turns again. Like Newton's law: motion continues until it meets an equal or greater force.

passages.h: Step: Where motion stops is your target
passages.t: If you buy at the demand wall, the next supply wall is where you take profit. No indicator is needed to know where motion ends.
Newton's law in market terms? - Price keeps moving until it meets a level with an equal or greater opposing force. Adam Smith's rule? - When supply exceeds demand at a price, price declines.
Mass and motion in markets? - Mass = supply and demand; motion = price moving between them. Who pays whom, in Sam's words? - Those who can't keep things simple pay those who can.

A live XLT session on May 20, 2009: the NASDAQ had rallied for days and new members wanted to buy, but the instructors planned a short at a daily rally-base-drop supply above. Price spiked up into it with large emotional green candles and then fell far and fast. There is a time to short in an uptrend: when price reaches a level where supply exceeds demand.

Shorting in an uptrend is valid only at a level where supply exceeds demand. Use the larger timeframe to find the level, the smaller timeframe to see novice buying into it. Mark the supply zone before the open and wait for price to come to it.

passages.h: Our job is to search, not to trade
passages.t: The job each day is to look for low risk, high reward opportunity, not to trade. Uptrends end at big supply; new downtrends begin there, so stay ahead of the masses. Buy in uptrends, but not when price is nearing major supply.

passages.h: Reading emotion on the small timeframe
passages.t: A series of rising green candles with the largest candles at the end of the run is a sign of novice, emotional buying.

passages.h: Reading emotion on the small timeframe
passages.t: Buyers at 'A' made the two mistakes: buying after a rally and buying at a level where supply exceeds demand.

passages.h: Reading emotion on the small timeframe
passages.t: Larger timeframes show the turning points; smaller timeframes show novices jumping on the bandwagon at the wrong time.
Know exactly what a low risk, high reward, high probability opportunity looks like on a chart (where the brick walls are). Have the self control not to jump on the bandwagon when everyone else does.
E-mini NASDAQ (@NQ) 30-min, evening of 5/19 to the morning of 5/20/2009, scale about 1388-1422.

Price grinds up from about 1388, pulls back to about 1395, then accelerates with large green candles; candle 'A' is a big green bar from about 1402 to 1413, followed by more large green bars to about 1420.
Same market from about 8:00 to 20:00 on 5/20: after 'A' price tops near 1424, drops in large red candles, makes a lower high near 1408, and falls to about 1386 by evening.
@NQ daily, late March to late May 2009, scale about 1180-1430, with a rising moving average labelled 'Uptrend'.
A black 'Supply (resistance)' line (about 1420-1430) is drawn across the early-May top, a rally-base-drop where price stalled and dropped to about 1340.
Price rallies back and at 'A' (about May 20) reaches just under the supply line, then turns down with a large red candle; last price 1359.

passages.h: Chart: NASDAQ E-mini 30-min, evening 5/19 to morning 5/20/2009 (before): price grinds up from about 1388, then accelerates with large green candles; candle A runs from about 1402 to 1413 and more large green bars follow to about 1420.
passages.t: The largest candles come at the end of the run: emotional novice buying. Those buyers are buying after a rally and into a daily supply level above.

passages.h: Chart: NASDAQ E-mini 30-min on 5/20/2009 (after): just after A price tops near 1424, falls in large red candles, makes a lower high near 1408 and drops to about 1386 by evening.
passages.t: The same move seen after the fact: the late buyers at A were the liquidity for the short. A short at the daily supply had a stop just above the top and reached the prior lows the same day.

passages.h: Chart: NASDAQ E-mini daily, late March to late May 2009: rising moving average marked "Uptrend"; a supply line about 1420-1430 across the early-May rally-base-drop top. At A (about May 20) price reaches just under it and turns down with a large red candle.
passages.t: Shorting in an uptrend is valid only at a level where supply exceeds demand. Use the daily to find the level, the 30-min to see novices chasing into it.
NASDAQ daily: the uptrend is intact, yet price rallies back into a rally-base-drop supply from early May. That is where the uptrend stalls and the short is planned.
Reading emotion on the 30-minute chart: green candles grow larger as the run gets older. The largest candles arrive right at daily supply, which is where the instructors sold to the late buyers.
Buying a strong uptrend right into major overhead supply. Chasing large green candles at the end of a run. Ignoring a pre-determined supply level because price was not there recently.
Is there daily supply just above current price? Are the biggest candles appearing late in the rally (emotional buying)? Am I fighting the urge to buy with the crowd?
“There is a time and a place to sell short during an uptrend.” “Our job is to wake up each day and search for low risk, high reward opportunity.”

Differs: Seiden shorts HTF supply in a daily uptrend; Kevin's course leans on trading with the trend unless the HTF zone and trend analysis justify a reversal. New: reading 'largest candles at the end of a run' as novice emotion.

Even in an uptrend, sell when price hits a big supply wall. The NASDAQ had gone up for days and new students wanted to buy. The teachers looked at the daily chart and saw a supply level just above, where price had dropped before. On the small chart, the green candles grew bigger and bigger as price ran up, which is what scared, excited buyers look like. The teachers sold to those buyers at the supply. Price then fell far and fast the same day.
It is like kids running faster and faster toward a closed door. The faster they run at the end, the harder they bump into it.

Our job each day is to search for low risk, high reward chances, not to trade. Uptrends end at big supply. Buy in uptrends, but not when price nears major supply. Big green candles at the end of a run show emotional novice buying into the wall.

passages.h: Step: The big chart shows the wall
passages.t: On the daily chart price rallied, stalled, then dropped. That rally-base-drop left supply above the market. Mark it before the open.

passages.h: Step: The uptrend is still on
passages.t: Price climbs back. The trend is up and most people only want to buy. But price is now heading toward the supply we marked.

passages.h: Step: Candles grow at the end
passages.t: Look at the candles: each one is bigger than the last. The largest candles at the end of a run are novices chasing. They are buying after a rally and into supply: the two mistakes.

passages.h: Step: Sell to the late buyers
passages.t: Price reaches the supply. We sell at the bottom line with a stop just above the top. The late buyers become the fuel for our short.
Price falls hard and fast from the supply, even though the bigger trend was up. There is a time to short an uptrend: at a level where supply exceeds demand.

Our daily job, per Sam? - Search for low risk, high reward opportunity, not to trade. Where do uptrends end? - At big supply levels. Largest candles at the end of a run mean? - Emotional novice buying. Two mistakes of the buyers at A? - Buying after a rally, and buying into supply.

A step-by-step S&P futures short from a live XLT Futures session on May 27, 2009. A rally-base-drop supply 'A' was confirmed by a fast decline 'B'; a steep rally 'C' back to it invited a short at 911 ('D') with a 4-point stop at 915 ('E') and a 3:1 target at 899 ('F'). With the whole trade pre-planned, the trader can walk away.

Supply = rally-base-drop; skip drop-base-drop bases in the middle of a move. Judge the level by how fast price left it. A steep rally back into supply with no demand inside it is a positive. Stop just above the supply zone; size so total risk is fixed in dollars. Target at least 3:1 before taking the trade.
Find the opportunity, apply the rules, execute like a robot, enter the entire trade, then go do something else.
This brings emotional detachment and a better life; watching trades keeps the biggest risk (you) alive.
Trading is like Las Vegas: the same action over and over, wins and losses, with gains larger than losses.

A: supply, because price could not stay there and had to fall. The pattern is rally-base-drop; drop-base-drop levels sit mid-move and typically do not work well. B: the rate of decline from A measures the imbalance; the faster, the better.
C: a strong rally back to A with no sign of demand inside it is the most inviting part; a steep rally usually falls back at a similar rate. D: short at 911 as novices buy after a rally into supply.
E: protective buy stop at 915, just above the zone, because price could not get above it before. 4 points = $200 per contract; 5 contracts = $1,000 risk.
F: target 899, 12 points = 3:1; 5 contracts = $3,000. Keeping goals at 3:1 or more also raises probability.

@ES 10-min, 5/20 to 5/28/2009, scale about 878-922. 'A': two black lines at about 911 and 915 around a small base after a rally on 5/20; the drop from it is shaded as ellipse 'B' (about 910 down to 899, continuing to about 888).
Price bottoms near 879 on 5/22 and 5/26; ellipse 'C' shades the steep 5/26 rally from about 879 back to about 910.
A dashed vertical line at 05/27/09 08:40 marks the open; 'D' is the short at the lower line (911), 'E' the stop line at 915.
Price holds just under 912 for a few hours, then falls; the blue line 'F' at 899 marks the 3:1 target, and price reaches about 891 (last 894).

passages.h: Chart: E-mini S&P 10-min, 5/20 to 5/28/2009: A is a small rally-base-drop base wrapped by lines at about 911 and 915; ellipse B marks the fast drop away; ellipse C the steep 5/26 rally from about 879 back to 910. D: short at 911 at the 5/27 open, E: stop 915, F: target 899 (3:1). Price holds under 912, then falls to about 891.
passages.t: Supply is the rally-base-drop at A; the speed of B measures the imbalance. A steep return (C) with no demand inside it tends to fall back at a similar rate.

passages.h: Chart: E-mini S&P 10-min, 5/20 to 5/28/2009: A is a small rally-base-drop base wrapped by lines at about 911 and 915; ellipse B marks the fast drop away; ellipse C the steep 5/26 rally from about 879 back to 910. D: short at 911 at the 5/27 open, E: stop 915, F: target 899 (3:1). Price holds under 912, then falls to about 891.
passages.t: Risk 4 points, target 12 points: 3:1, all orders entered before the open so the trader could walk away.
S&P 10-min walk-through: A is the rally-base-drop supply, B the fast decline away, C the steep rally back with no demand inside it, D the short at 911, E the stop at 915 and F the 3:1 target at 899.
Choosing the base: a rally-base-drop marks a turning point where supply overwhelmed demand; a drop-base-drop is a pause inside a move and is a lower-quality level.
Sitting in front of the screen watching open trades. Buying after a rally right into supply. Using drop-base-drop bases as supply.

Is the zone a rally-base-drop (not drop-base-drop)? Was the departure fast? Is the return to the zone steep with no demand inside it? Stop just beyond the zone; risk fixed in dollars? Is the target at least 3:1? Are all orders in so I can walk away?
“Money always ends up in the hands of its rightful owners.” “Sitting and watching your trades keeps the largest risk in your trading world alive.”

Similar: Kevin's set-and-forget approach matches 'enter the whole trade and leave'. New: rejecting drop-base-drop as supply (continuation zones are part of Kevin's course). New: a steep return into the zone counts in favour of the trade.

Plan the whole trade, enter every order, then walk away. Sam explained a trade with six letters. A is the supply where price stalled after a rally and had to fall. B is how fast it fell. C is the steep rally back with no buying zones inside it. D is the short, E is the stop just above the zone, and F is the target three times the risk. Once all the orders were in, the trader went to do something more important.
It is like setting the oven timer: put the food in, set the time, and go play. Standing and staring at the oven does not cook it faster.
Supply is a rally-base-drop. Drop-base-drop bases in the middle of a move usually do not work well. The faster price left A, and the steeper it returns with no demand inside, the better.
Fixed dollar risk, at least 3:1 target, all orders in, then walk away. Watching trades keeps the biggest risk (you) alive.
Price rallied, paused for three candles, then could not stay there. This rally-base-drop is the turning point where supply beat demand.

passages.h: Step: B: the rate of decline
passages.t: Price fell fast and far from A. The faster the drop, the bigger the imbalance at the base.
Price rallies steeply back toward A, with no base (no demand) forming inside the rally. A steep rally into supply tends to fall back at a similar rate.

passages.h: Step: D, E, F: the full order set
passages.t: D: short at the bottom line. E: protective stop just above the zone, because price could not get above it before. F: target three times the risk. Size so the dollar risk is fixed, then walk away.

passages.h: Step: The trade works without you
passages.t: Price holds under the zone for a while, then drops through the target. Nobody had to watch it.

Supply pattern Sam trusts? - Rally-base-drop. Why skip drop-base-drop? - It is a pause in the middle of a move, typically a weak level. Best kind of return into supply? - A steep rally with no demand forming inside it. Minimum target? - 3:1 or more. After all orders are in? - Walk away and do something more important.

Most big mistakes come from not paying attention to the reality in front of you. In the June 16, 2009 XLT Futures session a quiet cluster in the S&P collapsed with a big red candle, so lines were drawn around that origin as a supply zone. Hours later price rallied into it, the class shorted to novice buyers, and the target near 911 was reached; a student made 13.25 points.

Wrap the base where price was balanced before a sharp collapse; that is the supply zone. Short the first rally back into the zone; risk first, reward second. Pre-plan the trade before the market opens.
Focus on what price action shows, not on thinking too deeply. Market information is only given to those who listen.
Two lines are drawn around a cluster where price was balanced; then it collapsed with a big red candle.
That collapse says supply greatly exceeded demand at the origin of the decline: a 'supply zone' or 'sell zone'.

When price later rallied into it, buyers there made the two mistakes (buying after a rally, buying into supply); taking the other side is the high odds trade. Focus first on objectively assessing risk, then reward; not every trade works.
First short at 923 closed manually at 923.75 (-0.75) because it looked close to his 924 stop; he re-entered at 923. Price ranged 919-924.25, then fell to close at 909.75: +13.25 points.
Screenshot of the session hours before the US open: chat window on the left, an S&P E-mini chart on the right.
Two magenta lines (about 924-927) wrap a small cluster near the top; a big red candle drops out of it, and price then drifts sideways lower overnight.
@ES 10-min (Sep09 contract), 6/15 to 6/16/2009, scale about 906-927. 'XLT Supply Level': lines at about 924.1 and 927.3, with the circled big red candle leaving the level on the left.

Price chops 916-922, then rallies into the lower line around 9:00 on 6/16 ('XLT Sells Short To Novice Buyer' arrow at about 924). Price falls hard to a 'Profit Target' line at 911.00 and on to about 907; last 908.75.

passages.h: Chart: Live XLT session screen hours before the US open: chat on the left, S&P E-mini chart on the right with two magenta lines (about 924-927) around a small cluster; a big red candle drops out of it and price drifts lower overnight.
passages.t: The zone is drawn before the open, around the balance that preceded the big red candle. The plan is waiting for price to come back, not a reaction to it.

passages.h: Chart: E-mini S&P 10-min (Sep09), 6/15 to 6/16/2009: XLT supply level lines at about 924.1 and 927.3 with the circled big red candle leaving it. Price chops 916-922, rallies into the lower line about 9:00 on 6/16 (XLT sells short to novice buyer), then falls through the 911 profit target to about 907.
passages.t: First return to a fresh supply after a collapse candle is the high odds short. Entry at the lower line, stop above the upper line, target the 911 demand. Buyers at the arrow bought after a rally and into supply.
S&P 10-min supply built in advance: a quiet cluster collapses with one big red candle, two lines wrap the cluster, and hours later the rally into it is shorted to novice buyers with a target at 911.
Not noticing the obvious reality on the chart. Acting on advice from people paid for advice, not trading. Buying after a rally into a fresh supply zone.
Was there balance (a cluster) before a big departure candle? Is this the first return to the zone? Is the profit target at the next demand defined? Have I assessed risk before reward?
“This important market information is only given to those who listen.” “Success is a choice.”
Similar: drawing the zone around the base before an explosive candle matches Kevin's zone drawing.
Differs: Seiden calls it 'supply' or 'sell zone'; Kevin adds qualifying rules (e.g. trendline/HTF) before trading it.

Watch what price shows you. A quiet pause, then a crash, marks supply. Hours before the market opened, Sam's class saw price resting quietly in a small cluster. Then one big red candle crashed out of it. That told them sellers were in charge there, so they drew two lines around the cluster. Hours later price rallied back into those lines, and they sold to the buyers. Price dropped to their target and a student made 13 points.
It is like a dog that was calm and then suddenly ran out of a yard. Something in that yard scared it. If it walks back in, expect it to run again.

Most big mistakes come from not paying attention to the reality in front of you. Balance (a cluster) followed by a big collapse candle = supply at the origin. Short the first rally back into it. Assess risk first, then reward.
Price sits in a small cluster. Buyers and sellers are balanced here. Nothing exciting yet.
Then price collapses with one big red candle. That candle says supply greatly exceeded demand at the origin of the decline.

passages.h: Step: Draw the sell zone before the open
passages.t: Wrap the cluster with two lines. That is the supply zone, drawn in advance while price chops lower. Now we just wait.
Price rallies into the bottom line. Entry there, stop above the top line: that is the risk. The target is the next demand below. The buyers here bought after a rally and into supply.
Price drops to the target and beyond. The market gave the information to anyone who listened.

Cluster + big red candle means? - Supply at the origin of the decline (a sell zone). Order of assessment? - Risk first, then reward. When is the zone drawn? - Before the open, before price comes back. Who gets market information? - Only those who listen (pay attention).

Supply and demand analysis also protects long-term wealth. A tech mutual fund can be bought at pivot-low demand, but a fund priced in dollars can still lose buying power when the US Dollar Index hits supply. Likewise, when the S&P revisits supply you can hedge a stock portfolio by shorting SPY or S&P futures or buying puts.
Buy funds or stocks at pivot-low demand, not after declines into it with the crowd selling.
Check the currency your assets are priced in; a dollar at supply is a risk to dollar assets. When the index revisits supply, hedge (short ETF/futures or buy puts).
The strongest turns and largest moves happen where demand and supply are MOST out of balance. You can chart almost anything that is bought and sold, including mutual funds.

Schwab Tech Fund: 'A' is pivot-low demand; whoever sells at 'B' is a novice selling after a decline and into demand. You do not need to know what the fund holds; price says it is about to rise at 'B'.

A fund rising in dollars can still lose buying power if the dollar falls. US Dollar Index: 'A' is supply and 'B' the first revisit; expect a decline at 'B', so dollar assets lose buying power. Ignoring currency risk transfers buying power to those who do not.

SPY: 'A' supply, 'B' the revisit. A decline from B drags global stocks and your retirement account down. Hedge choices at 'B': short SPY, short S&P futures, buy S&P puts, and more. All that matters at the end of the day is your buying power versus your neighbours.

passages.t: SWTFX monthly, 2002 to 2007. Price falls to a 2003 low, rallies into 2004, then pulls back to a pivot low at 'A' (late 2004), wrapped by two black lines.

passages.t: 'B' (2005) is the return into the upper line; price then climbs steadily to new highs in 2007.

passages.h: Chart: US Dollar Index monthly (Figure 2, p188)
passages.t: A sharp 2008-09 rally reaches 'B' (about 88-89), the first revisit, and price turns down to about 80 (last 80.28).
SPY daily, mid-September to late November 2007, scale about 141-157. 'A' supply: lines at about 155 and 157 around the October top.
Price drops to about 149, rallies to 'B' (about 155, around Nov 1), then declines steadily to about 141 by late November.

passages.h: Chart: Schwab Technology Focus Fund (SWTFX) monthly, 2002 to 2007: pivot-low demand A in late 2004 wrapped by two lines; B (2005) is the return to the upper line, after which the fund climbs to new highs in 2007.
passages.t: Mutual funds can be bought at demand like any stock; the holdings do not matter. Whoever sells at B is selling after a decline and into demand.

passages.h: Chart: US Dollar Index monthly, 2004 to mid-2009: supply A between about 89 and 92.5 at the late-2005 top, a long decline to about 71, then a sharp rally to B (about 88-89), the first revisit, and a turn down toward 80.
passages.t: Dollar assets can rise in price and still lose buying power when the dollar falls from supply. The first revisit of a fresh monthly supply is where the currency risk is highest.

passages.h: Chart: SPY daily, Sep to Nov 2007: supply A at the October top (lines about 155-157); price drops to about 149, rallies back to B around Nov 1 and then declines steadily to about 141.
passages.t: When the index returns to supply, hedge: short SPY or S&P futures, or buy puts. The revisit B was a lower high under the zone, a clean hedge entry with a nearby stop.
Supply and demand for a nest egg: buy a fund at its pivot-low demand on the first return (B); when the index returns to supply (B), hedge the portfolio with a short or puts.
Ignoring currency risk because it seems complicated. Selling a fund after a decline into demand.
Is the asset at demand or supply on the monthly chart? Is the currency it is priced in near supply? Is the S&P at supply, and do I need a hedge?
“All that matters at the end of the day is your BUYING POWER.” “The REAL demand and supply equation is always right in front of your face.”
New: using supply and demand for hedging and currency risk on long-term holdings; not covered in Kevin's course.

Use levels to protect your savings, not just to trade. Supply and demand works on anything people buy and sell, even a slow retirement fund. You can buy a fund when it drops into its demand, without knowing what it holds. But watch the money it is priced in: a fund can go up in dollars while the dollar itself falls from supply. And when the stock index comes back up to supply, you can protect your account with a hedge.
It is like wearing a raincoat when you see dark clouds. You still go out, but you do not get soaked.

The biggest turns happen where demand and supply are most out of balance, on any chart, even mutual funds. Watch the currency: dollar assets lose buying power when the dollar falls from supply. When the index returns to supply, hedge: short SPY or futures, or buy puts.

passages.h: Step: A: supply on the index
passages.t: The index rallied, paused at the top and dropped away. That base is supply: A.
Price rallies back up to A for the first time. Many people feel happy as their accounts grow. But this is exactly where supply waits.
You do not have to sell your long-term holdings. At B you can short SPY, short S&P futures or buy puts, with a stop just above the zone.
The index falls from B. Your hedge gains while the portfolio drops. What matters at the end of the day is your buying power.
Can you use levels on mutual funds? - Yes; almost anything bought and sold can be charted.

What is currency risk? - Dollar assets losing buying power when the dollar falls from supply. Hedge choices at index supply? - Short SPY, short S&P futures, buy S&P puts. What matters at the end of the day? - Your buying power.

Occam's Razor and the lemonade stand: trading should be as simple as buying low and selling high as a child. A student shorted Alcoa (AA) at 12.08 when it returned to daily rally-base-drop supply near 12, with targets at 3:1 (10.85) and 5:1 (10.03). The buyers made the two classic mistakes.

Supply = rally-base-decline (pivot high); short the return into it. Set targets as multiples of risk: target 1 at 3:1, target 2 at 5:1. Apply the same logic in markets as when buying anything in daily life.
The simplest answer is usually right; most people take illusion for reality. Much of his teaching is peeling away layers of illusion rather than giving rules.
As a child you sold lemonade costing $0.05 for $0.50 or more; that is solid buying and selling.
Instead of advice from people paid for advice, bring that simple logic back to the markets.
AA came into daily supply; short at 12.08, target 1 at 10.85 (3:1), target 2 at 10.03 (5:1). The supply is a rally-base-decline pivot high near $12; price could not stay there.
Buyers bought after a rally (like offering $40,000 for a $30,000 car) and into supply (like hitting the gas toward a concrete wall).
AA daily, late 2008 to July 2009, scale about 5-13. 'XLT Supply Level': a box at about 11.9-12.4 around the early-January 2009 spike top (rally-base-decline).
Price falls to about 5.2 in March, then rallies through April-June back into the box ('Shawn Short Entry' arrow, early June). Price turns down to about 9.0-9.5; last 9.46.

passages.h: Chart: Alcoa daily, late 2008 to July 2009: XLT supply level box (about 11.9-12.4) around the early-January rally-base-decline spike top. Price falls to about 5.2 in March, rallies back into the box in early June (Shawn short entry at 12.08) and turns down to about 9.0-9.5.
passages.t: A pivot high where price could not stay is supply; short its first return. Targets as multiples of risk: 10.85 (3:1) and 10.03 (5:1). Buyers in the box bought after a rally and into supply.
Alcoa daily: a rally-base-decline pivot high near $12 is supply. When price rallies all the way back into it, short at 12.08 with targets at 3:1 and 5:1 of the risk.
Buying after a rally (paying above the sticker price). Buying at a level where supply exceeds demand (accelerating into a wall). Following paid advisers instead of simple logic.
Is the supply a rally-base-decline pivot high? Has price rallied back into it (buyers after a rally)? Are targets at 3:1 and 5:1 room before the next demand?
“Simple logic always beats complex illusion.” “Do you step on the gas pedal or the brakes?”
New: fixed multi-R targets (3:1 and 5:1); Kevin targets the next opposing zone and avoids a fixed R:R.

Buy low and sell high, like a lemonade stand. Simple wins. As a kid you bought lemons for a nickel and sold lemonade for fifty cents. That is good trading, and nobody had to teach you. A student used the same logic on Alcoa: price came back to a high where it could not stay before. He sold there, with targets three and five times his risk. The buyers paid too much, right into a wall.
Buying after a big rally into supply is like offering $40,000 for a $30,000 car, then pressing the gas toward a concrete wall.

Occam's Razor: the simplest answer is usually right. Peel away illusion. Supply is a rally-base-decline pivot high where price could not stay. Short its return. Set targets as multiples of risk: target 1 at 3:1, target 2 at 5:1.

passages.h: Step: A high price could not keep
passages.t: Price spiked up, paused for a moment and fell hard. A rally-base-decline pivot high: supply was much bigger than demand there.
Months later price rallies all the way back. Buyers get excited after the rise. They are paying the sticker price and more.

passages.h: Step: Sell where it is too expensive
passages.t: Short at the bottom line, stop above the top line. Target 1 sits at three times the risk, target 2 at five times.
Price turns down and reaches both targets. Simple logic beat complex illusion.

Lemonade logic? - Buy low (wholesale), sell high (retail). AA short: entry and targets? - 12.08; T1 10.85 (3:1), T2 10.03 (5:1). Supply shape in this lesson? - Rally-base-decline pivot high. Gas pedal or brakes at supply? - Brakes: do not buy into a wall.

Buying the breakout itself is usually the 'sucker bet': high risk, low reward. Instead, let the breakout happen, because it reveals where the buyers are, then buy the return to the origin. Setup: 20-period MA uptrend, drop-base-rally demand at the origin, a profit margin to the breakout high; buy at the top line, stop below the bottom line, target the breakout high.

Trend filter: 20-period MA for direction. Demand must be drop-base-rally (a decline before the base). Entry at the proximal line on the first return; stop just beyond the distal line. Target = high of the initial breakout (low of the breakdown for shorts). Check the higher timeframe curve first.

Why do prices move? They turn where demand and supply are out of balance. Who is on the other side? Trading transfers money from those who do not know to those who do; make sure a novice is on the other side.
Area 'A' is the origin of a strong rally; most traders buy as price breaks out from it. By the time you buy the breakout, price has moved so far that it is high risk, low reward.
Wait for price to return to 'A' ('C'); the seller there is selling after selling and into demand.
Longs: uptrend defined by a 20-period moving average. Draw two lines around the origin of the strong move (demand 'A'); it should be a drop-base-rally (preceded by a decline) for higher probability.
Profit margin = distance from 'A' to 'B', the highest high of the initial breakout before the return.

Buy at 'C' when price touches the top line; protective sell stop just below the lower line; size to acceptable loss; target at 'B' (exit at 'D'). Shorts are the mirror image: short the pullback to pivot-high supply, not the breakdown.
Works in any market and timeframe, but always know where price is on the larger timeframe supply/demand curve.

Unlabelled candlestick chart with a rising 20-period moving average. Grey box 'A' with two black lines around a small base after a dip (drop-base-rally); arrows marked 'Breakout' show price leaving it with long green candles.

'B' is a horizontal line at the high of the initial breakout; price consolidates, then a sharp red candle drops back to the top line of 'A' at 'C'. Price rallies from 'C' through 'B'; 'D' marks the profit exit at the B level.
'Buying the Breakout': buy as price leaves pivot-low demand (origin of imbalance) = higher risk, lower reward, lower probability.
'Buying the Retracement': after the breakout, buy the pullback to the zone = low risk, high reward, high probability.
'Shorting the Breakdown' vs 'Shorting the Retracement' from pivot-high supply: same contrast mirrored. Page 197 is blank.

passages.h: Chart: Breakout example: a rising 20-period MA, grey demand box A (two lines) around a small drop-base-rally base, long green "Breakout" candles, B the high of the initial breakout, a sharp red candle back to the top line at C, and the rally to the B level where D marks the exit.
passages.t: Do not buy the breakout; it shows where the buyers are. Buy the first return at C, stop below the bottom line, target B. The trend filter is the rising 20-period MA, and the base should be preceded by a drop.

passages.h: Chart: Slide: "Buying the Breakout" (buy as price leaves pivot-low demand: higher risk, lower reward, lower probability) versus "Buying the Retracement" (buy the pullback to the zone after the breakout: low risk, high reward, high probability).
passages.t: The same zone, two entries; the pullback puts the entry next to the stop.

passages.h: Chart: Slide: "Shorting the Breakdown" versus "Shorting the Retracement" from pivot-high supply: the breakdown short is higher risk and lower reward; the short on the pullback to the zone is low risk, high reward.
passages.t: Mirror rule for shorts: let price break down, then short the return to the origin.

Same demand, two entries: buying the breakout candle puts the stop far away for little reward; letting the breakout happen and buying the first pullback to the zone keeps the stop tight and the reward large.

The full setup: uptrend by a rising 20-period MA, demand A is a drop-base-rally at the origin of the breakout, B is the high of the initial breakout. Buy C at the top line, stop under the bottom line, exit D at B.
Buying the breakout candle (the sucker bet). Letting emotion push you into the initial rally. Ignoring where price is on the larger timeframe.

Is the 20-period MA rising (or falling for shorts)? Is the zone at the origin of a strong move, with a drop before the base? Is there enough room to the breakout high? Is this the first return? Where is price on the higher timeframe?
“This type of breakout entry is typically the 'sucker bet'.” “I sit back and let the breakout happen.”
Differs: Kevin also teaches a breakout entry (order above supply with stop below the base) when structure allows; Seiden rejects buying the breakout.
New: 20-period moving average as the trend filter; Kevin uses trendlines and structure, not MAs. New: target fixed at the initial breakout high.

Let the breakout go. Buy when price comes back to where it started. Most people buy the moment price breaks out. By then it has moved so far that the stop is miles away and the reward is small. Sam sits back and lets the breakout happen, because it shows him where the buyers are. When price comes back to the start of the jump, he buys with a tight stop. His target is the high of that first breakout.
It is like a bus pulling away. Do not chase it down the street. Wait at the bus stop; it comes back on the next loop.
Buying the breakout is usually the sucker bet: high risk, low reward. Setup: rising 20-period MA, drop-base-rally demand at the breakout origin, room to the breakout high.
Buy the top line on the first return, stop below the bottom line, target the breakout high. Shorts are the mirror.

passages.h: Step: Uptrend and a drop before the base
passages.t: The 20-period average is rising, so we look for buys. Price dipped, paused, then broke out. The dip before the base makes it drop-base-rally, the higher-probability kind.

passages.h: Step: The breakout: do not chase
passages.t: Big green candles break out. This is where most people buy. Their stop would have to go far below; the reward is small. We just watch and mark where it started.

passages.h: Step: Mark B: the profit margin
passages.t: B is the highest high of the first breakout before price comes back. The distance from A to B is our profit margin.
Price drops back to the top line of A. The seller here is selling after a decline and into demand. Buy at the top line, stop just under the bottom line.
Price rallies from C to B. That is the exit, D. Low risk, high reward, high probability.

The sucker bet? - Buying the breakout candle: high risk, low reward. Trend filter for this setup? - A rising (or falling, for shorts) 20-period MA. Target of the retracement buy? - B, the high of the initial breakout. Demand shape wanted? - Drop-base-rally at the breakout origin. Mirror for shorts? - Short the pullback to pivot-high supply, not the breakdown.

How long it takes depends on prior bad information: beginners with no experience learn fastest. A student's failed GENZ long shows three common errors: supply too close above, a third return to the demand after a weak rally, and the S&P not at demand. His reading list is Economics 101 and Psychology 101.

Need room: no nearby opposing level above a long. Be cautious on a third return to a level, especially after a weak bounce. Time trades with the S&P being at a matching level. Look for basing pockets of sellers between entry and the zone.

Those with little or no experience learn fastest; seminar and book veterans take longest because of bad 'decision filters'. Get the right information the first time; first impressions are hard to replace.
Use a simple logic filter: if it seems too complex or illogical, it is probably poisonous to your account.

Plan: long at 51.35 from the July 23 drop-base-rally demand, stop 51.00. Price opened 51.99 on Aug 3 after a downgrade and bad news, and the trade was stopped. 1) Supply was not far above, limiting profit and showing sellers nearby. 2) It was the third return to the level and the latest rally from it was weak: low odds. 3) The S&P was not at demand; timing with the S&P is not everything but very important.
The circled area was a pocket of sellers the student missed.
Economics 101 for supply and demand and Psychology 101 for how people decide. Most trading books are written by people who write books, not trade.
GENZ 30-min, 7/23 to early August 2009, scale about 50-56.5. 'Demand' lines at about 51.0 and 51.3 under the 7/23 low, where price launched to about 53.
Price climbs to about 56.5 by 7/30; 'Supply' lines at about 55.8 and 56.5 wrap the top cluster.
On 7/31 a huge red candle drops to about 52; a circled cluster (about 51.6-52.3) is the pocket of sellers. 'Student Bought' arrow at the demand line on Aug 1-3; price breaks through to about 50.

passages.h: Chart: Genzyme 30-min, 7/23 to early Aug 2009: demand lines about 51.0-51.3 under the 7/23 low; supply lines about 55.8-56.5 around the 7/30 top. On 7/31 a huge red candle drops to about 52 where a circled cluster (pocket of sellers) forms; the student bought at the demand line and price broke through to about 50.
