passages.t: Low odds: supply not far above, a weak latest rally and a repeated return to the level. The circled cluster between entry and supply was a pocket of sellers. The S&P was not at demand, so the trade was against the market timing.

The failed GENZ long: opposing supply sat close above, a pocket of sellers based between the entry and that supply, the latest rally from the zone was weak and repeated, and the S&P was not at demand.
Buying demand with supply close above. Trading a level that has been revisited several times. Ignoring the index. Learning from too many sources first.

How many times has price returned to this level? Was the latest move away strong? Is opposing supply far enough away? Is the index at the same kind of level? Any small base (pocket of sellers) just above the zone?
“If information seems too complex or doesn't make sense to you, chances are great that it is poisonous.” “Timing your trade to the S&P is not everything but it sure is important.”
Differs: Kevin keeps a zone until it is removed (closed through), not weakened by touches; Seiden lowers odds on a third return. New: requiring the S&P to be at demand for a stock long.

Before buying demand, check the room above, the visit count and the index. A student bought a stock at demand and got stopped out. Sam showed him three things he missed. Supply sat close above, so there was little room to profit. It was the third visit to the level, and the last bounce from it was weak. And the S&P was not at demand. A small pocket of sellers had also formed just above his entry.
It is like a cookie jar that has been raided three times already. The fourth time you reach in, there are only crumbs left.
People with no experience learn fastest; bad information from books and seminars must be unlearned.
Low odds: supply close above, many returns to the level, a weak latest rally, index not at a matching level.
Read Economics 101 and Psychology 101. If it seems too complex or illogical, it is probably poison.

passages.h: Step: A demand, but a short leg
passages.t: Price dropped, based and rallied, but only a little before it paused again. That pause is supply close above. Room to profit is small.
Price comes back and bounces, then comes back again. Each visit uses up buy orders at the level.

passages.h: Step: A weak bounce and a pocket of sellers
passages.t: The bounce after the second visit is weak, and price pauses in a small cluster just above the zone: a pocket of sellers between the entry and the supply.
The student buys the third visit. The S&P is not at demand. With so many warning signs the odds were low, and price breaks right through.

Who learns fastest? - People with little or no prior experience. Three GENZ errors? - Supply close above, third return after a weak rally, S&P not at demand. Pocket of sellers? - A small base between your entry and the opposing level. Sam's reading list? - Economics 101 and Psychology 101.
Simple logic filter? - If it seems too complex or illogical, it is probably poisonous to your account.

Schools train people to think alike, which loses in competitive markets. Two conventional tools used differently: judge trend health by the shrinking distance between pivot lows, and use a past moving-average cross as a pointer to look slightly left for the origin of a strong move, i.e. a supply or demand level.
Measure distance between pivot lows (uptrend) or highs (downtrend); shrinking spacing warns of trend end.
Never use an MA cross as an execution trigger; use it only to locate the origin of the move to its left.
No class teaches how to compete; herd thinking hands accounts to those who think differently. Conventional technical analysis is taught the same way, so it offers little edge.

Beyond higher highs/lows or MA slope, measure the distance between the pivot lows of an uptrend (pivot highs in a downtrend). Shrinking distance between pullbacks means the trend is weakening and likely to end soon.
A strong trend does not pull back often; a trend is an imbalance moving toward a level of temporary balance.

passages.h: Moving average cross as a locator
passages.t: MA slope and MA cross signals lag price and add risk if used for execution. MAs cross because of a strong move, whose origin is an imbalance. When you see a past cross above or below price, look slightly left of it for the level. He does not use these two tools himself; the point is to think differently from the herd.
Unlabelled long-term chart (months marked, several years), price rising from about 65 to about 150 with volume below.

Double-headed arrows join successive pivot lows (about 75, 98, 125, 135); the arrows get shorter: 'Decreasing distance between the pivot lows'. At the far right price stalls near 150 and turns down to about 130.

passages.h: Chart: DryShips daily with two MAs (Figure 2, p204)
passages.t: DRYS daily, June to mid-August 2009, scale about 4.9-7.6, two moving averages. Circled MA cross near 7.1-7.2 in mid/late June labelled 'Moving Average Cross & Supply (resistance) level'; two lines at about 7.1 and 7.45 mark the supply just left of the cross, where price topped before falling.

passages.h: Chart: DryShips daily with two MAs (Figure 2, p204)
passages.t: Price drops to about 4.9 in early July, then rallies; around 7/27 a big green candle reaches about 7.1 ('Selling Opportunity', circled). Price then falls back to about 6.1-6.5; last 6.48.

passages.h: Chart: Long-term chart rising from about 65 to about 150 with volume: double-headed arrows join successive pivot lows (about 75, 98, 125, 135) and get shorter, labelled "Decreasing distance between the pivot lows". At the right price stalls near 150 and turns down.
passages.t: Shrinking distance between pullbacks warns that the trend is weakening. A strong trend does not pull back often.

passages.h: Chart: DryShips daily, June to mid-Aug 2009 with two moving averages: the circled MA cross in late June sits just right of a supply level (lines about 7.1-7.45) where price topped. Price falls to about 4.9, then a big green candle on 7/27 reaches about 7.1 ("Selling Opportunity") and price falls back to about 6.1-6.5.
passages.t: Use a past MA cross only to look slightly left for the origin of the strong move. The return to that supply is the sell; the cross itself is never the trigger.
Same tool, different thought: measure the distance between pivot lows of an uptrend. When the distance keeps shrinking, the trend is losing its imbalance and is likely to end soon.
DryShips: two moving averages cross after a strong decline. The cross is not the trade; it points to the supply level just to its left, which is sold when price rallies back to it.
Using lagging indicators to time entries. Thinking and acting like the herd.
Are the pullbacks in this trend getting closer together? Is there a past MA cross nearby, and what level sits just left of it?
“A strong trending market does not pullback often.” “Look slightly to the left of the cross and investigate the price action.”
New: trend strength from pivot-low spacing; Kevin judges trend with trendlines and structure. New: MA cross as a pointer to a zone; Kevin does not use moving averages.

Use common tools in an uncommon way, so you do not think like the herd. Schools teach everyone to use the same tools the same way, and the same crowd loses together. Sam shows two twists. First, in an uptrend measure the gaps between the dips: if dips come closer and closer together, the trend is getting tired. Second, when two moving averages cross, do not trade the cross; look a little to its left to find where the strong move started.
A runner who stops to rest more and more often is about to quit the race. Count the rest stops, not just the steps.
Thinking like the herd hands your account to people who think differently. Shrinking distance between pivot lows (uptrend) or pivot highs (downtrend) means the trend is weakening.
A moving-average cross is never the trigger. It only points slightly left, to the origin of a strong move.

passages.h: Step: A strong trend rarely pulls back
passages.t: Price climbs with long runs between dips. The first gap between pivot lows is wide: the imbalance is strong.
Each new pivot low comes sooner than the last. The trend is moving toward balance.
Now the dips are almost on top of each other. Risk of buying is rising and the trend is likely to end soon.
Price stalls and turns down. The shrinking spacing warned us before any lagging signal did.

Trend health check? - Measure distance between pivot lows (uptrend) or highs (downtrend). Shrinking distance means? - The trend is weakening; risk to join it is rising. Use of an MA cross? - Only as a pointer: look slightly left for the level. Why not trade the cross? - It lags price and adds risk.

Most people lose because conventional technical and fundamental analysis make them buy with the herd after good news, and because they drop the everyday logic they use when buying a car or cheese. On August 19, 2009 the NASDAQ (QQQQ) gapped down into demand and CSCO sat at demand aligned with it; both were bought 'wholesale' and rallied.
Buy wholesale (at demand), sell retail (at supply). Align a stock's demand with the index's demand. Treat a gap down into demand as a sale, not a reason to sell.
Books and seminars teach buying after rallies, lagging indicators, and buying after good news when price is already high.
People throw out simple logic: nobody offers $30,000 for a $20,000 car, yet traders wait for confirmation of higher prices and then buy. To profit, others must buy after you at higher prices.

A pizza chain owner: cheese averages $2/lb; at $4 he buys only what he needs, at $1 as much as he can store. He already knew how to trade; he only needed to see what that looks like on a chart. Bring your everyday shopping mindset (coupons, sales) into trading.
Pre-market top-down analysis an hour before the open. NASDAQ was gapping down into demand (circled): briefly on sale. Sellers on the gap down ignored supply and demand.
CSCO had demand aligned with the NASDAQ demand; despite bad news it was at wholesale prices that would not last.
Screenshot of the August 19 session: participants and chat on the left, several TradeStation charts on the right.
The main chart shows an uptrend with a horizontal two-line box drawn from a base on the left; on the far right price has dropped into the box (black circle at the gap down).
QQQQ 30-min, 7/22 to 8/24/2009. Two lines wrap the late-July base (around 7/23) from which price rallied strongly.
Price ranges through early August, then falls in mid-August and dips into the zone around 8/17-8/19. A large ellipse marks the rally out of the zone from 8/19 to 8/24 to new highs.
CSCO 60-min, 8/14 to 8/24/2009, scale about 20.6-22.6. Price drops from about 21.5 to a base around 20.7-20.8 on 8/17; two lines at about 20.65 and 20.82 wrap it.
On 8/19 a candle dips back to the zone (about 20.75) and price climbs steadily to about 22.6 by 8/24; last 21.93.

passages.h: Chart: Live XLT session screen, Aug 19, 2009: participants and chat on the left, several charts on the right; the main chart shows an uptrend and a two-line demand box drawn from an earlier base, with price gapping down into it at the far right (circled).
passages.t: The top-down plan is done before the open; the gap into demand is the sale.

passages.h: Chart: QQQQ 30-min, 7/22 to 8/24/2009: two lines wrap the late-July base from which price rallied strongly. Price ranges in early August, falls into the zone around 8/17-8/19, and a large ellipse marks the rally out of it to new highs by 8/24.
passages.t: Index at demand while the news is bad: buy wholesale. The first return to the origin of a strong rally produced another strong rally.

passages.h: Chart: Cisco 60-min, 8/14 to 8/24/2009: price drops from about 21.5 to a base near 20.7-20.8 on 8/17, wrapped by lines at about 20.65 and 20.82. On 8/19 a candle dips back to the zone and price climbs steadily to about 22.6.
passages.t: Stock demand aligned with the index demand on the same morning. Entry at the upper line, stop under the lower line, a very small risk for a large move.
Everyday logic on a chart: buy heavily when price is at wholesale (demand) and only a little or not at all when it is at retail (supply), exactly as a pizza owner buys cheese.
Aug 19, 2009: the NASDAQ dropped into its demand at the same time CSCO sat at aligned demand. Bad news made it cheap; both were bought wholesale and rallied to new highs.
Buying after good news when price is already high. Waiting for confirmation of higher prices before buying. Selling a gap down into demand because of bad news.
Is price at wholesale (demand) or retail (supply)? Is the index at matching demand? Am I reacting to news or to the level?
“If proper market speculating was as easy as reading a book, wouldn't every librarian be a millionaire?” “Make sure you are the author.”
Differs: Seiden argues against waiting for confirmation; Kevin's course includes confirmation entries in some contexts.

Shop for stocks like cheese: buy a lot when it is on sale. A pizza shop owner pays about $2 for a pound of cheese. At $4 he buys only what he needs, and at $1 he buys all he can store. He already knew how to trade; he just had never seen it on a chart. One morning the NASDAQ gapped down into demand on bad news, and Cisco sat at its own matching demand. Sam bought both at wholesale prices and they rallied.
Waiting for a price to go up before you buy is like waiting for the sale to end before you go shopping.
People lose by buying after good news and rising prices, and by dropping the logic they use when shopping.
Buy wholesale (demand), sell retail (supply). Others must buy after you, higher, for you to profit. A gap down into demand is a sale, not a reason to sell. Line the stock up with the index.
Price dropped, paused and rallied strongly. That base is the wholesale price: where demand far exceeded supply.
Up here price is retail. Buying after good news at these prices is like paying $4 for cheese.

passages.h: Step: The sale: a gap into demand
passages.t: Bad news gaps price down straight into the zone. The index is at its demand too. This is the coupon. Buy at the top line, stop under the bottom line.

passages.h: Step: Sale prices do not last
passages.t: Price rallies back toward retail. Those who sold the gap down sold their cheese for $1.

Wholesale and retail on a chart? - Wholesale = demand, retail = supply. Two reasons people lose? - Conventional analysis teaches herd buying after good news, and they drop everyday shopping logic. A gap down into demand is...? - A sale, not a reason to sell. The pizza owner at $4 cheese? - Buys only what he needs.

A parable of Foolsville, a box-shaped town where everyone thinks and trades the same way: buy on good news, rising prices and bullish indicators. On September 1, 2009 the S&P had a gap-down supply zone; the financial sector, Goldman Sachs and Citigroup had matching supply. Price rallied into supply, the 'Foolsville' buyers bought, the XLT sold short, and all four fell hard.
Look for the index, sector and stocks all at supply (or demand) together. If price opens away from the level, wait for it to rally into it; do not chase. A gap away from a base marks strong supply.
To command a higher income, learn to do something others can't, which requires thinking differently.
In Foolsville everyone eats, drives and trades the same way; from inside the box you never see the box. Money flows out of Foolsville to those who buy when they sell and sell when they buy.
S&P supply above price: price could not stay there and gapped down, meaning too much supply.
Price opened below the level, so a rally was needed, plus buyers buying after a rally right at supply.
The financial sector (XLF) had the same supply; GS and C had clear supply just above the open. Index, sector and stocks at supply together stacked the odds.

SPY 15-min, 8/27 to 8/31/2009, scale about 102-104.2. Two black lines labelled 'S&P Supply' at about 103.1 and 103.5 wrap a small base on 8/28 late in the day. On 8/31 price gaps down from the base to about 102.0-102.4 and drifts there.
XLT Stock Mastery session screenshot with seven panes: XLF, C, BAC, COF on top and GS, JPM, MS below.
Callouts point to 'XLF (Financial Service Sector) Supply Level', 'Citigroup (C) Supply Levels' (two levels) and 'Goldman Sachs Supply Level', each drawn as horizontal lines above current price.
Same SPY zone (about 103.1-103.5). On Sep 1 price rallies from about 102 to about 103.2 into the lower line ('XLT Short Entry' arrow). Price then collapses to about 100.4-100.6.
GS: 'Supply Level' line at about 165.5-166 from an 8/28 top; on Sep 1 price rallies back to it ('XLT Short Entry') and falls to about 160.2.

C: 'Supply Level' lines at about 5.00 and 5.05 from a base on 8/28-8/31; Sep 1 rally into it ('XLT Short Entry') then a drop to about 4.55 by 9/2. Index bar at top: Dow 9310.60 (-185.68), Nasdaq 1968.89 (-40.17), S&P 998.04 (-22.58).

passages.h: Chart: SPY 15-min, 8/27 to 8/31/2009 (pre-market): two lines labelled "S&P Supply" at about 103.1 and 103.5 wrap a small base late on 8/28; on 8/31 price gaps down from it to about 102.0-102.4.
passages.t: A gap away from a base marks strong supply. Price opened below the level, so the plan waits for a rally back into it.

passages.h: Chart: Live XLT Stock Mastery screen with seven panes (XLF, C, BAC, COF, GS, JPM, MS); callouts mark the XLF supply level, two Citigroup supply levels and the Goldman Sachs supply level, all above current price.
passages.t: Sector and stocks were checked for supply matching the index supply.

passages.h: Chart: SPY 15-min (after): the same supply about 103.1-103.5. On Sep 1 price rallies from about 102 into the lower line (XLT short entry) and collapses to about 100.4-100.6.
passages.t: The rally into the gap-origin supply was the short; the buyers there bought after a rally into supply. Risk about half a point for a drop of more than two and a half points.

passages.h: Chart: Goldman Sachs 15-min and Citigroup 30-min: GS supply level about 165.5-166 from the 8/28 top, rallied into on Sep 1 (XLT short entry) and fell to about 160.2; C supply about 5.00-5.05 from the 8/28-8/31 base, rallied into on Sep 1 and dropped to about 4.55.
passages.t: Index, sector and stocks at supply together stack the odds. Each short was entered on the rally into the level, never on the way down.

Sept 1, 2009 plan: the S&P supply formed where price based and gapped down. Price opened below it, so the plan was to wait for the rally into the zone and short, with the sector and two bank stocks at matching supply.
Buying after good news, rising price and bullish indicators all line up (the Foolsville setup). Doing what everyone else does.
Is the index at supply? Is the sector at matching supply? Which stocks have clear supply just above the open? Am I waiting for the rally into the level?
“If you want to command a higher income, simply learn how to do something others can't do.” “You have to be outside the box to understand that there is a box.”
New: sector and multi-stock alignment with the index (no sector step in Kevin's course).

Do not trade like the town where everyone thinks the same. In the town of Foolsville, everyone eats the same food, drives the same car and buys when the news is good and prices are rising. Their money flows out of town to people who sell when they buy. One morning the S&P opened under a supply level where price had gapped down before. Sam waited for the rally back into it, while the bank sector and two big bank stocks sat at the same kind of supply. The Fools bought, Sam sold, and all four fell hard.
You have to step outside a box to see that it is a box.

To earn more, learn to do what others cannot. That needs different thinking. A gap down from a base marks strong supply. If price opens below it, wait for the rally into it. Index, sector and stocks at supply together stack the odds.
Price based and then gapped down. Price could not stay there: too much supply. Mark the base as S&P supply.

passages.h: Step: Open below: wait, do not chase
passages.t: Price opens below the level. Shorting down here would be selling low. We need a rally back into supply, with buyers buying after that rally.
The financial sector fund has the same supply, and two bank stocks have clear supply just above their open. Index, sector and stocks line up.
Price rallies into the bottom line. The Fools see good news, rising price and bullish indicators and buy. We sell to them with the stop above the zone.
Price collapses. The index, the sector and both stocks fell hard together.

Foolsville buy signal? - Good news, rising price and bullish indicators all together. Price opens below supply: action? - Wait for the rally into the zone; do not chase. What stacks the odds? - Index, sector and stocks at the same kind of level. To command a higher income... - Learn to do something others can't.

Newton's laws describe price: mass is supply and demand, motion happens between them. A strong S&P supply (gap away) worked on the first revisit 'A' and again on a gap into it 'B', but each revisit absorbed supply; at 'C' and 'D' the declines were shallow, so shorts were skipped. When price pushed deep into the level ('E'), they switched to buying smaller-timeframe demand on the 5-minute chart.
First revisit to a fresh level has the highest odds. Each further revisit absorbs orders; shallower reactions mean the level is failing.

Stop trading a level when reactions get shallow; when price goes deep into it, look for the opposite trade on a smaller timeframe. A gap into a level shows novice entries and can justify a trade on a later revisit.
On the CME floor, the largest stack of sell orders above price is where rallies stopped; the largest buy stack below is where declines stopped.
Price rises at levels where demand exceeds supply and falls where supply exceeds demand; motion occurs between them.
A gap away from the level means supply greatly exceeds demand. First revisit ('A') = highest odds; the class shorted and price fell.
Second revisit ('B') a week later was shorted because price gapped into it (novice buying), but there is less supply left.
Each move into the level absorbs some supply; at 'C' and 'D' declines got shallower, so shorting became high risk and was skipped.
When price pushed deep into the level ('E'), the mass was removed and motion higher was likely.
They looked for demand below on smaller timeframes; on the 5-minute chart price crashed into demand for a low risk long (entry close to stop, reward high because supply above was absorbed).
Image of the 1687 Principia page 'Axiomata sive Leges Motus' with Newton's first and second laws in Latin (source: Wikipedia).

SPY 30-min, about 8/28 to 9/9/2009, scale about 99.5-104, with volume. 'XLT Supply Level': two lines at about 103.0 and 103.45 around a circled base on the left; a circled gap below it is labelled 'Gap suggests supply level is strong'. 'A' (Sep 1): first revisit, followed by a fall to about 99.7 on 9/2-9/3.
Rally on 9/4; 'B' (9/8): a circled 'Novice Gap into supply', short taken; price dips to about 102.7.
'C' and 'D': further touches with shallower dips; 'E' (9/9): price pushes deep into the zone, then breaks above to about 104; last 103.76.
SPY 5-min, about 13:00 on 9/8 to 11:00 on 9/9/2009, scale about 102.75-104. 'Demand Level': lines at about 102.72 and 102.80 under a base around 14:00 on 9/8.
Around 8:30 on 9/9 a big red candle drops to the upper line; a circle marks the 'Low Risk Long Entry' at about 102.8. Price then rallies to about 103.95; last 103.76.

passages.h: Chart: Page of Newton's 1687 Principia, "Axiomata sive Leges Motus", with the first and second laws of motion in Latin.
passages.t: Mass (supply and demand) and motion (price between levels) frame the lesson.

passages.h: Chart: SPY 30-min, 8/28 to 9/9/2009: XLT supply level lines about 103.0-103.45 over a circled base; a circled gap below it ("Gap suggests supply level is strong"). A (Sep 1) first revisit, then a fall to about 99.7; B (9/8) a novice gap into supply; C and D shallower touches; E (9/9) price pushes deep and breaks above to about 104.
passages.t: First revisit (A) had the highest odds and the deepest decline. Each later touch absorbed supply; shallow dips at C and D said stop shorting. A deep push into the level (E) signalled that the mass was gone.

passages.h: Chart: SPY 5-min, 9/8 to 9/9/2009: demand level lines at about 102.76-102.85 under a base from 14:00 on 9/8. Around 8:30 on 9/9 a big red candle drops to the upper line (circled "Low Risk Long Entry") and price rallies to about 103.95.
passages.t: Once the larger supply was absorbed, switch sides and buy smaller-timeframe demand. Entry close to the stop, reward large because the supply above had been used up.

SPY 30-min: the gap-origin supply produced a big decline on the first revisit (A) and a smaller one on the novice gap (B). Reactions at C and D got shallow, and at E price pushed deep and broke through.
SPY 5-min: once the 30-min supply was absorbed, the class looked for demand on a smaller timeframe. A big red candle crashed into it, giving a long with the stop close by and plenty of room above.
Shorting the same supply again and again after it has been absorbed. Chasing pretty candlestick patterns instead of quantifying supply and demand.
How many times has price revisited this level? Are the reactions from it getting shallower? Has price pushed deep into it? If so, is there smaller-timeframe demand below for a long?
“Mass = Demand and Supply, motion occurs between demand and supply.” “Proper trading is easy; having the proper belief system is the hard part.”

Differs: Kevin keeps a zone valid until a candle closes fully through it; Seiden downgrades it as revisits make reactions shallower. New: switching to the opposite trade on a smaller timeframe once supply is absorbed.

Every visit to a level eats its orders. Shallow bounces mean it is nearly empty. Price had gapped away from a supply level, so lots of sell orders were waiting there. On the first visit price fell hard. On the second visit price gapped in and fell again, but not as far. On the third and fourth visits the drops were tiny, so the class stopped selling. When price pushed deep into the zone, they knew the sellers were used up and looked for a buy on a smaller chart instead.
A level is like a pile of sandbags holding back water. Each wave washes some away. When the waves start getting over the top, the wall is about to go.
Mass = supply and demand; motion happens between them. The first revisit has the highest odds. Each revisit removes orders; shallower reactions mean the level is failing.
When price pushes deep into the level, switch sides: look for smaller-timeframe demand below.

passages.h: Step: Strong supply: a gap away
passages.t: Price based and gapped down. The gap says supply greatly exceeded demand. Lots of sell orders are left there.
Price comes back for the first time and falls a long way. The first revisit has the highest odds.

passages.h: Step: B: a novice gap in
passages.t: A week later price gaps into the zone: novices buying. Worth a short, but less supply is left, and the drop is smaller.

passages.h: Step: C and D: shallow reactions
passages.t: Now each drop from the level is shallow. The sell orders are being absorbed. Shorting here has become high risk, so the class stops.

passages.h: Step: E: deep push, switch sides
passages.t: Price pushes deep into the zone and breaks above. The mass is gone. Now the plan is to buy fresh demand on a smaller chart, with little supply left overhead.
Mass and motion? - Mass = demand and supply; motion occurs between them. Highest-odds revisit? - The first one. Shallower reactions mean? - Orders are being absorbed; the level is failing.
Price pushes deep into supply: next? - Switch sides and look for smaller-timeframe demand to buy. What does a gap away show? - A strong level: supply greatly exceeded demand.

Losses belong in the 'winning' category: they are a necessary part of a profitable strategy. An AAPL weekly short at supply 'A' lost $960 when price rallied through, but the rules then shorted the next supply 'C' for +$3,020 with the stop moved to breakeven at 3:1. A futures day with one loss and one win still netted $1,562.50.
Size every trade so the loss is a small, comfortable amount (e.g. $1,000 or less). After a stop-out, keep applying the rules; take the next valid level. At 3:1 move the stop to breakeven.
Winners play to win; losers play not to lose (fear). A bad golf shot is part of the game; don't let it affect the next shot. Trying to eliminate losses also eliminated his winning trades.

Categorize each trading loss as part of winning. A loss should be small and no big deal; he keeps losses to $1,000 or less in one lower-risk account. If a loss makes you cringe, the position is too big for your comfort.
'A' looked like supply; short at 'B' when price rallied back, which was profitable for a bit, then stopped for a loss as price rallied through.
'A' had less supply than thought; price zoomed up to supply 'C', where the rules said short again.
Plenty of sellers at 'C'; price reached 3:1, the stop moved to breakeven (free trade), and it paid. Two trades per day, 50% accuracy, is fine with proper risk and odds, like a casino.
AAPL weekly, 2007 to mid-2009. 'D': circled top around the end of 2007 (the highest); 'C': circled flat top in mid-2008 just below it.
'A': two lines around a lower pivot high in late summer 2008 (below C), followed by a crash into early 2009. Price then rallies through 2009 back toward 'A' (the 'B' revisit is off the right edge).
Figure 2: TradeStation P&L line showing AAPL -960 as the loss was taken. Figure 3: the same line later showing AAPL +3,020 on the re-short at 'C'.
Figure 4: futures fill window, ES DEC09: sell 5 at 1063.75; buys of 2 and 3 at 1065.00, 5 at 1064.75, 2, 2 and 1 at 1063.75; sell 10 at 1068.00. Bought 15, sold 15, net 0, P/L 1,562.50.

passages.h: Chart: AAPL weekly, 2007 to mid-2009: D the circled late-2007 top, C a circled flat top in mid-2008 just below it, A two lines around a lower pivot high in late summer 2008 (about 175-181), the crash into early 2009 and the rally back to A at B on the right edge.
passages.t: A looked like supply but held less than expected; the short there was stopped. The rules then point to the next supply, C, for the next short.

passages.h: Chart: TradeStation P&L line: AAPL -960 as the short at A was stopped out.
passages.t: A small, planned loss is part of the strategy, not a failure.

passages.h: Chart: TradeStation P&L line later: AAPL +3,020 on the re-short at supply C.
passages.t: The next valid trade more than paid for the loss.

passages.h: Chart: Futures fill window, ES DEC09: sell 5 at 1063.75, buys of 2, 3, 5, 2, 2 and 1 between 1063.75 and 1065.00, sell 10 at 1068.00; bought 15, sold 15, net 0, P/L +1,562.50.
passages.t: One loss and one win in a day still nets a profit when winners are larger than losers.
AAPL weekly: the short at A was stopped for a small loss when price rallied through, but the same rules sold the next supply C, moved the stop to breakeven at 3:1 and paid far more than the loss.
Why losses belong in the winning column: ten trades at 50% accuracy with every loss at 1R and every win at 3R still net +10R, like a casino with an edge.
Treating a loss as failure and becoming paralysed. Trying to eliminate all losses. Risking an amount that makes a loss hurt.
Is my risk on this trade a loss I can accept calmly? If stopped, where is the next level for the next trade? Is the breakeven rule (at 3:1) set?
“To become a professional winner, you have to first become a professional loser.” “If you want to change, change your perception of loss.”
Differs: stop to breakeven at 3:1 here; Kevin's examples move to breakeven around 1:1 or use larger targets.

Small losses are part of winning. Take the loss, then take the next setup. Sam shorted Apple at a level that looked like supply, but price rallied through it and he lost $960. He did not get upset or quit. His rules pointed to the next supply above, so he shorted there. Price fell, he moved his stop to break even at 3:1, and he made $3,020. One loss and one win still left him well ahead.
A golfer who hits one bad shot does not quit the game. He lines up the next shot calmly, because one shot never decides the round.

Losses belong in the winning column: they are a normal cost of a profitable plan. Keep each loss small and comfortable. If it makes you cringe, the size is too big. After a stop-out, keep following the rules. At 3:1, move the stop to break even.
Price rallied, paused and dropped. A looks like supply, so the rules say short the return.

passages.h: Step: The short, then the stop
passages.t: Price comes back and the short is taken. It works for a bit, then price rallies right through A. The stop is hit: a small, planned loss.
A had less supply than it looked. Price zooms up to the next supply, C. No fear, no revenge: the rules say short again.
Price falls. At 3:1 the stop moves to break even, so the trade is now free. The winner is three times bigger than the loser.

Which column do losses go in? - The winning column: they are part of a profitable plan. Winners play to...; losers play...? - Winners play to win; losers play not to lose. Sam's typical max loss in his lower-risk account? - $1,000 or less. AAPL result? - -$960 on A, then +$3,020 on C. Break-even rule? - Move the stop to break even at 3:1.

A Q&A covering FESX (Euro Stoxx 50 futures) and its daily gap, scaling into a position versus adding to a loser, what changes for position trading (only the timeframe, and the need for large profit margins), the VIX as an odds enhancer, and why fresh levels from far back in time can be better than recent ones.

Scale in only with a written plan: entries, stop and total size fixed before the first fill. Add larger size nearer the stop when scaling in. Position trades need large profit margins. Use only fresh (unvisited) levels; a fresh level far back in time is high quality. Use the VIX at its own supply/demand as a confirmation for index trades.
Euro Stoxx 50 futures on Eurex; no overnight session, so a gap forms almost every day, which traders like. Each point is worth 10 euros.

passages.h: Scaling in vs adding to a loser
passages.t: Scaling in is smart only if it is built into the plan. Know all entry points and the exact stop first, then size the total so the risk stays acceptable. Unplanned additions are adding to a loser.

passages.h: Scaling in vs adding to a loser
passages.t: Entries need not be equal; he adds larger size the closer price gets to the protective stop.
Nothing different: same imbalance levels, just larger timeframes. Insist on LARGE profit margins (examples: British pound trades, the March S&P buy).
VIX high at supply while stocks are low at demand: strong odds stocks turn up. VIX low at demand while stocks are high at supply: strong odds stocks decline.
The public buys 'insurance' after the accident; a free delayed chart is enough. Check daily for day trading, weekly for swing/position.
The key is 'fresh' levels: not revisited since they formed. These are often recent but sometimes far back.
Levels from long ago are arguably better: price is far out on the curve (rubber band stretched).
He accepts a little more risk on distant fresh levels because the probability and profit margin are so good.
No charts in this Q&A (it refers back to the AAPL weekly chart from the previous article).
Scaling in versus adding to a loser: entries, one stop and total size are fixed in advance, with larger size placed nearer the stop, so the total risk is known before the first fill.
The VIX check: when stocks are low at demand and the VIX is high at supply, the odds of a rally in stocks are strong; the reverse warns of a decline.
Adding to a losing position without a plan. Ranking support/resistance by number of touches. Assuming only recent levels matter.

Is the level fresh (never revisited)? If scaling in, are all entries, the stop and total risk set in advance? Is the VIX at an opposing level that supports the trade? Is the profit margin large enough for the timeframe?
“This action would only be adding to a losing position if it was not planned.” “The rubber band is very stretched so to speak.”
New: the VIX as an odds enhancer; not in Kevin's course. New: planned scaling in with larger size near the stop.
Similar: fresh (untested) zones matter in both; Kevin also keeps far-back zones valid until removed.

Plan every entry before the first one. A fresh old level can be the best. A reader asked whether buying more as price falls is smart or silly. Sam said it is smart only if it was in the plan before the first order: every entry, one stop and the total size. Unplanned buying more is just adding to a loser. He also said a fresh level from long ago, never visited since, can be even better than a new one, because the rubber band is stretched so far.
Planned scaling is like a recipe that says add flour in three steps. Throwing in more flour because the cake looks wrong is panic, not cooking.
Scaling in is smart only when all entries, the stop and total size are set before the first fill. Add larger size nearer the stop.
Fresh means never revisited. A fresh level far back in time is high quality: price is far out on the curve.
VIX at supply while stocks are at demand favours a rally. Position trades need large profit margins.

passages.h: Step: A level from long ago
passages.t: Price dropped, based and rallied strongly. Then it wandered for a long time, never coming back to this base. It is still fresh.

passages.h: Step: Write the scaling plan first
passages.t: Before the first order: entry 1 at the top line (small), entry 2 deeper in the zone (larger, closer to the stop), and one stop below the zone. The total risk is known now.
Price falls deep into the zone. Both planned entries fill. This is scaling in, not adding to a loser, because it was planned.

passages.h: Step: The stretched band snaps back
passages.t: Price rallies hard. A fresh level far out on the curve gave a big profit margin.

When is scaling in OK? - Only if entries, the stop and total size are planned before the first fill. Where goes the larger size? - Closer to the protective stop. Fresh level? - One that has not been revisited since it formed.
VIX as odds enhancer? - VIX at supply + stocks at demand = rally odds; reverse warns of a decline.
What changes for position trading? - Only the timeframe, and it needs large profit margins. FESX point value? - 10 euros; no overnight session, so it gaps most days.

A satire of the herd's scoring system: seven criteria (downtrend, red candles, volume, bad news, bad earnings, reversal candle, S&P falling) worth 10 points each, with 70 meaning 'sell' at the lows. On Sept 11, 2009 the XLT bought a pre-planned NASDAQ (QQQQ) demand level exactly when the Fools yelled 'sell short', revealing who is on the other side of the trade.
Pre-plan the demand level before the open and buy there on a gap or drop into it. Ignore the crowd's checklist of news, candles and indicators; ask who will buy after you.
Everyone drives the same car; the town pools funds and makes one trade at a time together.

Their sell setup awards 10 points each for downtrend, 3+ red candles, above-average volume, bad news, bad earnings, a reversal candle and the S&P declining; 70 is their best signal. The buy setup is the mirror; when it scores 70, price is 'very high'.
Key question: if you buy high, who buys from you? To profit, others must buy after you at higher prices.
Pre-market news of a China-US trade dispute caused selling in S&P and NASDAQ futures. QQQQ had clear demand a bit below the prior close: a low risk day trade buy if reached.
Price fell into the level just as the Fools shouted 'sell short'; demand held and price rose.
'Make decisions based upon the actions of others, after they make it.' Change starts with thoughts: think in reality-based terms, not conventional ones; pay attention to the present.
Candles: a decline, a bounce of green candles, a red reversal candle, then several red candles; a circle at the last red candle (near the prior low) marks their 'High Odds Shorting opportunity'.
Panel: Downtrend 10, 3 or more red candles 10, above average volume 10, bad news 10, bad earnings 10, reversal candle 10, S&P declining 10 = 70 points.
XLT Stock Mastery session screenshot with the participant list, chat (joined September 14, 2009, 7:31 AM) and several chart panes; one pane shows two horizontal lines under a base.
QQQQ 5-min, 9/10 to 9/11/2009, high 42.60, low 41.60. 'XLT Demand': two lines (about 41.7 and 41.95) under a base from 10:00-12:00 on 9/10, from which price rallied to about 42.6.

On 9/11 price drops from the highs to touch the upper line around 11:45; arrows from the same candle are labelled 'Foolsville Sell Signal' and 'XLT Buy Signal' with money flowing from one to the other. Price then rallies back to about 42.4.

passages.h: Chart: Slide "Foolsville Sell Setup": a decline, a green bounce, a red reversal candle, then several red candles; the last one is circled as the "High Odds Shorting opportunity". Panel: downtrend, 3+ red candles, above-average volume, bad news, bad earnings, reversal candle and S&P declining, 10 points each = 70.
passages.t: The crowd checklist fires after the move is done, near the low. If you sell low, who will sell to you even lower?

passages.h: Chart: Live XLT Stock Mastery screen, Sept 2009: participants, chat and several chart panes; one QQQQ pane shows two horizontal demand lines under a base.
passages.t: The demand level was drawn before the open, ahead of the news selling.

passages.h: Chart: QQQQ 5-min, 9/10 to 9/11/2009: XLT demand lines at about 41.20 and 41.25 under a 10:00-12:00 base on 9/10, from which price rallied to about 41.6. On 9/11 price drops back to touch the upper line around 11:45 (Foolsville sell signal = XLT buy signal) and rallies to about 41.55.
passages.t: The same candle was a sell to the crowd and a buy at pre-planned demand. Entry at the upper line, stop below the lower line, target the prior highs.
The Foolsville checklist scores 70 out of 70 exactly when price reaches pre-planned demand, so the crowd sells at the low and the XLT buys from them, as on QQQQ on Sept 11, 2009.
Selling after a decline into demand because news, candles and the index all look bearish. Making decisions after others have acted. Following the crowd (the long airport line).
Is my signal built from lagging news, candles and volume after the move? Is price at pre-planned demand while others are panicking? Who will buy from me (or sell to me) after I enter?
“Make decisions based upon the actions of others, after they make it.” “Do you trade like a Fool or do you trade with a Fool?”

When the crowd's sell checklist is perfect, price is usually at the bottom. The people of Foolsville score a sell signal with seven checks: downtrend, red candles, big volume, bad news, bad earnings, a reversal candle, and the S&P falling. Ten points each, and 70 means "sell now!" But all those things are only true after price has already fallen. One morning bad trade news made the Fools shout "sell short" just as the NASDAQ hit Sam's pre-planned demand. He bought from them, and price rose.
It is like a weather forecast that only says "rain" after you are already soaked.
The crowd's checklist fires after the move is done, near the low (or the high). Ask: if I sell low, who sells to me even lower? If I buy high, who buys from me higher?
Pre-plan the demand level before the open and buy when price drops into it while others panic.
Before the open, mark the demand: a base that launched a strong rally. Nothing is happening there yet.

passages.h: Step: The Foolsville checklist fills up
passages.t: Price turns down. A red reversal candle, then three red candles in a row, bad news and the S&P falling. The Fools add up 70 points.
Price reaches the demand. To the Fools this is the perfect short. To us it is pre-planned demand. Buy at the top line, stop under the bottom line.

passages.h: Step: Who was on the other side?
passages.t: Demand holds and price rises. The money flowed from the Fools who sold low to the buyer at demand.

Foolsville sell checklist? - Downtrend, 3+ red candles, high volume, bad news, bad earnings, reversal candle, S&P falling: 10 points each. Where does 70/70 usually fire? - Near the low, at demand. Foolsville belief? - Decide based on the actions of others, after they act. Key question before selling low? - Who will sell to me even lower?

A reader Q&A collection. Seiden answers five student emails: taking profit early at a 60-minute index level, slippage on a spot-FX cross, whether turns need high volume, hesitating at a valid signal, and how to scale up position size. The common thread is to follow a rule-based plan, accept that nobody catches the whole move, and grow size slowly.

Only take opening trades when price opens into a demand or supply level. Take profits when the broad market/sector reaches its own higher-timeframe (e.g. 60-minute) level. Treat a 3:1 reward with a 40% win rate as a fully acceptable plan. Prefer low-volume turns at levels as a sign of a large imbalance. Increase size in steps of about 10x at most (10 -> 100 shares), not 100x.
Use set-and-forget orders to remove emotion.
She bought two stocks a minute after the open at lower levels, trailed stops to 2:1 and exited when the related ETF was 10 cents from a 60-minute zone, banking 3:1 and 5:1.
Trading right at the open is smart only if price opens INTO a demand or supply level; that is when demand and supply are most out of balance.
Exiting because the sector/broad market is nearing a 60-minute level is the right call even if price later runs further.
A plan that wins only 40% of the time at 3:1 is already a fantastic income; chasing more of the move usually invites more losses.

passages.h: Slippage in spot Forex (W. Jones, GBPCHF)
passages.t: A long at demand on GBPCHF from a Sunday class made about $2,800 on 2 contracts but suffered ~10 pips of slippage on a market order after limit orders did not fill.

passages.h: Slippage in spot Forex (W. Jones, GBPCHF)
passages.t: Reason 1: in spot FX the broker is on the other side; when you buy at real demand the broker knows it is selling at a bad price and will fill you where it cannot lose. Reason 2: non-major pairs are thinner, so slippage is more likely. Set-and-forget orders mean you do not have to sit at the screen and they remove emotion.

Seiden corrects the idea that he plays every turn that comes with volume. The most significant turns usually happen on LOW volume: the bigger the imbalance at a level, the less time price spends there and the fewer trades print. He actively looks for low-volume turns as evidence of a large imbalance.
Student marks daily levels, plans on the 30-minute chart, enters on the 5/15-minute, but freezes wondering if the level is wrong.
There is no certainty; once you truly accept that, you look for better odds instead of guarantees.
Build a rule-based plan that stacks odds, then execute; set-and-forget orders make this easier.

passages.h: Scaling up size (Keith, BBBY and QLD)
passages.t: Keith's 10-share trades: BBBY long 39.75 to 39.97, short 39.99 to 39.93 (he admits the target was too close), long 39.97 to 40.17, plus QLD 52.18 to 52.43. Do not jump from 10 to 1,000 shares; go 10 to 100 and stay rule-based. Scaling too fast is one of the biggest causes of complete failure.

Second-guessing a valid exit because price later went further. Expecting high volume to confirm a turn. Waiting for certainty before entering a valid setup. Taking trades whose target is too close (poor reward). Scaling position size up too fast.

Is the open happening into a demand or supply level? Where is the index/sector relative to its 60-minute levels (exit trigger)? Is the target far enough for at least 3:1? Is position size only a modest step up from what I have traded successfully?
“No one will ever get the entire move, all the time.” “The most significant turns in price happen with low volume most of the time.” “Don't move from 10 to 1000. Instead, move from 10 to 100.”
Low volume at the turn is a positive sign for Seiden; Kevin's course does not use volume at all.
Exit when the related index/ETF reaches its own 60-minute level - an inter-market exit rule not in Kevin's material. Explicit scaling guidance (grow size about 10x at a time) is new.

Follow the plan, take profit at the next level, and grow your size slowly. Barbara bought two stocks right after the open because price opened straight into demand. She sold when the sector fund got close to its 60-minute level, even though price later ran further. Sam said that was right: nobody catches the whole move. Another student froze at a good signal because he wanted to be sure; Sam said certainty does not exist. And one more wanted to jump from 10 shares to 1,000; Sam said go to 100 first.
Growing your trade size is like learning to swim: go from the shallow end to the middle, not from the shallow end to the ocean.

Trade the open only when price opens INTO a demand or supply level. Exit when the index or sector reaches its own level. 40% winners at 3:1 is already a great plan. The biggest turns often come on LOW volume. Grow size 10 to 100, not 10 to 1,000.
Demand below, and a 60-minute supply above that will be our exit area. All drawn while the market is closed.
The new session gaps down straight into demand. This is when demand and supply are most out of balance, so trading the open is smart here. A set-and-forget buy order fills.

passages.h: Step: Exit at the bigger level
passages.t: As price nears the 60-minute level, take profit. It is the right call even if price runs further later.

passages.h: Step: Nobody gets the whole move
passages.t: Price did go a bit higher after the exit. That is fine. Chasing every last tick invites more losses.

When to trade the open? - Only when price opens into a demand or supply level. When did Barbara exit? - When the sector ETF was 10 cents from its 60-minute zone. Volume at the biggest turns? - Usually LOW. How to grow size? - 10 to 100, not 10 to 1,000.
Cure for freezing at a valid signal? - Accept there is no certainty; stack odds and use set-and-forget orders.

Bull and bear traps: an event (news or a popular breakout) invites the crowd to buy right into objective supply with plenty of room below, or sell into demand. Seiden sells to those breakout buyers. Example: the S&P breaking above the prior day's high into supply formed at the origin of a weekly gap down.
When a significant event invites buyers, price is at supply and there is an adequate profit margin below: sell short.

When a significant event invites sellers, price is at demand and there is an adequate profit margin above: buy. Check the larger timeframe first to know which side carries the better odds. Use the opposing level (first demand below) as the first target.
Floor traders call it being 'hung': buying right into supply before a collapse or shorting into demand before a rally.
A bull trap needs two things together: a positive event pulling buyers in, and price at a level where supply exceeds demand with a significant profit margin below.
Once the last buyer buys there are no more buyers; price falls and trapped buyers sell at a loss, pushing price lower still. The 'event' can be news or a popular chart pattern such as a breakout.

Figure 1 (p247): TradeStation screen from an XLT Stock Mastery session on 'Advanced Bull and Bear Trap Strategies'. Right panel: SPY weekly (about 70-130), price rallied from the lows right up to a horizontal line labelled 'Gap Supply' around 105-108 - the origin of a gap down from the prior year.

Left panel: SPY 15-minute (about 108.6-110.2, 10/15-10/21). A white-shaded 'Supply' zone at the top (about 109.6-110.0) marks that gap origin on the small timeframe; a 'Demand' box at the bottom (about 108.5-108.9) is the target.

A circled high labelled 'Trap' pokes above the prior day's high into the supply box - the breakout that makes the crowd bullish. Price then drops sharply (red bars) toward the demand box; last price shown about 108.25.
The demand level below was the first target and was reached; risk was small had it failed.
Like a car dealer, you want customers who do not know true value: first-time buyers driven by emotion.
Sell to them when price is at a level you know is too high; buy from them when it is too low.

passages.h: Chart: SPY: weekly chart (right) rallies up to 'Gap Supply' at the origin of a prior-year gap down; the 15-minute chart (left) shows that supply as a box at about 109.6-110.0, a circled 'Trap' high above the prior day's high, and a 'Demand' box about 108.5-108.9 as the target.
passages.t: The breakout above yesterday's high is what makes the crowd bullish - and it happens right inside higher-timeframe supply.

passages.h: Chart: SPY: weekly chart (right) rallies up to 'Gap Supply' at the origin of a prior-year gap down; the 15-minute chart (left) shows that supply as a box at about 109.6-110.0, a circled 'Trap' high above the prior day's high, and a 'Demand' box about 108.5-108.9 as the target.
passages.t: Short into the trap with the stop just above the supply box; the demand below is the first target and was reached.

passages.h: Chart: SPY: weekly chart (right) rallies up to 'Gap Supply' at the origin of a prior-year gap down; the 15-minute chart (left) shows that supply as a box at about 109.6-110.0, a circled 'Trap' high above the prior day's high, and a 'Demand' box about 108.5-108.9 as the target.
passages.t: Check the larger timeframe first: the weekly gap origin is what gives the small 15-minute box its power.
Bull trap: a breakout above the prior day's high runs into supply at the origin of a weekly gap down; short at the proximal line, stop above the distal line, target the demand below.
Buying a breakout above the prior day's high when it runs into higher-timeframe supply. Trading with the crowd after an exciting event. Ignoring where price is on the larger timeframe.

Is there an event (news, breakout) inviting the crowd in? Is price at objective higher-timeframe supply/demand? Is there a significant profit margin to the opposing level? Is the breakout running INTO the level rather than away from it?
“Gaps represent the picture of a strong supply and demand imbalance.” “Be the seller to these buyers as they are falling for a trap.”

Fading a prior-day-high breakout into higher-timeframe supply is framed as a named setup (bull/bear trap); Kevin's course treats it only implicitly through zone entries. Gap origin explicitly used as the supply zone on the weekly.

A breakout into big supply is a trap. Sell to the people who fall in. Floor traders call it getting hung: buying right before a collapse. A bull trap needs two things at once. First, an exciting event, like news or a breakout above yesterday's high, pulls buyers in. Second, price is sitting at real supply with lots of room below. When the last buyer has bought, there is nobody left, so price falls and the trapped buyers sell at a loss.
It is like a shop that puts a flashy "SALE" sign on things that cost more than anywhere else. The sign pulls people in; the price is the trap.
Bull trap = an exciting event inviting buyers + price at supply + a big profit margin below. Bear trap is the mirror.
Check the larger timeframe first: a weekly gap origin gives the small-chart zone its power. Short at the zone, stop above it, first target the demand below.
On the big chart price based and gapped down. The origin of that gap is strong supply. Price has now rallied back toward it.

passages.h: Step: The event: a breakout above yesterday's high
passages.t: Price pushes above the prior day's high. The crowd sees a breakout and gets bullish. But the breakout runs INTO supply, not away from it.
At the zone we sell to the breakout buyers. Stop just above the top line. The demand below is the first target, far enough for a big margin.

passages.h: Step: The last buyer has bought
passages.t: With no buyers left, price falls. Trapped buyers sell at a loss and push it lower, down to the demand target.

Being "hung"? - Buying right into supply before a collapse (or shorting into demand before a rally). Bull trap recipe? - Event inviting buyers + price at supply + big margin below. What gives a small-chart zone power here? - It sits at a higher-timeframe gap origin. Gaps represent? - A strong supply and demand imbalance.

Using an Alcoa (AA) daily chart, Seiden contrasts an XLT member's short at daily supply (a pivot high followed by a gap down) with the textbook double-top entry below the neckline. The textbook entry sells after a decline and into demand, exactly backwards. Wrap supply and demand rules around any pattern to enter before the pattern traders.

Short when price rallies into supply, not after it breaks down from a pattern. Use a pivot high followed by a gap down as evidence of strong supply. Set targets that give at least 3:1, with a second target near 5:1.
If you like a conventional pattern, wrap supply/demand rules around it to enter before pattern traders.

Shawn shorted AA at 12.08 when it rallied into daily supply; target 1 at 10.85 (3:1) and target 2 at 10.03 (5:1). The supply was a clear pivot high followed by a gap down, showing a big imbalance. He sold to novices buying after a rally into supply, then covered at the circled targets.

passages.h: Why the double top is flawed
passages.t: By the books the double top is only confirmed much lower, and the short is taken when price breaks the neckline.

passages.h: Why the double top is flawed
passages.t: That means selling after a decline and selling into demand (support) - something no consistently profitable trader would do.

passages.h: Why the double top is flawed
passages.t: The people buying back from Shawn at his targets were likely the book readers selling the neckline break. Conventional entry rules nearly always get you in well after the move is underway.
Figure 1 (p251): AA daily (NYSE), Jan-Jul 2009, price scale about 6-12.5. A 'Supply' box at the top left (about 11.8-12.3) from the early-January pivot high that gapped down.
Price falls to about 5 in March, then rallies back through April-June into the same supply box at the top right; arrow 'Shawn (XLT member) Short Entry' at that box (~12.08).
Two small circles just below (about 10.8 and 10.0) are labelled 'Profit Target 1' and 'Profit Target 2'.

Arrows label the two highs 'Double Top' and a horizontal 'Neckline' near 9.3; the textbook 'Double Top Short Entry' arrow points at the neckline break, which is also labelled 'Demand Level' - shorting into demand.

passages.h: Chart: Alcoa (AA) daily, Jan-Jul 2009: 'Supply' box about 11.8-12.3 from the January pivot high that gapped down; in June price returns to it for the XLT member's short entry, with profit targets 1 and 2 near 10.8 and 10.0. The textbook 'Double Top Short Entry' at the neckline (~9.3) is also the 'Demand Level'.
passages.t: The supply short sells at the top of the move with a stop just above the box; the double-top short sells after most of the decline is over.

passages.h: Chart: Alcoa (AA) daily, Jan-Jul 2009: 'Supply' box about 11.8-12.3 from the January pivot high that gapped down; in June price returns to it for the XLT member's short entry, with profit targets 1 and 2 near 10.8 and 10.0. The textbook 'Double Top Short Entry' at the neckline (~9.3) is also the 'Demand Level'.
passages.t: The neckline is where buyers previously stepped in - shorting the break means selling into demand. Use patterns only to locate levels; enter at the level, before the pattern traders.
Wrap supply/demand rules around the double top: short the return to the first pivot's supply; the textbook neckline break sells into demand after the move is done.
Selling the neckline break (after a decline and into demand). Following popular books simply because everyone teaches it the same way. Entering after the move is already underway.
Am I entering at the level, before the pattern completes? Is my short entry above demand, not into it? Do T1 and T2 give at least 3:1 and 5:1?
“You can't be consistently profitable buying and selling where everyone else does.” “Why in the world would we want to sell after a decline in price?”
Direct critique of the double-top/neckline entry, with the neckline identified as demand; Kevin does not discuss classic patterns. Two-target layout (3:1 and 5:1) shown on a stock swing trade.

The textbook double top sells too late, right into buyers. Sell the top instead. Books say a double top is only real after price breaks below the neckline, so they sell down there. Sam's student sold up at the second top, where the first top had left strong supply and gapped down. By the time the book readers sold the neckline, most of the drop was over. And the neckline was where buyers had stepped in before. The book sellers were the ones buying back the student's shares at his targets.
It is like buying a ticket for a train after it has already left the station. You paid, but the ride is over.
Short where price rallies into supply, not after a pattern breaks down. The neckline is demand. Selling its break means selling after a decline and into demand.
Like a pattern? Wrap supply and demand rules around it and enter before the pattern traders.

passages.h: Step: Top 1: a pivot high that gapped down
passages.t: Price spiked to a pivot high, paused and gapped down. A gap away shows a big imbalance: strong supply.

passages.h: Step: The low between the tops is demand
passages.t: Price based and rallied from a low. That low will become the "neckline" in the textbook. It is really demand.
Price rallies back into the first top's supply. Short at the bottom line, stop above. T1 at 3:1, T2 at 5:1.

passages.h: Step: The textbook short is backwards
passages.t: Price falls to the targets near the neckline. That is where books say to sell, after the decline and into demand. Price bounces from there.

Textbook double-top entry? - Sell the neckline break: after a decline, into demand. Sam's double-top entry? - Short the return to the first top's supply. Neckline is really...? - Demand (support). AA targets? - T1 10.85 (3:1), T2 10.03 (5:1) from 12.08.

At an OTA event Seiden runs a 'hard right edge' game: EBAY opens with a doji gapping up into obvious 5-minute supply. Graduates mostly sell; newcomers copy the first trader and mostly buy. Price fills the gap lower, and graduates outperform newcomers by over 400%: herd behaviour, not chart reading, drives the losers.

When price opens with a gap into obvious supply and stalls (doji), favour the short. You do not have to trade the first candle; patience is allowed. Decide from the level, never from what other traders are doing. Learn, practise on a demo, then start small and low risk.
Proper trading needs an edge over the competition: a rule-based way to buy before others buy and sell before others sell.
He is happy when people do not join, because markets need people who sell at demand and buy at supply.
Candles are revealed one at a time; attendees raise a hand to buy or sell once. Graduates mostly sell: gap up, into obvious supply to the left, with a doji.
New prospects copy whoever moves first, usually buying, despite being told they need not trade the first candle.
Afterwards losers admit they 'knew' it was a doji into resistance but bought because others did.

Figure 1 (p253): EBAY 5-minute (NASDAQ). Prior afternoon a small base at about 24.45-24.51 (boxed 'Supply (resistance)') drops hard to about 23.95 on 9/21, then chops 24.00-24.20 for the rest of the day.
At the hard right edge the new session opens with a gap up straight into the supply box, arrow labelled 'Doji Candle' at about 24.45-24.50.

Figure 2 (p255): same chart scrolled forward (9/22). After the doji at supply, a string of red candles falls from about 24.45 to about 24.15, filling the gap - sellers of the doji profit, buyers lose.
Graduates' performance is more than 400% better than newcomers'. Fear and greed will always keep enough people buying where he sells and selling where he buys.

passages.h: Chart: EBAY 5-minute, hard right edge: the prior afternoon's small base at about 24.45-24.51 ('Supply (resistance)') launched a drop to about 23.95; the next session opens with a gap-up doji straight into that box.
passages.t: This is the decision point of the game: a strong-looking open into a level that previously sent price sharply lower.

passages.h: Chart: EBAY 5-minute, hard right edge: the prior afternoon's small base at about 24.45-24.51 ('Supply (resistance)') launched a drop to about 23.95; the next session opens with a gap-up doji straight into that box.
passages.t: Graduates sold; newcomers copied the first trader and bought - the herd, not the chart, drove their decision. Small bases that launch big drops are the cleanest intraday supply.

passages.h: Chart: Same EBAY 5-minute chart scrolled forward: after the doji at supply a string of red candles falls from about 24.45 to about 24.15, filling the gap.
passages.t: The outcome confirms the setup: shorts at 24.45 with a stop above 24.51 made several times their risk. Opening gaps INTO a level are where demand and supply are most out of balance. The gap fill (prior close area) is the natural first target.
The EBAY game in a diagram: a base that launched a sharp drop is supply; next morning price gaps up into it with a doji - sell at the proximal line, stop above, target the gap fill.
Copying the first trader (herd mentality). Buying a gap up into supply. Feeling forced to act on the first candle.
Is the open gapping into a supply/demand level? Am I acting on my rules or on what others do? Is there room for price to fill the gap (profit margin)?
“It's herd mentality live in action.” “This has nothing to do with reading a chart.”
Gap at the open into an intraday supply zone treated as a high-odds short; Kevin does not cover opening gaps on stocks. Herd behaviour illustrated with live audience statistics (400% better).

Decide from the level, not from what everyone else in the room does. At a big event Sam played a game: he showed a chart one candle at a time and people raised a hand to buy or sell. The market opened with a gap up straight into a supply level, and the first candle was a doji. Graduates mostly sold. Newcomers copied whoever moved first, and most bought. Price filled the gap lower, and the graduates did over 400% better.
It is like following the person in front of you through a door marked "wrong way" just because they went first.
An edge is a rule-based way to buy before others buy and sell before others sell. A gap open into obvious supply with a doji favours the short; the gap fill is the first target.
You never have to trade the first candle. Herd behaviour, not chart reading, makes the losers.
Yesterday afternoon a small base launched a hard drop. That base is clean supply.

passages.h: Step: The rest of the day
passages.t: Price chops quietly below. We mark the close; the gap fill will be our target.

passages.h: Step: Hard right edge: gap up doji
passages.t: The new session gaps up straight into the supply and prints a doji. Graduates see: gap up, into supply, stalling. Newcomers see others buying and copy them.
A string of red candles drops to the prior close. Sellers of the doji made several times their risk.

Hard right edge game? - Candles revealed one at a time; decide buy or sell once. Gap up doji into supply favours? - The short, target the gap fill. Graduates vs newcomers? - Graduates did more than 400% better. What drove the losers? - Herd mentality, not chart reading.

Day, swing and longer-term position trading compared with pros and cons. The strategy never changes across them: buy low/sell high at quantified supply and demand imbalances. Seiden personally finds swing trading the most profitable and comfortable.

Day traders: focus on 1-3 quality opportunities, typically near the open. Swing traders: do analysis while the market is closed and use set-and-forget orders. Use price charts and supply/demand, not news, as primary tools for longer-term positions. Keep the same rule-based strategy whatever the timeframe.
Exit before the session close; needs fast connections, backups, real-time data, direct access and multiple monitors.
Pros: suits high-energy, disciplined people; profitable day traders take 1-3 quality trades, usually near the open, not 10-100.
Cons: get-rich-quick appeal, high emotion, competing with market makers, most time-consuming, needs quick decisions.
Hold from one day to a couple of weeks or longer; real-time data helpful but not required.

Pros: where he sees the most students succeed; least competition (too long for day traders, too short for institutions); an hour or so of analysis two or three times a week; set-and-forget orders; best analysis is done when the market is closed.
Cons: can feel boring; stock setups come in bunches, e.g. when the S&P pulls back to demand in an uptrend most stocks set up at once and vanish once it rallies.
Hold weeks to months; buy and hold can be the best style if you buy at the right time. Pros: fully pre-planned, least time-consuming.
Cons: many rely on news and opinions and end up buying high/selling low; results take time; capital tied up (opportunity cost).
A strategy that works in one market or timeframe should work in any. Everything comes down to objectively quantifying demand and supply to find turning points.
Day trading for the get-rich-quick thrill. Over-trading (10-100 trades a day). Long-term investing driven by news and opinions. Believing each style needs a different strategy.
Which style fits my time, temperament and decision speed? Is my analysis done before the market opens/while it is closed? Am I limiting myself to a few quality trades?
“The consistently profitable day traders are the ones who tend to take the 1-3 quality opportunities.” “The best time to perform your swing trading analysis is when the market is closed.”
Swing trading framed as the least competitive niche (too long for day traders, too short for institutions). Observation that stock swing setups cluster when the S&P sits at demand.

Day, swing or long term: the style changes, the strategy never does. Day traders close everything before the bell and need fast tools and fast decisions. Swing traders hold for days or weeks and can plan when the market is closed. Position traders hold for months and need the least time. Sam likes swing trading best, because there is the least competition and he can use set-and-forget orders. In every style the rule is the same: buy low at demand and sell high at supply.
Walking, biking and driving are different ways to get to school. The address of the school stays the same.
Same strategy in every style: buy low and sell high at quantified imbalances. Good day traders take 1-3 quality trades, usually near the open, not 10-100.
Swing: plan while the market is closed and use set-and-forget orders. Setups come in bunches.
The market is closed. On the daily chart, mark the demand that launched a strong rally. No emotion, no rush.
Place a buy at the top line, a stop under the zone and a target. Then go live your life.

passages.h: Step: The order fills by itself
passages.t: Days later price pulls back into the zone. The order fills while you are not watching. When the S&P pulls back to demand, many stocks set up like this at once.
Price rallies to the target over the next days. A swing trade with an hour of analysis.

Three ways to speculate? - Day trading, swing trading, longer-term position trading. Sam's favourite style? - Swing trading. Swing trading con? - Can feel boring; setups come in bunches. Position trading con? - News-driven decisions, slow results, capital tied up. What never changes? - The strategy: quantify supply and demand to find turning points.

Follow-up Q&A on trading styles. Seiden explains that 'the basics never die' (Newton and Adam Smith said the same thing), that swing traders should pair a daily/weekly chart for direction with a 60-minute chart (no smaller) for entry, and that swing trading uses the same analysis as day trading at a slower pace.
Swing trading: daily or weekly for direction, 60-minute (no smaller) for entry. Refine a weekly zone on the 60-minute chart to reduce stop size. Do swing analysis while markets are closed.
Price movement is a function of an ongoing demand/supply equation; opportunity exists when it is out of balance.
Newton (objects stay in motion until met by equal or greater force) and Adam Smith (supply exceeding demand drives price down) described the same reality.
Use a larger timeframe (daily or weekly) to see where price is on the supply/demand curve and so which side to trade. Example: a stock near weekly demand likely offers a quality swing buy.
Use a smaller timeframe such as the 60-minute chart, but no smaller, to pinpoint entry and shrink the stop inside the weekly zone.
Focus on where most of the trading activity sits inside the demand level, as the turn is likely there. Moving averages are not part of his answer; the levels decide.
No: same larger/smaller timeframe combination, but slower and done while the market is closed, which removes emotion. Process: find levels, assess trend, plan and take trades per rules.
Looking for the 'best' moving average to swing trade. Using too small a timeframe for swing entries. Analysing while the market is moving and emotions are high.
Is price near weekly/daily demand or supply? Have I refined the zone on the 60-minute chart? Was the plan prepared while the market was closed?
“The basics never die.” “A 60-minute chart (but no smaller) in your swing trading analysis.”
Explicit floor for swing entries: no chart smaller than 60-minute.

Big chart picks the side. The 60-minute chart picks the exact spot. A swing trader asked how to pick timeframes. Sam said: look at the daily or weekly chart to see where price is, near demand or near supply. That tells you whether to buy or sell. Then zoom in to the 60-minute chart, but no smaller, to find where most of the trading happened inside the big zone. That smaller zone gives a much smaller stop.
A map of the country shows you which city to go to. A street map shows you the exact house.
The basics never die: Newton and Adam Smith described the same supply and demand reality. Swing: daily or weekly for direction, 60-minute (no smaller) to refine the entry and shrink the stop.
Swing uses the same analysis as day trading, just slower and done while the market is closed.

passages.h: Step: The weekly zone is wide
passages.t: On the weekly chart, demand covers a wide area. The stop below it would be large.
Inside the weekly zone, find where most of the trading sat: a tight base. Draw it with the same rule: top on the highest body, bottom on the lowest wick.
Entry at the refined top line, stop under the refined bottom line. Same trade idea, a fraction of the risk.
Price returns and turns right inside the refined zone, where the activity was. No moving average was needed.

Swing timeframes? - Daily or weekly for direction; 60-minute (no smaller) for entry. Why refine on the 60-minute? - To shrink the stop inside the bigger zone. Where is the turn likely inside a zone? - Where most of the trading activity sat. The basics never...? - Die.

A competitive edge has two parts: mental (reality-based thinking, self-control, focus) and strategic (a rule-based plan). In late 2009 the S&P made repeated breakouts to new highs into an October 2008 supply level; XLT members sold each breakout. Three factors: origin of a strong decline, breakout buyers trapped, and no other advisory service watching that level.
Carry strong supply/demand levels forward until price returns to them. Sell breakouts to new highs that occur inside a known supply level. Keep the same stance at the level regardless of news.
Treat lack of attention from other services, and bullish consensus at supply, as an odds enhancer for shorts.
Mental: reality-based thinking free of illusion, extreme self-control, focus. Strategic: a rule-based strategy that wins over the opponent.
1) The supply was formed in October 2008 at the origin of a strong decline, so supply far exceeded demand; carry such levels forward.
2) Each rally into the level made new highs; breakout buyers bought after a rally and into supply. His standing XLT line: bearish and a seller on breakouts to new highs within this supply level.

3) Weekly review of competitor advisory services found nobody else pointing out the level, and most were bullish (good jobs/earnings news, a TV host calling Apple to $300) - more buyers to sell to and less competition for the fills.
A member (Scott H.) reported over $10K in a month shorting @ESZ09 off this supply, starting from a clean chart with no indicators.
Figure 1 (p265), left: @ES 60-minute, early October 2008 (10/2-10/9). A circled small rally/base around 1,120-1,130 labelled 'XLT Supply' is followed by a collapse to about 960.

Figure 1, right: @ES 240-minute, Nov-Dec 2009 (about 1,050-1,120). Two black horizontal lines carry the supply forward at about 1,106.9 and 1,118. Five circled highs (mid-Nov, ~11/18, ~11/24-25, early Dec, ~12/4) poke into the band; each is followed by a decline toward 1,085-1,090 or lower (one drop near 1,060 in late November). Last price about 1,098.

passages.h: Chart: E-mini S&P: left, 60-minute Oct 2008 with a circled 'XLT Supply' base around 1,120-1,130 before the collapse to about 960; right, 240-minute Nov-Dec 2009 with the supply carried forward as two lines (1,106.94 and 1,118). Five circled breakouts to new highs poke into the band and each one turns lower.
passages.t: A level from more than a year earlier still holds unfilled sell orders if price left it fast and never returned.

passages.h: Chart: E-mini S&P: left, 60-minute Oct 2008 with a circled 'XLT Supply' base around 1,120-1,130 before the collapse to about 960; right, 240-minute Nov-Dec 2009 with the supply carried forward as two lines (1,106.94 and 1,118). Five circled breakouts to new highs poke into the band and each one turns lower.
passages.t: Every breakout to a new high was a bull trap into objective supply - XLT members sold each one.

passages.h: Chart: E-mini S&P: left, 60-minute Oct 2008 with a circled 'XLT Supply' base around 1,120-1,130 before the collapse to about 960; right, 240-minute Nov-Dec 2009 with the supply carried forward as two lines (1,106.94 and 1,118). Five circled breakouts to new highs poke into the band and each one turns lower.
passages.t: Three factors made the edge: origin of a strong decline, trapped breakout buyers, and nobody else watching that level.
S&P late 2009: repeated breakouts to new highs ran into the supply that started the October 2008 crash; each poke into the band was a short.
Buying breakouts after a rally and into supply. Letting good news override the level. Trading levels that every advisory service is publicising (crowded fills).

Is this level the origin of a strong move? Is the current move into it a breakout that excites buyers? Is the crowd/news bullish into my supply (or bearish into my demand)? Is anyone else publicising this level?
“I would be bearish and a seller on BREAKOUTS TO NEW HIGHS within this supply level.” “When we sell short, we want many to buy.”
Checking competitor advisory services for crowding is an extra odds enhancer not in Kevin's course.
