Repeated short entries at the same supply on multiple revisits; Kevin's zone-removal rules would usually treat later touches as weaker.

Think differently from the crowd and carry strong old levels forward. A trading edge has two parts: a clear, calm mind, and a rule-based plan. In late 2009 the S&P kept making new highs, and each new high pushed into a supply level from October 2008, where the crash had started. Everyone was bullish on the good news, and no other advisory service was watching that level. Sam's members sold each breakout to new highs, and each one turned lower.
It is like knowing about a hidden speed bump that is not on anyone's map. Everyone else drives fast; you slow down and wait on the other side.
Edge = mental (reality-based thinking, self-control, focus) + strategic (a rule-based plan). Carry strong levels forward until price returns, even more than a year later.
Sell breakouts to new highs inside a known supply. A bullish crowd and nobody else watching the level add odds.

passages.h: Step: The origin of a crash
passages.t: A rally, a small base and a collapse. Supply far exceeded demand. Draw it and carry it forward to the right.
Price spends a long time below and then climbs back. The good news grows and the crowd turns bullish.
Each push to a new high runs into the old supply. Breakout buyers buy after a rally and into supply. Sam's line: bearish and a seller on breakouts to new highs within this supply.
One after another, the new highs fail inside the band and price drops.
Mental edge? - Reality-based thinking, self-control, focus. Strategic edge? - A rule-based plan.
Sam's stance at old supply? - Bearish and a seller on breakouts to new highs within the level. When we sell short, we want...? - Many to buy.

Beyond trading, supply/demand analysis helps everyday financial decisions. Crude oil daily shows a short at supply targeting demand near $68, which also signalled when to fill up on fuel or hedge (airlines, truckers). The 10-year note daily short at supply after a novice gap up signals rates about to rise, relevant for mortgages and refinancing.
Use the opposing level as the target for a short and as a fresh entry for the opposite trade.
A novice gap up into supply that sits high on the larger-timeframe curve adds odds to the short. Remember price/yield are inverse in bond futures.
XLT shorted crude at daily supply targeting the demand below; the trade made over 12 points. The demand target was also a long swing entry for some members.

Families: fill tanks (and spare cans) when crude reaches demand. Airlines: buy crude futures at the $68 demand as a hedge - effectively flying at $68 while competitors pay $73. Truckers/taxis: buy fuel ahead.

Price rallied into a clear supply well placed high on the larger-timeframe curve, with a novice gap up just before reaching it. Price and yield are inverse: when the note falls from supply, rates rise.
Use it to time a home loan or refinance, or to lock a fixed rate on an adjustable mortgage before rates rise.
Figure 1 (p268): @QM (e-mini crude) daily, Sep-Dec. Top: 'XLT Supply' box about 80.5-82 from the October rally top; circled 'XLT Short Entry' at about 81-82 in early November.

Price declines through November-December to a bottom box 'XLT Demand' about 66.5-68 (the late-September base that launched the rally), circled 'Short Profit Target and Buying Opportunity' near 68; last price about 73.6 after the bounce.

Figure 2 (p270): @TY (10-year note) daily, Apr-Dec. 'XLT Supply Level' two lines about 120'08-121'08 at the top left (origin of the March spike and decline to ~111). Price rallies back through Oct-Nov; arrow 'XLT Short Entry' where it touches the band near 120'00, then drops to about 117'15.

passages.h: Chart: E-mini crude (@QM) daily, Sep-Dec: 'XLT Supply' about 80.5-82 at the October rally top with a circled 'XLT Short Entry' in early November; price falls to the 'XLT Demand' box about 66.5-68, labelled 'Short Profit Target and Buying Opportunity'.
passages.t: Short at supply, target the next demand: the whole move is mapped before entering. The demand that ends the short is also the next long - and a signal to buy fuel or hedge costs. A large margin between supply and demand is what makes the trade worth taking.

passages.h: Chart: 10-year note (@TY) daily, Apr-Dec: 'XLT Supply Level' about 120'08-121'08 at the origin of the March spike and decline; in November price returns and the 'XLT Short Entry' arrow marks the touch near 120'00, followed by a drop to about 117'15.
passages.t: Falling bond prices mean rising rates - the supply level warned of higher mortgage rates. The level was months old but untouched, so the sell orders were still there. The same analysis serves trading and everyday financial decisions.
Crude oil daily idea: short the return to supply, target demand, and use the same levels for real-life decisions like fuel purchases or hedging.
Treating supply/demand only as a trading tool and ignoring real-life cost decisions. Buying fuel or borrowing at variable rates without checking where price sits on the curve.
Where is price on the higher-timeframe curve (high = short, low = long)? Was there a novice gap into the level? Is the opposing level far enough for a good profit margin?
“Price and yield are inversely related in this market.” “No one entity controls this market.”
Using a gap into the zone as an odds enhancer (novice buyer) is not in Kevin's material. Non-trading applications (hedging fuel, timing mortgages) are new.

Levels help you trade, and also show when to buy fuel or lock loans. The class shorted crude oil at supply and took profit at demand far below, making over 12 points. That demand was also a good place for some members to buy. Sam said families could fill their tanks when oil reaches demand, and airlines could lock in cheap fuel there. With bond futures, a fall from supply means interest rates are about to rise, which matters if you are about to take a home loan.
It is like a farmer reading the sky: the same clouds tell you when to plant and when to bring the washing in.
The opposing level is both the target of one trade and the entry of the next. A novice gap into supply that sits high on the larger curve adds odds to the short.
Use the same levels for life: fuel buying, hedging, timing a mortgage. Bond price and yield move opposite.

passages.h: Step: Map the whole move first
passages.t: Demand below, supply above. The trade is mapped before entering: short supply, target demand.
Price rallies into supply. Sell with a stop above; the demand far below is the target. A large margin makes it worth taking.
Price falls to demand. The short is covered, and the same level is a fresh buy: for traders, and for anyone who needs fuel.
Price bounces from demand. Someone who filled up or hedged there paid the low price while others paid more.

Demand target of a short is also...? - An entry for a long. Bond price vs yield? - Inverse: price falls, rates rise. Everyday use of crude demand? - Fill the tank (or hedge fuel) when crude reaches demand. Crude short result? - Over 12 points, from supply to the demand near $68.

End-of-year Q&A. Book advice: learn mechanics from books, but learn speculation from Economics 101 supply and demand. Quality levels are found by how price leaves a level: the stronger the move away, the bigger the imbalance. Moving averages are only secondary for trend; the larger-timeframe level matters more, and he only takes levels meeting his reward minimum.

Find momentum first, then mark its origin as the potential level. Grade a level by the strength of the departure from it. Use moving averages only as a secondary filter. Only trade levels meeting your minimum risk/reward.

Mechanics (platforms, contract specs) can come from books. Becoming a profitable speculator should start from basic supply/demand and seeing retail vs wholesale prices on a chart, not from pattern recognition and indicators.

Reader recalled: a level cannot be in the middle of a move, and repeated tests weaken it. Additional key point: look at how price leaves the level - the more out-of-balance, the stronger price moves away; gradual departures mean small imbalance. Search for periods of momentum first, then go to the origin of that momentum.

A reader uses a 50-SMA on the daily to choose sides on 4H/60-minute charts. MA is acceptable only as a secondary tool; primarily judge trend by where price is relative to larger-timeframe levels, because trends start and end at those levels.
He does not trade every level - only those offering his required risk/reward; when found, trend is a distant consideration.
Learning speculation from conventional books full of patterns and indicators. Treating every level as tradable. Letting a moving average override a strong larger-timeframe level.
Did price leave the level strongly? Is the level at the origin of a momentum move? Does it meet my minimum reward requirement?
“Simply learn to see the difference between retail and wholesale prices on a price chart.” “When I find it, trend is a distant consideration.”
Seiden ranks risk/reward above trend ('trend is a distant consideration'), whereas Kevin's course puts more weight on trend alignment.

Find the fast move first, then go back to where it started. Learn the buttons of your trading platform from books. But learn speculating from basic supply and demand: spotting wholesale and retail prices on a chart. To find a quality level, first search for momentum, a fast strong move. Then go to the origin of that move. If price left a level slowly, the imbalance there was small; if it shot away, the imbalance was big.
If you see a crowd of people sprinting down a street, look where they came from. Something big happened there.
Books for mechanics; Economics 101 for speculation. Learn to see wholesale vs retail on a chart. Find momentum first, then mark its origin. Grade the level by how strongly price left it.
A level cannot sit in the middle of a move, and repeated tests weaken it. Moving averages are only secondary.
Price based for a long time and drifted away slowly. A gradual departure means only a small imbalance. Skip it.
Here price shoots up with big candles. That is momentum. Now look back to where it started.
The small base before the momentum is the level. It is the origin, not the middle of a move, and it is untested.

passages.h: Step: Trade only if it meets your reward minimum
passages.t: There is plenty of room back up to the high, so it qualifies. Price returns and rallies. Trend was a distant consideration.

Where to learn speculation? - Economics 101 supply and demand, not pattern books. First step to find a level? - Search for momentum, then go to its origin. Gradual departure means? - A small imbalance. Two old criteria for levels? - Not in the middle of a move; repeated tests weaken it.

The rule most plans miss is to define a demand or supply level with numbers. Seiden's rule: a demand level qualifies only if the initial rally away from it is at least three times the zone height (entry-to-stop), i.e. 1:3. Crude oil and 10-year note daily trades show the grey-shaded initial move compared to the zone.

A demand level counts only if the initial rally is at least 3x the zone height (1:3); same for the initial decline from supply. Enter at the proximal line, stop just beyond the distal line. Ignore levels that fail the minimum requirement. Bigger initial moves mean higher probability of reaching T1.
Students can describe drop-base-rally and rally-base-drop but then jump straight to entries, stops and targets. Quantifying exactly what counts as a level is part of an edge.
A significant profit margin both measures risk/reward and raises probability, because price is far from equilibrium.
Buy at the top demand line and place the stop just below the lower line; that distance is the risk.
The initial rally from the level shows there is no significant supply until its top, opening a profit margin.

The initial rally must be at least 3x the zone (e.g. 2-point zone needs at least a 6-point rally) or the level is ignored. He uses 1:3; you may require 1:4 or more. T1 does not have to be the top of that rally.
Figure 1 (p276): @QM crude daily, Oct-Dec 2009. Lower left: 'XLT Demand Level' between two black lines about 66.5-69.5, a clear drop-base-rally in late September/early October.
A grey-shaded rectangle covers the initial rally from about 69.5 to about 82.5 in October - far more than 3x the zone height.
Price returns in mid-December: 'XLT Long Entry' at the upper line (~69.5), arrow 'XLT Protective Stop' just below the lower line.
Blue lines mark T1 (~77) and T2 (~78.5, at a prior December pivot); price reached both, last about 78.5.
Figure 2 (p278): @TY 10-year daily, Apr-Dec. 'XLT Supply Level' about 120'08-121'08 at top left; grey-shaded initial decline from about 121 to about 111 (Apr-June).
In November price returns: 'XLT Short Entry' at the lower supply line, 'XLT Protective Stop' above the upper line; blue T1 near 115'24, reached in December.

passages.h: Chart: Crude (@QM) daily, Oct-Dec 2009: 'XLT Demand Level' between lines about 67.6 and 69.7; the grey-shaded initial rally runs from about 69.5 to 82.5. In December price returns to the 'XLT Long Entry' line with the 'XLT Protective Stop' below the zone, then rallies to T1 (~77) and T2 (~78.5).
passages.t: The grey box measures the initial rally: about 13 points versus a 2-point zone - far more than the 3x minimum.

passages.h: Chart: Crude (@QM) daily, Oct-Dec 2009: 'XLT Demand Level' between lines about 67.6 and 69.7; the grey-shaded initial rally runs from about 69.5 to 82.5. In December price returns to the 'XLT Long Entry' line with the 'XLT Protective Stop' below the zone, then rallies to T1 (~77) and T2 (~78.5).
passages.t: Enter at the proximal line, stop below the distal line; the long fills on a wick and never looks back. T1 does not have to be the top of the initial rally - here it is a prior December pivot.

passages.h: Chart: 10-year note (@TY) daily: 'XLT Supply Level' about 120'08-121'08 with a grey-shaded initial decline from about 121 to 111; in November price returns for the 'XLT Short Entry' with the 'XLT Protective Stop' above, and reaches the blue T1 near 115'24.
passages.t: The initial decline is many times the zone height, so the supply qualifies under the 1:3 rule. The same qualifier works for supply: measure the drop away versus entry-to-stop. A qualified level plus a big margin gave a multi-R swing trade.
Quantify the level: a demand zone counts only if the initial rally is at least three times the zone height (1:3); otherwise skip it.
Calling any drop-base-rally a demand level without measuring the move away. Assuming T1 must be the top of the initial rally. Not writing numeric definitions of supply/demand into the plan.
Measure zone height (entry to stop). Measure the initial move away from the zone. Is move away >= 3x zone height (or my own multiple)? Is T1 placed within that profit margin?
“A demand level only becomes a demand level if the initial rally is at least three times the demand level.” “Few actually define what supply and demand levels are to them.”
Hard numeric qualifier: initial leg out must be at least 3x the zone height. Kevin uses 3:1 for targets but not this specific test of the departure.
Explicit idea that a large profit margin itself raises probability (price far from equilibrium).

Measure it: the first move away must be three times the zone. Many students can name drop-base-rally, but never say exactly what counts as a level. Sam's rule uses numbers. The zone height is the distance from the entry line to the stop. The first rally away from the zone must be at least three times that height, or he ignores the level. A 2-point zone needs a rally of at least 6 points.
It is like a high-jump bar. If the jump does not clear three times the height, it does not count.
Write numeric definitions of supply and demand into your plan; that is part of an edge. The initial move away must be at least 3x the zone height (1:3), or skip the level. You may demand 1:4.
Enter at the proximal line, stop beyond the distal line. T1 does not have to be the top of that rally.
Box the base. The zone height, entry to stop, is about 1.2 points.
The first rally runs about 17.77 points above the zone top: far more than 3 x 1.2. The level qualifies.
The rally shows no big supply until its top, so there is a big profit margin. Price is also far from balance there.
Price returns, the long fills at the top line, and it reaches T1. T1 was a pivot inside the margin, not the very top.

The key overlooked rule? - Define a level with numbers. Sam's demand qualifier? - Initial rally at least 3x the zone height (1:3). Zone height? - Entry (proximal) to stop (distal). Must T1 be the rally top? - No; it can be a pivot inside the margin. Crude example? - About 2-point zone, about 13-point initial rally: qualifies easily.

Like travel, many routes reach the same destination. The same 10-year note short at daily supply (gap into the level) is shown with price only, then with Bollinger Bands, CCI and Slow Stochastics. Indicators may add comfort, but price reaching supply/demand is the real reason for the turn; filter every indicator signal through levels.

Price is the primary decision tool; indicators are optional secondary confirmation. Only act on an overbought/oversold reading when price is also at supply/demand. Exit at the opposing level, not on an oscillator reading.
The supply was well placed on the daily curve, odds enhancers rated it high probability, and price gapped into the level, showing novice buyers. Price and volume alone gave everything needed.

Bollinger: at the entry price pierced the upper band (overbought) at supply with a large margin below - higher odds; act on band piercing AND a level, called an 'All Star' setup by the options instructor.

CCI: overbought at entry and oversold at the target, but earlier overbought/oversold readings failed; price turns because of supply/demand, not because CCI is overbought. Using CCI alone would have entered early and exited early.
Stochastics: sell cross lined up with entry and buy cross with the target - but they were not needed.

Figure 1 (p280): @TY daily, Apr 2009 to Jan 2010. 'XLT Supply' two lines about 120'08 and 121'12 at top left (March spike origin). Decline to about 110'16 in June, rally into November, 'XLT Short Entry' at about 120'08. Price falls to a 'Target' line about 115'20 (a late-October pivot low) in December, then bounces to about 116'30.
Figure 2 (p281): same chart with Bollinger Bands; at the short entry the high pierces the upper band; at the target price touches the lower band near 114'29.

Figure 3 (p282): same chart with CCI(14, +/-100). Red circles: overbought spike (~+200) at the entry and oversold (~-150) at the target; many earlier overbought readings to the left came with no turn.
Figure 4 (p283): same chart with Slow Stochastics (14,3,3; 80/20). Red circles: bearish cross above 80 at entry and bullish cross below 20 at the target.

passages.h: Chart: 10-year note (@TY) daily, price only: 'XLT Supply' about 120'08-121'12 from the March spike; price rallies back in November to the 'XLT Short Entry' near 120'08 and falls to the 'Target' line about 115'20 (a late-October pivot low) before bouncing.
passages.t: Price and the level alone gave the entry, stop and target - no indicator was needed. Price gapped into the level, a sign of novice buying at supply. The target is the nearest opposing demand, the October pivot low.

passages.h: Chart: Same @TY chart with Bollinger Bands: at the short entry the high pierces the upper band at supply; at the target price touches the lower band near 114'29.
passages.t: A band pierce AT a supply level with a big margin below is the 'All Star' setup. Band pierces elsewhere on the chart did not produce turns - the level is what matters. Use the band only as a comfort filter on top of the level.

passages.h: Chart: Same @TY chart with CCI(14, +/-100): circled overbought spike (~+200) at the short entry and oversold (~-150) at the target; many earlier overbought readings came with no turn.
passages.t: Price does not turn because CCI is overbought - it turns because it reached supply. Trading CCI alone would have meant entering early and exiting early many times. Filter every oscillator reading through the supply/demand map.

passages.h: Chart: Same @TY chart with Slow Stochastics (14,3,3; 80/20): circled bearish cross above 80 at the entry and bullish cross below 20 at the target.
passages.t: The stochastic lined up with the trade, but it was not needed to find it. Many crosses on the left would have been losing trades without a level behind them. Many routes reach the same destination - the level is the destination.
Many routes, one destination: filter every oscillator signal through supply/demand - act only when the overbought reading coincides with price at supply.
Shorting just because price pierced the upper band or CCI is overbought. Taking profits because an oscillator is oversold. Not filtering indicator signals through supply/demand levels.
Is price at a qualified level before looking at any indicator? If using an indicator, does its signal coincide with the level? Is the target an opposing level rather than an oscillator reading?
“Price does not turn lower because CCI is overbought.” “Did we need Stochastics for this trading opportunity? No.” “Filter those signals through proper supply and demand analysis.”
Indicator-plus-level 'All Star' setup (band pierce at supply) - Kevin's course does not use Bollinger/CCI/Stochastics.
Seiden accepts indicators as a comfort tool if filtered by levels; Kevin's course is pure price.

Indicators are just different roads. The level is the place you are going. Sam showed the same bond short four times: with price only, then with Bollinger Bands, CCI and Stochastics. On every chart the reason for the turn was the same: price reached supply. The indicators sometimes agreed, but many of their earlier signals failed when no level was there. Price alone gave the entry, the stop and the target.
You can get to Grandma's house by plane, train or car. The house is the same; only the ride changes.
Price at a qualified level is the real reason for a turn. Price does not turn because CCI is overbought.
Use an indicator only as comfort: act on an overbought reading only when price is also at supply (the "All Star"). Exit at the opposing level, not on an oscillator reading.
A spike, a pause and a hard drop left supply. It sits high on the daily curve.
Months later price rallies back. Indicators will flash overbought many times on the way up; without a level, those signals fail.
Price reaches supply. Short at the bottom line, stop above. Target: the nearest demand, a prior pivot low. If a band is pierced here too, fine, that is extra comfort.
Price falls to the target. Price and the level did all the work; the indicators were optional.

Primary decision tool? - Price at supply and demand levels. When to act on overbought? - Only when price is also at supply. All Star setup? - Bollinger pierce at a supply level with a big margin. Did the trade need Stochastics? - No.

Beliefs drive behaviour which drives actions, and the biggest illusions sit inside conventional technical and fundamental analysis. Three illusions are dismantled with charts: moving averages as support/trend, bad news meaning lower prices, and good fundamentals/upgrades meaning buy. Seiden closes with his three laws of price movement.
Buy the first return to an objective demand origin even if MAs slope down. Never buy near supply on the first rally into it, whatever the news or upgrade.
Before any trade ask only: is price at a level with more demand than supply (or vice versa)? Treat indicators as derivatives of price; price alone is enough.
MAs are averages of past data and lag; slope-based trend filters make you skip the best buys.

Waiting for price to get back above the 200-day MA means higher risk, lower profit potential, and paying the person who bought at demand. When an MA lines up with real demand/supply it only appears to work.
Strong news leads to strong emotion. Once the last seller sells at a level with more willing buyers, price must rise.
Strong news often creates powerful turns opposite to what most expect, because one side exhausts itself into an objective level.

Good earnings, strong balance sheet, solid management, rising price, an upgrade and a strong economy create the illusion of a quality investment - usually when price is already high. When perceived risk is lowest, actual risk is often highest, and vice versa.
Illusions lead to two mistakes: buying after rising prices and buying where sellers outnumber buyers.
1) Price in any free market is a function of an ongoing supply/demand relationship. 2) Every influence on price is reflected in price.

3) Change in price originates where one of the two forces (buyers or sellers) becomes zero at a specific price. 'Act like a goose': follow rules mechanically like geese flying south, without debating.

Figure 1 (p286): S&P 500 daily with 20 MA (blue) and 200 MA (red), about 1,120-1,240. 'A' arrows mark two demand bases between green lines: a lower one about 1,145-1,150 at the start of a strong rally and a higher one about 1,180-1,185 after a gap/rally step.

Circled 'B' points are the first returns to each level: the upper B while the 20 MA slopes down, the lower B well below the 200 MA with the 20 MA sharply down. Both launch strong rallies to about 1,240 - the MA filters would have said do not buy.
Figure 2 (p289): NASDAQ daily, about 1,440-1,640. 'A' is a small demand base between green lines about 1,477-1,488 before a strong rally to about 1,600.
'B' marks the day of the London bombings: a long lower wick spikes down into the A zone (~1,480) and closes higher; price then rallies to about 1,630.
Figure 3 (p291): CTXS 30-minute with a Yahoo Finance upgrades table (Needham Hold to Buy, $40 target, 21-Apr-08). Two black lines mark supply about 32.65-32.85 from an earlier high on 4/18.

On 4/21 price gaps up into that supply with the upgrade ('Public Buys' / 'OTA Student Sells') and then collapses in a long red bar to about 31.0. Side panel: risk to buy perceived low, actual HIGH; profit potential perceived high, actual LOW.
Figure 4 (p293): a list (good earnings, strong balance sheet, solid management, price moving higher, brokerage upgrade, strong economy) bracketed as 'the illusion of a quality investment'.

passages.h: Chart: S&P 500 daily with 20 MA (blue) and 200 MA (red): 'A' marks two demand bases between green lines (about 1,145-1,150 and 1,180-1,185); circled 'B' points are the first returns to each, both while the 20 MA is falling and the lower one well below the 200 MA. Both launch strong rallies toward 1,240.
passages.t: An MA trend filter would have rejected both of the best buys on the chart. The first return to a fresh demand base is the trade; the moving average is just lagging history. Waiting for price to reclaim the MA means higher risk and lower reward.

passages.h: Chart: NASDAQ daily: 'A' is a small demand base about 1,477-1,488 before a strong rally; 'B' is the day of the London bombings, when a long lower wick spikes into the A zone and closes higher, followed by a rally to about 1,630.
passages.t: Bad news pushed price down - straight into demand, where buyers were waiting. News does not decide direction; it only moves price to the next level faster.

passages.h: Chart: NASDAQ daily: 'A' is a small demand base about 1,477-1,488 before a strong rally; 'B' is the day of the London bombings, when a long lower wick spikes into the A zone and closes higher, followed by a rally to about 1,630.
passages.t: Those who sold on the news sold at the low; demand buyers had a tiny stop and a huge margin.

passages.h: Chart: CTXS 30-minute with a Yahoo upgrades table (Needham Hold to Buy, $40 target, 21-Apr-08): on 4/21 the upgrade gaps price up into supply at about 32.65-32.85 from 4/18 ('Public Buys' / 'OTA Student Sells'), then a long red bar collapses it to about 31.0. Side panel: risk to buy perceived low, actual HIGH; profit potential perceived high, actual LOW.
passages.t: The upgrade made buyers feel safe exactly where risk was highest. The trained trader sold to the public at supply; the move down came within hours. Perceived risk and actual risk are opposites at the extremes.

passages.h: Chart: List graphic: good earnings, strong balance sheet, solid management, price moving higher, brokerage upgrade, strong economy - bracketed as creating 'the illusion of a quality investment'.
passages.t: These factors feel like quality but say nothing about where unfilled orders sit. By the time the good news is public, price is usually already at or near supply. Decide on price and levels, not on how comfortable the story feels.
Moving-average illusion: the first return to demand (B) happens while the 20 MA is still falling - the best buy is the one the MA filter rejects.
News/fundamental illusion: a brokerage upgrade gaps price up into supply; the public buys what feels safe while the trained trader sells to them.

Using MA slope or the 200-day cross as a trend filter for entries. Selling on bad news into demand or buying good news into supply. Buying because fundamentals look great after a big rise. Buying a gap up into supply.
Is this the first return to the level? Am I being pulled in by news, upgrades or an indicator rather than the level? Is the stop small and the distance to the opposing level at its maximum?
“When perceived risk is lowest, actual risk is often highest.” “Price is all that needs be considered.” “The many illusions are nothing more than risk disguised as opportunity.”
The 'three laws of price movement' framework is Seiden-specific. News-driven spikes into demand (London bombings) framed as the best buys; Kevin generally advises avoiding news events.
Explicit rejection of MA slope as a trend filter, while Kevin's course uses swing structure.

Trade what price shows, not what the news or averages make you feel. Our beliefs drive what we do, and the biggest false beliefs hide in normal chart and company analysis. Moving averages lag, so waiting for them means skipping the best buys. Bad news often pushes price into demand, where it turns up. Good earnings and an upgrade feel safe, but they usually arrive when price is already high. Sam sums it up in three laws of price.
A moving average is like driving while looking in the rear-view mirror. It shows where you were, not the wall in front of you.
Three laws: price is a function of supply and demand; every influence is in price; change starts where buyers or sellers become zero at a price.
Buy the first return to fresh demand even if the MA slopes down. MAs only appear to work when they sit on real levels.
When perceived risk is lowest, actual risk is often highest: upgrades into supply, bad news into demand.
Price dropped, based and rallied hard. That base is objective demand. The moving average is still sloping down.
Price drifts back toward the base while the MA still falls. A slope filter would say do not buy. That filter is lagging history.

passages.h: Step: Bad news spike into demand
passages.t: Bad news! A long lower wick dives into the zone and closes higher. The last seller has sold at a level with more willing buyers, so price must rise.
Price rallies strongly. Follow the rules mechanically, like geese flying south, without debating the news or the average.

Law 1 of price movement? - Price is a function of an ongoing supply/demand relationship. Law 2? - Every influence on price is reflected in price. Law 3? - Change starts where buyers or sellers become zero at a specific price. Perceived vs actual risk? - When perceived risk is lowest, actual risk is often highest. "Act like a goose" means? - Follow your rules mechanically, without debating.

Two edge-building tools. Trend health: in an uptrend, shrinking distance between pivot lows (pullbacks) signals the trend is weakening and nearing supply; the mirror applies to downtrends. Volume: the biggest turns come on LOW volume because big imbalances leave little time for trades; he prefers below-average volume at his entry.
Uptrend: shrinking distance between pivot lows means risk to buy rises and the trend is nearly over.
Downtrend: shrinking distance between pivot highs means risk to short rises and the trend is nearly over. Prefer below-average volume as price returns to your level.
He rejects higher-highs/higher-lows as a lagging method and uses his own real-time trend analysis.
Strong trends do not pull back often; if pullbacks become frequent the trend is weakening.
A trend is a supply/demand imbalance moving back into balance; works on any market and timeframe.
Books say turning points come with above-average or climactic volume; he says the opposite.
The more out of balance a level, the less time price spends there, the fewer transactions, the lower the volume. He often wants below-average volume at his supply/demand entry.

Figure 1 (p297): a long-horizon uptrend chart (monthly-style labels M J S N), price from about 65 to 150 with volume beneath. Vertical dashed lines mark pivot lows; double-headed arrows between consecutive pivot lows get shorter ('Decreasing distance between the pivot lows'). The final arrow ends near the top (~140-150), after which price stalls and turns down.

Figure 2 (p298): schematic 'Buying at Demand': red candles decline into a base of two green and one red candle between two white lines; price rallies, then a red candle pulls back into the zone labelled 'Buy Pullback'. Volume bars below shrink at that pullback (circled 'Low Volume'), then rise as price rallies.

passages.h: Chart: Long-horizon uptrend from about 65 to 150 with volume below: vertical dashed lines mark pivot lows, and arrows between consecutive pivot lows get shorter ('Decreasing distance between the pivot lows'); after the last one price stalls and turns down.
passages.t: Shrinking distance between pullbacks means each rally travels less - the trend is tiring. This usually happens as price approaches higher-timeframe supply. Mirror it in downtrends: shrinking distance between pivot highs warns demand is near.

passages.h: Chart: Schematic 'Buying at Demand': red candles drop into a base between two white lines, price rallies, then a pullback into the zone is labelled 'Buy Pullback'; volume bars below shrink at that pullback (circled 'Low Volume').
passages.t: The best turns come on low volume - a big imbalance leaves little time for trades. Below-average volume on the pullback into demand is a plus, not a warning. Buy the first pullback into the base after a strong move away.
Pivot-low spacing: when each pullback low in an uptrend comes sooner than the last, the trend is weakening and nearing supply.
Low-volume pullback into demand: shrinking volume at the zone signals a large imbalance - Seiden prefers below-average volume at his entry.
Waiting for higher highs/lows to confirm trend. Requiring climactic volume to confirm a turn. Buying late in an uptrend whose pullbacks are getting closer together.
Are the pivot lows/highs getting closer together? Is volume below average as price returns to my level? Is the trend old and close to a higher-timeframe level?
“A strong trending market does not pullback often.” “The larger the supply and demand imbalance at a given price level, typically, the lower the volume.”
Pivot-spacing trend-exhaustion tool is new; Kevin judges trend with structure, trendlines and momentum. Volume filter (low volume on the return) - Kevin's course does not use volume.

Watch how often a trend rests, and want quiet volume at your level. Sam has two tools you will not find in most books. First, a strong trend does not stop to rest often; when the dips in an uptrend come closer and closer, the trend is getting tired near supply. Second, books say big turns come with huge volume, but Sam says the biggest turns come on low volume. When a level is very out of balance, price spends little time there, so few trades happen.
The best sale in town sells out in minutes. Few people get to shop, so the till rings only a few times.

Shrinking distance between pivot lows (uptrend) or highs (downtrend) = trend weakening, risk to join rising. Big imbalance = little time at the level = few trades = low volume. Seiden often wants below-average volume as price returns to his level.
Red candles fall into a small base, two green and one red. Then price rallies away.
Price pulls back toward the base. The pullback candles are small and quiet: low volume. Few people are selling.
At the zone, buy at the top line, stop below. Below-average volume here is a plus, not a warning.

passages.h: Step: Volume returns with the rally
passages.t: Price rallies away; now the activity picks up. The turn itself was quiet.

Volume at the biggest turns? - Usually low. Volume Sam likes at his entry? - Below average. Uptrend dips getting closer? - Trend weakening; it is nearing supply. What is a trend? - A supply/demand imbalance moving back toward balance.

Q&A on timeframes, single-stock day trading, and trend. Use two or three timeframes suited to your style (e.g. weekly/monthly for the curve, daily/hourly for entries when swing trading futures). Trading one stock (RIMM) needs index analysis (QQQQ) and a larger timeframe. Stop agonising over trend methods; trends begin and end at supply/demand levels.

Use 2-3 timeframes: larger for direction, smaller for entry. For stocks, analyse the index first and align stock levels with index levels. Day traders still check 60-minute or daily levels. Qualify every level with an odds-enhancer checklist.
Depends on style; always use more than one - two or three. Larger timeframe shows where price is on the curve (longs or shorts); smaller finds low-risk entries.
His XLT futures swing set: weekly and monthly for the curve, daily and hourly for demand levels with big profit margins.
Reader trades the first 15-minute candle high/low with a 1/3 stop and $0.90-1.00 targets using 5 and 15-minute charts.
First do supply/demand on the index (NASDAQ/QQQQ), then find the matching turns in the stock to filter weak levels.
Even a day trader needs a larger timeframe (60-minute or daily); a perfect 5-minute buy at daily supply will likely fail. Use a checklist ('odds enhancers') to qualify levels.
Conventional HH/HL and MA slope are high risk, low reward, low probability entry methods. In everyday life nobody buys only after prices rise; doing so in markets transfers money to others.
Every trend begins and ends at out-of-balance levels; get in before the conventional buyers.
Trading a stock without looking at its index. Using only 5- and 15-minute charts. Spending years searching for the perfect trend method.
What is the larger-timeframe picture? Does the index agree with the stock setup? Has the level passed the odds enhancers?
“Every trend begins and ends at price levels where supply and demand are out-of-balance.” “Use more than one time frame; typically two or three are perfect.”
Index-first analysis for individual stocks (QQQQ before RIMM) is new; Kevin trades FX/indices directly.
Seiden's futures swing set (monthly/weekly + daily/hourly) differs from Kevin's timeframe combos.

Use two or three timeframes, and check the index before any stock. A reader day traded one stock using only 5 and 15-minute charts. Sam said even day traders need a bigger chart, like the 60-minute or daily. A perfect-looking 5-minute buy that sits right under daily supply will likely fail. For a stock, look at its index first, then find the stock levels that match the index turns. And stop hunting for the perfect trend method: trends begin and end at supply and demand levels.
A small puddle can look like a lake if you only look at it up close. Step back and you see how small it is.
Always use two or three timeframes: larger for direction, smaller for entry. For stocks, analyse the index first and line the stock levels up with it.
Every trend begins and ends at out-of-balance levels. Get in before the conventional buyers.
On the daily chart there is supply above, where price fell hard before.
On the 5-minute chart a neat demand zone forms. It looks perfect, but it sits right under daily supply.
With daily supply just above, there is no room and the bigger sellers are waiting. The 5-minute buy is fighting the larger picture.
Price breaks down through the small zone. The larger timeframe won.

How many timeframes? - Two or three. Larger timeframe tells you? - Where price is on the curve: longs or shorts. Stock day trade first step? - Analyse the index, then align the stock. Where do trends begin and end? - At out-of-balance supply and demand levels.

Most automated systems fail because they are curve-fitted rather than built on how markets work. A good system needs a novice on the other side. Seiden's simple mechanical template: a 50-period MA slope is the 'switch' (ok to buy or ok to sell) and an oscillator cross in oversold/overbought territory is the 'trigger', ignoring counter-trend signals. With supply/demand, the switch is price reaching the level and the trigger is the entry.

Define a switch (permission to buy or sell, never both) and a trigger (entry). Uptrend: only oversold buy signals; downtrend: only overbought sell signals. Build systems on logic of who is on the other side, not on backtest optimisation. Do not keep adjusting settings or adding indicators after losses.

Backtests often show 80%+ winners but lose fast with real money. Traders then tweak settings and add indicators - a path to disaster. The foundation must be how markets work: supply and demand out of balance.
Buy rule: MA sloping up -> take stochastic crosses in oversold territory, ignore every overbought sell signal.
Sell rule: MA sloping down -> take crosses in overbought, ignore every oversold buy signal.
Logic: in an uptrend the oversold buy signal shows someone selling after a decline in an uptrend - a novice to buy from. Switch = on/off permission for one side; trigger = actual entry.
For a level-based system: switch = price reaching the level; trigger = arrival at the level, a reversal candle, etc.
Summary table: uptrend+overbought ignore, uptrend+oversold buy; downtrend+oversold ignore, downtrend+overbought short.

Figure 1 (p305): QQQQ 5-minute, 50-period MA rising, Slow Stochastics 14,3,3 (80/20). Price rises from about 44.6 to 45.75, then a sharp drop to about 44.95 (circled) near the rising MA; stochastic crosses up below 20 (circled) and price rallies back to about 45.7. Earlier overbought readings during the rise would have been losing shorts.
Figure 2 (p307): QQQQ 5-minute, MA falling from about 45.2 to 43.2; price grinds down to about 42.5. Circled stochastic crosses down from above 80 mark short entries; oversold crosses are ignored.

Figure 3 (p308): @NQ (e-mini NASDAQ-100) 5-minute, MA sloping down (about 2,027 to 2,007). Two vertical lines at about 11:55 and 14:25 where CCI(14) spikes above +100 (circled) and price then falls - from about 2,020 to 2,000 and from about 2,010 to 1,990.

Figure 4 (p309): USDJPY 5-minute (FOREX), MA rising from about 105.20 to 105.45. Vertical lines at about 18:15 and 22:35 where CCI drops below -100 (circled) near the MA; price then rallies to about 105.55. Figure 5 (p310): a 2x2 summary table of oscillator signals by trend.

passages.h: Chart: QQQQ 5-minute with a rising 50-period MA and Slow Stochastics (14,3,3; 80/20): after a rally to about 45.75, a sharp drop to about 44.95 near the MA (circled) coincides with a stochastic cross up below 20 (circled); price rallies back to about 45.7.
passages.t: Switch: the MA slopes up, so only buy signals are allowed. Trigger: the oversold cross is the entry; earlier overbought crosses during the rise are ignored. In supply/demand terms the switch is price at demand and the trigger is the entry order.

passages.h: Chart: QQQQ 5-minute with a falling 50-period MA: price grinds from about 45.2 down to about 42.5; circled stochastic crosses down from above 80 mark short entries while oversold crosses are ignored.
passages.t: With the switch set to sell, every oversold reading is a trap for buyers. Overbought crosses in a downtrend line up with pullbacks to supply. A simple, logical rule set beats a curve-fitted system.

passages.h: Chart: E-mini NASDAQ-100 (@NQ) 5-minute, MA sloping down: two vertical lines where CCI(14) spikes above +100 (circled); price then falls from about 2,020 to 2,000 and from about 2,010 to 1,990.
passages.t: Same switch-and-trigger idea with a different oscillator. Each trigger came on a counter-trend rally into the falling MA - a pullback to supply. The tool matters less than the logic behind it.

passages.h: Chart: USDJPY 5-minute (FOREX), MA rising: vertical lines where CCI drops below -100 (circled) on pullbacks near the MA; price then rallies to about 105.55.
passages.t: Uptrend switch plus oversold trigger = buy the pullback. The same template works on forex, futures and stocks because it is built on how markets work. A good system needs a novice on the other side - here, the trader selling the dip.

Seiden's mechanical template: the MA slope is the switch, the oversold/overbought cross is the trigger; counter-trend signals are ignored. With supply/demand, the switch is price at the level and the trigger is the entry.
Taking every indicator signal. Curve-fitting parameters to past data. Shorting overbought readings in an uptrend. Adding more indicators when a system loses.

Is the switch on for this side? Did the trigger occur in the right territory (oversold in uptrend, overbought in downtrend)? Am I ignoring counter-switch signals? Is the rule logical about who is on the other side?
“Whatever the strategy, there is always a 'switch' and 'trigger.'” “There is no perfect trading system and there doesn't need to be.”
Switch/trigger framework and an indicator-based mechanical template - Kevin's course has no indicator system.
Seiden here accepts an MA slope as a trend switch inside a system, unlike his discretionary articles.

Every system needs a switch and a trigger, built on simple market logic. Most trading robots look great on old data and then lose fast with real money, because they were bent to fit the past. Sam's simple template has a switch and a trigger. The switch is the slope of a 50-period average: up means only buys are allowed, down means only sells. The trigger is an oscillator turning in oversold (for buys) or overbought (for sells).
With supply and demand, the switch is price reaching the level and the trigger is the entry.
A light switch decides if the room can be lit. Pressing the lamp button is the trigger. If the switch is off, pressing the button does nothing.
Systems fail when curve-fitted. Build on how markets work: a novice must be on the other side.
Switch = permission for one side only. Trigger = the actual entry. Ignore every counter-switch signal.
Uptrend + oversold = buy; uptrend + overbought = ignore. Downtrend + overbought = short; downtrend + oversold = ignore.

passages.h: Step: The switch is set to buy
passages.t: The 50-period average slopes up. The switch says: buys only, no shorts.
The oscillator goes overbought on the way up. In an uptrend those are sell signals we ignore. Shorting them would lose.

passages.h: Step: The trigger: oversold in an uptrend
passages.t: A sharp drop toward the average pushes the oscillator oversold and it crosses up. Someone is selling after a decline in an uptrend: a novice to buy from. That is the trigger.
Price rallies back to new highs. In supply and demand terms: the switch is price at demand, the trigger is the entry order.

Switch? - Permission for one side only (e.g. MA slope, or price at a level). Trigger? - The actual entry (e.g. oscillator cross in the allowed zone). Uptrend + overbought? - Ignore. Downtrend + overbought? - Short. Why systems fail? - Curve-fitting instead of logic about who is on the other side.

Q&A: add a 'flat MA' state for sideways markets in which both oscillator signals are taken; gaps in the middle of moves - find the nearest drop-base-rally to the gap origin; longer-term demand must have room below supply and some overhead supply absorbed; and hand charting builds feel for supply and demand.
Define a numeric MA slope threshold for up, down and flat. For a gap, mark the nearest drop-base-rally at or just below the gap origin.
For long-term investing, require margin to supply and wait for overhead supply to be absorbed.
Define trend by a numeric MA slope; between the up and down thresholds the market is sideways.
In sideways mode take both oscillator buy and sell signals; switch back to trend mode once the slope returns.

Be careful with gaps in the middle of moves. Find the nearest demand (drop-base-rally) to the gap origin; often at the origin, sometimes just below it - that is the low-risk entry. Reverse for gap downs.

Two equal considerations: a demand level below with significant upside margin to supply, and waiting for some or all of the overhead supply to be absorbed before investing for a big move up. Reaching demand does not mean price will break the big supply above.
He used graph paper and coloured pencils; it makes you aware of levels where demand exceeds supply.
Lagging computer signals put people into high risk, low reward trades that pay the tape reader who bought at demand.
For a gap in the middle of a move, the demand is the nearest drop-base-rally at the origin of the move into the gap, not the gap edge itself.
Using trend-mode rules in a flat market. Treating any gap origin as demand without finding the actual base. Assuming price will pass big supply because it bounced at demand.
Is the MA slope up, down or flat by my numeric definition? Where is the actual base near the gap origin? Is there overhead supply that has not been absorbed?
“Be careful with those gaps in the middle of moves.” “Most will go with the high risk entry - people are people.”
Rule for gaps: use the nearest base to the gap origin, sometimes just below it. Waiting for overhead supply to be absorbed before long-term investing.

For a gap mid-move, buy the real base below it, not the gap edge. Readers asked three things. In a sideways market, define flat with numbers and take both buy and sell signals. When a gap sits in the middle of a move, do not just buy the gap edge; find the nearest drop-base-rally at or just below where the gap started. For long-term money, you need room up to supply and some of that overhead supply used up first. And Sam built his feel for levels by drawing charts by hand.
A gap is like a jump on a ski slope. The jump is not where the skier started; look back up the hill to the real starting gate.
Define up, down and flat with a numeric MA slope. In flat mode take both signals. Be careful with gaps in the middle of moves: mark the nearest drop-base-rally at or just below the gap origin.
Long-term buys need margin to supply and overhead supply absorbed. Hand charting builds the feel.

passages.h: Step: A base, a push, a gap
passages.t: Price dropped, based, pushed up a little and then gapped higher in the middle of the move.

passages.h: Step: Gap edge is not the level
passages.t: Most people would buy the gap edge. But the gap is mid-move; the real imbalance began lower.
Look just below the gap origin: the base after the drop. That is the demand. Draw it with the usual rule.
Price slices through the gap edge and turns at the real base. That is where the low-risk entry was.
Flat market rule? - Define flat by a numeric MA slope and take both signals. Gap in the middle of a move? - Find the nearest drop-base-rally at or just below the gap origin.
Two conditions for long-term buys? - Margin to supply above, and overhead supply absorbed. Hand charting tools? - Graph paper and coloured pencils.

Markets spend most time near equilibrium and little time at strong imbalances, so patience is needed to wait for those levels. GOOG daily swing short on March 12: five odds enhancers lined up (S&P near supply, novice gap-up buying, gap-down origin, VIX at demand, large profit margin). The entry was taken at the level before the red confirmation candle.

Wait for price to reach the level; enter at the level, not after confirmation. Stack odds enhancers: index at a level, novice behaviour (gap after rally), strong departure (gap), sentiment (VIX), large profit margin. For stock shorts, the index should be at or near supply.
Fast platforms tempt home traders to over-trade. Low risk, high reward, high probability only exists at extreme imbalance, which is rare; patience and probability go together.

passages.h: Odds enhancers for the GOOG short
passages.t: 1) S&P nearing supply - most stocks likely to decline. 2) Novice buying - gap up after a strong rally and into supply. 3) Gap down from the supply originally - stronger departure, bigger imbalance. 4) VIX near demand - complacency; when everyone has bought the market must fall.

passages.h: Odds enhancers for the GOOG short
passages.t: 5) Large profit margin to demand - the further from equilibrium, the higher the probability. Not every opportunity has all of them.

The entry day closed red at supply; next day gapped down to T1. Most wait for the red candle before shorting the next day; the astute speculator is already short and those late sellers help push price down.

Figure 1 (p316): XLT swing-trading screen, 12 March. Circled grey S&P chart (upper left) nearing supply; circled VIX chart (lower left) near demand; a GOOG chart circled with labels 'Supply' and 'Short Entry' where price meets the supply line; watch list on the right.
Figure 2 (p318): GOOG daily, Dec 2009-Mar 2010. Price peaks about 625 in early January, falls to a small base; 'Supply Level' two lines about 580-592 in mid/late January.
A circled 'Gap' just below the zone shows the gap down from the base to about 565, then lows near 525 in February.
In March price rallies, gaps up into the zone; arrow 'Novice Buyer' at a candle reaching about 588. Next candles red, the last gapping down to about 557.

passages.h: Chart: XLT swing-trading screen, 12 March: circled S&P chart nearing supply, circled VIX chart near demand, and a GOOG chart circled with 'Supply' and 'Short Entry' where price meets the supply line.
passages.t: Check the index and VIX before a stock trade: S&P at supply and VIX at demand both favour shorts. Stack odds enhancers across markets before pulling the trigger. Patience: wait for the few moments when several imbalances line up.

passages.h: Chart: GOOG daily, Dec 2009-Mar 2010: 'Supply Level' about 580-592 at the base before a circled gap down in January; in March price rallies and gaps up into the zone ('Novice Buyer' arrow at about 588), then the next candles are red, the last gapping down to about 557.
passages.t: The base before a gap down is strong supply - price left it with no trading at all. The gap up into it shows novice buying; Seiden sells to them at the level.

passages.h: Chart: GOOG daily, Dec 2009-Mar 2010: 'Supply Level' about 580-592 at the base before a circled gap down in January; in March price rallies and gaps up into the zone ('Novice Buyer' arrow at about 588), then the next candles are red, the last gapping down to about 557.
passages.t: He entered at the level without waiting for the red confirmation candle - waiting would have cost much of the move.
GOOG swing short: a gap up into the base that preceded a gap down, with five odds enhancers lined up; the entry is at the level, before the red confirmation candle.
Over-trading in balanced markets. Waiting for a confirmation candle before entering. Ignoring the index and sentiment context.

Is the S&P/NASDAQ at a matching level? Is the VIX at an opposing level (demand for shorts)? Did price leave the zone with a gap? Are novices gapping in after a rally? Is the profit margin to the opposing level large?
“Patience and probabilities go hand-in-hand.” “With patience comes high probabilities.”
Entry at the level without confirmation - Kevin's course often uses confirmation entries on a lower timeframe. VIX as a sentiment odds enhancer and S&P context for stock trades are new.

Strong levels are rare. Wait patiently, then enter at the level, not later. Markets spend most of their time calm and balanced, and very little time at big imbalances. So you need patience. For a Google short, five things lined up: the S&P near supply, novices gapping up after a rally, a level that price had gapped away from, the fear index (VIX) at demand, and a big room down to demand. Sam sold at the level. Most people waited for a red candle first, and their late selling helped push price down.
Fishing is mostly waiting. When the fish bites, you pull right away, not after it swims off.
Low risk, high reward, high probability only exists at rare extreme imbalances. Patience and probability go together.
Stack odds: index at a level, novice gap after a rally, strong (gap) departure, VIX opposite, big margin. Enter at the level. Waiting for a confirmation candle gives away much of the move.

passages.h: Step: A base that gapped down
passages.t: Price based and gapped down: no trading at all as it left. That is strong supply.
Price spends a long time far below. Nothing to do. Most of the time the market is near balance.
Price rallies and gaps up into the zone: novice buying. The S&P is near supply, the VIX is near demand, and demand is far below. Sell at the level.
The entry day closes red; the next day gaps down toward the target. Those who waited for the red candle sold late and helped push it lower.

Patience goes hand in hand with? - Probabilities. VIX near demand means? - Complacency; good for shorts. Entry timing? - At the level, before the confirmation candle. Strongest kind of departure? - A gap away from the base.

Starts here and continues into the next part. For stock day trades, time entries to S&P/NASDAQ turning points. On March 24 the S&P and INTC both reached yellow-shaded supply (origins of declines) with demand much lower, so XLT shorted both; S&P reached its demand target.
Only short stocks when the S&P/NASDAQ is also at supply (and long when at demand). Plan pre-market: index level, distance to opposing level, stock level. Supply = origin of a decline.
Supply levels are the origins of price declines; price cannot stay there because supply exceeds demand.
INTC worked because the S&P was also at supply with demand lower - an acceptable (not great) profit margin. Shorting INTC when the S&P/NASDAQ is not at supply is very low probability.
Figure (p320): composite of XLT screens. Left labels: 'XLT Pre Market Planning: 1) S&P at supply 2) Demand much lower 3) INTC at supply'; 'XLT Trading: 1) Short S&P 2) Short INTC'.
Grey S&P charts show yellow supply boxes; circled 'S&P Supply (short entry)' where price returns, and a blue line below marked 'S&P Demand (target met)' that price later reaches.
White INTC charts (three timeframes) show yellow supply with a circle at 'INTC Supply (short entry)'. Order ticket: Sell 5 at 1,167.25 and Buy 5 at 1,163.00 - a 4.25-point S&P futures short.

passages.h: Chart: Composite of XLT screens for March 24: pre-market plan '1) S&P at supply 2) Demand much lower 3) INTC at supply'; S&P charts with yellow supply boxes and a circled 'S&P Supply (short entry)', a blue 'S&P Demand (target met)' line below; INTC charts with circled 'INTC Supply (short entry)'; order ticket Sell 5 at 1,167.25 / Buy 5 at 1,163.00.
passages.t: Plan before the open: index at supply + room to demand + stock at supply = short both. Stock day trades work best when timed to S&P/NASDAQ turning points. The index's own demand is the exit for both trades.
Inter-market alignment: when the S&P reaches supply with demand far below and a stock is also at supply, short both; exit when the index reaches its demand.
Shorting a stock at supply while the index is mid-range or at demand. Lacking patience for index and stock to line up.
Is the S&P/NASDAQ at supply (for shorts) or demand (for longs)? Is demand far enough below for an acceptable margin? Is the stock at its own matching level?
“Timing your entries in stocks to the S&P and NASDAQ supply and demand levels is the key.”
Index-to-stock alignment as a requirement; Kevin's course trades instruments standalone.

Short a stock only when the index is at supply too. On March 24 the S&P reached a supply level, the place where an earlier decline began, with demand far below. Intel was at its own supply at the same time. So Sam's class shorted both. The S&P fell to its demand target and the trades paid. Shorting Intel while the S&P was not at supply would have been very low probability.
A stock is like a boat in a harbour. When the tide (the index) goes out, almost every boat goes down with it.

Supply = the origin of a decline: price cannot stay there because supply exceeds demand. Time stock entries to S&P/NASDAQ levels: short stocks when the index is at supply, buy when it is at demand. Plan pre-market: index at a level, room to its opposing level, stock at a matching level.
The index has supply at the origin of an earlier decline, and demand much lower. That is enough room.
The stock also has supply at the same moment. Index at supply + room + stock at supply = short both.
Price rallies into the zone. Sell at the bottom line, stop above. The exit is when the index reaches its demand.
The index falls to its demand and the stock follows. Both trades are closed there.
Key to timing stock entries? - The S&P and NASDAQ supply and demand levels. Stock short needs the index at? - Supply.
Pre-market checklist? - Index at a level, room to the opposing level, stock at a matching level. Exit for both trades? - When the index reaches its demand.

Seiden shares one odds-enhancing rule: a supply level with another supply level sitting just above it (or demand with demand just below) is stronger than a lone level. He shows an S&P (SPY 5-minute) short taken at stacked supply and explains how to enter when two levels are stacked. (Page 321 opens with the last lines of the previous article; this lesson starts at the new heading.)
A supply level with another supply level just above it is typically stronger than an isolated supply level.
A demand level with another demand level just below it is typically stronger than an isolated demand level.
With stacked levels, either scale in (part at lower level, rest at upper, stop above upper) or enter fully at the upper level.
Never put the full position at the lower level with the stop just beyond it - your stop would sit where the next entry belongs.
The only reason to study trading is to gain an edge over the competition; this is one rule rarely found in conventional books.
Stacked supply levels are like a bank vault with two steel doors instead of one: price arriving at the lower supply meets a 'thick' area of supply.
The buyer he sold to had bought after a strong rally straight into that thick supply - a very novice mistake, 'a plastic hammer' against two vault doors.
The same logic applies to demand: a demand level with another demand level just below is typically stronger.

Option 1: scale in - part of the position at the lower (proximal) supply level, the rest at the upper level, with the stop above the upper level. Option 2: enter the whole position at the upper supply level.
Never enter the full position at the bottom level with a buy stop just above the bottom level - that puts your stop exactly where you should be adding/entering short.
A tongue-in-cheek 'mayor of Foolsville' story: the copy-paste crowd was buying at $119.00 SPY on a 'buy signal', exactly where he planned to short.

Certainty does not exist in trading or life; search for better odds with objective, rule-based supply/demand analysis ('motion into mass'). Not every trade wins, but levels on top of levels dramatically increase the odds.

322): SPY 5-minute (TradeStation, S&P ETF used to represent the S&P futures trade, 4/7/10). 05 created by another small base (D) before a further decline. 00 at about 12:30. Arrows labelled 'Novice Buyers' point up into the level and 'Low risk Short Entry' marks the top. 38 on the axis). 50.

passages.h: Chart: SPY 5-minute, 4/7/10: a rally-base-drop 'Supply' near 119.10-119.20 (R-B-D upper left) with a second 'Supply' just below at ~119.00; the midday rally back up is marked 'Novice Buyers' and the 'Low risk Short Entry' arrow sits at the stacked supply. Price then falls into the close (~118.0). Statement: net +$2,132.50.
passages.t: Two supply levels stacked on top of each other: the lower one is the entry, the upper one protects the stop. The rally into supply is where the 'buy signal' crowd buys - Seiden sells to them.

passages.h: Chart: SPY 5-minute, 4/7/10: a rally-base-drop 'Supply' near 119.10-119.20 (R-B-D upper left) with a second 'Supply' just below at ~119.00; the midday rally back up is marked 'Novice Buyers' and the 'Low risk Short Entry' arrow sits at the stacked supply. Price then falls into the close (~118.0). Statement: net +$2,132.50.
passages.t: The short had room to run: the earlier 10:00 low (~118.40) and then the session low were the downside targets.

Stacked supply: price rallies into Supply 1 with Supply 2 sitting just above. Short part at the lower proximal line and the rest at the upper level, stop above the upper distal line, target the prior low.
Wrong vs right: a full position at the lower level with a stop between the levels gets stopped by the spike into the upper level; scaling in with one stop above the upper level survives it.

Buying after a strong rally straight into stacked supply. Copying 'buy signals' from the crowd without checking where supply sits. Placing the protective stop inside the second (stronger) level. Searching for certainty instead of better odds.

Is there a second supply level just above (or demand just below) my level? Am I scaling in across both levels or entering at the outer level? Is my stop beyond the OUTER level, not between the two? Did price arrive after a strong move (novice buyers/sellers on the other side)?
“Would you rather have your money in a bank vault that had one steel door, or... two steel doors?” “We must not search for certainty, but instead search for better odds.”
Kevin's Q&A covers stacked zones; Seiden adds the explicit entry choice: scale in across both levels or enter only at the upper one, with the stop beyond the outer level.
Seiden frames stacking as an odds enhancer (stronger level), not just a zone-drawing question.

Two supply levels stacked together make a stronger wall than one. Imagine a bank with one steel door, and another bank with two steel doors. A robber with a plastic hammer will not get through either, but two doors make it even harder. On a chart, a supply level with another supply level just above it is that two-door bank. The crowd buys after a rally right into it and bounces off. You sell to them, with your stop above both doors.
It is like a goalkeeper with a second goalkeeper standing right behind him. If the ball gets past the first, the second one stops it, so never stand between them.
Supply with more supply just above (or demand with more demand just below) is stronger than one lonely level.
Scale in at both levels, or enter all at the outer level. One stop beyond the outer level. We do not look for certainty. We look for better odds.

Price rallied, paused for two small candles and then dropped. Price could not stay there, so supply was bigger than demand. Wrap the pause: bottom line on the lowest body, top line on the highest wick. That is Supply 2.

passages.h: Step: A second door just below
passages.t: On the way down price paused again for two candles and fell hard. Now there is a second supply sitting just under the first one. Two steel doors instead of one: levels on top of levels.

passages.h: Step: Plan before price comes back
passages.t: Price fell far, to the prior low. The plan is made now, not later: sell part at the bottom line of Supply 1, sell the rest at the bottom line of Supply 2, and put ONE stop above the top of Supply 2. The target is the prior low.
A steady rally climbs back up. The crowd sees a buy signal and buys after a rally, straight into thick supply. That is a plastic hammer against two vault doors. Entry 1 fills.

passages.h: Step: The spike fills entry 2, the stop holds
passages.t: Price spikes up into Supply 2. A trader with a stop between the doors would be stopped out right here. Our stop sits above both doors, entry 2 fills, and price falls to the target.
Supply with supply just above it is...? - Typically stronger than a lone supply level. Demand with demand just below it is...? - Typically stronger than a lone demand level.
Stacked levels: option 1 entry? - Scale in: part at the inner level, the rest at the outer level. Stacked levels: option 2 entry? - Enter the whole position at the outer level.
Where is the stop with stacked supply? - Above the upper (outer) level, never between the two. What do we search for instead of certainty? - Better odds.

A long-term call: in March 2009 the S&P reached monthly demand (wholesale) with a huge profit margin to the next fresh supply, so XLT bought. Thirteen months later price was approaching large monthly supply, which he zoomed into on the weekly chart to find two stacked supply levels, so he expected the rally to stop and turn lower. Bad news at demand and good news at supply are opportunities against the crowd.
Measure profit margin as the distance between the fresh demand level and the fresh opposing supply level.
Investigate large higher-timeframe levels on smaller timeframes to locate the precise proximal and distal levels inside.
Bad news with price at demand is a buy context; good news with price at supply is a sell context. If a forecast level fails, switch to buying pullbacks into the newly created levels.
Profit margin is assessed as the distance from the fresh demand level to the fresh supply level; in March 2009 it was huge, giving ideal risk/reward.
XLT members were alerted on March 4th; one member bought a basket of stocks also at larger-timeframe demand and had double-digit gains within two months.
Wall Street says 'you can't time the market' - Seiden disagrees; timing via real supply and demand analysis is the key.

passages.h: Zooming into a large monthly level ('x-ray')
passages.t: A large monthly supply area is investigated on smaller timeframes - like a doctor taking several x-ray pictures of the same elbow from different angles.

passages.h: Zooming into a large monthly level ('x-ray')
passages.t: Inside the monthly supply, the weekly SPY shows two clear supply levels: a lower (proximal) one not far away and an upper (distal) one just above.

passages.h: Zooming into a large monthly level ('x-ray')
passages.t: If he is wrong and price rallies through monthly supply, simply buy pullbacks to new demand levels.
March 2009 news was terrible (worst jobs reports since 1945, record foreclosures, AIG 'collapse') - yet that was the time to buy.

Two facts matter: you profit by buying at wholesale (demand) and selling at retail (supply), and you must quantify supply/demand on a price chart to find turns in advance. Bad news + price at demand = turn higher; good news + price at supply = turn lower. Keep analysis 'real' and 'simple'; the price chart contains all needed information.

Figure 1 (p.325): $INX/SPX monthly, 1997-2010. A yellow-shaded 'Demand - (wholesale)' zone is drawn at the very bottom-left (1990s base around the 700 area) and carried right; the March 2009 low (~670) reaches it. A second yellow box labelled 'Supply - Retail' is drawn around 1,200-1,250 at the base where price broke down in 2008. Price has rallied from the 2009 low to about 1,200, just under that supply.
Figure 2 (p.325): a short email from an XLT member (May 6, 2009) saying most positions were entered the week of 3/9-3/13 in an IRA that was in cash.
Figure 3 (p.325): the member's position list (DRYS, AA, HYG, NUE, DLN, PBT, PBR, TBT, PCU) showing percentage gains roughly 5-59%.

Figure 4 (p.326): SPY weekly ('09-'10). Two yellow supply boxes: upper 'Supply - Retail' around 138-145 (distal) and lower 'Supply - (retail)' around 124-131 (proximal), both origins of the 2008 declines. Price has climbed steadily from the 2009 low near 68 to 121.02, approaching the lower supply.

passages.h: Chart: $INX (S&P 500) monthly 1997-2010: 'Demand - (wholesale)' box at the 1990s base (~700) reached by the March 2009 low; 'Supply - Retail' box near 1,250-1,300 at the origin of the 2008 collapse, with price rallying toward it (1,208 on the right).
passages.t: Monthly demand at the origin of a multi-year rally = wholesale price, bought on the worst news. The profit margin from demand to the next fresh supply was enormous. The retail supply above is where the rally is expected to stall.

passages.h: Chart: Email from an XLT member (May 6, 2009): most positions were entered the week of 3/9-3/13, in an IRA that had been all cash.
passages.t: Buying at monthly demand meant buying when the news was worst - the week of the 2009 low.

passages.h: Chart: The member's position list (DRYS, AA, HYG, NUE, OLN, PBT, PBR, TBT, PCU) showing gains of roughly 5-59% two months after the March 2009 entries.
passages.t: Low-risk entries at demand produce large percentage gains without needing to predict the news.

passages.h: Chart: SPY weekly 2008-2010: two yellow supply boxes - 'Supply - Retail' (~138-145) and 'Supply - (retail)' (~124-131), both origins of 2008 declines; price has rallied from the 2009 low to ~121, just under the lower box.
passages.t: Zooming from the monthly to the weekly chart reveals levels on top of levels inside the monthly supply. Seiden expected the rally to stop at the lower supply and turn lower.
S&P monthly logic: buy the return to the wholesale demand base on bad news, target the retail supply at the origin of the collapse; the distance between them is the profit margin.
Seiden zooms from the monthly supply into the weekly chart and finds two stacked supply levels (both origins of 2008 declines), so he expects the rally to stop and turn lower.

Believing the market cannot be timed. Letting dramatic news stop you from buying at wholesale prices. Treating a large monthly zone as one entry price without zooming in. Complicating analysis instead of keeping it real and simple.

Where is the nearest fresh opposing level (profit margin)? Is the HTF level large? Have I zoomed in to find the inner levels? Is the news pushing price INTO my level (crowd on the wrong side)? What will I do if the level fails (buy/sell new pullback levels)?
“Real bad news and price at or near demand (wholesale prices) equates to a turn higher in price.” “The trick is to keep your analysis 'real' and 'simple.'”
Kevin's MTF is about refining entry-TF zones inside HTF zones; Seiden uses the same idea for long-term investing calls on monthly/weekly index charts.
Kevin says don't trade the news; Seiden treats extreme news pushing price into a level as part of the opportunity (on HTF swing/position horizons).

Buy at wholesale on bad news, sell at retail on good news. A shop owner buys toys cheap from the factory and sells them dear in the store. The factory price is demand, the store price is supply. In 2009 the news was the worst in decades, and the S&P fell all the way back to its old factory price. Seiden bought there while everyone else sold. A year later price was near the store price, so he expected it to stop.
It is like buying winter coats in summer when nobody wants them, then selling them when the first snow falls and everyone panics for a coat.

Profit margin = distance from fresh demand to the next fresh supply. Zoom into a big higher timeframe level to find the exact levels inside it. Bad news at demand means look to buy; good news at supply means look to sell.

passages.h: Step: Wholesale: the base that launched the rally
passages.t: Long ago price paused for two candles and then rallied hard for years. Demand was much bigger than supply at that pause. That is wholesale demand on the monthly chart.

passages.h: Step: Retail: where the collapse began
passages.t: At the top price paused and fell, paused again and fell harder. Those pauses are retail supply. Zoom in like a doctor taking more x-rays of one elbow: the big monthly area holds two supply levels, one on top of the other.
Price falls all the way back to wholesale demand while the news is the worst in decades. The crowd sells. The rule: bad news plus price at demand means a turn higher. Buy here.
The profit margin is the distance from fresh demand up to the next fresh supply. Here it is huge, so the reward is many times the risk. That is why this was the ideal long-term buy.

passages.h: Step: The rally meets retail supply
passages.t: Price rallies for months and reaches the lower of the two stacked supply levels as the news turns good. Good news plus price at supply means a turn lower. If it breaks through, simply buy pullbacks to the new demand.

Profit margin (Seiden)? - The distance from fresh demand to the next fresh opposing supply (or the reverse). Bad news + price at demand = - A likely turn higher. Good news + price at supply = - A likely turn lower.

Why zoom into a big monthly zone? - To find the exact levels inside it, like several x-rays of the same elbow. What if the forecast level fails? - Buy pullbacks to the new demand levels. Wholesale and retail mean? - Wholesale = demand (buy), retail = supply (sell).

Introduces the XLT 'All Star' entry: a strong supply/demand level combined with price piercing the outer Bollinger Band and a significant profit margin to the opposing level. Two live trades (RIMM 60-minute, INTC daily) illustrate it. 'Lite' because two further rules are withheld for XLT members.
Buy: price at a strong demand level, piercing the lower Bollinger Band, with a significant profit margin above.
Sell short: price at a strong supply level, piercing the upper Bollinger Band, with a significant profit margin below. Place profit targets just before the opposing level, not at it.
1) Supply and demand; 2) Bollinger Bands. Supply level chosen because price fell from it in strong fashion - a big imbalance.

When price returns to supply AND pierces the upper Bollinger Band, it is both at a level of excess supply and statistically at an extreme likely to revert to the mean - the combination makes it high probability.
The profit target (blue line) is placed just ABOVE the demand level below for a short - buy back before demand, not at it.
At demand there is competition to buy, so your cover order is more likely to fill just in front of it.

INTC had a significant supply level (price fell strongly and far from it). Price rallied back into it on a good earnings announcement while piercing the upper band; mean reversion happened quickly and target one was reached.
However good the news, when price reaches a level where supply exceeds demand, price falls.

Figure 1 (p.329): RIMM 60-minute with Bollinger Bands (red midline). A yellow 'Supply' box around 73.80-74.20 sits at the 4/15 peak, origin of a strong drop to ~69. Price later spiked back up on 4/27 into supply and above the upper band (circled) - labelled 'XLT Short Entry'. A blue 'Target' line sits around 69.6, just above the lows/demand near 68.9. Price turned down from the entry (last 71.36).

Figure 2 (p.331): INTC daily, roughly two years, with Bollinger Bands. Yellow 'Supply (resistance)' box at the upper-left peak (~24.3), origin of a steep collapse to ~12.
