Price grinds back up over a year and finally reaches the supply at the far right (circled, 'XLT Short Entry') while poking outside the upper band. Two blue target lines, T1 (~22.9) and T2 (~21.6), are drawn below; price drops to T1 quickly.

passages.h: Chart: RIMM 60-minute with Bollinger Bands: yellow 'Supply' ~73.8-74.2 at the 4/15 high; on 4/27 price spikes back up into supply and pierces the upper band (circled 'XLT Short Entry'). A blue 'Target' line sits near 69.6 at the opposing demand; price is already back to ~71.4.
passages.t: All Star: strong supply + price outside the upper band + big margin to demand. Entry at the supply, stop just above it, target the demand that launched the spike.

passages.h: Chart: INTC daily with Bollinger Bands: 'Supply (resistance)' box at the upper-left peak (~24.3), origin of a collapse to ~12. A year later price grinds back up, pierces the upper band and reaches supply ('XLT Short Entry' circled at ~24); T1 and T2 lines drawn below (~23.3 and ~22.5).
passages.t: The same All Star logic works on a daily chart: a fresh level from long ago is still fresh. Targets step down: first near the midline, then lower.
All Star: price spikes back into fresh supply and pierces the upper Bollinger Band while there is a big margin down to demand; short the proximal line, stop above the distal line.

Buying after a big rally outside the upper band and into supply. Placing the cover/exit order right at the opposing level where competition is greatest. Letting great earnings news override a supply level.

Is the level strong (sharp, far move away)? Is price piercing the outer Bollinger Band on arrival? Is there a significant profit margin to the opposing level? Is my target placed just in front of the opposing level?
“We want to buy back our profitable shares just before price reaches demand, not at demand.” “When price reaches a price level where willing supply exceeds demand, price will fall.”
Kevin trades pure price action with no indicators; the All Star adds Bollinger Bands as a statistical-extreme filter.
Explicit target placement just in front of the opposing zone (to avoid competition) is a Seiden detail.

Strong level plus a band poke plus room to run makes an All Star. Think of a rubber band stretched way out. Let go and it snaps back. When price races back into a strong supply level and pokes outside the upper Bollinger Band, it is stretched AND it hit a wall of sellers. Seiden sells there and buys back just before the demand level below. Great news on the way up does not change it.
A ball thrown hard at a wall far from where you stand: it hits the wall (supply), it is going too fast to stay (band), and it rolls all the way back to you (margin).

All Star = strong level + outer band pierce + big profit margin, all together. Place the target just before the opposing level, not at it. Good news does not beat a level where supply is bigger than demand.
Price paused for two candles and fell hard and far. A sharp, fast drop means a big imbalance: much more supply than demand. That is the first tool.

passages.h: Step: 2. The opposing demand and the margin
passages.t: Price based low and launched a fast spike up. That base is the demand below. The space between supply and demand is the profit margin, and it is big.

Price spikes back into supply and pokes outside the upper Bollinger Band. Now price is at excess supply AND at a statistical extreme likely to snap back to the mean. Both tools agree: short at the bottom line of supply.

passages.h: Step: The target goes just before demand
passages.t: Put the buy-back order just ABOVE the demand, not at it. At demand many traders compete to buy, so you want to be filled in front of them.
Price falls back quickly to the target. However good the news was on that spike, price fell because it reached a level where supply was bigger than demand.

The two tools of the All Star? - Supply/demand levels and Bollinger Bands. All Star short trigger? - Price returns to strong supply and pierces the upper band. Where to put the profit target? - Just before the opposing level, not at it. Why not at the opposing level? - Competition to buy there; your order may not fill. Why is it called "Lite"? - Two more rules are kept for XLT members.

Reader Q&A: why time-at-level and distance-before-return matter, how to handle conflicting trends across timeframes, when old supply becomes demand, and how a newbie should start (simulator, QQQQ, small size).
Prefer levels with few candles in the base (little time at level). The farther price travelled before returning, the bigger the profit margin and the better the level.
A broken supply becomes demand only with strong breakout, big profit margin and good HTF location. Use moving averages at most as a background guide, never the primary trend tool.
Prove platform, execution and profitability on a simulator before real money; start small.

passages.h: The four questions (from his 'Market Traps' talk)
passages.t: 1) How did price leave the level? 2) How much time did price spend at the level? 3) Levels on top of levels? 4) How far did price move before returning to the level?

passages.h: The four questions (from his 'Market Traps' talk)
passages.t: These questions explain why he takes some levels and ignores others - the ignored ones are not levels at all under these tests.
Where supply and demand are badly out of balance there will be very few transactions - few candles in the base.
This contradicts books that say the best turns come with heavy/climactic volume: big imbalance means one side is mostly missing, so few trades occur. Look for levels with fewer candles, not many.

It quantifies profit margin: a long rally from demand shows the supply in that rally was absorbed, so you know where sellers are and are not. The farther price moved away before returning, the greater the profit margin.

Trends confuse many people; an uptrend on one timeframe is a downtrend on another. Waiting for a rising moving average means buying after price is already expensive - the opposite of shopping for a sale.
Identify where the trend begins with supply/demand levels; a larger-timeframe MA as a general guide is fine but not as the primary tool.

When demand absorbs all supply and price breaks through, the old supply becomes demand only if: there is significant profit margin, the breakout was strong, and the level is well placed on the larger-timeframe curve. Missing any of these makes the new level weak.
Decide your style (day, swing, position) and use a simulator first to: get comfortable with the platform, execute the strategy as planned, and prove the rules are profitable.

Then start with the stock market, e.g. QQQQ (liquid, low price); if you can't profit on QQQQ you won't on individual stocks. Start small with position size until your data shows you are consistently profitable.

Expecting strong turns at heavy-volume, many-candle areas. Waiting for a rising MA before buying (buying expensive). Assuming every broken level flips polarity. Trading real capital before proving the plan in a simulator; oversizing early.

How did price leave the level? How many candles are in the base? Is there another level stacked on top/below? How far did price travel before returning? For a flipped level: strong breakout, big profit margin, good HTF location?
“When looking for strong levels of supply or demand, look for levels with fewer candles in them instead of many.”
“The farther price moves away from our level before returning back to the level, the greater the profit margin.”
Kevin limits basing to about six or seven candles; Seiden gives the reason (few transactions = big imbalance) and rejects heavy-volume S/R logic.
Seiden's conditions for a broken supply flipping to demand (strong break, profit margin, HTF placement) are an explicit filter not stated in Kevin's notes.

Ask four questions about every level before you trust it. A good detective asks the same questions at every scene. Seiden asks four about every level: how did price leave, how long did it stay, is there another level on top, and how far did it go before coming back. A quiet spot with only a couple of candles is where one side was missing. If the answers are weak, it is not a level at all.
It is like checking a used car: how it drives away, how long it sat in the lot, whether it has a spare, and how far it can go on a tank.
Four questions: how it left, time at the level, levels on top, distance before return. Few candles at a level means a big imbalance. Many candles means balance.
Old supply becomes demand only with a strong break, big margin and good higher timeframe location.

passages.h: Step: Q1: How did price leave?
passages.t: From this little pause price fell with two big red candles. A strong move away shows supply was far bigger than demand.

passages.h: Step: Q2: How much time was spent there?
passages.t: Only two candles. Where supply and demand are badly out of balance, very few trades happen, so there are few candles. The busy area on the left had many candles: buyers and sellers agreed there, so it is not a level.

passages.h: Step: Q3 and Q4: stacked levels and distance
passages.t: Check for another level on top. Then ask how far price went before coming back: here it fell a long way. That long fall shows where buyers were absorbed, and it is the profit margin.

passages.h: Step: Shop for a sale, not a rising average
passages.t: Waiting for a rising moving average means buying after price is already expensive. Seiden finds where the trend begins with the levels themselves. Here the return to supply is the sell.

passages.h: Step: The answer on the chart
passages.t: Price touched the quiet two-candle supply and turned down. All four questions said yes, which is why this level was taken and the busy one ignored.
Strong level: few or many candles? - Few candles. Why few candles? - A big imbalance means one side is missing, so few trades happen. What does distance before return measure? - The profit margin.

Three needs for old supply to become demand? - Strong breakout, big profit margin, good higher timeframe location. Role of moving averages? - At most a background guide, never the main trend tool. First step for a newbie? - Simulator, then small size on a liquid market like QQQQ.

Entry location is the key to everything else (stop, size, target): enter as close to the turn as possible. Seiden lists three checks for a level where price should turn: how price left, how much time it spent there, and how far it moved before returning - each with its logic.

Gap away > strong big-candle move away > gradual move away. Fewer candles at the level = stronger level. Use the distance from the level to the extreme before return as a profit target. Enter as close to the turn as possible to maximise size and reward for given risk.

Entering close to the turn allows the largest position for the least money at risk. It also puts you farthest from the target, making the reward side as big as possible. Price turns where supply and demand are most out of balance.

passages.h: 1) How did price leave the level?
passages.t: Logic: the stronger the move away, the more out of balance the level. Three ways to leave: gradual move, strong move with big red/green candles, or a gap - the gap is strongest.

passages.h: 2) How much time did price spend at the level?
passages.t: Logic: the less time at the level, the bigger the imbalance. Contrary to books seeking lots of activity and volume: big imbalance means fewer transactions and lower volume. 'Don't believe everything you read' - the herd once thought the world was flat.

passages.h: 3) How far did price move before returning?
passages.t: Logic: the farther the move away before return, the greater the profit margin and probability.

passages.h: 3) How far did price move before returning?
passages.t: Such a level is far from equilibrium on the supply/demand curve - a stretched rubber band likely to snap back. On return to a supply level you are selling to someone buying after a very large rally.

passages.h: 3) How far did price move before returning?
passages.t: Measure from the supply level to the lowest low before the rally back - that distance becomes one of the profit targets.
His Lessons from the Pros and SFO articles, the free recordings, an Economics 101 book, the XLT, and Adam Smith's 'The Wealth of Nations'.

Seiden's three checks: price should leave the level strongly (big candles or a gap), spend little time there (few candles), and travel far before it returns (big profit margin). The bottom row shows the weak versions to skip.
Choosing levels with lots of activity and heavy volume. Entering far from the turn and shrinking the reward side. Trading levels that price barely moved away from.
Did price gap or leave with large candles? Is the base only a few candles? Did price travel far before coming back? Is my target based on the distance to the prior extreme?
“The stronger price moves away from a price level, the more out-of-balance supply and demand are at the level.” “The less time price spends at a level, the more out-of-balance supply and demand are.”
Kevin grades the move away and counts basing candles too; Seiden explicitly ranks a gap as the strongest departure and uses the 'stretched rubber band' curve idea.
Target from the distance between level and the lowest low before return is a Seiden-specific target method.

Good entry is everything: buy right where price turns. If you buy a toy right at the cheapest moment, you can buy more of them and still risk little money. Seiden says the entry decides your stop, your size and your target. So he checks three things to find where price will turn. Did price leave fast or with a gap, did it stay only a moment, and did it go far before coming back?
A trampoline jump: the harder you bounced off, the shorter you touched the mat, and the higher you flew, the better the trampoline.

Entry location decides stop, size and target, so enter as close to the turn as possible. Gap away beats big candles, which beat a gradual move. Few candles and a far run before the return mean a strong level and a big target.

passages.h: Step: Check 1: how did price leave?
passages.t: Three ways to leave a level: a gradual drift, big candles, or a gap. Here price GAPPED away. A gap is the strongest exit and shows the biggest imbalance.

passages.h: Step: Check 2: how long was it there?
passages.t: Only two candles. The less time price spends at a level, the more out of balance it is. Draw the zone: top on the highest body, bottom on the lowest wick.

passages.h: Step: Check 3: how far before returning?
passages.t: Price ran far up before coming back. The level sits far from balance, like a stretched rubber band. The distance from the level to that high is a profit target.

passages.h: Step: Enter as close to the turn as you can
passages.t: Buy at the top line, stop just under the bottom line. Entering at the turn gives the most size for the least risk and puts you farthest from the target.
Price turned at demand and ran back to the prior high. Gap, few candles, far distance: all three checks passed.
Strongest way to leave a level? - A gap. Less time at a level means? - A bigger imbalance.

Far run before return means? - Bigger profit margin and higher probability (stretched rubber band). Target from check 3? - Level to the extreme reached before the return. Why does entry matter most? - It decides stop, size and reward.

Q&A: include after-hours levels (especially S&P futures overnight) when trading stocks; supply/demand applies in every market worldwide; and why he says supply/demand instead of support/resistance, plus where to learn the rules.
Include overnight/after-hours levels in analysis, especially S&P futures when trading stocks.
Discard a stock level if the index futures already traded well beyond the corresponding level overnight. Only consider levels that meet minimum quality standards.
Yes, include after-hours supply/demand levels; most line up with day-session levels anyway.
When trading stocks, check the S&P futures overnight chart: a level that looks good on a small stock chart can be invalid because S&P futures already moved well beyond it overnight.
If the market is open, supply and demand are at work, whatever the time a level forms - but every level must meet minimum standards (see The Check List).

passages.h: Does it work in all markets? (Asian markets)
passages.t: A solid yes: supply and demand ('motion into mass') is the same underlying equation everywhere. Behind every market and asset class are people pushing buttons.

He avoids support/resistance because people define them differently (pivots, Fibonacci, Elliott Wave, sloping MAs). Calling it what it is - demand and supply - avoids reinforcing inaccurate definitions.
Rules can be learned from archived articles, free recordings, or the paid XLT where strategy is executed live 3-4 times a week.
Ignoring the overnight session and trading 'levels' already invalidated. Using fuzzy support/resistance definitions (pivots, Fibs, MAs) as if they were supply/demand. Treating every swing as a level.

Did I check the overnight/after-hours chart for levels and for price already beyond my level? For a stock trade, where is the S&P futures relative to its levels? Does the level meet the check-list standards?
“Behind all these markets around the world and different asset classes are just people pushing the buttons.” “Make sure your definition of supply and demand is correct.”
Checking the S&P futures overnight chart before trading a stock level is a Seiden equity-specific filter; Kevin's course is forex-focused.

Supply and demand work all night, so check the night chart. A shop that is open 24 hours still sells things at 3 a.m. The market is the same: if it is open, buyers and sellers are at work. Seiden includes after-hours levels, and before a stock trade he checks the S&P futures overnight. If the futures already went far past their level in the night, the stock level may be used up.
Checking the night chart is like checking whether the cookie jar was raided while you slept before you promise cookies to a friend.
Include after-hours levels; most line up with the day levels anyway. Skip a stock level if index futures already traded well beyond theirs overnight.
Supply and demand work in every market. Say supply and demand, not support and resistance.

passages.h: Step: Look at the night session too
passages.t: The shaded candles traded after hours. While the market is open, supply and demand are at work, whatever the clock says. Many traders only watch the day session and miss this.
Overnight price paused for two candles and rallied hard. It passes the check list: strong exit, little time. Draw it like any other demand.
In the day session price falls back to the overnight demand for the first time. Day-only traders do not even see the level. Buy at the top line.
Price turns up. Stocks, futures, Asian markets: behind every market are just people pushing buttons. Call it what it is, supply and demand, not fuzzy support and resistance.
Do after-hours levels count? - Yes, if they meet the check list standards. Trading a stock: which overnight chart to check? - The S&P futures.

When is a stock level invalid? - When index futures already traded well beyond their level overnight. Does supply and demand work in all markets? - Yes. People push the buttons everywhere. Why not say support and resistance? - Too many different definitions (pivots, Fib, MAs).

From his CME floor days handling Yen order flow, Seiden learned that intervention in free markets never works for long and often produces the opposite move. He treats intervention or bailout news as a cue to look for a supply level to sell, illustrated by a 6/21/10 S&P E-mini short after the Yuan-peg news gap.

When intervention/bailout news drives a rally, look for a nearby supply level to sell short (and vice versa for declines). A gap below the entry implies little demand in that space - a large profit margin. Small supply levels formed after a news gap are valid if the profit margin is large.
He facilitated institutional order flow in currencies (Yen, CAD, GBP, DEM, CHF); the Yen was the most volatile due to Bank of Japan activity.
The BOJ would sell hundreds of millions of Yen to weaken it; the Yen fell to their target, then rallied back to pre-intervention levels and much further.
Lesson: intervention in free markets never works for more than a short period; the 'invisible hand' brings price where it should be.

Before the March 2009 low, every time a bailout was announced students were to find a supply (resistance) level in the S&P and prepare to short. The market would rally on the news, reach supply and decline.

Headline: US equities rally on Yuan intervention; indices gapped up (S&P +1.5%). Reasons to short at the small supply level: novice buying on news; price at a level where supply exceeded demand (low risk); the gap below meant a large profit margin because there is no demand inside a gap.
Intervention is a sign something is broken: an initial move one way, the big move the other way.

passages.t: Intervention news creates the initial move; the supply it leaves behind gives the low-risk short. Enter on the retest of the base, not into the news itself.
6/21/10-style fade: intervention news gaps the market up, price bases at the high (retail supply), and the short on the first retest rides the move back down.
Buying a news-driven gap because an authority 'intervened'. Believing central banks/governments can hold price away from free-market value.
Is the move news/intervention-driven (novice participation)? Is price at a fresh supply/demand level? Is there a gap or empty space giving profit margin toward my target?
“Intervention in free markets never works.” “All I had to see was the word 'intervention' and that was a sell signal for me.”

Kevin: don't trade the news. Seiden deliberately fades intervention-driven rallies at supply (after the news, not into the release). Using a gap as evidence of no opposing demand (profit margin) is a Seiden concept.

When you hear "intervention", look for supply to sell. Imagine a kid holding a beach ball under the water. He can push it down for a while, but his arms get tired and the ball shoots back up. Governments and central banks pushing on prices are that kid. Seiden saw the Bank of Japan push the Yen down, and then it came right back and went much further. So when news says "intervention" lifts the market, he finds the supply it leaves and sells the retest.
A sandcastle wall against the tide: it holds for a moment, then the sea goes where it was always going.

Intervention in free markets never works for long; expect the opposite big move. Sell the first return to the supply that the news rally leaves, not the news itself. There is no demand inside a gap, so a gap below is profit margin.

The headline says the government intervened. The market gaps up hard at the open. Seiden learned on the floor that intervention in free markets never works for long; it often brings the opposite move.

passages.h: Step: Price cannot stay up there
passages.t: At the high price based for three small candles and then slipped. Supply is bigger than demand there. Draw the supply around that base: retail prices.

passages.h: Step: Sell the retest, not the news
passages.t: Do not trade into the release. Wait for the first return to the base and sell there. Novices buy because of the news, at a level where supply exceeds demand.

passages.h: Step: The gap is the profit margin
passages.t: Inside a gap there was no trading, so there is no demand inside it. That empty space below is a big profit margin, all the way back to where the gap began.
Price slides back down through the gap. Initial move one way on the news, the big move the other way.

Does intervention in free markets work? - Never for more than a short time. The word "intervention" means to Seiden? - A sell signal: find supply to short. What is inside a gap? - No demand (or no supply): empty space = profit margin. Trade into the news release? - No. Sell the first return to the supply after it. Intervention pattern? - Initial move one way, big move the other way.

Follow-up Q&A on the 6/21/10 E-mini short: why the origin of the earlier gap-up was not a buy (no profit margin because of supply after supply above), why a big candle appears at the end of moves (the bandwagon), and why a weak-departure supply was still tradable (news rally, big profit margin, levels on top of levels).
Only buy a demand origin if there is upside profit margin (no stacked supply right above).

A big profit margin can compensate for a weaker departure, especially with news-driven extension and stacked levels. Enter before the bandwagon - big end-of-move candles show where the late crowd acts.

passages.h: Why not buy the gap-up origin? (JP)
passages.t: The origin of a strong move up is where demand exceeds supply - the area of interest, not the big green candles themselves.

passages.h: Why not buy the gap-up origin? (JP)
passages.t: But when price came back to that origin, there was supply level after supply level above - no upside profit margin - so it was not a buy and price likely keeps falling.

passages.h: The big candle at the end of a move (Beth)
passages.t: It shows the bandwagon: most traders buy aggressively after a rally into supply and sell aggressively after a decline into demand.

passages.h: The big candle at the end of a move (Beth)
passages.t: People are taught to wait for a strong trend before acting; Seiden's strategy enters well before this crowd, when risk is low.

Ideally the move away from supply is very strong; here it was weak. Compensating factors: the news-driven rally brought price way up the curve; a big profit margin below; levels on top of levels. Primarily the big profit margin made up for the weak departure.
He had no mentor; he asked questions like 'where is buying low?' and answered them from the chart (a demand level). Humans love to complicate and to follow others - both kill accounts.

Two yellow-shaded 'Supply Levels' near 1,126-1,128: one at the high just after 6/21 open and a second small base slightly lower to the right (levels on top of levels).

The gap-up origin is real demand, but with supply level after supply level just above it there is little upside profit margin, so the return is not a buy.
The largest candle usually prints at the end of a move: the bandwagon chases the rally into supply (or the decline into demand), which is where XLT takes the other side.
Buying the origin of a gap-up when several supply levels sit overhead. Buying the big green candle after the move or selling the big red candle after a decline. Overcomplicating and copying others.

Is there clear space to the next opposing level? If the departure is weak, do I have compensating odds (profit margin, stacked levels, extended news move)? Am I entering before or after the bandwagon candle?
“You are identifying the 'bandwagon' on a price chart.” “Ask the right questions, get the right answers and life is good.”
Kevin requires a strong move away to qualify a zone; Seiden lets a large profit margin plus stacked levels compensate for a weak departure.

Demand alone is not enough; you need room to the next supply. Imagine a great parking spot, but a wall is right in front of it so you cannot drive out. A demand level with supply just above is that spot: good level, no room to go. Seiden also notes that the biggest candle comes at the end of a move, when the bandwagon jumps on. He gets in before the bandwagon, and a big profit margin can even make up for a weak exit.
Party crowd: the most people pile onto the dance floor just before the music stops. Be there early, and leave when they rush in.
Only buy a demand origin if there is room up to the next supply. The biggest candle at the end of a move is the bandwagon arriving late.
A big profit margin, a news-stretched move and stacked levels can make up for a weak exit.

passages.h: Step: The gap-up origin is demand
passages.t: Price paused, then gapped up with long green candles. The origin of a strong move up is where demand exceeds supply. The area of interest is the pause, not the big green candles themselves.

passages.h: Step: But look what sits above
passages.t: Right above the gap there is supply level after supply level. Those are the places where price fell before. If you buy at the gap origin, where will price go? Into supply almost at once.
Price touched the lower supply and fell back to the gap origin. Demand is there, but the profit margin up to the supply is small. Small reward for the risk: it is not a buy.
The origin did not hold. With heavy supply overhead, buyers had nothing to gain, and price fell through. The margin decides.

Demand origin with supply right above? - Not a buy: no profit margin. Area of interest in a strong move up? - The origin (the base), not the big green candles. Big candle at the end of a move shows? - The bandwagon: the late crowd chasing. Main thing that offset a weak departure? - A big profit margin. Two account killers? - Complicating things and following others.

We are conditioned to buy cheap everywhere except in stocks, where we wait for good company, strong earnings, uptrend and rising MAs - i.e. high prices. Intel's quadrupled earnings gapped price straight into the origin of a huge prior decline: the right action was to be a seller.

When all the 'good stock' criteria are true, assume price is likely high - check for supply. A positive news gap into the origin of a strong prior decline is a sell, not a buy. Before buying, ask whether someone will buy it from you higher.

With cars and houses we negotiate down and seek wholesale prices. With stocks we are taught to wait for good company, strong earnings, healthy balance sheet, quality management, uptrend and rising MAs - when all true, price is high. That is paying $50,000 for a $30,000 car.

passages.h: INTC earnings (April 15 Hour With The Pros)
passages.t: INTC earnings quadrupled to 43 cents vs 38 expected; revenue +44%; price gapped up. The gap went right into the origin of a huge, strong decline - supply exceeds demand there. Buyers made two losing mistakes: buying after a rally and buying into supply. Ask: 'If I buy here, will someone buy it from me higher?'

passages.t: The supply was identified in advance, live, before the earnings gap arrived.

passages.t: Great news delivered price to retail supply: a sell, not a buy. Targets sit at prior swing areas below; the first was hit within days.
INTC: quadrupled earnings gap price up into the supply where a large decline began; the low-risk action is to sell there with targets below.
Buying because earnings, fundamentals and trend all look good. Buying after a rally into supply. Getting lost in pattern recognition instead of simple buy-low/sell-high logic.
Is the news pushing price into a fresh supply/demand origin? Did price rally into supply (or fall into demand) before my entry? Will someone pay me more from here?
“If I buy the stock here, will someone buy it from me higher?” “The only question that matters, however, is this: Should you be the buyer or the seller?”
Kevin's lessons treat news as something to avoid trading; Seiden uses earnings gaps into supply as swing short setups.

Great news can deliver price to a terrible buying price. When you buy a car, you haggle to pay less. When you buy a stock, you are taught to wait until everything looks perfect, which is exactly when the price is high. That is paying $50,000 for a $30,000 car. When Intel posted amazing earnings, price gapped straight into the spot where a huge fall had started. The smart move was to sell, not buy.
Buying an umbrella for ten dollars during a rainstorm when it cost two dollars on a sunny day.
When every "good stock" box is ticked, price is probably high. Check for supply. A good-news gap into the origin of a big decline is a sell. Ask: if I buy here, will someone buy it from me higher?

passages.h: Step: Where did the big decline start?
passages.t: Price paused for two candles at the top and then collapsed. Supply was far greater than demand right there. Mark it before anything else happens.
Price grinds back up for months. Good company, rising trend, rising averages. This is when most people are taught to buy, and it is exactly when price is high.

passages.h: Step: Great earnings gap price into supply
passages.t: Earnings quadruple and price gaps up straight into the origin of the big decline. Ask one question: if I buy here, will someone buy it from me higher? With fresh supply right here, probably not.
The buyers make two mistakes: buying after a rally and buying into supply. Sell to them at supply, stop above it, with targets at prior swing areas below.
Price fell to both targets. The news was real, but the price was retail.

All "good stock" boxes ticked usually means? - Price is high. Positive news gap into the origin of a strong decline? - A sell, not a buy. The question to ask before buying? - Will someone buy it from me higher? Car analogy? - Waiting for perfect news is paying $50,000 for a $30,000 car. The only question that matters? - Should I be the buyer or the seller here?

The lowest-risk buys are far down the supply/demand curve, and price usually gets there on very bad news. BP's oil-spill collapse reached a fresh monthly demand level ($26-28) and XLT bought, deliberately skipping a closer grey area that was not fresh.

Only buy at FRESH demand; skip areas already traded through repeatedly. Very bad news pushing price far down the curve into fresh demand is a buy context. Prefer the deeper, fresh level over a closer, used one.
Prices turn where supply/demand are most out of balance; buying far down the curve gives huge upside margin and low risk.
Price rarely falls to such levels and does not stay there long, because demand greatly exceeds supply.
Stocks usually reach those levels on very bad news - the worse the news, the lower the price.

XLT identified demand at the $26-$28 range on the monthly chart. The grey area higher up was skipped because a key rule requires a 'fresh' demand level, which it was not. The logic is simple; acting is hard because the news is so bad. An XLT member sold at 38.47 for an $11 per-share gain.
Wall Street says turning points can't be timed; Seiden argues the average person can time them with a high degree of accuracy using rules - not always right, but with high odds.

passages.t: The grey area is not fresh demand - price had already traded there repeatedly. Very bad news drove price far down the curve into fresh monthly demand: the lowest-risk buy.
BP monthly logic: the closer grey area had been traded through repeatedly and was not demand; the fresh base far below was, and that is where the bad-news collapse was bought.
Buying the first visible support that is not fresh. Selling at wholesale prices because the news is terrible. Letting emotion about the event decide the trade.
Is my demand level fresh (not repeatedly revisited)? Is price far down the curve with large upside margin? Am I acting despite bad news, based on the level?
“The demand level in question must be a 'fresh' demand level.” “Price simply dropped down to deep discount, wholesale prices.”
Matches Kevin's fresh-zone emphasis; Seiden adds the 'No Demand' labelling of a used area and applies it to multi-decade monthly investing.

Buy only at fresh demand far down the curve, even on awful news. Imagine a bakery where the cookie tray was emptied at lunch, and another tray in the back nobody has touched. If you want a cookie, go to the full tray. A fresh demand level is the full tray: its buy orders have never been used. When BP collapsed on the oil-spill news, Seiden skipped the closer, already-emptied area and bought the fresh level far below.
Fishing in a pond nobody has fished, instead of the one where everyone has been fishing all week.

The lowest-risk buys are far down the supply/demand curve. Only buy FRESH demand; skip areas price has traded through again and again. Price usually gets that low on very bad news. Act on the level, not the feeling.

passages.h: Step: The fresh base far below
passages.t: Years ago price paused for two candles and rallied strongly. Price has never been back. That is fresh demand, far down the curve.

passages.h: Step: The grey area is not fresh
passages.t: Higher up there is an area price traded through again and again. It looks like support, but the buy orders there were used up long ago. A key rule: demand must be fresh. Skip it.
A disaster hits and price collapses. The worse the news, the lower the price. Price drops into the grey area, and it does not hold.

passages.h: Step: Buy at fresh, wholesale demand
passages.t: Price reaches the fresh base far down the curve. Demand greatly exceeds supply here, so price does not stay long. The logic is simple; acting is hard because the news is awful. Buy.
Price rallies strongly from the fresh level, as the XLT member who sold at 38.47 for an $11 gain saw.

Lowest-risk buys sit where? - Far down the supply/demand curve, at fresh demand. A level traded through many times is? - Not fresh: skip it. How does price usually reach deep demand? - On very bad news. Why is acting hard at these levels? - The news is so bad that emotion says sell. BP: which level did XLT buy? - Fresh monthly demand around $26-28.

Strategy is a direct function of your belief system. News, earnings, upgrades and indicators are 'invitations' to buy or sell; profitable traders filter them through the objective supply/demand picture. Examples: the 6/21/10 Yuan-news S&P short, the INTC earnings short, and the BP oil-spill buy.
Filter every news item or indicator through the objective supply/demand picture before acting.
Negative news into fresh demand = look to buy; positive news into fresh supply = look to sell.
Avoid the two novice mistakes: buying after a rally and buying at supply (mirror for selling).
Market invitations based purely on supply and demand (reality). Everything else: news, earnings, upgrades/downgrades, tips, indicators (illusion and a trap).
A good earnings report or buy rating does not equal demand; a downgrade may be a low-risk buy.

Ask two questions: what does the news suggest I do (buy), and what would a consistently profitable buyer/seller of anything do at this price (do nothing or sell)? Near the top price based sideways and could not stay - more willing supply than demand.
Buyers at the short were buying after a significant advance and at supply - the two novice mistakes.
Your psychological belief system IS your strategy; beware even the slightest illusion. Failing to follow rules is usually not a lack of discipline but a conflict between rules and beliefs.
All influences on price are reflected in price: news -> thoughts/perceptions -> action (buy or sell). Filter through true supply/demand before forming a perception.
Conventional S/R (clusters of activity) is not necessarily true supply/demand; a unique simple pattern shows peak supply/demand.
Negative news that brings price to fresh demand is typically a buying opportunity. Positive news that brings price to fresh supply is typically a selling opportunity.
INTC: very positive earnings and a strong uptrend, yet the gap reached supply (origin of a strong decline) for the first time - those buyers lost.
BP: bad oil-spill news pushed price to the origin of a strong rally; XLT bought at wholesale.
Price must DECLINE to reach fresh demand; most people only buy after rising prices and good news.
A strategy that works is not market- or time-specific; coupon cutters already have the right belief system.

passages.t: Example 3: catastrophic news at fresh monthly demand was an invitation to buy.
Seiden's flow: every input is only an invitation that passes through your beliefs; the profitable trader filters it through the objective supply/demand picture before acting.
Treating news, upgrades or earnings as buy/sell signals. Blaming lack of discipline when the real problem is conflicting beliefs. Equating clusters of trading activity with true supply/demand.

What is the news inviting me to do, and what does the level say? Is price at FRESH supply/demand? Am I buying after a rally or selling after a decline? Do my beliefs agree with my rules for this trade?
“Your psychological belief system IS your trading and/or investing strategy.” “The objective supply and demand relationship in markets is revealed most clearly in price and price alone.”
Seiden's belief-system/invitation framework is broader psychology than Kevin's mindset notes; it explicitly classifies news and indicators as illusion inputs.

News is an invitation; the level decides whether you accept it. Every day the market sends you party invitations: earnings, news, tips, upgrades, indicators. A wise kid does not go to every party; she checks who is really there first. Seiden checks where price sits: at fresh demand, at fresh supply, or in the middle. Bad news at demand is a buy invitation, and good news at supply is a sell invitation. Everything else, he stays home.
A coupon cutter does not buy because the ad is loud; she buys because the price is low. She already has the right belief system.

Your belief system IS your strategy. News, earnings, upgrades and indicators are only invitations. Filter them through supply and demand. Negative news into fresh demand = buy; positive news into fresh supply = sell.

passages.h: Step: Reality: where are the levels?
passages.t: Before any news, read price. This base launched a rally: demand. At the top price based sideways and could not stay: more willing supply than demand.
Good news hits and price rallies back toward the top. The news invites you to buy. That is only an invitation, and it passes through your beliefs before it becomes an action.

Ask two questions. What does the news suggest I do? Buy. What would a consistently profitable buyer of anything do at this price? Not buy: price is at fresh supply after a big advance. Positive news into fresh supply is a selling opportunity.
Price turns down. The buyers bought after a significant advance and at supply, the two novice mistakes.

Your strategy is a function of? - Your belief system. News, tips, upgrades, indicators are? - Invitations (illusion), not signals. Negative news into fresh demand? - Typically a buying opportunity. Positive news into fresh supply? - Typically a selling opportunity. Not following rules is usually? - A conflict between rules and beliefs. Clusters of activity are? - Not necessarily true supply/demand.

Q&A: why ES 1083-1085 was a weak demand level versus 1073-1075, another odds enhancer (levels on top of levels), why little time at a level means strength, and what a 'fresh' level is (first or second return only).

Prefer levels with no recent price action to their left (fresh). Prefer levels lower on the curve with stronger initial departure. Trade the first (at most second) return to a level. Two stacked levels with a big profit margin beat a single level.

1083-1085 had plenty of recent price action to its left - likely not fresh. 1073-1075 was lower on the curve (higher probability and bigger margin) and its initial rally was stronger; it produced a 13-point rally.
Not perfect either - trading seeks better odds and large margins, not perfection; trading both robotically with stops/targets still nets a profit.
Levels on top of levels: like a sell stack at 1070 with an even larger stack at 1071 - more comfortable shorting.
Time at level: books say more activity = stronger; Seiden says the opposite - big imbalance means few transactions, few candles and low volume.
'Motion into mass' confusion is resolved: strong levels are where little trading happened.
Demand is a stack of buy orders; each return fills some of them, so willing buyers decrease with each visit.

Buy when demand is strongest: the first, or sometimes second, return. After that the level is not fresh and odds fall rapidly. Best: enter the first time price revisits a level that has significant profit margin.
A demand level is a pile of buy orders: the first return meets the most of them, the second fewer, and after that the level is no longer fresh and tends to break.
Buying a demand level with a lot of recent trading around it. Trading a level on its third+ visit. Seeking perfect levels instead of better odds.
Is this the first (or second) return? Is there recent price action to the left of the level? Is the level low on the curve with a strong departure? Are there stacked levels and a large profit margin?
“We are not looking for perfection, we are looking for better odds and large profit margins.”
“Focus on entering a position at a supply or demand level the first time price revisits that level.”
Kevin also weighs how many times a zone was tested; Seiden's order-stack explanation (orders get filled each visit) gives the mechanism and allows a second touch at most.

Buy the first visit to a fresh level; each visit uses up orders. A demand level is a pile of buy orders, like a pile of sandbags. Each time price comes back, it knocks some bags off. The first visit meets the most bags, the second fewer, and after that the wall is mostly gone. So Seiden trades the first (sometimes second) return. He prefers levels with no busy trading to their left, lower on the curve, with a strong first rally.
An all-you-can-eat buffet: arrive first and the trays are full; arrive third and only crumbs are left.
Fresh = first or sometimes second return. After that, odds fall fast. A level with lots of recent price action to its left is likely not fresh. We seek better odds and big margins, not perfection.
Two places look like demand. The lower base was left with a strong rally. The higher one has lots of price action around it.

passages.h: Step: Not fresh: busy to its left
passages.t: The higher level has plenty of recent trading to its left. Buy orders there have already been used. Likely not fresh, weaker.

passages.h: Step: Lower on the curve, stronger rally
passages.t: The lower level is further down the curve (bigger margin, higher probability) and its first rally was stronger. Plan the buy there.
Price comes down, pauses at the busy level and breaks through it.
Price reaches the lower, fresh demand on its first return and rallies. Not perfect, just better odds and a big margin.

Demand is a stack of? - Buy orders. Each return fills some of them. Best time to trade a level? - The first time price revisits it (at most the second). Recent price action to the left of a level means? - Likely not fresh. Lower on the curve means? - Higher probability and bigger profit margin. Seiden seeks perfection? - No: better odds and large profit margins.

Level II, Total View and the Matrix bid/offer ladders do not show the real willing buyers and sellers; they can be bluffs. A live AAPL example showed 1600 bid vs 200 offer right at supply, and price collapsed seconds later. Trust price. The article ends with an educational short idea in XLNX at daily supply aligned with QQQQ weekly supply.

Base decisions on price-defined supply/demand, not displayed bid/offer size. A big bid into fresh supply can be a lure for novice buyers - stick to the short. Check the index/sector for aligned supply/demand to raise odds on a single-stock trade.
On the CME floor he held real institutional orders, stacked by price; the largest buy stack below price was where it would turn higher.
Level II-type tools claim to show this, but market makers can post and pull bids and offers freely.
S&P E-mini shows hundreds-thousands on bid/offer but only 1-2 contracts trade at a time - not real.
If you truly saw real orders you would not be allowed to trade - he was monitored by cameras and recorded lines on the desk.
A 2-minute supply level formed where price could not stay; on the rally back it was the place to short.
At that moment the Matrix showed 1600 bid vs 200 offer - books say buy. Seconds later price collapsed. Institutions with too much to sell need novice buyers; a big displayed bid invites them.

XLNX rallied with the NASDAQ toward daily supply: entry $27.75, stop about $28.50, target around $25.50 unless new levels form. The NASDAQ (QQQQ) also approaching weekly supply raised the odds. Alternatives: short stock, buy puts, or a credit spread.

passages.t: The visible order book said buyers dominated; price at supply said otherwise - and price won. Level II sizes can be bluffs; trust the chart.

passages.h: Chart: Left: QQQQ weekly '08-'10 with 'Supply (retail prices)' near 49-51 at the 2008 high and price rallying back to 49.24. Right: XLNX daily with 'Supply (retail prices)' ~27.70-28.10 at the upper-left high and price rallying to 26.73 toward it.
passages.t: A stock short idea is stronger when its index is also arriving at higher-timeframe supply. Both charts: the rally is into retail prices, so the low-risk side is short.
AAPL example: the Matrix showed 1600 bid vs 200 offered right at supply; the visible orders were not the real sellers and price dropped hard. The chart is what you trust.
Buying because the bid is much bigger than the offer. Believing Level II/Matrix shows institutional intentions. Trading a stock level without checking the index level.
Is my decision based on price levels only? Is the related index also at an aligned level? Are entry, stop and target defined before the touch?
“To answer the question, 'Who can you trust?' The answer is simple. Trust price.” “These bids and offers are not exactly real!”
Kevin does not cover Level II or order-book data; Seiden explicitly rejects it as unreliable.
Index alignment (QQQQ weekly supply supporting an XLNX short) is a stock-specific MTF/correlation filter.

The order book can bluff. Price cannot. Trust price. Imagine a poker player who pushes a huge pile of fake chips into the middle to scare you. Level II and bid/offer screens can be like those fake chips: anyone can post a big order and pull it a millisecond later. Seiden once saw 1,600 bid against 200 offered right at supply. The book said buy, the chart said sell, and seconds later price collapsed.
A shop window that says "Huge crowd inside!" while the store is empty. Look at what people actually paid, not the sign.

Displayed bids and offers are not the real willing buyers and sellers. A big bid under fresh supply can be a lure for novice buyers. Check that the index is also at an aligned level to raise the odds.
Price rallied, could not stay at this level for more than two candles and fell. Supply is bigger than demand there.
Price rallies back toward the supply. This is the place to short.
At the touch the order book shows 1,600 bid and only 200 offered. Books say that means buy. But bids and offers can be posted and pulled in a millisecond, and real sellers do not show their size.
Seconds later price falls rapidly. A big displayed bid is often a lure: institutions with too much to sell need novice buyers.

Who can you trust? - Price. Are Level II bids and offers real? - Not exactly: they can be posted and pulled at will. Why show a big bid at supply? - To lure novice buyers for sellers with size. Extra odds for a stock short? - The index also at aligned higher timeframe supply. XLNX vehicles named? - Short stock, buy puts, or a credit spread.

Conventional TA says strong support/resistance has many candles and heavy volume; Seiden argues the opposite - the most out-of-balance levels have very few candles and low volume. An ES 15-minute short at a four-candle supply level illustrates it, followed by a SPY 240-minute idea at supply with no demand below.
Prefer levels with very few candles and low volume at the base. Short the first retrace into a small-base supply after a sharp drop.
Thin, little-traded areas below supply mean little demand - easy downside path (and vice versa).
Markets turn where supply and demand are 'most' out of balance; the more imbalance, the stronger the turn.
At a big imbalance all the potential is on one side, so actual trading activity is small: few candles, low volume.
Supply level of only four little candles before price dropped - price could not stay there.
He shorted the retrace into it, selling to a buyer who probably ignored the level because it had so little activity. That lack of activity is what makes it strong.
Price has rallied far and is near supply (yellow), whose initial decline was strong and had little time spent at it.
A circled area below with hardly any trading = no demand, so price can fall into it easily. Overhead supply plus no solid demand below suggests a pause or reversal.

Price falls, then rallies back to just under the level - arrow 'Amateur buying (my short entry)' - and collapses to ~1,187 by noon (last 1,185.75). passages.h: Chart: @ES 15-minute, 4/27/10: a small four-candle base (circled, ~1,207.5-1,210) right before a drop is labelled 'Supply (Retail)'; price gaps lower, rallies back just under it ('Amateur buying (my short entry)'), then collapses to ~1,186. Statement: net +$2,313.20.
passages.t: Few candles at the level = big imbalance = strong supply. The amateur buys the rally; the professional sells it at the supply.

passages.h: Chart: SPY 240-minute May-Oct 2010: yellow supply box at the May high (~117-118) carried across; price has climbed from ~102 (July) to ~116 by 10/6, just under supply; a circled area of sparse trading on the right (~114-115) shows no demand below.
passages.t: Approaching supply with no demand below: the short side has room. Thin price action means little time spent there, so no strong demand to stop a decline.
The ES 15-minute short came from a four-candle, low-volume supply; a long, busy sideways area is where buyers and sellers agreed (balance), not where price turns sharply.
Looking for many candles and heavy volume to find strong levels. Ignoring small levels because they are 'hardly noticeable'.
How many candles are in the base? Was the departure strong? Is the path to my target thinly traded (little opposing interest)?
“Lack of activity is what makes it such a strong supply level.” “Don't be afraid to question something everyone believes to be true.”
Kevin caps basing at about six or seven candles; Seiden argues the logic and adds 'thin areas with no demand' as a reason the target is easy to reach.

Fewer candles at a level means a stronger level. At a busy playground swing, kids line up and take turns for an hour: that is balance. But if the ice cream truck pulls up, every kid drops everything and runs at once, and the swing is empty in seconds. A level where price stayed only a few candles is that moment: everyone was on one side. Textbooks say lots of candles and volume make a strong level. Seiden says the opposite.
A hot stove: you touch it for half a second and leap away. The shorter the touch, the hotter the stove.

The more out of balance, the less trading happens: few candles, low volume. Long busy areas are balance, not strong turning points. A thin, little-traded area below supply means little demand to stop a fall.
Price traded sideways for a long time with many candles. Textbooks call that strong support and resistance. Seiden calls it balance: buyers and sellers agreed.
Then a small base of only four candles, and price gapped and dropped hard. Price could not stay. Hardly noticeable, and that is exactly why it is strong.
Where supply and demand are most out of balance, all the potential is on one side. Few trades happen, so few candles and low volume.
Price rallies back to just under the little level. The buyer probably ignored the level because it had so little activity. Short the first retrace.
Price collapses. Lack of activity is what made it such a strong supply level.

Strong level: many or few candles? - Few. Strong level: high or low volume? - Usually low volume. Long busy sideways area means? - Balance, not a strong level. Thin trading below supply means? - Little demand to stop a decline. What makes a tiny level strong? - Its lack of activity: a big imbalance.

Seiden recommends the 10-year T-note futures (TY/ZN): huge volume and liquidity make supply/demand levels clean and easy to identify. A 15-minute short at a yellow supply box made $750, and timing bond turns helps forecast interest-rate moves for mortgages and investments.
Prefer highly liquid markets where levels are clean. A sideways area followed by a drop is supply; sell the first rally back.
Know the contract specs (tick value etc.) but don't expect them to tell you where to trade.
One of the largest global treasury markets; it is where interest rates are set in a free market. Very liquid, so quality supply/demand levels are solid and easy to see.
Price traded sideways in a yellow area - looks balanced, but it is never balanced; the imbalance just takes time to show. The drop from the area proved supply exceeded demand (retail prices).
When price rallied back he sold to someone buying at retail; he took a quick $750 because he had a plane to catch. The supply level was so clear you could almost draw a box around it.
CME contract specs give value, months, tick value, hours, symbols - but never where to buy and sell. Bond prices up = rates down and vice versa; supply on TY means rates about to rise.
Investors would use larger-timeframe levels; key living-standard markets (rates, currencies, food, energy) are all futures.

Yellow 'Supply' box around 126'06-126'08 where price traded sideways after an early decline; price drops from it, then rallies back up; arrow 'Short Entry' at the top of the box. Price then declines to about 125'22. Volume bars below. Statement Oct 26, 2010: gross 812.50, 'Low Risk Profit: $750.60'.

passages.t: Drop-base-drop supply in a deep, liquid market gives clean, objective levels. Short the first return with the stop just above the box.

passages.h: Chart: CME 10-Year US Treasury Note futures contract specifications: $100,000 face value, tick 1/2 of 1/32 ($15.625), March/June/Sept/Dec cycle, open outcry 7:20-14:00 CT, Globex Sun-Fri 17:30-16:00, tickers TY / ZN.
passages.t: Know the contract: tick value and trading hours determine stop size and position sizing.
TY 15-minute: price paused sideways in a decline (supply), dropped, and the first rally back to the box was the short, with the stop just above it.
Thinking a sideways area is truly balanced. Confusing contract knowledge with a trading edge.
Is the market liquid enough for clean levels? Do I know the tick value and session hours? Is the level a clear box with a sharp departure?
“It is never a balanced equation. It simply takes time for this unbalanced equation to play out.” “You can almost draw a box around that level.”
Kevin's material centres on forex; Seiden promotes the TY note futures and links bond levels to interest-rate forecasting.

Deep, liquid markets draw clean boxes. Sell the first return. In a huge, busy lake the water is calm and you can see the bottom clearly. The 10-year Treasury note is one of the biggest markets on Earth, so its supply and demand levels are clean and easy to see. Seiden saw price pause sideways in a fall, then drop again. When it rallied back to that box, he sold and took a quick $750 before catching his plane.
Reading a sign in bright daylight versus fog: big liquid markets are the daylight.
Liquid markets give clean, objective levels. A sideways pause in a decline, then a drop, is supply; sell the first rally back. Know the contract specs, but they never tell you where to buy and sell.
In a decline, price traded sideways for a few candles. It looks balanced, but it never is; the imbalance just takes time to show.
Price fell from the area. That proves supply exceeded demand there: retail prices. In a deep, liquid market like the 10-year note, you can almost draw a box around it.

passages.h: Step: Sell the first rally back
passages.t: Price rallies back up to the box. Short at the bottom line, stop just above the top line. Know your tick value so you can size the stop, but the contract specs never tell you where to trade.
Price falls. Bond prices and interest rates move opposite, so supply on the note means rates were about to rise.

Why trade the 10-year note? - Huge volume and liquidity: clean, easy levels. Is a sideways area balanced? - Never; the imbalance just takes time to show. Bond prices up means rates? - Down (and the reverse). Contract specs tell you? - Tick value, months, hours, symbols, not where to trade. TY tick value? - Half of 1/32, about $15.625.

Hunter vs hunted: the Bull Trap is shorting when price breaks above an obvious high (here the Globex overnight high) straight into fresh supply just above. Breakout buyers provide liquidity. The 11/17/10 Pro Picks ES short at 1182 (stop 1184.25) hit both targets.
Bull trap: short when price breaks an obvious high (e.g. overnight/Globex high) into fresh supply right above it.
Bear trap (mirror): buy when price breaks an obvious low into fresh demand right below it. Carry supply/demand lines forward so you know where price will likely turn.

Like the polar bear at the seal's breathing hole or the crocodile at the waterhole, professionals set traps for novices. There are invitations to buy that are real opportunities and others that are traps.

Supply level = yellow shaded area where price could not stay and declined; two lines are wrapped around it and carried forward. The Globex (overnight) high sat just below the supply; most traders watch the S&P.
When the regular session rallied above the Globex high, breakout buyers rushed in - right into fresh supply.
Entry 1182, stop 1184.25, targets 1179 and 1175; 1182 became the high of the day and both targets filled.
Most are trained to buy a new high of the day and buy at supply; he is trained to sell there. Trading is a transfer from those who fall for traps to those who set them.

383): Pro Picks screen 11/17/2010, ES S&P E-mini, Short. Trends: short-term Down, long-term Up. 00. 00, P/L $1,350, +10 points. The chart shows a yellow 'Supply above Globex High' box carried right to 'Bull Trap Short'. Trade strategy text explains the bullish expectations above the Globex high.

passages.t: The plan was published before the trade: entry, stop and targets all objective. Bull trap: the break above the Globex high runs straight into supply.

passages.h: Chart: @ES 10-minute (Dec10): yellow 'Supply' ~1,182-1,184 at the left (origin of a sharp drop to ~1,172); price recovers and pokes above the prior high into supply ('Short Entry' circled ~1,182); it then declines to both circled targets (~1,176 and ~1,174). Statement: 'Low Risk Profit: $732.40'.
passages.t: Breakout buyers above the prior high provide the liquidity for the short. Small stop above supply, two targets below - a lopsided reward to risk.
Bull trap: price pokes above the overnight (Globex) high into supply just above it; short the proximal line with a small stop, T1 and T2 below.
Buying a breakout of the day's/overnight high without checking for supply above. Buying at supply because it looks like strength.

Is there an obvious high/low (Globex, prior day) just inside a fresh level? Will a break of it create breakout buyers/sellers who become my liquidity? Entry at the level, stop just beyond, targets set?
“This game is a transfer of accounts from those who fall for professional 'traps'.” “When there is a fresh supply level just above, this bullish thinking is a TRAP.”
Kevin teaches liquidity traps before zones; Seiden's version names a specific trigger - the Globex/overnight high just under fresh supply.

A breakout into fresh supply is a trap; be the hunter. A polar bear does not chase seals across the ice. It waits at the breathing hole where the seal must come up. Professionals do the same with traders: they wait where novices must act. When price breaks above an obvious high, like the overnight high, breakout buyers rush in. If fresh supply sits right above that high, those buyers just walked into the trap, and Seiden sells to them.
A crocodile at the waterhole: the animals come for a drink because they are thirsty, and that is exactly where it waits.

Bull trap: short when price breaks an obvious high into fresh supply just above. Bear trap: buy when price breaks an obvious low into fresh demand just below. Carry level lines forward so you know where price will likely turn.
Price paused at the top and fell sharply. Wrap two lines around that base and carry them forward. Now you know where price will likely turn.
Overnight (Globex) price made a high just below the supply. Most traders watch that high. A break of it will look like strength.
In the session price rallies above the Globex high. Breakout buyers jump in, straight into fresh supply. When fresh supply sits just above, that bullish thinking is a trap.
Short at supply with a small stop just above it, targets below. The breakout buyers provide the liquidity for the short.
The entry became the high of the day and both targets filled. Trading is a transfer from those who fall for traps to those who set them.

Bull trap? - Price breaks an obvious high into fresh supply just above: short. Bear trap? - Price breaks an obvious low into fresh demand just below: buy. Who provides the liquidity for a bull trap short? - The breakout buyers. Why carry lines forward? - To know in advance where price will likely turn. Trading is a transfer from...? - Those who fall for traps to those who set them.

Supply and demand never change; buy wholesale and sell retail like any business. A Pro Picks long in Euro futures at fresh daily demand (1.3085) was supported by the US Dollar index hitting fresh supply at the same time, yielding about $4,400 in shorter-term trades.

Buy at fresh demand (wholesale), sell at fresh supply (retail). Raise odds by confirming the inverse/related market is at the opposite level (EUR at demand while USD index at supply). A swing level can be used for multiple shorter-term trades.

If it looks, walks and quacks like a duck, it's a duck - no matter what experts or fancy math say. Adam Smith described supply and demand; it has never changed, like gravity. A gas station buys gum at $0.25 and sells at $1.00 - traders must do the same.

Euro futures had declined for days toward a fresh demand zone; Pro Picks long entry 1.3085 (range 1.3085-1.2970), stop 1.2965, targets 1.3300 and 1.3350. At the same time the US Dollar index was nearing fresh supply - higher odds.
Price reached the zone a day later and turned up; he used the level for several shorter-term trades.

Right 'Euro/US Dollar - Daily Chart' (@EC): yellow demand ~1.30-1.31 at the September base, price declining from ~1.42 to touch it (last 1.3127).
