passages.t: A long against both trends, justified by fresh demand and the margin above. The trade strategy notes the US Dollar is at fresh supply at the same time.

passages.h: Chart: Left: US Dollar index daily - yellow supply ~80.8-81.6 at the September high, price rallying from ~76 back up into it (~80.7). Right: Euro/US Dollar daily - yellow demand ~1.30-1.31 at the September base, price falling from ~1.42 back down into it (~1.31).
passages.t: Mirror image: dollar at supply while the euro is at demand. Correlated confirmation raises the odds of both turns.

passages.h: Chart: Euro FX trading platform DOM with the open P/L circled, plus the 11/30 statement of Euro currency futures trades; 'Low Risk Profit: $4,421.55'.
passages.t: Shorter-term trades taken off the daily demand produced the profit.
Euro long at fresh daily demand was backed by the US Dollar index hitting fresh daily supply at the same moment - the mirror image confirms the trade.
Complicating a simple supply/demand picture. Selling at wholesale levels because the trend is down.
Is the correlated/inverse market at an aligned opposite level? Is my zone fresh? Entry, stop and targets set before the touch?
“Gravity is always gravity.” “Maybe you're really just looking at a Duck, thinking it's a Babboon.”
Using the Dollar index at supply as confirmation for a EUR long is an inter-market filter not in Kevin's notes.

If it quacks like a duck, it is a duck: buy wholesale. A gas station buys a pack of gum for 25 cents and sells it for a dollar. That is the whole business, and trading is the same. Supply and demand have never changed, just like gravity. When the Euro fell for days into fresh demand, Seiden bought, even though both trends were down. At the same moment the US Dollar was hitting fresh supply, the mirror image.
A seesaw: when one side (the Dollar) is at the very top, the other side (the Euro) is at the very bottom.

Buy at fresh demand (wholesale), sell at fresh supply (retail). It never changes. An inverse market at the opposite level at the same time raises the odds. One swing level can give several shorter-term trades.
Price paused for two candles and rallied strongly: fresh demand. This is the wholesale price, like a gas station buying gum at 25 cents.

passages.h: Step: Days of decline into it
passages.t: Both trends point down and the Euro falls for days toward the demand. Selling here because the trend is down would be selling at wholesale.
At the same time the US Dollar index is rallying into fresh supply. When the inverse market sits at the opposite level, the odds of both turns rise. Buy the Euro at demand.

passages.h: Step: Many trades from one level
passages.t: Price turns up. One swing level can be used for several shorter-term trades, as Seiden did for about $4,400.

Gas station lesson? - Buy gum at $0.25, sell at $1.00: wholesale to retail. Does supply and demand change? - Never. Gravity is always gravity. EUR at demand while USD index at...? - Supply: a confirming mirror image. Can one swing level give several trades? - Yes, shorter-term trades off the same level. Duck rule? - If it looks, walks and quacks like a duck, it is a duck. Keep it simple.

A fuller restatement of the All Star strategy: proper supply/demand plus Bollinger Bands. Short at strong supply when price pierces the upper band, in a downtrend context, with significant profit margin; stop just above supply; T1 = band midline, T2 = the opposing demand. Shown on RIMM 60-minute.

Short at key supply when price pierces the upper Bollinger Band in a downtrend context with significant profit margin; stop just above supply. T1 = Bollinger midline, T2 = opposing demand level. Mirror everything for longs at demand piercing the lower band.
Big profits in sales come from selling to buyers who do not know real value; trading is the same. The strategy focuses on buying from and selling to novices who cannot assess real value.
Supply (yellow) is where price dropped strongly. Return to supply + pierce of upper band = supply exceeds demand, statistical extreme, and a novice buying at supply.
Nearest demand below defines the profit margin; T1 = Bollinger midline (the mean), T2 = demand.
The novice buyer makes two mistakes: buying after a rally outside the upper band and buying at retail prices.

At key supply, piercing the upper band, in the context of a downtrend, with significant profit margin below: sell short at supply with a buy stop just above supply. Targets: first the midline, then the opposing demand level. Opposite rules for longs.

Figure 1 (p.390): RIMM 60-minute (4/13-5/6) with Bollinger Bands (grey midline). Yellow 'Supply' ~73.8-74.2 at the 4/15 high. Yellow 'Demand' ~68.5-69.0 at the 4/26 low, origin of a strong spike up. That spike reaches supply above the upper band - arrow 'Short Entry'. T1 at the midline (~71) is reached, and T2 at the demand (~69) is reached in early May as price falls toward 67.

passages.h: Chart: RIMM 60-minute (4/13-5/6) with Bollinger Bands: yellow 'Supply' ~73.8-74.2 at the 4/15 high and yellow 'Demand' ~68.5-69.0 at the 4/26 low (origin of a strong spike). The spike reaches supply above the upper band ('Short Entry' ~74); price falls to T1 (~71.3, band midline) then T2 at the demand, and continues lower to ~67.
passages.t: Full All Star plan: entry at supply on the band pierce, stop above supply. T1 = band midline, T2 = the opposing demand level.
RIMM 60-minute logic: short where the spike pierces the upper band inside supply, stop just above supply, first target the band midline, second target the demand that launched the spike.
Buying after a rally outside the upper band. Buying at retail prices. Taking the setup without profit margin to the opposing level.
Key level with strong departure? Price piercing the outer band? Trend context agrees (downtrend for shorts)? Profit margin to the opposing level? T1 midline, T2 level set?
“Profitable traders buy at wholesale prices and sell at retail prices.” “Learn to spot the novice trader.”

Kevin uses no indicators and targets with R:R to the next zone; here T1 is the Bollinger midline and a trend-context requirement is added. Completes the earlier 'Lite' version by adding the downtrend context and stop placement.

Sell to the buyer who pays too much: supply, band pierce, downtrend, margin. The best salesmen make big money selling to people who do not know what things are really worth. Seiden's All Star does the same. In a downtrend, when price spikes back into strong supply and pokes outside the upper Bollinger Band, a novice is paying retail after a rally. Seiden sells to him, takes the first profit at the band's middle line and the second at the demand below.
A tourist buying a souvenir at triple price at the airport: you are the shop, not the tourist.
Short at key supply when price pierces the upper band, in a downtrend, with margin below. Stop just above supply. T1 = band midline, T2 = opposing demand. Mirror everything for longs.
Price is falling. In a downtrend we look to sell, so we look for supply.

passages.h: Step: Key supply and the demand below
passages.t: Price paused and dropped strongly: supply. Lower down, a base launched a strong spike up: demand. The space between them is the profit margin.

passages.h: Step: The novice buys outside the band
passages.t: The spike reaches supply and pierces the upper Bollinger Band. The buyer makes two mistakes: buying after a rally outside the upper band, and buying at retail prices. Sell short at supply, buy stop just above it.

passages.h: Step: T1 the midline, T2 the demand
passages.t: First target is the band midline, the mean that price tends to return to. Second target is the opposing demand level.
Price falls to the midline, then to the demand, and keeps going. Profits come from selling to buyers who do not know real value.

All Star short: four conditions? - Key supply, upper band pierce, downtrend context, profit margin below. All Star stop? - A buy stop just above the supply. T1 and T2? - T1 = band midline; T2 = opposing demand.
Two novice mistakes at the spike? - Buying after a rally outside the upper band, and buying at retail. All Star long? - Mirror: demand, lower band pierce, uptrend, margin above.

A clearer restatement of the time odds enhancer with a two-level example: Supply 2 (big, many candles, conventional favourite) was broken, while Supply 1 (two candles) held and produced the short. Little time at a level means a big imbalance.

Ignore levels where price spent a lot of time; they are not out of balance. Favour small, few-candle levels and sell/buy the first retrace into them. Time is one of several odds enhancers deciding level quality.
The more out of balance supply and demand, the stronger and quicker the turn. At big imbalance, activity is low: few candles and usually low volume.
Supply 2: many candles, sharp fall - conventional TA loves it. On the return, price based sideways and broke up through it. XLT ignores such levels because too much time was spent there.

Supply 1: just a few candles, hardly noticeable - most ignore it. Price spent little time there, so a big imbalance; shorted on the retrace (circled), and price dropped hard. The buyer probably followed books that dismiss low-activity levels.
393): candlestick chart (instrument unnamed, prices ~131-140). 8, from which price fell to ~131. 14 marker on the axis).

passages.h: Chart: Candlestick chart (~131-140): 'Supply 1' - a two-candle box ~137.3-137.8 after a decline from ~139.5; 'Supply 2' - a long box of ~15 sideways candles ~134.8-135.8 from which price fell to ~131. On the return price chops at Supply 2 and breaks through it, then spikes into Supply 1 (circled ~137.5) and drops immediately to ~134.
passages.t: The long, busy base failed; the quiet two-candle level held. Less time at a level = more out of balance = stronger turn.
Supply 2 had many candles and was broken on the return; Supply 1 had just two candles, so the imbalance was big, and shorting the first retrace into it produced the drop.
Choosing the big, obvious, many-candle zone. Ignoring small levels because they are barely noticeable.
How many candles are in this base vs other candidate levels? If a long-base level is in the way, do I expect it to break? Is the few-candle level fresh with a strong departure?
“That lack of activity is what makes it such a strong supply level.” “By thinking the simple logic through, you will always arrive at truth.”
Kevin includes all basing candles and caps them at about six or seven; Seiden's example shows a long-base zone simply being disregarded as not a level.

The quiet two-candle level beats the big busy one. Two doors: one is a giant, colorful door that everybody notices, and one is a tiny plain door. Behind the giant door people have been coming and going all day, so it barely holds. Behind the tiny door, nobody has been in, and it is locked tight. On the chart, the long sideways base got broken, while the little two-candle level held and sent price down.
A trail that hundreds of hikers walked is worn flat; the untouched path still has its fence.
The more out of balance, the quicker and stronger the turn. Ignore levels where price spent a lot of time. Favour small, few-candle levels and trade the first retrace.
At the top, only two candles before price fell. Most traders do not even notice it.
Lower down, price spent a long time going sideways, then fell sharply. Conventional TA loves this big obvious zone. XLT ignores it: too much time was spent there.
Price rallies back, chops sideways at Supply 2 and breaks up through it. Many candles meant balance, not a big imbalance.
Price spikes into Supply 1. Little time there means a big imbalance. Short the first retrace, stop just above.
Price drops hard. The buyer probably followed the books that dismiss low-activity levels.

Big imbalance means activity is? - Low: few candles, usually low volume. Long many-candle base? - Ignore it: balance, likely to break. Few-candle level? - Favour it; trade the first retrace. What decides how quick the turn is? - How out of balance supply and demand are.

Actions come from behaviour patterns, which come from beliefs; the strongest illusions sit inside conventional technical and fundamental analysis. Covered here: moving averages (lagging, not support/resistance) and the news (BP at $27 demand). The article continues into Fundamental Analysis beyond page 400.

Do not use MAs as support/resistance or trend filters for entries; use price-defined supply/demand. Buy the first return ('B') to a base that produced a dramatic rally ('A'). Treat strong news into a fresh level as a likely exhaustion turn.
Mastering conventional technical/fundamental analysis is an illusion that layers subjective complexity - walking east-west near the equator trying to reach the North Pole.
Strategies that work don't change with market conditions; the core is supply/demand and human behaviour. Beliefs -> behaviour patterns -> actions; change beliefs, not just actions.
Illusion: MAs act as support/resistance or trend filters (crosses, slope). At the 'B' areas the 20 MA sloped down (a 'downtrend') exactly when the low-risk buy appeared - MA users would skip it.
MAs lag; waiting to buy above the 200-day MA means higher risk, smaller profit, and providing profit to those who bought at B. When an MA lines up with real supply/demand it only seems to work.

Reality: 'A' areas are sideways bases followed by dramatic rallies = demand; 'B' is the first return = low-risk buy with small stop, maximum profit potential and highest probability. Indicators are just derivatives of price and volume; price is all you need.

News is the most powerful illusion because strong news creates strong emotion. BP: oil-spill news drove the majority to sell; XLT bought for a long-term hold at $27.00 demand. Once the last seller sells where demand exceeds supply, price rises.

Strong news creates powerful turns opposite to what the majority expects, because one side exhausts itself into an imbalance level. Bad news + collapse in price into demand = low risk, high reward buy.

Two 'A' arrows mark a sideways base at ~1,145-1,150 and a base ~1,180-1,185 that both launched dramatic rallies (green lines drawn as demand zones). Two circled 'B' points mark first returns to each zone - one at ~1,185 and one at ~1,150 (below the 200 MA, with the 20 MA sloping down) - after which price rallied toward ~1,240.

Price rallies back to it - arrows 'Short Entry' and 'Novice Buyer' at the touch - then declines toward ~1.3650. Statement 02/09/10: gross 18,250.00, net 18,034.40.

passages.h: Chart: S&P 500 daily with a blue 20 MA and red 200 MA: two 'A' arrows mark sideways bases (~1,145-1,150 and ~1,180-1,185) that launched dramatic rallies (green demand lines); two circled 'B' points are the first returns to them - one below the 200 MA with the 20 MA sloping down - after which price rallies to ~1,240.
passages.t: The MA said 'downtrend' at exactly the lowest-risk buy. Moving averages lag; demand levels are the objective information.

passages.h: Chart: BP monthly 1996-2011: yellow 'Demand Level' ~26-28 at the 1996 base, carried right; the 2010 oil-spill collapse touches it ('We Bought' circled) and price rebounds to ~47.
passages.t: The news created the fear; the demand level created the buy. Bad news plus a collapse into fresh demand = low risk, high reward.

passages.h: Chart: EUR/USD 30-minute (Feb 2010): 'Supply Level' rectangle ~1.3825-1.3850 at the upper-left high, origin of a drop to ~1.3600; price rallies back to it ('Short Entry' / 'Novice Buyer' arrows at the touch) and falls toward ~1.3680. Statement 02/09/10: gross $18,250, net $18,034.40.
passages.t: The novice buys strength into supply; the short sells to him. Supply/demand works the same in forex as in stocks and futures.
S&P daily logic: the A base launched a dramatic rally (demand); at the first return B the lagging MA still points down, so MA traders skip the low-risk buy that XLT takes.
Skipping a demand buy because the 20 MA slopes down or price is below the 200 MA. Waiting for an MA crossover and buying far above demand. Selling into bad news at wholesale prices.
Is my bias from a level or from an MA/indicator? Is this the first return to the base? Is the news pushing the crowd into my level? Stop small, profit potential to the opposing level maximal?

“Indicators and oscillators are nothing more than a derivative of price and volume.” “No matter how bad the news is, when the last seller sells at a price level where demand exceeds supply, prices rise.”
Agrees with Kevin's no-indicator stance and adds an explicit S&P example where the MA trend filter would block the best buy.
Seiden treats bad-news exhaustion into demand as a buy; Kevin's notes focus on avoiding news releases.

Moving averages lag; the demand level is the real information. Imagine steering a car by looking in the rear-view mirror. You would always turn too late. A moving average is that mirror: it only shows where price has been. At the best buy of all, the first return to a base that launched a rally, the moving average still pointed down. People who trust it skip the buy and pay higher later.
Hearing thunder after the lightning: by the time the indicator speaks, the event already happened.

Do not use moving averages as support, resistance or trend filters for entries. Buy the first return (B) to a base that launched a dramatic rally (A). Strong news into a fresh level often marks an exhaustion turn.

passages.h: Step: A: base plus dramatic rally
passages.t: Price went sideways for three candles and then rallied dramatically. That is demand, the objective information on the chart.

passages.h: Step: The moving average turns down
passages.t: Price pulls back. The moving average now slopes down, so MA traders call it a downtrend and will not buy.
Price returns to A for the first time. This is the low-risk buy: small stop, maximum profit potential and the highest probability. The MA says no at exactly the best buy.
Price rallies strongly. Those who wait for the MA to turn up again buy higher, with more risk and less profit, and they pay those who bought at B.
Do MAs act as support and resistance? - No; they only seem to when they line up with real supply/demand.

A and B in the S&P example? - A = base + dramatic rally (demand); B = first return = low-risk buy. Indicators are? - Derivatives of price and volume. Most powerful illusion? - The news, because it creates strong emotion. Bad news + collapse into demand? - Low risk, high reward buy.

Starting from a friend's 'copy - paste' remark about US chain stores in Dubai, Seiden argues that losing traders copy crowd behaviour and conventional technical-analysis books, while winners think differently and focus only on supply and demand. He walks through an XLT short in the QQQ: a supply level that price left by falling, a pre-planned short when price rallied back, and the cover at the demand level below.

Draw a supply zone only after price has declined from the level; wrap two lines around it and extend them forward. Plan the short before price returns: sell when price rallies back into the supply zone. Place the protective buy stop just above the zone's upper (distal) line. Use the opposing demand level below as the final target; cover the short there.
Enter only where the counterparty is buying after a rally and into supply (or selling after a decline into demand).

Losing traders watch what others do, copy those novice actions into their own belief system and end up with a 'copy - paste' mind and life. The first step to trading success is simply to think differently from most people.
Very few people make consistent low-risk income from conventional TA books, yet more people buy them every day and repeat what they suggest.
Successful people ignore what the crowd is doing and repeat the actions that produced their own success, because they focus on what is real: price moves only through supply and demand.
A level where supply and demand looked balanced; then price declined from it, which revealed that supply was greater than demand.
After that decline, wrap two lines around the level and extend them to the right: this is the supply zone, a potential future turning point.
The plan, made in advance: sell short when price rallies back up to that zone. When it did, risk was low, reward high and odds strong.

The odds come from knowing who is on the other side: a buyer who buys after a rally and into a level where supply exceeds demand, the two classic losing-trader mistakes. One XLT member shorted 2,500 shares at the supply level, per the pre-set plan.
Price then fell to demand, where the short was covered by buying from the 'copy - paste' sellers who were selling after a decline into demand.

Left: participant list (Sam Seiden as moderator) and the chat window; the last chat line, boxed in green, reads roughly 'shorted 2500 qqq 57.70'. Right: the shared whiteboard with several TradeStation windows; the highlighted one is the QQQ chart with a yellow 'Supply' box at the upper left and a yellow 'Demand' box at the lower right.

On the left, after a run up to about 57.90, a small yellow 'Supply' base sits between black lines at about 57.73 (proximal) and 57.81 (distal); price then dropped hard in long red candles to about 57.30 and on to about 57.03.

Figure 2 continued: price bounced to about 57.47 on 4/5, then fell into a yellow 'Demand' base around 57.01-57.12 (late 4/5). On 4/6 it gapped higher at the open and rallied straight back up to the supply's lower line: 'Short Entry' circled at about 57.73.

Figure 2 trade marks: red 'Buy Stop' line just above the zone at about 57.82; blue 'Target 1' at about 57.57; blue 'Target 2' at about 57.15, just above the demand zone's top line. Price fell in large red candles through both targets into demand (last price 57.14). Risk about 9 cents against about 58 cents to Target 2, roughly 6:1.

passages.h: Chart: OTA XLT live room: participants and chat on the left (the boxed line reads 'shorted 2500 qqq 57.70'); the shared whiteboard on the right with the QQQ chart highlighted, a 'Supply' box top-left and a 'Demand' box bottom-right.
passages.t: The trade was posted before price got there: the plan (sell supply) existed in advance and a member simply executed it. The chart in the window is the same QQQ 15-minute setup shown full size on the next page.

passages.h: Chart: QQQ 15-min, 4/3-4/6: supply base about 57.73-57.81 after a run to 57.90, then a hard drop to about 57.03; demand base about 57.01-57.12 late 4/5. On 4/6 price gaps up and rallies straight back to supply: short entry 57.73, buy stop about 57.82, Target 1 about 57.57, Target 2 about 57.15 just above demand.
passages.t: Price fell away from the supply in long red candles, so supply clearly exceeded demand there.

passages.h: Chart: QQQ 15-min, 4/3-4/6: supply base about 57.73-57.81 after a run to 57.90, then a hard drop to about 57.03; demand base about 57.01-57.12 late 4/5. On 4/6 price gaps up and rallies straight back to supply: short entry 57.73, buy stop about 57.82, Target 1 about 57.57, Target 2 about 57.15 just above demand.
passages.t: The entry is at the proximal (lower) line; the stop sits just above the distal line: about 9 cents of risk. Target 2 is placed just above the opposing demand zone: about 58 cents, roughly 6:1.

passages.h: Chart: QQQ 15-min, 4/3-4/6: supply base about 57.73-57.81 after a run to 57.90, then a hard drop to about 57.03; demand base about 57.01-57.12 late 4/5. On 4/6 price gaps up and rallies straight back to supply: short entry 57.73, buy stop about 57.82, Target 1 about 57.57, Target 2 about 57.15 just above demand.
passages.t: The buyers at 57.73 bought after a rally and into supply; the sellers at 57.15 sold after a decline into demand.
QQQ short: supply base, drop, return; sell at proximal, buy stop above distal, Target 1 midway and Target 2 just above demand (about 6:1).
Counterparty logic: the novice buys after a rally into supply and sells after a decline into demand; you take the other side.

Copying the crowd and conventional TA books instead of thinking independently. Buying after a rally in price. Buying into a level where supply already exceeds demand. Selling after a decline into a demand level.
Did price leave this level with a clear decline (supply) or rally (demand)? Are the zone lines drawn and extended forward before price returns? Is the entry, stop and target set in advance?
Is the counterparty buying after a rally into supply (or selling after a drop into demand)? Is there an opposing zone to use as the final target?

“Those who know what they are doing in trading get paid from those who don't.” “Proper market speculation is simple; actually having the right knowledge and discipline to do it is not easy.” “The first step in successful trading is to simply think different than most.”

The 'copy - paste mind' psychology framing is not in Kevin's course. Target 1 here is a level partway down (not a fixed 3:1); Kevin takes 25% at 3:1 and holds the rest to the next HTF opposing zone. Both end at the opposing zone.

Don't copy the crowd; sell where they buy, buy where they sell. A friend in Dubai saw the same American chain stores on every corner and called it a "copy - paste" city. Many traders have copy - paste minds too: they copy what others do and what the books say, and they lose. Seiden thinks differently. He marked supply after price fell from it, planned a short in advance, and when the crowd bought the rally back up, an XLT member sold them 2,500 shares.
In musical chairs, the kid who watches the music, not the other kids, gets the seat.

Think differently from the crowd; price moves only through supply and demand. Draw the zone only after price leaves it, extend it right, and plan the trade before the return. Your profit comes from the trader making the two mistakes on the other side.

passages.h: Step: Price leaves the level by falling
passages.t: After a run up, price paused for two candles. It looked balanced. Then it dropped hard in long red candles, which revealed supply was greater than demand.

passages.h: Step: Wrap two lines and extend them
passages.t: Only after the decline do we draw it: wrap two lines around the base and extend them to the right. This is the supply zone, a future turning point.
The plan is made before price returns: sell short at the bottom line, buy stop just above the top line. The demand below is the final target, with Target 1 halfway.
Price gaps up and rallies straight back to supply. The buyer is buying after a rally and into supply: the two classic losing mistakes. The pre-set short fills.
Price falls through Target 1 to Target 2, just above demand. You cover by buying from copy-paste sellers who sell after a decline into demand. About 6 to 1.

Copy-paste mind? - Copying the crowd and conventional books into your own beliefs. First step to trading success? - Think differently from most people. When is supply revealed? - When price declines from the level. The two buyer mistakes? - Buying after a rally, and buying into supply. QQQ short reward to risk? - About 9 cents risk for 58 cents: roughly 6:1. Who pays those who know? - Those who do not.

Seiden says the entry is the key decision in a trade: entering as close to the turn as possible gives the largest size for the least risk and the biggest distance to target. Price turns where supply and demand are most out of balance, and he lists three XLT 'Odds Enhancers' to find such levels: how price left, how long it stayed, and how far it went before returning. No charts in this article.

Enter as close to the turn in price as possible. Grade the departure: gap away > big-candle move > gradual move. Prefer levels where price spent little time and traded low volume. Prefer levels price moved far away from before returning.
Use the extreme of the move away (lowest low for supply, highest high for demand) before the return as a profit target.
Stops, targets, duration, risk and position sizing all depend on getting the entry right. Entering right at the turn lets you trade the largest position with the least money at risk.
It also puts you farthest from your profit target, so the reward side is as large as it can be.

passages.h: Odds Enhancer 1: how did price leave the level?
passages.t: The stronger the move away, the bigger the imbalance at the level. Three grades of departure, weakest to strongest: a gradual move; a strong move with big red or green candles; a gap away. A gap away is the strongest and shows the biggest imbalance.

passages.h: Odds Enhancer 2: how much time did price spend at the level?
passages.t: Less time at the level means a bigger imbalance. This contradicts the books that favour busy, high-volume levels: if price could spend a long time there, supply and demand cannot have been very out of balance.

passages.h: Odds Enhancer 2: how much time did price spend at the level?
passages.t: A strong imbalance means few transactions and so lower volume: look for levels with little activity and low volume.

passages.h: Odds Enhancer 3: how far did price move away before returning?
passages.t: The farther price ran before coming back, the greater the profit margin and the probability.

passages.h: Odds Enhancer 3: how far did price move away before returning?
passages.t: A far run means the level sits far out on the supply/demand curve, away from equilibrium: a stretched rubber band that is more likely to snap back.

passages.h: Odds Enhancer 3: how far did price move away before returning?
passages.t: For a supply short: the buyer on the return is buying after a very large rally, a big mistake that helps the seller.

passages.h: Odds Enhancer 3: how far did price move away before returning?
passages.t: Measure from the supply level to the lowest low made before price rallied back: that distance becomes one of the profit targets.
His Lessons from the Pros and SFO Magazine articles, the OTA website recordings, a basic Economics 101 book, and the XLT live-market program.
Odds Enhancer 1: gradual move (weakest), big candles (strong), gap away (strongest).
Odds Enhancers 2 and 3: a short, quiet base beats a long busy one; the run before the return becomes a target.

Looking for levels with lots of trading activity and high volume, as conventional books suggest. Entering far from the turn, which means smaller size, more risk and less reward. Believing something just because most people believe it (herd thinking).

How did price leave: gradual, big candles, or a gap? How many candles did price spend at the level (fewer is better)? Was volume at the base low? How far did price run before returning, and is that distance a usable target? Is my entry as close to the zone (the turn) as possible?

“The stronger price moves away from a price level, the more out-of-balance supply and demand are at the level.” “The less time price spends at a level, the more out-of-balance supply and demand are.” “The more it is stretched, the more likely it is to snap back.”

Low volume at the base as a quality sign: Kevin's course has no volume logic. Using the run-out extreme (lowest low before the return) as a profit target is new; Kevin targets 3:1 and the next HTF opposing zone.
The departure grading (gradual / big candles / gap) and few basing candles match Kevin's 'explosive move away' and short-basing ideas.

Find turning points in advance with three odds enhancers. Stretch a rubber band a little and let go: it barely moves. Stretch it far and it snaps back hard. Seiden finds levels where price ran far away, left fast (best of all with a gap), and spent almost no time. Those levels are the most out of balance, so price turns there. He enters right at the turn, so his stop is small and his target is far.
A dog that bolts out of the yard the moment the gate opens: it really did not want to stay there.
The entry decides everything else: get as close to the turn as possible. Departure grades: gradual < big candles < gap away. Little time and a far run mean a bigger imbalance and a bigger target.

passages.h: Step: Odds Enhancer 1: how did price leave?
passages.t: Gradual move is weakest, big candles are strong, a gap away is strongest. Here price gapped down from the level. The stronger the move away, the more out of balance the level.

passages.h: Step: Odds Enhancer 2: how much time?
passages.t: Only two candles. If price could have spent a long time there, supply and demand could not have been very out of balance. Little activity, low volume: strong.

passages.h: Step: Odds Enhancer 3: how far before returning?
passages.t: Price ran far down before coming back. The level is far from equilibrium, a stretched rubber band. The distance to the lowest low before the return becomes a target.
Short right at the level, stop just above. The buyer here is buying after a very large rally. Entering at the turn gives the biggest size for the least risk and the most room to the target.
The rubber band snaps back to the target. All three odds enhancers were strong.

Odds Enhancer 1? - How did price leave the level? Odds Enhancer 2? - How much time did price spend at the level? Odds Enhancer 3? - How far did price move away before returning? Strongest departure? - A gap away. Rubber band idea? - The more it is stretched, the more likely it snaps back. Why the entry matters most? - Stops, targets, size and risk all depend on it.

Using an OTA Pro Pick short in USDCHF, Seiden shows what 'trade with the trend' means as a rule: in a downtrend, only look for supply levels to short. Of many visible supply levels only one met the odds-enhancer criteria; price rallied to it, turned and fell over 100 ticks for 25 ticks of risk. The buyers on the other side made three mistakes, the third being buying in a downtrend.
Downtrend: only short at supply. Uptrend: only buy at demand. Pick only the level that meets the odds-enhancer criteria, not every visible level.
Require quality level + profit margin + good risk/reward + trend in your favour before shorting. Example sizing of risk: 25 ticks risked for 100+ ticks of potential.
Stand aside (cancel pending entries) going into a major announcement such as the FOMC until the market settles (from the Pro Pick note).

passages.h: The rule behind 'the trend is your friend'
passages.t: OTA core strategy: supply (retail), demand (wholesale) and trends. When the trend is down, only look for supply (resistance) levels, because you only want to sell short.

passages.h: The rule behind 'the trend is your friend'
passages.t: Many supply levels may appear on a chart; only the one that meets the odds-enhancer rules is chosen.

passages.h: Four reasons to sell the USDCHF supply
passages.t: A quality supply level with several odds enhancers. A significant profit margin below. An ideal risk/reward. A strong downtrend.
Price rallied back to supply, stopped and fell well over 100 ticks to the targets while risking only 25 ticks.
He disputes the claim that turning points cannot be timed: quantify where supply and demand are out of balance, because that is where price turns.
The buyers made three mistakes: buying after a rally; buying where supply exceeded demand (worse than the first); buying in the context of a downtrend.
In a downtrend the odds are with the shorts. Those who trade against the trend tend to pay those who trade with it.

Figure 1 (p. 411): OTA Pro Picks screen dated 5/11/2011, Forex intraday, USDCHF Short. Trends panel: short term Down, long term Down. Trade parameters: pick date 4/27/2011, entry .8827-.8852, stop .8857, target 1 .873, target 2 .87.

Strategy note: 30-minute timeframe, 'trending down strongly', cancel the trade going into the FOMC announcement until the market settles, and a confirmation-entry stipulation. Figure 1 chart: a long decline from a top on the left, a small yellow 'Supply Zone' marked about 0.88276-0.88550, and a grey 'Target 1' line about 0.87293 below, with price already dropping to it.

Figure 2 (p. 412): USDCHF 30-minute TradeStation chart, 4/25 evening to 4/27 evening. A yellow 'Supply Zone' early on 4/26 between black lines at about 0.8832 and 0.8850: price jumped up into a short base, then fell in long red candles to about 0.8780.

Figure 2 continued: a bounce to about 0.8810, then a further drop to a spike low near 0.8660 (afternoon 4/26). On 4/27 price climbed steadily back up to the zone's lower line around 10:00, circled as 'Short Entry' near 0.8832, then fell back to about 0.8695 by the evening.
The run from the zone to the 0.8660 low is the 'distance before return' odds enhancer; the 25-tick stop vs 100+-tick move gives roughly 4:1 or better.

passages.h: Chart: OTA Pro Picks, USDCHF short (4/27/2011): trends short and long term Down; entry .8827-.8852, stop .8857, Target 1 .873, Target 2 .87. Results: closed for profit, +214 points. The small chart shows a long decline, a yellow 'Supply Zone' about .8828-.8855 and the Target 1 line about .8729.
passages.t: Every parameter (zone, stop, two targets) is set before the trade, with the trend panel confirming Down on both timeframes. Trade note: cancel the order going into the FOMC announcement until the market settles. Log: T1 hit, stop moved down to .8795, rest exited at .8710.

passages.t: Of the supply levels on the chart, only this one qualifies: short base, fast drop, and a long run away before returning.

passages.t: The rally back up is the buyer's triple mistake: after a rally, into supply, against a downtrend. About 25 ticks of risk (stop above .8857) against 100+ ticks to the targets.
Downtrend: ignore demand and weak supply; sell the rally back into the one qualifying supply with 25 ticks of risk for 100+.
Buying after a rally in price. Buying at a level where supply exceeds demand. Buying in the context of a downtrend. Trading every supply level on the chart instead of the one that qualifies.

What is the trend on my trading timeframe and above? Am I trading in its direction? Which single supply/demand level meets the odds enhancers? Is there a significant profit margin to the target? Is the risk small relative to the target (e.g. 25 vs 100+ ticks)? Is a major announcement (FOMC etc.) due? If so, wait. Is the counterparty buying after a rally, into supply, against the trend?
“Those who trade against the trend tend to pay those who trade with the trend.” “The professionals say you can't time the markets turning points; we say you can.”
“If you would not take this novice action when buying things in any other part of life, don't do it when trading.”
Same direction rule as Kevin (trade zones with the trend; counter-trend is lower odds). The 'buyer's third mistake = buying in a downtrend' counterparty framing is new.
Pro Pick note to cancel the order going into the FOMC: Kevin's news handling differs; check your own news rule.

In a downtrend, only sell, and only at the one supply that qualifies. Swimming in a river is easy if you swim with the current and very hard against it. In a downtrend the current flows down, so Seiden only looks for supply levels to sell. A chart may show many supply levels, but he picks only the one that passes the odds enhancers. Price rallied to it, turned and fell more than 100 ticks while he risked only 25.
Riding a bike down a hill: you pick the smooth path, and you do not try to ride back up.

Downtrend: only short at supply. Uptrend: only buy at demand. Pick only the level that meets the odds enhancers, not every level. Need: quality level + profit margin + good reward to risk + trend in your favour.
The trend is down on this timeframe and above. So we only look for supply levels to sell. Demand levels are ignored.
Supply B spent many candles and left slowly: ignore it. Supply A is a short base, a fast drop, and a long run away before returning. Only A meets the odds enhancers.

Short at A's bottom line, stop just above its top. The risk is small next to the room down to the low: about 25 ticks for 100+. If a big announcement like the FOMC is due, cancel and wait until the market settles.
Price climbs back up. The buyer buys after a rally, buys where supply exceeds demand, and buys in a downtrend.
Price turns at A and falls to the target. Those who trade against the trend tend to pay those who trade with it.

Trade with the trend means? - Downtrend: only short supply. Uptrend: only buy demand. Four reasons to sell the USDCHF supply? - Quality level, profit margin, ideal risk/reward, strong downtrend. Many supply levels on the chart? - Take only the one that meets the odds enhancers. Before FOMC? - Cancel pending entries until the market settles. Who pays whom? - Those against the trend pay those with the trend.

After hearing another speaker list six factors for a Euro trade, Seiden says he needs only two: the quality of the supply/demand level (where price will turn) and the profit margin (where price will go). A gold short and his March 2011 S&P buy call during the Japan disaster show both: a fast departure from the level, and a 'rally with no basing' meaning open space. He bought against the downtrend and the news because both factors were present.
Take a trade only when both a quality level and a clear profit margin are present. Judge level quality mainly by how quickly price left it.
Judge profit margin by the price action between entry and the opposing level: a move with no basing means no opposing orders and open space.
A quality HTF demand with clear margin can be bought even in a downtrend and against bad news. Example risk/reward: risk $400 to make $1,200 (3:1).
1) Quality of the supply or demand level: tells you where price will turn. 2) The profit margin: tells you where price will go.
If both are present he takes the trade and typically considers nothing else; everything else is secondary.

passages.h: Reading the profit margin from price action
passages.t: The supply was high quality because price declined from it so quickly: willing supply far greater than willing demand.

passages.h: Reading the profit margin from price action
passages.t: Below it, the rally had no basing: nothing on the chart suggests strong demand in that price range.

passages.h: Reading the profit margin from price action
passages.t: As fast as price rallied through that range, expect it to fall back through it at the same rate next time.

passages.h: Reading the profit margin from price action
passages.t: On a CME trade desk this looks like a big stack of sell orders at supply and no significant buy orders until many points lower.

On March 15, 2011, at the height of the tragedy, Barron's/WSJ asked whether the global sell-off was the start of a larger decline. News was real and awful, the trend was down and TV pundits called for lower prices.

But price had declined to a quality demand level and there was a clear profit margin above, so he called it a very good buying opportunity. Price rallied strongly from demand, through the margin and beyond.
Lesson: ignore most conventional TA and news analysis; apply how you profit buying and selling anything.

Figure 1 (p. 415), left: @GC gold 30-minute COMEX chart around 12/29-12/30. A yellow 'Demand (wholesale)' base at the bottom near 1,403-1,404; from it a big circled rally in tall green candles with no basing up to about 1,414. A yellow 'Supply (Retail)' base at the upper right around 1,411.5-1,413.5 marked 'Sold Short'.

Figure 1 continued: price dropped fast from the supply back down through the no-basing rally area; a bracket 'Took Profits' sits around 1,404-1,407, just above the demand. Right: the trading platform/DOM with filled orders and a highlighted P/L, 'Low Risk Profit: $1,200'. Banner: 'Risk $400 to make $1,200' (3:1).

Figure 2 (p. 416): Barron's article 'Steer Clear of a Radioactive Japan Stock Play' (3/15/2011) with Seiden's highlighted quote that markets collapse into high-quality demand levels that turn out to be buying opportunities.

Right: S&P (@ES E-mini) daily chart, Dec 2010-Mar 2011: strong uptrend from about 1,200 to about 1,340 in February, then a drop with large red candles (circled) into the upper of two yellow 'Demand Zones' (about 1,250-1,262); a lower demand sits about 1,205-1,225. An arrow labels the touch 'Interview Day'.

Figure 3 (p. 417): the same S&P daily chart later: the 'Demand Zone' around 1,240-1,250, the circled touch on interview day, then a strong rally to about 1,320-1,330 by early April. Caption: the market was down hundreds during the interview and the news was very bad, the strategy said buy, and the Dow then rallied over 800 points.

passages.h: Chart: Gold (@GC) 30-min: demand (wholesale) about 1,402-1,404 at the bottom, a circled rally with no basing up to about 1,410-1,414, then a supply (retail) base about 1,411.5-1,413 where he sold short. Price drops back through the empty rally range; profits taken about 1,404-1,407 just above demand. Platform: 'Low Risk Profit: $1,200'. Risk $400 to make $1,200.
passages.t: Quality: price left the supply quickly, so willing supply far exceeded willing demand. Margin: the circled rally had no basing, so no buy orders were left in that range to stop the fall. Profits were taken just above the demand that launched the rally: 3:1.

passages.h: Chart: Barron's interview (3/15/2011) with Seiden's highlighted quote: markets collapse into high-quality demand levels that turn into buying opportunities. S&P (@ES) daily: uptrend from about 1,200 to about 1,340, then a sharp drop (circled) into the upper of two demand zones (about 1,241-1,253) on 'Interview Day'; a lower demand sits about 1,205-1,220.
passages.t: At the moment of the call, the news, the short-term trend and the pundits were all bearish.

passages.h: Chart: Barron's interview (3/15/2011) with Seiden's highlighted quote: markets collapse into high-quality demand levels that turn into buying opportunities. S&P (@ES) daily: uptrend from about 1,200 to about 1,340, then a sharp drop (circled) into the upper of two demand zones (about 1,241-1,253) on 'Interview Day'; a lower demand sits about 1,205-1,220.
passages.t: Price had fallen to a fresh daily demand with a clear margin above to the prior high: both factors present.

passages.h: Chart: Same S&P daily chart a few weeks later: the circled touch of the demand zone (about 1,241-1,253) on interview day, then a strong rally to about 1,325-1,330 by early April. Caption: the strategy said buy; the Dow rallied over 800 points from that news-driven sell-off.
passages.t: Price turned at the demand, not at any news change: the level, not the headline, decided the turn.

passages.h: Chart: Same S&P daily chart a few weeks later: the circled touch of the demand zone (about 1,241-1,253) on interview day, then a strong rally to about 1,325-1,330 by early April. Caption: the strategy said buy; the Dow rallied over 800 points from that news-driven sell-off.
passages.t: The rally ran up through the open space to the prior high: the profit margin seen in advance.
Gold short: fast departure from supply (quality) and a rally with no basing below (margin); risk $400 to make $1,200.
S&P March 2011: buy fresh daily demand with clear margin even with bad news and a short-term downtrend.
Over-analysing with many factors (six-factor Euro analysis) instead of the two that matter.
Letting bad news, the trend and TV opinions stop you buying at quality demand with margin. Ignoring what lies between entry and target (bases there reduce the margin).

Did price leave the level quickly (quality)? Between entry and target, is there any basing (opposing orders)? None = clear margin. Where is the opposing zone (target), and is the reward at least 3x the risk? If the trend or news is against me, is this a quality HTF level with a clear margin?
“The quality of the Supply or Demand level itself - this tells me where price will turn.” “The profit margin - this tells me where price will go to.” “There is just a rally in price with no basing.”
Seiden's minimum filter is only quality + margin; Kevin uses a fuller qualify process (removal, HTF alignment, trend).
He bought against a daily downtrend because quality + margin were present; Kevin treats counter-trend as lower odds (allowed only with HTF support).
Defining the margin as 'no basing between entry and target' is close to Kevin's 'clear path' idea but stated here as an explicit rule.

Only two things matter: where price turns and where it goes. Another speaker used six factors for one trade. Seiden needs only two. First, the quality of the level, which tells him where price will turn. Second, the profit margin, which tells him where price will go. If a rally shot up with no pauses, there are no buyers waiting in that space, so price can fall right back through it.
Before you jump off a diving board, check two things: is the board springy (quality) and is the pool deep enough (margin)?
Part 1: level quality, judged mainly by how fast price left. It tells you where price turns.
Part 2: profit margin, judged by the price action between entry and target. It tells you where price goes. With both present, buy even against bad news and a short-term downtrend.

passages.h: Step: Part 1: quality of the level
passages.t: Price left this supply very quickly. Willing supply was far greater than willing demand. Quality tells you where price will turn.

Look below. The rally up to here had no basing at all, so there are no buy orders in that range. As fast as price rallied through it, expect it to fall back through it. The margin tells you where price will go.
Short at supply with the stop above. Take profit just above the demand that launched the rally. Risk about $400 to make $1,200. Nothing else needs checking.
Price falls straight through the empty range to the target. On a trading desk this is a big stack of sell orders at supply and no real buy orders until much lower.

The two most important parts of a setup? - Level quality and profit margin. Level quality tells you? - Where price will turn. Profit margin tells you? - Where price will go. A rally with no basing means? - No opposing orders in that range: open space. Gold trade risk and reward? - Risk $400 to make $1,200 (3:1).

Reader Q&A that follows up 'The Two Most Important Parts of a Trade Setup'. Seiden covers timeframe pairs for day and swing trading, what happens to a level after the first revisit, win rate on larger timeframes, when to trade a reversal, touch count versus penetration depth, counter-trend trades, Fibonacci and pivots, and candlestick patterns. No charts in this article.

Day trading: hourly or daily for direction, 5-minute for entries. Swing trading: weekly for direction, daily for entries. At or near HTF supply, only look for LTF shorts; at or near HTF demand, only LTF longs.

A level weakens with each revisit; expect a fast move to the next level once its orders are used up. Ignore touch count; keep trading a level whose returns only touch and leave strongly. Stop trading a level once price has penetrated 25% or more into it.
Trade counter-trend only when the trend reaches a fresh larger-timeframe supply/demand level.
Do not use Fibonacci retracements, pivot points or conventional candlestick/chart patterns.

Day trading: pair a larger timeframe (hourly or daily) with a small one (5-minute). The larger timeframe shows where price is on its supply/demand curve, which decides whether to look for buys or sells on the small timeframe.
Example: price at or near larger-timeframe supply, so go to the 5-minute chart and short quality supply levels with good profit margin. Swing trading: daily and weekly charts should be fine.
CME floor example: a large stack of S&P buy orders at 1245 with the market opening at 1260. The first time price reaches 1245 it bounces higher.
Each later decline to 1245 fills more of those orders: demand weakens, 'layers of the floor' are removed. Once all orders at 1245 are filled, price falls quickly to the next demand level.
Win rates are usually higher on daily, weekly and monthly charts because the levels are very clear.
Larger-timeframe levels trump smaller-timeframe ones: a good HTF demand with margin is not undone by small-timeframe noise.
The reverse is not true: a 5-minute demand with supply far above is not enough information; check where it sits on the HTF curve.
LTF buy near HTF demand: typically works very well. LTF buy at or near HTF supply: very low odds.

passages.h: Strong vs weak levels and reversal trades
passages.t: Trends always end and begin at fresh larger-timeframe supply and demand levels. That is where you stop trading with the trend and trade against it, anticipating the reversal and entering the new trend before it gets going. First make sure your own definition of a quality level is correct.
He rejects the textbook 'touch count' / '3 taps' rule as less objective. Watch how deep price goes into the level on each return.
If price just touches the level and leaves strongly, the imbalance is still big: trade it again on the 2nd, 3rd and later returns.
Once price trades 25% or more into the level, take no more trades there: the imbalance is no longer strong enough.
Counter-trend: only when the trend is reaching a larger-timeframe supply or demand level, meaning it is about to end.

Fibonacci and pivots: not used. They are calculations that ignore willing supply and demand, and they give several lines to choose from; the one that works is always the one lining up with real supply/demand, so why use the Fib?
Candlesticks: no conventional patterns. Focus only on the picture of where demand exceeded supply or vice versa.
Head-and-shoulders and double tops make you wait for a big decline before selling (selling low) instead of selling high at supply.
Almost every trading question is answered by asking how you profit buying and selling anything: use your 'bag of logic'.
Penetration depth: shallow touches keep the level tradable; 25%+ penetration ends it, and price then runs to the next level.
HTF location decides direction: at HTF supply only take LTF shorts at LTF supply with margin below.

Taking a 5-minute buy that sits at or near larger-timeframe supply. Relying on touch count ('3 taps') instead of how deep price goes into the level. Using Fib or pivot lines that ignore actual supply and demand. Waiting for H&S or double-top patterns, which make you sell low after a big decline. Trading reversals without a fresh HTF level or a correct definition of quality.

Where is price on the higher-timeframe supply/demand curve? Is my LTF setup in the same direction as the HTF location? How deep did earlier returns go into this zone: under 25%? If counter-trend, is the trend arriving at a fresh HTF level? Am I relying on Fib, pivots or candle patterns instead of the zone itself?
“Trends always end and begin at 'fresh' larger time frame demand and supply levels.” “Larger time frame levels trump smaller time frame levels.”
“Why do I need the Fib line when I am always taking the one that lines up with real demand or supply?”

Freshness by depth: Seiden says 25%+ penetration ends the level but touch count does not matter; Kevin's 0/25/50/75/100 grid treats ~25% as a 'mid' zone, over 75% as out, and also counts the number of tests.
Counter-trend allowed explicitly at a fresh HTF level ('trends end and begin there'); Kevin calls counter-trend lower odds.
Specific timeframe pairs (H1/D1 with M5; W1 with D1) differ from Kevin's own HTF/entry pairs.
Kevin uses the Fibonacci tool only as a drawing tool (levels 0 and 1), not for retracements, so no conflict with Seiden's 'no Fib' rule.

Big chart picks the direction; watch how deep price digs into a level. Think of a stack of pancakes on a plate. Each time a hungry kid visits, he eats a few. If he only nibbles the top, there are plenty left for next time. If he digs a quarter of the way in, the stack is nearly gone and the next visit finds an empty plate. Seiden ignores how many visits; he watches how deep each visit goes, and he lets the bigger chart decide whether he is buying or selling.
A map and a magnifying glass: the map (bigger timeframe) tells you which way to go; the glass (small timeframe) finds the exact step.

Larger timeframe location decides direction; smaller timeframe gives the entry. HTF trumps LTF. Ignore touch count; stop trading a level once price goes 25% or more into it. Counter-trend only at fresh HTF levels. No Fibs, pivots or candle patterns.

passages.h: Step: A stack of buy orders
passages.t: Picture a big stack of buy orders at this level. The first time price comes down, it bounces higher.
Draw a line 25% into the zone. Return 2 only touches and leaves strongly: the imbalance is still big, so trade it again. Ignore the "3 taps" rule.

passages.h: Step: 25% or more: no more trades
passages.t: Return 3 trades deep into the zone, past the 25% line. Many orders are filled; the layers of the floor are being removed. No more trades at this level.
Once the orders are all filled, price falls quickly to the next demand level.

Day trading timeframe pair? - Hourly or daily for direction, 5-minute for entries. Swing trading timeframe pair? - Weekly and daily. When to stop trading a level? - Once price penetrates 25% or more into it. Touch count or depth? - Depth. Ignore "3 taps". HTF vs LTF? - Larger timeframe levels trump smaller ones. Fib, pivots, candle patterns? - Not used.
Where do trends end and begin? - At fresh larger timeframe supply and demand levels.

Chapter 1 argues that indicators are not where trading edge comes from. Leading oscillators (RSI, Stochastic) throw false signals, lagging ones (MACD, moving averages) get you in late, and the few indicator traders who make money do so because of risk management and plan discipline. Indicators also make you predictable to professionals who hunt the stops the crowd places.
The book's alternative: read supply and demand directly from price and put stops beyond the zones.
Do not build entries on indicator signals; read supply and demand from price. Treat risk management and plan discipline as the real edge, whatever method you use.

Place every stop beyond a zone (below demand for longs, above supply for shorts), never at the obvious indicator or swing level. If you keep an indicator, it must sit on top of the zone rules, not replace them.

passages.h: What indicators are and why they disappoint
passages.t: Indicators are decision aids for entries and exits: oscillators, moving averages, trend lines and more complex formulas - well over 100 of them.

passages.h: What indicators are and why they disappoint
passages.t: Two families: leading (oscillators such as RSI and Stochastic) and lagging (anything built from moving averages, such as MACD). Lagging indicators get you into the trade late; leading indicators fire false signals.

passages.h: What indicators are and why they disappoint
passages.t: Learning them all costs time and money and leaves you not much better off - a busy-looking screen does not make a better trader.

passages.h: What indicators are and why they disappoint
passages.t: Weather analogy: forecasting crunches huge amounts of data and gets worse the further ahead it looks; Baker says his local forecasts are right about half the time. Indicator forecasting has the same problem.

passages.h: What really makes the profitable minority profitable
passages.t: Baker accepts that some indicator traders make money consistently, but calls them the exception. Their edge is risk management and sticking to a trading plan, not the indicator.

passages.h: What really makes the profitable minority profitable
passages.t: Thought experiment: a trader with the same strict risk rules whose whole plan is 'buy pullbacks in uptrends, short pullbacks in downtrends' could get the same results.

passages.h: What really makes the profitable minority profitable
passages.t: If you are experienced and like your indicators, you can keep them and add the zone rules from this book to raise your hit rate.
Craps example: some gamblers pull their bets when the dealers change, then credit the new dealers if a seven comes. The odds of a seven stay 16.7% (one in six) no matter who deals.
Same behaviour in trading: a trader buys on a MACD crossover, credits the crossover when it works and blames something else when it does not.
Psychology names it confirmation bias and gambler's fallacy - acting as if a ritual controls a random outcome.
Professionals know what the popular indicators are saying and where the crowd's stops sit.

They also know where the nearest supply and demand zones are. If the zone is far enough from current price, they have the capital to push price through the crowd's stops and get filled at a better price.
The classic experience - stopped out right before price turns and goes your way - is often exactly this.
Defence: always put the stop below a demand zone (long) or above a supply zone (short). That is the bridge into the rest of the book.

passages.h: Chart: Book cover chart: a demand zone (blue band) at the base of a move.
passages.t: Price sits briefly on the blue band, then leaves it with large green candles - the 'move away' that marks demand.

passages.h: Chart: Book cover chart: a demand zone (blue band) at the base of a move.
passages.t: No indicator is needed to see where buyers stepped in; the volume histogram below is the only study on the chart.

Indicators lag, zones lead. The moving-average crossover only fires after a large part of the move is gone. The demand zone (the whole pivot candle) marks where buyers took control, so the entry and the stop are known at the turn.

Why obvious stops get hunted. Stops parked just under the visible swing low (where indicator traders put them) are swept as price runs down to the real buyers in the demand zone. A stop a few cents below the zone survives the run.
Collecting indicators (100+ exist) instead of learning where supply and demand are. Entering on a lagging crossover after the move has largely happened.
Crediting the indicator for winners and blaming outside events for losers (confirmation bias). Parking stops where every indicator trader parks them, making them easy to hunt.

Is this trade based on a zone, not on an indicator signal? Would the trade still make sense with every indicator removed from the chart? Is my stop beyond a supply or demand zone rather than at an obvious level? Am I following my written plan, or reacting to a signal?
“Lagging indicators get you into the trade late and leading indicators are prone to false signals.” “The best professional traders stick to their trading plan and never deviate from it.”
“By always placing your stop below a demand zone or above a supply zone, it makes you more immune to stop hunters.”

Agrees with Kevin: both trade pure price action with no indicators. Kevin's only allowance is that an indicator can matter at a higher-timeframe zone; Baker lets seasoned traders keep their favourites as long as the zone rules sit on top.
Baker's case against indicators is about risk and discipline (the winners win through risk management, not the tool) - Kevin's course does not argue this point, it simply never uses them.

Stops beyond the zone are justified here by stop hunting. Kevin and Seiden put the stop just past the distal line for the same structural reason (the order stack has to fail first), so the placement matches.
Seiden frames the same idea as institutional order flow versus retail 'novice' behaviour; Baker uses simpler analogies (weather, craps) and no institutional vocabulary.

Read the buyers and sellers on price itself, not on gadgets. You want to know if the ice-cream shop is busy. You could ask a weather machine that is right only half the time. Or you could just look at the line of kids at the door. Baker says indicators are the weather machine, and price is the line of kids. And if you hide your piggy bank where everyone hides theirs, the bully finds it first.
An indicator is a weather forecast that is right about half the time. A zone is looking out the window at the real crowd.

Lagging indicators get you in late. Leading indicators give false signals. Winners win because of risk rules and sticking to a plan, not because of a gadget. Put your stop beyond a zone, not where the crowd puts theirs.
Look at the turn at the bottom. Buyers took over right there. A moving-average crossover only lights up after a big part of the rally is already gone. That is what "lagging" means: it tells you late.

passages.h: Step: The zone shows entry and stop up front
passages.t: Baker skips the gadget and boxes the candles where the turn happened. This is a demand zone: a place with more willing buyers than sellers. The near line is the proximal line, the far line is the distal line.

passages.h: Step: Where the crowd hides its stops
passages.t: Most traders put their stop just under the obvious swing low. Professionals know this. A bunch of stops sitting in one obvious place is like candy on the floor.

Price is pushed down through the obvious low. The crowd is stopped out, and the professionals buy their shares cheaply near the real demand zone. Then price turns up. A stop a few cents below the zone was never touched.

What are the two families of indicators? - Leading (oscillators like RSI, Stochastic) and lagging (built from moving averages, like MACD). Lagging indicator problem? - They get you into the trade late. Leading indicator problem? - They fire false signals.
What is the real edge of winning indicator traders? - Risk management and sticking to the trading plan.
Odds of a seven in craps after the dealer changes? - Still one in six (16.7%). The ritual changes nothing.
Where does Baker put the stop on a long? - A few cents below the demand zone (on a short: a few cents above the supply zone).
Why are obvious stops dangerous? - Professionals know where they sit and can push price through them to get a better fill.

Chapter 2 cuts candlestick analysis down to three single candles: the doji (indecision, supply and demand in balance), the shooting star (bearish reversal) and the hammer (bullish reversal). Body colour does not matter. Any multi-candle reversal pattern can be merged into one candle, and the result is always a hammer or a shooting star - just formed more slowly.
Because faster moves in and out of a pivot mean a bigger imbalance, Baker only wants the single-candle versions.
Use only three candle shapes: doji, hammer, shooting star. Ignore body colour when classifying them.
To read a multi-candle pattern, merge it: first open, last close, highest high, lowest low. Prefer the single-candle reversal: faster in and out of the pivot = stronger imbalance.
A candle carries the same four prices as a bar: open, high, low, close - drawn so the relation between open and close is visible at a glance.
Green body: closed above the open (bullish for that period). Red body: closed below the open (bearish). A candle can be a month, a week, a day or any intraday interval.
Wicks matter too: they show how far traders pushed price during the period before it came back to close inside the body.

Doji: a small body roughly centred between long wicks. Price went above and below the open and closed near it - supply and demand are in balance for the moment. Three shapes count (small green body, small red body, plus-sign).

Shooting star: long upper wick, small body at the bottom. Buyers were in control up to the top of the wick, then sellers took over and pushed price back down to or below the open. A small lower wick is allowed.

Hammer: long lower wick, small body at the top. Sellers were in control down to the bottom of the wick, then buyers took over and pushed price back to or above the open. For all three, the colour of the body is not important.
Most named reversal patterns use several candles. Baker says you do not need to learn them.
Merge a pattern into one candle: open of the first candle, close of the last, the highest high and the lowest low of the group. Close below open = red, otherwise green.

Bullish engulfing and morning star merge into a hammer; bearish engulfing and evening doji star merge into a shooting star. So every multi-candle reversal is a hammer or shooting star that took longer to form.
Later chapters show that the faster price moves into and out of a pivot, the stronger the supply/demand imbalance there.
A single hammer or shooting star is the fastest possible version of a reversal, so those are the only candles Baker uses for setups.
These candles reappear later as the pivot candle that defines a zone (chapter 3) and as the with-trend entry trigger for swing trades (chapter 4).

passages.h: Chart: Candle anatomy: bullish (close above open) and bearish (close below open).
passages.t: High and low are the wick ends; open and close are the body ends. The order of open and close flips between the green and red candle.

passages.h: Chart: Shooting star, shown in both colours.
passages.t: Long upper wick, small body near the low - buyers lost control at the top of the wick. Both colours are shooting stars; colour is ignored.

passages.h: Chart: Bearish engulfing merged into one candle.
passages.t: A small green candle followed by a larger red candle that engulfs it. Merged (first open, last close, high, low) it becomes a shooting star.

passages.h: Chart: Evening doji star merged into one candle.
passages.t: Green candle, small doji gapped above, then a red candle. Merged it is a shooting star with a small green body - colour does not matter.

passages.h: Chart: Bullish engulfing merged into one candle.
passages.t: A small red candle followed by a larger green candle. Merged it becomes a hammer: a long lower wick under a body near the high.

passages.h: Chart: Morning star merged into one candle.
passages.t: Red candle, small candle below, then a strong green candle. Merged it is a hammer: the long lower wick shows where demand took over.

Candle anatomy and the only three single candles Baker uses: the doji (small, centred body = balance), the shooting star (long upper wick = sellers took over at the high) and the hammer (long lower wick = buyers took over at the low). Body colour is irrelevant for all three.

Combining a multi-candle bullish pattern into one candle: open of the first candle, close of the last, the highest high and the lowest low. A bullish engulfing and a morning star both collapse into a hammer: a long lower wick where demand took over.

The bearish mirror: a bearish engulfing and an evening doji star each add up to a shooting star. That is why Baker only needs the hammer and the shooting star: the multi-candle patterns are the same footprint formed over more time, and the faster single-candle version shows the bigger imbalance.
Memorising dozens of named patterns that all reduce to a hammer or shooting star. Rejecting a hammer or shooting star because its body is the 'wrong' colour.
Calling a candle a doji when its body is large relative to its wicks or not roughly centred. Treating a slow, multi-candle turn as equal to a sharp single-candle rejection.

Is the body small relative to the wicks? Doji: is the body roughly centred? Hammer: long lower wick? Shooting star: long upper wick? If it is a multi-candle pattern, what single candle does it merge into? Did the reversal happen in one candle (fast) or over several (slow)?
“the color of the candle is not important to us” “the faster the price moves in and out of a pivot point, the stronger the imbalance of supply and demand”

Conflict with Kevin: Kevin says he does not use candlestick patterns (hammers etc.) and will not teach them; his confirmation is an opposing lower-timeframe zone or trendline being removed. Baker uses the hammer and shooting star both as the zone itself and as a with-trend entry trigger.
Seiden does not use candle patterns as a filter - his entries are fixed rules at the level. The 'merge candles into one' technique is new to the app's material.

Common ground: all three mentors say fewer candles at the turn means a bigger imbalance. Baker's single-candle preference is the same idea as Kevin's 1-3 basing candles and Seiden's 'time at the level' odds enhancer.

Only three candles matter: the doji, the hammer and the shooting star. Two teams play tug-of-war every hour, and each candle is one hour. If the rope ends right where it started, nobody won: that is a doji. If one team drags the rope far to its side but the other team pulls it all the way back, the second team won: that is a hammer or a shooting star. The long wick is how far the losing team got before it lost.
A candle is a tug-of-war picture. The wick is how far one team pulled; the body is where the rope ended up.
Doji means balance. Hammer means buyers won. Shooting star means sellers won. Body colour does not matter for these three.
Every multi-candle reversal merges into a hammer or shooting star. One candle is faster, and faster is stronger.

passages.h: Step: What one candle tells you
passages.t: A candle shows four prices: open, high, low and close. The body runs from open to close: green if it closed higher, red if lower. The thin wicks show how far traders pushed price before it came back.
A small body roughly in the middle of long wicks. Price went up, went down, and closed near where it opened. For that moment, supply and demand are in balance.
Long lower wick, small body at the top. Sellers were in charge down to the bottom of the wick, then buyers took over and pushed price back up to or above the open. Colour does not matter.

passages.h: Step: The shooting star: sellers win
passages.t: Long upper wick, small body at the bottom. Buyers pushed price up to the top of the wick, then sellers took over and pushed it back down to or below the open. A small lower wick is allowed.

passages.h: Step: Merge many candles into one
passages.t: You do not need to learn named patterns. Merge them: the open of the first candle, the close of the last, the highest high and the lowest low. A bullish engulfing merges into a hammer. A bearish engulfing merges into a shooting star.

A two-candle turn is just a hammer that took longer to form. Baker wants the single-candle version: the faster price moves in and out of a turning point, the stronger the imbalance of supply and demand.
The three candles Baker uses? - Doji, hammer, shooting star. Doji means? - Small centred body: supply and demand in balance.
Hammer shape and meaning? - Long lower wick, small body at the top: buyers took over from sellers.

Shooting star shape and meaning? - Long upper wick, small body at the bottom: sellers took over from buyers. Does body colour matter? - No, not for these three candles. How to merge candles? - First open, last close, highest high, lowest low. Bearish engulfing merges into? - A shooting star.
Why only single-candle reversals? - The faster price moves in and out of a pivot, the stronger the imbalance.

Chapter 3 opens with what Baker calls the most important chapter of the book. Against the Random Walk view (prices are unpredictable, buy an index fund), he argues that past price action does predict - not through indicators, but because it shows where excess supply and excess demand sit.

He restates the economics of supply and demand, then applies it to charts: every change of direction is a change in the balance between willing sellers and willing buyers, and sideways tight trading is balance.

Treat every swing high as supply overpowering demand and every swing low as demand overpowering supply. Treat tight sideways ranges as balance - no imbalance to trade inside them. Plot supply and demand zones from past price action before looking for trades. Read the zones through the four laws: imbalance moves price; balance does not.

Random Walk Theory / Efficient Market Hypothesis: prices already reflect all known information (earnings, expectations, dividends), new information arrives at random, so nobody can consistently beat the market; buy and hold an index fund.
Its opponents believe past price action predicts future price action and lean on technical indicators, chart patterns and trend lines.
Baker: the opponents are partly right - history does predict, but through the areas of excess supply and demand it reveals, not through indicators.
Whichever camp you are in, knowing where excess supply and demand sit improves decisions in any market.
Supply and demand set price in every market: price settles where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied (equilibrium).

Four basic laws: demand up with supply flat = shortage, higher price; demand down with supply flat = surplus, lower price; supply up with demand flat = surplus, lower price; supply down with demand flat = shortage, higher price.

Supply = willing sellers; demand = willing buyers. Every time price changes direction, the balance between them has changed. At swing highs supply became greater than demand; at swing lows demand became greater than supply, forcing a reversal. Uptrend: demand stronger than supply. Downtrend: the opposite. Tight sideways trading = supply and demand in balance.
The edge comes from knowing where these areas are - plotted as supply zones and demand zones - and then picking the zones most likely to produce a profitable trade.

passages.h: Chart: Price/quantity diagram: supply slopes up, demand slopes down, equilibrium at P and Q.
passages.t: The four laws describe what happens when one curve shifts and the other does not.

passages.h: Chart: XOM daily with pivot dots and a 'supply and demand in balance' box.
passages.t: Red dots mark swing highs (supply took over); blue dots mark swing lows (demand took over). The blue box is a short sideways cluster: supply and demand in balance. Every reversal on the chart is one of these balance changes.

The textbook picture: price settles where the quantity buyers want equals the quantity sellers offer. When demand rises and supply does not (amber line), a shortage pushes the equilibrium price up from P to P2. The four basic laws are listed on the right.

On a chart every change of direction is a change in the balance between willing buyers and willing sellers: red dots where supply overpowered demand, green dots where demand overpowered supply. Tight sideways trading is the two in balance. Uptrend = demand stronger; downtrend = supply stronger.

Skimming this chapter: Baker says to re-read it until it is fully understood. Assuming that because price is hard to forecast, nothing on the chart has predictive value. Looking for trades in the middle of a tight balanced range.

Where did price last change direction, and which side won there? Is the market trending (imbalance) or trading in a tight range (balance)? Have I marked the supply zones above and demand zones below current price?
“This is the most important chapter in the book.” “The forces that drive price action in a market are supply and demand.”

All three mentors start from the same law (imbalance moves price). Kevin explains it with bank order stacks left at a level; Seiden with institutional orders and 'novice' traders; Baker with the textbook price/quantity curve and the Random Walk debate.
Baker compares zones to support and resistance (supply = resistance, demand = support). Kevin, by contrast, shows a classic S/R box as an example of what S&D is not.
Baker uses no basing vocabulary: no DBR / RBD / RBR / DBD names. His zone types are pivots, tight ranges, mid-trend dojis and gaps (next lesson).

Price moves because buyers and sellers are out of balance. Imagine a lemonade stand. If lots of kids want lemonade and there is only a little, the price goes up. If there is a giant pile of lemonade and nobody is thirsty, the price goes down. When the number of thirsty kids matches the cups, the price sits still.
