How the plan changes by trading style, using the examples Baker gives in chapters 4 and 7. Dashes mean the book gives no figure for that cell.

Trading without a written plan and deciding exits in the moment. No symbol list or filters, so any moving chart becomes a 'setup'. Leaving the minimum ratio vague. Trading forex around the clock with no schedule. Never checking whether trades followed the plan.

Is this instrument and symbol on my written list? Is this the timeframe my plan uses for this style? Does the setup meet every written condition? Is the risk the planned percentage, and the ratio at or above my minimum? Do I know how I will move the stop and when I will exit? Is it within my trading hours? After the trade: did I follow the plan?
“Write down the exact conditions that must be met before you can enter a particular trade.”
All three mentors insist on a written plan; Baker's ten-part template is the most explicit, and fits the app's journal (the evaluation step = the journal's 'followed plan?' field).
The symbol filters (ATR above 3% of price, 10 million+ shares a day, options open interest above 10,000) are stock-specific and new to the app.
Minimum ratios of 3:1 for day trades and 5:1 for swing trades are stricter than Kevin's 2:1-or-better.
Trailing at each new pivot or moving to a small profit after a set move, versus the bot's fixed break-even at 1R and Kevin's roughly 2R.

Write the rules down first, then only play by the written rules. Before a board game, everyone reads the rule card, so nobody argues in the middle of the game. A trading plan is your rule card. It says which games you play, when you play, what counts as a good move, how much you can lose, and when you stop. After each game you check: did I follow the card?
A trading plan is a recipe. If you add random things while cooking, the cake fails; follow the recipe and it comes out the same every time.

A written plan keeps you from mistakes, overtrading and impulsive decisions. Write exact setups, risk per trade, minimum reward-to-risk, stop moves, exits and hours. Review every trade against the plan.

Parts 1 and 2: which instruments (stocks, currencies, futures, options), and which exact symbols. Example filters: day trade stocks with ATR above 3% of price and at least 10 million shares a day; swing trade stocks with options open interest above 10,000. Write the names down.
Part 3: weekly for long-term investing, daily (maybe hourly) for swing trading, daily plus intraday for day trading. One section per timeframe if you use several.
Part 4: write the exact conditions that must be met before you can enter. For example: swing trades only with the trend, with a reversal candle on a pullback into a zone.

Part 5: decide the risk per trade in advance so the size follows. Part 6: the minimum reward-to-risk at exit 1, for example at least 3:1 for day trades and maybe 5:1 for swing trades. The higher your win rate, the lower it can be.

Part 7: how you watch the trade, for example move the stop at every new pivot. Part 8: exact exit conditions (a price, a trailing stop or a time of day), so you neither leave too early nor hold too long.
Part 9: trading times. Forex never closes, so set a schedule; a stock day trader might work four hours from the open. Part 10: a comment box or checklist on whether you followed the plan.

Why write a plan? - It prevents mistakes, overtrading and impulsive decisions. Plan part 4: setups? - Write the exact conditions that must be met before entering. Example minimum ratios? - At least 3:1 for day trading, maybe 5:1 for swing trading.

Plan part 7: monitoring example? - Move the stop at every new pivot, or to a small profit after a set move. Plan part 8: exits? - Exact conditions: a price, a trailing stop, or a time of day. Plan part 9: trading times? - A fixed schedule (forex never closes). Plan part 10? - Evaluation: did I follow the plan?

Chapter 8 presents options as a risk tool: for any position held overnight, Baker says an option is always less risky than the stock. 34 call caps the loss at $34, where 100 shares exposed to an overnight gap could lose far more - and stock plus a put gives the same cap.
For overnight holds, consider a call (or stock plus a put) instead of naked stock to cap gap risk. Know the intrinsic and extrinsic parts of the premium before buying.
Prefer in-the-money options when replacing stock; treat out-of-the-money premiums as fully at risk. Include the bid/ask spread in your risk.
Over 2,000 stocks and most ETFs have options. Used properly, options are always less risky than holding the same position in stock.
An option is a contract giving the buyer the right, not the obligation, to buy or sell an underlying asset at a set price on or before a set date. Listed options cover 100 shares.
Like stocks: securities that trade with bids and offers in a listed market. Unlike stocks: derivatives with expiration dates, no fixed number outstanding, and no voting or dividend rights.
Call: the right to buy at the strike. Like a security deposit on a rental - it secures the price; if you never use it you lose only the deposit (the premium). Calls usually gain as the stock rises.
Put: the right to sell at the strike. Like car insurance - you pay a premium and are protected if the asset is 'damaged' (the price falls). If nothing happens, the premium is the only cost.
Symbols combine the stock, expiration date, call/put flag and strike; in TradeStation, AA 130518C8 is the Alcoa $8 call expiring May 18, 2013.
Alcoa at $8.27, three weeks to expiry, the $8 call at 34 cents: one contract costs $34 plus commission (per-share price x 100).
Price = intrinsic + extrinsic value. Call intrinsic = stock - strike (27 cents here); put intrinsic = strike - stock.
The remaining 7 cents is extrinsic (time) value, driven mainly by volatility and time left - more volatility, more value; it decays as expiry nears (like a 1-year vs a 5-year insurance policy).

In the money: call strike below the stock, put strike above it - only these have intrinsic value. At the money: strike equals the price. Out of the money: call strike above, put strike below. At- and out-of-the-money options expire worthless.
At $8.27 at expiry the call is worth 27 cents; at $7.98 it is worthless. The $8 put (AA 130518P8) costs 7 cents, all of it time value - the same 7 cents of extrinsic value as the call.
View: Alcoa to $9 by the third Friday of May. 100 shares make $73 at $9. One $8 call instead costs $34; at $9 it is worth $100, a $66 profit - $7 less than the stock.

If Alcoa falls, the call can never lose more than $34. A stop at $7.50 does not protect the stock from an overnight gap to $5 - you get filled near $5, not $7.50. (The book quotes the stock losses as about $50 at $7.50 and $300 at $5; from an $8.27 entry they work out to $77 and $327.)
Stock plus an $8 put (7 cents = $7) gives the same result: $73 - $7 = $66 at $9; below $8 the loss is capped at $27 on the stock plus $7 for the put = $34.
Baker rarely uses spreads; for more depth he recommends Lawrence McMillan's 'Options as a Strategic Investment'.

Baker's Alcoa example. Owning 100 shares at $8.27 makes $73 if the stock reaches $9, but the loss is open-ended - and an overnight gap jumps straight over a stop order. One $8 call for $0.34 ($34) makes $66 at $9 and can never lose more than $34. Owning the stock plus an $8 put for $0.07 produces the same capped profile.

Option pricing in one picture. The Alcoa $8 call at $0.34 is 27 cents of intrinsic value (stock $8.27 minus the $8 strike) plus 7 cents of time value; the $8 put costs 7 cents, all of it time value. Moneyness depends on where the strike sits relative to the stock price, and on options the bid/ask spread must be added to your risk per share.
Believing options are inherently riskier than stock. Relying on a stop order to protect a stock position from overnight gaps.
Buying out-of-the-money options that are worthless at expiry unless the move comes quickly. Ignoring time decay and wide spreads.

Will this position be held overnight? Would an option cap the gap risk? Call or put? Strike in, at or out of the money? How much of the premium is time value, and how much time is left? Spread between bid and ask - added to my risk? Is the stop still based on the stock's zone?
“If used properly they are always less risky than holding the same position with stock.”
Options are absent from Kevin's FX course and are only a side topic for Seiden; everything in this lesson is new to the app's material.

The claim that an option 'always' has less risk than stock holds for capped downside on overnight gaps; it says nothing about time decay costing money on trades that do not move, which Baker addresses only by preferring in-the-money contracts.
Kevin manages gap risk in FX with position size and stop placement; an option-based cap is not available on spot FX/CFD accounts.

An option lets you lose only a small, known amount, even overnight. You want to rent a house next month. You pay a small deposit to hold the price. If you change your mind, you lose only the deposit. That is a call. A put is like car insurance: you pay a little each year, and if the car gets smashed, you are covered. At night, when you are asleep, a stock can jump far past your stop, but a deposit or insurance never costs more than you paid.
A call is a deposit that holds a price; a put is insurance against a falling price.
An option is a right, not an obligation, usually for 100 shares, until a set date. Price = intrinsic value + time value. Only in-the-money options have intrinsic value.
For overnight holds, a call (or stock plus a put) caps the loss; a stop cannot stop a gap.

passages.h: Step: What the price is made of
passages.t: Alcoa is 8.27 and the $8 call costs 34 cents: $34 for one contract. Intrinsic value is stock minus strike: 27 cents. The other 7 cents is time value, which grows with volatility and time left and melts as expiry gets close.

passages.h: Step: In, at and out of the money
passages.t: A call is in the money when its strike is below the price; a put when its strike is above it. Only those have intrinsic value. At- and out-of-the-money options expire worthless. The $8 put costs 7 cents, all of it time value.
You own 100 shares with a stop at 7.50. Bad news comes overnight and the stock opens near 5. Your stop fills near 5, not 7.50. A stop order cannot protect you from a gap.

One $8 call costs $34 and can never lose more than $34. Or own the stock and buy an $8 put for $7: below $8 the loss is capped at $27 on the stock plus $7 for the put = $34. If Alcoa hits $9, the call makes $66, only $7 less than the stock.

What is an option? - The right, not the obligation, to buy or sell at a set price on or before a set date; 100 shares per contract. Call vs put? - Call = right to buy (deposit). Put = right to sell (insurance). Option price = ? - Intrinsic value + extrinsic (time) value. When is a call in the money? - When its strike is below the stock price.

Why can a stop fail overnight? - A gap opens past the stop and it fills at the gap price. Max loss on a $0.34 call? - $34 (plus commission). Options and the stop? - Keep the stop based on the stock price and its zone. Add what to option risk? - The bid/ask spread.

com). This final lesson pulls the book into one routine - find, draw, grade, choose timeframe, check the path, stop and exits, minimum 3:1, 1% sizing, manage and review - and lists where Baker's rules differ from Kevin's and Seiden's so trades can be journaled against the right rulebook.

No zone, no trade; no fresh strong zone, no counter-trend trade. Stop beyond the zone, set before entry, entered with the order. At least 3:1 to the first exit. 1% risk per trade. No more than two or three positions at once. Journal every trade against the plan.
1. Find a fast move away from a level: a pivot candle, a tight range, a mid-trend doji or a gap.
2. Draw the zone on the full candle(s) it started from; refine an oversized daily zone on the hourly, keeping the distal at the extreme.
3. Grade it: left fast, arrived fast, fresh (look left up to five years), little time inside.
4. Pick the style and timeframe: weekly for investing, daily for swing, daily zones with 5-minute/hourly execution for day trades. 5. Check the path: do not buy into supply or sell into demand.

6. Stop one to a few cents beyond the zone; three exits, each one cent before an obstacle. 7. Reward-to-risk to exit 1 at least 3:1 (Baker's swing example: 5:1) - otherwise skip. 8. Size: 1% of the account / risk per share, including fill, commission and spread. 9. Manage: trail the stop behind new pivots; review whether the plan was followed.
With-trend swing: rejection candle with its wick in the zone, enter after the close. Counter-trend swing: strong zone only, limit as close as possible to the far edge, no confirmation.

Day trade: strong fresh daily zone, execute on the 5-minute; a second chance often comes after the first touch. Conservative: wait for price to break back through the proximal line. Gap through a zone: wait for the opening pullback, stop beyond the day's low/high. All-time high/low: wait for a new strong zone and trade its first return.
Practice: plot zones on many stocks and timeframes and study the first returns; re-plot your recent losers. Proficiency takes time; Baker's site zone-trades.com (free sign-up) has further articles.

The whole book as one routine: find a fast move away, draw the zone on the candle(s) it started from, grade it, choose your timeframe, make sure nothing stands in the way, set the stop and three exits from the zones, demand 3:1 to the first exit, size at 1% risk, then manage and review.
Where Baker differs from the app's main mentor (Kevin) and from Sam Seiden - the details you must not mix up when journaling which rulebook a trade followed.
Mixing rulebooks: using Baker's tight stop on a Kevin-style zone, or Kevin's 2:1 minimum on a Baker setup. Skipping the grading step because a zone 'looks obvious'. Expecting quick proficiency.

Which zone type and which grade (fast out, fast in, fresh, time)? Which entry style from the book am I using? Path clear of opposing zones? Stop, three exits, ratio to exit 1, size at 1%? Which rulebook (Baker, Kevin, Seiden) does this trade follow?
“it takes time to become proficient at it”

Zone box: Baker uses the whole pivot candle; Kevin wraps tightly around the basing candles (four parts: basing, explosive move, stay-away candle, space); Seiden draws around where most trading happened before a strong departure.
Entry: Baker deep in the zone or after a candle; Kevin a limit just before the proximal; Seiden at the proximal.
Candles: Baker uses hammers and shooting stars; Kevin uses no candle patterns; Seiden uses fixed entry rules.
Broken zones: Baker trades the flip; Kevin treats them as void; Seiden flips them only with conditions.
Gaps: Baker reads them as one big candle; Kevin says no zone; Seiden calls them the strongest imbalance.
Minimum ratio: Baker 3:1 to exit 1 (5:1 swing); Kevin 2:1 or better by opportunity; Seiden 3:1 to target 1.
Market: Baker writes for US stocks and options; Kevin trades FX, gold and oil; Seiden covers stocks, futures and FX.

Find it, box it, grade it, check the road, fence it, size it, review. Building a sandcastle has steps. Find good wet sand, draw the outline, check the sand is strong, make sure no wave is coming, build a wall, use only the bucket you can carry, and afterwards look at what worked. Baker's whole method is the same kind of routine, done the same way every time. It takes time to get good at it, and that is normal.
The routine is a pilot's checklist: every flight, every step, no skipping because it "looks fine".

No zone, no trade. No fresh strong zone, no counter-trend trade. Stop beyond the zone, at least 3:1 to exit 1, 1% risk, no more than two or three positions. Journal every trade against the right rulebook (Baker, not Kevin or Seiden).

passages.h: Step: 1. Find a fast move away
passages.t: Start where price left a level fast: a pivot candle, a tight range, a mid-trend doji or a gap.
Box the full candle or candles the move started from, wick to wick. If a daily zone is too wide, refine it on the hourly but keep the distal line at the extreme.
Did price leave fast? Did it arrive fast? Is it fresh (looked left up to five years)? Did price spend little time inside? Do not skip this because a zone "looks obvious".

passages.h: Step: 4. Pick the style and timeframe
passages.t: Weekly for investing, daily for swing trading, daily zones with 5-minute or hourly execution for day trades.
Do not buy into supply or sell into demand. If an opposing zone sits right in the way, wait for the break or skip.

Stop one to a few cents beyond the zone. Three exits, each one cent before an obstacle. Reward to exit 1 at least 3:1, or skip. Size = 1% of the account divided by risk per share, including fill, commission and spread.
Trail the stop behind new pivots. After the trade, journal it: did I follow the plan? Proficiency takes time; keep plotting zones on many charts and study the first returns.

Baker's first rule of the routine? - No zone, no trade. Counter-trend needs? - A fresh, strong zone. Minimum ratio, Baker? - At least 3:1 to the first exit. Risk per trade? - 1% of the account. Conservative entry style? - Wait for price to break back through the proximal line.
Day-trade entry style? - Strong fresh daily zone, execute on the 5-minute; a second chance often comes. After every trade? - Journal it against Baker's plan.
How long to become proficient? - It takes time. Practise plotting zones and studying first returns.
All Star: Seiden: S/D level + Bollinger Band pierce + trend context + margin; T1 = the BB midline
Arrival (Seiden): How price comes back: sharp and base-free = good; stair-step = bad
Arrival zone: Kevin / drill: a zone that broke a trendline AND took out a high / low or a zone: the strongest
Base / basing: The short pause (1-6 candles) before the move away. Candle body < 50% of its range = a basing candle (bot)
Breakout entry: A stop order through a level. Kevin: beyond the removed opposing zone. Seiden: prefers the return to the origin
Bull / bear trap: Seiden: a breakout above an obvious high (e.g. the Globex high) into fresh supply, which is sold
Chain / qualification: Kevin: a zone counts only if its move removed an opposing zone or a trendline, or made an all-time high / low
Confirmation entry: Wait for proof at the zone. Kevin: an opposing ETF zone / trendline removed. Seiden: a leave-the-zone trigger. Baker: a rejection candle
Curve: Where price sits between the HTF demand and the HTF supply (0-100%). Buy low, sell high; the middle is equilibrium
DBR / RBD: Drop-Base-Rally (demand) / Rally-Base-Drop (supply): reversal zones, also called VP (valleys and peaks)
Distal line: The far edge: the extreme wick of the base / leg. The stop goes just beyond it
Emotional candle: A candle with range > 3 × ATR; its wick does not test or remove a zone (bot)
Equilibrium: Balanced trading: no edge
ETF / ITF / HTF: Entry / intermediate / higher timeframe (e.g. 15m / H1 / H4)
Flip / polarity: A broken zone that switches side (old supply → new demand)
Fresh / tested: Fresh = not revisited since it formed. Tested = price returned to the proximal
Initial profit margin / run-out: How far price ran from the zone before it first came back (Seiden's qualifying rule: ≥ 3 × the zone height)
Leg-in: The move *into* the base. Fast is better (Baker)
Leg-out / move away / departure: The move *out* of the base. Its strength (legRatio, gap, big bodies) shows how big the imbalance was
Levels on top of levels: Two same-side zones stacked together (Seiden: stronger; Kevin: ~50/50)
Liquidity trap: An obvious S/R just before the zone, where retail stops sit and fuel the reaction
Look left: Check older price for opposing levels (margin) or an older zone under the base (origin freshness)
Motion into mass: Seiden: each visit fills resting orders, so the level weakens until it breaks
Novice / two mistakes: Buying after a rally AND into supply (a third mistake: against the trend). The S/D trader takes the other side
Odds enhancer: A scored factor that raises the probability of a level (Seiden's sheet; bot ZScore 0-15)
Overextended / golden area: Kevin's channel: from the trendline to its 50% line = golden; beyond 50% = overextended
Parity rule: Repo rule: ZoneBot must trade exactly the zones ZoneVision draws, so drawing changes go into both
Penetration depth: How far a return went into the zone (0-100%). Seiden: ≥ 25% = done; Kevin: > 75% = void
Pivot vs cluster: Seiden: a pivot (price could not stay) is a strong level; a cluster (long sideways block) is weak
Profit margin: Room from the entry to the nearest opposing level, in R
Proximal line: The zone edge price reaches first: the top of demand, the bottom of supply. Usually the base body edge; the limit order sits just before it
R, BE, MFE / MAE: R = initial risk. BE = stop moved to entry (+ costs). MFE / MAE = max favourable / adverse excursion of a trade
RBR / DBD: Rally-Base-Rally (demand) / Drop-Base-Drop (supply): continuation zones, also called CP
Removed: A candle body (close) beyond the distal: the zone is void
Set & forget: Pending limit with stop and target placed in advance, then left alone
Space / gap (Kevin): The distance between the stay-away candle and the proximal; small = drawable only (InpMinGap)
Stay-away candle: The candle after the leg-out that does not come back to the proximal (Kevin's 3rd part)
X-ray: Seiden: inspect a big HTF zone on lower TFs to find its proximal / distal sub-levels
